<meta>This page serves as the introductory dedication and preface by Marsilius Ficinus for his translation of Iamblichus's "On the Mysteries." It establishes the connection between Neoplatonic philosophy and the Medici family.</meta>

## Marsilio Ficino of Florence humbly commends himself to the Most Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Giovanni de' Medici, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. <note>Giovanni de' Medici (1475–1521) later became Pope Leo X. Ficino was the head of the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note>

When I had decided to write a letter to you to congratulate you on the Cardinal's dignity recently bestowed upon you, and was considering to whom I might best give it to be delivered to you—someone who would make our congratulation much more pleasing—I suddenly betook myself to the Academy, hoping that at least in its innermost sanctuaries some greeter most acceptable to you would not be lacking. There, by a certain divine chance, I first encountered Iamblichus <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist philosopher known for his interest in theurgy and ritual.</note>, known among the Academics as "the Divine," and a great priest there. To him indeed I said, "Greetings, Iamblichus, great priest. At present (as you see) I am about to congratulate Giovanni de' Medici, a new prelate of the Christian religion; I pray you, if I ask what is right, that you will make our otherwise meager congratulation fuller with your divine words and mysteries." He assented to my prayers, and with this sentiment that great priest comes to you: "Giovanni, great priest." You, therefore, joyfully receive such a great greeter, and after the first greeting, after reading the letter, listen more attentively, if you please, to what that divine man says. For he promised that, to speak in a manner worthy of both his person and yours, he would express to you in brief what the Egyptian and Assyrian priests felt concerning religion and divine matters.

### ARGUMENT <note>A summary or introduction to the contents of a book.</note> ON THE BOOK OF IAMBLICHUS.

Porphyry <note>A student of Plotinus and a major Neoplatonic philosopher.</note>, who among the Platonists is called "the Philosopher" on account of his excellence, sent a long letter to Egypt to the priest Anebo, full of various and weighty questions looking toward all parts of philosophy, especially toward God, as well as angels, demons, and souls; toward providence, fate, prophecies, magic, miracles, sacrifices, and vows. Iamblichus, his pupil, responded to Porphyry's questions. He introduces Abamon, an Egyptian priest, responding to Porphyry on behalf of his disciple Anebo, to whom Porphyry had sent the letter. Therefore, of this entire inquiry and truly divine response—as if still too occupied with Plotinus <note>Ficino had recently completed a massive translation and commentary on Plotinus.</note>—I have translated almost every thought rather than every word. Thus it should not be thought strange if the speech appears disjointed in places, especially among the very beginnings of the disputation where the loss of words is lighter. From here on, the context of the words will appear more continuous. I was, however, occasionally forced to insert some word of my own for the sake of continuity or understanding. Furthermore, Pierleone <note>Pierleone Leoni, a famous physician and scholar close to the Medici.</note>, a man most desirous of all secrets, was also a cause for this swifter edition. But that which I especially admire is that he always seems to strive for those things which he already possesses. For by a certain divinity of intellect, he attains the secrets of the philosophers, both Greek and foreign <note>original: "barbarorum," referring to non-Greek traditions like the Egyptian or Chaldean.</note>, even before they are read.

# IAMBLICHUS ON THE MYSTERIES
<note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who defended the use of ritual and theurgy to reach the divine.</note>

## On the Knowledge of Divine Matters

<margin>}</margin>
<image-desc>Ornate historiated initial letter 'A' depicting two figures, one seated and one standing, in a classical architectural setting surrounded by foliage.</image-desc> Egyptian writers, believing that all things were discovered by Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure conflating the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth</note>, inscribed their books to Mercury. Mercury is the god of wisdom and eloquence. Pythagoras, Plato, Democritus, Eudoxus, and many others approached the Egyptian priests. The doctrines of this book belong to the Assyrians and Egyptians and are taken from the Pillars of Mercury. Pythagoras and Plato learned philosophy from the Pillars of Mercury in Egypt. The Pillars of Mercury are full of teachings. Before any use of reason, there is naturally implanted in us a notion of the gods. Indeed, there is a certain "touch" of divinity that is better than mere knowledge, from which the natural appetite for the Good is incited, as well as reasoning and judgment. The essential knowledge of divine things is perpetual to the soul; and in truth, this is not merely "knowledge" by which we enjoy God. For in knowledge there is "otherness" <note>The philosopher distinguishes between knowing *about* something (subject vs. object) and a direct, unified experience</note>, but this is a certain essential and simple contact. For we cannot reach Unity itself except by something most unified and by a unity of the mind, which exists above the specific properties of the soul and the mind. The Unity of the gods itself unites souls to itself from eternity through their own unities, according to a proximity so proper and effective that it appears to be a continuity. The divine Intellect gives being to the soul through its own essential act of understanding. Therefore, the being of the soul is a certain understanding—namely, of God, upon whom it depends. Our being is to know God, because the principal being of the soul is its intellect, in which "being" is the same as "understanding divine things" in a perpetual act. From that principal being, however, the discursive powers of the soul are derived. After the gods, we place demons, heroes, and pure souls; these three orders are the attendants of the gods. We cannot reach these attendants of the gods—the demons, heroes, and pure souls—by the usual wanderings of human reason. Instead, it is necessary to rise up to essential and eternal intelligence.

<margin>}</margin>
Just as the gods are always reached by an innate notion, so the spirits that attend the gods are only reached when the soul has laid aside its mobile mode of cognition—which belongs to the rational power formed by the intellect and intelligence, which they call the "acquired intellect" <term>intellectus adeptus: a technical term in medieval and Renaissance philosophy for the human intellect when it has been perfected by receiving universal truths</term>. For the first knowledge consists in the "active intellect." Since knowledge occurs through a process of making things equal <note>the mind conforming to the object</note>, it follows that we reach eternal and immobile things through an eternal, immobile, and simple notion. The knowledge by which we know "separate substances" <note>beings without physical bodies, like angels or celestial intelligences</note> is of a different kind than that by which we know other things.

The knowledge of divine things was always in the soul through a simple intuition.

<summary>This page introduces the Egyptian origins of sacred wisdom and argues that knowledge of the divine is not reached through logic, but through an innate, essential "touch" or unity with the divine that precedes human reason.</summary>
<keywords>Iamblichus, Hermes Trismegistus, Neoplatonism, divine unity, active intellect, Pillars of Mercury, Egyptian priesthood, hierarchy of being</keywords>

--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of divine and separate substances, likely following a discussion on the limitations of human perception in reaching the divine.</meta>

# IAMBLICHUS

...or by contact. Some people think they will attain knowledge of separate substances <note>The "separate substances" refer to immaterial beings like angels or celestial intellects that exist apart from physical matter.</note> through a certain method of opposition—namely, that material things are mobile, local, and subject to suffering, and so on; therefore, separate substances are immobile, and so on. In this way, one certainly learns what they are *not*. However, what they actually *are* is acquired in the rational power through a certain application, according to the adequacy of cognition toward that which is naturally present in the soul through the intellect. This is achieved not so much by the service of comparison and conjecture, as by the service of separation and purification. There was also a method of disjunction: namely, that the gods and divine things are either temporal or eternal. They are not temporal, therefore [they are eternal], and so forth. Yet even this method, by its own mobility, does not suit immobile beings.

### On the properties of the one cause of the higher beings

If any composition exists in contrast to separate and separable substances, it does not consist of a genus that is indeterminate in itself and a terminating difference <note>In Aristotelian logic, a definition is usually made of a "genus" (a broad category) and a "difference" (the specific trait that narrows it down). The author argues divine beings are too simple for this kind of "parts-based" definition.</note>. For those substances are complete species, entirely in a determinate and complete act. If separable substances, being simple, do not differ among themselves through specific differences under the same genus, then they do not differ through individual differences under the same species either. Therefore, each one is, as it were, a single genus or species existing by itself. They differ, however, by themselves and by the order of their grades, and insofar as they are referred to the First <note>The "First" refers to the Neoplatonic "One" or God, the ultimate source of all existence.</note> in different ways. Intelligences do not agree or differ among themselves by genus or any differences—for they are most simple—but only insofar as they are referred to the First by either the same or a different rationale; some are arranged in prior grades of perfection, others in subsequent ones. 

The differences of things among themselves in actions and passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to being acted upon or receiving an impression, rather than emotion.</note> must everywhere be resolved into differences of powers, and these into differences of essences. One must not rest anywhere in subsequent things, but must proceed to the prior. Neither in the higher substances nor in our soul is there any passive motion, but the whole is an effective act. The motion of the soul, by which it is moved from itself, is not divided into a mover and a moved, or into "moving" and "being moved"; rather, it is an essential act proceeding temporally. Accidents <note>Technical term for non-essential qualities, like color or size, which can change without changing what a thing is.</note> belong to composite things and forms that exist in a subject; they do not suit immaterial forms. Whatever is in separable forms is "being" and is essential by a certain principal and equal lot. Neither is any accident or consequence found there. 

Motions and actions are different because of the differences of natures, not the other way around. If we were to say there is one single genus of separate things, we would confound theology. Separable substances do not agree in one certain genus in which they might be distinguished by differences, but are distinguished by themselves and by the order of their grades, insofar as they are referred to the First through different grades of perfection. They agree, however...

<summary>This page discusses the nature of divine and immaterial substances, arguing that they cannot be understood through standard logic or physical categories, but only through their relationship to the "First" cause. It emphasizes that these higher beings are pure "act" and lack the accidental qualities found in the material world.</summary>

<meta>This page begins a discussion on the Neoplatonic hierarchy of being, specifically focusing on the distinctions between gods, demons, heroes, and human souls. It follows the introductory definitions of divine essence.</meta>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

Those things are more closely related to one another which are referred in a more similar manner to the first and the last. Goodness is twofold: that which is above essence <note>original: "super essentiam"; referring to the Neoplatonic "One" which transcends being</note>, and that which is according to essence. Essence is the property of all the gods. But the Good itself is above essence: and it is called the cause of good—namely, the principle of essential good. Accordingly, the ranks of the gods are distinguished among themselves according to the degrees of essence. In the lowest rational souls, essential good is not present as it is in the gods, but rather a participation in the good according to intellectual beauty; yet this is present in them immovably.

### On the order of the superior beings.

<margin>a</margin><insert>a</insert>Our souls are counted among the genera of divine beings. Heroes are greater than men, therefore demons are much grander. The first of the divine beings is the Good itself, and the gods following it. The last are the particular rational souls. Between these two are the intermediates: namely, heroes near to the souls, and demons near to the gods, just as air and water exist between fire and earth. Although heroes excel us in power, virtue, beauty, and magnitude, they nevertheless greatly agree with our soul and its life. Demons are superior to heroes, and are the ministers of the gods—who act as architects—in the worldly office. Those things which in the gods are ineffable and hidden, the demons express and make manifest. Demons and heroes adapt the universal, simple, and immovable gifts of the gods for inferior beings. They reconcile all things, and are the authors of harmonic consent and the mutual compassion <note>term: "compassion" (compassio); here meaning a cosmic "sympathy" or resonance between different parts of the universe</note> of all things. They translate divine things to us, and equally lead our affairs up to the divine. Furthermore, they equally distribute the grades in the gifts of the superiors and in the preparation of those receiving them.

The diverse genera of divine beings differ among themselves through a triple mode of properties: namely, as pertains to their essences, their virtues <note>note: "virtues" here refers to inherent powers or capacities</note>, and their actions. The property of the gods is unity, permanence in themselves, and an eminent providence that is the immovable cause of motions, having nothing in common with those things for which it provides; and this property is preserved in them according to essence, virtue, and action. The property of souls is an inclination toward multitude and motion, and a conjunction with the gods, as well as receiving something from others and being filled by them with vital motion, and agreeing everywhere with all things—partly with those that remain, and partly with those that flow—and tempering all things in and through itself. This property is preserved in them according to essence, virtue, and action. The properties of demons are to contain within themselves the gifts of the gods in a manner lower than the gods, but to contain the conditions of inferior things under the form and reason of those gifts; namely, while they are indeed multiplied, they are mixed unitedly, and though mixed, they remain unmixed. Finally, they are moved, but stably...

<summary>This page outlines the Neoplatonic "Great Chain of Being," ranking entities from the transcendent Good and the gods down through demons and heroes to human souls. It defines each group by its relationship to essence, unity, and its role in mediating divine influence to the physical world.</summary>
<keywords>Neoplatonism, hierarchy of being, gods, demons, heroes, rational souls, essence, divine providence, Iamblichus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic discussion of the celestial hierarchy, specifically defining the middle beings (daemons and heroes) that bridge the gap between the divine and the human soul.</meta>

# IAMBLICHUS

<image-desc>A narrow, vertical woodcut illustration positioned in the left margin. It depicts a multi-tiered classical architectural pillar or tower with detailed segments including cornices, rusticated masonry, and decorative moldings, resembling a lighthouse or a monument.</image-desc>

Heroes, on the other hand, possess unity, identity, stability, and excellence under the condition of multiplicity, motion, and mixture. Daemons and heroes are closest to the extremes: the former to the gods, the latter to souls. The differences between daemons and heroes are primarily these: heroes sometimes decline more toward particular and changeable things than daemons do. These two intermediaries—namely daemons and heroes—are composed of the properties of the extremes, that is, of gods and souls; but in daemons there is more of the divine, while in heroes there is more of the human.

### How the actions of superior beings are distinguished among themselves.

<margin>d</margin>
The gods hold the highest rank of beings, souls the lowest. The gods are capable of all things, united in a single moment; souls, by contrast, are capable neither of all things, nor in a single <margin>ti.</margin> moment, nor are they united. The gods act upon and care for all things without being inclined <note>original: "non inclinati" - meaning they act without losing their transcendent nature or becoming burdened by the material world</note> toward them. Souls act with a certain inclination and turning toward their objects. The gods are the primary causes; souls depend perpetually upon the will of the gods. The gods, with the swiftest vigor, encompass their innermost ends together with their beginnings. Souls proceed from one thing to another, from the imperfect to the perfect. The gods cannot be grasped by any measure or form. Souls are held back and overcome by inclination, habit, and will; they are touched by a desire for lesser things and by familiarity with them, and they contract certain qualities from that contact.

### Concerning the Intellect and the Soul.

<margin>i</margin>
The Intellect <note>The "Intellect" (Nous) here refers to the divine creative mind that shapes the universe.</note>, the maker of all things, is always present to all the gods most fully through a single act remaining within itself. The soul is a participant in an intellect that is more divisible and multiform, adapted for governing, and it naturally provides for inanimate things, being affected by various forms. Likewise, order and beauty itself (or the causes of both) are present to the gods from superior causes; but to the soul, order and intellectual beauty are present as gifts. Likewise, in the gods there is a measure powerful over all things; the soul, however, is defined by that measure and acts through it upon specific things. Daemons and heroes, as intermediaries between gods and souls, are composed in competent proportion relative to the extremes and to themselves, consisting of the properties of both souls and gods which we described above. Therefore, if you wish to apprehend the appearance of the gods, think of the properties of the lowest rational soul and attribute the opposites in perfection to the gods. If it pleases you to compose the likeness of a daemon, compose it from both, while attributing more of divinity. If, finally, the likeness of a hero, compose it from both but bringing in more of the conditions of the soul. He <note>Iamblichus</note> criticizes Porphyry...

<meta>catchword: ...ry for separating</meta>

<summary>This page defines the Neoplatonic hierarchy of beings, explaining how daemons and heroes act as bridges between the perfect, unchanging gods and the striving, changeable human souls. It contrasts the effortless, universal power of the divine Intellect with the limited, step-by-step progression of the soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical defense of the divine hierarchy, likely from Iamblichus's "On the Mysteries," arguing that higher beings are not defined by the physical bodies they govern.</meta>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

<note>original: "DE MYSTERIIS"</note>

...distinguishing separate essences by their relationship to bodies—namely, gods by their relationship to ethereal bodies, demons to airy bodies, and souls to earthly bodies. This is incorrect because primary things and causes should not be defined by what comes after them or by their effects. Incorporeal substances are not *in* bodies; rather, they lead them from the outside and give something to them without receiving anything in return. Therefore, they are neither changed along with them, nor are they distributed according to the distribution of those bodies. For they are not "habits" <note>In this context, 'habits' refers to accidental qualities or states of being</note> of bodies or material forms, but are self-subsisting and separable. Indeed, they are already separate and live before bodies exist. Separate and separable substances do not become such because they chose a certain lot or province, or were assigned one; rather, it is the other way around. Just as a soul, before entering a body, brings forth from itself a certain life and form into action, so it obtains a corresponding organic body and a nature following its own, which is subjected to the perfection of that soul's life. The rational soul <note>original: "anima rationalis"</note> enters into a body that is already alive, but only imperfectly so. Divine beings naturally generate within themselves their entire distinct work before they bring it forth. Among those things which hold the status of a universal principle, the lower things exist within the higher: corporeal things within the incorporeal, and the works within the creators. They are directed within those higher beings that contain them in a circular fashion. Therefore, the celestial circuits are reduced to the circuit of the celestial souls. Truly, the souls of the worlds—that is, of the spheres and the stars—as they approach their own intellect, are comprehended by it inwardly and are first generated within it. The particular intellect is contained in the universal intellect, and that in turn in higher things. Since subsequent things are always turned toward the first and higher things as their models, and the lower are led by them, certainly essence and form are produced by the higher and are present in the lower. In all cases, subsequent things are produced first within the better things. Therefore, order and measure in subsequent things depend on the higher, and not the other way around; thus, the properties of the higher are not to be assigned based on the lower. Therefore, an incorporeal essence cannot be distinguished by the qualities of bodies, with which it has nothing in common.

Divine principles grant to their works not only essence, but their entire distinction and formal order. An essence that is present to bodies non-locally is not distinguished by physical places; and that which is not restrained by the particular boundaries of subjects is by no means contained particularly by the parts of the world. An incorporeal nature is suddenly present wherever it wishes, with nothing anywhere prohibiting it.

Every divine and incorporeal thing is everywhere.

<margin>m</margin>
Even more so, divinity is constrained by no limit that would prevent it from being everywhere.
Likewise, those things which are among us cannot be made or formed unless there is one thing which...

<note>Signature mark: a iiii</note>

<summary>This page argues that divine and incorporeal substances (gods, demons, and souls) precede and govern physical bodies rather than being defined or limited by them. It asserts that the higher spiritual realms contain and organize the lower material realms through a process of intellectual and formal generation.</summary>

<keywords>Neoplatonism, Iamblichus, incorporeal substance, rational soul, divine hierarchy, celestial spheres, emanation, causality</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the nature of divine substances. The catchword "fis aliena" suggests the next page will begin with a discussion of how divine power becomes "alien" or externalized in lower forms.</meta>

# IAMBLICHUS

...a certain living creator, and that the participation of the Forms <gloss>specierum</gloss> <note>In Platonic philosophy, 'Forms' or 'Species' are the eternal patterns of all things</note> is diffused through all things. Finally, unless these things are divine, the power of sacrifice is everywhere abolished, for sacrifice consists in a certain communion <gloss>communione</gloss> of the gods with human beings. The gods contain all things precisely for this reason: because they themselves are nowhere contained <note>A central Neoplatonic paradox: the higher contains the lower by surrounding it with its power, but the lower cannot 'grasp' or contain the higher</note>. Since earthly things are created and exist <gloss>consistunt</gloss> by the gift of divine beings, whenever they are made more ready for the divine, they suddenly obtain the gods as existing <gloss>existentis</gloss> within them—and this occurs even before the specific, proper natures of those earthly things are manifest. Moreover, since in any god there is infinite power and a nature that is both indivisible and incomprehensible, they cannot rightly be confined to certain fixed places. Likewise, there would be no true union of universal providence among the gods unless all were equally present everywhere. It is also said that some gods are of the air <note>aerei</note>, others of the water <note>aquei</note>, not because they reside only there, but because they reign most especially <gloss>maxime</gloss> in those realms. Priests used to call upon earthly and subterranean gods; they are certainly called <gloss>dicuntur</gloss> such not because they are only there—for they are all everywhere—but because different gods operate most powerfully <note>original: "potissimum operantur"</note> in different places. For even the soul of any particular star is everywhere, though it acts more directly in that star. Through statues, a certain divine illumination is received.

---

->On providence and how the gods are everywhere:<-

<margin>q</margin> When the gods are said to have specifically allotted various parts of the world, cities, temples, or statues, you must understand that their essence <gloss>essentiam</gloss> and power, flourishing everywhere <gloss>ubique</gloss> in itself, illuminates this or that place most especially. Just as light, remaining in itself, illuminates various things here and there without any mixing or division of itself, so do the gods. Just as the light of the sun is the same continuous whole everywhere, and can neither be divided into parts, nor enclosed anywhere, nor separated from its own source, nor mixed with the air (even though it is present there), so it is with the divine. Indeed, while the sun leaves nothing behind, the heat remains in the objects after the heater has departed; in the same way, the light of each god, as an indivisible whole, is inwardly present to the entire world, even though it grants its power <note>original: "vires"</note> more specifically to a certain part that is most suited to it. Meanwhile, it fills all things in a certain way due to its perfect power and its absolutely immense causal transcendence <note>original: "excessum causalem"</note>. Whence it perfects all things and joins the furthest extremes with other extremes, comprehending all things in itself through intermediaries and reflecting itself back to itself as an entirely unified whole. The world also imitates this gift through its circular motion, and through a certain connection and reconciliation of parts that transfers elements into other elements in turn, sending the virtue of higher things down to the lower. He who accepts this manifest statue of the gods, which is entirely unified everywhere, ought to revere it; I shall say nothing [disparaging] of the gods...

It argues that sacrifice and providence depend on the gods' ability to be everywhere present while remaining indivisible.</summary>

# ON THE MYSTERIES
<sig>4</sig>

...alien to their duties, <note>original: "officiis aliena"</note> namely, that they are locally (so to speak) separate. For if there is no communion of the world with the divine spirits <gloss>numina</gloss> in regards to their essence, power, or action, and no shared distribution or fellowship, then certainly there is no co-extension or shared distribution according to place. As far as that is concerned, mutual containment and intermingling cannot be imagined by species or genus. However, those things which differ entirely from one another do not admit any reciprocal distribution, mixture, or containment at all. When the distribution of divine spirits <gloss>numina</gloss> occurs through different regions of the world, understand that different regions receive the gifts of the gods in different ways, according to their own properties. Indeed, the art of sacred works <note>Refers to theurgy, or 'god-working,' the practice of using rituals to communicate with or draw down divine power</note>, considering this, uses specific invocations that seem appropriate to such a distribution and to the property of the divine spirits. Any part of the world receives something from any god, for every god is present in his entirety to every part of the world. But some parts receive from him in one way, and others in another; the Ether <note>In ancient science, the 'fifth element' that fills the space of the universe above the sphere of the moon</note> receives in an ethereal manner, while the Air receives in an aerial manner. For the gifts of the gods are naturally attracted by specific materials and specific invocations.

### That all things divine are removed from passions.

<margin>n</margin>
The divine spirits <gloss>numina</gloss> superior to us have nothing in themselves that is "passible" <term>passibile</term> <note>From the Latin 'pati' (to suffer/undergo); it means the capacity to be acted upon or changed by an external force, such as an emotion or physical injury</note>. They possess this impassibility (so to speak) not as a virtue they have acquired, but by their very nature. Not even the soul, which is the last of the divine things, has anything passible in it—I mean the soul that is pure and separate from bodies. Such a soul is not even touched by the disturbance of pleasure, which is merely a restoration to a natural state. Since its life is supernatural and unbegotten, it is not subject to any dissolving pain, as it exists outside of every body and the nature surrounding the body. It is divided from the harmony that descends into the body, being itself the principal harmony of the soul. Nor does it require the passions that precede the senses. For it is not contained by a body, nor is it forced to perceive bodies through external instruments. Indeed, since it is an individual and uniform essence, remaining incorporeal according to itself and sharing nothing with the body, it naturally admits no passions of division, alteration, or any change.

### Concerning the soul separated from the body.

<margin>a</margin>
The soul does not suffer <note>original: "patitur"; meaning to undergo change or be affected by emotion</note> even while it is present in the body, nor do the seminal reasons <term>rationes seminales</term> <note>The 'blueprints' or formative principles that govern the growth and development of physical matter</note> which it delivers to the body. For these are species, simple and uniform, which admit no disturbance or departure from themselves...

# IAMBLICHUS

...wise ones. Whatever passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to "pathos"—the state of being acted upon or changed by external forces, including emotions and physical suffering.</note> exist in a living creature do not exist in the soul, whatever its nature may be, but in the body. The body, existing under the soul, possesses a certain quality through which it both suffers and acts. There is no passion in the soul, neither destructive nor disturbing. The soul does not only acquire this "impassibility" <note>The state of being unable to suffer, change, or be harmed by external influences.</note> through choice, but possesses it by its very nature, which is far superior to bodies. Demons and heroes are impassible and eternal. For they always follow the gods in preserving the order of the world; where there is passion, a perpetual order cannot be maintained.

Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) and student of Plotinus who often questioned the efficacy of rituals.</note> suspected that the demons who govern the world were somehow affected by the things offered to them in sacred rites. Iamblichus <note>The author of this work and a defender of theurgy, who argued that divine beings are essentially unchanging.</note> denies this because where there is perpetual order, there is no passion, which an incorporeal essence cannot receive through eternal things. Perhaps, however, he would concede that the lowest and evil demons, who are deprived of governance, are touched by "effective passions"—not indeed in their soul, but in a body constituted by the presence of the soul.

Just as nature makes manifest things from hidden reasons, so the Priest <term>Sacerdos; here referring to the theurgist or ritual practitioner</term> employs manifest things to signify the hidden. The Priest often performs many actions to create something similar and appropriate to the divine, and through this kinship, he draws down something from the divine. Meanwhile, he also performs many works to purify the soul and turn away evils from us.

Demons, who are superior to us, receive no natural utility from us; for they either have no needs, or they themselves abundantly supply their own needs everywhere. Truly, they never suffer any change from corporeal things. Within us, there are certain principles of disturbances; if these are restrained too violently and suddenly from the start, they eventually break out more sharply, like a suppressed flame or stifled laughter. Therefore, they should be corrected more gently. Heraclitus <note>An early Greek philosopher known for his doctrine of change and his cryptic style.</note> calls sacrifices "medicines" because they purge the soul from the diseases gathered in this realm of generation <note>The physical world of birth, death, and constant change.</note>.

Porphyry suspected that not only demons but even the gods are touched by some passion, since they are "moved" during invocations. However, the will for good in God and the gods (who are goodness itself) is more excellent and thus freer than our own life of choosing concerning the good. Therefore, the gods are not moved to provide good to men because they are invoked. Instead, they provoke us toward the good of their own accord, and they freely meet us when we have turned toward them through invocation; they show us something and grant their bounty. Men think they are free to ask. So be it; therefore, the gods are even freer to give. Because of their free will for the good and their eternal and perfect action, the gods benefit everyone as soon as they are turned toward them by invocation. The soul, reaching the contemplation of divine things through supplications, transforms its prior life, which was subject to passions, into a divine one.

<meta>This page continues the technical debate between the Neoplatonists Porphyry and Iamblichus regarding the nature of divine beings. ->OF THE MYSTERIES<-

...in a life free of passion <note>original: *passionis experte*. In this Neoplatonic context, "passion" refers to *pathos*—the state of being acted upon or changed by external forces, rather than just strong emotion.</note> while it undergoes the action and life of the gods. How, then, do our supplications touch the gods through passions, when they even render souls—which were previously subject to passions—free from them? Supplications make the soul fit for the influence of the gods, which arrives easily and of its own accord because of the divine friendship that connects all things.

---

### Concerning the anger of the gods.

When we turn away from the beneficent care of the gods—as if from the light of the sun—we are immediately in darkness, and it is said that God is "angry" with us. To appease the anger of the gods is therefore to return to them through prayer. Appeasement of this kind brings no passion to the god; rather, it frees the soul from its prior passions. The gods and divine demons <note>The term "demons" here refers to *daimones*, intermediary spirits between gods and humans, who help manage the cosmos. They are not the evil spirits of later folklore.</note>, when humbly adored and worshipped, repel many evils that would otherwise occur naturally.

---

### Concerning the necessity and liberty of the gods.

It is necessary for the gods to be as they are, not by a necessity forced upon them from the outside, but by a natural necessity that is best for them. This is therefore a most voluntary state, such that they would never wish to be otherwise even if an option were presented. Porphyry and many philosophers say that gods are pure intellects, while demons are either intellects or animate "participations" <note>A philosophical term meaning a lower being that takes on some of the qualities of a higher being.</note> of intellect. However, Iamblichus objects that the nature of demons is not correctly defined in this way; for souls are also animate intellects and certain participations of intellect itself. Nor is the nature of the gods correctly defined by these philosophers, for the gods preside over even the pure intellects.

---

### Concerning the difference between gods and demons according to the Greeks and the most devoted.

The gods are not correctly defined according to the reasoning of the intellect itself, but rather by unity, goodness, and the intelligible object <note>The *intelligibile*, or the highest spiritual reality that the mind can perceive.</note>. Porphyry suspects that pure and separate intellects have no relationship with physical things, nor do they hear prayers. Nevertheless, the primary worship must still be offered to these "separate substances" <note>Beings that exist independently of matter.</note>; in this worship, the highest part of the soul is awakened and joined to the highest being. The supreme being comprehends and knows all our affairs in its unity. The actions of religious prayers are contained within the divinity itself; they do not depart from themselves, but remaining within themselves, they are readily present to the intention of those praying. Indeed, it is most fitting to acknowledge our own nothingness <note>original: *nihilitatem*</note>; when we compare ourselves to the higher beings, it makes us pray most earnestly, so that we may conform ourselves to them entirely and become like them through constant habit. ### IAMBLICHUS

Truly, prayers sent by divine grace, in which a divine power resides, bring me benefit. This stands in opposition to Porphyry, who thinks we should worship the gods of this world specifically because they have sensory perception <note>original: *quia sentiunt*. Porphyry argued that if gods didn't have senses like ours, they wouldn't hear our prayers.</note>. Likewise, while Porphyry thinks that petitions do not suit the purity of divine minds, Iamblichus believes they are appropriate because of the "inner sense" <note>An intuitive or spiritual perception rather than a physical one.</note> contained within prayers, especially those given by divine inspiration. Pure intellects know physical things through their higher mind, without needing physical senses.

->Again concerning supplications.<-

Porphyry says that since material objects are used in prayers <note>Referring to offerings like incense, herbs, or stones used in theurgic rituals.</note>, such prayers must only be directed to those gods who are "living beings" <note>original: *animalia*. In this sense, beings that possess an *anima* (soul) and a body.</note>. Iamblichus responds that within these material things, beyond their physical qualities, there lie hidden incorporeal and divine principles, forms, and measures. It is through these higher qualities that the materials used are made compatible with the gods. Indeed, whenever something is offered that is in any way harmonious with and similar to the gods, the gods are immediately present; they join with it, display their gifts, and hear the prayers. A small degree of harmony between our world and the gods is enough for us to draw something from them. For the gods are always most ready for this, owing to their natural goodness and marvelous power. A powerful cause acts even upon matter that is only slightly prepared. Porphyry distinguishes "Demons" <note>original: *Dæmones*. These are intermediary spirits, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note> from gods by saying the former are incorporeal while the latter are corporeal; Iamblichus argues that their true nature and properties cannot be distinguished by such simple categories.

->On the difference between gods and demons, and concerning celestial beings.<-

The celestial gods can be called incorporeal because no hindrance from their bodies interferes with their superior actions or their happy lives. Rather, just as the gods tend toward "the One" <note>The ultimate, transcendent source of all existence in Neoplatonism.</note>, their bodies spontaneously strive toward that same goal. These bodies do not "contain" the souls; rather, they are contained by the souls in a most excellent way. A celestial body is the most closely related of all physical things to the incorporeal realm, because of its simple, undivided, and constant nature, and its single action—namely, its circular motion—and its inherent life and light. In the heavens, there is no composite "third nature" formed from soul and body; instead, the body is drawn entirely into the nature of the soul. It is, as it were, a kind of "visible soul." Perhaps the heaven is light itself, without matter and without dimension. Dimension appears there only because of the vastness of its presence. Thus, the soul of heaven comes from above, adapting itself to our eyes and to fleeting things, and its circular path is the path of the soul; its light is the soul's intellect. Just as in the lowest physical body a "form" becomes material, so in the highest realm "matter" becomes formal. It is an "ensouled body" rather than a "bodied soul"—if indeed there is any matter at all in the heavens. Just as the highest air becomes fiery, so the celestial fire becomes "ensouled" <note>original: *aialis* (animale). Meaning it is filled with life or soul.</note>. That intellectual soul becomes the Intellect itself.

<summary>Iamblichus defends the use of material objects in prayer by arguing they contain divine principles, and he describes the heavens as "visible soul" where matter is entirely subordinate to spirit.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus's explanation of how divine and celestial influences interact with the material world. It specifically addresses why "evil" or harm appears to exist on Earth if the heavens are purely good.</meta>

### OF THE MYSTERIES

...the mind is made <term>good-formed</term> <note>original: *boniformis*. Having the shape or character of the Good.</note>. Celestial <term>living beings</term> <note>original: *animalia*. In the ancient view, the stars and planets were considered living, ensouled entities rather than just rocks or gas.</note> can be called incorporeal. All the celestials are good and beneficial, looking only toward the Good itself and acting with this eternal intuition. Inestimable powers are found within them, both inherent in these celestial beings and within their bodies, and then descending through influences into all things without hindrance down to the lowest reaches, communicated both to individuals and to entire species. They are everywhere immutable, even while ruling over changeable matter; they govern generation in a perpetual order and are always beneficial. 

Accordingly, when the flow of heaven enters into matter that is full of discords, something dissonant to us results. Temporal things receive eternal things in a temporal way. Bodies receive incorporeal things in a bodily way. These material things receive the immaterial powers of the heavens in a changeable and disorderly fashion. Those things that are shaped in the divine world are not truly "figured" <note>Meaning they have no physical shape or geometry in the higher realms.</note>, even though they are received as having figures in heaven; likewise, celestial things are not evil, even though they are received here as evil. All powers of the celestials descend as good from that source, but in this mixture of contraries, they are changed. Therefore, the quality that causes harm on earth is something other than the quality that originally arrived from heaven. 

First, what is given is one thing within the giver, but another thing once it is outside—even if the giver remains unchanged within itself—and it is also diminished. Second, while it is received in a baser subject, it also becomes baser. Third, because of the diverse nature of the receiver, it is received in a diverse manner. Fourth, it is affected by the differing qualities that are captured together by that same subject. Fifth, as the subject is acted upon, the influence itself is affected. Sixth, from all the factors combined within the subject, a different final result eventually emerges. 

Celestial influences extend into material things. Indeed, the power of **Saturn** is restrictive <note>original: *contentiua*. A power that holds things together, binds, or limits.</note>, while the power of **Mars** is motive. The former often causes harm by accident when it is received by colder matter, while the latter harms when received by hotter matter. Likewise, the former [Saturn] hurts when it is received in the manner of a congealing or freezing, while the latter [Mars] hurts through parching heat; this happens according to the disposition of the matter—that is, when that matter is not warm enough and is too dense, whereas the latter power is itself hotter and subtler. 

Just as the light and color of the sun may seem to offend a weak eye, they are nonetheless necessary for life. Similarly, all celestial influences arrive as health-giving, even if the impurity of the receiver corrupts them, or if weakness prevents someone from easily enduring the efficacy of the higher powers. All motions contribute to the universe and to the necessary parts of the universe, even if, in the meantime, among the smallest particles under this motion, one is hurt by another, or such particles cannot easily withstand the motion of the whole. It is like a dance where every person dances harmoniously and matches their gestures to the whole choir; yet a finger or a foot might be extended and struck, or if something weak enters the movement, it is trampled down.

# JAMBLICHUS

...of intelligence and of a will that is quite effective and perpetual. And therefore they rule without effort, which is clearly apparent from the always constant order. Thus affected, they are joined to the separate gods rather than to bodies. Governance over the heavens cannot distract the gods from the focus of intelligence, since they rule more powerfully and easily the more attentively they contemplate there. For from this proceeds that. The same would also happen to our <term>living beings</term> <note>original: *animalibus*. Refers to any ensouled creature, including humans.</note> if they contemplated their own cause, from which comes even the power of growth.

->Confirmation of the Foregoing.<-

<margin>Mind</margin> The divine Mind, through its own Ideas, procreates the souls of the celestial gods, and through them the celestial bodies, and keeps both perpetually joined to itself. The <term>worldly gods</term> <note>original: *Dii mundani*. These are the gods that inhabit and govern the physical cosmos, such as the planets and stars.</note>, who are also named <term>intellectual forms</term> <note>original: *intellectuales species*.</note>, are united among themselves, both because they all look upon the same Exemplar in which the intelligible Forms exist, and because that Exemplar thrives everywhere as a whole in every worldly god. Neither space nor diverse subjects prevent any incorporeal essence from being present within each other everywhere. The worldly gods are in one another and in their own Ideas, partly because they come from the One and are referred back to the One, partly because the divine unity that prevails everywhere unites them, and partly because they proceed among themselves, turn back toward each other, and receive from one another. In natural compounds, unity is <term>added from without</term> <note>original: *adventitia*. Something not inherent but granted by a higher power.</note>, depending on higher things and being overcome by multiplicity. In separable forms, unity surpasses multiplicity, and in the gods it surpasses it to such an extent that their very being is a kind of unity—I say "a kind of," because the <term>First Principle</term> <note>The One, the highest source of all existence in Neoplatonism.</note> is Unity itself in its absolute simplicity. Since, therefore, unity so prevails within the gods, it rightly overflows from the prior ones into those that follow. Thus, the latter consist in the unity of the former—a unity in which, as if it were common to all, they are all one by a certain act, just as bodies are one among themselves by a certain material potential. The celestial gods are deeply united with the invisible gods, both because the celestial souls are outside of bodies and because the higher gods—that is, the Ideas—possess an infinite unity, insofar as all are in each, through which unity they join the following gods to themselves and to each other. For since all gods are defined by unity, one common unity is extended into all, through which they are one in the action of all directed toward a single object, principle, and end, all at the same point and moment. 

### Concerning providence, and concerning gods and demons.

Their providence is universal, while that of <term>demons</term> <note>original: *dæmonum*. In the ancient sense, these are not "evil" spirits but intermediary beings between gods and humans.</note> is <margin>demons</margin> particular. The First God gives all things to all; the following gods bestow some things on all. Demons and souls bestow only some things on some beings. There are invisible gods, and there are visible gods in heaven, and there are also demons. Indeed, the gods visible in heaven exist in that very union with the hidden gods. But the demons are far removed from them, just as from pure contemplators they...

# ON THE MYSTERIES

...they are more readily occupied in pure actions. Therefore, they are far distant from the visible gods <note>original: *diis conspicuis*. These are the "manifest" gods, such as the planets and stars.</note>. Likewise, the essence of both types of gods, as well as their power and providence, is universal, extending through all things. The nature of daemons <note>In this context, *daemons* are not evil spirits, but intermediary beings between gods and humans.</note>, however, is a particular providence concerning specific things and regions. Likewise, the gods so greatly transcend their bodies, and their bodies are so obedient to them, that they are said to be separate from bodies. Daemons, however, are more significantly affected by and joined to bodies. Likewise, the gods are the architects, while the daemons are the ministers. Daemons are hidden from the senses; the gods are hidden even from human reason. If, by chance, the gods should ever appear around the earth, they will still be more excellent than the daemons of the air. For a change of place or office does not change the divine nature. Finally, the gods are free from the powers flowing into the process of generation <note>The cycle of birth and physical becoming.</note>. Daemons, however, are not. He refutes the arguments that Porphyry <note>A philosopher and student of Plotinus who wrote a letter of inquiry to which this text responds.</note> had brought forward from history: namely, that many things are done toward the gods as if they were passible <note>original: *passibiles*. Meaning capable of being acted upon or feeling "passions" like anger or desire.</note>. Because the law of sacred rites commands one to be free from passions during sacrifices. This law was indeed given divinely, even by the first father of the world, from whom also come all the symbols in sacrifices signifying something most occult <note>Hidden or secret.</note>. Finally, those things which are properly done in sacred rites have a divine cause so remote from passion that reason cannot even reach it. The common people cannot grasp the reason for ceremonies divinely instituted. Nevertheless, they attempt to assign one. By assigning reasons based on their own passions, they attribute passions to the gods. The crowd uses gestures of veneration toward the powerful, and uses these same gifts toward the gods. But they do this toward men because of their own passions and because of the passions of their superiors. They think that similar passions exist in the gods as exist in powerful men, and that because of similar passions in subjects and worshipers, such things are offered to the gods. But in truth, ceremonies divinely instituted are not performed because of any passion, but rather out of admiration, veneration, and a thoroughly constant intelligence and a joy very much like it.

### How Daemons, Heroes, and Souls Differ

<margin>8</margin> There are in the gods generative and demiurgic <term>powers</term> <note>original: *uires generatiuæ opificesq;*. The powers responsible for creating and ordering the world.</note>; there are also life-giving powers, which are contained more sublimely in the former. The first are spread more widely than the second. The second are defined through the first. Daemons begin after a long process of these, where they are already derived into a very great division. Heroes are defined through the second—that is, the life-giving powers—before they arrive at the end. For in their end, souls begin. The office of the daemons, therefore, is the work of crafting regarding worldly natures, to carry out and perfect everything down to individual details, and to bind souls to bodies. But the office of Heroes is to give life, to reason, and to guard souls, and [to lead] them from...

<meta>This page continues the technical distinction between various classes of spiritual beings, focusing on the soul's ability to ascend the hierarchy and the specific visual characteristics (epiphanies) of gods, angels, daemons, and heroes when they appear to a practitioner.</meta>

to release from bodies. The duty of daemons <note>In this Neoplatonic context, *daemons* are not evil, but intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between gods and the physical world.</note> is wider than that of heroes. The former act more concerning the universe; the latter focus more on souls. We do not say that souls are created by them, but rather that they receive something from daemons and heroes, and add much more from themselves, beginning their own duty near the end of the divine works. This is not because divine actions do not reach further, but because souls are recruited into the final ranks of divine duties. Likewise, the soul can bring forth such various forms of living from itself that it may inhabit individual regions of the world according to their suitability. It can both meet with those it wishes, and return into itself, and join itself both to gods and to those inferior to itself, insofar as it brings forth the reasons <note>original: *rationes*. These are the 'logoi' or rational principles that govern the cosmos.</note> of the divine like an inferior. And if it is often joined to the gods through daemons and heroes, it can also join itself to the gods through certain intermediaries of its own that differ from them. The soul sometimes reconciles itself to the divine through other harmonies of its essence and actions than those by which daemons join themselves to those above. And if the soul does not maintain a course of life so similar, it nonetheless, often illuminated by the beneficent will of the gods, transcends the daemons toward an angelic life rather than an animal one. Although a soul may seem to exhibit all reasons and entire forms <note>original: *species*. Referring to the Platonic Ideas or archetypes within the soul.</note> within itself, it is nonetheless always determined according to some one thing—that is, one specific form. And meanwhile, from preceding causes, it coordinates itself with others, moving itself.

### When Different Divinities Appear and Act Differently.

All the higher beings, when invoked, come into view: but some appear under different forms and powers. The souls of the stars also move our sight in certain new ways. The visions <note>original: *visa*. The manifestations or apparitions seen during a ritual.</note> of the gods appear uniform and most simple. Those of archangels are somewhat less uniform or simple. Those of angels are even less so. Those of daemons are varied. Now, those of the principalities <note>original: *principatuum*. A specific rank of spiritual authority.</note> are more varied, but with a wonderful order of variety. Those of heroes are somewhat similar to these. The variety of the principalities is very ordered, but little ordered for the heroes. The souls of particular beings are, of course, "all-formed" <note>capable of taking any shape or form</note>. For since the higher beings are different in nature and action, and appear in their own way, they rightly meet individuals in different ways. The gods come into view as entirely salutary <note>original: *salutares*. Meaning health-giving, saving, or beneficial.</note>; the archangels appear both terrifying and gentle at the same time. The angels are milder. The daemons are to be feared. The heroes are to be venerated, though less than the principalities, which are stupendous; the "princes" <note>lower, often more earthly spirits</note> are harmful and hostile. Souls are similar to heroes, although inferior. The images of the gods appear completely immutable in magnitude, form, and action. Those of archangels and angels are gradually less immutable, but close to the gods. The images of daemons are indeed mutable in magnitude and form; for to some they appear one way, and to others another, yet they are recognized as the same. The images of the principalities are immutable; those of the heroes

### CHAPTER 9

The forms of souls are varied in many ways, almost like the leading daemons, but they are far more changeable than those of daemons. The **Gods** appear with a certain stillness and order. **Archangels** appear with the same, but they apply an efficacy <note>original: *efficaciam*. In this context, it refers to the active power to produce a divine result.</note> to them. **Angels** appear with the same, namely adding an ordered and moderate movement to that stillness and order. **Daemons** appear with a disturbance that breaks through order. **Principalities** <note>original: *principatus*. These are the *Archontes* or "Rulers" who govern the cosmic elements.</note> appear with stability and constancy within themselves. **Heroes** appear with motion and haste. **Princes** <note>original: *principes*. These are lower-ranking rulers, often associated with more material or sublunary realms.</note> appear with tumult. **Souls** appear almost like heroes, but with less stability and order.

To the **Gods**, there occurs a beauty that is inestimable, incomparable, and admirable, delighting beyond all measure. That of **archangels** and **angels** is similar, but varies by degree of rank. **Daemons** and the spirits of **heroes**, when appearing by themselves, possess beauty in specific defined forms; however, the former [daemons] possess it according to the principles of their essence, while the latter [heroes] possess it according to an act of fortitude. The beauty of **principalities** is primary and innate, while that of **princes** is artificial, adorned, and labored. The beauty of **souls** consists in specific principles, yet it is more fragmented than the form of heroes, though still contained under a single appearance.

The actions and effects of the **Gods** are faster than the intellect can grasp, yet meanwhile, they remain entirely stable. The speed of **archangels** is mixed, in a way, with effective actions. That of **angels** involves movement, and they do not possess the power to fulfill a task at the same time it is spoken. The actions of **daemons** appear faster than they truly are in effect and truth. **Heroes** proceed magnificently toward an action, yet they perform more slowly than daemons. **Principalities** come to act with authority and command. The effort of **princes** has much outward show <note>original: *emphasim*. This suggests a grand appearance that lacks substantive power.</note>, but fails in actual effect. The actions of **souls** are more mobile than those of heroes, but weaker.

The magnitude of the appearing **Gods** seems to occupy the whole sky, and as they proceed, it is thought that even the earth cannot sustain them. When **archangels** appear, certain parts of the world are moved, and a light precedes them that is divided within itself. They themselves display a magnitude of light and form proportional to the greatness of their dominion. The **angelic** form and light is both smaller and more divided. The magnitude and form of **daemons** is even more divided and smaller. That of **heroes** is again narrower, yet with a magnanimous appearance. **Principalities** appear very large and vast; **princes** appear inflated, proud, and insolent. The figures of **souls** are unequal and smaller than those of heroes. Finally, each being displays a magnitude of form and light according to the greatness of their power and the breadth of their command.

The sights of the **Gods** appear extremely bright to us, shining to the highest degree, wonderfully distinct in splendor, and more lucid than they actually are. Those of **archangels** are true and perfect. The figures of **angels** maintain the same appearance, except...

...because they fall short in the distinction of recognition due to a lack of full knowledge. The manifestations of **daemons** are fleeting and as if falling; those of **heroes** are even more fragile. Those of **principalities** <note>original: *principatuũ*. These are the "Archontes" or cosmic rulers who govern the spheres of the world.</note> are clear, while those of **princes** <note>original: *principum*. Lower-ranking rulers or "sublunary" powers often associated with matter.</note> are obscure, though both types are impious <note>original: *impiosa*. In this context, it suggests they lack the "piety" or pure divine alignment of the higher gods.</note>. Those of **souls** are shadowy. The images of the **Gods** flash with the greatest splendor. Those of the **archangels** are pre-eminently bright, and those of the **angels** are likewise bright. **Daemons** appear as a turbulent fire. **Heroes** possess a light mixed from many sources. **Principalities** show a purer light, whereas **princes** show a light confused by dissimilar and contrary elements. **Souls** return a fire that is full of many mixtures of generation <note>original: *generationis*. This refers to the process of being born into the physical, changing world.</note> and is divided.

The images of the **Gods** appear as an indivisible fire, ineffable <note>original: *ineffabilis*. Too great or sacred to be expressed in words.</note> and filling the entire depth of the world. The fire of **archangels** is also undivided, having around itself—either before or behind—a very great multitude. The fire of **angels** is divided, but exists within the most absolute forms. The fire of **daemons** is even more divided, but is narrowly circumscribed and easily described; it is easily contained by those who have seen higher things. The fire of **heroes** has some qualities similar to these, but not equal. The fire of **principalities** is exceptionally bright, while that of **princes** has something opaque. The fire of **souls** is greatly divided, multiform, and mixed from many natures of the world.

The fire of the **Gods** is entirely stable in its appearance. That of **archangels** partakes in stability. That of **angels** moves in a stable manner. That of **daemons** is unstable. That of **heroes** is more rapid. That of **principalities** arrives quietly, but that of **princes** is tumultuous. The fire of **souls** is changed by many movements. The **Gods** purify most perfectly; **archangels** recall us upward; **angels** only release us from the chains of matter. **Daemons** drag us toward nature; **heroes** lead us to the care of sensible <note>original: *sensibilium*. Things perceived by the physical senses rather than the intellect.</note> resources. **Principalities** exhibit a presidency over worldly affairs, while **princes** show a devotion to material things. **Souls**, when they appear, contend and drag us into generation.

Whatever is pure and firm in the image meeting us should be attributed to the superior kinds. Indeed, attribute that which is pre-eminently bright and firmly remains in itself to the **Gods**. That which shines and remains, but as if in another, attribute to **archangels**. That which remains in another, to **angels**. That which is mobile, wandering, and full of alien natures, attribute everywhere to the inferior orders. **Daemons** have mixed within themselves the vapors of the world and are carried unstably alongside or near the motion of the world. To **heroes**, generative compositions of spirits are mixed, around which they themselves are moved. **Principalities** remain in the same way, showing the worldly nature they possess; **princes** are full of material fluids. **Souls** are filled with superfluous stains and alien spirits; whenever each of these kinds appears, it shows itself by these qualities. **Gods** consume matter suddenly; **archangels** do so gradually; **angels** release from it and recall to the heights; **daemons** diligently adorn it; **heroes** adapt themselves to it in fitting ways...

...everywhere managing it <note>Referring to the divine order or light from the previous page.</note> vigorously and appropriately with measures. **Principalities** <note>original: *principatus*. High-level cosmic administrators.</note> stand by them, excelling over them, and in this way they show themselves. The **princes** <note>original: *principes*. Lower cosmic rulers associated with the physical realm.</note> show themselves to be completely filled with **matter**. **Pure souls** indeed come apart from matter. But **impure souls** show themselves to us entangled in matter. 

Furthermore, different beings exhibit different things to us. The **Gods**, when present, give health to the body, virtue to the soul, and purity to the mind. They call back all our parts to their own proper principles. What is cold and death-bearing in us, they destroy; they foster heat and make it more effective for life. They also cause all things of the soul and mind to agree and be measured by these same principles; they pour out light with an intelligible harmony. That which is not a body, they show as if it were a body to the eyes of the soul itself through the eyes of the physical body. 

**Archangels** do the same things, but not as sufficiently, nor as permanently, nor beyond our human proportion. **Angels** distribute more particular goods separately, and produce an effect that is much weaker than the innermost vigor of those higher beings. 

**Daemons** by their presence weigh down the body, afflict it with diseases, or punish it in other ways. They also drag souls toward nature and do not depart from bodies and their related senses; and those who strive toward the celestial or divine fire, they detain in the lower regions, nor do they release them from the bonds of fate. 

**Heroes** do other things similar to daemons, but they have this unique quality: they rouse us to certain noble and great works. **Principalities**, when appearing, bestow worldly goods and supply all the things of this life. **Princes** provide material and earthly goods. 

When **souls** appear, if they are **pure souls** established in the angelic order, they call us upward; they provide salvation to souls, sacred hope, and the sacred gifts that are hoped for. **Impure souls** twist the observer toward "generation" <note>original: *generationem*. The cycle of physical birth and change.</note>; they frustrate hope by taking away its fruits, and they fill the soul of the observers with passions that bind it to the physical body.

The order which each being holds is also designated by how they appear. The **Gods** show gods or angels standing around them. **Archangels** present angels either preceding, surrounding, or following them, or some other crowd of angels like guards encircling them. **Angels** present works appropriate to their order. **Good daemons** bring into view their works and the goods they bestow. **Avenging daemons** show types of punishments. Other **daemons** who are in any way depraved appear surrounded by deadly and voracious wild beasts. **Principalities** show certain provinces of the world with them. **Princes** bring into view with them the condition of matter, lacking order and wandering. 

Indeed, a **whole soul**, not held in any particular form, shows a fire without a certain shape around the whole world, by which the nature of the mundane soul <note>original: *mundanae*. The soul of the world itself.</note> is signified as undivided, one, and attached to no particular form. A **purified soul** shows a fiery figure, pure fire, and a sparkling light, yet stable; and she herself follows along with a sublime leader, rejoicing with good will. And so in her works...

When each of these beings appears, they show the provinces and lots which they have been allotted to inhabit. The **aerial** beings show an aerial fire; the **earthly** ones a terrestrial and black fire; and the **heavenly** ones a more splendid fire. All their ranks are distributed within these three boundaries. The **Gods** demonstrate the principles of all ranks within themselves when they appear. **Angels** declare that they depend upon **archangels**. **Daemons** and **heroes** reveal that they serve those above them, though the former do so differently than the latter. **Principalities** <term>original: *principatus*; high-ranking cosmic administrators</term> and **princes** <term>original: *principes*; lower cosmic rulers focused on matter</term> show their prefectures. The former are concerned with the world, the latter with matter. The **soul** declares that it holds both the higher and the lowest places; thus, together with themselves, the first souls designate the first places, the second souls the second, the third souls the third, and the rest following in the same order.

The **Gods** shine with a light of such subtlety that the eyes of the body cannot grasp it. They are affected much like fish pulled from murky, thick water into the thinnest air; for those who look upon the divine fire, being unable to breathe the subtlety of that divine fire, seem to fail in their strength as soon as they begin to look, and their innate spirit is entirely cut off. **Archangels** also emit a splendor more subtle and pure than can be endured, though it is not as intolerable as that of the **Gods**. **Angels**, when they come forward, create a tolerable mixture of air, so that **priests** <note>original: *sacerdotes*. Refers to theurgists or those performing divine rites.</note> are able to reach it. When **daemons** appear, the whole air is not affected at all, nor does the surrounding air become more subtle, nor does a light run before them in which their form shines out by anticipating the air. Nor does the air shine all around them. When **heroes** appear, certain regions of the earth are shaken and sounds ring out all around. However, the whole air does not become more subtle, nor does it become so unsuitable for the priests that they cannot endure it. 

Under the **principalities**, a circular motion of many uniform things runs around them, which is difficult to endure, and a cosmic volume of this kind surrounds them. Around the **princes**, however, there is a terrestrial atmosphere, yet it possesses neither the supra-cosmic subtlety nor the subtlety of the highest elements. When **souls** appear, the visible air is more akin to them and, being adapted to them, it takes on their description. 

The states of mind of those who summon the **Gods** bring back an exceeding perfection, action, divine love, and incredible joy. From **archangels**, they receive intellectual contemplation and a most pure, unchanging power. From **angels**, they receive rational knowledge and virtue placed in the highest order. From **daemons**, they receive a desire for generation <note>original: *appetitū generatiōis*. The urge toward physical life and reproduction.</note> and from **heroes**, similar things, along with an interest in the governance of the state. ->### 4<-

...worldly or material beings act for the sake of nature and the completion of fated works for souls; they provide the appetites of generation and the pursuits of caring for bodies. The appearance of the **Gods** strengthens truth, power, and actions to the highest degree and offers the most ample goods. That of **archangels** <note>original: *arcāgelorū*. In the celestial hierarchy, these are the messengers above the rank of angels.</note> is similar, but more particular, offering knowledge and power not in a general way, but for a specific purpose, place, time, and manner. Those of **angels** are even more restricted and specific. The gifts of **daemons** <note>original: *dæmonū*. Middle-tier spirits that act as intermediaries between gods and men; here they are associated with the physical world.</note> are not goods for the soul, but for the body and bodily things, when the worldly order permits. The gifts of **heroes** concern the affairs of the worldly or earthly republic. Those of **principalities** <term>original: *principatuū*; high-ranking cosmic administrators</term> concern worldly matters and all the comforts of life; those of **princes** <term>original: *principū*; lower cosmic rulers focused on the material</term> provide inferior things—that is, an abundance of more material goods. Those **souls** which contribute to human life come forward in an entirely familiar way.

**Porphyry** <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a series of skeptical questions about Egyptian and Chaldean rituals which Iamblichus is answering here.</note> recounted an opinion stating that it is common to gods, angels, daemons, and finally all higher beings, that when they appear they show off and boast wonderfully, producing an imaginary likeness of themselves. **Iamblichus** refutes this on both counts. A **God**, **angel**, or **good daemon** teaches a human when they appear what their essence truly is and what kind it is, speaking nothing beyond or short of the truth. For just as light naturally and constantly follows the sun, so truth follows God and his attendants, especially since they are perfect and full; they neither lack anything, nor can they claim for themselves more than what they are.

When errors are made in **theurgy** <term>original: *theurgia*; from the Greek for "god-working," the practice of rituals intended to invoke the presence of gods</term> (that is, in the deific and priestly faculty), then it is not the good divinities who are desired, but inferior and evil ones who encounter us under the pretext of being good. For evil spirits often transform themselves into the likeness of good ones; they come boasting and claim for themselves more than what they are. Indeed, where a primary corrupted beginning arises, a great deal of lying proceeds from that perversity. **Priests** must examine the appearances of spirits by the rule of the whole order, and remember that boastful arrogance is in no way proper to true and good spirits. They must also take care never to stray from the sacred rite. And if, through an error in the apparition, some insolent beings suddenly arrive, it is not right to judge the common and entire nature and condition of the divinities based on their specific behavior. For what has been proven in the sacred rites over many centuries and with laborious effort is a sacrilege <note>original: *nephas*; a violation of divine law.</note> to change by judging rashly based on some things that happen suddenly. 

And even if false spirits lie, the good ones are truthful and lawful concerning the fire <note>The "fire" refers to the divine light or the element used in theurgical invocation.</note>. For in every genus, the primary things begin first from themselves; they provide for themselves what they exhibit to others, and this occurs in essence, life, and motion. Likewise, the higher beings, exhibiting truth to all, first speak true things about themselves and reveal their very essence especially to those contemplating. Therefore, they duly demonstrate the fire to the priests, to be seen in its own proper form. For it is not the nature of heat to make cold, or of light to darken and hide; nor is it the nature of anything that acts by essence to sometimes do the contrary. A **phantom** <term>original: *phantasma*; here used to mean a deceptive image or simulacrum</term>—that is, a simulacrum sent by someone without...
