<meta>This page continues the discussion of divine manifestations, transitioning from the specific gifts of spiritual beings to the nature of their appearance and the philosophical debate between Porphyry and Iamblichus regarding knowledge versus ritual action.</meta>

# IAMBLICHUS

[...does not reveal] its true nature: but only by way of a mirror-like idol <note>original: *idoli specularis*; an illusory image that reflects something without possessing its essence, like a reflection in a glass.</note> it vainly draws away the mind of the beholder, and it deceives; while it feigns itself to be something, it has nothing of that nature. Therefore, it is the cause of falsehood, which in no way belongs to any true essence. For this reason, neither the gods nor their followers reveal thin and empty images, but rather reveal natural and true images of themselves. These are not indeed mirror-like (as I said) or vain—for why would they be sent? It is not to demonstrate their essence and power, for those images fall short of that throughout all nature. Nor are they for the benefit of the beholders; for what utility is there in a lie combined with deception? Finally, they do not send them because it is their nature to thus emit an idol from themselves. Surely an essence that is firm, consisting in itself, and is thus the cause of essence and truth for all else, in no way sends into another any fallacious and deceptive imitation of itself, which claims to be something whose nature it does not possess. Therefore, neither the gods nor their followers transform their nature into any likenesses, nor do they produce these likenesses out of themselves into something else; rather, they illuminate and demonstrate the true forms of themselves in the true characters <note>original: *moribus*; can also mean the 'dispositions' or 'ways' of the soul.</note> of the soul.

<margin>Note this similar point: that in the heavenly homeland, the blessed mind sees the divine essence not through an image created by it (which would be entirely deficient), but through the essence itself; just as he who sees light through light, in light. It is not like one who perceives heat through light, or one who sees a body in a mirror.</margin>

Separate substances <term>original: *substātiæ separatæ*; spirits or intellects existing independently of physical matter</term> have no genus in common with one another. Likewise, gods, angels, and good daemons do not appear in a phantastic <note>original: *phantastico mō*; referring to the 'phantasia' or the imaginative faculty which can be prone to illusion.</note> manner, but in a manner entirely proper and true. Truly, evil spirits appear in a phantastic and deceptive way; nor is it fitting to judge, from the condition in which these appear to us, the manner in which the good beings form the soul by their presence.

**Porphyry** says that the knowledge of divine things is indeed sacred, while ignorance is profane. **Iamblichus** approves of these things: because since the gods act upon beings through intelligence, we rightly please the gods and are approved through the intelligence of beings. But he places religious operation <note>original: *operationem religiosam*; the practice of theurgy or sacred ritual.</note> before intelligence, as that which alone is effective for acquiring the deifying union <term>original: *deificam unitatem*; the mystical state of becoming one with the divine</term> of the soul with God. So great is the virtue of sacred rites rightly performed for God that even if you are ignorant of these, yet observe them piously, they have no less efficacy. For intelligence does not join the sacrificers to God; otherwise, philosophers would achieve deifying union [by study alone].

->### On the virtue of the sacraments.<-

A fitting observance of the precepts and divine works which exceed all intelligence, and the power of symbols and sacraments—known only to the divine powers—grants us deifying union. When we labor in sacred rites, we do not perform them through intelligence...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that true divine manifestations are not deceptive illusions but true illuminations of the soul. He further contends that mystical union with the divine is achieved through sacred ritual and symbols (theurgy) rather than through mere intellectual understanding.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical defense of theurgy (divine ritual), specifically addressing how rituals work independently of the human mind. It marks the transition into a new chapter regarding the origins and nature of prophecy (vaticinium).</meta>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

<note>The first paragraph of this page contains horizontal pen strokes through several lines, indicating a possible correction or a passage the scribe or a later reader intended to delete, though it remains fully legible.</note>

[...un]derstanding to the sacrament; otherwise their action would be intellectual and would be provided by us. On the contrary, even when we do not understand, these sacraments perform their own work, and the power of the gods to which these things are referred recognizes its own ineffable images within itself, not being excited by our intellects. For universal causes are not moved <gloss>a</gloss> by particular effects; hence divine things are not principally moved to action by our intellects. But it is necessary for intellect, the best disposition, and purity to precede them as certain contributing causes. Those things which principally provoke the divine will are the divine <term>sacraments</term> <note>original: *sacramenta*; in this context, Iamblichus refers to theurgical rituals or sacred signs that bridge the gap between humans and gods.</note> themselves; and thus divine things are incited by themselves, nor do they receive the principle of action from anything subordinate. Therefore, do not think that the whole authority of effective reasoning in the sacraments lies within us, nor that their true work is completed in the truth of our intellect, or that these things are measured by our deception. For even if we knew which things follow each genus, we would not suddenly attain the truth of their operation.

Without knowledge, effective unity with divine things never arrives; yet it is not entirely the same thing. Wherefore divine purity is not produced through correct knowledge—just as the purity of the body is not produced through health—but purity is united and purified above knowledge, that is, through a power superior to knowledge. Therefore, nothing else human in us contributes anything to the end of divine actions. Conclude the opinion of <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who defended the use of ritual (theurgy) against the more intellectualized approach of Porphyry.</note> the Egyptian for the Assyrian: just as in agriculture, medicine, the art of images, or human intercourse, a human prepares the matter opportunely, but a superior and universal cause applies the form—so it is in sacrifice, when symbols and <term>synthemata</term> <note>original: *synthemata*; divine "tokens" or "passwords" embedded in the material world by the gods to allow the soul to communicate with them.</note> (that is, seals) and sacraments are made. The priest applies certain material things in the order the ritual established, but God impresses the effective power upon the sacraments.

### ->What Prophecy Is and From Where It Comes<-

Prophecy itself is not produced by art, nor by nature, nor by natural or animal reasons or movements; nor does it happen in any [accidental] way, but it is always sent to us from the divine. The entire prophetic power is referred back to the gods, and all its authority consists in them; thus it is handed down and perfected by divine works or signs. It possesses divine spectacles and contemplations endowed with true knowledge. All other things are subjected as instruments to the gift of prophecy sent from the divine, whether they pertain to the soul, the body, or are in the nature of the whole or in specific natures. Indeed, places and certain such things are required for prophecy in the role of matter; it is not fitting to derive prophecy without a cause—namely, from things having no foreknowledge inherent in themselves. But it is fitting to contemplate prophecy as distributed throughout the whole world and through all the diverse natures in the world, so that the principal and most common cause of prophecy exists, possessing in itself whatever it exhibits to those who participate in it...

IAMBLICHUS

...principally providing the truth which is required for prophecy, and especially its essence; for since it possesses in itself the cause of those things that come to be, a perpetual following of presage necessarily proceeds from it. Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus, whose questions to the Egyptian priest Abammon (actually Iamblichus) frame this entire work.</note> says that when we sleep, we sometimes foresee the future without any notice of our present state, even if we are not at all driven into an ecstasy. He thinks, I believe, that this presaging comes not so much from an external divine influence flowing in, as from the nature of the soul and mind itself. Iamblichus says that dreams which arise from human causes—whether through our nature or through our emotions, thoughts, and actions—touch upon the truth only very rarely and obscurely, and more often by a kind of chance.

### On dreams.

Dreams are sometimes stirred in us by our innate intellectual reasonings, or by the imaginations and cares of the day, which sometimes attain the truth but are mostly deceptive; these arise from human principles and happen to those who are sleeping, having no part in wakefulness. But dreams sent by the divine do not happen in this way; instead, they come either between wakefulness and sleep, or between sleep and wakefulness, or even during wakefulness itself. Then, brief voices are heard, advising what should be done; and sometimes a certain spirit <note>original: *spiritus*; here referring to a non-physical breath or essence.</note>, neither fleshy nor touchable, surrounds those lying down. It is not, however, seen by sight, but is perceived by another kind of sense and awareness through a certain impulse that enters as a shared feeling, surrounding from all sides without touch; it wonderfully drives out the passions of the mind and body. At other times, a pure and genuine light shines forth, under which the physical sight is closed, while the sight of the soul is opened.

But the other senses remain awake and perceive how the gods show themselves in the light, and they perceive what the gods say and do with continuous awareness. This whole process is discerned more perfectly when the sight also looks upon them, and the strengthened intellect follows what is happening, and those who watch are moved in a similar way. Such great differences as we have described are not human. They occur when our sleep is a certain heaviness or nodding of the head, or a closing of the eyes, or a middle state between wakefulness and sleep, or a sudden awakening, or wakefulness itself. All these states are divine, suitable for receiving the gods and sent from the divine. Yet some such things precede the divine appearance as parts of it.

Dreams proceeding from human causes suffer from two defects: they happen to those who are completely asleep, and we do not then clearly or fully notice either what occurs or our own state there. But when dreams are mixed from the divine, we are not truly asleep; we grasp and notice things more clearly than we are accustomed to when awake. Therefore, prophecy is most especially placed in dreams of this kind. The soul has a double life: one shared with the body, the other separable from every body. When we are awake, we use...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of divine revelation and the mechanics of the soul's perception. The previous page established that while ordinary dreams are often deceptive products of the mind, divine dreams occur when the soul is partially detached from the body. This page explores how the soul accesses "seminal reasons"—the underlying blueprints of reality—to foresee the future or receive divine healing.</meta>

For the most part, life is shared with the body, except perhaps when we are thoroughly separated from it, either because we understand or because we think with pure reasons; but in falling asleep we can be thoroughly released, as if from bonds applied to the soul, and then utilize a life separated from the world of generation <note>original: *generatio*; in Neoplatonism, this refers to the physical world of birth, death, and constant change.</note>. Since in a certain way the soul is released from the body for those who sleep, then that form of life—remaining according to itself, separable and separated, whether it be intellectual or even divine—immediately wakes up in us and acts according to its own nature. 

Because the intellect contemplates beings, and the soul embraces the reasons of things to be generated within itself, it rightly foreknows future things—which are ordered within its own preceding reasons—by comprehending the cause. Something has been said regarding the presages of the soul returning into itself in a state similar to sleep. "Into itself," I say, that is, into seminal and intellectual reasons <note>term: *seminal reasons* (Latin: *rationes seminales*); these are the generative blueprints or "seeds" of all things that exist in the physical world, stored within the soul and the divine mind.</note>, but thus far under a form proper to the present life—that is, under the form of this particular action and life. 

But if the soul soon unfolds the universal form of reasons and thoughts, according to how it once lived, it will then report presages pertaining more to the universal condition of worldly affairs, under which it can also see particulars here and there. If, again, through such a universal form, it is joined to the very minds of the gods, it will see moreover those things which look toward the higher world, and those which look toward this one; likewise, through those as through principal causes, it will understand more absolutely. In this state, not only will thought be perfect, but the imagination also will have pure images of corporeal and divine things.

Because the reasons of things to be generated are in the soul according to its power—both in terms of their effects and their cognition—and since these reasons depend on the reasons which are in the gods, the soul joined to these gods stirs the reasons within itself into action. This results in the most ample knowledge, achieved under the mode of divine providence <note>original: *diuina prouidentia*; the divine "foresight" or plan that governs the universe.</note>, through which the soul considers the past, the future, and all temporal things, as well as their actions and experiences, the remedies for suffering, the cures for illnesses and vices of the soul, the statutes of laws, and the arts necessary for the human race. 

Thus, in the temple of Aesculapius <note>Asclepius, the Greek god of medicine. In antiquity, the sick would sleep in his temples (a practice called *incubation*) to receive healing dreams.</note>, dreams are received by which diseases are cured; indeed, the art of medicine itself was obtained through divine dreams. The army of Alexander [the Great] was about to perish from disease when it escaped through the discovery of a remedy provided in a dream by the god Dionysus. King Lysander was besieging the city of Aphytis, and in a dream he was commanded by Ammon <note>Zeus-Ammon, an oracular deity of the Libyan desert.</note> to lift the siege. Many similar things happen daily, beyond human speech and reason.

...so that they may also use their senses. However, in the meantime, they are not in control of human reason. Iamblichus says that souls truly presaging <note>The act of perceiving or foretelling the future.</note> and inspired, even when they seem to sleep, do not sleep; and when they seem to wake, they do not wake in the proper sense. Nor do they use their senses in the human manner. Souls divinely inspired and stirred up, being thoroughly breathed upon by God, submit their life entirely to Him. Therefore, whether they have submitted themselves as a vehicle or as an instrument, they have laid aside their previous mode of life and have either exchanged their own life for the divine life, or they lead their own life entirely toward God. Therefore, they neither use their senses, nor are they awake in the way those with wakeful senses are, nor do they themselves presage or move by any human impulse or custom, nor do they perceive their own state, nor do they produce any knowledge or action of their own. But everything there is conducted under a divine form and action.

->Many miracles are performed by prophets.<-

¶ That those divinely inspired do not live a human life at that time is clear from the physical life itself. For many of them are not burned when fire is applied—evidently because God, breathing within them, repels the fire—or if they are burned, they do not feel it, nor do they perceive pricking, or scraping, or any torments. Likewise, it is clear that their actions are not human, since they walk through pathless places, and are carried through fire untouched, and cross rivers miraculously, as the priestess herself does in the *cataballa* <note>original: *cataballis*; This refers to the ecstatic rites at Castabala in Cilicia, where priestesses of the goddess Artemis Perasia were famously said to walk over hot coals without injury.</note>. Through these things, it is clear that they do not live a human or animal life burning with senses and impulse, but a divine one, as if their soul is at rest, and God is there in place of the soul, and moves them as if He were a more excellent soul.

The species of those divinely inspired are various, partly due to the variety of the gods—for some inspire in one way and others in another—and partly due to the difference in the modes of inspiration. These modes are as follows: for either God himself occupies us, or we dedicate ourselves to him and become entirely his, or we perform a common action with God. Likewise, we either become masters of the lowest divine powers, or the middle, or the supreme. Also, sometimes it is the naked presence of God; sometimes a communion occurs beyond presence; and sometimes a union is achieved beyond this. Again, either the soul alone becomes part of the inspiration, or the body also subsequently becomes a participant in a certain way, or the <term>common animal</term> <note>Latin: *commune animal*; in Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to the composite entity formed by the union of the soul and the physical body.</note> becomes equally a participant. According to the diversity and difference of these, there are signs, effects, and works of the inspired. According to the aforementioned diversity of the inspirers and the inspiration, some of the inspired are moved either in their whole body or in certain limbs, or on the contrary, they are at rest. Likewise, they perform dances and harmonious songs, or the opposite. Again, their body seems either to grow in height or in width, or to be carried through the heights <note>A description of levitation or the sensation of physical expansion during a trance.</note>, or the opposite. Likewise, they produce voices, either level and continuous, or uneven and interrupted by silence. And then

The inspired person is free from their own action and holds God in place of their soul.

<margin>But the greatest sign of divine breathing <note>The term used is "afflation," from the Latin *afflatio*, meaning a divine breath or inspiration.</note> is that the one who leads and introduces the deity sees the spirit descending, perceives its size and quality, and is mystically taught and guided by it.</margin>

~~Furthermore, he who receives the deity sees a certain appearance of fire before the reception.~~ But sometimes this is also observed by those present, whether the god is arriving or departing. From this sign, those skilled in these matters most truly discern the power of the deity, its rank, and the truths about which it speaks or the things it accomplishes. However, those who introduce spirits secretly without such spectacles, as if lurking in the darkness, cause confusion. They do not understand what they are doing, except for certain small things—that is, some signs in the body of the inspired person himself. Therefore, when the excellence of the divine fire and a certain appearance of ineffable light rests upon the possessed person from the outside, it fills him entirely and dominates him from within. It embraces him on all sides, so that he cannot perform any action of his own. What sense, perception, or personal observation could possibly remain in the soul that receives the divine fire? What human motion, passion, distortion, imagination, or "alienation" of the mind could there be, such as some people suspect? Porphyry <note>A Phoenician Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note> defines divine breathing as follows: "a motion of the mind along with demonic inspiration." Iamblichus <note>A Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who responded to Porphyry’s critiques of theurgy.</note> says that in a soul divinely inspired, neither human mind nor thought is moved, if it is truly possessed in this way. Nor is it an inspiration of demons, but of the gods; nor again should it be defined as a "departure" or "alienation." For these terms signify a fall for the worse, but rather it should be called a "reduction and restoration" for the better. Therefore, inspiration is nothing other than the souls being entirely occupied and held by God. From this, "ecstasy" <note>From the Greek *extasis*, meaning to stand outside oneself.</note>—that is, a departure or a certain alienation—follows later as an accidental consequence of the breathing. Plato in the *Phaedrus* says that the ancients called prophecy <term>mania</term> <note>Meaning madness or fury.</note>. This is because only those seized by divine fury truly prophesy. Later people, however, by adding the letter "t" <note>The Greek letter tau (τ).</note>, called it <term>mantia</term> <note>Divination or prophecy.</note>. Likewise, priests, sibyls, and prophets, as long as they are "sane," foresee very little and obscurely, or nothing at all; but when they are carried away by God, they truly prophesy. Hence, among many nations, they have foreseen dangers imminently threatening by divine will, warned the people, and appeased divine Nemesis <note>The goddess of retribution and balance.</note> through sacrifices. He also says that prophecy made by art is called "conjectural estimation," and it is of no importance if compared with divine inspiration and prophecy. Iamblichus says that divine breathing and prophecy are not in the mind or soul as a quality in a subject, nor as an action in an agent...

# IAMBLICHUS

But [he argues that] it is entirely an act of the god himself, depending simply on God. I mean an act performed by God in the mind or soul simply, as if they were instruments free from all their own motion. In this way, true prophecies are given. But if a motion from the body or soul—or a certain quality of that kind—is meanwhile inserted or precedes the event, the visions are seen to be confused. There will be no true prophecies, nor is there a legitimate divine inspiration <term>afflatio: literally a "breathing upon," referring to the divine breath or spirit entering a human</term> where anything human is mixed in.

Generally, there were three opinions regarding inspiration and divine prophecy:
1. The first attributed the cause to the soul.
2. The second to the body.
3. The third to the composite <note>The "composite" refers to the human being as a combined unit of both body and soul.</note>.

The **first** opinion places inspiration in that state where the whole soul is reduced into its divine part, or into the mind; or when its action has become more intense or more ample; or when thought has become sharp and its motion very swift; or when the mind has become "heated."

The **second** opinion places its cause in the body when it has a certain constitution <term>complexio: the physical temperament or balance of humors in the body</term>—namely, either melancholic or balanced—or a certain elemental quality, or furthermore a specific quality or a certain spirit <note>original: "spiritum," here likely referring to the *pneuma*, a subtle substance thought to circulate in the body.</note>.

The **third** opinion says the cause is a certain proportion by which the body and soul are joined together.

**Iamblichus** says that inspiration is not the work of the soul, or the body, or the composite, nor does it have its cause in them. For that prophetic inspiration acts—both in foretelling the future and in bringing things to pass—beyond all the custom of human nature. A man, or anything belonging to a man, cannot progress beyond his own limits toward divine limits. Nor can superior things be generated from inferior ones. 

Therefore, the cause of this is solely divinity itself: namely, when lights descend from the gods into us and spirits are transmitted by them. An absolute dominion and power from that higher realm is present with us, embracing everything that is in us and utterly exterminating our own personal attention and motion. It brings forth speeches through the human, indeed, but not with the human's own thought; rather, it speaks itself through the mouth of the one in a frenzy <note>original: "furentis," referring to the *theia mania* or "divine madness" described by Plato.</note> who is placed outside of himself. This happens while whatever is in us serves the whole deity and yields to the sole dominant divine action.

**Porphyry** says that music brings passions to the soul and likewise calms them, and that different sounds suit different souls and characters. Likewise, he says it changes the constitutions and affections of the body; it moves madness and it restrains madness.

**Iamblichus** concedes these points. But he denies that these are the causes of divine inspiration. Because these things are human—partly natural and partly artificial—they do not have anything divine in themselves. This is what Porphyry seems to suspect when he says some are inspired when they hear flutes <note>original: "tybias," the *aulos*, a reed instrument often used in mystery cults.</note>, or cymbals, or drums, while others are moved by different melodies. These correspond to various orders of the gods in the world

<meta>catchword: in the world</meta>

<summary>Iamblichus rejects the idea that prophecy originates from the human soul or body, arguing instead that it is an external divine force that completely replaces human agency. He also disputes Porphyry's suggestion that music is the cause of inspiration, viewing it instead as a mere human tool that corresponds to divine orders.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of divine inspiration, moving from a general categorization of theories to a specific analysis of how music and external elements serve as conduits for the gods, rather than being the causes of inspiration themselves.</meta>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

In the world, there are various types of motions, and specific motions belong to specific things. From these, various melodies flow out. These correspond similarly, through their own movements, to certain gods in order—who are the principles of motion. Since these gods are everywhere and impart their own gifts especially to those things belonging to them, they are present especially in the melodies that most agree with them. Stealing into our spirits <note>original: "spiritibus," referring to the "pneuma," a subtle substance linking body and soul</note> when they are affected by these melodies, the gods take possession of the human and soon fill him completely with their own essence and power. The cause of this inspiration <term>afflatio: literally a "breathing-upon," referring to the divine breath or spirit entering a human</term> is not so much a human passion excited by music as it is the very agreement of the music with the god, to which the god is naturally present.

Things that come to the sight are too much like images and rather represent intellectual things <note>referring to the "intelligible" realm of Platonic Ideas or Forms</note>. Things perceived by the senses below hearing are too material. But things belonging to hearing are intermediate and agree with the soul. Having worked their way into the spirit through motion, emotion, and meaning, they powerfully affect the soul on one hand, and the body on the other. Hence the whole human, according to the properties of the melodies, becomes a vessel <term>susceptaculum: a receiver or container</term> for this divinity or that. Those who are inspired behave differently in motion, rest, and other states, primarily according to the diversity of the divinities by whom they are inspired rather than the difference in the music. 

For the influence of the sound has already ceased when the god acts. In the intelligible world, the soul heard divine harmony, which it remembers here when it hears melodies possessing a trace of the divine; by remembering, it is strongly moved toward it—if it is among the number of those souls that especially contemplated the very Idea of Harmony in their homeland <note>referring to the soul's pre-incarnate state among the stars or gods</note>. Made familiar with the god by an affection of this kind, it is then inspired by a certain singular presence of the god. From this, the soul performs wonders. Therefore, the cause of this inspiration and miracle is not a passion brought on by sounds, nor is it the nature of the soul being composed of harmony, but its likeness to God and the presence of God.

It must also be said much less that inspiration consists in this: that through music and the inspiration itself, certain superfluous things hardened in the soul and body are purged. The authority of prophecy is not derived from a certain physical temperament <term>complexio: the balance of humors in the body</term>. For the gifts of the gods are not breathed in differently according to bodily variety. For the divine gift is impassive and is given above the power of nature through God's own action. Neither water, nor air, nor any other physical thing provides prophecy; rather, the sacred rites performed around these things—or rather, the purification of the mind together with the purification of the vehicle <note>the "spirit-vehicle" or *pneuma* that carries the soul</note> and the intention toward God—receives the divine power, which is everywhere and always most ready. When the inspired mind speaks and acts above and against the habit of nature, the cause of such inspiration is not natural—not from our body, nor the quality of the place, nor from the celestial arrangement <note>astrological configuration</note> at the person's birth or during their work—but these things happen from the presence of God. Hence, the various types of inspired people do not follow the natural variations within us.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the mechanics of divine inspiration. Having previously established that music acts as a conduit for the gods rather than a cause of human passion, Iamblichus now addresses how specific physical oracles—using water, vapor, or sacred seats—facilitate the descent of the divine presence into the human soul.</meta>

->### IAMBLICHUS###<-

...but there are different species, both of the inspiring spirits and of the modes by which we are made participants in the divine presence. Thus, among those divinely inspired, some become quiet while others are stirred up; some seek out mountains and deserts, and others behave in various different ways. This does not proceed from differences in the natural causes within us, or from locations, or from the music they have recently heard or are hearing. Rather, it arises from the various properties of the gods by whom the inspired are ruled, and from the various modes of inspiration <term>afflatus: literally a "breathing-upon," the process of a divine spirit entering a human</term>. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus who questioned the validity of theurgy and oracles</note> brings forward three oracles out of many: one at Colophon, where prophecy came from drinking water; another at Delphi, where the priestess prophesied sitting at the mouth of a cavern; and a third at Branchidae, where they prophesied by drawing vapor from the water. Each of these acts according to the mode of its own nature concerning its own effects and works. Therefore, the spirits themselves, which, depending on the gods, rouse and stir men, exceed every natural and human movement in this very work; and this action of theirs is in no way similar to the usual actions known to men.

There was in Colophon a subterranean place in which there was a spring. The priest, therefore, sacrificed on appointed nights; afterward, he would taste the water. Finally, he would prophesy there, having become invisible to those present. It might seem to someone that the divine spirit passed through the water into the priest. However, it is not actually so. For the divine does not run through those things that participate in it according to physical distance or division; rather, it encompasses from the outside and illuminates and fills the water from within with a certain power contributing to prophecy—namely, a purifying power. Thus, when the priest drinks, it purifies the **luminous spirit** <note>original: "luminosum spiritum," referring to the "pneuma," the subtle, light-like vehicle of the soul that bridges the physical and the divine</note> implanted within us and adapts it to God. By this purification and adaptation, we are able to receive God. But there also exists another presence of God beyond the power infused into the water, which is prior, and from above, shining around and within. This is absent from no one, provided they can attain it through congruity. Thus He is suddenly present and uses the prophet as an instrument; the prophet, meanwhile, is neither in control of himself nor notices what he says; he is even ignorant of where he is, which is why he barely recovers himself after the response. Indeed, even before drinking the water, he abstains from food for a day and a night, and withdraws to certain sacred rites inaccessible to the common people. Therefore, because of this sequestration from human affairs, he renders himself pure and fit for receiving God. From these things, it is gathered that a man is prepared for God in two ways: one through the purifying water made such by God, which purifies the spirit; the other through sobriety, solitude, the separation of the mind from the body, and an intention toward God.

The Sibyl at Delphi used to receive God in two ways: either through a certain thin and fiery spirit that broke out somewhere from the mouth of a cave, or sitting in the inner sanctum <term>adyto: the most sacred, restricted part of a temple where the oracle spoke</term> upon a bronze seat having three or four feet and dedicated to the god; and in both cases, she exposed herself...

...by the divine spirit, by which she was illuminated by a ray of divine fire. Therefore, sometimes a great amount of fire, flying out from the cave all at once, surrounds her on all sides and fills her with divine splendor. At other times, while she remains seated upon the seat sacred to the god, through which she is made ready for the god, she is joined to the stable prophecy of the god. In both ways, through this, the **Sibyl** <note>original: "sibylla" — the Sibyls were famous ancient prophetesses who spoke in riddles under the inspiration of Apollo</note> becomes entirely of the god. From this, the god is suddenly present, yet remaining separate in the meantime, distinct from the fire, the spirit, the seat, and all the equipment of that place, whether crafted or natural. 

The woman who is a prophetess at **Branchidae** <note>original: "branchis" — a reference to the oracle of Apollo at Didyma, managed by the priestly clan of the Branchidae</note> either sits upon an axle or holds a wand in her hand given by some god, or dips her feet or the hem of her garment in the water; or she inhales a vapor from certain water, and in these ways she is filled with divine splendor. Having obtained the god, she prophesies. For through all these things she becomes prepared for the god, whom she receives from the outside. 

That prophecy does not arise from any physical power or any soul's own power, nor from the instruments of the places, but from the presence of the god coming from without, is clear from the fact that the priestess herself, before giving oracles, performs many sacrifices according to ritual, observes holiness, is washed, and abstains entirely from food for three days. She dwells in seclusion and already begins to be gradually illuminated and to rejoice wonderfully. Through these things, it is clear that the god is called from the outside so that he may arrive, and that he does arrive from without. And even before the priestess comes to the place of the water, she is inspired in some way; and in that place, while a certain spirit flies out from the water of the spring, it is certain that the god is something else besides these things, separated from all of them: the cause of the place, the spring, and the entire prophecy. 

The power which inspires prophecy in us is absolute, free from places and times. Otherwise, it would not be able to express all places and times at once. For if it were inseparably attached to the nature of places or materials, or proceeded according to a movement determined by number, it would not be able to foreknow things that are everywhere or always, nor would it itself be everywhere and always equally. But if it is absolute from these things, just as it is superior to those things that happen in time or are contained in space, it is present to all waters wherever they may be, and it is present to those things that happen in time from all sides at once, and in one moment it comprehends the truth of all things, because of its essence, which is entirely separate and surpasses all things. 

The divine power, the origin of prophecy, is whole everywhere and whole always. This power is not from the body nor from the soul addicted to the body, but from the absolute—that is, from **angels** <term>angelos: in this Neoplatonic context, these are intermediary beings that bridge the gap between the supreme God and the human world</term> and from God, who are everywhere; or at least the power itself is wherever any angel is, and he is everywhere. It is separate from all bodily things yet present to all. Not comprehended by place or body or soul, which is addicted to some particular form. But this very prophetic power belongs properly to god, and is separate from all things; and therefore, the whole is present everywhere at once to those who are able to participate. It illuminates from without and fills all things, running through all elements, leaving no living thing or nature upon which it does not imprint something of itself according to its capacity, contributing to the foreknowledge; but it is able to fill all things equally because it is equally absolute from all things.

-># IAMBLICHUS<-

Porphyry, besides publicly celebrated prophecies, mentions some private ones—specifically those who claim they will attract spirits for prophecy through certain **symbols** <note>original: "characteres" — in this context, these are magical signs, sigils, or inscribed characters believed to have the power to compel or summon spirits</note>, which Iamblichus rejects. He does so because, while these people entirely neglect religion and holiness and rely solely on **symbols**, they are unable to attain the actual presence of any god or good **divine power** <term>numen: a Latin term for a deity or a divine presence that exerts influence over the world</term>. True prophecies are usually given through such presence, but these practitioners are deceived; although they use symbols appropriate to the gods and focus their mental intention, they only bring back a certain tiny and obscure imaginary apparition from the higher powers. Furthermore, since they neglect holiness in the meantime, they fall under the power of evil spirits who lie and deceive. These spirits pervert and confuse whatever small amount of signs or apparitions might have come from the gods. 

But those who are granted the true presence of the gods bring back a true and unchangeable foretelling, which cannot be disturbed by evil spirits. For just as when the sun rises, the darkness cannot withstand its presence but suddenly flees away without hindering the sun at all, so when the power of the gods shines from every side—filling all things with goodness—every disturbance that usually arises from evil spirits has no place, but is suddenly destroyed. When good divinities are fully present, evil spirits vanish; they are neither able to move themselves nor to cloud the divine splendor. 

He condemns those who neglect all contemplation and religious holiness, trusting only in symbols, by which they hope they will enclose the very substance of some god to be present while they prophesy. Porphyry also disapproved of the confidence of such people. He also relates that, besides these, there are others in whom the **imagination** <term>phantasia: in Neoplatonic philosophy, this is the faculty of the soul that receives and stores images, acting as a bridge between the senses and the intellect</term> is sometimes stirred up when they use certain materials. Even if their minds are otherwise sound in other matters, they are caught in a frenzy of the imagination during sacred rites. This happens, for instance, when they have hidden in darkness, or drunk certain potions, or used songs or specific structures. Then, in their frenzy, they imagine hidden and future things—some seeing them in water, others on a wall, others under the open sky (that is, in the clear air), others in the sun, and others in various stars. 

This divine light properly enters the imagination; if we see anything marvelous externally, it happens through the sense of sight following the lead of the imagination. The gods move the soul either by their presence alone, without any medium, whenever they wish it to be prepared; or they pour a certain light from themselves into the **ethereal vehicle** <note>original: "aethereum animae uehiculum" — the 'astral body' or 'spirit-body' believed by Neoplatonists to be the soul's intermediate housing between the physical body and the pure intellect</note> of the soul, by which images are moved in the imagination according to the gods' own will. In both cases, the divinity itself is never enclosed or confined. When those things appropriate for prophecy are employed, the attention and thought of the soul notice what is happening, even when the divine light does not properly reach these things—that is, the...

# ON THE MYSTERIES

...rational powers, but meanwhile the imagination rages, alienated from itself, because it is incited from above beyond human custom. Sometimes this state holds a person in darkness for the purpose of prophesying, for in these cases, nothing stands in the way of the coming light. At other times, the gods keep them in the light while they prepare them, so that there may be a greater likeness to the divine light; then the revelation is received in the light of the sun, or the moon, or a clear night, or in water prepared for its **transparency** <term>diaphanon: a term used to describe a medium, like water or air, that allows light to pass through</term>, or even on a wall prepared with **sacred characters** <note>original: "sacris charecteribus" — magical sigils or symbols believed to act as anchors for divine energy</note>. Here, because of the wall's solidity, that which is once divinely received is retained for a longer time.

Furthermore, they bring forward certain things related to the gods to be introduced, and they provide those about to prophesy with potions, certain compositions, and chants or incantations suitable for preparing the **receptacle** <note>original: "susceptaculum" — a physical or mental vessel intended to host a divine presence</note> and for accommodating the presence and appearance of the gods. This is done so that their hidden light may become manifest to the senses somewhere, but always according to the will of the gods—whether it be drawn from the ether, the air, the sun, the moon, or another celestial sphere. Insofar as it pleases the gods, who give freely as the primary authors, they move the imagination, and through it sometimes the senses toward appropriate objects; and sometimes through the sense itself, magical images made from solid matter preserve their power longer. The higher beings give gifts to those who are prepared, not only naturally, but through the intellect and free will of the gods themselves.

The gods give signs of future things in **sacrificial entrails** <note>original: "extis" — the internal organs of animals, such as the liver, used by "haruspices" to interpret divine will</note> and birds, and in new prodigies of the stars. From these, human sagacity conjectures events by the proportion of the signs to what is coming—such as the fall of a bird indicating the fall of a man, or a lack of limbs in the entrails indicating a failure or loss of status. The gods imprint signs of the future in things through the ministry of universal nature and individual natures, or by the service of **spirits** <term>dæmonum: intermediary beings that bridge the gap between the divine and material worlds; not necessarily "evil" in this Neoplatonic context</term> who serve the gods and preside over the elements, animals, and all similar things, which act easily according to the will of the gods.

And if they declare the will of the great god and future events **symbolically**—as Heraclitus says—they meanwhile represent the method of the divine workmanship. For just as they make things through firm images and pre-signify events, so too they do so through new portents and signs of all kinds; and meanwhile, for the same cause and occasion, they sharpen our own insight. The viscera in portents are transmuted against nature in animals by their souls, and by the spirit presiding over them, and by the motion of the air and the heavens, beyond nature and according to the will of the gods for the purpose of warning men. That this is done divinely is clear, because often certain principal organs necessary for life are not found in the animals; these are suddenly removed by a miracle, even though they must have been present just a moment before. In capturing **auguries** <note>original: "auguriis" — the ancient practice of interpreting the flight and songs of birds to discern the future</note>, birds are miraculously moved by their own soul, by a presiding spirit, and by the motion of the air and the sky, from which sky a power descends through the whole air, shaping and moving it...

# IAMBLICHUS

...opinion regarding the production of signs. I speak of an opinion pre-signified and decreed from the beginning: thus birds often cast themselves down, or dash themselves against things, or otherwise kill themselves while contributing to the act of **signification** <note>The belief that animal behavior, even self-destructive acts, were directed by the gods to provide omens (augury).</note>. They do not do this of their own accord, but are drawn by a divine power. Certain flames, made in the likeness of stars by divine power, are sometimes very easily created in the air at the command of the celestial gods for the purpose of signaling future events; the upper air is ignited there, which is very easy to guide and format—especially by the gods—and it turns into fire. In the meantime, certain influences from the celestial bodies descend into this air, leading to the creation and movement of "stars" of this kind, which are similar to the actual celestial bodies in their light, power, and motion.

The **World-Animal** <note>original: "Mundanum animal" — the Platonic concept of the universe as a single, living, interconnected organism.</note> is so united with itself that its members sympathize with one another; even those parts that seem remote from each other are moved together as if they were close, like the limbs of the same animal. And this union and **sympathy** <term>compassio: not "pity," but the Greek concept of 'sympathia', where a change in one part of the universe affects all other parts.</term> serves the gods in exhibiting signs to men, first through the heavens, and then through the air. The gods do not act immediately, but through intermediate instruments—namely, **daemons** <note>original: "daemones" — intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between the divine and the human; they were seen as messengers rather than "demons" in the modern sense.</note>, souls, natures, and all things depending on these—to create signs for men, starting from a single principle. 

And from there, they subsequently diffuse the motion descending from themselves wherever they wish. Therefore, without any attachment or coordination with things subject to change, they rule each such thing. Just as in craftsmanship and providence, so in exhibiting signs, their intellect is not turned aside toward our affairs; rather, while the divine intellect remains within itself, it converts all signs and prophecy back to itself, noticing those things that proceed from itself.

<margin>Porphyry wonders that the gods so serve men that prophets sometimes even prophesy by means of flour <note>This refers to 'aleuromancy', an ancient form of divination using flour.</note>. Iamblichus responds that the gods do not provide this out of subservience, but through an excess of power and goodness. And since the First Cause contains all things in itself, while the gods remain in themselves without turning toward lower things, they bestow gifts and signs upon them according to the level of preparation of the recipient, just as the sun gives light to transparent things and to the eyes, and similarly provides heat. Because we see men care for their subjects by "turning" toward their work—being distracted by various tasks, drawn away from themselves, and laboring—we therefore wrongly suspect that the gods provide in the same way. On the contrary, insofar as they are turned toward themselves and their single Form (which is the cause of all lower things), to that extent they act, move, and rule all things. They are not distracted by variety, but vibrate all things from a single principle and a simple command, with a certain succession of events depending on that command. They are not bent toward the subjects; instead, by their status and absolute fixity, they render all things similar to themselves. God supplies various modes of prophecy; he is not distracted himself, but suggests all modes by an individual command and simple form. He suggests different modes at different times, but is not himself varied by time; rather, by the same eternal stroke of mind and will, he inspires all things, even though these are unfolded at various times.</margin>

All prophets confess that they obtain prophecy through gods or daemons, because no one can see the future except those who are the causes and masters of the future. It is through them that others may see.

<summary>Iamblichus explains that divine signs in nature, such as the movement of birds or atmospheric "stars," occur because the universe is a single living organism where all parts sympathize. He argues that gods do not labor or "turn" toward humans to provide these signs; rather, signs flow naturally from their overflowing power and fixed, eternal intellect.</summary>

### ON THE MYSTERIES

<sig>c ii</sig>

...[is revealed]. Nor is the divinity confined or distracted by these omens, but rather, by embracing all signs within its own unified form, it expresses them from within itself. Remaining consistent within its own being, it transmits all things through a single act of **will** <note>original: "uoluntatis"</note>. So great is the abundance of **Providence** <note>original: "prouidentiæ" — the divine guidance of the universe.</note> in showing us signs that it provides indications of the future even in pebbles, rods, pieces of wood, stones, grain, and flour. In these instances, it miraculously appears to grant a soul to the inanimate, movement to the immovable, and a certain intelligence to those things lacking reason—almost as if these objects seem to know the future they portend for us.

And just as God often speaks wisdom through foolish men—declaring that it is not the man speaking there, but God—so He portends future events through even the most lowly things. He remains entirely superior to these things, yet He instructs our intellect through all of them. God reveals through the lowliest things, which lack their own knowledge, certain matters that are higher than knowledge, thereby testifying that He far surpasses nature. While He provides diverse signs, He is not confined by them, nor distracted through them; but standing in His own single and indivisible form, He comprehends all signs there. From that place, with a single and simple nod, He unfolds all things, offering us proofs everywhere of things past, present, and future.

---

->No work of any efficacy occurs in sacred rites except through the power and, indeed, the presence of some divinity.<-

In religion, no work of any miraculous efficacy can be performed unless some one of the higher beings is present as an observer and fulfiller of the work. Indeed, the **gods** <note>original: "dii"</note> lead the perfected works; the **angels** <note>original: "angeli"</note> lead the intermediate works; and the **demons** <term>daimons: in this Neoplatonic context, these are "dæmones"—intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between gods and humans, rather than evil entities.</term> lead the third class of works. Human nature cannot even grasp the reasoning or speech concerning the gods without the gods themselves, much less be capable of performing divine works without them. For human nature is so weak and dull that it has no remedy for its own nothingness, except for a certain portion of divine light descending from above, without which nothing divine is done by us. Just as those who trust they can create a soul from inanimate things or a mind from the mindless are deceived, so too are those who believe they can perform divine works from non-divine things, or the works proper to the gods without the gods—such as **prophecies** <note>original: "uaticinia"</note>, **miracles** <note>original: "miracula"</note>, and similar things like **apparitions** <note>original: "apparitiones"</note> and **purifications** <note>original: "expiationes"</note>.

---

->When divinities are invoked, they are present to us not by compulsion but by their own will.<-

<margin>c</margin>
It is a confessed truth that the works of religious efficacy are perfected by the presence of gods, angels, and demons. <meta>This page continues the discussion of divine interaction with the material world. The previous page established that God expresses His will through a single act and uses even the lowliest objects as signs. This page transitions into a specific defense of theurgy—sacred ritual—against the idea that humans can "force" the gods to act, specifically addressing the philosophical disagreements between Iamblichus and Porphyry.</meta>

# IAMBLICHUS

...[to be] drawn to these things by some necessity of invocation. Iamblichus denies that necessity is imposed either by man or by the world upon the deities <note>original: "numinibus" — divine powers or lesser gods in the Neoplatonic hierarchy.</note>, for since they are immaterial, they do not receive an order that comes from outside themselves. Likewise, invocation and sacred ritual do indeed move the priests toward the deities through a process of assimilation <note>original: "assimilatione" — the act of becoming like the divine through ritual purity.</note> and a certain familiarity; yet no violence is done to the priests, let alone to the deities. God and the entire chorus of deities joined to God <margin>1</margin> exist above any necessity that comes from the outside.

Prophecy <note>original: "Vaticinium"</note> is perfected while the priest performs sacred rites. At that time, no "passion" <note>original: "passio" — in this context, it refers to being "acted upon" or experiencing emotional/physical disturbance.</note> falls upon the priest or the diviner when they are divinely inspired. Even less so does it fall upon the deities, who do not glide into souls unless those souls are empty of passion. Nor should it be said that the prophetic soul is a "middle instrument" or an effective tool of the divine; nor that the priest who invokes is the "effective cause" of divine works. Rather, God is all and can do all; He fills all things with Himself. Human nature has no effectiveness in these matters.

Indeed, compared to the divinity, these things are like a game <note>original: "ludus" — implying that what seems miraculous or difficult to humans is effortless "child's play" for the divine.</note>. We mock those who say that God is present for some people by the chance power of a "celestial figure" at their birth <note>original: "in genesi" — a reference to judicial astrology, where one's fate is tied to the stars at the moment of birth.</note>. For it is not fitting that uncreated and universal causes should be enslaved to anyone through a specific birth, or its cycle, or through external causes. 

Some people, because they did not wish to "burden" God with chores, and did not perceive any mode of the Creator's **Providence** <note>original: "prouidentiæ"</note> other than the kind characterized by human worry, denied that the gods act or provide for us. Similarly, those who do not see the excellent way in which the gods are present without labor or change to themselves would deny that the gods take part in prophecies and miracles. However, the manner in which the gods are present throughout all these things is known only to the gods themselves.

**Porphyry** <note>A philosopher and student of Plotinus who wrote a famous letter questioning the validity of Egyptian and Chaldean rituals.</note> says that divine works, such as prophecies and miracles, are sometimes merely "passions" of the soul excited by small sparks, and that the soul is able to imagine, speak, and do these things by its own power. Iamblichus, however, says that a divine work is not produced by chance (since it is ordered) nor by a human being (who is far inferior). For it is necessary that a divine work be performed by divinity. Therefore, all works similar to divinity do not sprout from human nature, but from divine nature.

The works of miracles and prophecy are not produced by any power of the stars, the body, or the soul, but by the pure and free power of God.

The human soul is both confined to a single species and is greatly overshadowed by the falling body. Therefore, it has no effective power for divine work. If ever we seem [to be able to do] such a thing in some way...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that divine acts like prophecy and miracles are the result of God's free power rather than human effort or astrological necessity, rebutting Porphyry's claim that such phenomena are merely products of the human soul.</summary>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

</header>

<warning>Faded text and ink loss in the middle-left section of the page (lines 7-10).</warning>

...to be able to do anything of ourselves. We only act by divine illumination flowing down from above, through which we seem to be participants in divine action. If divine works were performed by the soul by its own nature, then by its own power, any soul possessing virtue and prudence—or even all living creatures—would perform them. But in truth, not every soul does so; even a soul that appears perfect is still imperfect in the face of divine matters. Therefore, it is not the soul, but divinity itself that is the cause of divine works. Otherwise, religion would not be necessary for us; <unclear>without</unclear> God and worship, we would be capable of divine works if they were brought about by our own power. 

Finally, if the soul performed divine things by its own power, it would either do all things, or it would perform those things which belong to its own virtue and perfection: namely, knowledge, art, prudence, and the moral character acquired through prudence. But as it stands, it is not such people who perform these works, but rather those who are divinely inspired <note>original: "concitati" — literally "stirred up," referring to the state of divine frenzy or prophetic ecstasy.</note> and withdrawn <note>original: "abstracti" — those whose minds are pulled away from worldly senses.</note> from the world. 

Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a philosopher who often questioned the efficacy and logic of theurgical rituals.</note> had proposed three possibilities regarding divine works: 
1. First, that the soul is merely an instrumental cause.
2. Second, that the soul is sometimes the principal cause.
3. Third, that the soul can be an equal co-cause, such that from it and the divine spirit, a certain third type of substance or "subsistence" is created.

Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was the author of this defense of ritual, arguing for the absolute superiority of the divine over the human.</note> says that when one single thing is made from many, those many parts must be related and changeable; just as a "fifth element" is made from the mixing of the four elements. He notes that many souls might merge into one whole—perhaps a vegetative, sensory, or motive soul—and in us, they yield to the intellectual soul and are brought into its action. Or perhaps from all of these, a vital harmony results in the body; or perhaps souls in their heavenly homeland conspire into one single Idea of all souls. 

Divinity, however, acts as the Exemplar for all things and does not "merge" into a unity with them. Porphyry's third point fails because the soul has already fallen from its original state, and divinity—being vastly different—does not enter into a mixture. Furthermore, because divinity is immutable, it is not changed into something else that is common to both. 

It was said previously that divine forms <note>original: "species diuinas" — the archetypal patterns or shapes of the divine.</note> are awakened in the soul by "tiny sparks"; let it be so, but these would not be translated into purely divine forms if they were merely bodily or natural in origin. Finally, where it is said that the soul and divinity meet to form a third thing, the soul is made equal to God. This would mean admitting that God is changed there and receives something from the soul, just as the soul is changed and receives something from God. This is absurd—especially because it would mean the gods, like mere elements, would combine in their effects to create a form that exists only for a time. It would mean that eternal beings are contained within a temporal thing <note>This refers to the philosophical problem of how an eternal god could be "trapped" in a ritual that happens at a specific moment in time.</note>, whenever it is said that something temporal is made from the soul and God (or the gods) together. We must ask whether something new results beyond the parts coming together, or not; if nothing results...

<sig>c iii</sig>

<vocab>Porphyry, Iamblichus, divinity, soul, elements, on the mysteries</vocab>

<summary>Iamblichus refutes Porphyry's suggestion that the human soul and the divine combine to form a "co-cause" in ritual. He argues that God is immutable and cannot "mix" with the human soul, maintaining that all divine effects are the result of God's power alone.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical debate between Porphyry and Iamblichus regarding the origins of divine power. # IAMBLICHUS:

<warning>Faded and illegible text at the bottom left of the page.</warning>

Then no true union will occur, nor a true unity; just as in a craft that depends only on the art itself, if eternal things fall from their stable state, something temporary is created. Unless they are changed, a third thing does not result; indeed, it is completely absurd to claim that something which is created through a kind of temporal generation is actually eternal. Yet, it is not proper to categorize it as temporal, lest eternal things become servants to the temporal. Nor is it proper to claim that this thing is dissolvable, having been made from eternal things on both sides. And yet, through a new generation, it would seem to be dissolvable. Therefore, that opinion is absurd.

Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a critic of certain ritual practices, whose questions Iamblichus is answering here.</note> says that the soul sometimes generates a <term>daemonic power</term> <note>original: "potestatem essentiamque dæmonicam" — referring to a spirit-like essence or power that acts as an intermediary.</note> that imagines future events through certain motions. I say "generate" in the sense that the soul brings together certain materials that possess such powers within themselves, especially materials taken from living creatures. 

Iamblichus denies that <term>daemons</term> <note>In this context, daemons are not "demons" in the modern sense, but spirits that bridge the gap between gods and humans.</note> are generated or destroyed. For he denies that daemons, who are superior to both bodies and the soul, can be generated by the soul from bodily forces. He also denies that the actions of an individual soul—one confined within a physical body—can result in essences that exist independently outside the soul. He denies that the powers of bodies, which are entirely tied to matter, can be released from them to generate daemons. 

Furthermore, he asks what power it is that releases these material forces from matter and fuses them back into one to generate a daemon. In such a case, this power itself would appear to be daemonic; thus, the daemon would exist even before it was supposedly generated. A soul, especially a prophetic one, cannot be generated from things that lack a soul and the power of divination. The more excellent cannot be procreated from the inferior. No essence or substance can be constituted from the motions of the soul and bodily forces, which are themselves neither substances nor essences. Likewise, nothing that is sown through generation possesses anything greater than what was granted to it by its primary generating cause. Therefore, since neither the body nor the soul possesses the power of divination by itself, the soul cannot procreate a prophetic daemon from its own motions and bodies. 

Perhaps someone will say that daemons are not generated by us, but that they preside over living things in an orderly way; and so, when materials from animals are appropriately offered to this daemon, he is drawn to these things as if by a <term>shared feeling</term> <note>original: "compatientem" — referring to "sympathy," the Stoic and Neoplatonic idea that all parts of the cosmos are linked and react to one another.</note>. Iamblichus says that daemons who are subject to such shared feelings to such a degree cannot prophesy the truth. For true prophecy <note>original: "uaticinium"</note> does not belong to a nature that is <term>passive</term> <note>original: "passibilis" — meaning a nature that can be affected, changed, or moved by external physical influences.</note> or confined by any body, place, or time; rather, it is free from all these things, so that it can look upon things happening in any place or time with equal and simple foresight.

<summary>Iamblichus refutes Porphyry’s suggestion that human ritual or animal materials can create or "generate" spirits (daemons). He argues that because daemons are superior to matter, they must be eternal and independent of human action or physical sympathy.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the general nature of intermediary spirits (daemons) to the specific phenomenon of divine dreams. It continues the structured debate between Porphyry, who seeks psychological or naturalistic explanations for prophecy, and Iamblichus, who insists on the purely external and divine origin of such revelations.</meta>

# CONCERNING THE MYSTERIES

->On divine and human dreams.<-

Porphyry says that the foreknowledge found in dreams comes partly from within ourselves and partly from an external source. Iamblichus, however, argues that it comes solely from an external source. He reasons that we often study and perform various actions to "hunt" for this foreknowledge, yet it is not granted to us; conversely, it is often given to those who are not seeking it at all. If the effects of dreams originated from our own nature and human will, they would occur when we planned for them. Instead, they are sent by the gods according to their own will—specifically when and how they wish—to demonstrate the future through a certain divine kindness. The Orphic hymn declares this same truth.

Porphyry claims that the cause of <term>prophecy</term> <note>original: "uaticinii" — refers to the act of foretelling the future or divining divine will.</note> is a certain <term>passion</term> <note>original: "passionem" — in this philosophical context, a "passion" is not necessarily an intense emotion, but a state of being "acted upon" or a passive modification of the soul.</note> of the soul. Iamblichus denies this, saying that passion is by its very nature unstable, disordered, and disturbed. Prophecy, he argues, must be entirely stable and ordered; therefore, it cannot reside in a state of passion. Furthermore, when the soul is wise and constant, acting according to its higher powers—namely the intellectual and rational faculties—it does not look into the future. How, then, could the soul achieve this foresight when it is suffering under disordered and disturbed movements? 

Additionally, passion contributes nothing to the contemplation of true beings and truth; rather, it acts as a hindrance. Moreover, if the things of the world were constituted by passions, then a passion in the soul might reach them through a kind of similarity. But since things are constituted and governed by <term>reasons and forms</term> <note>original: "rōnīb⁹ speciebusq;" (rationibus speciebusque) — referring to the Platonic idea that the world is structured by rational principles and ideal forms.</note>, surely a different kind of foreknowledge exists that is entirely foreign to all passions. Again, passion only perceives the present. Since prophecy also reaches into the future, it is not involved in passion.

Porphyry says that prophecy is a certain passion arising in the <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "phantasiæ" — the faculty of the mind that processes images.</note>, arising either from our own thoughts, or from the instinct of our physical nature, or occurring by chance, just as it happens that the "frenzied" (those with brain fever) sometimes prophesy. To support this, he points to signs: in the state of prophecy, the imagination acts intensely, while the senses are meanwhile occupied and restrained. He also notes that <term>suffumigations</term> <note>original: "suffumigationes" — the ritual burning of incense or herbs to produce smoke.</note> are used by the one about to divine, presumably to affect the imagination. Likewise, invocations are used to stir the same state. Furthermore, he notes that not everyone is fit for this, but rather the young and the simple. 

Iamblichus replies that the "occupation" of the senses is actually a sign that no *human* mental image is present at that time. Vapors are used to create a harmony with the god, not to affect the soul of the person watching. Invocations do not stir up thoughts or physical passions within us; for those are unknown to us, and known only to the god who is being called. As for the fact that only simpler people are chosen, it is because they are more exposed to the divine spirit coming from the outside. Regarding Porphyry's claim that prophecy is a passion of the imagination similar to what often happens to "melancholics" and the deluded who speak as if they were prophets, he misuses...

# IAMBLICHVS
Kk 3

...is perfected by the divine gift of prophecy, while a state of <term>alienation</term> <note>original: "alienationē" — a state of being 'outside oneself,' often referring to a trance or ecstasy.</note> produced by God for a better purpose is compared to an alienation resulting from diseases, drunkenness, or madness, which happens for the worse. Alienation arising from our own <term>passions</term> <note>original: "paffionibus" — here meaning internal emotions or physical disturbances.</note> casts the soul down below the human state; but that which is caused by God raises man above man and joins him to God. The former makes a person unstable and completely immerses them in matter; the latter makes them constant and master of order, freeing them from matter.

---

In no way should it be said that divine <term>inspiration</term> <note>original: "afflationē" — literally a 'breathing upon' by the divine.</note> has anything in common with the alienation caused by the <term>humors</term> <note>original: "humorib⁹" — in ancient medicine, these were the bodily fluids thought to dictate health and temperament.</note>, drunkenness, or rage. For these states are distant from God by a gap greater than can be imagined. Therefore, such madness is just as far removed from divine inspiration; they have nothing similar or in common. Alienation caused by bodily causes is a corruption of the soul occurring from weakness. But that which is caused by God is the health of the soul occurring from the fullness of power. In the former state, when the soul attempts its own operations, it produces them in a perverse and turbulent way. In the latter state, however, while the soul is at rest from its own life and intelligence, it exposes itself to a superior power to be used. In short, as much as divine things are distant from the lowest natural things, so too are the actions and effects of the divine distant from the effects of nature.

Therefore, the alienation induced by God has nothing in common with that which occurs humanly. When you think of the divine kind, you must completely separate from it all the defects and accidents of the human kind. Furthermore, when you contemplate the sacred sobriety and vigilance received from God, do not compare it with the sobriety of ordinary men. In both cases, remove from the soul anything similar to those <term>imaginations</term> <note>original: "imaginationibus"</note> which the humors and similar causes stir up. Likewise, do not think the ambiguous state of a man—halfway between a sober mind and an alienated one—is similar to the state of a sacred soul looking upon God with a single intuition. Nor should you believe that the most certain visions of divine things are similar to the mental images raised by the <term>sorcerous arts</term> <note>original: "arte uenefica" — refers to witchcraft or the use of potions/charms.</note>. For those things we imagine when fascinated have no truth of action or essence beyond the mere image. For the goal of such magic is not to truly create something, but merely to extend mental images until they appear real.

One must not think that the divine <term>prophet</term> <note>original: "uatem"</note> happens upon the truth by chance, as madmen sometimes do, nor even by a certain natural "suffering," just as animals often "suffer" or are affected by certain parts and forces of the world when something in the future is beginning to stir—already acting in the air, as it were, before it happens on the earth. By being affected in this way, animals sometimes sense coming earthquakes and storms, especially those animals that are either easily affected or possess sharp senses. For foreknowledge arising from chance or from such natural sensitivity is rare, disordered, and inconsistent, and it remains entirely obscure. Divine prophecy, however, follows the continuous order of the universe...

He also contrasts true prophecy with the hallucinations of sorcery and the natural instincts of animals sensing weather changes.</summary>
