# IAMBLICHVS
Kk 3

...and firmly connected, which it beholds with reason. If any faculty were innate in us for perceiving the future, it would not for that reason be <term>prophecy</term> <note>original: "uaticinium"</note>; for such a faculty is not always truthful, but only occasionally, and not in all things, but only some. True prophecy, however, is always and in all things truthful. Likewise, <term>foreknowledge</term> <note>original: "prenotio"</note> achieved by skill attempts to catch the future from signs that are not entirely reliable, because they do not always have a guaranteed outcome joined to them. But the effect produced by divine providence beholds its outcomes from their causes, connecting all changeable and temporal things—even those distant from one another—with a firm, present, and entirely continuous gaze, anticipating future things as if they were present. Someone might say that the future can be predicted from four gifts joined together: namely, from a specific human nature, from a skill applied to it, from the common <term>sympathy</term> <note>original: "compassione" — the Stoic and Neoplatonic concept that all parts of the universe are interconnected like a single living body.</note> of things among themselves as if they were parts of the same living creature, and from that disposition of bodies by which some provide signs to others. But in truth, even when these factors concur and signs are clearly perceived, such a perception only has something similar to prophecy. Indeed, the universe holds traces of prophecy everywhere, but they are not clear everywhere. Just as the image of the Good itself reflects God in all things, so there is some trace of prophecy in all things.

Yet the one, unmixed divine species of prophecy should not be defined by these likenesses sent down into the <term>realm of generation</term> <note>original: "generationem" — the physical world of birth, death, and change.</note>, and much less by the fantasies of those who are delirious. For all these are deceptive. **Prophecy itself** must be defined by a single principle and a single order: one divine species and one <term>intelligible</term> <note>original: "intelligibilem" — referring to things that can only be understood by the mind/intellect, rather than the physical senses.</note> and immutable truth. On the other hand, every changeable perception must be separated from it as being undefined, and in no way fitting for the gods or divine things. When we perform some work natural to us, the seeds and preparations for it are certainly granted from the beginning by nature itself, which is the cause of such work. Therefore, no such preparations or seeds have been given by nature—whether universal or human—for that prophecy which is above nature and human custom. For nature lacks intelligence; it is not the primary author of things that happen, especially insofar as nature exists within us. But prophecy is more than intellectual; it touches the very causes of events and, in a single and sudden gaze, embraces the order of the entire universe. Such work is proper to God, who acts this within us while we ourselves are then "vacant" from our own personal actions. **Presentiment** <note>original: "Pręfagiū" (praesagium)</note>, if any occurs to us by natural instinct or is produced by skill, may certainly have a preparation and aptitude within our nature. But this presentiment is very narrow and obscure, and is experienced to a greater or lesser degree. Divine prophecy, however, is most ample and certain, and it possesses one stable—that is, the highest—degree everywhere. Therefore, it could not have been implanted in us by nature. **Porphyry**

...conjectured that a certain affection of our nature, whether bodily or psychic, contributed especially to <term>prophecy</term> <note>original: "uaticinium"</note>. This was based on the fact that those who summoned prophecy into a human being used to carry certain small stones and herbs, tied sacred knots, and then untied those that were bound. They also changed the intentions of those who had received such things from them, turning bad circumstances into better ones. But Iamblichus turns such observations and effects back into a counter-argument: namely, that the inspiration of prophecy comes from outside, from another source, and from above. For such things <note>referring to the stones and herbs used in rituals</note>, being in harmony with certain deities, adapt us to receive that inspiration when they are applied to us.

Porphyry says that one should not despise the art which, at specific times and near a fire under favorable stellar influences, makes <term>images of gods</term> <note>original: "deorū idola"</note> appear immediately in the air. These are somewhat similar to the gods and possess a certain similar efficacy. Iamblichus, however, says these images are held in low esteem by priests who have perceived the true forms of the gods. Nor can any excellent good be found in that which sprouts from matter and the forms within it, or from the powers of such forms combined with human art. For what is made by man is inferior to man; and what is made in this way, like a magical image, is a certain shadow—appearing rather than truly existing—and while it exists, it is immediately vanishing. It is not made by the <term>creative art</term> <note>original: "arte opificia"</note> which fashions true essences, but rather by an imitative art which merely renders images of those essences.

Indeed, God, the <term>craftsman of the world</term> <note>original: "mundi opifex" — the Demiurge</note>, does not fashion all things through celestial motions, nor through particular matter, nor through powers so divided. Instead, He brings forth worlds by intellects, wills, and immaterial species, and through the eternal soul—both the one that is above the world and the one within it. The maker of such magical images is said to act through the stars, but not in the same way that God creates the stars, as might perhaps seem to be the case. For since there are innumerable powers in the heavens, the lowest of all is the natural power. 

Under this natural power of the celestial gods are <term>principles</term> <note>original: "rationes" — the logoi or formative patterns that guide nature</note>, both "seminal" <note>generative seeds of form</note> and generative of shapes, as well as certain other immobile principles that precede the seminal ones in the same hierarchy of forms. The authority of both these principles therefore precedes universal generation. After them, in the celestial bodies, are qualities, powers, and motions; and from these come the dominant <term>emanations</term> <note>original: "defluxus" — the "flowing down" of celestial influence</note> which serve the principles for the adornment of all worldly things. The lowest power of the heavens, however, which is called <unclear>virtue</unclear>, leads the generation of earthly things. 

Many arts—such as medicine, gymnastics, agriculture, and whatever else clearly cooperates with the operation of nature—use quantities and powers transmitted to lower things through these celestial emanations. And so, the maker of images himself draws from these celestial emanations some generative portion, however small and weak. For he does not use the motions of the heavens themselves and <unclear>those...</unclear>

He explains that while magicians use low-level celestial emanations and herbs to create temporary apparitions, God creates the world through eternal intellect and soul.</summary>

### ON THE MYSTERIES

...by the powers themselves and those things that are within them, or by powers that are naturally distributed around the celestial motions. It cannot reach the highest powers, but is occupied with certain forces that have flowed down from the nature of the stars to the very last, falling into the lowest place of the world. This practitioner uses a certain art, but it is not a pious or divine one. Indeed, these lowest of the celestial powers, conspiring around a particular piece of matter, can transmute, transfigure, and transform it in various ways.

Furthermore, they take up a transposition of those powers which are in particular things from some to others. When someone constructs <term>idols</term> <note>original: "Idola" – in this context, these are not just statues but "simulacra" or artificial apparitions intended to channel spiritual forces</note> of this kind from many materials and under celestial influences, then the variety of celestial actions from one side, and of material powers gathered from the other, does indeed produce something. But this action falls far short not only of <term>divine craftsmanship</term> <note>original: "opificio diuino"</note>, but even of natural production. For Nature performs its own work with a single, steady course and a simple action. Therefore, this manufacture of idols is an artificial mixing involving the final outflow of celestial things, and those things which are moved and recede to the furthest point from celestial nature.

Since man is of a better nature and created from better things, he ought not to devote himself to the making of idols. These things are not truly alive, but are inflated with a mere show of life. They are held together not by an internal and true harmony, but by an external and fake one, meant only to last for a brief moment; they possess nothing true or legitimate, since they are fashioned by human art alone. Only what is simple and uniform in action or composition prevails within them. Therefore, they are greatly deficient, because they are forced together from widely diverse and contrary qualities, and they do not possess any perfect power. Because a multitude of such outflows is snatched from many sources and mixed into something thin and weak, these idols have no stability; indeed, they vanish more quickly than reflections in mirrors. For when <term>fumigation</term> <note>The use of incense or sacrificial smoke to provide a "body" or medium for a spirit to appear.</note> is applied to the exhaling vapors, they are immediately assembled, but when the vapor spreads more widely through the air, they are suddenly dissolved.

The making of such <term>prodigies</term> <note>original: "prodigiorum" – meaning unnatural marvels or artificial monsters</note> in the form of idols is entirely unworthy of a seeker of truth. For whoever schemes these things—if he recognizes their utility yet still takes pleasure in them—becomes like them; or if he worships them as gods, he is guilty of a deed and word that is unspeakable. No divine light shines into a soul occupied with the dark phantasms of idols. <margin>Porphyry says that the makers of idols observe the course of the heavens...</margin> Porphyry says that the makers of idols observe the course of the celestial bodies in their construction, saying by which particular path of the heavenly beings...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that creating magical idols is a low, unstable art that uses the "residue" of celestial forces rather than true divine power. He warns that such practices are unworthy of the human soul and produce only fleeting, artificial phantoms.</summary>

...you, and with what or whom it concurs, true or false prophecies will result. Likewise, regarding the things that happen there: whether they are significant and effective, or on the contrary, empty of significance and efficacy. Although they construct <term>idols</term> <note>original: "idola" — here meaning artificial apparitions or magically charged statues</note> from chosen materials by observing the stars, these things nevertheless have nothing divine in themselves. For the materials moved here by heaven are the last in the order of generation, and they suffer according to the final outpourings <note>original: "defluxus" — the "dripping down" of celestial influence to the material world</note> from heaven. For such <term>phantasms</term> <note>original: "phantasmata" — illusory or temporary appearances</note> are so easily changed that at the slightest nod they are either inert or, on the contrary, prophetic, whether significant or effective. Surely such easy passivity and rapid mutability declare that they possess nothing of divine power. There are no powers in materials that are the basic elements of <term>demons</term> <note>In the Neoplatonic sense, "daimones" are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense</note>, nor can these demons be generated from particular bodies; on the contrary, these bodies are generated and guarded by the demons. Nor can man by his own <term>machines</term> <note>original: "machinis" — referring here to the "tools" or "artifice" of the magical craft</note> procreate the very forms of demons; rather, we ourselves are formed by demons according to our physical bodies. One must not think that from the union of elements some multitude or composition would flow together having a power proper to demons in itself. For the demon himself—simple, uniform, and self-consistent—gathers diverse elements into one, generates composites from them, and bestows whatever perseverance exists within them. Nor is it fitting to call these idols "demons." For the author of idols is one thing, and the demon—the great leader of demons—is another; and the very substance of demons is different from the phantasms of idols, as you also, Porphyry, confess: that neither a god nor any demon is drawn downward. Therefore, this manufacture of idols, since it is devoid of both god and demon, provides neither prophecy nor any sacred work.

Even if Porphyry does not approve of this opinion, he nevertheless mentions it while consulting the Egyptian <note>The "Egyptian" refers to Abammon, the persona Iamblichus adopts to answer Porphyry's doubts</note> on this matter as well. <meta>This page continues Iamblichus's defense of theurgy against Porphyry's skepticism. Having previously discussed the nature of material "idols," he now explains how genuine purification through sacrifice separates the practitioner from lower, malevolent spirits and aligns them with the divine light of the gods.</meta>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

...having been expiated through sacrifices, with whom the gods associate; by their company, the gods drive far away all wickedness and passion, and by their own splendor, they keep dark spirits at a distance. For evil spirits flee from the entering light of the gods just as darkness flees the sun, and they can no longer disturb the pious sacrificer, who is free from all wickedness, perversity, and passion. 

However, those who are pernicious and who meanwhile insolently invade the sacred rites against the established order and rituals, these surely cannot reach the gods because of the weakness of their actions and their lack of power. Instead, due to certain impurities, they are both repelled by the gods and matched with evil <term>demons</term> <note>original: "daemonibus" — here referring to malevolent intermediary spirits</note>, by whose foul breath they are completely filled. From this, they emerge as utterly wicked—profane, dissolute, and unjust alike—possessing a desire unlike that of the gods, and in all things most similar to the wicked demons with whom they constantly associate. 

These people, therefore, being full of passions and wickedness, draw evil spirits to themselves through their very kinship; soon occupied by these spirits, they are incited again toward every iniquity. In this state, one helps and strengthens the other in turn, like a circle joining its beginning to its end, and returning an equal exchange in the same manner. 

**Thus far the Chaldeans.** <note>original: "hucusque caldei" — Iamblichus is noting the end of a section citing Chaldean wisdom</note> 

When the profane handle sacred matters against the rituals, the outcome is frustrated. For in place of the gods, other entities are celebrated, and in place of good spirits, evil ones insinuate themselves. Therefore, the errors of these people ought not to be mentioned when discussing legitimate sacred rites, nor should what happens to them be considered a law. Just as sacrilege is the opposite of divine worship, so too are those occupied by deceptive evil demons—the authors of intemperance—the opposites of legitimate priests. From these priests, every wicked spirit, wickedness, and passion is far removed; instead, the presence of good deities is at hand, and from above they are filled with truth by the **divine fire**. 

To these priests, therefore, evil spirits bring no hindrance to the goods of the soul; nor is the smoke of pride suggested from that source, nor "soft flattery," nor are they deceived by <term>suffumigation</term> <note>original: "subfumigatione" — the ritual use of incense or smoke to attract spirits</note>, nor disturbed by any force. Rather, all these evils are immediately destroyed and vanish when the good deity is present, as if struck by a lightning bolt. To such men, therefore, comes a **truth-telling prophecy**, with which no other can be compared in any part, and which must be studied rightfully with that holiness we have described. 

For by this means alone is unshakable truth acquired in divining, and a thoroughly perfect virtue in the soul. By these two things, the priest ascends to the **intelligible fire**, which ought to be set forth as the goal of every ritual and sacrifice. You have thought much too rashly, O **Porphyry**, where divine prophecy is concerned, that the opinion of those who...

...lest they think a prophecy is granted by an evil <term>demon</term> <note>original: "daemone"</note>. For these spirits have always dwelled in darkness from the beginning; they can neither discern truth from falsehood, nor understand the principles from which these things arrive.

### Invocations and Commands of Men Against Spirits.

Porphyry wonders why we sometimes humbly invoke spirits as if they were our superiors, and yet at other times command them with orders as if we were their superiors. Iamblichus distinguishes the matter in this way: The Gods indeed—and all those superior to our nature—grant what is fitting to worthy souls out of a fullness of goodness, a will for good things, and a certain kindness. They cherish the religious as their own offspring, pupils, and disciples, and they take pity on those who labor. 

There are, moreover, certain middle classes of divinities who are <term>ephors</term> <note>original: "ephori" — a term for "overseers" or "guardians," borrowed from Spartan magistrates</note> and presiding officers of discernment and judgment. They deliberate on what is proper to do and what to avoid. They assist in just causes and recall men from unjust ones; often, they justly turn back upon wicked men the very injuries those men try to inflict, so that they suffer the same things they were attempting to do. 

There is, again, another class of spirits surrounding us that is indiscriminate and unthinking, which has received a single, specific power because of the way they are distributed from the individual parts of the universe. Because of this, each one is devoted to only one task. For just as a sword only cuts and does nothing else, so among the spirits distributed in the world—by the necessity of their divisible nature—this one only divides, while that one only collects the things that are made and generated. 

Therefore, since these hidden spirits have each received a different power, they perform only that specific task for which they were ordained. If anyone, therefore, takes those powers which agree with the whole in their distributed order and deflects them elsewhere, or transgresses by a sort of <term>prevarication</term> <note>original: "praevaricando" — acting in bad faith or deviating from a natural duty</note>, the result follows naturally, and the damage belongs to the one using the power badly. 

But let us return to the question. To answer: commands and violent orders are directed toward spirits that use no reason of their own, nor possess the principle of judgment and discernment. Since our own thought possesses the nature of reasoning and discerning the condition of things—and encompasses many powers of life within itself—it is accustomed to command those spirits that do not use reason and are limited to only one specific action. 

We invoke them, therefore, as superiors, because we attempt to draw from the universal world that contains us those things that contribute to the whole, concerning certain matters that are divided and contained in particulars. On the other hand, the practitioner commands them as inferiors, because our intellectual nature is more excellent than that which lacks intellect, even if those spirits occupy a wider place in the world...

<meta>catchword: have</meta>

<summary>Iamblichus explains the hierarchy of spirits, noting that while gods are invoked with reverence, lower irrational spirits are commanded by the human intellect because they lack independent reason and are confined to single, mechanical functions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of theurgy by Iamblichus. Having established that there are different classes of spirits, he now addresses the "double persona" of the practitioner—how a mere human can command divine forces—and responds to Porphyry's concerns regarding the apparent injustice of the gods.</meta>

<header>ON THE MYSTERIES</header>

possesses action. Likewise, there is a double persona in the priest, or rather a twofold character: one indeed human, the other divine. He puts on the divine character through the <term>sacraments</term> <note>original: "sacramentis" — in this context, the physical objects or rituals used in theurgy</note> in which divine power is hidden, lifting his mind upward toward the divinity and joining it with God. Therefore, by applying this divine character to his soul—a character he has put on—he is able, under the guise of God, to command spirits of that kind as a superior. Nevertheless, as a man, he is accustomed to petition them, invoking them as his superiors insofar as he calls upon powers from the universe. 

But we may solve the question more truly in this way: a certain communion of harmonious benevolence and an unbreakable bond of unity contains the whole of the sacred operation, so that this effect is divine and exceeds every limit of human capability. Therefore, we ought to remove all human limitations from this process. The priest does not summon a host of spirits as if he were someone distant, nor does he mandate that something be completed by a separate entity—as men usually do with one another. Rather, a single and identical action of divine fire shines forth and acts of its own accord, being ready and present through itself. It acts in the same way through all things simultaneously: both through those who subsequently pass it on to others, and through those who are able to receive a portion of it. 

Therefore, the divine works that are fulfilled in the sacred rites are not accomplished through the opposition of one thing to another, as occurs in the world of generated things. Nor is the spirit summoned through a difference between the caller and the mover; rather, the movements are transformed into something else, unlike how human affairs usually go. Instead, this whole work is fulfilled through identity, union, and consensus. Once all discrepancy is removed, that which acts and that by whose power it is acted upon is a common and simple thing everywhere. 

Porphyry asks why the higher beings often command their worshippers to be just, yet sometimes, when entreated, they inflict injury upon others. Iamblichus responds that they do not inflict injuries, but rather just punishments. And if by chance the actions are unjust, they are not the work of gods, but of wicked <term>demons</term> <note>original: "daemones" — intermediate spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense, though "improbos" here implies they are malicious</note>. The gods do not view only a single part of this life, but the whole; and not this life alone, but the entire life of the soul from age to age. Thus, they often punish a person in a subsequent life for merits or debts contracted in a previous one, whether they are asked to punish or not. 

Meanwhile, we who see nothing beyond the present moment imagine that adversities sometimes happen to us without merit. However, we often suffer in this life for what we have already inflicted in another, and what we do now, we shall one day suffer. Furthermore, many sins of men are hidden from us, which are not hidden from the gods at all. Likewise, we define justice as each person doing his own duty according to the present laws of the country. But the gods define justice much more broadly, looking to the entire order of the universe; they look especially to that principle by which souls may be led back to the gods, and they carry out judgment from that perspective. And so great is the difference between divine judgment and human judgment.

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s explanation of how divine justice operates in theurgy. # IAMBLICHUS

...of justice itself and our own, so that we are unable to reach it. Now indeed, even the gods themselves weigh what is just differently when looking at a single soul compared to the entire kinship of souls. For if a communion of the same nature exists among souls—both those living in a body and those placed outside the body—it creates a certain embrace that is the same and common to all toward the entire life of the world and the mundane order. It is therefore necessary to require the execution of judgment from the whole; that is, it would be required from the universal order and from the necessity of souls among themselves. This is especially true where the magnitude of crimes committed by a single soul exceeds the punishment expected as a consequence. The gods, therefore, never bring punishments unless they are just. For since they possess the **Good** according to their very essence, they cannot be the cause of evil or injustice. 

But if someone should happen to prove, through the imprecations <note>original: "imprecationibus" — refers here to ritual curses or petitions for harm</note> made to the higher powers, that certain adversities happen to people unjustly, we shall be compelled to seek other causes besides the gods and the good <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "numina" — spiritual powers or divinities</note>. If by chance we do not find these causes, we still ought not to suspect anything of the gods that is unworthy of their divine nature and that certain knowledge of the goodness of the gods which is innate in our intellects. In this, without a doubt, all Greeks and barbarians agree. Therefore, since the species of evils are diverse and conflicting, they must be referred not to one cause, but to several different causes.

If what we were saying about <term>idols</term> <note>original: "idolis" — in Neoplatonism, these are "images" or phantoms, often deceptive spiritual projections</note> and wicked spirits <note>original: "dæmonibus"</note> is true, then a manifold origin of evils surely arises from here. For they simulate the presence of the gods and of good spirits. Therefore, they command their worshiper to be just so that they themselves may seem good, just like the gods. However, because they are evil by nature, when they are asked to bring about evil, they do so willingly and lead us toward unjust acts. These are the ones who lie in oracles, deceive us, and advise or perform shameful things. 

The gods and good spirits, however, never deceive, nor do they contribute to iniquity. Furthermore, the nature of evil spirits is inconsistent within itself, unstable and disagreeing with itself, persuading one thing at one time and another at another. The nature of the higher beings, however, is consistent with itself and always preserves the same tenor in its action. The corporeal parts of the world are not void of power <note>original: "virtute vacuæ"</note>; rather, insofar as they are larger, more beautiful, and more perfect than our bodies, they possess greater forces and actions. Therefore, each one of them has distinct powers separately and produces diverse actions. Likewise, by a certain relationship, they are able to accomplish much more together. Indeed, a certain multiform action descends from the whole parts of the world into the particles, and it descends most easily because of the similarity of their powers. That is to say, the powers that follow in degree correspond to those that precede them. Especially where...

He introduces the concept of the "Harmony of the World" to explain how natural forces can be misused by humans (sorcery) without the divine source being at fault.</meta>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

<page-num>5</page-num>

...moreover, the recipient is adapted to the active agent. Therefore, out of the necessities of the body, certain evil and destructive things happen to specific parts from the whole—things which are actually salutary to the entirety and in tune with the **harmony of the world** <note>original: "harmoniæ uniuersi"</note>, though harmful to the parts. This happens either because the parts cannot sustain the actions of the whole, or due to a mixture occurring in the lower realms, or because of the natural weakness inherent in the lowest things, or because the parts are not proportional to other parts. Furthermore, beyond the body of the world itself, the nature of the world can do many things. For the concord of similar things and the discord of dissimilar things produce no small number of effects; indeed, the gathering of many things into the one animal of the whole, and whatever and of what kind the powers flourishing in the world may be, they perform one action in the whole and another in the parts because of the very weakness of the parts, distributed and divided to the last degree. **Friendship** of the whole, as well as love and contention and similar things, are active "actions" within the wholes, but in the parts, they are "passions" <note>original: "passiones" — here meaning the state of being acted upon or suffering an effect</note>. Likewise, those forms and pure reasons that exist in the **divine intellect** <note>original: "intellectu diuino"</note> participate in a certain material deficiency within the nature of the universe. In individual things, they eventually fall into shapelessness, and those things which are united in the wholes become divided in the particulars. Moreover, certain parts are corrupted so that the whole, constituted according to nature, may be preserved; certain parts are also crushed and pressed, while the wholes, arising therefrom, remain meanwhile free from suffering.

When a **sorcerer** <note>original: "veneficus" — literally a poisoner or one who uses drugs/charms for harm</note> brings down some calamity from above upon someone through his imprecations, by using certain natural and physical powers of the universe for this purpose, the transmission of such an action indeed comes from above without any choice or malice. Nevertheless, the evildoer using this very power diverts the transmission toward entirely contrary and evil ends. That transmission and action descending from above is moved by a certain compassion through similarity under the passions of contrary things. However, the sorcerer, by his own choice, draws what has been transmitted toward evil, contrary to justice. Indeed, that transmission itself acts according to the single **harmony of the world**, so that even the most distant things cooperate. If someone, detecting this, strives to pull the strong parts of the whole toward other parts, thereby causing injury, the universe is not the cause of such damage, but rather it is **human abuse** <note>original: "abusus humanus"</note> transgressing the order of the universe and perverting what is lawful. Therefore, the gods do not bring evils upon us, but rather natural bodies do, which depend upon the divine. And these bodies do not send down their outflows to the lowest realms as evil, but as good and salutary to the world; yet those who receive them transform them by their own mixture and perversity, so that what was given is received in a contrary condition.

After this, you ask why the higher natures do not listen to the one invoking them unless he is **pure** <note>original: "castum" — ritually clean or chaste</note>, yet they meanwhile help those who have been prayed to for illicit unions. Nor should it shame them to incite their worshippers to foul lusts. When

<meta>This page continues the exploration of how natural, cosmic forces can be diverted toward "evil" ends without the divine source being responsible. Specifically, it addresses the origin of unlawful sexual desires and the influence of sorcery (magic) and lower spirits.</meta>

# IAMBLICHUS

By hidden causes we are incited to unlawful intercourse—unlawful, that is, according to human laws, but perhaps "lawful" according to the laws of the universe, specifically when it results in something necessary for mankind. Indeed, the instinct for love <note>original: "uenerem" (Venus), referring to sexual desire or the goddess of love</note> in the universe tends toward friendship and harmony. In the individual parts <note>referring to individual beings or humans</note>, however, it becomes more intense because these parts, due to their own constitution <term>complexionem: the physical and temperament balance of a body</term>, too easily and mutually suffer alongside each other and the whole. Finally, that which descends from the heavens for a good purpose is here often turned toward evil. The world is one single living being <note>original: "unum animal"</note> in which the parts, though distant in location, are nevertheless drawn toward one another because of their shared nature.

And yet, that very conciliatory power of the world and the common cause of all mixing draws the parts toward each other by its own nature. Such a pull and appetite can, by a certain art <note>referring to "ars" or magic/sorcery</note>, be increased beyond its proper order. This reconciling force infused in all things is inherently good and is everywhere the cause of fulfillment, community, harmony, mutual love, and the union of the world—all of which are created by the command of the governing power. However, in the individual parts, because of their distance from one another and from the whole, and because of their weak and needy nature, this force brings about a mutual coming together through shared suffering.

From this, a sharper appetite is naturally born in many people. Thus, **Art** <note>here meaning the art of the magician or sorcerer</note>, discovering this power of "binding" <note>original: "coaguli"</note> scattered everywhere in nature, contracts it from all sides, collects it, and directs it into one place. In this way, it takes the naturally moderate appetite for a necessary union and, through its own mechanisms, renders it unrestrained. It does this by applying materials that especially contribute to procreation <note>original: "genituræ"</note> and by mixing together different natural forces from everywhere. By this mixture, the art governs and produces unions for procreation according to its own will.

Accordingly, since there are powers in herbs and stones that are both dissolving and, conversely, binding—and since these powers are much greater in larger things and natures—it is certainly possible for the urge toward intercourse to be intensified when such things are used. Through these very things, even without the labor of sorcery, love can be ignited and a "pull" created. We have discovered that **wicked daemons** <note>original: "dæmones improbos"—in this context, intermediary spirits that are low-ranking or malevolent</note> can have the greatest power over procreation and earthly or human affairs.

Therefore, it should not seem surprising that a burning for unlawful intercourse is frequently ignited in us by them. Certain forces of the soul can also contribute to this: both those living in this body and possessing a miraculous power of attraction, and also those souls already released from here but still wrapped in a turbulent and moist spirit <note>original: "spiritu turbido humidoque"—referring to the "pneuma" or ethereal envelope of the soul that can remain weighted down by earthly desires</note>, wandering about the places of procreation and thus committing such things.

Therefore, let no one say that either the gods or the daemons who follow them are the causes of unlawful love and intercourse. Instead, blame either the depraved natural instincts within us, or the art of sorcery <note>original: "ueneficam artem"</note>, or evil daemons, or souls not yet purified.

### On sacrifices: whence they derive their power and what they contribute.

¶ It is asked by what reason sacrifices are both appropriate to the higher beings <note>original: "superis," referring to the celestial gods</note>, how they benefit men, and what they accomplish in the world. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus who often questioned the literal efficacy of traditional rituals</note> says that not only the prophets, but also the "hypophets"—that is, all priests who hand down a prophecy received from others—must abstain from [eating] animals, lest the gods be contaminated by the vapors exhaling from them. However, contrary to this opinion is the common saying that the gods are especially soothed by the savory vapors <term>nidoribus: the smell of roasting meat from a sacrifice</term> of animals, as if by bait, and are thus "captured." Iamblichus condemns both views: namely, that the gods are either infected or ensnared and baited by the smells of flesh. The World Soul and the celestial souls <note>original: "Anima mundi coelestesque"</note>, by virtue of the fact that they are present to their bodies, neither receive passions from them nor are they distracted from the higher intellects. Individual souls <note>human souls</note>, however, suffer both. Indeed, one would stray too far who attributed similar defects to the higher souls; for the condition of universal beings and particular beings—or of causes and effects—is not equal. To feed upon bodies formerly joined to a soul <note>eating meat</note> undoubtedly brings a burden and a stain <note>original: "inquinamentum"</note> to us, and a leaning of the soul toward the physical, through which it melts and succumbs to pleasures and produces many other diseases in the soul. But the vapor exhaling from animals and the sacred incense-smoke, when the rite is performed correctly, does no harm to the gods or to the worldly and universal causes. For the vapor does not contain or order the higher beings toward itself; rather, it is contained by them, and is coordinated toward the universe just as the gods are. And thus, by their command, the ritual can be adapted to the higher beings and agree with them harmoniously. Therefore, religious people abstain from animals, yet not because the gods could be defiled by animal vapors—for the power of the gods, before anything material can touch it, disperses that matter even without contact. Not only does this divine power destroy and delete these physical things before they come near it, but even the celestial bodies themselves <note>the stars and planets</note> do not take any material element into themselves. They neither admit anything foreign nor lose anything of their own. Furthermore, the vapors of earthly things, having progressed barely five stadia <note>A Greek unit of distance; five stadia is roughly 3,000 feet or 0.6 miles</note>, flow back down; they do not infect or nourish the material and revolving body [of the heavens]. That celestial body has in itself no power for change <note>In ancient cosmology, the heavens were made of a "fifth element" (ether) that was changeless and incorruptible, unlike the four elements on Earth</note>, nor does it have anything contrary to itself, nor is it carried away from or toward the center, but must either remain at rest or revolve. Therefore, the bodies below the moon <note>the "sublunary" realm of Earth</note>, since they are composed of conflicting powers and motions, and are entirely changeable and carried up or down, have nothing in common with heaven—neither nature, nor power, nor action. Therefore, neither vapor from them nor anything else reaches the heaven, which is entirely separate from them. And deservedly [is it called] unborn...

<summary>Iamblichus refutes the idea that gods are either polluted or enticed by the physical vapors of animal sacrifices, arguing that the divine realm is ontologically superior and immune to material influence.</summary>

# IAMBLICHUS

...they take no change from things that are subject to generation. How, then, can the nature of the gods be defiled by vapors of this kind? For they repel material vapors with a single blow (so to speak). Such things are therefore not harmful to the higher beings <note>original: "superis," referring to the celestial or higher gods</note>, but to us. For these vapors are divisible, material, and akin to us; they share something in common in terms of being acted upon or acting upon similar things. But against celestial and divine beings—which are placed in a different category of essence, endowed with different natures and powers, and which utterly surpass us—these vapors can neither act in any way nor communicate anything.

->**What is the reason and utility of sacrifices?**<-

<margin>P</margin> **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a Phoenician Neoplatonist who often sought rational, ethical explanations for religious rituals</note> thinks that sacrifices are offered for a twofold reason: so that we might venerate the gods with gifts of this sort (as we are often accustomed to doing for our elders), and also that we might return thanks for the good things received from the divine, rendering good things in exchange for good things. <margin>1</margin> **Iamblichus** <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was the author of "On the Mysteries" and argued that rituals have a divine power beyond human logic</note> says that a reason of this kind is drawn from the common customs of men toward other men, and does not suit the nature of the gods, which surpasses human behavior beyond all measure. Truly, such methods and explanations of sacrifice do not fully demonstrate the greatest efficacy of sacrifices. I speak of that efficacy without which we are not liberated from plague, famine, or poverty, nor do we obtain timely rains <note>original: "hymbres," a variation of "imbres"</note>; indeed, it is through this efficacy that we attain the purification and perfection of our souls, and freedom from this realm of generation <note>the material world where things are born and die</note>. Therefore, one would not greatly approve of these reasons from your assignment, as if you had assigned a worthy cause for their effects. And if by chance one did approve of them, he would certainly accept them in a secondary place, as if they were consequences or secondary factors adapted to the primary and most ancient causes of such works. We desire, therefore, the reason why sacrifices have the efficacy to bring things about, and from whence they are aligned with the chief gods, who are the causes and principles of what is done.

Someone will say that because the world is one living being <term>animal: used here in the sense of a "soul-bearing" organism</term> and possesses one and the same life everywhere, it therefore possesses a communion of similar powers, or even a distance between dissimilar ones. Or perhaps it possesses a certain fitness of the agent to the patient <note>the one who acts and the one who is acted upon</term> to move similar things in the same way, while it clearly runs according to a single sympathy <note>original: "compassionem," used in the philosophical sense of "feeling together" or "cosmic sympathy"</note> even from the most remote thing to the most remote, just as if these too were close together. For among these things as well, the communion of life is an equal allocation of this sort. He speaks truly, indeed, regarding what necessarily follows from sacrifices. Nevertheless, the true mode of sacrifices is not shown in this way. For the very essence of the gods is placed neither in nature nor in natural necessities, through which an obligation would exist arising from natural passions, or extending through the whole of nature...

<summary>Iamblichus rejects Porphyry's view that sacrifice is merely a social exchange of gifts with the gods, arguing instead that it has a profound metaphysical power to purify the soul and avert disaster.</summary>

Here, Iamblichus begins to explain the "sympathy" between physical objects and higher powers.</meta>

# IAMBLICHUS

<sig>d iii</sig>
<meta>catchword: however (autem)</meta>

...be moved by extended powers. But beyond these things, the divine nature is determined according to itself, having nothing in common with these lower things, whether in essence, power, or in simultaneous action and passion <note>original: "actione simul & passione," referring to the philosophical concept of acting upon something and being acted upon in return</note>. Some add to the above explanation that certain things in the lower realms correspond to those above, and therefore contribute to the efficacy of sacrifices; for example, they say the number six <note>original: "hexagonarius numerus"</note> in the crocodile corresponds to the Sun. In the dog, again, and in the baboon <note>original: "cynocephalo," literally "dog-head," the Egyptian baboon associated with the god Thoth</note>, there are certain physical reasons and powers held in common with the Moon. Likewise, in other things, there are certain material species—as in sacred animals—where colors, figures, and forms might suit one of the superior beings, or perhaps some specific limb of an animal, such as the heart of a cock <note>original: "cor galli," traditionally used in solar rituals due to the bird's association with the dawn</note>. And other such natural things employed in sacrifices are said to be the causes of miraculous works. 

From the above assignment of causes, however, the divine cause is not truly assigned—for that cause is entirely supernatural and is not moved by natural motions. Instead, what is being described is a certain natural power contained within matter and bodies, which is therefore stirred up and calmed by bodily movements and material things; I speak here of natural things and those which exist alongside nature. If any such result follows from a sacrifice, it is joined to the preceding causes merely as a "co-cause" <note>original: "concausa sine qua non," a necessary condition but not the primary driver</note> without which the work would not occur. 

It is better, therefore, to say that the miraculous effects of sacrifices proceed from a certain friendship, accommodation, and conciliating habit <note>original: "habitudine," a state of being or relation</note> which joins the craftsmen to their crafts and the parents to their offspring. When, therefore, with this common principle leading the way, we take some animal or other living creature born from the earth that preserves the will and purpose of the Creator <note>original: "effactoris," referring to the Demiurge or divine maker of the world</note> sincerely and exactly, we then move the appropriate creative cause presiding over this creature by means of such an object. 

While there are many such causes—some presiding closely and familiarly, such as spirits <note>original: "demonia," intermediate beings between gods and humans</note>, while others are superior to these in an ordered fashion, such as divine causes—and while one most ancient cause presides over all of them, certainly in a perfect sacrifice, all these causes are moved in order. According to the order which each has obtained, they are familiarly accommodated and (so to speak) appropriated to the sacrifice by a certain kinship of condition. 

But if a sacrifice be imperfect, it rises only to a certain degree and does not transcend further. This is why many people think that sacrifices are made only to good spirits, and many think they are made to the final powers of the gods. Others think they are made to the worldly or earthly powers of spirits or gods. These people are explaining one real part of sacrifice, yet they are ignorant of their total power and all the benefits that expand deep within the whole divine realm. We, however, admit all these things while simultaneously encompassing the natural causes.

<summary>Iamblichus explains that while physical symbols like the "number six" or specific animals have a "sympathy" with the gods, the true power of sacrifice comes from a divine friendship and a hierarchy of causes—from local spirits to the ultimate Creator.</summary>
<keywords>Neoplatonism, theurgy, sacrifice, sympathy, Iamblichus, Porphyry, sacred animals, divine hierarchy, spirits (daemons)</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s explanation of how ritual acts interact with the cosmos. He is currently moving from the idea of "natural sympathy" (where physical objects simply react to one another) to a higher "divine cause" where sacrifices are part of a grander, intelligent design managed by higher beings.</meta>

# IAMBLICHUS

...indeed, and those things which are moved together—as if in a single living creature—according to their natural aptitude, or shared feeling <note>original: "compassionem," referring to the philosophical concept of *sympatheia*, where parts of the universe react to one another</note>, or shared reaction <note>original: "repassionem"</note>, we accept as simply being subordinate, following and serving the effective cause that appears in the sacrifices. However, we accept that **daimons** <note>In this context, *daimonia* are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between gods and humans</note> and the divine powers surrounding the terrestrial world are those placed in charge closest to our own rank. Yet, we judge that the most powerful causes of effective sacrifices belong to the most perfect and **demiurgic** powers <note>original: "opificiisque potestatibus," from the word for "craftsman" or "maker." These are the powers that structure and build the universe</note>. Because those highest demiurgic powers embrace all causes in order within themselves, we believe that all efficient causes are moved together with them in a single stroke.

Since, in a perfect sacrifice, the lower causes in the hierarchy are moved along with the highest demiurgic causes, a common benefit then flows from all of them into the whole realm of **generation** <note>original: "generationem," the physical world of birth, death, and change</note>. Sometimes these blessings reach through whole cities, peoples, and nations of every kind—or larger or smaller regions. At other times, however, these good things reach households or individual men, with the higher beings bestowing them out of an abundantly kind will. They do not distribute these gifts out of emotion <note>original: "passione"</note>, but rather, with an **impassible mind**, they judge that they must give according to what is appropriate, familiar, and related to each recipient. 

There is a certain internal **friendship** <note>original: "amicitia," representing the cosmic bond that holds the universe together</note> that contains all things and creates this connection through an ineffable communion. These explanations are certainly truer and participate more in the essence and power of the gods than what you suspect—namely, that the higher beings are primarily enticed by the **smoke and odors** <note>original: "nidoribus," the fatty steam from burnt offerings</note> of animals in a sacrifice. 

For if the daimons are indeed wrapped in some kind of body—which some believe is nourished by sacrifices—that body is surely immutable, impassive, luminous, and lacking nothing; so much so, that nothing flows out of it and nothing needs to flow into it. And even if there were some need, why would it be necessary for it to flow in through sacrifices? For the world and the air within it have a never-failing exhalation rising from the earth, diffused everywhere around it. 

Furthermore, even if the bodies of daimons were to experience such an "outflow," sacrifices would not restore them in equal measure, nor would they maintain the natural balance between excess and deficiency for the daimons, nor keep their proportions similar. Finally, since the **Maker of the world** <note>original: "mundi faber," the Creator</note> has provided abundant nourishment for all creatures of land and sea, would he leave those beings superior to man without food? When he has established that the daily food of other living things be provided copiously through their own natural workings, why would he want an external nourishment to be provided by humans for the daimons alone? 

Indeed, if we were to neglect such nourishment, would the bodies of the higher beings starve and perish? Therefore, if we were the ones who nourished the daimons, we would also [be the cause of their] **generation**...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that sacrifices do not "feed" the gods or daimons, but rather align the practitioner with the demiurgic powers and cosmic friendship that govern the universe. He mocks the idea that immortal beings depend on the smoke of burnt offerings for their survival.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page regarding whether gods "need" sacrifices. The incomplete word "househo-" from the previous page likely concluded as "households," and the Latin text begins by completing a conditional thought: "If we were to [nourish] them..."</meta>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

d iiii

...[if we were to nourish] them, we would be their superiors. But the reality is quite the opposite. For they themselves nourish us. Indeed, higher things everywhere nourish the lower, just as celestial things nourish terrestrial ones. The **soul** <note>original: "Anima"</note> is perfected and nourished by the **intellect** <note>original: "intellectu"; in this philosophy, Intellect is the higher divine mind that feeds the Soul with truth</note>, and the soul in turn perfects nature. Furthermore, the offering of sacrifices through fire consumes the material matter. It makes that matter entirely like itself; it does not make itself similar to the matter. It leads the offering back toward the divine, celestial, and immaterial fire, and it does not decline in any way downward toward matter and **generation** <note>original: "generationém," the realm of physical birth, decay, and constant change</note>.

For if the exhalation of vapors from sacrifices were meant to be material nourishment, it would be necessary for the matter to remain intact. In that case, a more abundant influx of nourishment would flow to those intended to receive it. But as it stands, all the matter is burned and consumed, and it is completely transformed into the very purity and subtlety of the fire. This indicates the exact opposite of what you were saying. For the higher beings are free from **passion** <note>original: "passiois," meaning they cannot be affected or "suffered" by external physical forces</note>, since it pleases them for matter to be dispersed and consumed by fire. They make us strangers to such passions, and they make whatever is in us like the gods—just as fire makes all things that are hard and opaque look like bodies that are subtle and bright. 

It lifts us upward through sacrifices and through their consumption by fire toward the gods; just as fire attracts fire, it leads back what is heavy and hard toward things divine and celestial. The corporeal **vehicle** <note>original: "Vehiculū," the "spirit-body" or subtle energetic shell that surrounds the soul and allows it to interact with the physical world</note> provided for **daimons** <note>intermediary spirits between gods and humans</note> consists neither of matter, nor of elements, nor of any body known to us. Therefore, it is impossible for nourishment to be provided to daimons from elemental essence, as it is completely foreign to them. Rather, just as the gods divide matter with lightning-fire and separate from matter all things that are immaterial by their essence but bound to matter—rendering those things incapable of suffering which were previously capable of it—so too our fire, imitating the action of divine fire, destroys whatever material it finds in the sacrifice. It purifies the things brought near and releases them from the bonds of matter; because of the purity of its nature, it makes them fit for communion with the gods. 

In the same way, it releases us from the chains of the physical world, makes us like the gods, and renders us fit for the friendship of the gods, lifting our material nature toward an immaterial nature. This general reasoning concerning sacrifices is sufficient, I believe, to enable those who are gifted and capable to wisely investigate the specific nature of each sacrifice from this common rule. Nevertheless, being indulgent toward those with slower minds, we shall add certain specific points to these, bringing clearer explanations into the open. 

The very first principle of all these things is that which the structure of the sacrifices declares, being connected in sequence to the order of the gods. We propose that some gods are material, while others are immaterial. The material gods are those who encompass matter within themselves and adorn it. The immaterial ones are those who are entirely separated from matter. Therefore, according to the **priestly art** <note>original: "sacerdotiā artē," referring to theurgy, or ritual acts intended to unite the soul with the divine</note>, it is proper to begin sacrifices with the material gods; for otherwise, one cannot ascend to the immaterial gods...

the path of ascent is open. These [gods] therefore have a certain communion with matter insofar as they preside over it and hover over it. These same beings also rule over those things that happen within matter: such as division, the impact of a strike and its recoil, change, **generation** <note>original: "generationi"; the philosophical term for the cycle of birth and the coming-into-being of physical things</note>, corruption, and all material bodies. If, therefore, one wishes to worship these beings rightly, one must provide a worship that is material—in a material way, so to speak—according to their nature and their leadership. For in this way, we are led into a proper familiarity with them in their entirety, and we shall offer a kinship in worship that is suitable to them. Therefore, bodies deprived of life, the slaughter of animals, the multiform transformation and corruption of bodies, and the total casting off of preceding matter is fitting for the **material gods** <note>original: "materialibus diis"; in Neoplatonic thought, these are the deities who govern the physical cosmos and the elements</note>. Not indeed for their own sake, but for the sake of the matter over which they preside. For even if they are most especially separated from it, they are nonetheless present to it at the same time. And even if they contain matter within an immaterial power, they nevertheless exist together with it. For indeed, things governed are not foreign to their governors, nor things adorned to those who adorn them. Furthermore, things that serve as instruments are easily adapted by their proportions to those who use them. For this reason, it is foreign to use matter in sacrifices for the **immaterial gods**; but for all the material gods, it is entirely consistent.

In addition to these things, it is worthwhile to consider the dual condition of our own life. Sometimes we are made entirely **soul** <note>original: "animus"</note>, placed outside the body and elevated in mind; together with all the immaterial gods, we are raised up through the sublime. But at other times, we are bound by the earthly body, and we are corporeal, clearly held fast by matter. Similarly, there will be a twofold reasoning for divine worship: one will be simple, incorporeal, and pure from all generation, suited to pure souls. The other, however, is full of bodies and material action, fitting for those who are not yet pure, nor yet purged from all generation. There are, therefore, two species of sacrifice: the most pure sacrifices belong to men who are highly purified (which indeed happens rarely to one, or to very few, as **Heraclitus** <note>Heraclitus of Ephesus was a pre-Socratic philosopher known for his difficult, paradoxical sayings about the nature of the universe</note> says), while material sacrifices, which involve change, belong to those still occupied by the body. Therefore, for **cities** <note>original: "ciuitatibus"; referring to the general public or the political community as a whole</note> not yet purified—perhaps because of their physical association and companionship—unless you give sacrifices of this kind, you will wander away from both immaterial and material goods alike. The former they cannot receive; to the latter, they do not offer what is proper and consistent. Added to this is the fact that everyone should care for their own **essence** <note>original: "essentiæ"; the fundamental nature of what a thing is</note> based on the reason of what they are, not what they are not. It is not right, therefore, to transgress this proper measure and nature of the worshiper. I judge that a constitution properly fitted between the humans who perform the care and the powers who are cared for will choose a mode of worship suitable to itself. For a constitution of this kind, tempered in an immaterial way...

->### ON THE MYSTERIES<-

...it chooses the immaterial, inasmuch as it is joined to purely incorporeal things by purely incorporeal powers. A connection of that kind, physically adapted to bodies, chooses a similar form of worship for the **essences** <note>original: "essentias"; the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing</note> that preside over bodies. Often, for the necessary use of the body, we make vows and perform works toward the gods who govern the body and the good **daemons** <term>daemons: in Neoplatonic philosophy, these are benevolent intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between gods and humanity, not "demons" in the modern sense</term>, specifically when we strive to purge the body of certain stains and old filth, or to release it from diseases, and to apply health, or to remove heaviness and sluggishness, and to provide lightness and efficacy, or to procure some other good for the body. 

Then, therefore, we will not treat the body rightly through some intellectual and incorporeal reasoning. For it is not so designed that it can be cured in these ways; but when it obtains things akin to itself, then the body is cured and purged by bodies. Therefore, the rite of sacrifice for such a use will necessarily be physical, and thus it will purge the excesses of the body and supply what is lacking according to necessity, and reduce whatever is scattered to its proper proportion and order. 

We often sacrifice while asking the heavenly beings for things suited to human life, namely those things which are necessary for food or pertain to those things we desire for the sake of the body. What, then, will come to us from the gods themselves, who are entirely separated from all human **generation** <note>original: "generatione"; the cycle of birth, growth, and decay in the physical world</note>? Will it be something that helps us banish poverty or sterility, or brings abundance, or leads to other necessities of life? Nothing at all. They are released from all things and do not handle gifts of this kind. 

If, however, someone should say that those immaterial gods encompass within themselves gods who are entirely immaterial, and that they encompass the gifts of these gods according to one primary cause, he would surely say that a certain abundance of divine gift descends from there to the lower realms. But it must be granted to no one to say that they, in handling these things, carry out human life and actions in a direct way. For the distribution of such things that are here is divided and particular, and is carried out with a certain turning toward these things; it is neither entirely separated from bodies, nor can it admit a pure and sincere governance and oversight. 

Therefore, the mode of sacrifice suitable for such things is one that has commerce with bodies and **generation**, not one that is entirely separated from matter and the body. For he who is entirely pure transcends such things and has no **proportion** <note>original: "proportionem"; a mathematical or harmonic relationship/correspondence</note> to them. But he who uses bodies and their powers is most akin to all things of this kind. He is able to supply certain prosperous things for life, and to avoid the adversities threatening us, and to provide a moderate temperament for the human race. The vast multitude of men is subject to universal nature and is governed by natural powers, and proceeds further down to the works of nature...

<header>IAMBLICHVS :</header>

...which takes up the administration of fate and the order of fatal works, and exercises practical reason only concerning natural things. Very few, relying on a **supernatural** <note>original: "supnaturali"; Iamblichus refers to a power that transcends the laws of the physical world</note> power of the mind, depart from nature and betake themselves to the separate and unmixed intellect. From this, they emerge superior to natural powers. Some, however, hold the middle path between pure intellect and nature; and of these, some follow each in turn, while others lead a life mixed from both. Others are freed from lower things and transfer themselves to better ones. 

Therefore, those who are governed by universal nature and lead a life devoted to their own nature, enjoying the powers of nature, will practice a worship appropriate to nature and fitting for bodies moved by nature. Choosing for this purpose specific locations, qualities of the air, matter, the powers of matter, bodies, the qualities and habits of bodies, appropriate movements, and the changes of those things involved in **generation** <term>generation: the process of coming-into-being in the physical world, often contrasted with the eternal state of the divine</term>, and similar things both in other parts of divine worship and in the ritual of sacrificing. 

But those who live by the mind alone, freed from the bonds of nature, will contemplate an intellectual norm of worship, free from bodies, in every part of religion. Those who lead a middle life between intellect and nature will also follow a middle religion, and according to the differences of their middle life, they will seek different modes of worship through middle ways. For they will either treat both in turn, or they will decline from one to the other, or they will touch upon lower things so that through them they may attain better things, believing that they cannot otherwise attain the more sublime. 

In the class of <unclear>essences</unclear> <gloss>for</gloss> and divine powers, some have the soul and nature subject to them—namely, serving their handiwork as far as they wish; others are entirely separate from soul and nature, not only from the mundane and **generative** <note>pertaining to the cycle of birth and physical existence</note> soul, but even from the divine soul and its nature. Others, finally, hold the middle ground and bring about a union between the extremes, either according to one indissoluble bond, or according to an abundant tradition of the greater beings, or according to a lesser reception that is not hindered, or according to both joined together by agreement. 

When we worship the gods who rule over the soul and nature, it is not improper to offer them natural powers, and to consecrate to such gods bodies and all things that are ruled by nature. For all the works of nature both obey them and contribute something to their administration. But when we desire to venerate the gods who are far secluded and gathered in their own unity, we ought to venerate them with honors entirely released from matter. Intellectual gifts are owed to these: an incorporeal life, perfect virtue, consummate wisdom, and their proper duties. To the middle gods, however, and the leaders of middle goods, as we have said, middle things are appropriate. 

Starting therefore from another principle—namely, from the world—concerning the distribution of the mundane gods, from the common lot of the four elements in the world made according to the measures of the elements, from the circumference of the circle...

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus's explanation of the relationship between the human soul and the cosmos. Having previously categorized souls into those bound to nature, those of pure intellect, and those in between, the text now argues that since humans are composed of the world's elements, their religious practice must generally reflect that cosmic structure.</meta>

<header>ON THE MYSTERIES</header>
<page-num>30</page-num>

...revolving in order from the center, we have easy access to the truth of sacrifices. For if we are in the world, and are contained in it as parts, and are first generated by it and perfected by all its powers, and are composed of its four elements, and possess a certain portion of life and nature obtained from it, then surely we ought not to omit the world and the mundane orders in divine worship. 

Let us therefore establish that around every part of the world there is indeed a body, as we see; and moreover, there are incorporeal powers distributed in order within those bodies. The law of sacred rites, therefore, duly distributes **like things to like things** <note>original: "similia similibus"; a fundamental principle of ancient magic and medicine where things of a similar nature act upon one another</note>, and it proceeds from the highest to the lowest through all the intermediate steps. It applies bodily things to bodily things and incorporeal things to incorporeal things, evidently rendering to each its own proper due. 

Nevertheless, if a religious person attains a **super-mundane** <term>super-mundane: "supra-mundane" or existing above and beyond the physical world and its laws</term> deity—which happens very rarely indeed—this person, being placed apart from bodies and matter, surely follows such a worship, united by a super-mundane power to the super-mundane gods. But that which scarcely happens to one person at the very end of their **priesthood** <note>original: "sacerdotii"; referring here to the culmination of a long spiritual and ritual training</note> should not be established as a common law for everyone at the beginning or in the middle of their religious life. For these others perform worship that is, in some way, bodily. 

Every person skilled in the priesthood will therefore confess that it is necessary to offer worship to the higher beings that is neither partial nor imperfect, but suitable and complete. Since, therefore, before the gods are present and descend to earth, all the powers lying beneath them are moved and precede them as precursors and processions, it follows that he who does not distribute to all what is fitting for each, nor honors each with their own specific honor, does not attain the presence of the gods themselves. 

But he who renders all the deities favorable to himself, offering to each grateful and most similar gifts, is surely not frustrated in the outcome, but receives the divine choir in its complete and full presence. Since these things are so, the ritual of religion ought not to be simple or composed of only a few things, but multiform, consisting of every **harmony** <note>original: "harmonia"; used here in the Pythagorean sense of a mathematically ordered cosmic arrangement</note>, and constituted from all things everywhere in the world (as we have said). 

For if it were something simple and of only one order, then that which is invoked in the priesthood and moved toward us would also be simple, and a simple mode of sacrificing would suffice. But in truth, the great multitude of powers that are usually aroused when the gods descend and are moved is known to none but those priests who have already experienced it through the work itself. These men alone, therefore, know what constitutes the perfect fullness of worship, and how much we are frustrated in the outcome if even a few things are omitted. Just as in a musical harmony, if one string is broken, the whole suddenly sounds dissonant; so, if one deity is omitted, the religion itself, without the common ritual, does not achieve its desired end. While this one thing is lacking, the sacred work interrupts its structure...

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus's argument from the previous section, where he explained that because humans are composed of cosmic elements, they must honor the diverse powers of the world. He now addresses the consequences of neglecting any part of the divine hierarchy and begins to explain how material things can participate in the divine.</meta>

-># ON THE MYSTERIES<-

...and does not possess its integrity. When the divine powers are about to descend openly to the senses <note>original: "palàm ad sensum"; referring to a visible manifestation of a god, or theophany</note>, a clear loss occurs for us if we neglect any of the higher powers without honor. Similarly, when they come secretly during a **sacred work** <term>sacred work: "opus sacrum," referring to theurgy, a ritual practice intended to invoke the presence of the divine</term>, it is dangerous if you honor one indeed, but do not honor another according to their dignity and order. For whoever cheats any power of its proper honor throws the entire work of religion into confusion, while dissipating a single and whole arrangement; nor, as one might think, is the work of receiving the divine then only imperfect, but the structure of the whole perishes.

What then? Does not the very summit of holiness return to the supreme principle itself—the **One**—which stands above the entire multitude of deities? And does it not worship all divine essences and lordships together in that One? Undoubtedly. Truly, a summit of this kind arrives quite late, and to very few; and we must think we have fared best if such things happen to us at the **close of life** <note>original: "vitæ calce"; literally "at the heel of life," a classical metaphor for the very end of one's journey</note>. 

The present discussion, however, does not set down laws for a man of that kind. For such a man is superior to the law; but for those in need of some law, it ordains these laws of sacred rites for the present. The multitude of deities is like a world of its own, having many orders conspiring into a single order. Similarly, sacrifices ought to have a number and order likewise conspiring into a single order, so that individual things may rightly correspond to individual deities. 

Likewise, those things that are around us and within us are manifold, and they should not correspond to the divine causes of our affairs only in some part, but suitably in all parts, and thus ascend to the supreme leaders. Religious observance, therefore, acts in various ways around us and within us. For it either perfects as if by propagating, or it cuts away, or it cleanses, or it organizes things that lack order, or it separates them further from **mortal error**. Finally, it reconciles all things to the whole of the heavenly realm through familiarity. 

But when both come together into one—the divine causes from one side, and human preparations equally from the other—then absolute religion accomplishes everything and brings back immense blessings from the sacrifices. Certainly, the abundance of power in the highest causes of the universe is such that, just as it surpasses lower things in other respects, so too does it greatly surpass them in this: namely, in the very magnitude of its presence. Thus, the causes of all things are most present of all to all things, to such an extent that the very power of each cause is present everywhere, in its entirety, and always, apart from any impediment. By this reasoning, therefore, the first of all things also shine upon the last. **Immaterial principles** are present non-materially in material things. 

Let no one wonder if we say that some matter is pure and divine. For since matter itself was also made by the **Father of all** <note>original: "opifice patre"; the "Craftsman-Father" or Demiurge who created the universe</note>, it has deservedly acquired a certain perfection of its own, fit for receiving the gods. Furthermore, nothing prevents...
