<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous section, where Iamblichus discussed the necessity of honoring the entire divine hierarchy. Here, he begins to explain the "theurgical" principle that matter is not inherently evil or separate from the divine, but can serve as a bridge or receptacle for spiritual powers when properly prepared.</meta>

-># ON THE MYSTERIES<-

...prohibits the higher beings from spreading their light to the lower. Therefore, they do not permit matter to be entirely devoid of the higher powers. For this reason, whatever part of matter is perfect, pure, and **godlike** <term>godlike: "deiforme," possessing a structure or quality that mirrors the divine nature</term> is not unsuited for the reception of the gods. Since it was necessary that even earthly things should by no means be without a share in divine communion, the earth itself also received within it a certain divine portion sufficient for receiving the gods. This **wisdom of sacred rites** <note>original: "sacrorum sapientia," referring to the knowledge of theurgy</note>, having contemplated these things and thus diligently finding **receptacles** <term>receptacles: "susceptacula," physical objects like stones or plants used in rituals to anchor divine presence</term> suitable for each of the gods according to their harmony, often composes into one: stones, herbs, animals, spices, and other similar things that are sacred, perfect, and godlike. And then, from all of these, it fashions a pure and complete receptacle. For it is not right to loathe all matter, but only that which has become alienated from the gods. Indeed, it is fitting to choose what is appropriate to them, seeing as it can harmonize and contribute to the dwellings of the gods, the foundations of statues, and the works of sacrifice. For otherwise, no possession or portion from the divine can reach earthly places and the men living here, unless such a foundation has first been laid.

One must believe the **secret discourses** <note>original: "archanis sermonibus," likely referring to the Chaldean Oracles or Hermetic texts</note> which testify that, through **blessed visions** <note>original: "beata spectacula," referring to direct mystical encounters or theophanies</note>, a certain kind of matter was handed down by the gods themselves. This matter is therefore kindred to those who handed it down. A sacrifice of such matter rouses the gods to reveal themselves, and immediately calls them to our understanding, and captures them as present, and demonstrates them perfectly. One can learn these same things even from the distribution according to places which has been divinely effected, and from the very **governance** <term>governance: "praefectura," the divine administration of specific parts of the world</term> which is divided among individual things. Whatever things, according to diverse orders, whether greater or lesser, have obtained lots of this kind in various places. For it is evident to the gods who are rulers of certain places that a sacrifice from the very things that are born there will be fitting in manner; the things governed will please the governors, and those things which belong to them will be pleasing. To creators, their own works are always most pleasing. And those who first beget certain things hold such things as primarily acceptable in return. Whether, therefore, they be certain animals, or plants, or other things which are distributed by the oversight of the powers above, they have at the same time obtained a governance under them; and they procure for us an indivisible communion with the powers above. Therefore, some of these, as long as they are preserved and held, increase the familiar affinity of those who hold them toward the gods—namely, as many as preserve the power of communion between men and gods by remaining intact. Such are certain animals among the Egyptians, and everywhere the **holy man** <note>original: "sacer homo"</note>; while other things, being sacrificed and burned, create a clearer affinity, namely all those which, through their resolution into the **prior elements** <term>prior elements: "priorum elementorum," the fundamental spiritual building blocks of the universe</term> and principles, create a closer kinship with the higher causes.

# IAMBLICHUS 1

...and more sacred according to the rite. For everywhere, the more that **appropriateness** <term>appropriateness: "proprietas," the natural affinity or "sympathy" between a material object and a specific god</term> and familiarity are perfected, the more perfect are the goods that descend to us from there. Nor are these merely the inventions of men, nor have they gained authority through human customs; rather, God himself, duly invoked during the sacred rites, is the author of such laws. Around him, many gods and angels move, and under him, throughout whichever nations exist on earth, some divinity has obtained leadership and a common province.

A specific divinity is also assigned from that source to each temple. Likewise, of the sacred rites we perform for the gods, a particular god is the spectator and governor. Those rites pertaining to **angels** <note>original: "angelos," here referring to high-level celestial intermediaries in the Neoplatonic hierarchy</note> are overseen by an angel; those to **demons** <term>demons: "daemones," not "evil" spirits in this context, but middle-tier spiritual beings who mediate between gods and humans</term> by a demon; and in other cases, in the same manner according to their own kind, a perfected being has obtained a kindred leadership.

Since, therefore, we conduct sacrifices under the gaze and authorship of the divinities of sacred things, we must revere the laws of divine holiness and the legitimate sacrifices. Because of this, we may hope for success in these rites, as we sacrifice under the sovereignty of the spirits and the gods. In the meantime, we must take the utmost care lest we offer anything unworthy of the higher beings, or anything foreign to them.

In short, we provide this warning: that we should diligently look around at every single thing within us and around us, as well as the things in the world—likewise the gods, angels, and demons distributed among the nations. In this way, we may offer a friendly sacrifice to each one accordingly. For only by this method is the holiness and religion worthy of each divinity preserved.

**Vow**, or **adoration**, and **prayer** <note>original: "Votum, siue adoratio, & oratio," the three stages of theurgical invocation</note> complete every work of sacrifice; they contribute above all to the whole of religion and forge a sacred and indissoluble communion between souls and the gods. Of this, there are three species:
1.  The first gathers us together and provides us with contact and knowledge of the divinity.
2.  The second binds a consenting communion to the divine and calls down gifts sent from the divine, which perfect our entire work even as we speak and understand.
3.  The third accomplishes an **ineffable unity** <term>ineffable unity: "ineffabilem unitatem," a mystical union that transcends language or intellectual understanding</term>, placing all authority within the gods, and perfectly places and confirms our soul within them.

Indeed, in these three stages—by which all divine things are measured—a harmony is forged for us with the gods, and a triple sacred utility is brought to us from them. One pertains to **illumination**, another to the joint execution of works, and the third to the perfect fullness derived from the **divine fire** <note>original: "igni diuino," a reference to the Chaldean Oracles' concept of spiritual energy</note>.

Likewise, adoration and its power sometimes precede the sacrifices themselves, sometimes are inserted in the midst of sacrifices, and sometimes complete the end of the sacrificing. Indeed, no work in the sacred rites is ever performed without the supplications of adoration. Finally, adoration, when practiced for a long time, nourishes and perfects our intellect, making the soul much more spacious for receiving the divine...

...reveals [divine truths] to humans. It accustoms us to receive the splendors of divine light. It gradually perfects those qualities within us that allow us to reach the deities, until it leads us to the very summit. Moreover, it gradually withdraws our human habits of thought and implants divine ways of being; it also generates a persuasion, a communion, and a friendship that is perpetual and without interruption. It further increases divine love; it kindles and elevates what is divine in the soul, and purges whatever is contrary and adverse to the soul. And from the **ethereal spirit** <note>The "ethereal spirit" or "pneumatic vehicle" was believed by Neoplatonists to be a subtle body that carries the soul through the heavens.</note> itself, which is wrapped around the soul, it shakes off whatever leans toward **generation** <term>generation: "genitura," the physical realm of birth, decay, and material existence, as opposed to the eternal realm</term>. It even provides good hope and perfects our faith concerning the divine light. Finally (to speak briefly), for those who pray frequently, the power of adoration makes them familiar companions and disciples of the gods.

Since adoration is of this nature and has such a deep connection with sacrifices, it is clear that the goal of sacrifices is to participate in contact with the **Creator** <term>Creator: "opificium," referring to the creative power or the Demiurge—the divine craftsman who orders the cosmos</term>. For through these ritual works, the soul is made suitable for the gods. Thus, the benefit of sacrifice is as great as the good that is sent from the higher causes and creative powers to the human race. And from this, the power of adoration appears once more as **reductive** <note>original: "reductiua," in the Neoplatonic sense of "leading the soul back" or "returning" from the material world to its divine source</note>, perfecting, and fulfilling; it shows how it is effective and the producer of union, and how it acts as a common bond from the gods. It also shows how adoration and sacrifice mutually confirm each other and together bestow the power of the wonderful effects of religion. From this, it appears again that the priestly discipline and its operations possess a harmony in their parts no less than a living animal has in its limbs; nor can any part of it complete its work without the whole.

## Concerning the sacrifice of animals.

Porphyrius asks why it is required by the law of sacred rites that someone who is about to behold divine things must not touch a lifeless body at that time. Nevertheless, through the bodies of dead animals, the invocations and attainment of divine things are frequently carried out. Iamblichus solves the problem in this way: the prophets command that the spectator of divine things should not touch a lifeless body that has not been consecrated for the sacred rites. But they permit the touching of that which is consecrated. Furthermore, they forbid even looking at human bodies that the soul has already left. For a certain trace, image, or demonstration of divine life in the body is extinguished by death. However, no religious law forbids touching the dead bodies of other animals, since they did not participate in a more divine life while alive. Besides, insofar as we rise up to the immaterial gods, it is beneficial not to have touched such a body. But insofar as we strive to approach the material gods, touching [them] fre...

->On divination through animals.<-

<margin>q</margin> When divination is performed through the bodies of sacred animals, such as the inspection of entrails <note>original: "utasturum," likely a corruption of "ut extorum," referring to the practice of extispicy or reading animal organs</note>, it must not be thought that the gods approach these things. One should not imagine that universal providers descend to a divided, particular, material, and proportional care concerning individual animals. Rather, it is spirits—and these indeed are greatly divided and distributed individually to individual species of animals—who have obtained the most immediate care and oversight of those animals. For these spirits have obtained a lordship that is by no means entirely self-sufficient or free from matter. And therefore, they are accustomed to touch such instruments in a fitting manner. 

To this end, therefore, so that we may obtain such divination through animals from these spirits, it is necessary to prepare for them a seat through which they can be present among humans and communicate with us. But this seat must be incorporeal, so that the incorporeal spirits may be present with us through it. This seat will therefore be the soul of such animals, now released from the body. For insofar as this soul is itself in some way separated from the body, it accords <gloss>is in harmony</gloss> with the spirits, and it also accords with us because of a certain kinship of life. Therefore, acting as a medium, it serves the presiding spirit by suggesting the omen to the human and declaring the commands of the spirit; thus, it reconciles us with the spirit. 

But the soul that uses such divinations does not only hear or receive the prophecy. It also contributes no small amount from itself toward the execution of the work. For it is moved and cooperates, and at the same time foresees through a certain **sympathetic necessity** <note>The concept that all parts of the universe are interconnected, allowing one part to "feel" or signal what is happening in another.</note>. These are matters placed in divided nature, and however many things are now carried along together within the realm of **generation** <term>generation: "generationem," the physical world of birth, death, and constant change</term>. ...is pure, it is especially accustomed to grasp what is to come. ### How those who pray used to threaten the spirits.

<margin>n</margin> Porphyry relates that priests were accustomed to use certain violent threats against the spirits, such as: "Unless you do this, or if you do something to the contrary, I shall shatter the heavens, or I shall reveal the secrets of Isis, or I shall divulge the hidden mystery concealed in the abyss." Or: "I shall stop the *baris*" <note>original: "barī," a sacred Egyptian boat used in religious processions and believed to carry the gods across the sky or the Nile.</note>, or: "I shall scatter the limbs of Osiris to Typhon" <note>Typhon is the Greek name for the Egyptian god Set, who in myth murdered Osiris and scattered his body parts across Egypt.</note>, and other similar things. Iamblichus adds that those who utter these curses are not accustomed to direct such threats toward the Sun, the Moon, or other celestial bodies, as Porphyry thinks. Rather, there is a certain class of powers in the world that is greatly divided, lacks discernment, and is unthinking. This class receives reason <note>original: "rationem," implying a governing logic or command</note> or speech from another and listens to it, but it possesses no intelligence of its own. It distinguishes neither truth from falsehood, nor the possible from the impossible. Therefore, when this class is provoked by threats, it is immediately stirred up and "stunned," because it is naturally moved by forceful words, and it is led and dragged along by a certain dull and unstable imagination. Furthermore, the priest often commands and threatens these worldly spirits not with human power, but with the divine power of ineffable sacraments. He is then situated within the order of the higher gods; and for this reason, he employs commands and threats natural to a more magnificent status. He does not do this as if he were actually going to perform what he asserts, but to declare how much power he has obtained through his union with the gods—a power gained, evidently, from the knowledge and possession of ineffable symbols or seals, which we call sacraments. Likewise, the spirits <term>spirits: "daemones," here referring to intermediary beings that act as guardians of the natural order.</term> are divided by provinces and regions, guarding different parts of the world. Each has such great care for the parts entrusted to them that they cannot tolerate even a single word contrary to that order and eternal arrangement. They have received an immutable duty because the order of the gods remains immobile within them. Therefore, in the realm where these spirits exist—whether they are of the upper air or distributed around the earth—this order is such that they cannot even bear to hear threats. Consequently, these spirits zealously manage the guardianship of ineffable and secret mysteries. They do so with such great observance because they understand that the order and arrangement of the universe is chiefly contained within such mysteries. To the extent that these deities are represented allegorically through these words—

But the Egyptians, who mix demonic speech with divine sacraments, sometimes turn to such threats.

### Exposition of the symbols of Egyptian theology.

<margin>i</margin> Imitating the very nature of the universe and the workmanship of the gods, the Egyptians also display certain images of mystical and hidden notions in the fashioning of symbols. Just as nature expresses hidden principles in apparent forms as if in symbols, and the gods explain the truth of Ideas through manifest images. Since, therefore, they perceive that all higher things delight in the likeness of lower things, and moreover they desire to be filled with goodness from the higher beings, so that they might imitate them according to their strength, they rightly offer a manner of acting convenient to the higher ones when they insert hidden mysteries into manifest symbols. In interpreting these, dismiss the words and receive the meaning. When, therefore, they name "mud" <note>original: "lutum"</note> in their sacred rites, as they bring it in, understand this to be the body of the world and the matter and the generative power inserted into it, which is agitated and flowing, or even the primary cause and placed as a foundation of the elements and elemental powers. Since this is so, the god himself of generation and of the whole of nature's powers which...

...of all things that are inherent in the elements, as the cause that towers above all these things; he is himself immaterial, undivided, immobile, and unbegotten, whole from himself and whole within himself. He clearly precedes all these things and leads them, encompassing all things in himself. Because he encompasses all things and bestows from his own nature upon all worldly things, he has shone forth from them. 

Since he indeed towers above all and shines forth, he is set apart from all worldly things, proceeding alone by himself through the heights. This is also confirmed by the symbol that follows, where the god is introduced sitting upon a **water lily** <note>original: "loton aquaticam"</note>, a plant which signifies that the god, by his own sovereignty, exceeds the worldly mud <note>The "mud" represents the heavy, changing nature of physical matter</note> and does not touch it while governing. Instead, he holds a sovereignty that is entirely intellectual and **empyrean** <term>empyrean: the highest, most spiritual part of the heavens, associated with pure light and fire</term>. For all things in the lotus are round, both the fruits and the leaves; by this is signified the circular action of the mind, which always returns to itself and remains in the same state. The god himself, therefore, stands above even this action within himself, surpassing such a sovereignty; he is holy and venerable, resting entirely within himself, which is signified by the act of sitting. 

Accordingly, when they introduce the god as the **pilot** <term>pilot: "gubernatorem," a common metaphor for a divine mind steering the "ship" of the universe</term> of a ship, they signify his sovereignty as the governor of the world. For just as a pilot, separated from the ship and the rudder, moves, rules, and directs the vessel from every side in one easy moment, so the god himself directs the world from above—namely, from the first principles of nature—providing the primary causes of all motion. 

Since indeed all parts of heaven and the **celestial beings** <term>celestial beings: "animalia cœlestia," referring to the constellations or stars, which the ancients viewed as living, divine entities</term>, and the whole motion of the universe, and time itself according to which the world moves—finally all things contained in the whole—receive powers descending from the sun, some mixed within them and others surpassing any mixture, for this reason the symbolic mode of expression brings these things forward too. In words, it designates the sun as being shaped according to the celestial animals, and changing forms in turn through the **seasons** <note>original: "oras," likely referring to the hours or the zodiacal divisions of the year</note>. Meanwhile, it demonstrates his immutable and simultaneously whole transmission through the entire world. 

But since those who look up at the sun—some in one place and some in another—are carried around the indivisible transmission of the god, and they themselves, according to the diversity of their natures and motions, receive multiform powers from the sun, therefore symbolic tradition holds that through the multitude of gifts, one god enters, and through multiform powers, one power of God is present. Therefore, it says that he himself remains one and the same, but asserts that the changes of forms and transfigurations result from the recipients themselves. For this reason, the tradition says he is changed according to the animals and towards the seasons, as if such mutations vary around the god according to the different ways the god is received. ### On Divine Names

<margin>p</margin>
Porphyry asks why priests use certain names that signify nothing. Iamblichus responds that all such names signify something to the gods, even though in some cases the meaning is unknown to us. However, there are some known things for which we have received an interpretation through divine inspiration. In general, however, the manner of signifying within them is **ineffable** <term>ineffable: that which is too sacred or great to be expressed in human words</term>. It is not according to human imaginations, but according to the intellect, which is divine within us—or rather, in a simple and superior way, according to an intellect united with the gods. 

Therefore, one must remove from divine names all human inventions, discursive reasonings, and natural analogies of the voice itself—those rooted in things found in nature. Just as the symbolic character of divine likeness is intellectual and divine in itself, so must we suppose and accept this same character in all names. Whatever of this is within us, this very thing is most to be venerated; for it is more excellent than can be broken down into our common understanding. 

Indeed, in those divine names for which we have received a resolution <note>original: "resolutionem," referring to the explanation or decoding of a name's meaning</note> through divine inspiration, we possess within them the entire knowledge of the divine essence, power, and order encompassed by the name itself. We should also keep the mystical and ineffable image of the gods as a whole within the soul, and through these names, we lift the soul up to the gods and, having raised it, join it to them as much as we are able.

Next, the question is asked why we prefer **barbarian** <term>barbarian: in this historical context, "barbarian" refers simply to non-Greek peoples, specifically the Egyptians and Assyrians, whom the author considers more ancient and spiritually pure</term> names over others among the names of the gods. This is because, clearly, the gods have approved the entire speech of sacred nations, such as the Egyptians and Assyrians, as being most suitable for sacred rites. For this reason, we believe that these common expressions and ways of speaking should be applied to the speech and prayer that is akin to the gods, especially since this mode of speaking existed as the oldest and first. 

Also, since these specific names were received through divine inspiration when they were mixed with their own language as something familiar, the gods handed them down to be preserved by us forever, tempering them with a voice that is consistent with them. And so, we must duly preserve the rule of tradition itself from then on. For if anything else is fitting for the gods, that which is eternal and immutable is most akin to them above all others.

Among these points, Porphyry says that he who hears the sound of divine names looks only to what they signify; therefore, the mental concept itself, remaining the same everywhere regardless of the specific word used, should be sufficient. Iamblichus responds in this way: "It is not as you think. For if names..."

But if they were adapted to the very nature of reality, those that align most closely with it are also most beloved by the gods. From this it is clearly evident that the speech of the sacred nations <note>Iamblichus refers primarily to the Egyptians and Assyrians, whom he considers the oldest and most "priestly" civilizations</note> is rationally preferred over all others.

For names do not preserve exactly the same meaning when translated into another language. Instead, there are certain properties unique to each nation that cannot be expressed through speech to other nations. Furthermore, if we were able to translate these specific meanings into another language, they would still not preserve the same power when changed. Moreover, "barbarous" names <term>barbarous: used here in the ancient Greek sense to mean "foreign" or "non-Greek," particularly referring to the Egyptians and Chaldeans</term> possess a great deal of **emphasis**—that is, an effectiveness in suggestion and demonstration. They also possess a concise brevity. Because they have the least amount of ambiguity, variety, and wordiness, they are most suitable for the higher beings for all these reasons. 

Therefore, set aside the false suspicions you hold, where you suspect that the Egyptian language is used there only because the person invoking is Egyptian, or used Egyptian speech when the god was invoked. Rather, consider that because the Egyptians were the first of all to be allotted the presence and participation of the gods, the gods are therefore most pleased when they are invoked according to the Egyptian rite. 

One must not say that these "barbarous" and obscure names of the divine are the inventions of tricksters or sorcerers; for how could things that are most closely joined to the gods—and which join us to them, possessing a power almost equal to the higher beings—be mere figments of the imagination, without which no sacred work can be completed? Nor are such veils and coverings <note>original: "prætegmina inuolucráque," referring to the words as "garments" or "wrappers" for divine truths</note> created through our own human emotions, as if we attributed them to the divine based on our own reputation. We do not start from the things we suffer ourselves; rather, we attribute these expressions to the gods as they are fitting to them according to their own nature. We do not hold notions contrary to the divine—that is, contrary to how the divine truly is—but we persevere in them exactly as their nature is, and just as those who first handed down to us the laws regarding the holiness of religion attained the truth about them. 

For if anything else in sacred laws and rites pleases God, stability itself pleases him most and is especially fitting. It is necessary, therefore, to always preserve the ancient rites of worship as sacred and untouched, neither taking anything away nor adding anything from elsewhere. For this has recently been the cause of nearly everything—both names and prayers—becoming weakened: because they are constantly changed, and never cease being changed, due to a violation of tradition and a lust for innovation. 

For the Greeks are by nature seekers of new things, and they are carried away headlong in every direction, like a ship lacking ballast <note>original: "instar nauis saburra carentis" - ballast is the weight in a ship's hull that keeps it stable; without it, the ship is prone to capsizing or drifting aimlessly</note>, possessing no stability, nor do they preserve what they have received from others. But even this quickly...

### The Opinion of the Egyptians concerning God and the gods.

<margin>Question</margin> Porphyry then asks what the Egyptians consider the first cause to be: whether it is Mind <note>original: "intellectum"</note> or something beyond Mind. Likewise, whether it is one single thing alone, or one along with something else, or others. Again, whether it is incorporeal, or perhaps corporeal. Furthermore, whether the One is the same as the Creator of the world <note>original: "opifice mundi," referring to the Demiurge or divine craftsman</note>, or if it is superior to the Creator; and whether all things flowed forth from one or from many. Finally, whether they consider the first foundation to be matter that is entirely formless, or bodies of some quality, and whether matter itself is ungenerated <note>eternal</note> or generated. To these questions, Iamblichus responded thus: I will first tell you why the sacred and ancient Egyptian writers have held various views on these matters, and why the wise men of this current age do not speak of them in the same way. For since there are many essences in the universe, and they differ from one another in many ways, it is only right that many principles for them have been handed down, possessing different orders, and different principles given by different priests. Indeed, the principles are total or universal, as Seleucus relates. Mercury <note>The Latin "Mercurius" here refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage to whom thousands of Egyptian hermetic texts were attributed</note> himself recorded them in twenty thousand volumes, or as Meneteus recounts, he handed them down in thirty thousand volumes—and even in six thousand, five hundred and twenty-five—and in those, he demonstrated everything perfectly. However, other ancients have introduced various specific principles of particular essences here and there. Therefore, it is necessary to declare the truth briefly concerning all these matters, and first regarding what you first asked. The first god, prior to Being <note>original: "ante ens"</note> and alone, is the father of the first god, whom he generates while remaining in his own solitary unity; and this is beyond the intelligible <note>that which can be perceived by the mind alone</note>. He is the exemplar of that god, who is called his own father and his own son, the father of the one, and a god truly good. For He is the greater and the first, the fountain of all things, and the root of those things which are first understood and which understand—namely, the Ideas. From this one, <unclear>also</unclear>, the self-sufficient god unfolded himself. And therefore he is called "self-sufficient," "his own father," and "prince through himself." For he is the principle, the god of gods, a unity derived from the One, existing above essence, the principle of essence. For from him comes essence; therefore he is named "Father of Essence." For he himself is the transcendently existing principle of the intelligible. These are the most ancient principles of all, which Mercury places before the ethereal, empyrean, and celestial...

...gods: composing one hundred books on the empyrean gods, as many on the ethereal gods, and a thousand on the celestial gods. According to another order, he places the god Emeph <note>likely a Latinization of the Egyptian Kneph or Kmeph, often identified as a creator deity</note> before the celestial gods as their leader, whom he says is the Mind <note>original: "intellectum"</note> thinking itself and turning its thoughts inward. Before this one, he places the one indivisible thing, which he calls the first model <note>original: "exemplar"</note>, or expression, or image; this he calls Ic-thon. In whom is the first thinking thing and the first thing thought <note>the subject and object of divine thought</note>, which is worshiped in silence alone. Beyond these, however, other leaders preside over the making of visible things. For the Craftsman <note>original: "opifex"; the Demiurge who shapes the physical world</note> in the intellect, who is both the lord of truth and wisdom, insofar as he proceeds into the process of creation <note>original: "generationem"</note> and brings the hidden power of latent principles into the light, is called **Amun** in the Egyptian tongue. Insofar as he accomplishes all things without falsehood and with skill alongside truth, he is called **Phtha**; the Greeks call him **Vulcan**, considering only his craftsmanship. Insofar as he is a doer of good, he is called **Osiris**, and he has other names according to his different powers and actions. There is also another lordship among them over all the elements involved in creation and their powers: four of these are masculine and four are feminine <note>This refers to the Ogdoad of Hermopolis, the eight primeval deities representing the qualities of chaos</note>. They attribute this lordship to the Sun. Likewise, another lordship over all nature involved in creation is assigned to the Moon.

**Marsilio** <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century translator and commentator, adds a clarifying note here</note>: You can arrange these in an order consistent with Proclus in this way. 
1. First is the **One** itself, above being and above all that can be known. 
2. Second is **One-Being**, or the unity of being, in which its unity is placed before its being; it can also be called the "Intelligible Intellect" and its own father. 
3. Third is the **Intellect** that is both intelligible and intellectual at once, the united intellect and expression, the first Ic-thon. 
4. Fourth is the **Intellectual Intellect** already unfolded, the leader of the celestial gods, Emeph. 
5. Fifth is the **Craftsman-Intellect**, the immediate leader of the worldly craftsmen, who are the celestial, empyrean, and ethereal gods; this is perhaps the intellect of the World Soul, which is named Amun, Phtha, Vulcan, and Osiris.

**Iamblichus**: But those who divide the heavens into two parts, or four, or twelve, or thirty-six, or doubles of these, or in any other way, also establish rulers for these, whether few or many. Again, they place one leader over these, and thus the Egyptian treatise on first principles, proceeding from above to the final things, descends from the One into the many. It is governed by the One, namely by God; everywhere, an undefined nature is held by a certain defined boundary under his command. Especially by the supreme cause of all, Unity. God produced Matter from materiality, namely...

### IAMBLICHVS:

...derived from a secondary essence, which the **Craftsman** <note>original: "opifex"; refers to the Demiurge or divine creator</note>, taking it up as a vital force, used to make the simple and impassible spheres. However, he took the final part of this same essence for the making of bodies that are subject to birth and decay. With these things thus distinguished, the doubts you mention having conceived regarding the Egyptian books are easily resolved. For those works circulated under the title of **Mercury** <note>original: "mercurii"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note> contain Mercurial opinions, even if they often speak in the style of Greek philosophers. Indeed, they were translated from the Egyptian language into Greek by men not unskilled in philosophy.

I would wish, truly, that whoever reaches for the first causes of worldly things would also declare the ultimate principles. Likewise, whoever treats the planets, the zodiac, the decans, the horoscopes, and the powerful stars as leaders should pass on the specific distributions of the principles. Furthermore, the teachings in the *Salaminiaca* <note>likely referring to the *Salemeschoiniaka*, a lost Egyptian astrological text</note> are very brief and contain a portion of the Mercurial arrangements. Similarly, those matters treated concerning the appearances or disappearances of the stars, or the waxing or waning of the moon, have their assignment of causes among the latest Egyptian records.

Certainly, the Egyptians do not believe that all things are merely natural; instead, they distinguish intellectual life and animal life from nature—not only in the world at large, but also in human beings. Since they have placed intellect and reason at the head as entities existing by themselves, they believe that whatever happens occurs in this way. They assert that the **Craftsman** is the first or chief father of those things involved in the process of creation. He also knows the vital power, both that which is in the heavens and that which exists above the heavens.

Likewise, they place pure intellect above the world: one indivisible intellect in the whole world, and another distributed through all the celestial circles.

Now, they are not accustomed to observing these things through mere speech and reason alone; rather, they further advise and teach that our nature can progress toward higher, more universal, and superior things beyond fate—to God himself, the **Craftsman** of the world. In this state, one carries no matter with them, nor anything else except the observation of the opportune time. They teach us that we achieve this through **sacred works** <note>original: "sacrorum opera"; this refers to theurgy, or rituals intended to unite the practitioner with the divine</note>, and they perform these works simultaneously. Mercury himself handed down this path to us. But the **prophet Bitis** <note>The OCR reads "prophetabitis," likely a conflation of "propheta Bitis," a legendary figure who translated Hermetic texts</note> interpreted it for King **Ammon**, having found it in the inner sanctuaries of the temple in the city of **Sais** <note>original: "Sayn"</note> in Egypt, and he presented it to us inscribed in sacred characters. The name of God runs through the universe. There are also many other orders of these same things. Therefore, you do not seem to me to be correct in reducing all the traditions of the Egyptians to natural causes alone. For among them, there are many things and many essences; there are also super-worldly powers which they worshiped through religious principles and actions.

->On free will and how we are released from fate.<-

After these things, Porphyry says that many Egyptians also subjected our own free will to the movement of the stars. Iamblichus responds, according to the Hermetic <note>original: "mercurialibus"; referring to the teachings of Hermes Trismegistus, known to the Romans as Mercury</note> opinions, in this manner: man has two souls, as the Hermetic writings teach. One, indeed, is from the first intelligible <term>intelligible: a philosophical term for the higher realm of pure thought and divine reality, which can only be understood by the mind, not the physical senses</term>, and participates in the power of the Creator himself. The other, however, is imparted to us from the circuit of the celestial bodies, into which the contemplative soul creeps by a divine influence, etc. Therefore, the soul descending into us from the worlds follows the world's circuit. But that soul which comes from the intelligible is present in an intellectual way, and stands above the circuit of generation <term>generation: the physical world of birth, change, and decay</term>. Through this higher soul, we are both released from fate and ascend to the intelligible gods. 

We possess a religion that reaches toward eternal things; therefore, one must not think—as you were doubting—that all things are bound together by the unbreakable chains of necessity, which they call "Fate." For the soul has a principle within itself proper to it, by which it may commit itself to the intelligible, and indeed depart from those things that are created, and approach Being itself and the divine. Nor, again, do we attribute fate to the gods, whom we worship in temples with sacrifices and statues as those who release us from fate. The gods themselves dissolve fate. However, the lower natures descending from them, which are already entangled with the physical generation and the body of the world, carry out the decrees of fate. 

Rightly, therefore, we offer all holiness to the gods, so that they alone—ruling over necessity through intellectual persuasion—may release the evils looming over us from fate. For not everything is bound in the nature of fate; rather, there is another principle of the soul, superior to both nature and generation, through which we can be joined to the gods, surpass the worldly order, and participate in the eternal life and action of the celestial gods. Through this, therefore, we are able to exempt ourselves from fate. For when the more excellent parts of what is within us are active, and the soul is called back to its own more excellent parts, then it is completely separated from those things that bind it in the world of generation; it moves away from the lower things and exchanges one life for another. It inserts itself into a different order of existence while entirely abandoning the former one. 

What then? Is it possible to be released from fate through the gods who move in circuits <note>referring to the planets and stars</note>? And to think of those same gods as the leaders and authors of fates, binding lives completely with unbreakable chains? Perhaps, truly, nothing prevents it being so. For since the gods embrace many essences and powers within themselves, what prevents there being within them other differences and contrarieties beyond our estimation? Now indeed, one may also say this: that in each of the gods, even the visible ones <note>the stars and planets</note>, there are certain intelligible principles of essence, through which the souls may achieve flight from the generation of the worlds and obtain freedom. If, however, someone distinguishes two orders of gods...

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s explanation of how the soul can be liberated from the constraints of Fate. He argues that while the soul is partially bound by the physical laws of the universe, it can be freed through the intervention of higher, "super-mundane" gods.</meta>

<header>IAMBLICHUS</header>

...does not admit to the office of release. Namely, it admits both worldly and super-mundane <term>super-mundane: gods or powers that exist above and beyond the physical world</term> gods; at least through the super-mundane gods, a release will eventually be achieved. But these matters are explained more thoroughly in the *Treatise on the Gods*. There, we discuss which gods are primarily responsible for leading us back to the higher realms, to what place they call us back, by what powers they do so, and in what way they dissolve the bonds of Fate, and through which specific returns [to the divine] established by sacred operations. We also consider what the order of worldly nature is, and in what way perfected intellectual action dominates this order.

For this reason, we consider it a sin to say what you brought forward from the verses of Homer—namely, that the gods are "flexible" <note>original: "flexibiles"; a reference to the Iliad where Homer suggests gods can be swayed by human entreaty</note>. For by pure and intellectual laws, the holy works of religion have long been defined; and by a greater order and power, lesser things are dissolved. To the extent that we are translated into a better lot, by that much is a departure made from the lesser things. Nor does anything happen outside the rule established from the beginning, such that the gods are "turned" because of a sacrifice or worship performed later. Rather, from the first descent, God sent down souls on the condition that they should return to Him again. Nor do the ascent and descent of souls conflict with each other. For just as in the intellectual universe, "being" and "becoming" exist together—rather, all this is rightly connected—so too in the disposition of souls, their care for the world of birth agrees with their release from that world.

### Concerning the personal daemon of each person.

After this, Porphyry asked many things about each person’s personal daemon <term>daemon: in ancient philosophy, a guardian spirit or guiding "genius" assigned to a person at birth, not an evil entity</term>. Iamblichus responds to these things thus: The discussion concerning the daemon proper to each individual is twofold. One way is sacred, or god-making. The other is technical [astrological]. The former way invokes the daemon from higher causes. The latter from the planetary circuits involved in birth. The former does not use the exploration of an individual's birth-chart <term>geniture: an astrological chart of the sky at the moment of a person's birth</term>. The latter explores such things diligently. The former is universal and above nature; the latter worships and cares for a daemon more specifically according to nature.

Since things are this way, you seem to me to have absurdly transferred the more perfect worship [the sacred way] into a merely human manner, and you have limited your questions only to this lower path. Furthermore, where you seek or worship a daemon by the natural way alone, you seem to have accepted only a tiny part of such a path. For those who investigate and operate technically regarding nature are accustomed to call upon the daemon in an orderly way from the decans <term>decans: thirty-six ten-degree segments of the zodiac, often associated with specific spirits in ancient astrology</term> (that is, "the makers"), and from the dispensers of influences, the images of heaven, the stars, the sun, and the moon. Likewise, they call from the multifaceted <note>original: "polistotis"; likely a Latinization of the Greek word for "having many elements"</note> elements and the world. But you, choosing incorrectly a very small part of these—namely the "Lord of the Nativity" <note>the dominant planet in a birth chart</note>—bring questions about this alone. On this single supposition, you investigate in what way the Lord of the chart assigns the daemon, and according to what kind of life, power, or influence flows into us from him. Thus, you linger entirely in the exploration of the birth-chart, scrutinizing...

->On the judgments of astrologers and the daemon.<-

Porphyry says that if anyone knew the figure of their birth and the lord of that figure, they would find their daemon, and through it be released from the fate of their birth. But he adds that it is impossible to know those things, or to find this daemon, and that the rules of astronomy and astrology are incomprehensible and uncertain, even according to the witness of Chaeremon <term>Chaeremon: an Egyptian priest and philosopher who wrote on the influence of stars</term>. Iamblichus says that the daemon is neither known nor given by that birth figure and its demonic influence. Otherwise, it would not release us from the fate of our birth. Instead, the daemon is given from a more ancient and higher principle—namely, from the superior gods—and at the very moment when the soul first inclines toward sensible things before conception. He argues that we are released from fate not so much through the daemon, but through the worship of a superior deity. Indeed, those sayings of Porphyry not only disagree among themselves but also from the truth. For a daemon is not assigned to each person entirely from their own figure of birth; rather, this origin is also ancient. Likewise, if only this daemon were recognized, he who knew his "genetic" daemon <note>original: "genesicum"; relating to the *genesis* or birth chart</note> would not for that reason be happy. And who would accept this spirit as a guide to escape the things of fate, if the spirit himself was assigned to fulfill those very things? Truly, you entirely overlook the principal questions concerning the essence and order of the daemon; you only touch on the final points—where it descends from.

You inquire, furthermore, that countless rules of astrology are circulated, and there are doubts about the birth chart, from which it appears that knowledge of these things cannot be had. But I judge, first of all, that the most certain truth concerning the stars can be held through divine prophecy. Nor do we need a counting of rules <note>original: "regularum"</note> or artificial predictions. And I add further that you do not demonstrate that knowledge from there is entirely impossible as far as mathematical science is concerned, simply because diverse opinions are held among them, or because Chaeremon or whoever else speaks to the contrary. For in this way, because of conflicting opinions, we would be forced to say there is no science at all, in every science and art alike. But surely, everywhere, not only do false things disagree with each other, but false things also disagree with true ones, so that everywhere truth can be found besides the false. Porphyry says the rules...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical debate between Porphyry and Iamblichus regarding the "personal daemon" or spirit guide. While the previous page established Porphyry's skepticism about finding this guide through astrology, this page presents Iamblichus's defense: that while human astrology is flawed, divine revelation and sacred rites (theurgy) can reveal the spirit that governs a person's life.</meta>

# IAMBLICHUS:

...that even astronomy cannot be fully grasped, much less astrology, and that there are many disagreements among them and many people who challenge these arts. Iamblichus responds that divine prophecy <note>original: "uaticiniũ" (vaticinium); referring to direct revelation from the gods</note> can teach the nature and effects of the stars without the need for human art. Astronomy and other arts were once given by the gods, but over a long period, they have become confused by human opinions and retain very little of divinity or, finally, of truth. In astronomy, there is some truth, though a small amount, which is evident through the effects of the stars upon one another according to their measurements in the heavens, as was predicted before regarding the eclipses of the sun and moon and the "aspects" <note>the relative positions of planets that astrologers believe change their influence</note> of the planets. The rules of measurements, magnitudes, distances, progressions, comets, and similar things observed long ago among the Chaldeans <note>ancient Babylonian astronomers and astrologers</note> and among ourselves, testify that the science of astronomy is true. 

Porphyry says that the "lord of the figure" <term>lord of the figure: the specific planet that rules over a person's birth chart or horoscope</term>, or even if there are several such lords, cannot be grasped even by the judgment of astronomers and astrologers, but that the personal daemon must be sought from there. Iamblichus says that astrologers provide rules—some five rules, some fewer, others more—for finding or distinguishing these lords of the birth figures. I do not say, however, that the rules are actually possessed, or that these lords are truly found and distinguished; rather, it is so *thought* and handed down by them, contrary to what Porphyry asserted. What, then, prevents the lord of the figure and the daemon from being difficult to find through astrology, but very easy to find through divine prophecy and sacrifices? <note>original: "sacrificia"; in this context, it refers to theurgical rites used to communicate with the divine</note> 

Nor should it be thought that the daemon is assigned by the lord of the figure alone. For there are principles of the daemon more numerous and more ancient than this. We cannot find the personal daemon through human arts, but through divine ones. The personal daemon assigned to each person is not distributed by some particular part of the heavens or the elements, but by the entire disposition of the world, at the moment the soul descends while that world-order is reigning; the world-order itself accommodates a certain daemon as the "executor" <note>an official who carries out a decree; here, the spirit who carries out the soul's chosen destiny</note> of the life which the soul has chosen. This daemon joins the soul to the body and cares for the life communicated to the body. It directs the soul's own specific life and constantly provides the principles for our thoughts; we act in such a way as the daemon brings to our minds, and it governs us to the extent that, once we are perfected by sacred rites, we may exchange the "lord" <note>the daemon</note> for God. 

Then the daemon yields to God, and either ceases from its work or leads the soul toward that same divine goal. A person's "lot" <note>original: "fors"; their portion or destiny</note> is assigned to the soul as it descends from the whole body of the world and life as it then stands; that lot is led and fulfilled by a certain daemon. Therefore, it is impossible to judge certain events since we cannot grasp the concurrence of all causes, unless we attain that knowledge through divine inspiration.

---

->Whence the personal daemon comes, what it does, and whether it is unique.<-

The personal daemon is not assigned by some specific part of the heavens or the elements; on the contrary, it comes from the whole world, from the multiform life within it, and from the multiform bodies through which the soul passes as it descends into "generation" <note>the process of being born into the physical, changing world</note>.

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s response to Porphyry regarding the "personal daemon" (guardian spirit). # ->ON THE MYSTERIES<-

Is there not properly distinguished and decreed for us a certain lot of our own, distributed to us according to a specific governance? This spirit certainly existed in the ideal pattern before the souls fell into the cycle of birth. As soon as the soul receives its leader, the spirit himself stands by to fulfill the lives that follow. This spirit, as I said, binds the soul to the body as it descends. He takes care of the living being as a whole. He directs the soul's own life and provides the principles for whatever we reason; we act just as he brings thoughts to our mind. He governs us until, purified by sacred works <note>original: "sacris opibus"; referring to theurgy, ritual practices meant to unite the soul with the divine</note>, we receive a god as our leader instead of a spirit guide. After this, the spirit guide yields to the god in such a way that he either steps aside in the god's presence or contributes to the same purpose.

Next, you asked whether several spirits are present to each person, with different ones governing different aspects of a human being. To this we respond: the spirit does not merely preside over some specific part of us, but is present to the whole at once and leads the whole, just as he was assigned by the total orders that exist in the world. You conjectured that several spirits are present to us according to the number of our parts. Furthermore, you thought that even within the body itself there are different spirits: one caring for health, another for beauty, and others for certain habits within these; and that one spirit might preside over these equally in the body. In this way, you also thought that one spirit rules the body, another the soul, and another the intellect. 

However, it is better to understand that the body, soul, and intellect are all governed by the same spirit. Do not, therefore, divide them so that there is one spirit for the body, another for the soul, and another for the intellect. For it is absurd to think that while the living being is one, the divine power <note>original: "demonium"</note> set over that being is many-formed. Indeed, those things that hold the position of leadership are everywhere simpler than the things they lead. It is even more absurd if many ruling spirits were not joined together as one, but were disconnected from one another, like parts of a divinity. You would also introduce conflict among them, as if some of the ruling spirits were good while others were truly evil. Yet evil spirits never have a share in the "lot" of governance <note>original: "sortem præfecturæ"; the divinely appointed duty of a guardian</note>, nor are they distributed in opposition to the good ones with equal authority or number.

After this, you suspect that the personal spirit is a certain part of the soul—specifically the intellect—and that a man is happy <note>original: "εὐδαίμονα" (eudaimona), meaning "having a good daemon"</note>, that is, fortunate, who possesses a wise intellect. If this were so, there would no longer be any higher order presiding over man that is more excellent than man himself. Instead, a superior part of the soul would merely rule over the inferior parts. In that case, all parts would be of the same kind, and none would rule over the subjects with absolute authority. 

Next, you introduce the worship of the spirit as if it were directed toward several things—partly as if toward two spirits, and partly as if toward three. It is a forbidden thing <note>original: "nefas"</note> to partition the causes that preside over us, or to fail to bring that governance back to a single point. This is because unity dominates in all things. Now, concerning the one who views the spirit according to the body—

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s explanation of the personal spirit (daemon). The previous page ended with a discussion on whether a person has multiple spirits for different body parts; here, Iamblichus clarifies that the spirit is a single, unified governor for the whole individual.</meta>

### IAMBLICHUS

...and divides the administration of the body, he reduces its sovereignty to its narrowest part. Therefore, it is not fitting to consider the religious worship concerning the spirit <note>original: "daemonium"; in this context, a *daemon* is not an evil being but a mediating spirit or guardian that links the human soul to the divine</note> as being divided in such a way, since the very opinion on which that idea is founded wavers in its own weakness. Therefore, there is one personal spirit for each of us who acts as our own governor. It is not right to think that there is a spirit who is completely common and the same for all men—namely, one who is common in himself but joined to each person by a private condition. For the division of species and the diversity of matter do not allow for that identity and incorporeal unity that accompanies things that are truly unified in themselves.

->The Invocation of the Spirit<-

You ask next why we are accustomed to call upon the spirit with a certain common invocation used by everyone. This is because the invocation is performed through the one God who is the Lord of all spirits, who from the beginning assigned to each person their own spirit, and who reveals each person's spirit in sacrifices according to His own will. For in the order of sacred operations <note>original: "sacrarum operationum"; referring to theurgy, or "god-working" rituals</note>, the lower powers are always called upon through the higher divinities. Therefore, among the spirits as well, a certain leader among them—who holds sovereignty over the realm of generation <note>the material world of birth, change, and death</note>—sends down to each person their own personal spirit. Once the spirit is present to each person, he then reveals the worship that is suitable for himself, and makes known his own name and his own specific way of being invoked. And this is the proper order of spirits: one order is related to those who invoke them, another proceeds from more ancient causes, and another creates a harmony among them, contributing together to the same goal. 

Do not, therefore, imagine that divine invocations are similar to human ones, or compare the ineffable <note>words too sacred or great to be spoken</note> with the speakable. Do not compare those things that surpass every limit and every indeterminate mode with human commands and mandates, whether those commands are clearly defined or entirely vague. For the things that exist among us have nothing in common with the whole of their kind, nor with those things that exceed us according to the entire celestial order and surpass our whole essence and nature. Indeed, it is here that the greatest errors happen to men: when, out of human weakness, they try to reason about the powers of spirits, and they judge vast, great, and perfect things by things that are small, worthless, and divided.

->On Happiness<-

You suspect that perhaps some other path toward happiness <note>original: "beatitudinem"; a state of supreme, divine well-being</note> might lie hidden besides divine worship, and you ask what that path might specifically be. But indeed, if the essence and perfection of all good things are contained in the gods, and if the primary power and the first principle of all good resides there, then it is only right that we priests—and whoever has similarly devoted themselves to the higher powers and has lawfully achieved union with them—

# ON THE MYSTERIES #
7
L

...them we have followed, we diligently pursue the Good, which is the beginning and the end of all things. In this state, certainly, the contemplation of truth is present, along with the completion of intellectual knowledge <term>intellectualis scientiæ; here referring to "noetic" or spiritual knowledge gained through direct intuition rather than just logic</term>. And together with God and this knowledge, a turning back towards ourselves and an acknowledgment of our own nature follows. Indeed, you suspect in vain that perhaps a religious devotee depends on human opinions and favors. For what leisure could there be for a mind dedicated to the gods to listen to human praise?

-> Religion is true <-

Nor do you correctly doubt what follows—namely, whether the religious man himself might be deceived—when you say that the soul often invents great things by chance. What origin can there be for fabrications <note>original: "figmentorum"; mental inventions or fantasies</note> among things that truly exist? Is it not the imaginative power within us <term>potentia phantastica; the faculty of "phantasia" or imagination</term> that fashions and transforms images? Yet, when the intellectual life acts perfectly, no fantasy arises. Does not truth itself exist essentially with the gods? Is it not much more the case that truth is founded upon the harmony found in intelligible things? Therefore, such claims are spread by you and others in vain. Indeed, when you and others slander religious men as being deceivers <note>original: "præstigiatores"; literally "jugglers" or those who use sleight of hand to trick the eye</note>, vain, and boastful, you depart further from the truth. For just as in other arts, so too in religion there are those who profess it falsely. This false profession departs further from religion than anything else. For evil is more contrary to good than to that which is merely "not good."

-> Concerning natural, artificial, and divine foreknowledge <-

If any natural aptitude for foretelling the future exists within us—just as animals possess a natural foreknowledge of earthquakes, storms, and cold—such a foreknowledge does not seem to possess anything venerable. For such a natural presage <note>original: "præfagium"; a sense of what is to come</note> follows from the sharpness of the senses, or a shared physical sympathy, or some other disturbance of natural powers. Nor, if someone follows a path of reasoning or the observation of signs that precede certain effects—just as doctors are accustomed to foresee a fever from the contraction of the pulse and shivering—does such a foresight seem to be particularly honorable. For it proceeds from a human, suspect, and bodily condition. Therefore, only the prophecy <note>original: "uaticinium"</note> that arrives by divine means truly exhibits the divine life to us, as it possesses both foresight and divine understandings. It renders us truly divine and brings us the legitimate good. For the most blessed intelligence of the gods is filled abundantly with all good things. You might suspect, perhaps, that prophets inspired by the divine foresee what is to come, yet are not happy because of it. For they are able to foresee, yet not know the future...

# IAMBLICHUS #

...to use [falsehoods], but rather it must be asserted that every foreknowledge inspired by the gods belongs to good men, is filled with goodness, and is possessed of order and beauty. They suggest that it brings us utility, and along with the divine foretelling, it provides us a faculty for avoiding and turning away from those troubles that naturally threaten us. When it is necessary to practice virtue, and if ignorance of the future contributes to that goal, the gods hide future things so that the soul may become better. However, when it does not matter to this end, and it is beneficial for the soul to foresee things—specifically so that they may return safely to higher realms—then they deeply implant the gift of prophecy <note>original: "vaticinium"</note> within the very essences of souls.

-> The Way to Happiness <-

¶ You then asked what the way to happiness is, or in what thing happiness itself consists. Hear this, then: man himself, as an intellect capable of contemplation within himself, was once joined to the contemplation of the gods. But then he entered another kind of soul, fitted or tempered to the human form, and because of this, he is bound by the chain of necessity and fate <term>necessitatis, fatiq; uinculo; in Neoplatonism, the "chain of fate" represents the mechanical laws of the physical universe from which the soul seeks liberation</term>. It is therefore fitting to consider by what means above all he can be released from such chains. There is no release except through the knowledge of the gods themselves. For the very Idea of happiness <note>original: "fœlicitatis"; "felicity" or supreme blessedness</note> is to know the Good itself. Just as the idea of evils consists in the forgetting of good things and a deception regarding evil, so that knowledge [of the gods] meets with the divine. This forgetfulness and deception, however, are inseparable from that which is perishable. Likewise, that divine knowledge rightly measures the essences of intelligible things <term>intelligibilium essentias; realities that exist beyond the physical senses and can only be "seen" by the mind</term> through the sacred ways of holiness. But this forgetfulness, falling away from principles and being cast out, throws itself into measuring the physical world <term>corporalem ideam; literally "bodily idea" or the material form</term>. The former is the recognition of one's own parent; the latter is a departure, along with forgetfulness, far removed from God the Father himself—the one who is above all and sufficient unto himself. The former preserves true life, calling the soul back to the Father. The latter leads man, the chief of creation, down to that which never stays still and is in a perpetual state of flux <note>This refers to the material world, which is always changing, unlike the eternal stability of the divine realm</note>. Let this then be your first path to happiness, possessing the intellectual fullness of divine union within souls. Indeed, the sacred and deifying tradition of happiness is called the "gate" to the Creator God <note>original: "opificem deum"; a reference to the Demiurge or craftsman of the universe</note> of all, or the "place" and "hall" of the Good. It possesses as its first power a chaste and sober holiness of the soul, which is far more useful than the sober chastity of the body. Next, it offers the tuning of thought toward participation in and the vision of the Good, and at the same time, it works toward the expulsion of contrary things. Third, it offers union with the gods, the givers of all good things. Afterward, in a specific and proper way, both to the parts of the world and to the di[vine...]

<meta>This page concludes Iamblichus's discourse on the soul's ascent and the Egyptian mysteries. Picking up from the previous discussion on the "chain of fate," Iamblichus now describes the final stages of the soul's reunification with the divine mind and the role of the Creator.</meta>

...with divine powers spread throughout the various parts of the world, it <note>the soul</note> joins itself to the whole Creator <term>opifici; often translated as the "Demiurge," the divine craftsman who shapes the universe</term>. It provides harmony with Him on every side, and places the soul beyond all matter, joined now solely with the eternal Reason of the universe. This happens, for example, within the power of the Creator himself—which is self-generated, self-moving, sustaining all things, completely elevating the soul, and intellectually adorning all things equally. Likewise, once the soul is recalled to the truth of the intellect, it is again made perfect by that which is self-perfecting and effective. It is gradually adapted to the other powers of the Creator, according to the specific nature of each, so that in their actions, thoughts, and creative faculties, the purified and sacred soul is perfectly strengthened. And then, at last, he <note>the divine power</note> settles the soul within the Creator God in His entirety.

### Conclusion of Religion and Happiness among the Egyptians.

<margin>a</margin>
And here, among the Egyptians, is the end of the religious and sacred elevation. They consider the "Good itself" to be something divine: namely, the God who is understood before all else <note>original: "præ intellectum deum"</note>. On the other hand, they consider the "human good" to be the union with the Lord himself. This is exactly how the prophet Bytis explained it from the books of Mercury <term>mercurialibus; referring to the "Hermetica," the mystical and philosophical writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</term>. Therefore, this part of the path has not been neglected by the Egyptians, as you might suspect, but has been handed down to us in a manner consistent with religious duty.

Nor do the priests trouble the divine intellect with trivial matters, but rather concerning those things that pertain to the purgation <note>cleansing or purification</note>, liberation, and salvation of the soul. They do not meditate on difficult things that are useless to mankind; rather, they seek the most useful matters of the soul. Nor do the priests wander in hallucinations, clouded by some deceitful or seductive demon; for they completely surpass the deceptive and demonic nature in all things and ascend to the intelligible and divine realms.

Now that these matters have been thoroughly discussed, I pray to the gods that they may grant to me and to you a true guardianship and observance of the higher intellects <note>original: "intelligentiarum"</note>, which shall never fail at any time, and that they may provide the eternal truth of the heavenly beings forever. May they make us capable of the perfected understandings concerning the gods, in which the most blessed end of all good things is set before us, as well as the full authority and foundation of friendship and harmony between us.

->THE END<-

# PROCLUS

->Marsilio Ficino’s excerpts from the Greek commentaries of Proclus<-
->on Plato’s *First Alcibiades*.<-

The beginning of the Platonic dialogues and of all philosophy—its most excellent and firmest foundation—is considered to be the knowledge of our own nature. For once this is rightly understood, we will be able to know more perfectly what good is suitable for us, or what evil is discordant. Nature is so arranged that just as the essences of things differ from each other, so too do the specific perfections of things. Therefore, so that we may find what the perfection of our nature is and how it is obtained, we must first of all recognize our own essence. Indeed, this is the goal proposed in the *Alcibiades* and is the aim of all Plato’s teaching.

When we consider the essences of things, we must investigate whether the essence of a thing belongs to the number of those that are indivisible, or to the genus of those divided among bodies, or to those placed in the middle <note>This refers to the "Intermediate" status of the soul, which sits between the eternal, indivisible divine realm and the changing, divisible physical world.</note>. Likewise, we must ask whether the essence is eternal, or existing within time, or created in some part of time. Again, whether it is simple and existing before any composition, or whether it is composite—but composed with indissoluble bonds—or whether it can, in turn, be resolved back into the elements from which it is composed. And if we consider each thing in this way, we can then more easily judge what kind of good belongs to it. It is clear that for an entirely indivisible essence, the good is eternal; but for a divisible one, the good is also found within time and motion. Finally, for an intermediate essence, its perfection is determined according to the measures of its own substance. For such perfection indeed requires time, but "primary time" <note>original: "tpe primo"; in Neoplatonism, this is the fundamental measure of the soul's motion, distinct from physical time</note>, which can be properly measured in the circuits of the body. We remain ignorant of ourselves because we are occupied by "generational forgetfulness" <term>obliuione geneſica; the Platonic concept that the soul forgets its divine origins when it is born into the material world of "generation"</term> and are struck by the disturbance of life among the species of rational things. Yet we think we know many things among those we are ignorant of, because we possess the innate reasons <note>or "forms/principles"</note> of things within our essence.

There are three types of conversion <term>conuerſionis; the Neoplatonic concept of 'epistrophe' or the soul "turning back" toward its source</term>. For whatever is turned, either it is turned toward something worse than itself, falling away from its own perfection; or it rises toward something better because of the vigor of its own life and natural action; or it is reflected back toward itself because of a knowledge shared with itself and an intermediate kind of motion. Conversion toward the worse is a kind of suffering for the soul as it casts off its wings and is placed in forgetfulness, both of itself and of higher things. But conversion both toward oneself and toward the better belongs not only to souls, but also to the divine beings themselves, as Parmenides himself teaches us.

Plato indicates in the prologue that, among other things, a mind eager for truth produces forms of knowledge that are kindred to the things being known. He does not produce an immutable knowledge of changeable things, nor an ambiguous and wavering knowledge of necessary and stable things. Instead, just as Socrates taught in the *Republic*, with a knowledge that is indeed simple [and] uniform...

# ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.

f ii

...to know all intellectual things in a joined and uniform intellectual manner. Scientific and reflective knowledge, however, contemplates the middle ratios <note>original: "rationes regę medias"; in this context, these are the mathematical or logical laws that govern the intermediate realm of the soul.</note> by the unfolding and composition of forms. Thirdly, falling away from the truth through the power of the senses, the soul judges sensible things through its own appropriate instruments of knowledge. Finally, through the power of imagination, it apprehends the images of sensible things. Indeed, Timaeus <note>Referencing the character in Plato's *Timaeus* who explains the creation of the universe.</note>, distinguishing types of knowledge by a certain proportion to the things known, commands us to judge beings by intelligence and reason, but to judge those things that are not true beings—but are constantly becoming and perishing—by opinion and sense. He states that the reasons for those things which truly exist are fixed and firm, while the reasons for things flowing in the realm of generation are imaginary and contingent. For everywhere, reasons and speech imitate the things they explain.

And Socrates in the *Cratylus* says that concerning eternal things, names reach more toward the nature of the thing, but concerning mutable things, names also often change and depend more on human convention. Everywhere, different properties of the gods exist: for some are the architects of the universe and create the substance of the form of beings; others propagate life and generate various vital forces; others maintain an unchangeable order and guard the indissoluble connection of things. Finally, others, having been allotted different powers, preserve all things through their own kind of beneficence.

Likewise, the whole "Order of Love" is the cause of conversion <note>In Neoplatonism, "conversion" is the process by which a soul or thing turns back toward its divine source after being created.</note> for all things toward divine beauty and form, leading back all subsequent things to it, joining them to it, and confirming them once joined, and soon thereafter filling the subsequent things and radiating the gifts of divine light proceeding from there through all things. For this reason, it is taught in the *Symposium* that Love is a "Great Daemon" <note>original: "dæmonem"; in Greek philosophy, a *daemon* is a mediating spirit between gods and mortals, not a "demon" in the modern sense.</note>, since Love is the first of all to demonstrate this kind of mediating power in itself, being in the middle between the desirable thing itself and the one who desires, and being the cause of the return of later things to earlier ones. 

Therefore, the entire amatory cohort, stationed in the vestibule of the Cause of Beauty, calls all things toward it and forms a middle process between that which is lovable and those who are recalled by love. Wherefore it declares in itself the pattern of the whole daemonic order, holding this middle position in divine matters, which daemons hold between the divine and the mortal. Since, therefore, the entire amatory cohort has this property among the gods, we conceive of its summit as unique and hidden, coupled with the first and intelligible beauty among the supreme gods; but its middle progression shines with an intellectual condition above the gods of the world. Its third progression, however, is distributed in many ways around the world, producing from itself many orders and powers, and distributing gifts of this kind to the various parts of the world. For after the single and first principle of Love, and after the tripartite substance spreading out from there...
