<meta>This page continues Proclus’s discussion on how the soul relates to beauty and the divine hierarchy. It transitions from the different modes of knowledge to the "Order of Love" and how various beings—angels, daemons, and humans—are drawn toward the Intelligible Beauty.</meta>

### PROCLUS:

...shines with a varied crowd of Loves. From this source, the choirs of angels are made radiant with love. Even the crowds of daemons <note>In Neoplatonism, daemons are intermediary spirits between gods and humans; they can be good, acting as messengers, or "low" and deceptive.</note>, filled with this divinity, follow the gods, having been called back to that intelligible beauty <note>original: "intelligibilem pulchritudinem"; the pure, non-physical form of beauty accessible only to the mind.</note>. An army of heroes, along with daemons and angels, revels around this beauty. Finally, all things are stirred up, revived, turned green again, and grow warm through the inward flow of beauty itself. Indeed, the souls of humans, touched by this kind of inspiration and naturally akin to God, move constantly around the beautiful. They descend into the province of generation <note>original: "generationis"; the physical world of birth, death, and constant change.</note> to offer a benefit to imperfect souls and to provide for those things that seem to be in need of salvation. While the gods themselves and the followers of the gods remain in their own proper state, they benefit those who follow them and turn those followers back toward themselves. Human souls, however, having fallen downward and touched the realm of generation, display the beneficial providence of the gods as much as they are able. 

Therefore, just as some souls are established according to one god and others according to another, they purely govern these falling provinces and the souls wandering here. Some benefit the more imperfect souls through prophecy, others through rituals of purification and sacrifices, and others through the divine power of healing. In the same way, those souls that have chosen the life of a lover are moved by the god who presides over beauty to care for talented souls. From the beauty that appears to the senses, they are led back to divine beauty, calling those they love to join them. However, those souls that fall away from the heavenly gift due to a perverse education—even if they possess a nature suited for love—fall instead into the mere shadows of beauty. Because of their ignorance of true beauty, they admire and love bodily forms, remaining ignorant of their own true nature. Just as in the writings of Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) whose work Proclus is interpreting.</note> a downward flow of the mind creates mere astuteness, and a fallen portion of wisdom creates sophistry <note>original: "sophisticam"; the use of clever but false arguments.</note>, so too does the gift of love, when it falls into a corrupted vessel, produce a life of excess and tyranny.

->The higher cause acts upon a work before and after the lower cause, and acts together<-
->with it, and is more present to the work.<-

<margin>q</margin>Those things which are more perfect everywhere, and which hold the status of a model <note>original: "ratione exemplaris"; acting as the blueprint or Ideal Form.</note>, fully encompass the actions of their images. So much so, that the lower things are never present to anything unless the more perfect things have also handed down something of themselves much earlier. For even now, through all the orders of things, the "One" <note>The ultimate, absolute principle in Neoplatonism from which all existence emanates.</note> itself encompasses all other things; it acts before them, after them, and together with them.

...and drawing the soul toward that which is weaker, pulling it away from the contemplation of true beings <note>original: "entiũ cõtemplatiõe"; the act of mentally perceiving the eternal forms of reality</note> toward the imagination which is familiar with fleeting things. Just as in the elevation of love, a crowd of commonplace lovers acts as a hindrance by pretending to be the true lover—thereby twisting the soul of the younger person away from heavenly goods and toward dark, earthly things—so it is in the most holy purifications and sacred rites. Before the god himself is openly present, certain terrestrial spirits <note>original: "dæmonum... terrestrium"</note> appear. These strange sights disturb those who are being purified and initiated, turning them away from pure goods toward physical matter. For this reason, the gods command that you should not look upon those spirits until you have protected your eyes with the power of the sacred rites. Thus, the divine oracles <note>A reference to the Chaldean Oracles, a set of spiritual texts highly regarded by Neoplatonists.</note> say: "It is not profitable for you to look upon them before you have purified and hallowed your body," because those spirits, by charming the souls, turn them away from the sacrifices at every turn. Therefore, just as in the sacred rites the divine first appears only when we have driven out this entire demonic host that drags souls into matter, so too the "divine lover" meets the beloved only after the commonplace lovers have been rejected. Furthermore, just as a "good spirit" <note>original: "bonus dæmon"; in this context, a protective tutelary spirit or guardian angel</note> guards each person from childhood, examines all their actions and words, provides for them even before their parents do, and remains after their parents as a constant governor of their whole life—eventually serving as a guide to the judges after death—in this same way, Socrates conducts himself toward Alcibiades. Finally, just as a good spirit remains mostly hidden while providing for us secretly, counseling us in silence, and correcting us inexpressibly, so Socrates acts toward Alcibiades.

->The Intellect within us is always active by illuminating, even<-
->though we do not always notice it.<-

<margin>i</margin>
The Intellect <note>original: "Intellectus"; the highest faculty of the soul, capable of direct spiritual intuition</note> itself is indeed always active around us and always offers the light of understanding. This is true even before we fall into an irrational state, and when we live a life ruled by passions. Even when the passions are eventually calmed, we do not always notice this light; we notice it only when we have been purged of the great tumult of generation <note>original: "generationis tumultu"; the chaotic noise and distraction of the physical world of birth and decay</note> and live tranquilly. For it is then that the Intellect shines upon us; then it speaks with us, as it were; then it communicates its voice to us, having previously been present in silence.

One can consider Alcibiades in two ways: both as the soul simply, and as the soul making use of a body. For these two are not the same thing.

For that which is indivisible <note>original: "imparticibile"; refers to a principle that remains whole and does not descend into parts</note> differs entirely from that which is divisible. Furthermore, that which exists by itself differs from that which is considered alongside something else. Finally, that which is transcendent <note>original: "exemptum"; standing apart from or above a lower order</note> differs from that which has been assigned a shared rank with another. Since Alcibiades is understood in two ways—both as a soul simply, and as a soul using a body—in the sense that he is simply a certain soul, Socrates acts in the place of the Mind <note>original: "mentis"; the higher intellect (Nous)</note> for him. However, in the sense that he is a soul using a body, Socrates plays the part of a good spirit <note>original: "boni dæmōis"; a guardian daemon or guiding spiritual entity</note>. Thus, he is both a spirit in relation to the man, and an intellect in relation to the soul. Indeed, when we consider the intermediary nature of spirits, we place them between gods and men. But when we consider the intellect, we suspend the soul from the intellect itself at the highest level, and the body from the soul. You have, certainly, the first division in the *Symposium*, where it is taught that spirits exist as a middle ground between gods and men; you have the second in the *Timaeus*, which says the soul holds the middle place between the intellect and the body. Therefore, the same entity is both intellect and spirit: it is considered an intellect in relation to the soul, but a spirit in relation to the human soul.

### How the god Love is neither first nor last, and how in divine
### beings there is the Good, the Wise, and the Beautiful, as well as Faith, Truth, and Love.

<margin>a</margin>We ought to place Love, the master, neither among the first of beings, nor among the last. Not among the first, because the object of love <note>original: "amabile"; that which is worthy of being loved, such as the Form of Beauty</note> is higher than love itself. Not among the last, because the lover is a participant in love. It is necessary, therefore, to establish Love between the beloved and the lover, and to assert that it is later than the Beautiful itself, but prior to all those things which love. Where, then, did it exist from the beginning? In what way does it proceed through all things, and with what unities did it come forth? Since there are three substances <note>original: "substantiā"; likely referring to the three primary hypostases or levels of reality in the intelligible realm</note> among the intelligible and hidden gods: the first is marked by the Good—that is, the Good itself understanding from itself—where, as the sacred oracles <note>original: "sacra eloquia"; a reference to the Chaldean Oracles</note> teach, is the paternal unity. The second is designated by the Wise, where the first intelligence flourishes. The third is defined by the Beautiful, where the most beautiful of intelligible things resides, as the *Timaeus* <gloss>o</gloss> says. Doubtless, three unities also exist according to these intelligible causes: they reside uniformly in the intelligible realm according to their cause, but they shine forth first in the ineffable order of the gods—namely, Faith, Truth, and Love. Faith firms all things in the Good. Truth explains all knowledge in minds <note>original: "inentibus"; likely a printer's error for "mentibus"</note>. Finally, Love turns all things back and gathers them into the nature of the Beautiful itself. Indeed, such a trinity proceeds from here through all the [orders] of the gods...

...orders and radiates a union to all things toward the <term>intelligible</term> <note>The "intelligible" (intelligibile) refers to the highest realm of reality consisting of pure forms and divine thoughts, accessible only to the intellect rather than the senses.</note> itself. However, it declares itself differently through different orders, folding its powers everywhere into God according to their specific properties. In one place, it exists ineffably, unknowingly, and uniquely; in another, by the logic of containment and connection; in another, as if perfecting and forming. Here again, it acts intellectually and paternally; there, it is entirely moving, life-giving, and effective; in that place, it is imprinting and assimilating. There, it is absolute, deep, and pure; in another place, it is already multiplied and divided. Therefore, **Love** descends from above, from the intelligible realms even to the mundane, summoning all things to divine beauty. **Truth** also proceeds through all things, illuminating everything with knowledge. **Faith** proceeds through the universe, establishing all things individually in the Good. Here, the divine oracles <note>A reference to the *Chaldean Oracles*, a sacred text for Neoplatonists like Proclus.</note> hand down that all things are governed by these three—Faith, Truth, and Love—and consist within them. For this reason, the gods command those performing sacrifices to join themselves to God through a <term>trinity</term> <note>This Neoplatonic trinity of Faith, Truth, and Love was seen by scholars like Ficino as a pagan parallel to the Christian Trinity.</note> of this kind. Indeed, the intelligibles themselves, because of their inestimable unity, do not need a "loving" medium. But where there is both a unity of beings and a distinction between them, there Love exists; for Love is the binder and the reconciler of those things which are after it and those which are above it. It is the turner of following things toward those that came before, a guide back for the imperfect and a refiner for the perfect.

->Providence runs through each thing down to the smallest, and meanwhile is bound to none.<-

Those who are more diligent in assigning reasons to the King <note>Referring to the "King of All" or the supreme Divine Principle.</note> hand down these two most powerful elements of divine and <term>daemonic</term> <note>From the Greek "daemon," meaning a mediating spirit or guardian entity, not an evil "demon" in the modern sense.</note> providence:
<margin>q</margin>
First, that providence proceeds from above through all things to the very last, and does not omit even the smallest thing from its influence. Second, that it receives absolutely nothing from those things it governs, nor is it filled by their lower nature, nor mixed with them anywhere. For it is not the case that because it preserves and disposes all things, it is therefore stained by the things it governs. For the divine and daemonic nature is not subject to the passions of particular souls. Nor yet, while it stands separately above the things that follow it, does it leave anything among the lower things disordered or uncultivated. On the contrary, for this very reason, it adorns all things fittingly and yet remains free from the things it dispenses. For it is equally beneficent and pure: the adorner of all, yet meanwhile unburdened by the things it cultivates. It runs through all things, especially because it is nowhere restrained. Even divine men provide for their inferiors most diligently and yet calmly. What then must be said of the gods themselves and the good spirits? Are they not present to all things, yet free from all? Filling all things with themselves, they are nowhere mixed with any; running through the universe, they have nowhere surrendered their own life. Shall we not confess that the gods love their offspring? Just as the poets imagine Jupiter loving a girl, and Venus herself. Certainly, because love of this kind is a provider, a savior, a perfecter, and a contain[er]...

...by a torch <note>original: "torre"</note> divinely loved. Meanwhile, he is both beneficent and sincere, unmixed by any attachment to external affairs. I shall say even more: why would such a privileged amatory path belong to the souls of men, unless it first existed within the gods themselves? For whatever good and health-giving quality belongs to souls has its defined cause from the gods. For this reason, Plato proves that the **exemplars** <term>exemplaria</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, these are the perfect, eternal "blueprints" in the divine mind of which earthly things are mere shadows.</note> of all virtues and bodily goods—such as health, strength, justice, and temperance—precede us in the possession of God. How much more, then, shall we confess that the principal cause of the gift of love exists among the gods? Indeed, as Socrates says in the *Phaedrus*, this amatory affection is granted as a certain divine gift.

The gods, therefore, love the gods: the elder gods indeed love the younger through the gift of **providence** <note>The downward flow of care and guidance from a higher being to a lower one.</note>, while the younger in turn love the elder through a certain duty of **conversion** <note>The upward movement or "turning back" of a soul toward its divine source.</note>. To perfect those things that are worse and to provide for subordinates is a duty that belongs to souls insofar as they are souls; for this very reason they descend: for the sake of providing for generated things and caring for mortals. Yet, to provide in such a way—governing those you provide for without being mixed or affected as if enslaved, nor receiving anything from them—is the unique property of the gods and good **daemons** <term>daemonum</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, a "daemon" is a mediating spirit or divine power that bridges the gap between gods and mortals; it does not carry the modern negative connotation of "demon."</note>. Whenever this occurs in human souls, it happens through divine or demonic bounty.

In the most holy sacrifices, priests are accustomed to lead those present into admiration and **stupor** <note>original: "stuporem"; here meaning a state of ecstatic awe or being "struck" by the divine, which renders the soul receptive to God.</note>, either through words or through things shown to the eyes. For stupor is known to expose the soul to God. Socrates would never have lived such a perfectly amatory life unless he had chosen it through the inspiration of a certain daemon and held fast to that choice.

Love is the medium between the lovable and the lover; it is a great daemon binding all things together, and whatever things feel desire, Love—as the medium—first joins them to the object of desire.

Diotima <note>The wise woman described in Plato's *Symposium* who taught Socrates the mysteries of Love.</note> called this a "great daemon," since it everywhere fills the middle space between those who desire and those who are desired. That which is to be loved claims the first rank for itself; the lover takes the third rank from the beloved. Finally, Love occupies the middle between both, gathering and binding the desirer and the desired into one, and filling the lesser with the better.

-># ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.<-

It is a certain union, yet one that exists alongside a manifold distinction. For this reason, the sacred writings <note>original: "eloquia sacra"; likely referring to the Orphic hymns or Chaldean Oracles</note> are accustomed to call the fire of this love "the Joiner." For proceeding from the **intelligible intellect** <term>intellectu intelligibili</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, this is the highest level of Mind, which contains the perfect Forms.</note>, it binds all subsequent things to one another and to that source.

It reconciles all the gods to intelligible beauty, daemons to the gods, and us to the daemons; and it joins us to the gods. In the gods, it subsists first. In daemons, it subsists second. In particular souls, however, it exists through a certain third process originating from these principles. In the gods, moreover, it is **above essence** <note>original: "super essentiam"; meaning it exists in the realm of the One, prior to the existence of defined being.</note>, for every race of gods is of this kind. In daemons, however, it exists through essence. Finally, in souls, it exists through the effect of illumination. And this triple order appears similar to the triple power of the intellect. For one intellect stands as **unparticipable** <note>An independent principle that does not mix with lower things.</note>, absolute and free from all particular kinds. Another is **participated**, in which the souls of the gods share as something superior. Yet another is infused by this into souls, which is surely the perfection of the souls themselves. The divine Plato <note>original: "Timaeus ipse"; referring to the character in Plato's Timaeus.</note> signifies these three things regarding the intellect. Therefore, understand that the love implanted in the gods is consistent with the unparticipable intellect; for that too is absolute, both from all things that receive it and from those which are illuminated by it. Compare **daemonic love** to the participated intellect. For it is itself essential and perfected by itself as a pre-participated intellect, residing most closely to souls. Finally, you must render the third love as that which is infused into souls by illumination, according to their acquired habit. Nor do we consider love to be joined to the universal intellectual difference without justice. For it has its first and hidden substance in the **intelligible intellect**. For if it proceeded from there, it is also established there through it; and it seems to me that Plato also found this god in the works of Orpheus, where the same is called both Love and a **Great Daemon** <term>magnum daemonem</term> <note>In the Greek tradition, a 'daemon' is a mediating spirit between gods and humans, not an evil entity.</note>, and he himself seems to have been content with this hymn. Justly, therefore, does Diotima call Love a great daemon. And Socrates, where he disputes concerning love, also disputes concerning daemons.

Those holding the last places of the third and daemonic order have a varied and more rational...

### PROCLUS:

...and material nature. Formed of such a substance, they are divided according to the division of the gods, inasmuch as they perform the role of ministers to the gods. For they respond and serve the gods in different ways: some serve those who are entirely absolute <note>original: "penitus absolutis"; referring to transcendent gods who exist prior to the physical universe</note>, who initiate and lead all things before the world began. Others, however, serve the mundane gods who preside directly over the parts of the world, and who are distributed according to the twelve celestial gods. These daemons <term>daemones</term> <note>In Greek philosophy, a 'daemon' is not an evil spirit, but a mediating power or "spirit guide" that bridges the gap between the divine and the human.</note> are distributed according to all the properties of the mundane gods. For every mundane god commands a certain order of daemons, to whom he imparts his own power as to a neighbor. For the craftsman-god <note>original: "Deus opifex"; often referring to the Demiurge from Plato's Timaeus</note> bestows a crafting power; the immutable god exhibits an uncontaminated faculty; the perfecter god likewise grants a perfecting power. And around each and every god is an innumerable multitude of daemons, who carry the same titles as their leading gods. Indeed, they rejoice when they are named "Apollos," "Mercuries," or "Joves," <note>original: "Apollines. Mercurii. Ioues"; referring to the classes of spirits that follow the gods Apollo, Mercury, and Jupiter</note> since they express the property of their own gods within themselves. Consequently, through these divine daemons, mortal things obtain divine influences, and thus plants and animals are fashioned—some reflecting the images of one god, some of another. From a close position, these daemons bestow the gifts of their leaders; yet, from a more eminent height, the gods themselves preside over the daemons.

For this reason, the last things agree with the first in their affection <note>original: "in passione"; here meaning a shared quality or resonance rather than suffering</note>. For the marks of the first are found in the last, and the causes of the last are contained in the first. Indeed, the intermediate genera of daemons fill all things and connect them at once, and they themselves maintain the communion of all; for while they share in the gods, they are shared by those things that are fleeting. If anyone says, therefore, that the craftsman of the universe <note>The Demiurge</note> established the rank of daemons to be the firmament of the entire order, he will not wander from the truth. Since even Diotima <note>The wise woman mentioned in Plato's Symposium who teaches Socrates about Love.</note> attributed this order to them—namely, connecting divine and mortal things together, channeling the flowing streams from above, referring all subsequent things back to the gods, and finally filling the universe according to the connection of this very mediation.

*He refutes two opinions: the first, saying that there are no other daemons besides our souls released from the solid body; the second, that of Amelius, who thinks that daemons are certain wandering gods.*

We shall not, therefore, admit those who say that daemons are our own souls that have finished their habitations and transitioned into another state. For it is not fitting to equate a being considered a daemon through a certain habit <note>i.e., a soul acting like a daemon</note> with one that is a daemon by its very essence; nor is it fitting to establish the eternal mediation of all mundane things from a manifold life that is subject to change. For the daemonic guard itself always stands in the same manner, continuing the universe. A soul, however, does not retain its own order in such a way, as Socrates says in the *Republic*.

# ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.

...of the state. For at other times it chooses other lives. Nor will we again approve of those who think some daemons are gods, as if they were wandering gods, as Amelius <note>Amelius Gentilianus (3rd century AD), a Neoplatonic philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note> thinks. But we shall follow Plato himself, who calls the gods the masters of the universe, but subjects the flocks of daemons to the gods, and we will everywhere approve the reasoning of Diotima <note>The wise woman of Mantinea in Plato's *Symposium* who teaches Socrates about the nature of Love as a great daemon.</note>, who assigns the daemons a middle rank between the gods and mortals.

### On guardian daemons. Likewise, he enumerates five kinds of daemons and their various duties.

<margin>c</margin> Since therefore daemons are established in the middle, as we have said, the first and highest among them are the divine daemons, and they frequently appear as gods on account of their excellent resemblance to the gods. Indeed, in every order, the first member displays the form of the higher order. For the intellect presents itself out of itself as a god, and the most ancient part of souls exists as intellectual; therefore, the highest genus of daemons, as being closest to the gods, is uniform and divine. The second after these are the daemons already endowed with an intellectual property, presiding over ascents and descents <note>This refers to the journey of the soul as it descends into a physical body and eventually ascends back toward the divine realm.</note>, and declaring and handing down the works of the gods to all. The third are the daemons who distribute the effects of divine souls into the things that follow, and they complete the bond for those who look upward, and the downward flow from the gods to those souls. The fourth transmit the effective powers of universal natures into things capable of being born, and they breathe life, order, and reason into particular natures, and into the whole production of mortal things. The fifth are in some way corporeal, and they govern the outermost parts of bodies.

For in what way would eternal bodies be compatible with falling ones? How could the causes be joined with the effects, unless they were bound by a middle ground of this kind? For a nature of this kind, being in the middle, rules over corporeal goods and provides for all natural abundances. Most of them, however, from their number, are occupied with matter, and they contain and weave together the powers descending from celestial matter into the material world below. They subsequently guard it and preserve the variety and "painting" <note>original: "picturāmque"; a metaphor for the diverse appearances and "coloring" of physical forms in the material world.</note> of forms within this very matter.

### The five duties of daemons; the first daemons join souls to their own gods.

<margin>c</margin> Since therefore there are many and multiform daemons, as Diotima says, the highest indeed join the souls proceeding from the Father to the gods who are their leaders. For every god leads first the daemons, and then the particular souls. For as Timaeus <note>Referring to the speaker in Plato's dialogue *Timaeus*, who describes the creation of the universe and the sowing of souls into the stars.</note> says, the god who is the craftsman of these things sowed some souls in the sun, others in the moon, and others into the other gods...

# PROCLUS

Indeed, there are daemons who have been allotted souls according to their essence, which they join to their own leaders <note>In Neoplatonic thought, "leaders" or "hegemons" are the higher gods who guide specific chains of being.</note>. And every soul, even if it revolves around its own god, needs the benefit of such a daemon. Truly, the daemons manage the ascents and descents of souls, and many of the choices made by souls are mediated through them.

Surely, those most perfect souls who live their lives in the realm of generation <note>The physical world of birth, change, and decay.</note> without becoming entangled in its commerce, live a life according to a divine daemon, just as they chose a life agreeable to their own god. This daemon had already joined them to their own god while they still remained among the heavenly beings. For this reason, that Egyptian <note>A reference to an Egyptian priest in Rome who, according to Porphyry, sought to conjure Plotinus’s guardian spirit and was amazed to find it was a "god" rather than a lower daemon.</note> was filled with admiration for Plotinus, seeing him as one governed by a divine daemon. Therefore, regarding souls who live their lives here as if they are soon to return to the sublime heights, the daemon is the same here as it is above. But regarding less perfect souls, the daemon itself is one thing by its own essence, but another daemon accompanies the life recently brought forth into the world.

---

->The term <term>daemon</term><note>From the Greek *daimon*; in this context, it refers to a guiding spirit or intermediary power, not an evil "demon."</note> is used in three ways: by essence, by comparison, or by a certain disposition.<-

---

If these principles are correctly established, no one will now agree with those who say our rational soul is itself a daemon. For a daemon is something other than a human being, as Diotima <note>The priestess from Plato's *Symposium* who explains that Love is a "great daemon" bridging the gap between gods and men.</note> teaches, placing daemons in the middle rank between gods and humans. Socrates himself indicates this here, where he distinguishes a "daemonic cause" from a "human cause," saying that it was not a human reason, but a "daemonic obstacle" <note>Socrates famously spoke of his *daimonion*, a divine inner voice that warned him against making mistakes.</note> that held him back. Since a human is defined as a soul using a body, the daemon should not be thought of as being the same as the rational soul.

Furthermore, this is also manifest where Plato, in the *Timaeus*, says that the "daemon" of a living being is the reason established within us. However, we should only accept this as a matter of "comparison." For a daemon by its own essence is one thing, a daemon by comparison is another, and a daemon by habit or disposition is yet another. Indeed, it is customary to call "daemon" whatever stands immediately above something else in the daemonic order, looking down toward what is lower. By this usage, Jupiter <note>original: "Iuppiter"</note> in the writings of Orpheus called his father Saturn <note>original: "Saturnum"</note> a daemon; and Plato himself in the *Timaeus* called those gods "daemons" who arrange the process of birth nearby, where he says: "To treat of the other daemons, and to bring their generation into the light, is a task greater than human genius can bear."

A daemon "by comparison" is thus of such a kind that it provides immediate providence for an individual, even if that provider is actually a god, or inferior to a god. On the other hand, the mind is called a daemon "by disposition" when, through a certain likeness to the more wonderful daemonic race, it performs actions that surpass the human level and suspends its entire life from a daemon.

# CONCERNING THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.

By this reasoning, I believe Socrates in the *Republic* <note>Plato's *Republic*, specifically the Myth of Er in Book X.</note> called those souls "daemons" who have lived their lives well and have been transferred to a better lot and now inhabit more restricted places. Finally, the daemon itself, according to its essence, is not called a daemon because of its relationship to subsequent things nor because of some similarity to another, but it has obtained this property through itself; in its existence, it is distinguished by its own powers and different modes of action. Indeed, in general, the rational soul in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato's *Timaeus* 90a, where the highest part of the soul is called a daemon.</note> is called an "animal daemon" <note>Original: *daemon animalis*. This refers to the soul functioning as the guiding spirit of the living being.</note>. But we are investigating the daemon of the man himself—not the animal daemon—and that which directs the rational soul, not merely its instrument. And again, it is the one who leads the soul, once released from the living creature, to the judges. As Socrates asserts in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato's *Phaedo* 107d.</note>, when the living creature is no longer, the daemon leads each person to the judge—the very daemon, I say, which they had been allotted while living. For if the daemon found that same person while living, whom it also presents for judgment after death, it is clear that it had found not just an animal, but a man. Moreover, beginning from above and commanding, it governs our entire constitution.

->Against those who say the daemon is either an active part of the soul, or a part set over it.<-

But neither are those to be approved who, setting aside the rational soul, say the daemon is that which operates within the soul—as if for those living according to reason, the daemon is "reason"; for those living in anger, it is the "irascible" part; and for those in desire, the "concupiscible" <note>The three parts of the soul in Platonic thought: reason, spirit/anger, and appetite/desire.</note>. Nor should those be listened to who say the daemon is that which, in our life, presides most closely over whatever is active—for example, that reason presides over the angry, or the power of anger over the lustful. In the first place, to say that daemons are parts of human souls is the view of those who admire human life too much, and who do not approve of Socrates in the *Republic* when he places the heroic and human race after the gods and daemons, and when he rebukes the poets for introducing <term>heroes</term><note>In Greek mythology and philosophy, heroes were a class of being between humans and gods.</note> who are no better than men, but enslaved to similar passions. Socrates, therefore, rebuking such things, will be very far from the opinion that daemons—who are superior to heroes—should be placed among the parts and powers of the soul. For from this it would follow that things better by essence are received within to complete things that are inferior. Furthermore, changes in lifestyles would lead to various changes of the daemons. For a greedy man often changes to an ambitious life; an ambitious man to a habit of living by right opinion; and this one to a habit endowed with knowledge. The daemon would therefore be different at different times. For the very part acting in the soul is one thing at one time and another at another. If, therefore, either this active part itself or the part presiding closely over it were the daemon, then surely the daemons would change along with the changes of human life; and in the same life, several...

<sig>y</sig>
<page-num>47</page-num>

<summary>Proclus argues that the "guardian daemon" is a distinct, superior entity allotted to a person during life and after death, rather than being merely a psychological part of the human soul like reason or desire.</summary>

### PROCLUS.

The same soul will not obtain [different] daemons <note>original: *daemones*. In Greek philosophy, a *daemon* is a tutelary spirit or divine guide, not a "demon" in the modern sense.</note>, which can in no way happen. For never does the soul change the leadership of its daemon in the same course of life. Instead, the same daemon governs us from our very birth <note>original: *genitura*</note> until we stand before the judge of life. This is exactly what Socrates asserts in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato’s *Phaedo* 107d.</note>.

The daemon is not a particular intellect <note>meaning an individual human's mind or capacity for thought</note>, but a substance differing from the intellect, placed within the range of souls.

<margin>p</margin>
Therefore, those who think the particular intellect is the same as the daemon allotted to us do not seem to me to rightly confound the intellectual property with the daemonic substance. For all daemons are contained within the breadth of souls and exist as posterior to the divine souls. However, the intellectual order is something other than the soul; they have obtained neither the same essence, nor the same power, nor the same action. Furthermore, souls enjoy the intellect only when they have finally turned toward it, received light from it, and joined their own action to it. By contrast, souls are under the leadership of a daemon throughout their entire life, their whole way of living, and the cycles <note>original: *perioia*, likely referring to the *periodoi* or circuits of the soul</note> which proceed either from fate or from providence. For it is the daemon itself that rules our entire life, fulfills our choices made before birth, and bestows the gifts of fate and the favors of the lords of destiny. Indeed, it even suggests and measures out the illuminations provided by providence. Now, as certain souls, we depend upon the intellect alone; but as souls using a body, we also need a daemon. For this reason, Plato called the Intellect the "governor of the soul" in the *Phaedrus* <note>Plato’s *Phaedrus* 247c.</note>, but elsewhere called the daemon the "observer and curator of men." Truly, no one considering the matter rightly will find any other single providence closest to us that pertains to all things, except for daemonic providence and care. For the Intellect is participated in by the rational soul (as we have said) but by no means by the body; nature is participated in by the body, but not at all by the intellect. The rational soul rules over anger and desire; yet in matters of chance, it has no command. The daemon alone moves all things. It governs everything. It cultivates and arranges all our affairs; indeed, it perfects reason, tempers disturbances, inspires nature, preserves the body, supplies chance occurrences, fulfills the decrees of fate, and grants the gifts of providence. This daemon exists as the one ruler of the universe <note>original: *universo x*, possibly a scribal mark or abbreviation for *Christo* or a specific Greek term like *chi*</note>, holding the rudder of our entire life and everything within and around us.

->Three things concerning the daemon of Socrates: first, that it is also a god; second, that it appears through a voice; third, that it calls back but does not urge forward.<-

Concerning the daemon of Socrates, three things must be considered by us. First, that it is called a "god," as is clear here and in the *Apology* <note>Plato’s *Apology* 40a-c.</note>. Second, that it gave a vocal sign to Socrates, which appears in the *Theages* <note>A dialogue attributed to Plato, though its authenticity is debated by scholars.</note> and the *Phaedrus*. Third, that it "called Socrates back" <note>original: *revocabat*</note> but did not "urge him forward" <note>original: *provocabat*. Socrates's "divine sign" famously only acted as a deterrent, stopping him from doing things, rather than commanding him to act.</note>.

# ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.

...as the *Apology* <note>Plato’s *Apology*, where Socrates discusses his "divine sign" or daemon.</note> testifies. In the beginning, those divine souls who have chosen an intellectual life are "divine daemons," being the highest in the genus of daemons, and participants in the nature of the gods before all others. For just as there is a "daemon" among the gods, so too is there a "god" among the daemons; however, in the gods the substance is divine while the proportion is daemonic, whereas in the daemons the property is daemonic but the proportion declares a divine essence. Indeed, they so far excel the other daemons that they frequently appear as gods. It is for this reason that Socrates calls his own daemon both a "daemon" and a "god," <note>original: *daemonem suum appellat & deum*</note> as if it were the highest of the daemonic order. Therefore, Socrates was perfected, being governed by such a daemon and directing himself according to the norm of this daemon; thus, pay attention to what concerns that "voice" of the daemon.

Socrates truly first enjoyed the inspiration of the daemon through intelligence and the knowledge of <term>separate things</term> <note>original: *rerum separatarum*; in Neoplatonism, this refers to abstract, divine forms that exist apart from physical matter</note>, which continually called him back toward divine love. Secondly, in the business of life, it directed his providence toward inferior matters; and according to the action of the daemon itself—not only through intelligence or thought, nor only by the power of opinions—he received light proceeding from there, but also in his very spirit. While that daemonic inspiration proceeded suddenly throughout his whole life, it eventually moved his very senses. It is established that by the same action hanging over us from above, the reason is affected in one way, the imagination in another, and the sense in yet another; by the gift granted, each of the things within us is moved and acted upon by the daemon according to its own specific condition. Therefore, the voice did not fall upon Socrates passively from the outside, but was an inspiration proceeding from his innermost parts through the whole soul, and progressing all the way to the instruments of the senses, until finally it emerged as a "voice," coming into his awareness not so much by any physical sense as by a "con-sense" <note>original: *consensu*; a shared internal perception or harmony between the faculties of the soul</note>. For such are the illuminations that tend to happen from good daemons and gods.

->*Other daemons ordered under other gods have various duties among themselves.*<-

What has been said regarding the daemon of Socrates—namely, that it "called him back" <note>original: *revocare*; the daemon famously only told Socrates what *not* to do (the *apostatic* function)</note> and did not "provoke him forward"—is not a benefit common to all our daemons. Therefore, because Socrates’s own nature was full of charity toward men and was of its own accord ready for good deeds, he did not require a daemonic exhortation. Yet the daemon would discourage him whenever he might approach his teaching either unseasonably or toward those unfit for his discipline. He was, in other words, one who needed a bridle rather than spurs. Furthermore, some daemons possess a <term>purgative</term> <note>cleansing or purifying</note> and uncontaminable power, others a <term>generative</term> <note>creative or life-giving</note> power, others a <term>perfecting</term> power, others an <term>artificer</term> <note>original: *opificem*; crafting or building</note> power, and they are divided entirely according to the properties and powers of the gods under whom they are ordered. Now indeed, according to their substance, individuals are protected by their patrons for the sake of a blessed life—some moving us to care for lesser things, others drawing us back from external actions.

<summary>This page explores the nature of Socrates’s personal daemon, explaining it as a divine-daemonic hybrid that guided him from within rather than through an external voice. It further categorizes daemons into different functional roles—such as purifying or creating—based on the specific gods they serve.</summary>

# PROCLUS. 1

It seems, therefore, that the daemon of Socrates, having obtained a property of this kind, is the cause of a purgative <note>cleansing or purifying</note> and undefiled life; yet it is ordered under this power of Apollo, who presides over all purification with a uniform virtue. By this virtue, therefore, the daemon separates Socrates from excessive commerce with the common crowd and gathers him into the inner sanctums of the soul and toward an action separated from lower things. For indeed, just as in the teachings of Orpheus <note>The mythical poet Orpheus, whose "Orphic hymns" were foundational to Neoplatonism.</note> Apollo presides over Bacchus, recalling him from his progression into the Titanic multitude <note>In Neoplatonic thought, Bacchus (Dionysus) represents the soul's descent into fragmentation/multiplicity, while Apollo represents the return to unity and the "intellectual" world.</note>, so also does the daemon of Socrates, who is a follower of Apollo. For our intellect is the offspring of the Apolline deity.

To know the substances of deities and souls belongs to a perfectly purified intellect. Commonly, however, we know their powers through their actions, and through these powers we infer their essences.

<margin>i</margin>
Among these things, Socrates promises Alcibiades that not the substance, but the power of the daemon will be known. For the divine Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus of Chalcis (c. 245–325 AD), a key Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> says that it is most difficult for us to contemplate the substances of daemons and of all those generally superior to us, unless we possess a perfectly purified intellect. Since even the essence of the soul is not easy for everyone to grasp; thus, only Timaeus <note>The narrator of Plato’s *Timaeus*, who describes the soul's creation and nature.</note> declared its entire essence. For what sort it is, is altogether divine and requires a long exposition for its declaration, as Socrates says in the *Phaedrus*. However, it is easy to explain the powers of the deities, for we perceive those very powers from the actions of which those forces are the immediate "mothers." For <term>Power</term> <note>original: *potentia*; here used as a technical term for the mediating bridge between an object's being (essence) and its manifestation (action).</note> is the middle ground between action and essence, being produced by the essence and itself producing the action. Furthermore, power itself has the greatest kinship with daemons. For everywhere, power holds the middle position, just like a daemon. And in the realm of <term>intelligible things</term> <note>things perceived by the mind alone, rather than the physical senses</note>, it joins the Father and the Intellect. For power exists simultaneously with the Father, while the Intellect exists from the Father. In intellectual matters, however, it couples actions with essences; action is the offspring of power, while essence gives birth to powers from itself. Therefore, those spirits that are middle between us and the gods are properly designated by the name of Power, as they possess the middle ground everywhere. For true essence and true "being" belong to the gods. Power, however, rightly ministering to the gods, has its place in daemons. Finally, action and effect, having progressed outward through their power, reside in us.

> The knowledge of future contingents is certain and necessary among those above <note>original: *supos*, likely a contraction for *superos*, referring to divine beings or gods.</note>;
> and the divine Iamblichus and that leader of ours <note>Likely referring to Syrianus, the teacher of Proclus.</note> thus inquire and resolve.
> How is it not absurd to determine the differences of knowledge from the nature of the things to be known, and not the other way around? Namely, knowledge—

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic discussion regarding how higher beings (gods and daemons) possess knowledge. It transitions from the previous page’s focus on the powers of daemons to a general rule of epistemology: that knowledge is shaped by the nature of the knower rather than the object known.</meta>

# ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.
### 49
<sig>g</sig>

...it is necessary to divide the things to be known according to the differences among those who know them. Thus, that which is eternal and divine by its very essence knows all things in an eternal and divine manner. That which is human knows in a human way. That which is indivisible <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "indivisible" refers to the higher, unified realm of Intellect, as opposed to the "divisible" world of matter and time.</note> surely knows indivisibly, or rather, it anticipates things that are divisible. That which is eternal knows even temporal things beyond the constraints of time. That which is rational knows rational things, and does so through the faculty of reason. From these points, it is clear that gods and daemons know indefinite things definitely, and unstable things in a stable and firm manner. Do we not see that many things currently unknown to the beings below us are known to us? For irrational beings are unable to grasp the nature of the universal itself. We, however, are able to infer it. Why then do we wonder any further that the higher beings firmly comprehend those things which we only guess at with ambiguous and fallacious knowledge? For our own weakness is not the judge of their power, just as the irrational creature below us lacks the judgment of our reason. Who would allow their own intelligence to be moved by the irrationality within us or outside of us? It would be absurd if a conjectural foreknowledge of the future could be found in some places, but a stable, determined, and indubitable knowledge could be found nowhere. For the very nature of things cannot take its starting point from the imperfect, the impure, or from things mixed with their opposite. If, however, our "guessing" at the future is a partner to ignorance and is not certain, where then is that pure knowledge of the future that exists through itself? Where has that pure essence—from which even the lower beings and those who desire it have received their substance—been allotted its place, if not among the higher beings?

->The higher beings advise us well, even if they foresee that we will not obey them.<-

<margin>a</margin> The Pythian Apollo <note>Apollo as the god of the Oracle at Delphi.</note> responded to Laius <note>The father of Oedipus in Greek mythology.</note> advising him not to beget a son, for otherwise he would be subjected to the violence of the daemons. Meanwhile, the god foresaw that Laius would not obey the oracle. But Phoebus <note>A common title for Apollo meaning "bright" or "pure."</note>, as a good being, proposed to him the choice of a better life. And Laius, for his part, did not cause the god to err, but because of his own ignorance, he was caught in the midst of future dangers. Indeed, all actions of upright men turn toward their own innermost depths. Therefore, if a man has acted beneficially and divinely, he already possesses his goal within his own action, even if nothing was perfected externally. In a similar way, daemons often act concerning us. Hence, divine things frequently seem to meet and even precede lower things; meanwhile, they do not depart from their own seats, but while they remain within themselves, they seem to "approach" us because of the aptitude of the receiver. For both in the invocations of the gods and in spontaneous encounters, divinity itself seems in a way to approach us—though it is we, clearly, who have set out toward it.

<summary>This page explains that gods and daemons possess certain knowledge of the future because they exist above time, using the tragic story of Laius to show that divine advice remains good even when humans choose to ignore it. It concludes that the gods do not "descend" to us; rather, we experience their presence when we elevate ourselves to their level.</summary>

For Nature herself, who shapes bodies for souls, provides instruments suited to them and indicates the images of souls in the bodies; through these signs, those skilled in this art <note>This refers to physiognomy, the ancient practice of judging a person's character from their physical appearance.</note> can grasp the natural dispositions of souls.

### ->A dialectical rule concerning necessary and contingent propositions.<-

Those skilled in dialectics <note>The art of logical argument and investigation.</note> are accustomed to say that even if someone has used ten thousand necessary propositions <note>original: "propositionibus necessariis"; statements that must be true by logical necessity.</note> but a single contingent one <note>original: "contingentem"; a statement that might or might not be true depending on circumstances.</note> has been included, the conclusion will entirely turn out like the inferior part. Similarly, if the very thing we must know has something of a material and unstable nature mixed within it, it undoubtedly causes our knowledge of this very thing to be indefinite and ambiguous. For knowledge of unstable things is not secure against refutation, but such things are barely grasped through a kind of resemblance. Such also is natural virtue, because everywhere that which is imperfect, being related to matter, is very easily changed.

Self-sufficiency itself belongs primarily to the gods; for the gods are good, and they are certain "super-essential" goodnesses <note>In Neoplatonism, the gods are "super-essential" because they exist above the level of "Being" or "Essence."</note> and the fullness of all beings. It is through them that sufficiency reaches all others—intellects, divine souls, daemons, and ourselves. While other things are indeed sufficient by a certain participation <note>An ancient concept where lower things "participate" in the qualities of higher things, like a reflection in a mirror participates in the light of the sun.</note>, the gods are so by their very substance. Wherefore, the common and immutable opinion designates sufficiency with blessedness; for those to whom it belongs to be well, it is also fitting for them to have sufficiency.

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic discussion of the soul's rank and its relationship to the divine. # ON THE SOUL AND THE GUARDIAN SPIRIT. <note>original: "DE ANIMA ET DAEMONE." The word "daemon" here refers to a tutelary or guardian spirit, not a "demon" in the modern malevolent sense.</note>

...the distribution of fates <note>original: "sortes"; the "lots" or portions assigned to beings by the divine order.</note> descends even to the level of souls. And we say that some gods are indeed fiery, others ethereal <note>referring to the pure "upper air" of the heavens.</note>, others celestial, and finally others are of the earth. Likewise, we say some souls are from the solar sphere, others from the sphere of Mercury, and others indeed from the lunar sphere. And this distribution of souls according to their location is such that a person might truly take pride in it. This nobility, however, is not based on earthly parents and cities.

<margin>More perfect</margin> More perfect souls were carried <note>original: "latae fuerunt"; suggesting an orbital or celestial motion.</note> around the more sublime gods and spirits, and vice versa.

<margin>Socrates</margin> Among these things, Socrates points out the difference between the good spirits <note>original: "daemonū"</note> who preside over us according to their essence and the powers they were allotted in the world. Likewise, the more perfect souls are subject to the more powerful spirits, are preserved by them, and are directed everywhere as is beneficial. The less perfect souls, however, are subject to inferior spirits. For just as souls are fated to certain gods according to their worth, so too are they rightly ordered under spirits. And just as the Father and Maker of the world <note>The "Demiurge" or divine craftsman who shapes the universe in Platonic philosophy.</note> provided gods as leaders, so he is said to have set spirits as caretakers over souls. For this reason, Socrates calls the spirit and god assigned to him his "caretaker" <note>original: "curatorem"</note>. He clearly asserts to Alcibiades <note>A young, ambitious Athenian statesman who was a student of Socrates.</note> that this spirit alone is the true caretaker of a human being. This spirit is also the author of happiness because of its wonderful power—a power that surely no human being is able to provide for us.

The order of things requires that after the Ideal Cause <note>The perfect, unchanging "Form" or blueprint of a thing.</note> there are things that always participate in that Idea and are entirely stable; next are things that are ordered but are always subject to change.

<margin>Amor</margin> Love <note>original: "Amor"</note> that depends on bodily beauty is changeable, because that beauty is also changeable. Indeed, it is a violation of divine law for an effect to exceed the condition of its causes or to turn out better than them. For even where causes are well-ordered, disordered effects are often born; where causes are stable, the outcomes are often shifting; where causes are determined, they frequently result in the indefinite. Therefore, it is all the more certain that effects lacking order and stability will arise from causes that themselves lack a steady state or order.

The series of the universe descends from above through such steps until it reaches the extremes, which are finally of such a nature that they can be changed and claim for themselves a natural tendency toward mutation. Take, for example, the "Just": first, there is Justice itself <note>The pure, abstract Form of Justice.</note>, which is not "just" by participating in something else; second, there is that which is the primary participant in it and is *always* a participant; finally, there is that which is a participant only sometimes, and at other times falls away from that participation.

<sig>g ii</sig>

It also argues that the stability of an effect (like love or justice) depends entirely on the stability of its metaphysical cause.</summary>

# PROCLUS. <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was one of the last major Greek philosophers of late antiquity, known for his systematic presentation of Neoplatonism.</note>

->PROCLUS.<-

For it was not right that Justice itself should remain sterile, imparting nothing of its own property to anything else. Truly, none of the primary beings are of such a kind; rather, sterility itself belongs only to **matter**, as it is the lowest of all things. Nor, again, was it right that what was first to be shared by others should be shared directly by those things which only participate in it occasionally. For from that which remains entirely simple and immutable, that which is composite and mutable is certainly too far removed. Therefore, it requires a middle link to bridge the contact between them. Nor, furthermore, should that which is shared by things capable of being always illuminated from above end its gift only at those things, lest this very thing, which is always suspended from its principles, should be the very end of the universe. It is therefore necessary to establish a <term>threefold order</term> <note>Neoplatonists often used triadic structures—such as the Unparticipated, the Participated, and the Participant—to explain how divine qualities reach physical reality.</note> as we have said, not only concerning **Justice**, but also concerning the **Beautiful**, the **Equal**, the **Similar**, and finally all the **forms** of things.

<margin>¶</margin> Just as the gods bring healing for the diseases of souls—that is, for their **sins**—and provide fruits in their proper seasons, benefiting the souls thereby, so also do divine men seek the right <term>opportunity</term> <note>original: "opportunitatem," translating the Greek *Kairos*, meaning the "opportune" or "perfect" moment rather than just chronological time.</note> for teaching. But the gods themselves determine the measures of these opportunities through an intellectual and divine form, while humans pursue them through knowledge. There are also those among men who hunt for these moments through the inspiration of a **spirit**. <note>original: "daemonica"; referring to a guardian spirit or *daemon*.</note> For the presence and familiarity of **good spirits** has a primary power within us for infallibly seizing the opportunity everywhere, which is exactly what happened to **Socrates**. Now, just as a place is properly destined for each body by nature itself, so some parts of time suit some actions and others suit others. And just as certain circuits of the whole world are the causes of fertility or sterility for animals and plants, so for individual actions, one time is suitable and another is not for performing this or that task. Such a time is the "opportunity" of any action, bringing the good and the purpose to those who act and to the results. For this reason, the **Pythagoreans** also named the **First Cause**, from which good comes to all things, as "Opportunity" itself, since it grants that all things should be perfected. On such an occasion, Socrates, relying on his spirit, approached **Alcibiades** to speak with him, at the very moment when Alcibiades was thinking of going to him to ask the same things. For all things are joined together in this way, and thus the communion of goods is perfected everywhere for all, while the perfecting causes are most ready to bestow their gifts.

<summary>Proclus explains the metaphysical necessity of "middle links" between the divine and the material, focusing on "Opportunity" (Kairos) as a divine timing that allows spirits to guide human actions, using Socrates and Alcibiades as examples.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of divine participation and how higher causes interact with lower recipients. # ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.

->g iii<-

Truly, those things that are about to receive participation are awakened, and those higher beings in turn extend a perfecting power; whereas the former have received from nature a power of aptitude <note>The "aptitude" (aptitudo) is the internal readiness or capacity of a lower being to receive the influence of a higher one.</note>. For power is twofold: one belongs to the **agent**, and the other to the **patient** <note>In this context, the "patient" is the recipient of an action, not a sick person.</note>. The former is the mother of action, while the latter is the receptacle of perfection. Furthermore, it is necessary that what is to be the effector be so exuberant in itself and so ready to act that, even if no recipient were present, it would still remain perfect through itself and be spontaneously moved to give. Likewise, it is necessary that what is to be the recipient yearns for participation and moves itself toward that perfecting power; even if that power is not present, the recipient has still been awakened toward participation through a supreme aptitude.

Since there are two kinds of causes—some indeed immobile and present everywhere to all things, while others are mobile and sometimes present to the things to be perfected, but at other times distant—and certainly intelligible things <note>The "intelligibles" are the higher, non-physical realities like Forms or Ideas.</note> are similarly present everywhere and always bestow their gifts upon all in the same way, whereas sensible things <note>Physical things perceived by the senses.</note> are present to participants and can in turn be absent—just as the sun is now present and fills the world with light, and then departs—when, I say, things are so, whenever an aptitude is present in the prospective participant toward any of the immobile causes, then that cause is also present and the work of the efficient cause is completed. For in such cases, only the unsuitability of the subjects usually prevents the gifts; because those things which are to give are always giving, and are always everywhere in like manner. Therefore, whatever has become apt suddenly becomes a participant in the cause.

But when something is made ready for one of the mobile causes, it often happens that even if the recipient is prepared, that which was meant to give is absent. For it is necessary that the cause also be present in the moment, since it requires a specific place for its giving. In general, as we have said, it is necessary through all communions of goods that these two things precede: both the perfecting power of the giver and the consummate aptitude of the recipient. The perfection of the giver must concur with the preparation of the recipient, and through such a concurrence, the efficient cause itself is brought to the recipient according to its essence. 

Furthermore, such a concurrence is not fortuitous, nor does anything ordered usually arise from disordered or uncoordinated things (like those things which flow together by chance); rather, it is necessary that such a harmony <note>original: "conspirationé"; a "breathing together" or cosmic sympathy.</note> occur in some cases through nature, and in others through the intellect. Likewise, it may arise elsewhere from a <term>daemonic cause</term> <note>A "daemon" in Neoplatonism is a mediating spirit between gods and humans, not an evil "demon."</note>, or elsewhere rather from a divine one. Indeed, it was under this condition that **Socrates** opportunely met with **Alcibiades** <note>This refers to the beginning of Plato's dialogue *Alcibiades I*, where Socrates claims a divine sign told him to wait for the right moment to speak to the young Alcibiades.</note> for the same purpose; and a **good daemon** acted as the cause of this opportune meeting, determining the right moment <note>original: "opportunitaté", referring to the Greek concept of *Kairos*, or the "opportune moment."</note> for Socrates to encounter him. For opportunity itself, originating from divine things above, proceeds all the way to the lowest extremes; and some opportunities indeed...

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic discussion of how the soul interacts with divine influences. # PROCLUS

...unity is determined by the gods. Another kind is demonic; another is fatal <note>Governed by Fate or *Fatum*.</note>; and another is fortuitous. For Fortune, as it is said, and Opportunity govern all human affairs.

->The images of those things you had seen more intently in your homeland,<-
->you follow here before all others.<-

<margin>a</margin> Our souls wander here around the images of those things they saw in the first place <note>Referring to the Platonic "homeland" of the soul—the realm of Forms or the heavens where the soul exists before incarnation.</note>, and they are more strongly affected by those images whose archetypes <note>The original "examples" or divine Forms.</note> they had more intently contemplated there. For some souls are suited to some spectacles, and others to others. Therefore, some dwell upon certain images, and others upon others; for they love the likenesses of those things they had inspected in that higher realm.

Truly, those who were once the attendants of great Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus, the king of the gods, who leads the celestial procession in Plato’s *Phaedrus*.</note> on high, and lived together with him—who holds the leading rank among the twelve princes of the universe—these souls, having surely set out according to the form of their god, even here desire a commanding way of life. However, they are often ignorant of what is truly imperial, and instead they pursue the mere appearance of leadership among earthly images. If they happen to find wise teachers, this inclination leads them toward salvation through a return to the celestial realms. But if they linger too long among these earthly images, they decline into tyranny. Hence, Socrates says in the *Republic* <note>Specifically referring to the Myth of Er in Book X of Plato’s *Republic*, where souls choose their next lives.</note> that souls recently arrived from the heavens most especially choose "commanding" lives. For since they have only recently traveled with the celestial gods and inspected their powers ruling over all, they desire a life similar to theirs, ruling over others. And while many abuse this inclination, very few use it rightly. Plato establishes the **contemplative** life as the most excellent. The second is the **ambitious** life; the third is the **pleasurable** or **greedy** life. Souls coming from the heavens who were educated most rightly choose the contemplative life. Those coming from heaven but educated poorly choose the ambitious life; the rest, coming from the earth, choose the others.

->It is a natural conviction in all people that the gods<-
->know the hidden things of the soul.<-

All humans naturally speak their innermost thoughts, passions, and desires to the gods; they are clearly persuaded through unchanging preconceptions that divinity itself knows all things—even the hidden movements of our souls. Certainly, every bond and community formed by reason requires the presence of God. For what else unites many things and gathers together those things that are separate, if not divinity?

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic discussion of the soul's descent and its relationship to the divine order. # CONCERNING THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON
<sig>g iiij</sig>

### God confirms our free will by His providence.

<margin>d</margin>
They <note>Referring to the divine powers or daemons mentioned in the header.</note> set before souls various lives, and once the souls have chosen, they determine by a fixed lot whatever conditions are suited to those chosen lives. In this way, the freedom of the will is contained within the midst of providence; it is moved and determined from that source, and it revolves within that center. These matters are clearly described in the *Republic* <note>Plato’s *Republic*, specifically Book X.</note>, where the prophet <note>In the Myth of Er, the "Prophet" or spokesperson for the Fates who organizes the choosing of lives.</note> sets lives before the souls, taking the lots from the lap of Lachesis <note>The Fate who represents the past and determines the length of life's thread.</note>, <note>original: "atque clamans inter animas o animæ diurnæ & cætera."</note> and crying out among the souls, "O ephemeral souls," and so forth. Indeed, the proposal of lives is made from Lachesis through the intermediary of the prophet. However, the choice regarding the lives proposed there belongs to the souls themselves. Now, the prophet there—anticipating all the choices of the souls within himself—only then throws forth the lots. Surely, that which seems unstable and indefinite in this world is always previously comprehended in the higher and more perfect realms according to a single limit, and in a stable and orderly manner.

### Three opinions of Plato.

<margin>e</margin>
From the words of Plato we gather three things here: first, that evil itself is to be judged as entirely worse than non-existence. Second, that the separation of the soul from the body frees us from the evils that circulate in this decaying region <note>The "sublunar" realm of change and death.</note>, and from the obstacles that here prevent the achievement of a suitable goal. Third, that the appetites of the souls themselves have the greatest power over the forms of their lives; we are not such that we are formed and moved only by external things. For we bring forth choices from ourselves, through which we live our lives.

### Higher beings hold with certain judgment things that are uncertain in reality.

<margin>■</margin>
You will receive from this an admirable opinion: namely, that those things which are more excellent do, in a uniform way, everywhere anticipate inferior things, yet the inferior things never equal the power of the superior. Likewise, the knowledge of higher beings firmly comprehends within itself the actions of lower beings. However, the knowledge of lower beings can never comprehend the total action of the superior. That which is higher receives nothing from the inferior into itself, just as the heavens do not receive any "passion" <note>In the sense of being acted upon or changed by external force.</note> or change from the things below them. Neither does an immovable cause <note>The Divine or the First Cause.</note> admit anything worldly into itself from the motion of worldly things. Nor do those things which are eternal admit anything within themselves from things acting in time. Finally, that which is necessary—while it knows all things—does not undergo change even in the act of knowing that which is "contingent" <note>Things that might or might not happen; "chance" events.</note>.

It emphasizes that higher divine knowledge remains unaffected by the change and decay of the physical world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Proclus's Neoplatonic commentary, moving from the role of divine providence and free will to the logical and metaphysical methods of the soul's return to the divine. It explores how human reasoning mirrors the soul’s cosmic journey of descent into matter and its eventual ascent back to the Good.</meta>

->PROCLUS<-

# Double argumentation through negation and affirmation: the former resolves, the latter composes, and both agree with the very nature of the soul.

<margin>1. 8. 4</margin>
Alcibiades is unable to name a time when he thought he did not know those things about which he now deliberates; certainly, he never sought them out, nor did he ever learn them from teachers. But if he neither sought them nor received them from others, he surely neither learned nor discovered them. If he neither learned nor discovered them, he rightly does not know them; and if he does not know them, he is not a good judge in matters where he cannot assign a time when he thought himself ignorant. You see, then, how if the debate is conducted in this way, we proceed sometimes by composition <note>In Greek logic, *synthesis*; the process of building up from simple parts to complex wholes.</note> and sometimes by resolution <note>In Greek logic, *analysis*; the process of breaking down complex ideas into their primary principles.</note>: speaking by composition in the affirmative, and by resolution in the negative. This composition and resolution perfectly suit the nature of the soul, which indeed falls from perfections to lower states through the "composition" of reasonings and the adding on of certain foreign garments <note>A Neoplatonic metaphor for the layers of the "astral body" or material influences the soul gathers as it descends through the planetary spheres into the physical world.</note>, until it is enclosed in this dense and solid bond <note>The physical body.</note>. Conversely, it rises back to the heights through resolution and the casting off of those things that disagree with its own nature, until—emerging naked, as the sacred scriptures <note>Likely referring to the *Chaldean Oracles* or Orphic hymns, which Proclus regarded as divinely inspired.</note> teach—it is joined with the Forms <term>speciebus</term> <note>The eternal, archetypal patterns of things which exist entirely apart from physical matter.</note> which are entirely separate from matter. Therefore, argumentation proceeding through affirmation descends from perfections to imperfections, while that proceeding through negation conversely ascends.

# The Good itself, although it surpasses every intellectual essence, nevertheless reaches down even to the lowest things.

The Good itself—standing in itself as something above intellectual nature (if it is permitted to say so)—descends even to the last of things, illuminating, preserving, and adorning all things, while meanwhile turning them back toward itself. First, it is present to those things that truly exist <note>The highest realm of pure Being and the Forms.</note>. Second, it is present to divine souls. Third, to the deities presiding over the human race. Fourth, to our souls, and then to animals and plants, and to all bodies. Finally, even to formless matter—the very dregs of things—the Good itself secretly and ineffably performs its own gift to all before every order. All things participate in it everywhere, each in a different way according to its own order; and insofar as each is naturally suited, they carry away a portion of the Good from there—some more weakly, others more effectively; some more uniformly, others in a more divided state. Furthermore, some possess it eternally, others changeably; for just as more divine things have an indivisible essence, so they possess the Good undivided and unified. But those things that have departed further from the principles, being placed in a certain distance and division, acquire their own good. Wherefore, such things, in a certain gathering striving toward the same end and by mutual...
