<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic discussion of how the soul overcomes its limitations. It moves from the logical processes of the soul to the necessity of communal cooperation and the divine assistance provided by Mercury (Hermes) in the pursuit of knowledge and the recovery of innate truths.</meta>

->PROCLUS<-

# ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT.

<note>original: "DE ANIMA ET DAEMONE." In this context, "daemon" refers to a guiding spirit or intermediary divinity, not an evil "demon."</note>

<sig>y 4</sig>

...they completely lack harmonious cooperation. For since each individual thing does not possess the "sufficiency" <note>A technical term in Neoplatonism (*autarkeia*) meaning self-sufficiency or completeness, which belongs perfectly only to the One.</note> that constitutes the element of the Good, it must at least supply the defect of its nature through mutual communion. And so, it strengthens its own weakness (which was caused by division) through this cooperation. It is for this very reason that individual men, who are weak on their own, are gathered together into a common council, thereby joining their divided minds to one another, and striving to kindle a single light from many sparks. Indeed, a multitude can never provide for its own common benefit by itself unless it is organized around some single prevailing principle. This can be observed across the entire order of things: namely, that multiplicity is everywhere born from the One, and must be called back to that utterly absolute Unity through its kinship with the One. The Divine Good has therefore implanted a desire for itself in all things, so that through this longing it might be able to bestow its benefits upon us.

<margin>•</margin>
## Mercury is the author of discovery and instruction for us.

Mercury <note>The Roman name for the Greek god Hermes, the patron of messengers, interpreters, and secret knowledge.</note>, as the messenger of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus.</note>, explains the paternal will to our souls. In this way, he provides us with instruction, and likewise, as the author of inquiry, he grants the gift of discovery to his students. Now, when instruction comes into souls from the powers above, it is superior to discovery. But when it comes from our equals—such as from other men who merely awaken the cognitive power within us—it is inferior to discovery. Discovery, therefore, occupies a middle ground, being suited to the soul's nature, which is "self-moving" <note>A core Platonic definition of the soul: that which moves itself, unlike matter which must be moved by another.</note>. For through discovery, the very power that lives and operates within us by its own nature is most clearly revealed. Instruction, however, has a double character: it fulfills the soul according to a "better" mode when it comes from superior causes; but it awakens the vital power within us according to a "lesser" mode when it comes from those things outside of us that are themselves moved by something else. Moreover, the gods themselves often declare through their manifest presence and explanations that a certain knowledge of things is born in us from the heavens. They show the order of the universe to our souls and run before us like guides on the journey itself, hanging out processional torches as a signal for our path.

<margin>•</margin>
## Because of the innate notions of things, we think we know everything.

Our souls are weighed down by a double ignorance: they think they know a great deal because of the notions of things implanted in them from the beginning <note>The theory of *anamnesis* (recollection), suggesting the soul is born with innate knowledge of the divine Forms but forgets them at birth.</note>, yet they are actually ignorant because of forgetfulness. Therefore, he who is weighed down by this double ignorance seeks nothing further, just as the wise man himself does not "seek." In this respect, such a person is in a way similar to the wise man—just as matter is similar to God through a kind of "dissimilar similarity." For as some rightly teach: just as matter is formless, so too is God; and both are utterly infinite and unknown...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the soul's ascent. ->PROCLUS<-

Although all these things agree with the Divine according to what is better, they belong to the nature of matter according to what is worse.

## The soul becomes like the Intellect through the acquisition of knowledge; through double ignorance, it becomes like matter.

<margin>a</margin>Through knowledge itself, the soul indeed emerges as similar to the Intellect <note>original: "intellectui." In Neoplatonism, the Intellect (Nous) is the realm of pure, eternal forms.</note> by grasping that which is knowable through the very act of knowing, just as the Intellect grasps that which is intelligible. However, through **double ignorance** <note>A Socratic concept where one not only lacks knowledge but is also unaware of that lack, falsely believing they possess knowledge.</note> it becomes similar to matter; for just as matter appears to possess all things while in truth it possesses nothing, so too does the soul, when suffering from double ignorance, seem to itself to have what it does not. Consequently, there are two types of knowledge for souls. One is indistinct, occurring through simple and bare understanding. The other is clearly articulated, possessing true science and free from ambiguity. For we seem, as he himself says, to know all things as if in a dream, and yet to be ignorant of those same things in our waking state. This is because we possess the "reasons" <note>original: "rationes." Refers to the *logoi*, or the essential blueprints of things imprinted on the soul.</note> of things within our very essence—and from this source, we breathe out our understandings of them—yet in our actual practice and production of knowledge, we do not possess them sufficiently. Therefore, time does not precede the notion of the "species" <note>original: "specierum." Here meaning the eternal Forms or Types.</note> that are innate and constant within our essence, for we have held these from eternity. But time *does* precede the knowledge that is produced through the distinction and application of reason. Thus, we are able to assign a specific time when we first received this knowledge. For example, I might know what a circle is in itself, but I learned what the "form" of justice is at one time, and similarly for other things. These are the things of which we have knowledge through actual practice. Therefore, regarding the thing itself—the object we are recollecting—we do not fully remember the "time" of its origin. But regarding the act of **reminiscence** <note>original: "Reminiscentiæ." This refers to the Platonic theory of *Anamnesis*, where learning is actually the soul "remembering" truths it knew before being born into a body.</note> itself, there is certainly a determined point in time.

## The seven ages of man, corresponding to the seven planets.

<margin>a</margin>The order of the ages of life follows the order of the universe. The **first age** follows the power of the **Moon**; for then we live according to our nutritive and growth-oriented faculties. The **second age** is that of **Mercury**, when we apply ourselves to the study of letters, the lyre, wrestling, and similar games. The **third** is the age of **Venus**, when the limbs swell with the "seeds" of life and we are immediately urged toward procreation. The **fourth** is the **Solar** age, for then vigor reigns and the perfection of one's age hastens; this is the middle of life. The **fifth** is the **Martial** age (of Mars), in which we strive for power and victories. The **sixth** is the **Jovian** age (of Jupiter), which requires prudence and a life of action and civic duty. The **seventh** is the **Saturnine** age (of Saturn), in which it is natural to cease from procreation and to separate oneself from bodily concerns, transferring oneself to another, incorporeal life. The higher things are everywhere...

<meta>catchword: of the lower things (inferiorum)</meta>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the soul relates to higher powers. ->ABOUT THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.<-

[Higher beings] uniquely and more excellently embrace the cognitions of lower things. For whatever the sense perceives under material conditions, the imagination perceives in an immaterial way; what opinion considers without a cause, science <note>original: "scientia." Here meaning certain, causal knowledge rather than modern empirical science.</note> comprehends through a cause. In this way, more excellent things always contain within themselves, through absolute eminence, the entire cognition appropriate to lower things. Therefore, nothing of ours is hidden from the **daemon** <term>daemon: a guardian spirit or guiding divinity that mediates between the human and divine realms, acting as a personal overseer of a soul's destiny</term> appointed over us—neither the movements of the mind, nor natural power, nor accidental change. Rather, he uniquely surveys and governs all things. In this universe, all the ends of all things arranged within it lead toward the very end of the world. For as Timaeus <note>Referencing Plato's dialogue, the *Timaeus*, which describes the creation of the cosmos by a Divine Craftsman.</note> says, so that the world might be perfect, all living beings, both divine and perishable, were born. Similarly, in a well-ordered city, the ends of all parts serve the end of civic skill. Likewise, just as each thing involved in the process of generation has its being according to a single form and thus is not infinite, the intelligible itself is all things, since it possesses the causes of sensible things. So, too, any private craftsman is for the most part ignorant, even if once skilled; but the statesman is absolutely prudent. For he knows both his own end and the ends of others, and directs the other arts toward the single life of the city.

Through the harmony reigning in heaven, the higher beings harmoniously temper all remaining things.

<margin>c</margin>
The heaven is full of concord and the harmony of motions. Next, the divinities <term>numina: divine powers or spirits that inhabit or govern parts of the cosmos</term> superior to us participate in the harmony preceding from heaven. After this, a well-ordered human life receives from there a consonance of character and a harmony of actions; the gift of those same higher beings descends even to the brutes and plants. For these also naturally participate in harmony. For the higher beings contain and perfect all worldly things by a harmonic principle, and adapt them to each other and to the world. Indeed, they harmonize the body to the **Intellect** by means of the soul. To the "circuit of identity" <note>original: "circuitui identitatis." A reference to the "Circle of the Same" in the World Soul, representing eternal, unchanging truth.</note> which remains constant, they assign generation by means of the "circuit of alterity" <note>original: "circuitum alteritati." The "Circle of the Different," representing the changing, physical world of time and becoming.</note> (as I might call it). Finally, they bind earth to fire through intermediate links. Furthermore, they cultivate every soul with harmonic principles. And they join every body everywhere with similar measures. And they perform every movement everywhere with musical measures. Therefore, the musical disposition in us is a gift of the Muses, though it is the lowest reflection of them. For the artistic and contemplative dispositions within us have gods as their overseers and derive their origin from them.

# PROCLUS.

**He who is ignorant of the ultimate purpose, is ignorant of every cause.**

Ignorance of the final cause <term>final cause: the ultimate purpose or "why" for which a thing exists or is done</term> regarding any matter ensures that the other causes pertaining to it are similarly misunderstood. For the end (the goal) is the primary, most important, and most powerful cause; it is for the sake of this goal that efficient causes <term>efficient cause: the agent or force that brings something into being; the "how" or "who"</term> act, and for which things that are made are brought to completion. For this reason, Timaeus <note>The central figure in Plato’s dialogue of the same name, which discusses the creation of the universe.</note> considers such a cause to be the most excellent to be held among the wise. 

Plato teaches in the *Sophist* <note>One of Plato's dialogues, where he defines the philosopher vs. the sophist and discusses the nature of being and non-being.</note> that there is a twofold depravity of the soul. One of these is ignorance, which falls within the rational part of the soul; the other is discord, where the irrational part clashes with the rational. This sort of discord is a disease of the soul, while ignorance is a deformity. Since reason holds the order of a "form" <note>original: "speciei." Here meaning a defining blueprint or ideal type.</note> within the soul as a whole, the depravity of reason is rightly called the soul’s ugliness, just as the virtue of reason is the soul’s beauty. For ignorance arises because of the dominance of irrational power, whereas knowledge arises from the command of the rational part. This deformity of the soul occurs when reason is overcome—namely, when the soul produces actions that are clumsy, incongruous, ineffective, and unfit for their ultimate purpose. 

In cultivating the soul, once impediments are removed, one must move the soul entirely toward contemplation. For the knowledge of truth is inherent within us, but we are prevented from noticing it by the passions arising from our life in the world of change <note>original: "ex generatione." Literally "from generation," referring to the physical realm of birth, death, and material flux.</note> which stand in our way. I mean passions such as forgetfulness, mere opinion, false imaginations, and immoderate desires. Once these are expelled, the mind must be turned back into itself, and in this way, it suddenly enjoys the truth.

**The end of war is justice. The end of peace is friendship, which is more desirable than justice.**

Indeed, the goal of war is justice. But the goal of peace is a certain other, more excellent good: namely, friendship and union. For this is the end of all virtue, as the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who emphasized harmony and number as the basis of the universe.</note> teach and Aristotle confirms: once everyone has been made friends, we no longer have need of justice—specifically, when "mine" and "thine" have been abolished. Even if all people were just, there would still be a need for friendship to bring them together. 

That injustice is the origin of wars is demonstrated by war itself, which material forms wage against one another. For the hot fights against the cold—not when they are separated by space, but when one strives to occupy the "seat" or place of the other. Since a form lacks its own place in the material world, it rightly resists anything coming from the outside that tries to thrust it from its position. Because of this, the underlying principles <note>original: "rationes." In Neoplatonic thought, these are the "logoi" or spiritual blueprints that exist harmoniously in nature.</note> implanted in nature run together without rebellion, for each one persists within itself. However, because material forms cannot exist apart from matter, they rightly struggle over their "shared lodging," since matter cannot receive two contrary forms at the same time without confusion.

# ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT <note>original: "DE ANIMA ET DAEMONE." The word "daemon" here refers to a guiding spirit or a higher level of the soul, not a "demon" in the modern sense.</note>.

### How the soul is variously clothed in descending, and in turn is purified and returns.

<margin>d</margin>The descent of the soul into the body has indeed separated it from the divine souls, from which it used to be filled with intelligence, power, and purity. However, it has joined the soul to generation <note>The cycle of birth and physical change.</note>, nature, and material things, by which it has been imbued with oblivion, error, and ignorance. For as the soul descends, various "garments" and multiform ways of life from this world are attached to it, which pull it into a decaying composition and stand in the way of the contemplation of separate things <note>Non-material, divine realities that exist apart from the physical world.</note>. Therefore, the soul must be led back from here to that ever-watchful and upright nature, and it must prune away the secondary and tertiary powers that grew during its descent—just like the sea-god Glaucus <note>A mythological figure who became a sea-god; over time, his body became encrusted with seaweed, rocks, and shells, symbolizing the soul's accumulation of material "layers" that hide its true form.</note> grew covered in weeds, rocks, and shells. It must restrain those impulses that carry it outward and remember once again the essence of separate things and the divine nature from which its descent began, and toward which it is fitting for all life to strive.

->The soul is self-moving; the body is moved from outside. But because of their mutual exchange, each undergoes the condition of the other.<-

<margin>a</margin>The soul is, by its very essence, self-moving, but when joined to the body it has also become, in a certain way, moved from the outside. For just as the soul, by its presence, gave the body a final trace of the power to move itself, so too has the soul—because of its companionship with the body—taken on the mark of being moved from the outside. Therefore, because of its self-moving power, the soul is fertile, inclined toward discovery, and gives birth to reasons and sciences. But because of its condition of being moved from the outside, it frequently needs to be stirred by other things. Now, the perfections of the soul are more ready for discovery, while its imperfections need more external supports. For the former are more self-moving and share less in a degraded nature, while the latter move themselves less, suffering more of a bodily fate. Nevertheless, when these too make progress—rising, that is, from the body and gathering themselves out of matter—they immediately become more fertile and inventive regarding those things in which they were previously sterile and uncertain. This earlier state was due to a clumsy sluggishness of life caused by contact with matter and a filthy torpor contracted from the realm of generation. We, therefore, by observing the "mean" <term>mean: the middle state (mediocritas), or the proper balance of the soul's nature</term> of rational nature, assign the causes of its condition pertaining especially to its habits, its imperfections, and its perfections; and we judge such paths to lead to their perfection. Those who, in assigning reasons for these things, do not observe the mean at all, but either rise too high or sink too low, wander far from the truth of the soul. For we do not approve of those who...

# PROCLUS <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Plato.</note>

...[they believe] that the soul, having fallen into a moist body <note>Ancient philosophers often associated the physical body, especially in infancy, with "moisture" or "humidity" that clouded the soul's fire or intelligence.</note> and being hindered by that obstacle, is at the beginning senseless. However, as the moisture gradually evaporates due to innate heat and becomes more tempered, the prudent power of the soul grows stronger. Yet, this mode of perfection must be judged as bodily and material, for it assumes that the perfection of the soul proceeds from the tempering of the body. In truth, the soul possesses its own substance prior to the elements and the whole cycle of generation <note>The physical world of birth, death, and change.</note>. It is a kind of life that is mixed with neither the body nor nature. 

Nor, on the other hand, do we accept those who think that the soul is a certain part of the divine essence, and that this part is entirely unlike the whole <note>Meaning it remains perfect despite the "lower" state of the body.</note> and always perfect. They claim that turmoil and disturbances only concern the "animal" part of us. Those who say these things imagine a soul that is always perfect, always knowing, never needing recollection <note>term: recollection (reminiscentia); the Platonic idea that "learning" is actually the soul remembering knowledge it possessed before birth.</note>, always free from passion, and never corrupted. And yet, in the *Timaeus*, Plato says that the essence of our soul is not constituted entirely from the primary ranks <note>The highest, most divine levels of reality.</note>, as the higher souls are, but is composed of second and third ranks. 

And Socrates says in the *Phaedrus* that our powers are mixed with opposing goods and are full of mutual discord. For this reason, sometimes the better parts are accustomed to prevail, and sometimes the worse. What more? Does he not say himself that our charioteer <note>In Plato's famous allegory, the soul is a charioteer driving two horses—one noble and one rebellious.</note> is also sometimes corrupted, writing clearly that many souls go "lame" due to the depravity of the charioteer itself? Likewise, many lose their wings. Indeed, the power of the charioteer within us is more ancient [than the body]. It is this power which remembers divine things and uses the second and third powers as servants. We are plainly taught this in the *Phaedrus*. 

Certainly, as we have said, we must preserve the measures of the soul, assigning reasons for the soul's perfection and progress that are neither entirely derived from the bodily nor the divine, so that we may be true interpreters of Plato. We must not twist the philosopher’s words to fit our own opinions. Therefore, since the soul is at one time imperfect and again is perfected, and suffers the forgetting of divine things and then remembers them again, it is clear that time also contributes to its perfection. For in what way could it be transferred from imprudence to prudence, and into virtue from depravity, unless it worked these changes through time? For every change is acted out in a span of time. Let these things be said generally concerning the perfection of souls. From this, however, let us accept that he who knows what is just must have at some time passed from ignorance into the knowledge of it; he does not always have the logic of justice ready at hand. In this, we are unlike those beings superior to us. For we are born imperfect from the beginning. Nor, again, because of the change of the body itself, [does]

# ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT <note>Original: "DE ANIMA ET DAEMONE." In Neoplatonic thought, a "daemon" or spirit is a guiding entity or a level of being between gods and men, not an evil "demon."</note>

<meta>Catchword: knowledge</meta>

...that the knowledge of the just also falls to our lot. For our essence is not corporeal, nor is it constituted of material things. It is necessary that all changes of the soul be measured by time. Whence **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC) argued that change and movement are inextricably linked to time.</note> also places change in the soul—according to both **act** <note>The expression of a capability.</note> and **habit** <note>term: habit (habitus); a stable disposition or state of being, such as having the skill of geometry even when not practicing it.</note> and their opposites—within the realm of the temporal. Therefore, it is doubted by no one that the soul, when joined to the body and passing from the depravity of ignorance into their opposites, requires an interval of time. 

Some, indeed, judge that the soul itself, remaining apart within itself, does not require time for its actions, but on the contrary, that time is created from the soul itself. However, I believe this requires some further reasoning. For time is twofold: one is born together with natural life and the corporeal movement of the universe; the other proceeds through incorporeal life. This latter time, therefore, measures the circuits of even the divine souls. Again, it completes the actions of our souls even when they are separated [from the body]. However, according to that time which is extended along with natural life, it measures our life lived in conjunction with the body—but it in no way measures the life of the soul living according to its own nature. 

Yet, there is some knowledge within us that exists before all time. There is also that which occurs within time. **Socrates**, therefore, looking at knowledge expressed according to the **act**, inquires what time existed before this. **Alcibiades**, however, possessing at least that knowledge placed within his **essence** <note>Alcibiades is a character in Plato's dialogues; Socrates often tries to prove that Alcibiades already "knows" justice but has forgotten it.</note>—because of which he thinks he even knows those things which he does not—is unable to assign a time when he first received it. For we have held this knowledge from eternity <note>original: "ab aeuo"; referring to the *Aevum*, a state of existence between time and eternity proper.</note>. 

Wherefore, if one person speaks of one kind of knowledge and another speaks of another, both are true: namely, that time preceded knowledge [in practice], and yet you do not have a ready time that you can affirm preceded knowledge [in essence]. For before knowledge that is not yet fully realized, there is no time; but before knowledge perfected in act, time existed.

->**Many steps exist through which we ascend from the multitude to the One by contemplating.**<-

**Plato** and **Pythagoras** command us to flee the "multitude" <note>The "multitude" refers to the chaotic variety of the physical world and the distracted mind, as opposed to the "One," which represents ultimate truth and simplicity.</note> so that we may attain the simplest truth. Indeed, we must flee the multitude of the **exterior people** <note>The literal crowds and social distractions of the world.</note> who distract and deceive us in many ways. But much more so must we flee the multitude of the **interior people**; for these distract and deceive us even more. 

1. First, therefore, flee the varied multitude of the **passions** <note>original: "affectuum"; the emotional disturbances of the soul.</note>. 
2. Second, flee the multitude of the **senses**. 
3. Third, of **imaginations**. 
4. Fourth, of **independent opinions**. 

For every "multitude" already mentioned is so diverse within itself that some parts are contrary to others in any given respect. Whence it is better to betake oneself to the **sciences** <note>term: sciences (scientias); here meaning structured branches of philosophical or mathematical knowledge.</note>. In these, the multitude no longer possesses any contrariety. For even if passions are contrary to passions, senses to senses, imaginations to imaginations, and opinions to opinions, yet no branch of knowledge is contrary to another branch of knowledge.

# PROCLUS <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was one of the last major Greek philosophers and a head of the Neoplatonic Academy in Athens. His work sought to synthesize Platonic thought into a complex, unified system.</note>

...is found. In this multitude of propositions and notions, let us therefore gather the number of sciences into one, and connect them with a certain single bond. For they are so far from being contrary to one another that even one notion serves another; all the lower sciences serve the superior one and have their beginnings from them. Here, moreover, it is necessary to proceed from the many sciences—which presuppose a single higher one—to that one itself, which presupposes nothing further, and to rightly refer all things to this first science. 

After the study of science, however, it is expedient to lay aside compositions, divisions, and multiform discourses <note>term: discourse (discursus); in medieval and Neoplatonic logic, this refers to "discursive reasoning," the step-by-step process of logical thought, as opposed to direct intuition.</note>, and from there to ascend to the intellectual life and its simple intuitions and perceptions. For science is not the highest peak of knowledge. Above it is the **intellect**—I do not mean only the intellect that is separated from the soul, but also the very illumination of the soul infused from that source. Of this, **Aristotle** also says that it is the intellect by which we know the terms <note>Original: "intellectum esse, quo terminos cognoscimus." This refers to Aristotle’s *Posterior Analytics*, where he argues that the basic principles or "terms" of logic cannot be proven by logic itself, but must be grasped by a direct intellectual intuition (*nous*).</note>. And **Timaeus** <note>The main speaker in Plato’s *Timaeus*, a dialogue concerning the creation of the universe.</note> says that this very thing never happens in anything other than the soul. Ascending, therefore, to this intellect, let us contemplate the intelligible essence together with it, beholding the indivisible and simple kinds of beings with simple and indivisible perceptions. 

But indeed, after the venerable intellect, it is right finally to awaken the very highest existence of the soul (so to speak), through which we are "one" and under which our multitude is united. For just as through our intellect we touch the divine intellect, so also through our own "one" we may reach the first **One**—from whom unity is in all things—and, as it were, touch the "flower of our essence" <note>A famous Proclean metaphor: the "flower" (*anthos*) of the soul is its most divine part, the point where the human soul meets the ultimate source of all being.</note>. 

By this "one" of our own, we are most greatly joined to the divine. For everywhere, like can only be grasped by like: things knowable by science; things intelligible by the intellect; and the most unified measures of beings by the unity of the soul. Now indeed, this unity, through which there is action itself, is the summit of our actions; through this, we are made divine. Namely, when fleeing all multitude, we take refuge in our own unity and are made one, acting in a unified manner. 

Thus far, we have advised that multitude must be fled by proceeding through the degrees of knowledge in order. Next, let us proceed similarly through the degrees of knowable things to prove the same point. Flee all sensible things <note>Things perceived by the physical senses.</note>, for they are crowded together, divisible, and utterly changeable. Therefore, they cannot be held by pure knowledge. From these, therefore, transfer yourself to the incorporeal essence. For every sensible thing has only an accidental unity, and is dispersed through itself and full of infinity. Because of this, its "good" is divisible, accidental, and distant from itself—departing from itself and residing in a foreign seat. When, however, one has ascended...

### ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT <note>Original: "DE ANIMA ET DAEMONE." The word "Daemon" here does not refer to an evil spirit, but to a "daimon"—a guiding spirit or intermediary being in Greek philosophy.</note>

...[once you are led] there and have been placed among incorporeal things, you will behold that order of the soul which is mobile above bodies, acting of its own accord through itself, possessing its own substance in and from itself, yet multiplied and anticipating within itself a certain appearance of essence to be divided among bodies. There you will indeed see many relationships of reasons, various proportions, and many bonds. Likewise, you will see certain wholes: both parts and soulful circles, and a multiform variety of powers. Furthermore, you will see the perfection of souls—not eternal, not existing entirely as a whole all at once, but unfolded in time and turning in **discursive movements**. <note>term: discursive movements (discursionibus); this refers to "discursive reasoning," where the mind moves step-by-step from one premise to another, rather than grasping the whole truth instantly.</note> Such is the nature of the soul.

After the multiplicity belonging to souls, bring yourself to the **intellect** <note>term: intellect (intellectus); in this context, it refers to the Divine Mind (Nous), a level of reality above the soul where all truths are known simultaneously and eternally.</note> and the intellectual realms, so that you may possess the unity of things. There, indeed, be a contemplator of that nature. Behold a nature remaining in eternity, a vigorous life, a vigilant intelligence that lacks nothing of life, which does not require the cycles of time for its perfection. When you have inspected these things, and seen by how great an interval they are better than souls, you may then ask whether there is any multiplicity there and, since the intellect is one, whether it is also universal. Likewise, since it is uniform, whether it is additionally multiform. You will indeed find it to be so. 

When, therefore, you have perceived that intellectual multiplicity—though it is entirely indivisible and united—lead yourself back again to another principle. And above the intellectual essences, consider their unities. And finally, having progressed this far to the unity absolute from all things, you will have left behind all multiplicity and reached the very fountain of the **Good** itself. <note>In Neoplatonism, "the Good" or "the One" is the ultimate source of all existence, beyond even being and intellect.</note>

Since it is clear through these steps that the perfection of the soul is achieved specifically by fleeing all multiplicity—both external and internal, and the multiplicity of the universe itself—we can also conclude here that our souls do not merely gather knowledge from sensible things, nor find the "whole" and the "one" from particular and divided things, but rather bring forth learning from their innermost depths and correct what is imperfect in apparent things. For it is not fitting to think that those things which truly *are not* <note>meaning material objects, which are considered "non-being" compared to eternal truths</note> are the primary causes of the knowledge existing in the soul. Nor should things which disagree among themselves, and which require the soul’s reasons and arguments and are ambiguous, entirely precede a knowledge that remains the same. Nor can changing reasons produce truths consisting in the One. Nor can the indeterminate be the cause of determinate intelligence. Therefore, it is not fitting to receive the truth of eternal things from the "many," nor the judgment and discrimination of universals from sensible things, nor the judgment and sentence of good things from things lacking reason. But it is necessary for the soul to enter into itself...

# PROCLUS
80

...[the intellect], there to search for the true, the good, and the true reasons for all things. For the essence of the soul itself is full of these things. Yet they remain hidden because of a generic forgetfulness <note>original: "oblivione generica"; a reference to the Platonic concept of *anamnesis*, or the idea that the soul "forgets" its divine knowledge when it enters a physical body.</note>. Therefore, the soul seeks the truth while looking at external things, even though it possesses that truth within its own essence; and it explores the good outside itself, having deserted its own self.

From here, therefore, everyone ought to begin the knowledge of themselves. For if we distract our gaze upon the multitude of men, we will never discern the one form <note>term: form (species); in Platonic philosophy, this is the ideal or essential "blueprint" of a thing, which remains perfect even if individual examples are flawed.</note> among them, obscured as it is by the multitude, division, discord, <margin>1</margin> and the multiform change of things that participate in that form. But if we turn our sharp gaze toward ourselves, we will surely behold both the one reason and the one nature of men, removed from all disturbance. Rightly, then, does Socrates separate the soul far from the sight of the multitude to know what a human being truly is, and he refutes those opinions that hinder this contemplation. For the multitude is a hindrance to the soul’s turning back into itself and to the knowledge of its one form. Here, variety overshadows the one. Otherness obscures identity. Dissimilarity clouds similarity. For around matter, forms are confused, and the better things are mixed with the worse.

->The natural life proper to the soul is not in an earthly body, but in a sublime one; therefore, all forms here are sickly and delusional.<-

<margin>ii</margin> No one should wonder if, when we say that what is natural occurs more frequently than what is contrary to nature—and that the latter is confined to a <margin>iiii</margin> narrow space while the natural is amplified throughout the universe—we nevertheless admit that most men are ignorant and evil, while those of the opposite sort are very few. For it is not natural for souls to spend their life together with bodies and to be occupied in the world of generation <note>term: generation (generatio); the physical world characterized by birth, change, and decay, as opposed to the eternal world of the spirit.</note>. On the contrary, a separate, immaterial, and incorporeal life is rather what is suited to souls. <margin>vi</margin> Therefore, when they are occupied in the world of generation, they become like people inhabiting a plague-ridden region. Since they live outside of generation, they are—as Plato says—like those who dwell in blessed places. Just as, therefore, it is not surprising that among those who inhabit pestilential places, many are sickly while very few preserve their natural health, so too one should not wonder that most souls placed in the world of generation are subject to passions and are wicked. On the contrary, it would be astonishing if souls involved in such bodies, bound by these knots, and surrounded by such great change, were sometimes found to be sober, pure, and undisturbed. Is it not astounding for the soul to live immaterially within material things, and [to live] unchangingly among those that are falling—

->ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.<-
4
b ii

...to preserve itself unstained anywhere. And when it has already drunk from such cups <note>original: "pocula"; a reference to the "Cup of Forgetfulness" (Lethe) or the "Cup of Circe," which in Platonic thought represents the intoxicating and numbing effect of material life on the soul.</note>, it is not lulled to sleep by these potions. For in truth, oblivion, error, and ignorance are like a drug that diverts souls into a place of dissimilarity. Why then do you wonder that many are like wolves in their manner of life, many are like pigs, and many others are surrounded by some other species of brute? For the earthly place is the lodging for such as these.

And many souls, because of immoderate desire, have been baited by poisonous cups. But wonder rather at this: if any among mortals are found anywhere who have not been transformed by such potions, nor even ensnared. These are the ones who, relying on the gift of Mercury <note>original: "Mercurii munere"; Mercury (Hermes) is the god of reason, language, and the messenger who guides souls. His "gift" is the power of rational thought and philosophy to escape the "intoxication" of the senses.</note>, devote themselves to reason and knowledge. For just as you should not wonder if you look into Tartarus <note>term: Tartarus; in Greek mythology, the deepest abyss of the underworld, used here by the author to represent a state of total spiritual darkness or punishment.</note> and see tortured souls—for that is the place for such things—so also you should not wonder if many souls living in the realm of generation <term>generation (generatio): the physical world of birth, death, and constant change, contrasted with the eternal, unchanging divine realm.</term> are disturbed, ignorant, and mindless. For the realm of generation requires such souls; just as in heaven all souls are good, and in Tartarus all are wicked. Thus, in the realm of generation, the majority are depraved, while the fewer are upright. For generation does not decline toward the better and more divine of extremes, but toward the worse.

### The evil man agrees neither with others nor with himself.

The wicked man cannot agree even with himself. For it is necessary that he see the truth in some way because of his rational nature, yet because of his disturbed imagination, he must remain mostly ignorant and at odds with himself. Repentance, which arrives when his disturbances are relaxed, proves this. The intemperate man, therefore, sometimes thinks and speaks of divine things because of his kinship to the divine intellect. But because of his lust and his disturbed imagination, he departs far from divine temperance. And since he is always at war with himself, he certainly cannot agree with others.

### Whoever knows something, they agree entirely about that thing.

It behooves those who know something to be in concord about it. The first cause of this concord is the determined nature of the things themselves; the second is that the tools of judgment for cognition are the same in everyone. The third is that in first principles, the intellect is united to itself. Therefore, whatever possesses intelligence is a participant in that union. Knowledge is a certain illumination depending on the intellect, while concord is an illumination proceeding from unity. For concord is the union of different things. It is necessary, therefore, for those who share in the same knowledge to agree with one another.

<meta>This page transitions from the soul’s potential for corruption—discussed on the previous page—to Proclus’s core argument: that the soul is a self-moving, self-contained entity that holds the "Forms" of all things within itself. # PROCLUS.

->Each of us is a soul, and this soul contains within itself all forms, both divine and natural.<-

<margin>†</margin>
<margin>to produce from itself, and to recognize in itself all divine and natural forms</margin>
Plato’s entire purpose in this book is to call us back to the knowledge of ourselves, and to demonstrate that our essence consists of forms <term>forms (speciebus); in Platonic philosophy, these are the eternal, ideal blueprints of all things</term> and rational principles. Furthermore, he shows that the soul produces all sciences from itself and recognizes all divine and natural forms within itself. A perfect knowledge of ourselves would be to judge our powers by our essence, and our actions by those powers. However, we usually possess a more common knowledge of ourselves, coming to know our powers from our actions, and the essence of the soul from those powers. Indeed, these three—essence, power, and action—flow together in the soul. For its essence is active, and its action is essential. This action becomes intellectual according to its activity, and it is joined to the essence according to the soul's own perfection.

The soul leads itself with free motion; it provides good for itself, purifies itself, and educates itself, even when it seems to be educated from elsewhere.

<margin>a</margin>
Animals that are devoid of reason <margin>a</margin> are driven and governed by external forces and are cared for by others; they are moved by a motor in a condition where they lack the faculty to lead or preserve themselves. The rational soul, however, because of its property of being self-moving <note>original: "per se mobile"</note> and self-operating, is able by its very nature to act upon itself, to move itself, and to provide what is good for itself. Now, in truth, purification does not happen to us from external sources, but takes its origin from the innermost parts of the soul. For every evil happens from external things and is foreign to the soul, but good comes from the innermost parts. For the soul is naturally "good-formed" <note>original: "boniformis"; having the shape or nature of Goodness</note>, and the more perfect it becomes, the more it claims for itself a life that is moved from within. This is because it only becomes moved by external things due to its involvement and interaction with the body. Therefore, whatever it receives from the outside remains placed outside itself, just like the things perceived by the senses or the imagination. Only those things are truly in the soul which are made by the soul within itself and produced by it. It is therefore purified by itself, since reason, beginning from itself, ends in itself. For this reason, it is rightly understood what Socrates said—namely, among those disputing, that the one who answers is properly the one who speaks. If this person is refuted, and being refuted is purified, then surely while he is being purified, he purifies himself and frees himself from ignorance by applying the refutation to himself. This is indeed consistent with the nature of the self-moving soul. This saying also confirms that "learning is remembering" <term>Reminiscence (reminiscentia); the Platonic doctrine that the soul does not "learn" new things but recalls knowledge it possessed before birth</term>. Since those who answer speak all things from themselves, it is the greatest sign of "reminiscence"—namely, that souls bring forth reasons and discourses from within themselves, and only need someone to awaken them. Nor is the soul a blank tablet <note>original: "tabellas uacuas"; a reference to the *tabula rasa* or empty wax tablet</note> upon which characters are inscribed from the outside. For they are...

# ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT-GUIDE.

### 4

### h iii

For [the forms] are always inscribed, and the soul itself is the inner writer. Yet, not everyone can read what is inscribed, or even recognize that these things have been written. This is because, due to a birth-born forgetfulness <note>original: "geneficam oblivionem"; the Platonic concept that entering a physical body causes the soul to forget its divine origins</note>, the eye of the soul is clouded over with impurities, and through this forgetfulness, people fall into passions. Therefore, the only task necessary is to remove the obstacle placed in the way. It is not necessary to have knowledge forced in from the outside. Indeed, souls have within themselves the doors of truth, but they are closed off by earthly and material forms. If, then, someone demonstrates these matters with great diligence, the souls—roused from another source, yet producing the learned answers from within themselves—declare by this very act that the Platonic doctrine is true: that the soul knows all things and only requires someone to rouse it from the outside in order to respond. Furthermore, when someone is being educated and purifies themselves, this is the work of a daemonic power <term>daemonic power (daemonica potestas); in this context, it refers to a "daemon" or "daimon," a guiding spirit or guardian that acts as a bridge between the divine and the human</term>. For these spirit-guides do not act upon us from the outside, but they direct and govern us from within, as if from the stern of a ship. Nor do they purify us as if we were merely physical bodies whose movement comes from elsewhere; rather, they care for us as beings that move from within ourselves. For in this way, they provide good things and purge the passions. Socrates, therefore, acting in the place of a good spirit-guide, showed that a young man is refuted not so much by another person as by himself.

**Why the evil and ignorant man is at odds with himself and others; why the good man is in agreement, and why the wise are in harmony with one another.**

<margin>c</margin> Frequent discord with oneself happens to many people for good reason: because they admit some things from the senses, other things from the imagination, others frequently from opinion, some from anger, and many from desire. For such passions are not only moved in men by opinions, as the Stoics <note>the Stoics were a school of philosophy that taught that emotions resulted from errors in judgment</note> teach, but on the contrary, men often change their opinions because of certain passions and impulses, often carrying away the worst opinions in place of the best. These people, receiving multi-formed motions within themselves from many principles and powers—and the baser ones at that—undoubtedly possess a soul that is at odds and in discord. But those endowed with knowledge receive their entire understanding from a single, higher principle. For the Intellect <term>Intellect (Intellectus); the highest part of the soul, capable of direct, intuitive grasp of truth</term> hands down the principles to them. Indeed, all true opinions are the daughters of the intellect. Since, therefore, they all proceed from such a principle of simplicity, it is right that they are all in harmony with one another.

**Those who think that man is composed of soul and body consequently separate the "useful" from the "just"; those who hold that man *is* the soul join them together.**

<margin>u</margin> Whether the "just" and the "useful" are the same thing is a point where others disagree. The Platonists, however, judge them to be the same. For the Epicureans <note>followers of Epicurus, who prioritized pleasure and the avoidance of pain</note> and certain Stoics, placing our ultimate end in that which is according to nature...

<header>PROCLUS:</header>

...to live; and the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics; the followers of Aristotle, known for walking while teaching</term>, who define our "good" as being fulfilled by physical necessities, cannot easily confirm that the "just" and the "useful" are the same thing. It is similar for whoever claims that a human being is merely an "animated body," or a composite of body and soul. Such a person will flee from wounds or death, even if doing so is unjust, simply so that the "animal" <note>meaning the biological self</note> might be preserved. This is because the "good" for any animal is to exist according to its nature and to be preserved in that state. In this case, then, what is useful is at odds with what is just. 

However, those who place the ultimate goal within the soul itself—needing nothing from the body—and who believe that the human being *is* the soul using a body, these people certainly judge the just and the useful to be the same. For they place both within the soul, and they understand that the sufferings of the "instruments" <note>the physical body used by the soul</note> are separate from the users themselves. The logical argument proving that the just is useful proceeds like this: Everything just is beautiful; everything beautiful is good; therefore, everything just is good. And since the "good" and the "useful" are the same, everything just is useful.

### The soul takes on the form of the thing it adheres to; also concerning the "vehicles" of divine souls and our own.

<margin>a</margin> Souls also draw into themselves the qualities of those things to which they join themselves. Certainly, when they liken themselves to the Intellect, they soon claim for themselves a state of immutability <note>original: "immutabilitatem"; a state of being unchanging and eternal</note> in their opinions and their life. But when they couple themselves to the world of "generation" <note>original: "generationi"; the realm of physical birth, change, and decay</note>, they pursue novelty everywhere, and are carried now into these opinions, now into those. In this state, they rarely perceive the stable reasons of the soul itself. 

Plato signifies by this path that the more noble and gifted souls—those possessing an understanding of the inviolable purity of the gods and bringing this very quality into their own "idol" <note>original: "idolo"; here referring to the soul's lower reflection or its manifestation in the physical world</note>—are also accustomed to be occupied in a certain way with an apparent purity. For the essence of the divine "garments" <term>garments (indumentorum); in Neoplatonism, the soul is said to wear "vehicles" or "vestments" of light or spirit as it descends from the divine realm into the body</term> is inviolable, and their purity is immaterial; souls must surely put these on, cleansing their own inner garments and keeping their robes untainted by the world of physical change, rather than placing all their focus on the purity of external, physical clothes.

### Knowledge, while remaining one within itself, fills many without being diminished; from this we conclude that the soul is separate from the body.

<margin>e</margin> It is a lesser feat for a single branch of knowledge to persuade one person than to persuade many. This Platonic sentiment contains a kind of hymn and celebration of knowledge: how great and of what kind each science is becomes clear from the fact that, by imitating the Intellect itself, the same knowledge fills each individual and everyone simultaneously with understanding. It is indeed indivisible and rests confidently within itself, and meanwhile, it perfects all things that participate in it...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s Neo-Platonic commentary on the hierarchy of virtues and the nature of the soul. # PROCLUS.

...if it exists at all, it is nevertheless foul and deformed; it participates in the One, yet lacks <term>form; original "speciei", referring to the Platonic Ideal or structural blueprint of a thing</term>. But that which is perceived by the senses possesses traces of beauty, yet none of justice. For this reason, in the *Phaedrus*, Socrates says that among fleeting images there is no splendor of justice or <term>temperance; self-control or moderation</term>. But beauty alone has this privilege: to appear most clearly everywhere and to be the most desirable. Where therefore there is justice, there is beauty. Where there is beauty, there is the good—whether you choose to look at the first principles or at the illuminations of those principles stretching out to the furthest extremes. All things indeed participate in the Good itself, for it is the principle of all things; but only those things which have some form participate in beauty. Finally, only souls participate in justice.

Now indeed, in the very center of all things, which is the soul, all these qualities are connected to one another: the Good, the Just, and the Beautiful. And the Good of the soul is itself beautiful and just. The Just is also simultaneously both beautiful and good; similarly, the Beautiful is both good and just. Nor is this statement true only in a trinity of this kind, but also in many other cases. Just as among the principles, <term>Being; the state of existing</term> itself precedes Life, and Life precedes <term>Mind; original "mentem", the intellect or higher consciousness</term>. 

Similarly also in their effects: not everything that is a part of a composite possesses life, nor is every living thing immediately endowed with a mind. But in turn, through intelligence all things live and exist, and living things also exist by the act of living. Since there is such a difference in the furthest extremes, through this kind of trinity they flow together in the soul, where Being, Life, and Intellect exist; for there, Life is both intellect and essence. Intellect likewise is both essence and life. For there is one simplicity in the soul, one substance. Neither being, nor living, nor understanding is there as an <note>original: "adventicium"; meaning something added from the outside or accidental rather than being an inherent part of the nature</note> external addition. 

But its intellect is essential and living; its life is also intellectual through its essence. Finally, its essence is intellectual and living. Therefore, everywhere it is all things, and one thing out of all by a similar reasoning; its Good prevails through beauty and justice, and its Beautiful is the Good and the Just. And again, the Just is filled with the Good and the Beautiful. The subject is indeed one, but the <term>definitions; original "rationes", the logical explanations or aspects</term> are diverse. 

In this, we neither consider the identity of these three according to their definitions, nor do we think there is an "otherness" according to their subject; rather, we preserve their differing definitions among themselves, while the subject remains one. For this reason, these qualities concur everywhere through the actions of the soul; for just as the definitions of the virtues are different, yet there is one possessor of them all, it cannot happen that you participate in justice while being empty of temperance, or that you possess these two while the others...

# ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT.
<note>original: "DE ANIMA ET DAEMONE"</note>

...if you should not have it. In this way, such a <term>trinity; here referring to the triad of the Good, the Beautiful, and the Just</term> is bound to itself. Every good thing possesses both beauty and justice; and the same applies to the rest. This is why Socrates linked the "just good" through beauty, for beauty serves as their shared middle ground and bond. Timaeus, moreover, says that the most beautiful <term>knot; a metaphor from Plato's Timaeus for the mathematical or metaphysical bond that holds the universe together</term> is the one that most perfectly unifies itself and the things it binds. To evil, however, both evil and good stand as adversaries.

->He proves that everything just is, by its very nature, beautiful and good.<-

---

<margin>o</margin>We shall confirm that everything just is beautiful through the following arguments. Since the soul is a kind of multiplicity, there exists within it a first part, a middle part, and a final part <note>Proclus refers to the Platonic division of the soul into Reason, Spirit/Emotion, and Appetite</note>. Tell me, when do we say justice is established within it? Is it when the middle or the final parts attempt to dominate their superiors? Or is it rather when the first part—**reason**—commands the middle, and the middle part in turn commands the lower? 

If it were the case that the lower parts prevailed over the better, they would no longer be "lower" by their nature. For that which is fit to be called "better" is, by its nature, more honorable. Since it is impossible for the same thing to be naturally better and worse at the same time, justice must be found in the soul only when its best part holds the command over the entirety of life. The middle part, being subject to the better, then holds sway over the final part. In this state, every part of the soul possesses what is appropriate to it: the first part reigning, the second acting as a guardian, and the final part serving its superior. 

Therefore, the **Just** itself is by nature the distributor of what is fitting for each part of the soul. It is the cause of each part maintaining its own duty and receiving its proper dignity; thus, it is the preservation of the entire internal order. Such order and moderation, being in harmony with nature, is naturally beautiful. **Justice**, therefore, is the cause of beauty and is beautiful itself. 

Furthermore, justice is twofold. One type concerns contracts and preserves <term>arithmetic equality; a simple 1:1 ratio where everyone gets the exact same amount regardless of status</term>. The other type is concerned with distribution and relies on <term>geometric equality; a proportional ratio where rewards are given based on merit, value, or "dignity"</term>. In the first case, one observes arithmetic equality so that we do not cheat a partner in business dealings by receiving more than we gave. In the second case, one distributes unequal things to unequal people according to the dignity of each, maintaining a geometric proportion. Just as people differ from one another in merit, so should the things distributed to them differ. Thus, as we have said, everything just is equal...

<meta>This page continues Proclus's argument regarding the internal order of the soul. The previous page ended mid-sentence discussing the hierarchy of the soul's parts; this page begins by establishing that beauty arises from the "equality" or proper proportion of these parts, specifically when reason governs the lower impulses.</meta>

### PROCLUS

...everything equal is beautiful, for the unequal is disorganized and ugly. Therefore, everything just is beautiful. Moreover, beauty exists in physical bodies only when **form** overcomes **matter**. For matter itself is formless and ugly, and whenever form is overwhelmed by it, that form becomes filled with a certain shapelessness and deformity; it escapes as something nearly formless, having been made to resemble the chaotic nature of the matter beneath it. 

If, therefore, the intellectual part within us takes the role of **form**, while the irrational part takes the role of **matter**—for the intellect and reason are categorized under the order of the <term>Limit; in Pythagorean and Platonic thought, the "Limit" provides structure, while the "Infinite" is chaotic potential</term>, whereas the irrational is placed in the genus of the **Infinite**—it follows that beauty must shine forth in the soul specifically when reason reigns and those aspects of life lacking reason are subjected to it. 

Justice itself gives the command to reason and assigns servitude to the irrational. It attributes to each what is appropriate: sovereignty to the superior part, and obedience to the inferior. Since, in the crafting of the world, the irrational was made subject to us, the irrationality within us is subjected to reason like a <term>vehicle; a reference to the "chariot of the soul" or the "astral vehicle" that carries the rational spirit</term>. Thus, the just is naturally beautiful and is the very cause of the soul's beauty. 

Likewise, the **just** is something perfect and defined. For the **unjust** is judged to be imperfect and undefined; it wanders infinitely and never holds its ground, overstepping the boundary of justice. Therefore, justice imposes measure and limit wherever it is present, and in doing so, makes all things perfect. Since it possesses such a nature, it deservedly makes the soul beautiful. For beauty naturally follows that which is perfect and measured, just as deformity accompanies the unmeasured and the indeterminate. 

The just, therefore, is beautiful by nature. Finally, the <term>World-Maker; original: "mundi faber," referring to the Demiurge of Plato's Timaeus</term> himself adorned the whole universe through justice. He bound the world together with the most beautiful "knot" of all knots, and made it indissoluble because of the power of <term>analogical proportion; the mathematical harmony that links the different elements of the cosmos</term>, which contains the universe and makes it friendly to itself in every part. That which is similar to the world—the most shapely of all visible things—is surely beautiful itself. Therefore, what is just is necessarily also beautiful.

# ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT.

...and at first sight, it moves souls toward itself. This is confirmed in the *Phaedrus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on love and the soul.</note>. For in truth, the **beautiful** <note>original: $\kappa \alpha \lambda \dot{o} \nu$ (*kalon*)</note>—whether it is so called because it "calls out" <note>original: $\delta \iota \dot{\alpha} \space \tau \dot{o} \space \kappa \alpha \lambda \epsilon \tilde{\im{i}} \nu$ (*dia to kalein*); the author is using a Platonic pun linking the word for "beautiful" (*kalon*) to the verb "to call" (*kalein*), suggesting beauty summons the soul</note> to souls, or because it "soothes" those who gaze upon it—is certainly lovable by nature. Therefore, love is also said to lead "lovingly" toward the beautiful. Whatever is **lovable** is also **desirable**. For love is a certain strong and vehement desire for something. And whatever loves, desires something that it also lacks. Now, everything desirable is also **good**—whether it is truly good or only appears to be so. 

For many things that are not good present themselves to us as objects of pursuit, because they offer themselves to those who desire them as if they were good. It was clearly demonstrated by Socrates in the *Meno* <note>original: "Memnone," likely a transcription error for the dialogue *Meno*</note> that it is impossible for those who know the true nature of an evil to desire it. Therefore, every good is desirable. And if something is primarily desirable, it will also be primarily good. But if it is only an "apparent" desire, it will likewise be an "apparent" good; indeed, this distinction must be applied to every term: namely, whether it is **apparent** or **real**. 

For if something is both beautiful and apparent, then the lovable, the desirable, and the good associated with such beauty will also be apparent. But if it is beautiful by nature and lovable, then it is likewise good. But what then will be desirable? Surely not evil? Yet it is impossible for evil to be sought once its nature is known; for all things desire the good, and no desire is directed toward evil. Nor is desire directed toward anything that is neither good nor evil; for whatever is of that nature is done for the sake of something else, and it does not constitute an end in itself. 

Every desirable thing, however, is an **end** <note>In Aristotelian and Platonic thought, the "end" (*telos*) is the purpose or goal of an action</note>. And if any evil is desired, it is longed for as a good because it *appears* good; and if something not beautiful is loved, it is loved as beautiful because it *appears* so. Therefore, if everything beautiful is lovable, and everything lovable is desirable, and everything desirable is good, it follows that everything beautiful is good—and conversely, everything good is desirable, and the desirable is lovable, if indeed to love is to desire vehemently. 

Whence in the *Symposium* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the nature of love</note> Socrates says that the good is lovable just like the beautiful. If, I say, every good is desirable, and the desirable is in turn lovable, and the lovable is beautiful, it follows that every good is beautiful. Nor should anyone object to us now that the Good itself is superior to beauty, or again that what is called "lovable" is of two kinds; for we are not now disputing about the first principles of things, but about those beautiful and good things that exist within us. Therefore, the good that is within us is simultaneously desirable and lovable. 

Through love, therefore, we acquire and possess it; through love, I say, and an inclined zeal. And if anyone pays attention to himself, he will clearly see and recognize that this kind of good brings us sharper loves than those beauties manifest to the senses. For what...

# PROCLUS ON THE ALCIBIADES

...is good and is also beautiful. For this reason, Diotima <note>The wise woman from Plato’s *Symposium* who teaches Socrates about the nature of Love.</note> instructs lovers that, after encountering the beauty that meets the senses, they should transfer themselves to the beauty inherent in actions, duties, and sciences. There, they should vigorously exercise the "eye of the soul" <note>original: *amatorium animae oculum*</note> that is prone to love. From there, they should move toward the intellect; and there, they should see the primary and divine beauty reigning supreme, so that the "beautiful itself" <note>original: *ipsum re vera pulchrum*</note> may truly flourish within the soul in us. For what is more beautiful within us than virtue and knowledge? On the other hand, what is more foul than vice and ignorance?

->Man is a soul using a body as a tool. Therefore, the evils of the body do not belong to the soul or to the man himself, just as the defects of tools do not belong to the craftsman or his art.<-

<margin>f</margin>
But if most people consider wounds and death to be "evils," what part of these is truly an evil for us? If indeed such a thing does not pass into the soul—which is what we ourselves are—then the sufferings of the tools do not change the virtues of those who use them. Thus, a carpenter does not lose his art of cutting just because his saw <note>original: *seca*; a cutting tool or saw</note> becomes dull at some point. Furthermore, even if our happiness consisted in the craft of carpentry, we would not consider the carpenter unhappy simply because he lacked a saw. Now, just as the soul has the body as its instrument, so too the body has certain instruments through which it moves external things. Just as a defect in those external tools does not harm the good condition of the body, so too the sufferings of the body do not pass through into the soul. 

Therefore, even if death is an "evil" for the body, it is nevertheless not an evil for the soul. If, then, the beauty of an action resides in the soul, while an "evil" occurs simultaneously in something else <note>i.e., the body</note>, it has not yet been proven that the same thing can be both beautiful and evil at once. It is also possible to distinguish this through the method of logic <note>original: *dialectica ratione*</note>: it is one thing for something to be a certain way in itself <note>original: *secundum se ipsum*</note>, and another for it to be so by accident <note>original: *secundum accidens*</note>. For a brave action is beautiful in itself. But if it should ever be "evil," it is so by accident—since it merely happens that the one acting bravely dies. Even if you wish to categorize death among "evils," the brave duty is not an evil because of the very fact that it is brave (and therefore beautiful); rather, it is "brave" in itself and "evil" only by accident. Thus, one aspect is beautiful while the other is evil. It has not been shown that a thing is evil for the same reason it is beautiful, but rather it is called evil by accident because of the person's death. 

Consequently, anyone who separates the "Good" from the "Beautiful" is ignorant of the essence of man, placing one in one category and the other in another—placing the "Good" in the body and the "Beautiful" in the actions of the soul. But in truth, man himself is the mind itself, an essence set apart from the body, in which whatever is beautiful is also good.

# ON SACRIFICE AND MAGIC.

### How these two differ, namely "according to itself" and "insofar as it is itself."

<margin>d</margin> Phrases of this kind, namely **according to itself** <note>original: *secundum seipsum*</note> and **insofar as it is itself** <note>original: *qua ipsum*</note> are also distinguished in the works of Aristotle. For that which belongs to something **according to itself** might not belong to it primarily. However, that which is fitting for a thing **insofar as it is itself**, besides being fitting, also belongs to it primarily and is equal to it. Therefore, if beauty is the cause of proportion <note>original: *commensuratio*; a state of being balanced or in right measure</note> in the soul, and for this very reason it is called "beautiful," it ensures that the better part dominates the worse in the soul; it perfects us and purges the soul's deformity. By this very reasoning, it is "good"—not indeed by accident, but insofar as it is beautiful. For if that which is beautiful is proportionate, then insofar as it is proportionate, it is also good. Since "the Good" is the measure of all things, certainly insofar as a thing is beautiful, it exists also as good. Similarly, the foul <note>original: *turpe*; the ugly or morally base</note>, insofar as it is foul, is evil. For insofar as it is foul, it is formless, indeterminate, and disordered; and by this very reasoning, it is evil. Therefore, insofar as it is foul, it is certainly evil. Thus, the same thing is always both beautiful and good; and conversely, a thing is equally foul and evil. Keep this rule in mind here, which Aristotle used hereafter: **If any two things are interchangeable, then their opposites are also interchangeable.** Therefore, if the **beautiful** and the **good** are interchangeable with each other, it follows that their opposites—namely **evil** and the **foul**—are similarly interchangeable.

### The work of Proclus on sacrifice, translated by Marsilio Ficino the Florentine.

<margin>q</margin> Just as lovers progress by reason, step by step, from the beauty that appears to the senses toward divine beauty, so too the ancient priests—when they considered a certain kinship and "compassion" <note>original: *compassionem*; here meaning "sympathy," the Neoplatonic belief that all parts of the universe are interconnected and vibrate in harmony</note> in natural things, of some toward others and of visible things toward occult powers—found that all things exist in all things, and thus established their sacred science. For they recognized the highest things in the lowest, and the lowest in the highest. Indeed, they saw earthly things in heaven according to their cause and in a celestial manner, and they saw celestial things on earth, but in an earthly manner.

### Page 110

For why else do we think those plants which they call **heliotropes** <note>original: *heliotropias*; from the Greek for "turning toward the sun"</note>—that is, **sun-followers**—move toward the sun’s movement? Or that the **selenitropes**—that is, **moon-followers**—turn toward the moon? Truly, all things pray and sing hymns to the leaders of their own divine order <note>The Neoplatonic "chain of being," where lower things correspond to higher deities</note>. However, they do this in different ways: some in an intellectual way, some in a rational way, others in a natural way, and still others in a sensory way. 

Therefore, the sun-follower moves toward the sun however it is able. If anyone were capable of hearing the vibration made by the plant as it circles in the air, they would surely perceive that it produces a sound directed toward its king—a kind of melody such as a plant is capable of making. For this reason, one may look upon the sun and the moon on the earth, though according to an earthly quality. Conversely, in the heavens, one may see all plants, stones, and animals according to a heavenly nature, possessing an intellectual life <note>original: *uitam... intellectualem*; referring to the "living" or conscious essence of celestial bodies</note>.

The ancients, having contemplated these things, applied certain earthly things to certain celestial ones. From this, they drew down divine virtues into this lower realm through a certain similarity. Indeed, similarity itself is a sufficient cause for binding individual things to one another. 

For if someone heats hemp or papyrus and then brings it near a lamp, even if it does not touch the flame, he will see the hemp suddenly catch fire. Though it did not touch the fire, the ignition descends from above to the lower material. Let us therefore compare the heated hemp or papyrus to the kinship of lower things with higher ones; its approach to the lamp represents the proper use of things in the right time, place, and material. The movement of the fire into the hemp represents the presence of the divine light to that which is capable of receiving it. Finally, the "kindling" of the hemp represents the **deification** of mortals and the **illumination** of material things, which are then carried upward like the burning hemp because they participate in a certain divine seed.

But what shall I say of the **Lotus**? The Lotus folds its leaves into itself before the sun rises, but as the sun emerges, it unfolds them little by little. As the sun ascends to the mid-point of the sky, the lotus spreads its leaves wide; but as the sun moves from the midpoint toward its setting, the plant gradually contracts its leaves. It seems to honor the sun through this expansion and contraction no less than humans do through the expressions of their cheeks or the movement of their lips. 

Nor is this seen only in plants, which have a trace of life, but one may also observe in stones an imitation and participation in the lights from above. For example, the **sun-stone** <note>original: *helitis lapis*</note> imitates the solar rays with its golden rays. The stone called the **eye of heaven** or the **eye of the sun** has a shape similar to the pupil of an eye, and a ray flashes out from the center of that pupil. Furthermore, the **selenite** stone—that is, the **moon-stone**—possesses the shape of the crescent moon and follows the lunar mo... <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "motum" (motion) or "mutationem" (change)</note>

...not only plants, but also stones. Next, the **helioselenus** stone <note>original: *helioselenus*; literally "sun-moon" stone, likely a type of iridescent feldspar or labradorite</note>—that is, the "sun-and-moon" stone—imitates in a certain way the meeting of the sun and the moon, and represents this union through its color.
