Earthly things are indeed full of celestial things, while celestial things are full of "super-celestial" things <note>In Neoplatonism, "super-celestial" refers to the intellectual or divine realm beyond the physical stars</note>. Every order of things proceeds down to the very last. For those qualities that are gathered together into a single point above the order of things are subsequently expanded as they descend. In this descent, different souls are ordered under different deities.

Furthermore, there are many **solar animals** <note>Animals believed to be linked to the "chain" of the sun</note>, such as lions and roosters, which participate in the nature of a certain solar deity according to their own capacity. Wherefore it is marvelous how much lower things in the same order yield to the higher, even when the lower things are not inferior in size or physical power. From this, they say that the rooster is greatly feared by the lion and almost worshipped. We cannot assign the cause of this behavior to physical matter or the senses, but only to the contemplation of the higher order. Namely, it is because the presence of the **solar virtue** <note>The specific spiritual power or essence of the sun</note> belongs to the rooster more than to the lion. 

This is also apparent from the fact that the rooster, as if with certain hymns, applauds the rising sun and, as it were, calls out to it when the sun turns toward us from the mid-heaven of the antipodes <note>The people on the opposite side of the earth; the rooster "calls" the sun as it travels from their sky to ours</note>. Furthermore, sometimes certain solar **angels** have appeared endowed with such forms; and although these spirits are formless in themselves, they appear to us in specific shapes because we are beings shaped by form. Sometimes also solar **demons** <note>original: *daemones*; intermediate spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense</note> have been seen with the face of a lion. However, when a rooster was presented to them, they suddenly disappeared. This proceeds from the fact that things lower in the same order always revere the higher, just as many people, looking upon the images of divine men, are accustomed by that very sight to fear doing anything shameful. 

To speak briefly, some things revolve their "hearts" toward the revolutions of the sun, like the plants we mentioned; others imitate the shape of solar rays in a certain way, like the **date of the palm**; others reflect the fiery nature of the sun, like the **laurel**; others reflect something else. Truly, one may see the properties gathered in the sun distributed everywhere in the things that follow in the solar order—namely, in angels, demons, souls, animals, plants, and stones. 

Therefore, the authors of the ancient priesthood <note>The "theurgists" or divine-workers of late antiquity</note> devised the worship of higher powers from these visible things. In their rituals, they mixed some things and purified others. They mixed many things together because they saw that simple, single items had some property of a deity, but not enough on their own to successfully call that deity down. For this reason, through the mixture of many things, they attracted celestial influences. By composing one thing out of many, they were imitating the "One" <note>The Neoplatonic "One," the ultimate source of all existence</note> which stands above the many. They even fashioned statues mixed from many different materials and collected composite scents, using art to turn them into **divine symbols**. By making a single object that reflects the divine essence, they were able to...

# PORPHYRY

...comprehending, of course, as many powers as possible. Indeed, the division of these powers weakened each one, but their mixing restored them to the idea of the original archetype <note>The "exemplar" or divine pattern upon which natural things are modeled</note>. Sometimes, however, a single herb or a single stone is sufficient for a divine work. *Cnebison* <note>original: *Cnebison*; an Egyptian name for a specific herb</note>—that is, the thistle—is sufficient for the sudden appearance of a certain deity; for protection, however, laurel is used. *Raccinum* <note>original: *Raccinum*; likely a type of thorny shrub or buckthorn</note>—that is, a thorny kind of shrub—the sea onion, coral, diamond, and jasper are used; but for prophecy, the heart of a mole is used. For purification, however, sulfur and seawater are required.

Therefore, the priests, through the mutual kinship and "compassion" <note>The Greek concept of *sympatheia*, where objects in the universe are naturally "in tune" with one another</note> of things, would bring them together into one; through their natural repulsion, they would expel them, purifying when necessary with sulfur and asphalt—that is, bitumen—and sprinkling with seawater. For sulfur purifies because of the sharpness of its odor, while seawater purifies because of its fiery portion. They also employed animals for the gods that were appropriate for worship, and other things in a similar manner.

Wherefore, receiving powers from these and similar things, they first recognized the powers of the **daemons** <note>In this context, *daemons* are not evil "demons" but intermediate spirits that act as messengers between gods and humans</note>; they realized that these spirits are close to natural things and actions. Through these natural elements, to which the spirits are drawn, the priests summoned them into their presence. Then, from the spirits, they proceeded to the very powers and actions of the gods. They did this partly through the spirits teaching those who were learning, and partly by interpreting the appropriate **symbols** <note>original: *simbola*; ritual tokens or "passwords" in nature that resonate with divine power</note> through their own diligence. Thus, they ascended into the proper intelligence of the gods. Finally, setting aside natural things, actions, and for the most part even the spirits, they were received into the fellowship of the gods.

### Porphyry on the occasions, or causes, leading us to the intelligible world. Translated by Marsilio Ficino.

### On the nature of corporeal and incorporeal things.

Every body is in a place. But none of those things which are by their nature **incorporeal** <note>Non-physical entities, such as the soul or intellect</note>, or anything of that sort, is in a place.

Those things which are by their nature incorporeal—by the very fact that they are more excellent than every body and every place—are everywhere. They are not spread out over a distance, but exist in an indivisible condition. Those things which are by their nature incorporeal are not present to bodies in a "local" way <note>Meaning they do not take up physical space like a chair or a stone</note>. They are present to them whenever they wish, by turning and inclining toward those bodies, insofar as they naturally lean and incline toward them. But since they are not present to bodies by a condition of location, they are present to them by a certain "disposition" or "habit" <note>original: *habitudine*; a relationship based on state of being rather than physical proximity</note>.

# ON OCCASIONS <note>original: *De Occasionibus*; This refers to the "Sentences" or "Points of Departure" by the Neoplatonist philosopher Porphyry, which serve as introductory principles to metaphysical thought.</note>

Things which are incorporeal—lacking physical bodies—are certainly not present in bodies through their fundamental substance or essence. They do not physically mix with bodies; rather, through a certain "leaning" or inclination, as if in an instant, a specific power is established in the thing shared, becoming close to the physical realm. For this inclination itself substitutes a certain power into the bodies that are already nearby.

### On the nature, binding, and release of the soul.

The soul is a certain middle ground between indivisible essence <note>A reality that cannot be split into parts, typical of the divine realm</note> and the essence that is divided among physical bodies. The Intellect <term>Intellect: In Neoplatonism, the *Intellect* (or *Nous*) is the divine mind, containing the eternal forms and ideas of all things</term>, however, is an indivisible essence alone. But material qualities and physical forms are split up according to the bodies they inhabit. Not everything that acts upon another does so through physical closeness and touch; even those things which do act by approaching and touching use that closeness only incidentally, rather than by their true nature. The soul is bound to the body by a certain turning toward the "passions" <note>original: *passiones*; here meaning the sensations, sufferings, and physical experiences of the body</note> arising from the body. Conversely, it is released insofar as it ceases to be affected by the body. What nature has bound, nature herself releases. Similarly, what the soul has joined, the soul itself pulls apart. Nature binds the body within the soul, but the soul binds itself within the body. Therefore, nature separates the body from the soul, while the soul separates itself from the body.

All things are, in a way, present in all things, according to the capacity of the things they are inside of.

We do not understand "all things in all things" in the same way; rather, the essence of each thing relates properly to all others according to its own level: in the Intellect, it exists intellectually; in the soul, it exists rationally; in plants, it exists "seminarially" <note>original: *seminariæ*; through the power of seeds or the internal logic of growth</note>; in physical bodies, it exists through images. And in that which is above all these, it exists in a certain way that is "super-intellectual" and "super-essential" <note>Existing beyond the limits of thought or being itself</note>.

In the highest things, there is unity combined with power. In the lowest things, there is a great multitude combined with weakness.

When incorporeal substances descend, they are split apart; and their powers are multiplied and weakened in individual things. But when they ascend, they unite and run back together into a single point through an abundance of power.

### On the types of life.

It is not only in physical bodies that conditions vary; even "life" itself is described in many ways. For the life of a plant is one thing, that of an animal is another. There is the life of an intellectual essence, and finally the life of a superior nature. One kind belongs to the soul, another to the Intellect; for those higher things live as well, even if none of the things they create possess a life similar to their own.

Things that generate other things sometimes turn toward what they have created, and sometimes they do not at all.

Everything that generates by its own essence creates something lesser than itself, and...

# PORPHYRY.

Every created thing is by nature turned back toward its creator. Of those things that generate others, some do not turn back to their offspring at all; others are partly turned toward them and partly not; finally, some are turned only toward their offspring and, in the meantime, do not turn back toward themselves.

### Sensation, imagination, memory, and intelligence.

Memory is not a kind of preservation of imaginations <note>original Greek: ἀνὰ μελέτην προβάλλεσθαί τινας προβλήματα; "to put forward certain problems for the sake of exercise or practice"</note>, but rather it is the very propositions or the bringing into action of those things which the soul has contemplated, leading them forth into a new state of activity.

### The soul indeed possesses the reasons of all things.

The soul acts according to these "reasons" <term>Reasons: Translated from *rationes* (Greek: *logoi*); these are the formative principles or patterns within the soul that allow it to understand the world</term>, either being provoked to such activity by something else, or by turning itself inwardly toward its own reasons. When it is provoked by another, it allows the senses to introduce external things; but when it enters into itself, it reaches toward the intelligences—the pure concepts of the mind. Therefore, sensations do not exist outside of the imagination, nor—as one might say—do the intelligences, insofar as they belong to a living being. Again, sensations do not exist without the "passion" <note>original: *passione*; here meaning the physical experience or "undergoing" of a stimulus</note> of the sensory instruments. Likewise, intelligences do not exist without the imagination, unless there is an analogous condition—just as a physical shape is a consequence for a sensing animal, so a mental image is something that follows from the intelligence of a soul that is thinking within a living creature.

### The soul is immortal.

The soul is an unextended <note>It does not take up physical space</note>, immaterial, and immortal essence, possessing life from itself and likewise possessing its own existence.

### The passion of the soul and the body is far different.

It is one thing for bodies to suffer, and another for incorporeal things. For the suffering of bodies occurs through change or transformation; whereas the suffering of the soul is a certain accommodation and affection toward the thing itself, and a certain action, in no way similar to the heating or cooling of bodies. Therefore, if the suffering of bodies happens through physical change, it must be said that all incorporeal things are free from such suffering. For those things which are actually separated from matter and bodies remain the same. However, those things which approach matter and bodies are not themselves passive <note>They do not "undergo" change themselves</note>, but the things in which they appear do suffer. For when a living being feels, the soul seems like a certain harmony, separate and by itself, moving strings that are tuned together. The body, however, is like the harmony which is inseparable from the strings. But the living being seems to be the cause of movement because it is animate—possessing a soul. This is similar to a musician, who causes music because he is harmonious. The bodies which are struck through sensory suffering appear like the tuned strings. For there

And the musician certainly moves through that harmony which is within himself, yet the strings would not be moved by musical reason even if the musician wished it, unless the harmony itself dictated it.

### On the differences of incorporeal things.

The very name "incorporeal" is not used according to a commonality of one and the same genus (in the way that the word "bodies" refers to a specific category of things), but according to a bare privation of bodies <note>meaning "incorporeal" is defined simply by what it is *not*—namely, not a body</note>. Therefore, nothing prevents some among these incorporeal things from being "essence" <term>Essence: *essentia* (Greek: *ousia*); the fundamental reality or "being" of a thing</term>, while others are not essence; some exist prior to bodies, while others exist along with bodies. Likewise, some are separated from bodies, while others are not separated. Furthermore, some subsist through themselves, while others need other things in order to exist. Finally, some are identical in their self-moving actions and qualities; but others are changed in a certain way by disturbances and qualitative actions—namely, they are named according to the negation of those things which they are not, rather than the presence of those things which they are.

### The "passions" assigned to prime matter, similarly by Plotinus.

These are the properties of matter according to the ancients, which are indeed incorporeal. For matter is different from bodies; furthermore, it lacks life. It is neither intellect, nor soul, nor anything living through itself. Likewise, it is formless, changeable, infinite, and powerless. For this reason, it is not "being," but truly "non-being," a soft, appearing image. Since that which is first in mass <note>referring to physical bulk or volume</note> is itself powerless. Likewise, matter is a longing for substance, and it stands yet not in a stable state. Furthermore, it is always appearing within itself: now small, now large, now less, now more, now deficient, now exceeding—so that it is always becoming, but never remains, yet is unable to flee, since it is the lack of all being. Therefore, whatever it promises, it lies; and if it appears large, in the meantime it turns out small, for it is like a kind of game <note>original: *ludus*; Plotinus often describes the material world as a deceptive play or a shadow-theatre</note> fleeing into non-being. For its flight is not through space, but occurs while it falls short of being; wherefore the images within it are in turn within a worse image. Just as in a mirror that which is situated elsewhere appears elsewhere, and the mirror itself seems to be full and yet holds nothing, while it seems to hold everything.

### What suffers and what does not.

Passions <term>Passions: *passiones*; the state of being acted upon by an external agent</term> are all concerned with that which experiences both change and destruction. For the way toward destruction is the admission of passion, and to undergo this is to "suffer." However, no incorporeal thing undergoes destruction, but some among them either are or are not; therefore, none of them "suffers." For that which is suffering [passive] ought not to remain as it is, but must be such that it can be altered, and meanwhile be caught in the qualities of those things which enter it, and thus receive the passion into itself.

PORPHYRY:

For change does not occur to that which is within it by any random cause, nor therefore does matter suffer <note>original: *patitur*; in this philosophical context, to "suffer" means to be acted upon or to undergo a change from an external force</note>. For in itself, matter is devoid of quality, and so are the forms that enter into it and exit in turn. Instead, "passion" <note>the state of being acted upon</note> happens around the composite, and the being of the individual consists in its composition; for this individual seems to persevere in its existence amidst the opposing forces and qualities of the things that enter and bring about change. For this reason, those things whose life comes from external sources and not from themselves can certainly suffer both living and not-living. But for those things whose being consists in life, it is necessary that they remain living in spite of any suffering, just as it is appropriate for the absence of life not to suffer insofar as it is an absence of life. Therefore, just as changing and suffering happens to the composite of matter and form—that is, the body—yet this does not happen to the matter itself, so living and dying and suffering in this way is observed in the composite of soul and body. Yet this does not happen to the soul; for the soul is not something fashioned out of life and non-life, but consists of life alone, since it is a simple essence <term>Essence: *essentia* (Greek: *ousia*); the fundamental reality or "being" of a thing</term> and the very reason of the soul is a nature that moves itself.

## Every intellect contains all forms.

Intellectual essence is so similar in its parts that beings exist both in any particular intellect and in the universal intellect. But in the universal intellect, even particular beings exist by a universal reason. In the particular intellect, however, even universals and particulars exist together in a certain particular condition.

## Because the soul is life by essence, it does not die.

Regarding an essence whose being consists in life, and whose "passions" are certainly a kind of life, even death dwells within some quality of life. It is not a total privation <note>total absence</note> of life all at once. Because neither the passion nor the life is entirely directed toward non-living there, even though deprivation itself occurs in that state.

## Every incorporeal life remains immortal, however it may be changed.

In incorporeal lives, progressions are brought about while the prior things remain firm within themselves. They lose nothing of themselves, nor do they change in order to provide substance to lower things; wherefore those things which subsist from them do not exist with any loss or transmutation. Nor indeed is this produced like a "generation" <note>the process of coming into being in the physical world</note> that partakes in destruction and change. Therefore, they are unbegotten and incorruptible, and are produced as unbegotten and incorruptible according to this very principle.

## How that which is above intellect is to be understood.

Concerning that which is above the mind <note>Referring to "The One," the supreme principle in Neoplatonism</note>, many things are indeed said through the intellect; however, it is considered by a certain "void" of intelligence through a better kind of intelligence <note>This refers to the "Cloud of Unknowing" or apophatic theology: we understand the Divine best by realizing that our logical intellect cannot grasp it</note>.

For "like is usually known by like," since all knowledge is a kind of assimilation to the very thing that is being known.

->Non-being is either superior to being, as is God, or inferior, as with matter.<-

What is called "non-being" <term>Non-being: *Non ens*; in Neoplatonic thought, this refers to things outside the realm of "Being" (defined as the realm of Intellect and Forms). God is "non-being" because He is beyond being; Matter is "non-being" because it lacks true form.</term> is either something we devise ourselves by separating from "being" itself at some point, or it is something we understand while we possess "being." Therefore, if we are separated from "being," we do not understand "being" as that non-being which is above being, but rather we conceive of non-being as a false passion <note>original: *passionē*; an experience or state of being acted upon</note>, occurring to the one who wanders outside of himself. For just as each person, insofar as he exists—that is, truly and through himself—can be led back to that non-being which is superior to being; so, by wandering away from being and from himself, he is then carried over to the non-being which is the fall and ruin of being itself.

### Incorporeal substance is wherever it wishes.

The nature of the body does not hinder that which is incorporeal in itself from being everywhere and in any manner. For just as it is incomprehensible to a body that which is lacking in softness <note>original: *mollis*; likely referring to physical bulk or the "give" of material things</note>—it has nothing to do with it—so to the incorporeal, that which is physically distended is not an obstacle and lies there like non-being. For that which is incorporeal does not move about where it wishes by local condition <note>physical location or travel</note>. For "place" exists only together with mass. Nor, again, is it constrained by the limits of bodies. For whatever lies in mass can be confined to a narrow space and act through local change of position. But that which is entirely exempt from mass and magnitude cannot be contained by those things that are in mass; it remains free from local motion. Therefore, it is found in whatever specific disposition it has, wherever it is disposed. Meanwhile, it exists everywhere and nowhere at the same time. For this reason, by a certain specific affection <note>a state of being or inclination</note>, it is apprehended either above the heavens or in some part of the world. However, when it is held in some part of the world, it is not perceived with the eyes, but its presence is made manifest to men through its works.

### Incorporeal substance is constrained by no body, but produces a sustenance in the body through which it applies itself to the body.

If the incorporeal should ever be contained in a body, it is not necessary that it be shut in like animals in a pen; for no body can constrain it in such a way, nor can it be held like a wineskin draws in and contains some liquid or breath. Instead, it must supply powers emanating from its own union within itself, by which it is applied to the body as it descends. Therefore, its union with the body is fulfilled through an ineffable extension of itself. For this reason, not another...

...indeed any thing binds it, but it certainly binds itself. Therefore, it does not release the body itself when it is broken or perishes, but rather it unties itself when it turns away from its familiar affection <note>a "familiar affection" here refers to the soul's habitual attachment or emotional bond to the physical body</note> toward the subject.

## Universal causes do not turn toward effects but turn them toward themselves.

No substances which are universal and perfect turn toward their own offspring <note>original: *geniturā*; that which they have produced or generated</note>. All perfect substances, however, are led back to those that generated them, and this proceeds even down to the world-body. This body, since it is perfect, is led back to the soul—the intellectual soul, I say—and therefore it moves in a circle. The soul of the world, moreover, is raised up to the Intellect. The Intellect, however, is raised toward the Principle <note>The "First Principle" or "The One," the ultimate source in Neoplatonic thought</note>. Thus all things, starting from the furthest extremes, reach toward this very point as far as the capacity of each allows; they arrive in that elevation toward the first, having been led that far. This is usually accomplished either from nearby or from a distance. Therefore, these things can be said not only to desire God, but even to attain Him according to their powers. 

But in particular substances <note>such as individual human souls, as opposed to the "Universal Soul"</note>, which are capable of slipping into many things, there exists a tendency that deflects toward their offspring; therefore, in these things, "sin" <note>original: *delictū*; in this context, it refers to a metaphysical "falling away" or error rather than a moral transgression</note> is said to have occurred. In these, unfaithfulness is condemned. Matter itself, therefore, contaminates these things, because they are able to be bent toward it—even though they could have turned themselves toward the divine without error. For this reason, perfection—which is second to the things that come before—remains established by preserving those same things turned toward their superiors. Defect, however, deflects even the higher things toward the lower, and it causes them to love these very things while, in the meantime, turning away from what is superior.

## How God, Intellect, and Soul are everywhere in different ways.

God is everywhere because He is nowhere; the Intellect is everywhere also because it is nowhere; and finally, the soul is everywhere because it is both everywhere and nowhere. But God is everywhere and nowhere in relation to all those things which come after Him. He belongs only to Himself, just as He is and as He wills. The Intellect, however, is indeed everywhere in God, but in those things which come after it, it exists equally nowhere and everywhere. 

Finally, the soul is likewise everywhere in the Intellect and in God; but in the body, it is simultaneously everywhere and nowhere. The body, on the other hand, is in the soul, in the Intellect, and in God. Indeed, all things—both "beings" and "non-beings"—are from God. And yet, for all that, God Himself is neither these beings nor non-beings, nor does He exist within them. For if He were merely everywhere, He Himself would be all things and would be in all things. But because He is also nowhere, all things are surely made through Him, and they are made again in Him because He exists everywhere; yet they are also distinct from Him because He is nowhere. 

Similarly, the Intellect, existing everywhere and yet nowhere, is the cause of souls and of the things that follow souls; yet it is neither the soul itself, nor the things that come after the soul, nor does it exist within them—evidently because it is not only everywhere in relation to those things that come after it, but also nowhere. Again, the soul is neither the body, nor is it in the body, but it is the cause of the body; for while it is everywhere throughout the body, it is simultaneously nowhere in the body. Finally, the progression of the universe ends in that <note>the material realm</note> which is able to be neither everywhere nor nowhere at once, but instead becomes a participant in each by certain alternating turns <note>this refers to physical objects which are stuck in one specific place at one specific time</note>.

# ON STARTING POINTS. <note>original: *De Occasionibus*; This title refers to Porphyry's *Sententiae*, or "Points of Departure," which are short philosophical axioms designed to lead the student toward the intelligible world.</note>

## From Porphyry's work *On Abstinence from Animals*, translated by Marsilio Ficino of Florence. <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was a celebrated Italian scholar who revived Neoplatonism by translating the works of Plato and his followers into Latin.</note>

### The soul sleeps in this body.

<margin>a.</margin>We command abstinence from [eating] animals—not indeed for everyone, but at least for anyone who intends to contemplate divine things. Such a person truly observes the "poisonous charms" <note>original: *ueneficia*; suggesting the deceptive or distracting nature of the physical senses</note> of this dwelling place in which we live; furthermore, he recognizes that part of himself which is by nature perpetually awake, and he detects the "sleep" by which he is oppressed here. To this person, we shall surely hand down a way of upbringing and nutrition that is consistent both with the nature of this place and with the knowledge of his true self.

### Happiness is not the knowledge of divine things, but a divine life.

Blessed contemplation is not for us an accumulation of words or a multitude of studies, as someone might perhaps have thought; for it is not composed in that way. Nor does it receive its growth according to the quantity of arguments and words; otherwise, nothing would prevent those who have gathered all the academic disciplines from being happy. In truth, not just any study can fulfill a person with happy contemplation; nor do the doctrines concerning true things ever achieve this on their own, unless there is also present a life that has been transformed into the very nature of divine things. 

Indeed, the end goal of contemplation is Being itself <note>The ultimate reality or the "One"</note>, and to attain the Truth in such a way that an affection of this kind fuses the contemplator—according to the strength of his nature—into one with that which he contemplates. For the return is not to something else, but to his own true self; and the "breathing together" <note>original: *cōspiratio*; a mystical union or harmony</note> is not with something else, but truly with himself. And his true self is the Intellect <note>term: *Intellectus*; in Neoplatonism, this is the divine Mind or the first emanation of the One, representing pure, non-discursive thought</note>. 

For this reason, the end goal is to live by the Intellect. Speeches and studies applied from the outside provide us with a condition of purification <note>original: *purgatoria*; practices that cleanse the soul of material attachments</note>, but they are not the actual principle by which our happiness is fulfilled. Therefore, if happiness consisted in a heap of words and arguments, it would be possible for men to reach the happy end simply by maintaining a certain education and fixed duties. But since it is necessary to change the soul from this life into another, let us set aside words and arguments and work on those purifications; let us say which words and which works might best instruct us. Are they not those words and duties by which we are separated from things that move the senses and from the passions of the senses? And by which we are finally led back to the intellectual life, which is above the imagination and, as far as our strength allows, free from passion?

### Concerning the soul’s descent and ascent.

It is necessary for us—if we are to return to those things which are truly our own—to cast off entirely these things we have taken upon ourselves from our mortal nature, along with the affection that sinks down toward them, through which our descent occurred. Furthermore, we must remember the blessed and eternal substance; and while we strive to ascend toward the incorporeal, we must meditate on two things above all: by what reasoning we may cast off material and fleeting existence...

# PORPHYRY 30

...we are also able to see by what way we might especially return—namely, by returning through the contrary path to those ways by which we descended to these [earthly] things of ours. For we were, and still are, pure intellectual essences, free from all sense-perception, living by an [above-]irrational nature. But we have been joined to a sensible nature, both through the failure of an eternal continuation toward our intelligible realm, and through a power turning toward lower things. For all powers acting in concert with the senses and the body only then first sprout into effect when the mind has least dwelled upon the intelligible itself. It is like a land already corrupted, which, although it has often received wheat, at last yields only weeds <note>original: *lolium*; darnel or cockle, a common weed in grain fields often used in classical literature to represent moral or intellectual corruption</note>. And this happens through a certain depravity of the soul, which surely does not destroy its own essence while it sprouts this irrational seed; rather, through this very act, the soul is joined with the mortal while it is dragged from its own nature toward that which is foreign. 

Wherefore, if at any time we desire to return to our pristine state as much as we are able, it is necessary to separate the soul entirely from sense and imagination, and from every irrational condition and passion of that kind which follows from them, as far as the necessity of nature permits. We must rightly arrange and articulately compose those things which pertain to the mind, establishing tranquility and peace from this war against the irrational. In this way, we may not only hear about the intelligible things through the intellect, but also enjoy how great a power we are—namely, by the contemplation of the mind and by being restored into an incorporeal nature. Thus, we may truly live through the intellect and no longer falsely along with kindred, decaying natures. 

Therefore, we ought to loosen many garments from ourselves: both this visible garment [the body] and those inner robes still wrapped around us <note>The "garments" of the soul are a common Neoplatonic metaphor for the various layers of the personality and astral body that the soul "puts on" as it descends through the planetary spheres to Earth.</note>. For we ought not only to avoid vices by their effects, but to root out the effects themselves from the very source. Moreover, the departure from the body can indeed happen with violence, and it can also happen through a certain persuasion; indeed, it is rightly accomplished through a certain thinning out, or as one might say, through the oblivion and death of the passions. This is indeed the best departure, since it draws nothing with it from that which the soul is being torn away. For just as in things manifest to the senses, we see that whatever is plucked out by violence usually draws with it either a part or a trace of that from which it is rooted out <unclear>no less</unclear>.

### On the release of the soul.

The ancient sages diligently avoided all things that could bind them to the body. Thus, the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, known for their asceticism and belief in the transmigration of souls.</note> and similar wise men partly withdrew into solitude, and partly lived in temples and sacred groves, far from the crowds, so that they might be removed from all turmoil. Plato, however, chose the Academy <note>Plato’s school in Athens.</note> as his dwelling—a field not only solitary and apart from the city, but even (as it is said) unhealthy <note>Tradition holds that Plato chose an unhealthy, swampy location for the Academy to help keep the body weak, thereby preventing it from distracting the soul's philosophical focus.</note>. Others indeed did not even spare their eyes, so that they might maintain an internal contemplation, perpetual and interrupted by nothing. A philosopher indeed does not extract the soul from the body by violence...

...[it escapes;] for even if one has used force, the soul will nevertheless remain in that same place from which you have compelled it to exit. Nor will it think it of little consequence if, by fattening the body, it has fortified for itself a harsher prison. For it will take care lest the senses and their pleasures, should they grow strong, submerge the soul more deeply into the body. Indeed, if the activities of the senses did not impede the pure activity of the mind, what burden would it be to be in the body, provided you do not suffer the motions that occur through the body in the least? For in what way would you judge and say what you have suffered unless you actually suffer it—unless you were present to the things you were suffering? 

The Intellect <note>original: *Intellectus*; in Neoplatonism, this refers to *Nous*, the higher realm of pure being and thought</note> indeed remains within itself, even if we are not within it; but he who departs from the Intellect is already there where he has crossed over. Running to and fro, up and down, by the exertion of a certain focused perception, he is already present there where that perception itself takes place. Much less can he who descends to the experience of sensible things and acts through the irrational faculty simultaneously contemplate purely those things which pertain to the Mind. Nor do those who attribute two souls to us <note>A reference to the Platonic theory of a rational soul and an irrational/animal soul</note> permit us to have two simultaneous focuses of attention. Otherwise, they would have created two separate pairs of living beings. It might be possible for one soul to be intent on some things while the other did not claim the work of the first for itself. 

But why then would it be necessary to weaken the bodily passions, to die to them, and to meditate on this daily, if we could act according to the intellect while joined to mortal things without the intellect's oversight, as someone once declared? "The intellect sees, the intellect hears." <note>original: *Intellectus enim uidet, intellectus audit*; a famous fragment from the poet Epicharmus, often cited to show that the mind, not the eye, is the true organ of perception.</note> But if you eat luxuriously and gorge yourself on the sweetest wine, can you meanwhile apply yourself to divine things? Why are you not frequently among the divine while you cling to human things and commit those acts in social intercourse that are not even honorable to speak of? For everywhere there are the disturbances of the "child" within us <note>The "child" (*puer*) is a philosophical metaphor for the irrational, undisciplined part of the soul that seeks instant gratification.</note>; and because they are base, the contemplator cannot be distracted toward them and contemplate at the same time. For where sense-perception and such awareness are present, the Intelligible is absent; and the more the irrational faculty is excited, the further intelligence is removed. For it is not possible for someone carried here and there to be here and there simultaneously. For we do not achieve things with only a part of ourselves, but with our whole attention.

# PORPHYRY

...the body is struck by external things, and that impact reaches perception. For perception itself and the focused attention of the mind is the sound itself. Indeed, it cannot happen that the soul "sounds" <note>original: *sonet*; Porphyry uses the metaphor of the soul vibrating or resonating with the sensory input</note> unless it is entirely turned toward the sound and has directed its presiding eye toward this very thing.

When, however, the lack of many things has been removed as a cause, and we have been liberated from that abundance which is introduced into the body, and are now lightened of their weight—then the eye of the soul flashes out from the smoke and the bodily tide. It no longer needs delay or demonstration because of its own natural skill, which knows no rest.

Furthermore, the consumption of meat does not contribute at all to health, but rather hinders it. Since health is maintained by the same means through which it is recovered, and it is recovered through a very slender diet and by abstaining from meat, therefore health is preserved by this same practice. Even if abstaining from animals contributes less to the strength of a Milo <note>Milo of Croton was a legendary Greek wrestler famous for his incredible strength and massive consumption of meat</note>, certainly the philosopher has no need for an increase in such strength. If he is to be a contemplator, and does not give himself over to outward actions and lack of restraint, it is surely fitting to preserve health—not out of fear of death, but rather so that we are not blocked from the goods that proceed from contemplation. 

But an undisturbed state of soul and a disposition of thought directed toward that which Truly Is <note>referring to the Platonic concept of *To On*, or absolute reality</note> preserves health best of all. For much vigor overflows into the body from there, just as the experience of our own friends has proven. It has proven it to such an extent that they drove out the sharpest pains of the joints of both feet and hands—which for eight full years had forced them to be carried by others—as soon as they cast away their pursuit of money and external affairs in the court and turned their zeal entirely toward divinity. Thus, they expelled money, cares, and the disease of the body all at once. 

From this, it appears that a certain habit and state of soul contributes most—or rather everything—to health, and a thin and frugal diet contributes much to the same. But if it is necessary for us, fearing nothing, to confess the truth freely: it is not granted to reach the end <note>The "end" or *telos* of human life, which for Neoplatonists is union with the Divine</note> in any other way except when we are (if it is right to say) fastened to God and uprooted from the body and bodily pleasures. For since salvation <note>original: *salus*; can mean health, safety, or spiritual salvation</note> itself is acquired by us not through the mere hearing of words and reasons, but through deeds, I say we cannot be joined to God otherwise than through the purest abstinence. This applies not only to any particular god, but much less to the God who presides over all and exists simply above even corporeal nature. For as much as He is simpler, purer, more self-sufficient, and more distant from matter than all others, so it is necessary that the soul which is one day to enjoy Him be that much purer.

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s treatise "On Abstinence from Animal Food," transitioning from the health benefits of a slender diet to the theological arguments against animal sacrifice. # ON THE OCCASIONS FOR SACRIFICE

The first people to offer sacrifices did not use animals but herbs, first-fruits, and flowers; later, they used trees as sacrifices and burnt aromatic spices. Those who first began to feed upon animals did so out of a scarcity of crops, turning upon the animals for food. For previously, they lived on the fruits of the earth. There are three reasons why one must sacrifice to the gods: to venerate them, to return thanks, or to ask for necessities and ward off evils. To obtain these things, however, a vow of the soul is sufficient, to which small gifts from the fruits of the earth may be added. But to slaughter animals is a sin. <note>original: *nefas*; refers to an act that is contrary to divine law or moral right</note> Indeed, we too shall dedicate sacred things to the gods, but we shall offer different sacrifices, just as is fitting. We shall sacrifice differently to the various superior beings. 

To the God who reigns over all things—as a certain wise man said <note>This likely refers to Apollonius of Tyana, a Neo-Pythagorean sage</note>—we shall offer nothing perceptible to the senses. We shall use neither incense nor names. For there is nothing material that would not immediately be impure to him who is entirely immaterial. Therefore, even vocal speech is not suited to him, nor even the internal speech of the mind when it is stained by any passion of the soul. Instead, we shall worship him rightly through pure silence and by pure thoughts concerning him. 

It is necessary, therefore, that those who have become joined to and like God should dedicate this elevation of ours toward God as a sacred victim. This very act is both divine praise and our own salvation. In this contemplation of God, which is free from all passion, this sacrifice is fulfilled. 

However, to his offspring, who are the <term>intelligible gods</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, these are divine beings that exist between the supreme "One" and the physical world, accessible to the intellect</note>, we must now offer praise through speech. For a just offering of first-fruits is made to each of the divinities from those things which they bestow, and through which they nourish us and preserve our existence for the capacity of sacrifice. Just as farmers bring first-fruits from the things they gather—namely bundles of grain and the fruits of trees—to the divinities, so we shall dedicate to them the first-fruits of our intelligence and similar excellent gifts, giving thanks for those things they have bestowed upon us, namely the contemplation of the gods and their order. 

This is especially true since, through this inspection of them, they truly nourish us, being present everywhere and appearing to us, and favorably aspiring toward our salvation. But now, it even grieves many students of philosophy to labor at this; they worship fame rather than divinity and occupy themselves with statues. They neither consider whether or how such things should be approached, nor do they strive to learn from those who are powerful in divine wisdom how far and to what extent one should participate in these matters. 

We, however, shall contend with these people very little, nor shall we strive to discern anything of that sort. Instead, we shall greatly imitate the holy and ancient people, dedicating to the gods the first-fruits of that very contemplation which the higher beings have granted us, and the use of which is absolutely necessary for our true salvation. Thus, the Pythagoreans, being occupied with numbers and lines, dedicated many of these to the gods, naming one number Pallas, another Diana, another Apollo, and yet another Justice, another Temperance, and similarly in the end...

...and in this way, through similar sacrifices, they pleased the gods by the authority of God, so that they might call upon each one of them with their offerings. By the benefit of these gods, they frequently made use of prophecy and whenever they required something for examination. Regarding the gods who are within the heavens—whether moving in a certain way through the wandering stars <note>The planets</note> or the non-wandering stars <note>The fixed stars</note>, whose leader must be considered the sun first, and then the moon—we can appropriately consecrate fire to them as if it were a kinsman. And we must observe what the theologian <note>original: *theologus*; likely referring to an ancient authority like Orpheus or Pythagoras</note> commands. He says that no living creature <note>original: *animatum*; specifically meaning "having a soul," here referring to animals</note> is to be sacrificed, but only flour, honey, and the fruits and flowers of the earth. For he knows the man who is a true cultivator of piety. To the gods, indeed, no living thing was ever to be sacrificed, but rather to demons and others, whether good or evil. But let us set these matters aside. Indeed, it seems to me that those things which most of the Platonists have made public should now be asserted by my own talent. They hand down this manner: that the first God, since he is incorporeal, immobile, and indivisible, contained in nothing—not even in himself—needs nothing external; nor does the Soul of the World <note>A Neoplatonic concept of the spirit that animates the entire physical universe</note> need external things. For it possesses and contains that which is stretched out in three dimensions, and a faculty that moves naturally, and by its own nature it has decreed to be moved in a well-ordered and regular way, and to move the body of the world according to the best reasons. However, the Soul received the body into itself and embraced it, even though the Soul is incorporeal and free from all passion. To the other gods—namely the world, the wandering and non-wandering stars, which consist of soul and body and are manifest to our eyes—we must sacrifice with inanimate sacrifices for the reason we have stated.

### On the kinds of good and evil demons.

What remains is the multitude of invisible beings, whom Plato called "distinct demons." Some of these, named by men, have obtained honors equal to the gods and other forms of worship among various peoples. Others, for the most part, are not named, but secretly obtain names and worship from certain villages or cities. The rest of the crowd is commonly called by the name of "demons." There is a belief established among all people that these beings will certainly harm the human race if they become angry because they are neglected and do not receive legitimate worship. On the other hand, it is believed they will do good to men who have won them over through vows, supplications, sacrifices, and other following rituals. Since, therefore, this opinion concerning demons is confused and contains much slander against them, it is necessary to distinguish their nature by reason. For perhaps it is necessary, as they say, to declare the source from which error has fallen upon men concerning them. We must, therefore, distinguish them in this manner. Any souls that sprout from the total soul and govern large regions in the space below the moon—<gloss>resting</gloss> <note>original: *ἀμπαυομέναι* (ampauomenai); meaning resting, ceasing, or reposing</note> while living, whether adhering to or placed upon a spirit <note>original: *spiritui*; here referring to the *pneuma* or "astral body"</note>—but surpassing that spirit according to reason, these must be judged as good demons. They provide everything for the utility of those things that happen, whether they preside over certain...

### ON CIRCUMSTANCES.
<margin>451</margin>

...they preside over animals, or over specific fruits, or other things ordained for their sake, such as rains, temperate winds, clear skies, the balance of the seasons, and everything else that contributes to these things. Among us, in turn, they preside over the arts, the discipline of music, medicine, gymnastics, and similar pursuits. It is truly impossible that those who look after the utility and convenience of things should, in turn, inflict harm. Among these should be numbered the demons <note>original: *daemones*; in Neoplatonic philosophy, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits or "guides" that exist between gods and humans</note> whom Plato says "convey and report": human things to the gods and divine things to humans, while they carry our prayers to the gods as if to judges. Indeed, they bring down to us the commands and warnings of those gods along with prophecy <note>original: *vaticinio*; the foretelling of the future or divine will</note>.

However, whichever souls are not described as being bound to a spirit, but instead mostly cause destruction, these are said to be carried away and driven by this spirit when the impulses of anger and lust grow strong. These souls are themselves also demons, but they are properly named "maleficent" <note>evil-doing or harmful</note>. Moreover, both all these and those we have said are different from them are invisible and not at all manifest to human senses, for they are not clothed in a solid body. Furthermore, they do not all have a single form, but are marked by many shapes. And the forms that seal their spirit <note>original: *spiritum*; referring to the "pneuma" or the airy, subtle body that Neoplatonists believed spirits possessed</note> sometimes appear, and at other times not at all. Sometimes they even change their forms—namely those who are of the worse sort.

Their spirit, insofar as it is something corporeal, is subject to passion and is dissoluble; but because it is so bound by the souls, its appearance can endure for a long time, yet it is not eternal. It is consistent that something always flows out from it and is nourished [by it]. The body of the good [demons] consists in proportion, just like the bodies of things manifest to us; but the bodies of the maleficent demons are discordant. In a passive state, they inhabit a place near the earth. Therefore, there is no evil they do not dare to perpetrate. For they have an entirely violent and insane character, being abandoned by the guardianship of the better demons. For this reason, they plot and rush forth with many violent and sudden ambushes. And while they carry out their incursions, they partly try to hide and partly inflict violence. For this reason, the sufferings inflicted by them are sharp and swift. Healings and corrections from the better demons seem to be slower. For every good thing is easy and steady in its governance <note>original: *gubernatione*</note> and proceeds in order, nor does it overstep what is appropriate. If, therefore, you think about demons in this way, you will never fall into that most absurd opinion through which you might think that either evils happen because of the good or goods happen because of the evil. Nor is the discourse absurd only in this way; many, conceiving the same, even have the worst opinions about the gods...

-># PORPHYRY.<-

...opinions among many people. For this is one of the greatest harms brought about by **malevolent spirits** <note>original: *maleficis dæmonibus*; in Neoplatonic thought, these are lower, chaotic spirits that inhabit the air near the earth</note>. While they themselves are the authors of earthly disasters—such as plagues, famines, earthquakes, scorching heat, fires, and the like—they meanwhile persuade us that the gods who are actually the authors of fertility and prosperity are responsible for these calamities. In this way, they attempt to absolve themselves from being seen as the cause of our misfortunes, and they succeed in this through their schemes.

First, they strive to hide their own injustice from us. Then, they bend our minds toward prayers and sacrifices intended for beneficial gods, as if those gods were angry with us. They do these and similar things because they are eager to lead us away from a correct understanding of the gods and toward themselves. Indeed, they take great delight in all things done in such an iniquitous and discordant manner.

And assuming the masks of other gods, they take advantage of our ignorance to draw crowds into their company. Because of these kinds of cravings, they set human minds on fire with habits and desires for wealth, power, and pleasure. Furthermore, they entangle us in new and foreign opinions from which rebellions and wars are born, along with other things of that kind. But what is most serious of all is that they persuade us that such things are done by the higher powers, even to the point of subjecting the **supreme God** to such accusations. They claim that he throws everything, both above and below, into turmoil.

This happens not only to uneducated people but also to many students of philosophy. The cause of the error proceeds and is confirmed from both sides. For those practicing philosophy who have never separated themselves from the common crowd fall into the same errors as the public; meanwhile, the masses, hearing opinions similar to their own from praised writers, are even more confirmed in this view of the gods.

Moreover, the **craft of poetry** <note>original: *poeticum namque artificium*; Porphyry, following Plato, often criticized poets for depicting the gods as fickle or immoral</note> has even more sharply excited such suspicions in men, because it uses a style of speech that is powerfully suited for astonishment and a kind of magical attraction. It is easily able to soothe and entice minds, and therefore to bring us to believe in things that are entirely impossible. But we must firmly believe that the good never harms, nor does the evil ever benefit. For it is not the nature of heat (as Plato says) to make things cold, but rather its opposite; likewise, it is not the nature of the just to cause harm. Most just of all things, by nature, is divinity itself. Otherwise, nothing would be divine.

Must we not, therefore, distinguish between this power and the lot of the **beneficial spirits**? For a power that is naturally inclined toward the opposite is contrary to what is beneficial. Indeed, opposites never naturally occur in the same thing. Therefore, since spirits of this kind...

# ON OPPORTUNITIES <note>original: *De Occasionibus*</note>

In many matters, they injure human nature—at times significantly. Yet, the **good spirits** <note>original: *boni dæmones*; in Neoplatonic thought, these are guardian spirits or 'daemons' who act as intermediaries between gods and humans</note> never abandon their duties. They constantly signal the dangers posed by malevolent forces as much as they are able, revealing them through dreams or through minds divinely inspired, and through many other means. If anyone were able to distinguish these signs, they would discover and avoid all the schemes of the wicked. For these spirits signal to all people, but not everyone recognizes the meaning, just as not everyone can read what is written unless they have first learned their letters.

However, all forms of **sorcery** <note>original: *veneficium*; literally 'poisoning,' but used here to mean harmful magic or witchcraft</note> are brought about by the contrary spirits. Those who inflict harm through magic rituals usually honor these spirits and their leader most of all. These spirits possess an abundance of shifting shapes and images, and they skillfully deceive us with a machinery of wonders. Through their work, wretched people devise **erotic spells** <note>original: *erota amatoriáque*; Greek-derived terms for love-potions or magical charms intended to incite lust</note> and love-magic. Every form of intemperance, as well as the hunger for wealth and glory, grows strong through them—and especially deception. For lying is the natural characteristic of spirits such as these.

They desire to be seen as gods, and the very power presiding over them wishes to be regarded as the greatest god. These are indeed the ones who delight in libations and the **savor of meat** <note>original: *nidore carnium*; the smell or 'steam' of cooking meat from animal sacrifices</note>. For their spiritual body is said to grow fat upon these things; it lives on vapors and fumes, and in various ways (as is fitting) it draws strength from the smell of blood and flesh.

A wise and temperate man will therefore take care not to use such sacrifices, lest he attract these spirits to himself. Instead, he will strive to **purify his soul** perfectly. For these spirits never attack a pure soul, because of its total lack of similarity to them. If it should happen that cities find it necessary to win over these spirits, such practices have nothing to do with us. In the city, wealth and external or bodily comforts are considered "goods" by the citizens, just as their opposites are seen as evils; they care almost nothing for the perfection and purity of the soul.

We, however, will do without the "benefits" that these spirits provide as much as possible. Instead, through our soul and our external actions, we will strive with all our effort to become like God himself and those close to Him. This is achieved through tranquility of mind, a clear understanding of the truth of things, and a life focused entirely on these goals. We must become entirely unlike wicked men, malevolent spirits, and anything that takes pleasure in mortal and material things.

For this reason, we shall also perform sacrifices according to the traditions handed down by **Theophrastus** <note>A student of Aristotle who wrote extensively on piety and the history of sacrifices</note>. With him, the theologians also agree, recognizing that to the extent we neglect to purge the soul of its disturbances, we are coupled to a wicked power. From this, we are deservedly compelled to soothe this power further, so that—as the theo- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely continuing 'theologians'</note>

->PORPHYRY:<-

...those who depend on external things, and who are not yet masters over their passions, are compelled by this very condition to repel the onset of such a power from themselves. Otherwise, they will never be able to cease from their labors.

### On sacrifices to evil spirits and on abstinence and caution against evil spirits.

Therefore, theologians—if they ever permit the slaughtering of animals to wicked spirits <note>original: *daemonibus improbis*; in Neoplatonic thought, "wicked spirits" or "daemons" are lower spiritual entities associated with the material world and passions</note> for the sake of avoiding the evils they might inflict—forbid tasting such sacrifices. At the same time, they command that before you sacrifice in this way, you must purify the soul through fasting, and especially through **abstinence from animals**. For they believe that the holy purity of the soul is like a symbol <note>original: *symbolum*; a spiritual token or mark of recognition</note> and a divine mark by which you are guarded, so that you suffer nothing from those beings whom you approach while reconciling them through sacrifice. 

For when your disposition is the opposite of those for whom you perform the sacrifices, and you are purer (and thus of a divine nature), you continue unharmed in both body and soul, protected by pure holiness as if by a fortress. For this reason, even **enchanters** and **sorcerers** <note>original: *fascinatoribus etiam ueneficisque*; literally those who use "fascination" or charms, and "venefici" or those who use potions and poisons</note> have found such caution necessary, so that they might be safer from danger. Nevertheless, they cannot be entirely safe, for those who call upon wicked spirits are accustomed to all kinds of lewdness. Therefore, purity and holiness are not the proper domain of sorcerers and incantation-speakers, but certainly of divine men and those who contemplate divine things. 

Truly, **chastity and abstinence** protect their observers everywhere against evil spirits through a familiarity with the divine. Thus, if enchanters had resolved to practice this fully, they would certainly never dare to use enchantments at all, as they would have been called away by this purity from the very lusts for whose sake they pollute themselves in their religious acts. Therefore, being full of passions and scarcely (if at all) abstaining from impure foods, they—being entirely impure themselves—justly pay the price for their wicked transgression against the universe: partly through the spirits they themselves provoke, and partly through divine judgment, which looks upon all the works and counsels of mortals.

### On true worship, sacrifice, and caution against evil spirits.

A **divine man**, however, will fortify his soul both with divine wisdom and with abstinence from foods that incite passions in humans, and even by a likeness to God himself. He will consider his uncontaminated soul to be, as it were, a temple of God—specifically within this universe, which is the temple of God the Father. Accordingly, since every physical body brings to us certain "effluxes" <note>original: *defluxus*; outflows or emanations of material energy</note> of material spirits, it is certain that together with the impurity of nourishment drawn from **flesh and blood**, a demonic power is present with us, which is friendly to this impurity and easily...

<meta>The previous page established that the soul must be purified to resist the influence of lower, malevolent spirits. ->ON SACRIFICES<-

...connected because of a very familiar likeness and property. For which reason all theologians have rightly applied themselves first of all to abstinence; and the Egyptian <note>likely referring to Chaeremon the Stoic or Egyptian priestly traditions Porphyry frequently cites</note> revealed these causes to us, bringing forth a most natural reason which experience had proven. 

Namely, that a depraved and irrational soul which has left its body by violence, being stripped [of the physical form], then moves itself toward that very body and lingers there. Hence the souls of humans who have died by violence also linger around the body. This very thing warns us not to exclude the soul from the <unclear>body</unclear> by force. Since, therefore, the violent slaughter of living beings [compels] <margin>right margin obscured</margin> souls to love the bodies they have left behind, <unclear>nothing</unclear> however stands in the way of the soul [entering] wherever something kindred <margin>right margin obscured</margin> attracts it. For this reason, in many places, many souls [are seen] <margin>right margin obscured</margin> to lament. And the souls of humans lacking burial linger around their bodies; <margin>right margin obscured</margin> these souls, indeed, sorcerers <note>original: *malefici*; practitioners of "black magic" or harmful sorcery</note> frequently abuse to perform their service, compelling the souls by the placement of the body, or by the assumption of some ancient right. 

When these historical facts were discovered, and once they understood the nature of the depraved soul and its kinship to the body, as well as the pleasure it feels toward the body from which it was torn, they rightly fled from and condemned nourishment from animals. They did this so they would not summon to themselves foreign souls—violently torn away and impure—which are drawn toward what is kindred to them; nor would they be prevented from approaching the one and pure God, should they perhaps be driven away from God by the presence of disturbing spirits <note>original: *dæmonũ*; here meaning lower entities that disrupt spiritual focus</note>. 

Experience has taught theologians in many cases that the nature of a kindred body becomes a kind of incitement to attract the soul. For those who desired to take into themselves the souls of prophetic animals <note>animals believed to have divinatory powers, such as hawks or crows</note>, by swallowing their principal organs—such as the hearts of stags, or moles, or hawks <note>original: *asturum*; northern goshawks</note>—they immediately received the present soul prophesying in the manner of a god. This soul, indeed, along with the consumption of its body, thrust itself entirely into the human body. 

Rightly, therefore, does the philosopher and priest of the God who rules over all things abstain from all animals. He alone, indeed, through himself, strives to approach the one God, provided that no crowd of accompanying [spirits] diverts him. By this communion, he himself then understands the nature of things and divines the future. He has God within himself; whereby he possesses the confidence and pledge of eternal life. Entirely transformed toward God, and in the place of a seer, he now becomes an intimate of Jove <note>original: *Iouis*; Jupiter, representing the supreme divine intellect</note>. 

Accordingly, if any necessity looms, good spirits <note>original: *boni dæmones*; benevolent or helpful spiritual intermediaries</note> are not lacking to this intimate of divinity, meeting him everywhere and foretelling the future through dreams, signs, and voices, from which he may learn what is necessary to avoid. For one must only depart from evil, and recognize what is best and most worthy of veneration in the universe: the "Whole," which is entirely good, friendly, and approachable. However, wickedness and ignorance of divine matters compel a person to despise the things he does not know...

PORPHYRIUS:

...to condemn. But among those who are able to hear, nature itself cries out. Since nature is intellectual, it leads its cultivators deep into sacred matters through the intellect. The wise man certainly knows that evil demons delight in animal sacrifices and portend the future through them. The gods, however, do not need such victims; they look upon the character of the worshipers, considering the greatest sacrifice to be a correct judgment regarding the gods themselves and regarding reality. For among the gods, the best offering is a pure mind and a soul free from perturbations <note>original: *perturbationum*; refers to the "passions" or emotional disturbances like anger and fear that Stoics and Platonists sought to master</note>. Hence Plato says it is fitting for a good man to perform sacrifices and be present at divine rites, but for the evil man, to labor in sacrifices is in vain.

->From the third book.<-

### That souls are sensory, rational, and immortal

<margin>1</margin>In the third book, he says he brings forward the true and Pythagorean opinion: namely, that every soul endowed with senses and memory is rational, and possesses both reason and speech <note>original: *rationem orationemque*; this refers to the Greek concepts of *logos endiathetos* (internal thought) and *logos prophorikos* (external speech)</note>—both the internal and external kind—by which animals speak among themselves. It is no wonder that their words are not discerned by us, since we do not discern the speech of many foreign peoples <note>original: *barbarorum*; meaning those who did not speak Greek or Latin</note>, nor do we assume they are merely making indistinct cries. He adds that if we are to believe the ancients and those who lived in our fathers' time and our own, there are those who claim to hear the speech of animals and understand it, as was the case among the ancients with Melampus and Tiresias and such men. Recently indeed, Apollonius of Tyana <note>a famous Neopythagorean philosopher and wonder-worker of the 1st century AD</note> is said to have heard a swallow announcing to others, in a gathering of friends, that an ass laden with wheat had fallen near the city and the wheat was scattered on the ground.

He then contends that animals possess reason, both because they communicate meanings to one another and because they provide for themselves with diligent skill and foresee future needs; also because they learn much both from each other and from humans, and teach one another in turn. He joins to this Aristotle, Plato, Empedocles, Democritus, and others—whoever have scrutinized the truth about animals—who found a participation in reason and speech in animals. It appears, however, that there is a diversity in this. As Aristotle also said, they differ very little in essence, but rather by a diversity of "more or less" <note>original: *magis minusue*; a philosophical distinction meaning animals have the same kind of soul as humans, just less developed or sharp</note>, just as many think the difference between gods and humans lies in this. It is not a difference of essence, but rather according to a perfect or imperfect state of reason; thus we consider the nature of reason to be common to us and the animals, but we exist in a state of "more" and "less." Aristotle says those animals are more prudent—that is, more cunning—which excel in the sharpness of their senses. Indeed, differences of bodies make the soul more or less easily affected, and render the reason more or less prompt; but they cannot change the soul according to its essence. When

# ON SACRIFICES

Neither senses nor passions make souls differ fundamentally from one another, nor do they cause a perfected state to be overstepped. Let it be conceded, therefore, that there is a difference of reason <note>original: *rationis*; refers here to the faculty of logical thought</note> among these creatures according to "more and less," yet the remaining animals are by no means entirely deprived of reason. Simply because we might understand more than animals do, we should not for that reason believe they are entirely without understanding—just as we do not deny that partridges fly simply because hawks fly faster. 

One might indeed grant that the soul "suffers with" the body <note>original: *compati*; the idea that the soul and body are physically and emotionally linked</note>, and that it is affected for better or worse by the body's condition; however, the nature of the soul itself is by no means changed by this. If the soul merely shares these sensations and uses the body as an instrument, it will naturally perform many actions differently through that instrument depending on how it is arranged—performing things we ourselves are unable to do. Although it shares sensations through a body disposed in a certain way, its own fundamental nature does not change. 

Those who claim that "brutes" act rationally only by "nature" <note>original: *natura*; implying a blind, mechanical instinct rather than conscious thought</note> do not realize they are essentially saying these animals are rational by their very nature. It is as if reason were not also inherent in our own nature. While our own perfection grows as we are nurtured by nature, that which is divine does not become rational through training or discipline. There was never a time when the divine was not rational; rather, it existed and was rational simultaneously. Nor is a being prohibited from being rational simply because it did not acquire its reason through schooling. Indeed, among other animals just as among humans, nature itself has taught many things, while training has provided others. 

Some have reasonably attempted to show that many animals are even wiser than we are, depending on the places they were allotted by fate. For just as those inhabiting the ether <note>the "upper air" or heavens, where gods and celestial beings were thought to reside</note> are rational, they say the same of those living nearest to them—that is, in the air. After them, those in the water and those on the earth differ among themselves by degrees of reason. For if we measure the dignity of the gods in some way by their celestial location, we should likewise weigh the dignity of animals by theirs. 

Socrates, and before him Rhadamanthus <note>a legendary judge of the underworld known for his absolute justice</note>, used to swear oaths by animals. The Egyptians even considered certain animals to be gods—whether they truly believed them to be gods, or deliberately depicted the forms of the gods with the faces of oxen, the features of birds, and other animals so that people would abstain from harming animals no less than they would humans. Or perhaps there was another, more secret reason, just as the Greeks placed the horns of a ram upon the statue of Jupiter, and the horns of a bull upon the statue of Dionysus. They composed Pan from the forms of a man and a goat. They gave wings to the Muses and the Sirens, and they say that Mercury and Jupiter took the form of a bull, as well as an eagle and a swan. 

By these examples, the ancients testified that animals ought to be honored. Even Socrates was not joking when he said the swans were his "fellow servants." The Tablet <note>original: *Tabula*; likely referring to the "Table of Cebes" or Pythagorean doctrines on the soul's journey</note> indicates that animals share a soul with us, stating that due to the indignation of the gods, souls pass from humans into animals; and when they have passed through, the gods finally take pity. Through these and similar points, it is signified that animals are rational beings. In many, reason is indeed imperfect, but it is not altogether absent.

<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion on whether animals possess reason, this page transitions into the ethical consequences of that reasoning.
