# PORPHYRY

### It is wicked to kill animals.

It is unjust to kill animals since they are not entirely foreign to our own nature. We, however, acting as if we were wanton and insolent, frequently kill many animals everywhere as a sport in theaters and hunts. By doing this, the savage and ungentle force within us has grown more powerful, while our humanity and gentleness have withered away. The Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who were famous for their vegetarianism and belief in the transmigration of souls.</note>, however, practiced gentleness and mercy toward wild beasts as an example of humanity and compassion.

Everything that is inanimate, because it lacks reason and mind, stands in opposition to that which possesses a soul, reason, and a certain intelligence. For every living creature <term>animatũ</term> <note>literally "animated" or "having a soul"</note> possesses sensation and a form of imagination akin to reason. Nature, which does and has done all things for a purpose and for the sake of something, made the animal capable of sensation—not simply so that it might feel or be acted upon, but so that it might perceive what is beneficial and what is harmful, pursuing the former and fleeing the latter. Therefore, the senses bring the knowledge of both to each animal. 

As for those things that follow sensation—namely, the pursuit and capture of useful things and the avoidance of harmful ones—it must be believed that these cannot exist except in those who possess a certain power of reasoning, judgment, and memory. Even Strato the Physicist <note>Strato of Lampsacus, a Greek philosopher who argued that sensation is impossible without the mind's involvement.</note> says that sensation does nothing without intelligence. Indeed, we often do not perceive things present before our senses while we are focused on thinking about something else. Nevertheless, even if sensation did not require the mind for its basic action, when it directs itself toward what belongs to it and what is foreign, and places a distinction between the two—fleeing one and following the other, and sagaciously finding a middle way of pursuit or escape—we can conclude that reason is present within it. These actions are the proper functions of reason, and they are present in all animals, specifically those capable of movement <term>progressiuis</term> <note>original: *progressiuis*; refers to animals capable of walking or moving from place to place, as opposed to stationary life like sponges or plants.</note>.

### He who lives content with little and is innocent is like a god.

Since the goal of the soul is to become like God, and God lacks nothing and harms no one, surely he is most happy and most like God who so prepares himself that he needs as little as possible from others and harms as little as possible. Such a man, therefore, will feed only on the fruits of the earth, so that he does not harm men or animals; and as much as he is able, he will even spare plants and herbs. For the ancients themselves lamented even this: that we have need of the fruits of trees. 

The cause of this need was born from the fact that we were placed in a state of want through the process of <term>generationem</term> <note>In Neoplatonic thought, "generation" refers to the descent of the soul into the physical, material world of birth and decay.</note>, having become removed from the state of plenty. Poverty seeks salvation from external things. Therefore, he who requires many external things is more closely joined to poverty and is thus further separated from God. For he who is like God possesses true plenty by that very likeness. The man who is truly rich and enjoys his wealth brings injury to no one. Indeed, as long as he inflicts injury—even if he possesses all the money in the world and the entire...

<summary>Porphyry argues that killing animals is a moral failure that erodes human kindness and explains that because animals possess judgment and memory, they share in a form of reason. He concludes that a holy life involves minimizing one's needs and avoiding harm to all living things to achieve a god-like state of self-sufficiency.</summary>

->DE SACRIFICIIS.<-
<note>original: "ON SACRIFICES"</note>

->d 4<-

...he who occupies the land is to be considered poor, since he is a companion of want. Therefore, an unjust man is profane and polluted by every depravity. This vice was brought upon us by a certain fall of the soul as it descends into matter, departing from the Good. All things, therefore, are trifles insofar as one falls away from the Beginning. The mind is in need of everything so long as it does not look up toward that very fullness. That which is mortal in its nature gives way, insofar as it does not know how to revere itself. But he who has already become like God, and is content with the smallest amount of food, enjoys the prosperity of the Golden Age.

### A certain degree of reason exists even in animals.

Reason is indeed naturally present; however, right and perfect reason comes from meditation and teaching. Therefore, a certain participation in the rational faculty belongs to all animals. As for perfect righteousness and wisdom, one cannot find even a human who has fully attained them. Just as there are differences in sight itself and flight itself—for hawks <note>original: *Astures*</note> and cicadas do not see in the same way, nor do eagles and partridges fly in the same way—so too, not every rational being shares equally in sharpness and cunning.

### From the fourth book.

### The ancients abstained from animals.

Dicaearchus <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle.</note> the Peripatetic says that the ancient Greeks, being born closest to the gods, were the best by nature and lived the best life, so much so that their generation was judged to be "Golden." He adds that they killed no animals. Indeed, they believed nothing was better for health than to accumulate as few superfluities as possible. Thus, they did not wish to take in nutrition that would overpower nature, but rather that by which nature might be stronger. The ancient priests of the Egyptians also, who were devoted to the study of wisdom—of whom Chaeremon the Stoic <note>An Egyptian priest and philosopher who lived in the 1st century AD; he was a tutor to the Emperor Nero.</note> treats most diligently—abstained mostly from animals. Indeed, they revered many animals as divine, saying some were associated with certain gods, such as the hawk, the beetle <note>original: *cantharum* - likely referring to the scarab beetle.</note>, the ram, and the crocodile being associated with the Sun. For they understood that the soul of every animal is rational once it has been separated from the body, and that it foretells the future, divines for us, and is the producer of all things—just as the soul of a human is when released from the body. Therefore, they did not honor animals without reason, and they restrained themselves from them as much as possible.

### The sober life of the Essenes.

He then tells from the history of Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the Romano-Jewish historian whose works provide the primary account of the Essenes.</note> about the life of the Essenes <note>A Jewish sect known for their communal living and strict discipline.</note> among the Jews, who were religious men and philosophers. He describes how they held all things in common, practiced mutual charity and absti[nence]...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of ancient philosophical sects, moving from the Greeks and Essenes to the Indian Gymnosophists, exploring their ascetic practices and the metaphysical reasons for abstaining from meat.</meta>

<header>PORPHYRY: WHY THE ANCIENTS</header>

...that they cultivated self-restraint and patience above all things, always intent on divine worship. They were so strong in spirit that they preferred to be killed rather than deny God. They were even accustomed to laugh openly amidst their very tortures; those being tortured for this cause would release their spirits cheerfully, as if they were to receive them back again. For this conviction is firmly held among them: that souls are immortal, and that descending from the thinnest ether, they are attached to bodies by a *rush* <note>original Greek: ῥύμῃ (*rhume*), meaning a forceful movement or impetus</note>, drawn toward bodies by a natural impetus and instinct. But after they have emigrated from the prison of the body, they exult as if finally free from a long servitude, lifting themselves through the heights. They abstained both from many animals and from every kind of lack of self-control. Finally, from this life—which was both most temperate and most devoted to the study of truth and to God—many among them would foretell future events; for that reason, they were called prophets.

### Ancient sages despised the present life in hope of the future.

The sages of the Indians are named Gymnosophists <term>Gymnosophists: literally "naked philosophers," a term used by Greeks to describe Indian ascetics who practiced extreme renunciation</term>. Among them, those who advanced in the study of religion and wisdom through a certain hereditary succession are called Brahmans. However, those who professed the same path by choice alone were called Samaneans <note>likely referring to Shramanas, wandering monks of the Buddhist or Jain traditions</note>, whose life Bardesanes of Babylon describes at length. The Samaneans endured the time of this life as a kind of necessary servitude to nature, and they strove to release their souls from the body. Even when they felt the body was in good health, they would often depart from life with nothing forcing them to do so. Therefore, their kinsmen considered them blessed in death, and they wept for those who remained alive as if they were unhappy.

### Sobriety and contemplation join the mind to God.

### Besides other temperance and holiness, the Gymnosophists abstained from animals.

Indeed, the holiness that abstains from mortal things <note>referring here to the consumption of animal flesh</note> contains eternal life. But a fattened body forces the soul to go hungry, causing it to fall from the happy life. It increases the mortal element, and by expelling and hindering eternal life, it contaminates us, rendering the soul "corporeal" <note>heavy or material in nature</note> and turning it toward that which is different from the divine. Consider the magnet: the magnet stone imparts a certain spirit to iron when it draws near. Thus the iron, which is naturally very heavy, becomes light and is lifted by the "breath" of the magnet, pulling itself toward the stone. If, therefore, a person escapes into the incorporeal and intellectual realm by being suspended toward God, they rightly should not seek nourishment that makes the body fat, for that blocks the path to the mind. Instead, they will reduce the body to the minimum and most absolutely necessary food. Such a person will be nourished by divinity, joined to God more naturally than iron is to a magnet. Indeed, if we did not even require the smallest amount of food, we would be all the more blessed as we became more immortal. But as it is, living in this mortal state, we still secretly make ourselves (so to speak) even more mortal...

# THEY ABSTAINED FROM ANIMALS.

While we nourish the body and (as Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC) was Aristotle's successor and a pioneer in botany and ethics</note> says) while the soul, becoming familiar through <gloss>familiarization</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἐνοικειώσει (*oikeiōsei*), a technical term describing the process by which the soul becomes accustomed to or "at home" in the physical body</note> by dwelling with the body, contracts a great deal of necessity, and moreover devotes its whole self to it. 

But would that we had been able to lead a life entirely without food and drink, so that by restraining the physical waste of the body, we might immediately be joined to the highest things; among which God, being as He is, truly exists as God. 

But why indeed do we cry out and lament these things in vain to men, who are so blinded that they continually cherish their own misfortune? They hate themselves first, and then their own creator <note>original Latin: *genitorem*, which can mean biological parent or the divine progenitor of the soul</note>. Furthermore, they even hate those who advise and urge them to finally wake up from their drunkenness <note>a common philosophical metaphor used to describe the state of being overwhelmed by sensory desires and ignorance</note>. 

Democritus <note>the text reads "Democrates," but this is a common early modern variant or error for the pre-Socratic philosopher Democritus</note> says that to live imprudently, intemperately, and impiously is not so much to live badly as it is to die for a long time.

# MARSILIO Ficino the Florentine to the Great-Souled Lorenzo de' Medici sends greetings. 

<insert>s : . ⌝</insert> SYnesius, and Psellus, and Iamblichus, as well as Proclus and Porphyry—all Platonists—have long since entered your most spacious halls and greeted your noble sons. Up until now, they seem to have acted quite correctly. <meta>line flourish</meta> However, in leaving you yourself un-greeted, they have neither acted wisely nor turned out to be fortunate. Therefore, finally recognizing their own lack of wisdom, so that they may at some point be more fortunate, they now revisit your threshold to get to know the father, and in turn, to acknowledge the sons together with the father. Thus they will live more happily from now on. Indeed, they have recently discovered that even our own books *On Life* <note>original: *de uita*; Ficino refers to his famous medical-philosophical work *De vita libri tres*, dedicated to Lorenzo</note> did not wish to live without your patronage. Furthermore, Priscianus Lydus and Theophrastus accompany these five philosophers. For since they have long wished for my health <note>original: *valorem*, implying both physical health and the "value" or standing of his work</note> to be sound and have ardently desired it, they approach you today with eagerness. In this way, they will finally achieve their great wish: that they themselves, being safe in your care, might keep my health safe too—which, after God, desires to be sound primarily through you. Farewell, best of our patrons above all others, and listen happily to such great philosophers conversing in your presence.

# Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to the great-souled Piero de' Medici <note>Piero "the Unfortunate" (1472–1503), the eldest son of Lorenzo the Magnificent</note> sends greetings.

¶ Although you read many things daily that are better than ours, I think that almost none please you more than our own—if indeed it is true that one's own things usually please a person most. And a person’s own things are especially those that have been possessed the longest. Certainly, the works of Marsilio [Ficino] have been possessed by you for a very long time; I hope, therefore, that these will always be most dear to you, so that even if I send dreams <note>Ficino is playing on words regarding the subject of the book he is sending: Synesius' *On Dreams*</note>, these too might be held as true by you first, and through you, held as true by others. Since I desired that the Platonic philosopher Synesius' book *On Dreams*, which we recently translated from the Greek, should have authority and credibility primarily with its first reader, and through him with others, I sent it especially to you—you who are now the fourth generation after the great Cosimo <note>Cosimo de' Medici (1389–1464), the grandfather of Lorenzo and great-grandfather of Piero, who first sponsored Ficino’s Platonic Academy</note> to read our works, and who will immediately prove these things to everyone by your approval. I have added to the book *On Dreams* a book by the Platonic Michael Psellus *On Demons*, and not without reason, since the ancients believe that dreams are sent by demons <note>original: *demonibus*. In this Neoplatonic context, "demons" refers to spiritual intermediaries or "daemons" that bridge the gap between gods and humans, rather than purely evil spirits</note>. Farewell. April 15, 1489.

->SYNESIUS<-

### Synesius on Dreams, translated by Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Piero de' Medici.

It is an ancient custom, and a most Platonic one, to conceal the weightier mysteries of philosophy under a certain lowlier pretext <note>original: *viliori prætextu*; Ficino refers to the Neoplatonic practice of using allegories or simple stories to protect sacred truths from being misunderstood by the uninitiated</note>, lest perhaps those things which were discovered with the greatest labor should perish, or meanwhile be defiled if they were openly exposed to the common crowd. We have followed this custom in this work to the best of our abilities. Whether we have indeed achieved this, and whether we have treated the rest in the abundant manner of the ancients, those who read these things with a philosophical mind will be able to judge.

### Prophecy is the best of those things which humans pursue.

If dreams are prophets, and if those things seen in sleep provide humans with coverings <note>original: *involucra*; metaphors or "veils" of the future</note> for things to come, they will certainly be wise, though they will not be certain, insofar as the wisdom of dreams consists in that very uncertainty. For the gods have hidden the way of life from humans. Indeed, it is the unique good of divinity to achieve the greatest things without labor. Among us, however, not only virtues but also other excellent things are sought through sweat. 

Prophecy, however, will be seen as the greatest of goods. For by its very information—and by the faculty of knowledge itself—God excels over man, just as man excels over the beast. But for God, nature itself is sufficient for knowledge; for man, prophecy brings far more than common information can provide. For the common crowd knows only present things, while they merely guess at the future. Only **Calchas** <note>The legendary seer of the Greeks during the Trojan War</note> in the assembly of all the Greeks "knew what is, what was, and what is soon to come" <note>A reference to Homer’s *Iliad*</note>. For this reason, in the works of **Homer**, the affairs of the gods depend on their own will, since [Jupiter] existed earlier and knows more, precisely because he is more ancient. I believe that age in poems points to this: that by the benefit of time one happens to know more, since knowledge itself is surely the most honorable thing. 

If anyone, led by other poems, should think that **Jove's** <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> command consists in the power of his hands—because the poet says "he is superior in might"—that person interprets the poem poorly. He does not understand the philosophy within it, which says the gods are nothing other than **Minds** <note>original: *mentes*; in Neoplatonism, the gods are identified with divine Intellects</note>. Thus, when the poet says he excels in strength, he adds that he is also "prior in birth," since he calls Jove the "more ancient Mind." But what else is the strength of the Mind itself than **Prudence** <note>original: *prudentia*; here meaning practical wisdom or foresight</note>? Whoever is a god, and is deemed worthy to preside over others, commands by the excellence of his wisdom, since he is a Mind. Therefore, when the poet says, "He is more excellent in strength," and adds that "he knows more," it signifies the same thing to us. And because

->DE SOMNIIS<-

...therefore even the wise man is said to be like God, because he strives to be closer to Him in mind and exercises himself in that intelligence which constitutes the divine essence. By these reasons, let it be demonstrated that the prophecy toward which men strive is the most excellent.

## In the world, as if in one single living being, some things show signs to others.

---

<margin>s</margin>If indeed all things are signified by all things—since all things are kindred within the world as one living being—these things are like many-shaped letters, inscribed in the universe as if in a book. Some are Phoenician, some Egyptian, and some Assyrian. These the wise man himself reads. The wise man is he who understands the nature of things; one reads some things, another reads others; one more, another less. Just as one might read slowly, syllable by syllable, while another reads the whole word at once, and yet another reads the entire speech. In this way, wise men foresee the future: some by looking at the stars, others by flames—whether staying still or moving—others by examining the future in entrails, others in the chirping of birds, observing where they fly or where they land. There are also those who interpret clear signs of the future from voices, and from meetings, or from accidents that happen to another. Indeed, since all things are signified to all, if birds were wise, they surely would have gathered the art of prophecy from humans, just as we have accumulated skill from them. For we encounter them, just as they encounter us: recently, and long ago, and to the right, and to the left.

## Such is the harmony of the world that some things are drawn by others and work together in unison.

<margin>c</margin>Since this whole universe is sympathetic <note>original: *compatiens*; a Neoplatonic concept where all parts of the cosmos "suffer" or feel together, meaning they are interconnected</note> and breathes together <note>original: *conspirans*; literally "breathing together," referring to the cosmic spirit that links all things</note>, its parts must necessarily agree with one another, as they are parts of one and the same whole. It is worth considering whether lures or the "wagtails" of the magi <note>original: *motacillæ magorum*; likely a reference to the *iynx*, a bird used in ancient "sympathetic magic" to draw or attract objects or people</note> tend toward this. For just as worldly things are signified by one another in turn, so they are mutually charmed. Now, he is wise who holds the kinship of the worldly parts. For he draws one thing through another, holding present things like pledges for those far away—namely voices, materials, and shapes—just as in us, when something suffers internally, another part suffers with it. The pain of a finger often reflects in the nasal passage <note>original: *emunctorium*; literally a "cleaning place," referring to the sinuses or nose; an example of how distant parts of a body react to one another</note>, while many things between them do not suffer at all. Both of those parts are members of one living being, and they have something more kindred between them than with the others. And indeed, a certain stone or herb corresponds to one of the worldly gods, and by these, as if suffering with them, it yields to nature and is, as it were, enchanted. Just as one who strikes a deep note suddenly moves not the nearest <term>nine-to-eight ratio<gloss>original: *sexquioctauam*; the musical interval of a whole tone</gloss></term>, but the <term>four-to-three ratio<gloss>original: *sexquitertia*; the musical interval of a perfect fourth</gloss></term>.

<meta>This page continues Synesius’s argument regarding the interconnectedness of the cosmos. Having previously established that all parts of the universe act as "letters" for the wise to read, he now uses the metaphor of a musical instrument—the lyre—to explain how discord and harmony coexist within the world’s structure.</meta>

...and the sharp note called the *nete* <note>original: "netem." In ancient Greek music, the *nete* was the highest string or highest-pitched note of the lyre.</note>. For these things correspond closely to one another. Just as there is a certain harmony within parts, so too, above all, is there discord. For this world is not simply a single thing, but a unity made of many. In it, there are parts that agree for a time and others that differ; however, their disagreement contributes to the harmony of the whole, just as the structure of a lyre is a certain arrangement of dissonant and consonant tones. This "one made from opposites" belongs to harmony, to the lyre, and to the world itself.

-> Only what is connected to the world can be drawn by worldly things. <-

<margin>a</margin> Archimedes the Sicilian <note>The famous Greek mathematician and inventor (c. 287–212 BC).</note> desired a place to stand outside the earth, hoping that from there he could balance himself against the whole world <note>A reference to Archimedes’ famous boast: "Give me a place to stand, and I will move the earth."</note>. For he said that while he was upon the earth, he had no power against it. However, a man who is wise in any matter regarding the nature of the world would no longer have a way to use this wisdom if he were placed outside of it. For he uses it upon the world itself. Therefore, if the continuity is interrupted, this wisdom is in vain, and the signs observed for it lack life. Yet as much as the divine exists outside the world, it cannot be enchanted; one who is similar to this—who has been released—cares for nothing, for charms and allurements do not touch the nature of the mind. But that which is passive is soothed by charms and is drawn in. The multitude of things in the world, and the kinship of things that are united, provide the scope and breadth for prophecies and purifications. Regarding purifications and solemnities—let our discourse move nothing for the moment, keeping faith only with civil law—it is safe to accept prophecy, for its entire nature is proven through the things contained within. 

As for what concerns the present, one may choose the best and dwell more intensely on its consideration, while in the meantime we acknowledge that all prophecies have their own inherent obscurity. Thus, no form of prophecy should be rejected simply because it is obscure, as this quality is found equally throughout the whole of nature. Now, reason has declared that this is also to be revered: just as there is a secret in sacred rites, so too oracles are not open to everyone. For this reason, he who gives responses at the Pythia <note>The priestess of the Oracle of Delphi who delivered the messages of Apollo.</note> is called *Loxias* <note>original: λοξίας. An epithet of the god Apollo meaning "the Ambiguous" or "the Slanting," referring to the cryptic nature of his oracles.</note>, that is, "oblique" and "twisted." For even the "wooden wall" which Phoebus <note>A title for Apollo, the god of prophecy.</note> brought to the Athenians would have been heard by the common crowd in vain if Themistocles <note>The Athenian statesman who correctly interpreted the "wooden wall" as a fleet of ships, leading to victory against the Persians.</note> had not understood the hidden meaning of the oracle. Therefore, the prophecy of dreams should not be rejected because it is obscure, since it shares this obscurity in common with all other oracles.

<margin>s</margin> Truly, one must study this more than all other disciplines, since it is from within us, and is internal, and proper to each individual soul.

...themselves. For the intellect possesses the forms <note>original: "species." In this context, these are the ideal archetypes or "blueprints" of reality.</note> of all beings, just as ancient philosophy teaches. We can also add that, just as the intellect possesses the forms of those things which *are* (the eternal), so the soul possesses the forms of those things which *become* (the changing world). Indeed, the intellect is to the soul what Being is to the process of Becoming. Therefore, if we swap these—pairing the first with the third, and the second with the fourth—and exchange them in turn, we shall still speak the truth according to the established rules of science. Thus it will have been demonstrated, as we believe, that the soul possesses the forms of those things which are created; it possesses all of them, but it brings into action primarily those that are most fitting. It illuminates the imagination <note>original: "phantasiam." For Synesius, this is a "spirit-vehicle" that acts as a mirror for the soul's inner knowledge.</note> like a mirror, through which the living being perceives the things that remain within. 

Just as we do not notice the actions of the intellect itself until the presiding power communicates them to our common sense—and whatever does not reach that sense remains hidden from the living being—so too we are not accustomed to noticing the things in the primary soul before their imprints arrive in the imagination. And these images seem to exist as a kind of life that has slipped down a little and settled within its own natural property. Indeed, the powers of sensing belong to this faculty: for we see colors, hear voices, and perceive the most powerful strike and impulse while the physical instruments of the body are doing nothing. 

Perhaps, indeed, nothing prevents this type of sensing from being more sacred. For through this, we sometimes draw near to the gods as they warn us, foretell the future, or simply offer counsel. Therefore, if a "treasure" <note>original: "thesaurus." This can refer to a literal discovery of gold or a metaphorical discovery of wisdom through a dream.</note> or the gift of a dream should befall someone, I would not be at all surprised; nor if someone who is a stranger to the Muses <note>The goddesses of inspiration in the arts and sciences.</note> should fall asleep and, while slumbering, encounter them, emerging as a capable poet—partly speaking and partly listening. This is something our own age has produced, and it does not seem at all improbable. I pass over for now the well-known benefits of dreams, by which people are often delivered from ambushes, and how often sleep, acting as a physician, has driven away ill health. 

But when it opens a path for the soul—one it did not hope for or even contemplate—toward the most perfect contemplation of eternal things, this indeed is a gift that stands most eminent in the order of things: namely, to transcend nature and finally unite with the Intelligible <note>original: "intelligibili." The realm of pure, divine thought.</note> one who had wandered so far from there that he did not even realize from whence he came.

->### SYNESIUS<-

...to have that blessed commerce <note>original: "commercium." In Neoplatonic thought, this refers to the reciprocal exchange or communication between the human soul and the divine realm.</note> available to us, let him hear the sacred utterances, which show various ways for this purpose, and which, after the whole order of the narrative, offer opportunities from our innermost selves to ascend, through which it is granted to increase the inner seed. They say that God has given some the ability to learn the concept of light through study, while He has made others partakers of divine fruit and vigor even in their dreams. Do you not see how the eloquence of instruction is divided here into two paths? For it says that one person is taught while awake, while another is taught in sleep. 

But in wakefulness, the teacher is a human being; whereas, to the dreamer, God Himself makes him a participant in His fruit and vigor—as if learning and achieving were not the same thing; for to be nourished by fruits is much more than merely being taught. Truly, we have assumed this to affirm the dignity of the imaginative life <note>original: "vitae phantasticae." This refers to the life of the "phantasia" or imagination, which Synesius views as a spiritual faculty rather than just "make-believe."</note> against those who despair of it, even in the slightest degree. 

Now indeed, it is no wonder that those who possess an excessive and superficial wisdom feel this way—specifically those who have dealt in the very things condemned by the sacred utterances, where it is taught that sacrifices and the observation of entrails <note>original: "extorum." The practice of extispicy, or reading the internal organs of sacrificed animals to predict the future.</note> are vain and should be shunned. These people, acting as if they are superior to the common crowd, accept various other arts for foretelling the future and approve of such operations, yet they neglect dreams alone. They treat dreams as if they were something placed right before their eyes that is too common to be valued, because the ignorant and the wise partake in them equally. 

But what if the wisdom found here is actually greater for this very reason: because it is a more universal gift? Are not the other great goods, which are the greatest of all, also the most common? Nothing among all things seen is more divine than the sun, yet nothing is more common than the sun. If, however, to behold God Himself is a blessed gift, then certainly to perceive through the imagination is a gift of a more ancient and specific kind of inspection. 

For the imagination is the **sense of senses**, since the imaginative spirit <note>original: "phantasticus spiritus." This is the "astral body" or "spirit-vehicle" that Synesius believes mediates between the immaterial soul and the physical body.</note> itself is the most universal sensory organ and the first "body" of the soul. It is that which lies hidden, acting within, and it holds the governing principle of the living being as if from a citadel. For nature constructed the entire framework of the head around it. 

Hearing and sight are not actually senses themselves, but instruments of sense, serving the **common sense** <note>original: "communi sensui." This is a technical term for the faculty that binds together the data from the five individual senses into a single experience.</note> like doorkeepers and porters of the living being. They announce to the master the sensible things occurring from the outside world which strike the external sensory organs. Meanwhile, the internal sense is a complete sense in all its parts; it hears with the whole spirit, sees with the whole spirit, and is capable of all other sensations in the same way. It distributes various powers to different parts of the body, each of which is derived from the living being separately. These powers are like straight lines flowing out from a center and converging back at the center; they all spring from one common root, even though they become many through their progression. Therefore, the sense which occurs through the instruments openly displayed [the eyes, ears, etc.] belongs most to the animal nature, although it is not truly "sense" until it returns to the primary...

...into the first. For a sense produced without a medium is closer to the soul, and certainly more divine.

### Imagination is sharper than the outer senses.

<margin>a</margin>But indeed, if we honor the bodily senses for the sake of knowledge—since we know best those things we see—yet reject the imagination as less trustworthy than sense, we seem not to notice sufficiently that not even the eye itself truly reveals everything to us as it is. Sometimes it fails to show something, and sometimes it even lies, both due to the nature of the things seen and the nature of the organs themselves. Indeed, the same objects appear smaller or larger depending on distance; things seen through water appear larger to us, and a submerged oar appears broken; add to this the weakness of the eye. For a bleary eye presents objects as confused and indistinct. Therefore, whoever suffers from a weak imaginative spirit <note>original: "phantastico languet spiritu." In this context, "spirit" refers to a subtle physical substance that acts as the interface between soul and body.</note> should not demand clear and distinct visions. 

But what its illness is, and for what reasons it languishes or grows dull, or by what means it may be purged, refined, and restored to its natural purity, must be learned thoroughly from secret philosophy. By this philosophy, once purified through the mysteries, one emerges divine. Indeed, external influences flee before the spirit admits the divine; and whoever keeps this spirit pure by a certain natural way of life <note>original: "uictu quodam." Likely referring to dietary and behavioral self-discipline (ascesis) common in Neoplatonic circles.</note> uses it as something prepared by God, so that for this reason, such a gift is most common. For such a spirit also perceives the disposition of the soul itself and is not without sympathy toward it, just as the earthly body surrounding it is. For the body has conditions opposite to the higher dispositions of the soul. But its first and proper vehicle <term>vehicle: original "uehiculum" (Greek: 'ochema'). In Neoplatonic thought, the soul has a "star-carriage" or "astral body" made of light or ether that carries it down into the physical world.</term>, when the soul is in a good state, becomes refined and attains an ethereal condition; but when the soul is in a bad state, the vehicle grows dull and becomes earthly. In general, this is the gap between reason and irrational nature, between the incorporeal and corporeal levels, and the common boundary of both. Through this medium, divine things are joined to the lowest extremes; for this reason, it is difficult for philosophy to grasp its nature.

### The imaginative spirit is the soul's first vehicle.

<margin>u</margin>For this spirit claims something as its own, as if from both neighboring extremes; and things so far apart meet in a single nature. But nature extends the breadth of the imaginative essence through many ranks of things. It certainly descends even to animals that lack a higher intellect; in those cases, it is not the vehicle of a more divine soul, but it presides over the lower powers and is the very "reason" of the animal itself, and many things through this imagination...

the animal partakes of essence and acts with propriety; it is purified even in irrational beasts, so much so that something more excellent is inserted within them. Indeed, whole races of daemons <note>original: "dæmonum." In the Neoplatonic tradition, these are not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense, but mediating spirits between the human and divine realms.</note> derive their essence from such a life. For those beings are entirely "imaginary" in their whole existence, living among things that are imagined. Furthermore, man performs many actions through this faculty alone, or if he uses another faculty, he relies on this one even more. For we are not accustomed to produce thoughts <note>original: "intelligentias"</note> without the help of the imagination, unless perhaps someone briefly manages to touch upon a purely immaterial form. Truly, to surpass the imagination is a task no less difficult than it is blessed. Hence that Platonic ideal is especially desirable and satisfying: that even in old age, one might attain a mind and wisdom—meaning an intelligence that shines clearly without the need for imagination. Indeed, since our preceding and common life belongs to the imagination, or at least to an intelligence that uses imagination as its tool.

->The imaginative spirit is the middle ground between eternal and temporal things, and it is in this spirit that we mostly live.<-

Therefore, this animal spirit <note>original: "spiritus animalis." This refers to the "pneuma," a subtle substance believed to be the "vehicle" of the soul, bridging the gap between the physical body and the immaterial mind.</note>—which the blessed ancients have also called the "spiritual soul"—becomes a god, an all-shaping daemon, and a reflection <note>original: "idolum"</note>. In this spirit, the soul also undergoes its punishments. On this point, even the oracles agree, comparing the life of the soul in this state to the wandering visions of those who dream. Furthermore, philosophy proves that our preceding lives act as a kind of preparation for the lives that follow immediately after, while the best disposition or habit in souls makes this kind of spirit lighter and wipes away the density of a baser condition. 

By natural inclinations, therefore, the spirit is either raised on high because of heat and dryness. In Plato’s works, this is symbolized by the "growing of wings," and in Heraclitus, the same thing is signified by the "dry splendor" <note>original: "splendor siccus." Heraclitus famously stated that "a dry soul is wisest," associating dryness with the fire of intelligence and moisture with the dullness of the body.</note> or the wise soul. Alternatively, the spirit becomes thick and moist, whereby it is submerged into the recesses of the earth, hiding itself by its natural weight and being expelled into the subterranean region. For this place is most suitable for moist spirits. There, a wretched life is led, subject to punishments. However, through time, labor, and the purging of other vices, the purified soul may emerge again. For the soul runs its course through "twin lives," approaching better and worse things in turn. The soul borrows this kind of spirit from the celestial spheres when it first descends; boarding this spirit as if it were a boat <note>original: "cimbam"</note>, it enters into commerce with the corporeal world. But it engages in a struggle: it must either lead the spirit back up with it, or fail to remain united with it. Indeed, it can hardly happen that the spirit is dismissed without following the soul further, for it is a sacrilege not to believe the sacred signs. However, the return to the heavens would be shameful if souls did not return what was borrowed <note>original: "alienum"</note> but instead left behind near the earth that which they had received from above.

And this indeed may happen to one or to a second person as a gift from God and from the mysteries. For it is so ordained by nature that the soul, once implanted in this [spirit], either exerts an impulse together with it, or draws it along, or perhaps is drawn by it; in any case, it stays joined with it until it ascends again to the place from which it came. Therefore, when the spirit becomes heavy due to depravity, it drags down the soul that permitted it to be weighed down. This is the state in which the oracles <note>original: "eloquia." Synesius is quoting the *Chaldean Oracles*, a collection of philosophical and mystical texts highly regarded by Neoplatonists.</note> terrify the intellectual seed within us with these words: "Do not decline toward the dark world, beneath which lies a bottomless abyss, always unfaithful, and a black hell, filthy on all sides, which rejoices in senseless phantoms <note>original: "idolo demés." In this context, an 'idol' or 'image' refers to the lowest, most material form of existence.</note>." For in what way is a stupid and senseless life beneficial to the mind? Yet to the "idol"—that is, the phantom—the lower region is appropriate because of such a state of the spirit at that time. For like rejoices in like.

->The imaginative spirit can become purer and more impure, lighter and heavier.<-

Accordingly, if a single entity is forged from both through their union, the intellect <note>original: "intellectus." The highest, most divine part of the human soul.</note> also sometimes submerges itself for the sake of pleasure. This is the extreme of all evils: not even to notice the present evil. Those who are pressed down by this do not even attempt to emerge, for the disease has covered them in a very hard callus. And because they no longer feel any pain, they understandably do not strive for a cure. For this reason, repentance <note>original: "poenitentia." Here used in the sense of a philosophical "turning back" or change of mind.</note> has a peculiar power that leads one back to the higher realms. Indeed, he who endures his present state with difficulty will seek a way to escape. Therefore, the greatest part of purification is the will. By the gift of the will, both deeds and words lend a helping hand. If the will is removed, the entire mechanism of purification is lost to the soul, since the greatest pledge of reconciliation is missing. For this cause, both in this life and the next, punishments bring the greatest assistance to the order of things, while they oppose pain to pleasures and purge the stupid joy from our soul. Then truly, those misfortunes which are said to fall upon us beyond our merits contribute greatly to uprooting the affection we feel for these worldly fortunes. Certainly, among those who possess a mind, providence is confirmed by such things, while those who are mindless are usually led to distrust providence because of them. For no place is left for the soul to flee from matter if it should encounter no evil here. Therefore, one must believe that the rulers of the lower province <note>The "praesides" or "archons" who govern the material, earthly world in Neoplatonic thought.</note> have invented common prosperities as a trap for animals. Thus, while some might say that forgetfulness <note>An allusion to the River Lethe, the river of forgetfulness in Greek mythology.</note> happens to souls as they depart from here, the sweet and alluring condition of this life brings the drink of forgetfulness to the soul as it enters. When the soul has descended to its first life to labor for a reward, it willingly escapes its own nature through this mercenary status. This descent indeed...

<header>SYNESIUS</header>
<meta>catchword: is opposed</meta>

...it tended, so that it might fulfill the mystery of universal nature itself, according to the rules of the inevitable law which ordains these things. But fascinated by the gifts of matter, the soul is affected in the same way as those who, though they are free, are hired for a specific time to work for pay; then, captivated by the beauty of a certain handmaid, they wish to linger there, choosing to serve the master of that bitter girl. Now indeed, when by a deep-seated feeling external goods concerning the body seem pleasant to us, we appear to agree with the nature of matter that she is beautiful. She, however, signs our agreement as if in a secret contract <term>libellus: a small book or legal document, here used as a binding contract that "sues" the soul if it tries to leave</term>; and if we ever decide to depart from there as free men, she cries out that we are fugitives, and tries to recall us, and seeks us out like runaway slaves, bringing that contract into the open. Then, truly, the soul has the greatest need for courage and divine help.

For it is no light struggle to cancel one's own confession and pact. It happens, moreover, that force is applied. For material avenging punishments are then set in motion, according to fate, against those who rebel against the laws of fate. And this is exactly what the labors of Hercules signify, and the dangers which the sacred oracles <note>original: "sacra eloquia." Synesius refers to the *Chaldean Oracles*, which he viewed as divine revelation.</note> testify that Hercules had to endure—along with anyone else who bravely contends for freedom—so that he may lead the spirit to that point where the hands of nature can least reach out. But if a leap should occur within her boundaries, the soul is confined in a narrow space, and even heavier struggles are needed. For then she [nature] does not spare us, as if we appeared to be strangers; and if she despises our ascent, she demands punishment for the attempt and offers lives not from both jars—which Homer <note>Synesius refers to the two jars of Zeus in the *Iliad* (24.527), one containing blessings and the other evils. He suggests that in the material realm, the "good" jar is never unmixed.</note> secretly signifies by teaching that there are two portions of matter, distributing a double condition of fate, from which good is never pure. Now indeed, some also suffer a worse fate, though it be tempered.

### How beneficial is the repentance for sins, and how destructive is the love of mortals.

<margin>o</margin>
In general, all lives are involved in error—an error, I say, where there is no sudden return after the first descent. Consider how long this spirit deals with us. For when the soul is inclined downward, the oracle teaches that the spirit also grows heavy and is submerged until it enters a region dark on every side. But when the soul rises again, the spirit also accompanies it as far as it is able to follow. It is able, however, only until it reaches a step that is completely distant. Hear now what the oracles teach on this matter: "Nor shall you leave behind this most abject precipice <gloss>the precipice of matter</gloss>." But even for the image <note>original: "simulacrum," referring to the lowest, most material part of the human spirit.</note> there is a portion in the region bright on every side. This region, indeed, is quite opposite to the region dark on every side...

<summary>Synesius uses the myth of Hercules and the metaphors of legal contracts and Homeric jars to describe the soul's struggle to escape the gravitational pull of the material world. He explains that while the spirit can sink into darkness, it also retains a potential place in the divine light if it can be purified.</summary>

# ON DREAMS
## h
<meta>catchword: follows</meta>

...is opposed, even if in this place no one has interpreted it with excessive sharpness. For the sacred word <note>original: "eloquium." Synesius is likely referring to the *Chaldean Oracles*, which he treats as a primary philosophical authority.</note> does not seem to recall back to the spheres only that nature which first set out from there. Rather, it suggests that if the soul, while descending from on high before it was clothed in its earthly husk <term>cortex: literally a "shell" or "bark," referring here to the heavy, physical body that encases the soul</term>, contracted anything from the sublime fire or the air into its image-forming nature, then this very highest part—composed of air and fire—is recalled to the higher realms along with the soul's better part. For what is called the most abject part of matter cannot signify the divine body. 

Now indeed reason dictates that those things which communicate and contribute to a single end cannot lack a mutual relationship, joining, and persistence among themselves—especially those whose regions are neighbors, just as fire is closest to the circular body <note>The "circular body" refers to the ether or the celestial heavens, which move in circles.</note> and does not hold the extreme limit of things as the earth does. But if better things, sometimes yielding to worse ones, enjoy a communion, they create an indissoluble body in matter, as if formed by that which was permitted to rule in their meeting. Perhaps even the lower elements, not struggling against the action or activity of the soul, but being entirely tame, obedient, and following, exhibit a middle nature that cannot be scattered. Under the guidance of the primary soul, they are reduced together into an ethereal lot and are raised to the higher realms by a common pull; if not to the very summit of the universe, then at least they pass beyond the height of the elements and reach the region that shines on both sides. For the soul has (as it says) a certain portion in itself; that is, it is received into a certain order of the circular body. But let these things suffice concerning the portion and lot of the elements. While one may or may not believe these things, one cannot naturally deny that the corporeal essence, having set out from there, is lifted up at the same time as the soul flies back from the lowest depths and is fitted to the spheres—that is, it is poured back, as it were, into its own proper nature.

->**The soul has a celestial body as well as an aerial one, with which it flies back to the higher realms.**<-

<margin>h</margin> These indeed are the two extreme regions and lots. One is entirely dark on both sides, and the other is shining everywhere; these are the extremes allotted to happiness and unhappiness. But how many middle regions do you think exist within the world's capacity, which are dark on one side but shining on the other? In all of these, the soul lives its life together with this spirit <term>spiritus: the "pneuma" or subtle "vehicle" of the soul, which acts as a bridge between the immaterial mind and the physical body</term>, alternately changing its forms, habits, and lives. When, therefore, it returns to its own noble nature, it is a storehouse of truth; for it is pure, translucent, and altogether immaculate, becoming even a god or a prophet if it so chooses. But when it falls down, it is darkened, becomes erratic, and is prone to lying. For that which is misty in the spirit is unable to grasp the clarity of true things. Finally, when it holds the middle ground, it partly wanders and partly follows...

<summary>Synesius discusses how the soul's "spirit-vehicle" (composed of subtle elements like fire and air) can ascend back to the celestial spheres if it remains pure. He describes a hierarchy of existence where the soul fluctuates between the divine light of truth and the darkness of material delusion.</summary>
<keywords>soul's ascent, celestial spheres, astral body, pneuma, Chaldean Oracles, elements, spiritual purification, divinity</keywords>

# SYNESIVS

...d. You could also, by this reasoning, explore the demonic nature <note>original: "dæmonicam naturam." In the Neoplatonic tradition of Synesius, a *daemon* is not necessarily an evil "demon" but a mediating spirit between gods and humans.</note> and its order. In all things, to follow the truth or to err only a little is divine, or nearly divine. However, an erring condition in predicting the future necessarily belongs to those who are constantly inclined toward nature, whose condition is both subject to passion and utterly ambitious. For in this way, the soul enters subterranean places and abandons God and the more ancient guiding spirit. But by another means, the soul receives him, approaches him, and reaches the region dedicated to a more excellent nature.

### Concerning the Region Entirely Luminous, and Entirely Obscure, and Concerning the Middle Region, and How the Spirit is Revolved in Every Direction.

Accordingly, one can discern the order of the living soul in man from this: whenever the imaginative spirit <term>spiritus phantasticus: the "pneuma" or subtle "body" of the soul that acts as a bridge between the physical body and the intellect</term> is pure, composed, and watchful, it receives true images of things both while awake and asleep. Such a person then possesses a pledge by which they can assert that the very form of their soul enjoys a better lot. Moreover, we can determine with no small skill what the primary disposition of the animal spirit <note>original: "animalis spiritus," referring here to the spirit belonging to the *anima* or soul</note> is by observing the imaginations it especially produces and in which it occupies itself when it is not struck by any external influence. Philosophy, supplying a discerning judgment here, warns us to nourish and care for this spirit most diligently, lest it ever go astray.

The best education is to always act according to the intuitive and perceptive power, and to ensure that the primary act of the soul itself is always intellectual. We should always anticipate the absurd and reckless impulses of the imagination's concepts as much as possible. This means, first and foremost, turning toward the best and entering into no commerce with the worse, except as much as the utmost necessity compels. 

Intellectual intuition <term>intellectualis intuitus: the mind's direct grasping of higher truths</term> is something that, more than anything else, separates the physical accretions that have grown together in the spirit. For it thins the spirit itself more than can be expressed and directs it toward God. Once the spirit is made fit for this, it draws the divine spirit into commerce with our soul through a certain kinship. 

Just as when the spirit is constrained by some condensation and becomes too narrow to fill the seats assigned to it by the providence that fashioned man—those seats which are in the ventricles of the brain—then indeed, since nature does not tolerate a vacuum in things, an evil spirit creeps in. Then indeed, what might the soul not suffer, constantly pressed by an execrable evil? For nature has so arranged it that the seats of the spirit itself are filled either by something worse or something better. The former evil is the punishment of the impious who have ignored the divine within them; the latter good is either the goal of piety itself or, without doubt, near that goal.

# ON DREAMS

### How one might detect the purity or impurity of one's spirit, and by what means one may purify it.

---

<margin><unclear>O[...] u [...]</unclear></margin>
Since we have decided to discuss prophecy occurring through dreams—and so that men might not despise it, but rather cherish it as a beneficial aid to life—we have indeed carefully examined the phantastic nature. From this discussion, the immediate benefit may seem small, but the more excellent fruit is the return of a healthy spirit to the higher realms. It is surely such a sacred gain for the soul that it is a kind of religious practice to try to make such a spirit fit for prophecies. Now indeed, some, captured by a desire for prophecy for this reason, have preferred a sacred and mild table to a gluttonous one, and have loved a pure and entirely unspotted bed. Those who waited at the Pythian tripod <note>The tripod at Delphi where the priestess of Apollo sat to deliver oracles.</note> and the Phoebean couch for prophecy were certainly far from spending their nights there as witnesses to intemperance; rather, they entreated God and applied themselves more intensely to their vows. Because what is gradually accumulated eventually becomes great, and what is achieved through one means leads finally to something greater, we proceed to love God more vehemently and to encourage those who did not love Him before to join in this love.

->**Above all, we must strive to keep the phantastic spirit pure and fit for prophecies.**<-

<margin>n</margin>
Therefore, prophecy is not to be despised, as it leads us toward divine things and stands close at hand, being the most excellent power in the soul. Nor is the utility of the soul thus joined to God any less because it has been received into divine commerce <note>original: "diuinum comercium," referring to the interaction or exchange between the human soul and the divine realm.</note>. For it does not meanwhile abandon the living being, since it looks down upon lower things from its watchtower much more fully than if it were mingled with the worse parts. On this account, remaining unshaken, it will give images of the things that happen to the living being; and this is what is called "descending without descending," <note>A Neoplatonic concept where the higher soul cares for the body without being corrupted or fully "sinking" into the material world.</note> when a more excellent nature cares for a lesser one without being held fast by it.

I wish such prophecy to be present for me and to be firm for my children; to obtain it, we are not compelled to undertake a long journey, nor do we sail beyond the borders, as one does to the oracle of Pythian Apollo or Jupiter Ammon. Instead, it is enough to give oneself to sleep with joyful hands and after celebrating divine praises. She <note>Likely referring to the soul or the purified imagination.</note> first vows these joyful things to Minerva, having put on garments of pure color. Thus we shall long for a dream, just as Homer perhaps longed for one. Now indeed, if one is prepared, the God who is said to be far off will be present in an instant, since He becomes present everywhere to us even when we have performed no such rituals, but are merely sleeping. And these things...

<meta>catchword: us</meta>

<summary>Synesius argues that purifying the "imaginative spirit" through temperate living and religious devotion makes the soul a fit vessel for divine dreams. He emphasizes that this form of prophecy is superior because it is accessible to everyone at home, rather than requiring travel to distant oracles.</summary>

--- Page 169 ---
<meta>This page continues Synesius’s argument that dream-divination is superior to other forms of prophecy because it is accessible to all people, regardless of wealth or status, and requires no external tools or expensive rituals.</meta>

# SYNESIUS

The entire treatment of the mysteries is such that no one has ever complained of poverty in relation to them, as if they were less accessible to the poor than to the wealthy. Most states choose their high priests from the most noble and the richest citizens, just as the Athenians select their naval commanders; in those roles, there is a need for magnificent expenditures and <margin>|</margin> no small fortune to provide Cretan herbs, Egyptian feathers, and Spanish bone—and by Jupiter, whatever marvelous thing is born and nourished in the depths of the sea, whether where the sun sets or where it rises. For these and many other similar things are passed down concerning those who engineer prophecies received from the outside <note>original: "vaticinium acceptum forinsecus machinantur." Synesius refers to "technical" or external divination (like reading entrails or using exotic ingredients) versus "natural" divination through dreams.</note>. No private person’s wealth is sufficient to supply these materials. But a dream is seen by the lowly man just as much as by the one who possesses a great estate. The man struggling in extreme poverty sees them, as do the lookout and the hired laborer, the citizen and the foreigner alike. Indeed, in the eyes of God, there is no difference in the capacity for prophecy between an ox-driver, a slave, a madman, or anyone else. 

Because the condition of this prophecy is so suited to all people, it is certainly the most humane. Because it is simple and ready at hand by its very nature, it is truly philosophical. Because it is not violent, it is undoubtedly pious. And because it is present everywhere—not requiring us to employ water, or a rock, or a chasm in the earth <note>References to specific oracular sites, such as the spring at Didyma or the chasm at Delphi.</note>—it is rightly judged to be the most divine of all. 

It is also fitting to praise it for this primary reason: that for the sake of this kind of prophecy, we are not distracted from even a single business of life, nor do we waste any time. For no one goes home to bed for a scheduled dream after neglecting their necessary and present affairs. Instead, it is the very time that is necessary for a living creature to spend for the sake of restoring its nature—since our substance is not sufficient for the perpetual action of wakefulness—this very time, I say, grants us this gift of its own accord. As the saying goes, it joins a leisure greater than business <note>original: "ocium negocio maius." A play on the Latin terms 'otium' (leisure/contemplation) and 'negotium' (business/work).</note>, which is surely a thing to be desired: to combine well-being with simple existence. 

Conversely, regarding those omens that usually come through various instruments, we must consider ourselves lucky if, while they claim the largest part of our life for themselves, they <margin>.</margin> meanwhile concede anything at all to other life uses and actions. If you focus your mind entirely on those external methods, you will find it very difficult to be helped by this kind of prophecy. For it is not possible for everyone, at any time or place, to obtain the apparatus and equipment that serves those sacred rites. Nor is it easy to carry around the instruments necessary for such solemnities. And to omit other things: where punishments have recently been heaped up, there is a certain cruel burden <margin>|</margin> in a hollow ship <note>Synesius may be referring to the legal dangers of carrying divination tools during times when "magic" or certain pagan rituals were being prosecuted or suppressed by law.</note>, to which other parts of the rituals are added, namely designated men and witnesses—for this is the truth of the matter, since our current age is accustomed to announcing many things through the ministers of the laws.

<summary>Synesius argues that dream-divination is the most democratic and divine form of prophecy because it costs nothing and requires no exotic materials, unlike state-sponsored or "technical" oracles. He emphasizes that dreams occur during necessary rest, thus requiring no extra time or travel.</summary>

<keywords>divination, dreams, Synesius, poverty and wealth, Athenian navy, exotic rituals, religious law, philosophy of sleep</keywords>

<meta>Continues from page 83. The catchword "mi" on the previous page completes the opening word of this page, "mirum" (wonderful or strange), as Synesius continues his critique of external, "technical" divination rituals.</meta>

->DE SOMNIIS<-
->(ON DREAMS)<-

M ii

...it is a wonder how the works of rituals once kept secret have now come into the sight and hearing of the uninitiated common people. For besides the fact that it is harmful and wretched (as I think) to rely on these things, it is undoubtedly hateful to God. For to move someone not by their own will, but by external impulses and "levers" <note>Synesius uses the metaphor of "levers" (vectibus) to describe the forceful, mechanical way that external oracles or magical rituals attempt to "compel" a response from the divine.</note>, is nothing other than to offer violence. This is an act which even the human author of laws would not leave unpunished. Therefore, besides all these things, which are very difficult for those who search out the future in such a way, there is also the frequent interruption of the ritual itself, and the neglect of the art whenever we wander as exiles. For it is no light task for those wandering about to carry heavy packs of ritual supplies with them for such a journey.

But in the case of prophecy coming through a dream, each person is his own instrument. It is an oracle of such a kind that even if we wished to, we could not leave it behind; rather, it stays with those who stay at home and migrates with those who travel. It goes to war with the soldier, and simultaneously handles civil affairs, works in the country, and conducts trade. The laws of an envious city do not forbid this prophecy, nor could they forbid it even if they wished. For they have no grounds on which to condemn such a prophet. How, after all, do we do injury while sleeping? A tyrant could not prohibit us from seeing dreams unless he were to expel sleep itself far from the city—but it would be the mark of a madman to want the impossible, and of the impious to command nature and God to do things contrary to themselves.

### How useful and desirable prophecy is, especially through dreams.

<margin>a</margin> Therefore, it is fitting for women and men, the old and the young, the poor and the rich, private citizens and princes, rustics and city-dwellers, the elegant and the commoners alike to approach this prophecy. It rejects no race, no age, no fortune, and no particular craft. To everyone everywhere a ready prophet is present: a good and silent counselor, a teacher of sacred things, and a disciple all at once. It foretells good things, so that the dreamer, by anticipating their arrival, may enjoy the pleasure longer. It also foretells evil, so that we may be on our guard and repel the misfortune. Indeed, all things that are provident and useful are contained within dreams—whether they offer the best and most flattering prospects to nourish the human race, or whether they bring forth a useful fear. We are persuaded to hope by no other means as effectively as this, even though the capacity for hope is so great and salutary in nature that "elegant" <term>sophists</term> <note>Sophists were professional teachers and rhetoricians in the Greek world; here Synesius refers to their philosophical arguments about human nature.</note> proclaim that humans would not have even wanted to live if they were only affected by the conditions in which they were first created. They would have rejected life, driven by its difficulties, had not <term>Prometheus</term> <note>In Greek mythology, Prometheus gave humans fire, but also "blind hopes" to prevent them from despairing over their mortality.</note> inserted Hope itself into our nature as a remedy for persevering in life. Entangled by the allurements of hope, men judge what they expect in the future to be more "real" than their present state. Hope itself has such great power that even when someone is conquered by shackles, if it is ever permitted and hope should fall upon them, they are (so to speak) set free by dreaming of their wish.

<summary>Synesius argues that dream-divination is superior to ritual magic because it is internal, portable, and free from legal or tyrannical interference. He emphasizes that hope, often delivered through dreams, is a divinely-granted survival mechanism for humanity.</summary>

<keywords>dream-divination, internal oracle, legal freedom, Prometheus, hope, equality in prophecy, technical divination vs. natural divination</keywords>

<meta>Continues from page 84. The opening word "militat" (he serves as a soldier) completes the catchword "mi" from the previous page, where Synesius began describing how the imagination constructs elaborate fantasies while one is awake or asleep.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>SYNESIUS</header>

...he serves as a soldier, and suddenly makes double progress. A little later he commands a squad, soon he leads an army; he conquers, he slaughters, he is crowned, he hosts banquets, and he prepares a table—of figs if he pleases, or of Median delicacies <note>original: "medicam"; likely referring to Persian/Median luxury</note> if he prefers. Meanwhile, he has forgotten his feet, until the very moment he is about to lead the army. Yet this is truly the way of one who dreams while awake, and of a dream within wakefulness. For both revolve around the same subject, namely the phantastic nature <note>original: "naturam phantasticam"; Synesius uses this term to describe the imaginative faculty of the soul, which acts as a bridge between the senses and the intellect.</note>, which, as often as we decide to shape it with images, provides this one particular benefit: it defines our life with joy, flatters the wandering hope of the soul, and thus calls us away from the perception of troublesome things.

### An exhortation to acquire dream-divination, and concerning the power of the imagination.

<margin>¶</margin> When, however, the phantastic nature presides over us with its own proper function, <margin>q</margin> it stirs up hope within us, and this occurs specifically to those who are dreaming. We hold the promise of a dream as if it were a pledge from God <note>original: "dei pignus"</note>. On account of this, someone who eagerly prepares their mind—as if about to use the grander gifts proposed in the dream—gains a double profit: first, because they rejoice before the thing itself occurs, and second, because they knowingly use those things once they are obtained, since they have long meditated on them as being perfectly suited to life. 

Now, concerning that hope which Pindar <note>A famous Greek lyric poet (c. 518–438 BC).</note> praised—speaking, of course, about the fortunate man—saying that "sweet hope nourishes his heart and accompanies him," which "most of all governs the wavering mind of mortals everywhere": one might say that such hope, celebrated by him, is not that deceptive hope which tricks those who are awake (which we fashion for ourselves), but rather that this entire matter pertains to the dream-vision, and was said by Pindar to celebrate a small portion of dreams.

Therefore, pursuing dream-prophecy along with the art of interpretation makes what appears manifest a firmer vision, so that it does not seem to be of a lowlier kind. Penelope, indeed, in Homer’s writings, introduces two gates of dreams, and asserts that half are deceptive, because she did not possess the wisdom of dreams. For if she had approached these things with knowledge through the art, she would surely have led everything through the gate of horn <note>In the *Odyssey*, Penelope describes two gates: ivory for false/deceptive dreams and horn for true ones that come to pass.</note>. She is introduced there as being refuted and about to confess her ignorance regarding the vision itself, which she did not believe although she ought to have believed it: "The geese are the suitors; I, however, am the eagle." But this was her companion <note>Referring to Odysseus disguised as a beggar, who interprets the dream for her.</note>, and she was trifling with him regarding the vision. 

Indeed, I seem to hear Homer saying here that it is not right to distrust dreams, or to transfer the weakness of those who use them to the nature of the visions themselves. In Homer's work, not even Agamemnon <note>The leader of the Greeks in the Trojan War.</note> rightly accuses the dream of being deceptive when he had misunderstood the oracle concerning victory, which said: "I bid you to arm the helmeted Achaeans with breastplates." For now...

# ON DREAMS
<sig>M iii</sig>

...you would capture a most vast city. Agamemnon therefore hurried as if he were suddenly about to storm the city with his own strength, whereas he ignored and did not keep what was actually said by the oracle. For the oracle said he would certainly overcome it if he armed the entire army of the Greeks. But in fact, neither Achilles nor the phalanx of the Myrmidons <note>The elite warriors led by Achilles</note> went out to battle at that time—the most excellent part of the army, without a doubt.

---

->How much hope dream-prophecy provides us.<-

<margin>m</margin> I have certainly piled up many praises, yet I have behaved as if foolish. For as I said before, dream-prophecy sails with us, dwells with us, fights alongside us, trades with us, and serves everyone in everything. But I have not yet mentioned the benefits conferred upon me from there, although it is accustomed to communicate with men in nothing more than the exchange of philosophy. Many things that were doubtful during waking hours are either fully revealed after we have gone to sleep, or are partially debated with us; and now, indeed, the dreamer seems to ask and learn, and now even to discover. 

To me, indeed, it has often brought books together; for it instructed my mind and composed my speech. Sometimes it would describe a part of the day, or even change it. Sometimes it even corrected the entire foolish disposition of my tongue, which was swollen with the novelty of names because of an excessive love for the older and harsher Attic language <note>original: "attheæ linguæ"; Synesius refers to "Atticism," a stylistic movement that imitated the complex Greek of the 5th century BC. He suggests dreams helped him avoid a style that was too pompous or "swollen."</note>. Through God, this prophecy corrected me, partly by dictating and partly by showing what it was, smoothing over those artificial swellings of the tongue; it drove out the "tumor" <note>A metaphor for a bloated, overly rhetorical style</note> and applied a proper measure. 

And even when I was hunting at times, it supplied me with strength and strategies against wild beasts that were running or hiding through some craft. Sometimes, when I was exhausted and breaking camp, it commanded me to persist and promised success as a mistress, so that it was a pleasure to stay at the hunt with eager confidence. When such divination was lacking, Lady Fortune was present. She indeed showed the results of the provoked and captured beasts. 

To me, books and hunting are my life. I never desired to serve on embassies, considering it a waste to see three ill-omened years of one's life pass by. Yet even then, I was greatly assisted by this prophecy. For it rendered the plots of magicians <note>original: "magorum"; referring to sorcerers or political rivals using occult arts</note> who were plotting against me powerless, sometimes by revealing hidden things, and sometimes by freeing me from all dangers. Therefore, it even managed public affairs for me so that cities might be governed in the best way. It also reconciled me to the Great King <note>Referring to the Emperor in Constantinople, whom Synesius visited as an envoy</note> with greater confidence than any other Greek ever enjoyed.

<summary>Synesius argues that dreams provide practical guidance in all aspects of life, including solving philosophical problems, refining literary style, aiding in the hunt, and protecting against political conspiracies.</summary>
