<meta>This page continues Synesius of Cyrene's philosophical defense of dreams. Having previously discussed his personal success with dream-divination, he now transitions into a theoretical explanation of how the soul receives these divine messages and the "physics" of how images (eidola) from the world interact with the human imagination.</meta>

# SYNESIUS

Dreams provide us with prophecies in abundance. 
<margin>c</margin> While other matters require the care of specific specialists, this gift is present to everyone. A good guiding spirit <term>daemon: in Neoplatonic thought, a personal guardian spirit or divine intermediary between gods and humans</term> is present to each person; for those who, while awake, have meditated to discover something through their skill, this spirit appears as a teacher. The soul is such a wise thing when it takes its leisure, resting from the filth of the external senses <note>original: "colluuione forensium," literally the 'dregs of the marketplace' or the clutter of public life</note> which bring in foreign natures to the soul from every side. For whatever forms the soul possesses, and whatever it is accustomed to receive from the mind, it sometimes reveals clearly to those who have turned their gaze inward, translating those things that come from the divine. 

For the God of the world <note>the "Mundane God," referring to the divine principle immanent within the cosmos</note> joins himself completely to a soul in such a state, because the nature of the soul itself flowed forth from the same source as He did. These types of dreams are therefore considered more divine; they are either entirely or almost completely whole and clear, requiring very little help from the art of interpretation. But these indeed happen only to people who live in virtue, acquired either through wisdom or through disciplined habit. If, however, they occasionally happen by chance to someone else, it is rare indeed, though it may occur. But a noble dream does not happen to just anyone in a trivial way; the remaining kind, which is complex and very common, is entirely hidden. For the sake of this common kind, it is necessary to employ an art <term>art: referring to 'oneiromancy,' the technical skill or science of interpreting cryptic dreams</term>. For it has an origin that is absurd (so to speak) and monstrous. Since it sprouts from such things, it proceeds in a most obscure manner. For this is how the matter of dreams stands, as I shall explain.

->The prophecy of dreams is available to all.<-

<margin>a</margin> In all things <note>The Latin text reads "Somnibus," likely a printer's error for "Omnibus" (In all things), which fits the philosophical context of universal emanations</note> contained within the nature of the universe—whether they exist in the present, occurred in the past, or are spoken of as the future (for these too are modes of existence)—images flow out and are constantly vibrated forth from their substance. For if any perceptible thing is a form <note>original Greek: εἴδος (*eidos*), meaning the 'form' or 'species' of a thing</note>—that is, a species in matter, extended along with that matter—and we perceive that matter flows outward from the composite whole, reason certainly dictates that the nature of these forms is also derived externally through these images. This happens so that on both sides, those things involved in the world of "becoming" <note>generatione: the physical world of change, birth, and decay</note> decline from the dignity of true Being. 

Of all these images flowing from things everywhere, the phantastic spirit <term>phantastic spirit: the 'pneuma' or airy vehicle of the soul that acts as the organ of imagination</term> is certainly the clearest mirror. For otherwise, these images wandering about and slipping from their state—both because of their lack of defined existence and because they are known by no other existing being—as soon as they are ensnared in the "animal spirits" (which are themselves images, but have their seat in nature), they immediately lean upon them and rest as if in their own homes. Therefore, those things that have been done—since they have already proceeded into the act of being—are clear...

<summary>Synesius explains that while virtuous people receive clear, divine dreams, most people receive obscure ones that require interpretation. He introduces a Neoplatonic "physics of sight," where objects constantly emit "images" (eidola) that the soul's imaginative spirit captures like a mirror.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Synesius of Cyrene's exploration of the mechanics of dreaming. Having established that the soul is a divine thing that receives messages, he now moves into the "physics" of dreams, explaining how mental images (eidola) function like physical objects and how the "spirit-vehicle" of the soul must be prepared to receive them clearly. He transitions from theory to the practical "art" of interpretation.</meta>

# ON DREAMS

...clear images <term>idola: from the Greek *eidola*, these are the subtle forms or "films" shed by objects that travel to the soul</term> are sent forth in every direction, until they eventually become weak and small through the long passage of time. However, those that belong to the present arrive as much more powerful and manifest likenesses, since they still consist of their own substance; but the images of things to come are indefinite and quite indistinct. For these are like the first scrolls of things not yet present—a kind of blooming of a nature that is still imperfect, as if leaping forth and dancing outward, like the obscure markings of seeds still hidden. For this reason, an art <term>art: here meaning a systematic skill or science of interpretation</term> is needed for future events, because from them, shadowed images and dark likenesses proceed—certainly not as manifest as those from the present.

Images flow from all things, and their mirror and receptacle is the imaginative faculty itself <note>original: "species ipse phantasticus," referring to the *pneuma* or "spirit-vehicle" that acts as the seat of the imagination</note>.

<margin>m</margin>
The nature of images is indeed wonderful, as they are produced even from things not yet brought to pass. Therefore, something must now be said about this art, and by what method it may be acquired. First and foremost, it is best to have prepared the divine spirit <note>the Neoplatonic "pneuma," a subtle body that connects the rational soul to the physical body</note> in such a way that it becomes worthy for the intellect and God to become known to it and to preside over it. Let it no longer be a receptacle for indefinite images. The best education for the spirit is, first, to calm the disturbed movements of the soul through the study of philosophy—for when these are stirred up, the spirit itself is occupied like a conquered territory—and second, through a moderate and tempered diet, to affect the animal nature so that it is least prone to agitation. Thus, one should compose the outermost body so that it moves the waves as little as possible, for the ripple spreads all the way to the primary part of the soul. One must always strive to keep the primary part unshaken and undisturbed. However, since wishing for this is easy for anyone, but achieving it is more difficult than anything else, and because we desire that no dream be useless to anyone, let us now seek some boundary even within indeterminate things; that is, let us establish an art concerning these images. They behave in the following manner:

->How we can interpret dreams.<-

<margin>q</margin>
Those who frequently sail the seas, if they ever encounter a certain rock and, climbing upon it, glimpse a city from there, then whenever they see that same rock, they understand it to signify that same city. Furthermore, we often guess that army commanders, whom we do not yet see, are about to arrive by seeing their scouts; for in the past, the commanders have always been accustomed to follow when those same scouts ran ahead. By the same logic, we are accustomed to pre-signify future events through images. For precursors are the same as the things themselves, and similar things follow similar things. Just as it is a pilot’s laziness not to recognize a rock when it appears, nor to predict which shores he is approaching.

He uses the analogy of a sailor recognizing landmarks to explain how interpreters can recognize recurring patterns in dreams to predict future events.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Synesius’s argument that dream interpretation is a specialized skill. He moves from the general theory of images (eidola) to the practical application of this "art," comparing the dream interpreter to a navigator or a weather-watcher. He then begins a new section arguing that because every soul is unique and connected to different celestial origins, there can be no "one-size-fits-all" dream dictionary.</meta>

SYNESIUS

and such a navigator lacks the support of conjectures <note>original: "coniecturarum"; here referring to the rational inferences a pilot makes based on signs</note>. So it is with the person who frequently encounters the same vision: unless they have already marked out what specific outcome it portends for them—whether a feeling, a stroke of fortune, or an action—they use their life as senselessly as a navigator of that sort. We are also accustomed to noting signs of Jove <note>original: "iouia signa"; signs in the atmosphere or sky, as Jupiter/Jove was the god of weather</note> in the surrounding air; for instance, by looking at the circular area around the moon, we prophesy that there will be storms, since those who have looked at it frequently have found that winds follow. To this point tends that poetic saying: "from this a storm, from that a circular tranquility is designated." For a broken halo portends winds, while one that fades away portends calm. Two circles indeed precede a storm; however, a triple circle portends a more violent tempest, especially if it appears black, and even more so if it is broken. So it is in all things: both Aristotle and reason dictate that sense-perception produces memory, memory produces experience and skill, and from these, an art <term>art: a systematic branch of knowledge or "technē"</term> is finally established. We must proceed in a similar fashion regarding dreams.

**A common and identical rule for interpreting dreams cannot be applied to individuals.**

Most authors have composed many books on the observation of dreams in this manner. I, however, laugh at all these works, judging them to be of very little use. For the imaginative spirit <term>spiritus phantasticus: the "pneuma," a subtle, vaporous body that serves as the vehicle for the soul and the seat of imagination</term> is not like this ultimate physical body—that is, a coming together of reconciled elements—which can be subject to a universal art and a discourse that follows nature in a uniform way. For the physical body mostly suffers the same effects from the same causes, since in similar things there is little discrepancy; when something in them exists contrary to nature and falls ill, it is usually not hidden. Therefore, we do not use a single, guiding rule for the spirit; I say that the imaginative spirit itself does not behave that way, but from its very origin, one spirit differs from another. For one spirit aligns with one celestial sphere, while another aligns with a different one, insofar as in its temperament, this or that sphere prevails. Hence that poetic saying: "especially do the most blessed souls flow from heaven to earth, and those most wealthy, having been allotted unfathomable threads of fate." Whichever souls are less favored by the Splendid King <note>likely referring to the Sun or the Demiurge in Neoplatonic thought</note>, and those which come from Jove himself by the thread of powerful necessity—this was what he [Plato] secretly hinted at in the *Timaeus* <note>original: "timæns"; a likely OCR error for "Timaeo," referring to Plato's dialogue on the soul's origin</note>, where he assigned a companion star to each soul. But souls, having fallen from their own nature because they prefer to dwell near matter—this one less, that one more, insofar as each has used its own inclination of the scales—have unhappily stained the spirit. The spirit then inhabits bodies while thus affected, and the soul’s whole life is conducted in a state of error and disease...

<summary>Synesius argues that dream interpretation is an empirical "art" based on personal observation rather than universal rules. He explains that because each soul has a unique celestial origin and a different degree of material corruption, every individual's "imaginative spirit" responds to dreams differently.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Synesius’s argument against a universal "dream dictionary." He has just explained that because every person’s soul and its "spirit-vehicle" are unique, the images (eidola) they perceive in dreams will manifest differently. He is about to argue that dream interpretation must be a personal, autobiographical practice rather than a standardized science.</meta>

# ON DREAMS
67
4

...beyond nature, as far as the nobility of the species is concerned, but according to nature in terms of being a living creature. For a thing is animated by the spirit in this way—unless there is an inherent order to the spirit, it is ordered by itself, employing both depravity and virtue. Indeed, nothing is as easily moved or as changeable as the spirit. By what means, then, in things so unlike one another—whether by nature, by law, or by their passions—can the same results appear from the same sources? Certainly, it does not happen this way, nor can it. For how can water that is simultaneously turbid and clear, or agitated and still, be affected in the same way under the same form? But if the turbid condition differs from one person to another according to differences in color, and the motions themselves vary in their configurations, then surely there will be one general category of "straying" from a perfectly pure image, but the specific types of error will be diverse.

Therefore, whether Phemonoe, or Melampus <note>original: "Phemonoe, siue Melampus"; Phemonoe was legendary as the first priestess of Apollo at Delphi, and Melampus was a famous mythical seer who understood the language of animals.</note>, or anyone else claims to define a common rule for such matters and to organize them thoroughly, we shall ask them: can a mirror—whether it be straight or distorted, or made of different materials—return an identical image of the object? But these authors have not even begun to philosophize about the <term>spirit: the "pneuma" or subtle body that acts as the vehicle for the soul and the medium for dreams</term>. Instead, they think that their own individual spirit, however it may be disposed, is the rule and the standard for everyone. Now, I do not deny that some points of agreement can be found among things that are entirely different. However, that which is obscure and scattered only becomes more obscure; even from the beginning, the "idol" <note>original: "idolum"; here referring to the dream-image or reflection of a pre-existing reality</note> of a pre-existing thing was difficult to know. It is even more difficult to perceive something in every individual’s specific manner or habit that is entirely similar and perfectly suited to a common vision.

->Every individual observes their own dreams and the events following from them.<-

<margin>h</margin> For these reasons, one should in no way hope that universal laws of dreaming can be established for everyone alike. Instead, each person ought to treat themselves as the "material" of the art <note>Synesius suggests that the dreamer is both the artist and the canvas</note>, and they can record in their memory what kinds of visions have led to what kinds of outcomes. Indeed, it is not particularly difficult to gather a "habit" <note>original: "habitus"; a settled disposition or skill</note> regarding a matter that one contemplates through regular use or necessity. For use or necessity suggests the cultivation of memory, especially when the material is available everywhere. In the world of dreams, there is nothing more abundant, nor anything that draws the mind more strongly to itself. Dreams even compel the foolish to contemplate and care for them, to such an extent that it would be a shameful thing for men who have passed a decade since puberty to still require another <term>prophet: or "vates," a professional seer</term>, and not to have already accumulated for themselves many rules of this art. It would certainly be worthwhile to commit to writing, in detail, one’s visions and the things that happen—both while awake and while asleep—were it not that social custom looks down on the novelty of this practice...

<summary>Synesius argues that because the "spirit" (the medium of dreams) varies from person to person like different types of mirrors, there can be no universal dream dictionary. He concludes that every individual must become their own interpreter by keeping a record of their dreams and subsequent life events.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Synesius’s argument that dream interpretation is a personal, autobiographical endeavor. Having established that the "spirit-vehicle" (pneuma) is unique to each individual, he now introduces his famous practical advice: the keeping of "Night Books" or dream journals to complement one’s daily records.</meta>

# SYNESIUS

...dreaded of invention. By this indulgence, we judge that daily annotations should be joined every day with nocturnal annotations, so that the acts of both states of human life are kept recorded in commentaries. For reason has posited that a certain life is situated in the imagination—at times better than our "middle" [waking] life, and at other times worse, depending on how much health or disease the spirit possesses. <note>Synesius uses the word "spirit" (*spiritus*) here to refer to the "pneuma," the subtle substance that he believes links the physical body to the rational soul; if the pneuma is "clogged" by bodily passions, dreams become muddy or deceptive.</note> Thus, if we pursue this kind of observation with diligent effort, from which a personal art is gradually accumulated while nothing slips from memory, this will be an elegant delight and an exercise of the mind, as we honor the history of both our waking and our sleeping hours. Furthermore, this exercise contributes to eloquence. 

For those who care for the training of the tongue, there is (I believe) no invention more suited to exercising the faculty of speech in all matters. If the Lemnian sophist <note>original: "lemnius sophista"; likely Philostratus the Lemnian, a 3rd-century rhetorician who emphasized that a great orator should be able to speak on any subject, no matter how trivial.</note> teaches that daily writings are the best instructors for speaking aptly on every subject—because nothing, however small, is neglected, and one must learn to express everything, both grave and light—why then should we not also cultivate nocturnal annotations for the sake of interpretation?

->**How varied, deceptive, and playful imagination is in dreams.**<-

<margin>n</margin>
Someone might certainly ask how great a task he has undertaken who wishes to make his speech equal to the things seen in visions. In dreams, things which are naturally joined are separated, while those which are naturally distinct are joined together. Here, reason and discussion are needed so that a vision which is no longer present might be presented again; it is no light task to translate the prodigious and absurd motions arising in the soul into another mode of expression. 

When, through the <term>phantasia: the faculty of imagination or "image-making" in the mind</term>, things that actually exist are expelled from their state of being, and in turn, things that exist nowhere and can in no way naturally exist are introduced into being, what method is there to describe a nature within our thoughts that is entirely unnamable? These dreams show neither many hopes nor all things at once, nor do they present them in a logical sequence of time, even if they reach out and strike the dreamer. For we think that whatever the soul wishes occurs to it. In expressing all these things, one must linger at length—a task requiring the most perfect orator to avoid clumsiness. This boastful material exults in dreams against the very nature of discernment, bringing something more than simple estimation can bear. For we are not concerned with visions without feeling; rather, powerful constitutions and affections occur, no small hatreds arise, and frequent charms <note>original: "veneficia"; can mean poisons, sorcery, or magical charms—here referring to the "spell-like" intensity of dream experiences.</note> hang over those who sleep. Pleasure, indeed, then prevails most greatly, and this state of life is especially prone to the most alluring enticements—so much so that loves and hates may sprout in the soul that will endure even into waking life.

<summary>Synesius proposes that individuals keep "Night Books" (dream journals) to complement their daily journals, arguing that describing the strange and illogical nature of dreams is the ultimate training for an orator's eloquence and self-knowledge.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Synesius’s argument that recording dreams—his "Night Books"—is not only a spiritual exercise but a supreme rhetorical one. He is moving from the theoretical nature of the "spirit-vehicle" to the practical, wondrous experiences found in the dream state, comparing them to classical myths.</meta>

# ON DREAMS

## How wondrous is the variety of the imagination in dreams.

<margin>s</margin> If anyone intends to speak not in vain, but to fulfill the purpose for which their speech was begun, they will certainly need words that can move the listener and place them within that very state of feeling, perception, and thought. For indeed, in a dream, one may simultaneously conquer, fight as a gladiator, fly, or capture; all of this is the work of the imagination <term>phantasia: the faculty of the soul that creates and stores mental images</term>. Yet by what means shall a speech capture this? Someone sleeps a dream, and within that dream they see, and meanwhile the sleeper "rises" (as they suppose) and, while still lying down, shakes off the sleep. They philosophize, and they know both things regarding the appearing dream—that this is a dream, and that the other is a double dream. Then, they do not give it credit; they think that what is present is serious and that the things appearing are living beings. From this point, they struggle with all their might, both against themselves and to let go, or even to wake up and test themselves, attempting to catch the deception. They say indeed that the Aloadae <note>The Aloadae were twin giants, Otus and Ephialtes, who attempted to storm Heaven by piling Mount Pelion on top of Mount Ossa; they were punished in the underworld for their hubris.</note> pay the penalty because they built upon the Thessalian mountains against the gods. But for the sleeper, no law of unavoidable judgment ever forbids them from lifting themselves high from the earth, more fortunately than Icarus, and surpassing eagles in flight. You may even fly above the celestial spheres, where one may contemplate the globe of the earth from a distance—and not just as the moon sees it. It is permitted to argue with the stars and to meet with the hidden gods in the world. For when a thing is most difficult to do in reality, it becomes easiest there; then the gods clearly and openly meet with us, and there is no envy among them. A moment later, the dreamer sits back on the earth; they have not traveled, yet they are immediately there. For nothing is more characteristic of a dream than to cut out the "middle" <note>Meaning the travel time or the logical steps between two points or events.</note> and not to act within time. Thus, one speaks immediately with little sheep, and thinks their bleating is speech, and understands what they are saying. So new and so broad is the material for arguments and the province for treatment, if anyone strives to adapt their speech to dreams. I truly believe that fables also received their license and abundance from dreams—those stories in which a peacock speaks, or a fox, or the sea—even if these are small things when compared to the liberty found in a dream. And although fables are but a tiny part of dreams, they are nonetheless cultivated by the sophists <note>Professional rhetoricians and teachers in the Greek tradition.</note> and deemed worthy of interpretation. It would be fitting for those whose art begins with the fable to find their end in the dream. This is especially true since the faculty of speaking is not exercised in these matters in vain; just as in fables, nothing is done haphazardly, but some deeper meaning lies hidden there.

## That it is useful for both life and eloquence to note daily what dreams you see, what you do, and what happens to you.

<margin>a</margin> Therefore, let everyone to whom leisure is granted and who has the means of livelihood prepare themselves to write down all things that happen to them, whether waking or sleeping. Let them spend some time on this, which is indeed the best use of time, as elsewhere...

<meta>This page continues Synesius’s treatise on the spiritual and practical utility of dreams. Having established the "spirit-vehicle" and the imaginative power of the sleeping mind, he now argues that recording these experiences—creating personal "Night Books"—is a superior exercise for both the philosopher and the orator compared to the stale, repetitive themes of traditional rhetoric.</meta>

# SYNESIUS

Prophecy is acquired through intelligence; that is, by gathering together the art which we have praised. Indeed, nothing could be more useful than this; moreover, the method of speaking will not be hindered by this, but will gain a great weight of substance. For a philosopher, a study of this kind will be a game and a solace, serving to relax the excessive tension of the mind, just as Scythian archers are accustomed to unstring their bows. But for the rhetorician, we should establish such a practice as the very summit and peak of their demonstrations. For they seem to exercise their eloquence and vehemence on themes that are not always opportune—speaking of Miltiades <note>Miltiades was the Athenian general who led the victory at the Battle of Marathon.</note>, for instance, or Cimon <note>Cimon was an influential Athenian statesman and general, the son of Miltiades.</note>, and even certain obscure men; or arguing about the wealthy and the poor, or matters of the state that have become hateful. Regarding these things, I have even seen ancient men in the theater competing fiercely, even though they were venerable in the name of philosophy. Each of them (as it seemed) had grown a talent's weight of beard <note>original: "barbæ talentum" – a humorous exaggeration suggesting their beards were as heavy as a "talent" (a large unit of weight), marking them as overly performative "wise men."</note>. Yet the reverence for their profession did not prevent them from breaking out into insults and brawls, and immodestly waving their hands about while arranging their speeches with what I then thought were sufficient strengths. But as they later reported, or as I was later taught, they were not then, nor had they ever been, capable—not even from the beginning of their nature. For how can there be civility in a man whose victory gives him a reward for slaughtering a citizen who holds a different opinion about the republic? Now, truly, whoever at ninety years old still practices and contends with fictions—at what time shall they set aside words for the sake of the truth? 

In every way, they seem to me to understand the very name of "practice" [meditation] <term>meditatio: the rhetorical practice of preparing and rehearsing speeches</term> only when they say they are studying for the sake of something else; yet they have come to think of this preparation as an end without limit, and they have worshiped the path itself, which they ought to travel, as if it were the destination. For they have made practice itself the competition. It is as if someone, having exercised their hands vigorously in the wrestling school, were to profess mastery of the Pancratium <term>Pancratium: an ancient Greek martial art combining boxing and wrestling</term> at the Olympic games. Thus, both the aridity of the mind and an over-abundance of words have so occupied men that some seem powerful in speaking, yet have nothing worth saying. However, they ought to have prepared themselves as Archilochus and Alcaeus <note>Archilochus and Alcaeus were early Greek lyric poets known for writing about their personal lives, emotions, and political struggles rather than just myths.</note> did, both of whom spent the sweetness of their singing voices on their own lives; thus, posterity remembers what gave them joy and what caused them pain. For they did not pour out vain speeches on fabricated arguments, as this recent breed of "wise men" is accustomed to do, nor did they bestow their talents only upon others, like Stesichorus and Homer, who made the heroic race more illustrious through their poems—from which we too have made progress in imitating virtue. But those poets seem neglected in what concerns themselves, of whom we have nothing more to say except that they were vigorous poets. 

Therefore, anyone who desires to be remembered by posterity, and trusts that they can commit immortal things to letters, should follow the method of writing that we have approved at this present time, despite it being contrary to common custom. Let him boldly entrust himself to Time. For Time is a faithful guardian when something is entrusted to it in accordance with God.

<meta>This page transitions from the works of Synesius to a treatise by Michael Psellus, a 11th-century Byzantine scholar, as translated by the Renaissance philosopher Marsilio Ficino. While the previous pages discussed the "spirit-vehicle" and dreams, this text shifts to the physical nature of demons and angels, bridging Platonic thought with Christian theology.</meta>

### From Michael Psellus on demons; translated by Marsilio Ficino.

<margin>n</margin>
The nature of <term>demons</term> <note>In this context, "demons" (daemones) refers to a broad category of spiritual beings—not exclusively evil spirits—occupying the space between humans and the divine.</note> is not without a body; rather, it possesses a body and is occupied with bodies. This is what our venerable fathers also judged. There are even those who assert that demons have appeared to them in their own presence with bodies. Moreover, the divine Basil <note>Saint Basil the Great (c. 330–379 AD), one of the influential Greek Church Fathers.</note>, a contemplator of the mysteries hidden from us, attributed bodies not only to demons but even to pure angels, treating them as certain thin, airy, and pure spirits. As a witness, he brings forward David, who says: *He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flame of fire* <note>original: "qui facit angelos eius spiritus ac ministros eius flammeos" — a reference to Psalm 104:4.</note>. And this is indeed necessary, for as the divine Paul asserts, it is necessary for the "ministering spirits" who are sent out to have a body by which they may move, stand still, and appear openly; for they knew that these ministries could not be fulfilled otherwise than by a body.

And if you should read anywhere in Scripture that they are called "incorporeal," I respond that both our writers and others are accustomed to call thicker bodies "corporeal," while frequently naming those thin bodies—which escape sight and touch—as "incorporeal." Yet, the body of an angel and a demon is not of the same kinship. For the angelic body, emitting certain rays, cannot be sustained by human eyes but vanishes entirely from them. Whether a demonic body was ever such, I cannot say; however, it seems such a thing existed at some time, since Isaiah names the angel who fell "Lucifer" <note>original: "luciferum" — literally "the light-bringer," referring to the morning star and Isaiah 14:12.</note>. But now, it exists as something otherwise dark and shadowy. If it were offered to our eyes stripped of its joined light, it would appear troublesome to us.

The angelic [nature] is indeed entirely devoid of matter, and for this reason, it penetrates and passes through every solid thing; it is even less subject to suffering and external influence than a ray of the sun. For the sun’s ray, proceeding through diaphanous and translucent bodies, is held back by earthly and opaque obstacles so that it undergoes a "breaking" (refraction), inasmuch as it has a kinship with evil <note>This reflects a Neoplatonic idea that light becomes "corrupted" or weakened as it interacts with dense, material matter.</note>. But nothing of these things stands in the way of the angelic body, since it suffers no opposition from anything, because it does not agree with any of these things in order or nature.

Demonic bodies, however, although they are invisible due to their thinness, are nevertheless material in a certain way and subject to "passions" <note>In ancient philosophy, "passions" (passioni) refers to being acted upon by external forces or experiencing physical sensations and emotions.</note>, especially those that have entered subterranean places. For these have been thickened by God so that they may be subjected to touch and feel pain when struck, and they are burned when brought near fire—so much so that some of these even leave behind ash. History records that this happened among the Tuscans, a people of Italy. I do not speak of these things as if I were bringing forward poetic fables and monsters in the manner of the Cretans or Phoenicians, but I affirm these things because I am persuaded by the words of the Savior himself, who teaches that demons are tortured by fire.

<summary>In this passage, Michael Psellus (translated by Marsilio Ficino) argues that demons and angels possess "thin" bodies, distinguishing between the radiant, immaterial bodies of angels and the denser, material, and pain-capable bodies of demons.</summary>
<keywords>demonology, Michael Psellus, Marsilio Ficino, angels, Saint Basil, Lucifer, elemental bodies, spiritual physics</keywords>

### The six species of demons; how they transform themselves and introduce themselves to us; how they move us.

I have indeed received many accounts concerning these beings from those who have dedicated themselves to the study of summoning them to appear, even though I myself have never seen such a thing, nor do I desire to see demons. However, I have spent time with a man named Marcus, who led a solitary life in a region of Greece bordering the Chersonese. This man reported back to his river Mesim <note>Likely a local geographical reference or a transcription of a specific place name near the Chersonese.</note> and had made more progress than any other in the cult of demons, having inspected their manifestations. He had previously despised and loathed these things as empty and false; but later he sang a <term>palinode</term> <note>original: "palinodiã" — a poetic term for a retraction or recantation of one's former opinions.</term> and adhered to true doctrines and our own faith. 

This man, therefore, revealed many wonderful and indeed demonic things to us. To me, when I occasionally asked whether demons could suffer, he replied: "Most certainly, to such an extent that some demons even cast seed, from which certain tiny animals are born."

Then I said: "It is incredible that demons should have excrement and genital members." 

"They do indeed have members," he said, "but not of such a kind. Yet some excrement does emanate from them." Then he added: "Believe me." 

But I said: "They are in grave danger if they are nourished in our manner." 

"They are indeed nourished," Marcus said. "Some by inspiration <note>breathing in</note>, just as the spirit flourishes in the arteries and nerves; others by moisture, but not through the mouth as we do, but rather like sponges and oysters, sucking in the surrounding moisture from the outside. Again, they secrete what is more solid in the moisture. However, not all of them undergo this, but only the kinds of demons closest to matter: the kind that hates light, and the aquatic and subterranean kinds."

At this, I asked: "Are there many kinds of demons, O Marcus?" 

"Many," he said, "and diverse, both according to their forms and according to their bodies, so much so that the air above us and around us is full of demons; the earth and sea are full, as are hidden and deep places." 

"Unless it is too great a burden," I said, "enumerate them." 

"Generally, there are six kinds of demons," he said. "Nor do I know whether it is better to divide them by the places where they dwell, or rather by the fact that the entire genus of demons is affected by a love for the body. I know, however, that the number six is corporeal and worldly. For within it are the corporeal circumstances, and the world is composed through it. Either because this is the first number that composes a <term>scalene triangle</term> <note>A triangle with three unequal sides, here used as a symbol for imperfection or the material world.</note>." 

"I know that the divine and celestial nature belongs to the **equilateral** <note>A triangle with three equal sides.</note>, as it is equal to itself and is moved toward evil only with difficulty. But the **isosceles** <note>original: "æquicrurium" — a triangle with two equal sides.</note> is characteristic of the human race, which may wander from its purpose in one way, but through penitence becomes better."

<summary>In this dialogue, Michael Psellus interviews a former occultist named Marcus, who describes the physical needs of demons—including their breathing, "feeding" like sponges, and reproduction—and classifies them into six types linked to geometric symbolism.</summary>

->**The Six Species of Demons**<-

Indeed, he spoke of the **Scalene** <note>original: "Scaleni" — referring to a triangle with three unequal sides, used here as a geometric symbol for the "unequal" or disordered nature of demons.</note> as the specific demonic property, being unequal and in no way approaching the Good. Whether the matter stands in this way or another, he enumerated six types of demons in total. The first he named in an ancient, barbarian tongue *Leliureon*, that is, **"fiery."** He said this type wanders throughout the higher air, for everything demonic is banished from the lunar regions like something profane cast out of a temple.

The second kind is that which wanders in the air close to us, which is specifically named **"aerial"** by many. The third is **"terrestrial,"** which dwells mostly around the earth and opposes earthly things through many methods and schemes. The fourth is **"aquatic"** and **"marine,"** which immerses itself in moisture and willingly lives around lakes and rivers; it causes much destruction in the waters, stirs up waves and storms in the sea, and sinks ships laden with men, overwhelming many in the waves. The fifth is **"subterranean,"** which dwells in the hollows beneath the earth; it attacks those who dig wells and mines. It causes chasms in the earth, shakes foundations, and stirs up fire-vomiting winds. 

The sixth and last is the **"light-shunning"** <note>original: "lucifugum"</note>, which is inscrutable, entirely dark, and responds violently with cold passions. He said all these kinds of demons were so disposed that they hate the gods and oppose men; but some are worse than others. For the aquatic, the subterranean, and also the light-shunning are exceedingly evil and ruinous. These do not deprave and harm souls through fantasies and thoughts, but wandering like wild beasts, they hasten to the destruction of men. Thus, the aquatic demons drown those wandering in the waters and afflict them with the <term>falling sickness</term> <note>original: "morbo comitiali" — epilepsy, which in the medieval and Renaissance periods was often attributed to demonic possession or lunar influence.</note> and madness. 

The aerial and terrestrial demons, however, attack with a certain art and through calculated thought; they thus deceive human minds and bend them toward the most foul, unjust, and ruinous disturbances. 

Then I asked: "By what means and by doing what do they accomplish these things? Do they dominate us and carry us about like slaves wherever they please?" 

"They do not dominate us," he said, "but they secretly suggest things to us. For they approach the <term>imaginative spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritui... phantastico" — in medieval psychology, this was the faculty of the soul that processed sensory images and "whispers" from the spiritual realm.</note> that is within us, and since they themselves are spirits, they sound within us words of disturbance and pleasures. They do not emit a voice by physical percussion and sound, but instill their speeches without sound."

"But by what means," I said, "can they instill speeches into us without a voice?" 

"Why is it surprising," he said, "if you consider this: a person who speaks from a distance needs a louder shout. But having come closer, he speaks softly into the listener's ear by whispering; if he were able to be joined directly with the spirit of the soul, he would need no sound at all. Instead, his speech, conceived by the will, would glide into the listener with no sound whatsoever. They say this also happens to living beings when they have departed from the body <note>referring to the souls of the dead</note>. For these converse among themselves without noise. In this very way, demons converse with us: so secretly, in fact, that it is not even clear from where the war is being waged against us..."

...but to perceive deeply. No one who considers what happens to the air will doubt this. For just as the air, when light is present, receives colors and forms and transmits them to those things that are naturally able to receive them—as we see in mirrors and reflective objects—so too do the demonic bodies. By receiving figures and colors from the **imaginative essence** <note>original: "essentia phātastica"</note> within them, they transmit whatever forms they wish into our own animal spirit. They cause us much trouble by suggesting desires and plans, and by subtly indicating forms, they stir up memories of pleasures and frequently incite images of passions in those who are both awake and asleep. Sometimes, by tickling our thighs and groins, they incite and sharpen us toward insane and unjust loves, especially if they find **warm and moist humors** <note>In ancient medicine, the "humors" were bodily fluids that determined health and temperament; "warm and moist" was associated with blood and vitality, but also with lust.</note> conducive to this. The remaining kinds of demons, however, do not devise anything wisely, nor do they accomplish anything easily through cunning; instead, they are troublesome and utterly foul, harming in the manner of **Charonean breaths** <note>original: "charonei spūs" — referring to the toxic, suffocating vapors associated with the entrances to the underworld (Charon's caves).</note>. For just as they say this breath corrupts whatever comes near it—whether four-legged beast, man, or bird—so these demons, through their dreadful encounter, suddenly destroy whatever they meet, agitating bodies and perverting souls and natural habits. They often destroy not only men but also some brute animals by fire, water, or by casting them down a precipice. At this, I asked why these demons would invade brute animals. Indeed, the sacred scriptures testify that something of this sort happened to the pigs near **Gergesa** <note>A reference to the New Testament account of the "Gerasene demoniac," where demons were cast out of a man and entered a herd of swine.</note>.

To this he replied: since demons are the enemies of men, it should not seem strange to me that they insultingly harm even some brute animals—not so much out of a desire to hurt them, but out of a greed for **vital heat**. For since they dwell in the deepest places, which are extremely cold and lacking in moisture, they contract a great deal of dry coldness. Being thus obstructed and compressed into a narrow space, they crave moist and vital heat. To obtain this, they rush into animals, including those lacking reason, and flock to baths and pits. For they flee the heat of fire and the sun as if it were burning and drying; but they love the heat of animals, as it is moderated and mixed with a pleasant moisture—especially human heat, because it is more temperate. Therefore, by working their way into humans, they disturb them significantly, as the **channels** <note>original: "meatibus" — the pores or passages in the body through which the "animal spirit" or life-force was thought to flow.</note> where the animal spirit resides are blocked and filled. When the spirit itself is compressed and shaken inside by the thickness of the demonic bodies, it results in the bodies vibrating and shaking. The principal faculties perform poorly in their actions, and movements become dull and erratic. And if the demon that rushes in is **subterranean**, it shakes and destroys the person it has occupied; they cry out through the person, using the sufferer's

It was perhaps fitting for them to think that a sleep-inducing heaviness of the head, the anxieties of **black bile** <note>original: "atrae bilis"—associated with melancholy and depression.</note>, or the delusions of **frenzy** <note>original: "phreensis"</note> were the inconveniences of bad humors, which they are accustomed to soothe with baths, potions, evacuations, or plasters. However, the inspirations and possessions—by which the person who is occupied can do nothing by their own intellect, reason, imagination, or sense—are a different matter. Indeed, there is something else that moves and leads them, and moreover speaks things that the occupied person did not know, and sometimes predicts the future. How, I ask, can we say that these are merely the erratic motions of matter?"

### How demons occupy a man, speak, move, and transform themselves.

I, therefore, place my faith in Marcus—especially since I remember along with you what the divine Gospels hand down to us concerning demons, and what happened to the man of Corinth by the command of Paul, and finally, the many and deeply miraculous things read in the writings of our fathers concerning demons.

...[He spoke of] Livius, who had led him onto a mountain at night and ordered him to take a certain herb; then, he spat in his mouth and anointed his eyes with certain ointments, from which it happened that he saw crowds of demons. When someone observed that he had become a prophet—as if he were a musical instrument being played by sounding demons—he objected, saying: "All types of madness are merely the suffering of **corrupted matter** <note>original: "deprauatæ materiæ"—a reference to the medical theory that physical imbalance in the body's humors causes mental illness.</note>, rather than the tragic passions caused by demons." 

To this, he replied, "It should not seem strange if the followers of the physicians judge so, for they have never seen anything of the kind. A certain old man, who wore this same cloak—my elder brother—had a wife who was otherwise modest but troubled by frequent illnesses. Once, after giving birth, she was laboring violently; tearing her clothing, she began to **speak barbarically** <note>This is a classic description of "xenoglossia," the miraculous ability to speak a language one has never learned, often cited in historical texts as proof of possession.</note> in a language unknown to those present, so that everyone was uncertain what should be done in such a difficult matter.

She, in turn, responded to him in Armenian. At first, she boldly leaped from the bed, ready to fight him immediately. But that foreigner then made great use of **adjurations** <note>original: "adiurationibus"—formal commands or exorcisms used to compel a spirit.</note> and, as if raging, threatened that he would strike her. Then the woman withdrew, crouched down, and trembled; speaking more humbly now, she soon fell into a sleep. 

We, however, were stunned, wondering how that woman could have spoken Armenian—a woman who had never even seen an Armenian, nor had she ever left her family home. When she recovered, we asked her what she had suffered, and whether she had noticed what was done or remembered it. She replied that she had seen a dark demonic vision, appearing like a woman with disheveled hair, rushing at her; she had been terrified by this even before she got into bed. ...that I had perceived. For this reason, I began to doubt in this way: by what means did a demon appear as a woman to disturb a woman? Nor was it without cause that I doubted whether some demons are indeed male and others female, in the manner of mortal **animals** <note>original: "animalium caducorum"—literally "falling" or "perishing" animals, referring to biological creatures subject to death.</note>. Then Marcus, noticing my doubt, said: "No demon is male or female by its own nature. For such passions belong to **composite beings** <note>original: "compositorum"—beings made of a combination of different elements or matter and spirit, unlike the "simple" nature of demons.</note>. However, the bodies of demons are simple, easy to lead and bend, and naturally fit for every configuration. For just as we look up at the clouds and see them taking the shapes now of men, now of bears, now of dragons or other things, so it is with the bodies of demons. But there is this difference: clouds are driven by external winds and take on various shapes, but demons, by their own counsel and as they wish, vary the forms within their own bodies. At one moment they contract into a smaller mass, and then again they stretch themselves out into a longer one. 

This seems to happen in the same way as with **earthworms** <note>original: "lumbricis"—the author uses the flexibility of soft-bodied invertebrates as a biological analogy for demonic physics.</note>, owing to their better substance which is very easy to direct; nor does diversity occur in them only by size, but they also vary in multiform shapes and colors. For the body of a demon is prepared by nature for both. By the same principle that it is easily yielding by nature, it is thus transformed into various species of shapes; and because it is aerial, it takes on different colors like the air. But air is colored from the outside, whereas the body of a demon receives the appearances of colors from the internal action of the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasiae"—here meaning the power to project a mental image into physical form.</note>, just as our cheeks grow pale when we are terrified, or redden when we are affected by shame. 

For as the soul is affected in this or that way, it likewise transfers such passions into the body; we should think of demons in the same way. For they also transfer the appearances of colors from within into their bodies. Therefore, transforming its own body into whatever figure it has chosen, and bringing out a certain appearance of color to the very surface of the body, it thus appears now as a man, and soon it comes across as a woman; it roars like a lion, leaps like a leopard, or barks like a dog, and sometimes transfers itself into the form of either. And while it changes all forms of this kind in turn, it retains none of them as stable. For the body of demons is not solid, whereby it might retain the shapes it has received. But just as usually happens in air and water—namely, whether you pour in color or imprint a shape, it soon spreads and dissolves—something similar happens to demons. For in them also shape, color, and the appearance of things...

# PSELLUS 31

...of any of them quickly vanishes. Therefore, Marcus taught that these differences of male and female do not exist inherently in demons, but only appear so, and no such form remains stable within them. But if you hear from many people that a demon appears under a female form to all women in childbirth, know that while they take such shapes, not all demons have the same power or will, but in this they also differ greatly. Indeed, they exist in a certain proportion similar to that of **composite and mortal animals** <note>original: "composita caducaq; animalia"—referring to biological creatures made of multiple elements that eventually die or "fall."</note>. For just as among these, man—who is a partaker of intellectual and prudent power—possesses in addition a more general **phantastic** <note>original: "phantasticam uim"—the power of imagination or the ability to form and project mental images.</note> force, which is expansive and spread across almost all sensible things: both toward celestial things and those around and within the earth itself. 

However, the horse, the ox, and others of the same order have this power in a more specific way, operating toward certain recognizable images, by which they recognize their stable and their owners. Mosquitoes, mice, and similar creatures have this power even more narrowly and indistinctly; they do not recognize the hole from which they emerged, nor the place to which they traveled or where anything should be brought, but they have only a single imagination—namely, that of food. In the same way, the many and diverse kinds of demons differ among themselves. 

Truly, among these, the fiery and airy ones have a phantasy that is varied, distinct, and discrete, so that whatever imaginable form they choose, they shape themselves into that very thing. On the contrary, the **light-shunning** <note>original: "lucifugum"—referring to subterranean or deep-dwelling demons who avoid the sun.</note> genus of demons is different; for its imagination is very narrow. Therefore, it does not change into various forms, since it does not possess many "species" of imaginable things, nor does it possess bodies agile for movement and adapted for bending. 

The aquatic and terrestrial ones, holding a middle position between these demons, can indeed change into many forms, but they remain longer in those in which they take most delight. For those who live in moist places and lead a softer way of life make themselves similar to birds and women. For this reason, people call these **naiads, nereids, and dryads** <note>water and tree nymphs from classical mythology</note> of the female sex. But those who live in drier places and have parched bodies, which they say are <term>homoiozoous</term> <note>original: "ὁμοιοζώους"—meaning "of a similar life" or "animal-like."</note>, transform themselves into men. Sometimes they also show themselves as similar to dogs, lions, and other animals in which a masculine character is evident. Thus, it is no wonder if a demon attacking women in childbirth prefers a female form; for since it is impure and delights in filthy moistures, it takes on a form suitable to the life it finds pleasing.

->Demons imitate the language of the individual nations to whom they speak.<-

I believe, however, it will be clear from this that a specific language belonging properly to demons cannot be found—even if someone were to claim they speak Hebrew, Greek, Syriac, or some other foreign <note>original: "barbaram"—used here in the classical sense to mean any non-Greek or non-Latin language.</note> tongue. Furthermore, even those demons dwelling in Armenia, if they happen to move elsewhere, use the language of the local inhabitants.

But the question arises as to why demons fear threats and swords. # PSELLUS 30

...it is possible for light to exist within demons, but all of these are merely the fallacies and deceptions of those who deal in the occult. There are many who are commonly called the **Euchetae** <note>original: "Euchetae"—from the Greek word for "those who pray," also known as Messalians. They were a sect believed to hold that perpetual prayer was the only way to expel the demon every person was born with.</note>, whose fraudulent doctrine flowed from a certain madman named Mani <note>original: "Manete"—referring to Mani (c. 216–274 AD), the Persian prophet and founder of Manichaeism.</note>. From this Mani, several principles are handed down; in fact, two fundamental principles of all things were established by him: a God who is the maker of good things, and a God who is the artisan of evil. Thus, a God who is the Lord of the heavens is set against a God who is the lord of the sub-celestial realm. From this foundation, the wretched Euchetae added a third principle. According to them, there is not just one Father. They claim there are two sons, namely an elder and a younger. There are three principles: to the Father, only the supra-mundane realms are granted; to the younger son, the celestial realm; and to the elder son, the sub-celestial realms are assigned as their domains. This doctrine seems to differ not at all from the Greek myths, following that poetic line: *the rewards were distributed in a threefold number* <note>original: "ternario diſtributa ſunt præmia numero"—a reference to the division of the world in Homer’s Iliad between the brothers Zeus (heavens), Poseidon (sea), and Hades (underworld).</note>. 

But among the Euchetae, some worship both sons; for even if they say the two are currently at odds with one another, they nevertheless believe both ought to be adored. They argue that since both were born from the same Father, they must eventually be reconciled to one another. Others, however, worship only one—the younger son—as he rules over the better and more excellent province. They do not exactly despise the elder son, but they observe him with caution, taking care lest he should do them harm. Yet the very worst among them separate themselves entirely from the celestial deity and welcome only the terrestrial Satan <note>original: "ſathanã"</note> into their borders. They exalt him with the highest names they have, calling him the "first-born" and the one "separated from the Father." Likewise, they call him the maker of trees, animals, and all other composite things, even while admitting he is pestilential and hostile. 

But those who introduce these dogmas are blind in both the eyes and the ears of the mind. For they do not see, from the mutual kinship of all things, that there is but one Author of all; nor do they listen to the Holy Scripture which teaches this; nor do they reflect upon it with reason. It is evident that if there were two opposing creators of things, there would not be this single harmony and union binding all things together. And if demons promise us riches and glory, they can deliver nothing of themselves, seeing as they have no true power; rather, they offer only certain empty visions to their worshippers—various and unstable things—which the impious nonetheless mistake for divine spectacles.

### How magicians excite and draw forth demons.

<margin>NB</margin>
**Sorcery** and **magic** are not names chosen in vain, but they possess a certain power. For sorcery <term>Veneficium: while often meaning "poisoning," in this context it refers to low-level "goetia" or witchcraft involving material substances and the summoning of base spirits.</term> is an art concerned with material and earthly demons. It calls forth phantom images of demons into one’s sight; some it excites as if from the underworld, while others it draws down from on high. For our own discipline <note>Referring to the Christian or Orthodox perspective of the author.</note> considers every demon to be evil, having fallen from the angelic state and order due to an excess of pride and vanity. The Greek opinion <note>The "Greek" or pagan philosophical tradition, such as Neoplatonism.</note>, however, judges only a small portion of demons to be evil. They believe these are not evil by choice, but were assigned this nature by the primary division of the universe, acting as a kind of "torturer" against souls who have committed crimes. It is this portion of demons that the practitioner of prestidigitation <note>original: "præstigiator"—a jugler or illusionist.</note> calls into an imaginary appearance through sorceries, presenting these phantoms to the eyes of spectators. To some, they bring forth certain flowing waters that gush out from the beyond; to others, they promise the loosening of bonds, delights, and favor. These demonic powers are brought forth, yet they do not truly teach anything; in most matters they lie, though in a few they speak the truth.

**Magic**, however, was seen by the Greeks as a faculty composed of great power. Indeed, they hand down the tradition that this is the highest portion of the priesthood. It often brings certain visions to the sight which falsely display some form of divinity. For this faculty thoroughly investigates the nature, power, and quality of the elements and every thing created under the moon—including their parts, all animals, plants, seeds, and fruits, as well as stones and herbs—and, in short, the substance and virtue of every single thing. From these sources, magic performs its effects. It constructs statues that bring health—fashioned, of course, into all kinds of specific shapes—and it is skilled in other devices that bring on diseases, knowing which things conflict and which agree with one another. For the joining of many materials brings about a "union" in that art, while distance from a thing brings about a "separation." Now, among these practitioners, eagles and dragons are said to contribute to health, while cats, dogs, and crows contribute to wakefulness <note>original: "uigiliā"—used here to mean staying alert or warding off sleep.</note>. Likewise, wax and mud are often used by them for certain skilled configurations, since these materials possess certain properties by their own power. Frequently, there appears a channeling of celestial fire down to this place; then the statues seem to smile, and lamps are spontaneously lit with fires. Magic is also heavily equipped with much astronomy.

# PSELLUS.

He acts through that very faculty in great abundance. There is also a certain **divination by a basin** <term>Lecanomancy: a method of divination using a bowl of water, common in the ancient Near East and Byzantium.</term> through which even common folk often prophesy. Indeed, just as there is a certain kind of prediction made by sacred objects and by leaves, so there is a certain prediction made in a basin, a practice frequent and well-known among the Assyrians, which indeed possesses a certain affinity with demons that are closely bound to matter. The diviners, therefore, take a basin full of water, which is suitable for those demons that creep in the depths. That basin full of water somehow appears to "breathe" because of the sound it makes; for the water itself, once poured into the basin, does not differ in substance from external water, but by the power infused into it through incantations <note>original: "carminibus"</note> it excels greatly, and is thus made more fit to receive the spirit of the demons. 

That particular demonic spirit is of an earthly nature and is attracted by material compositions; as soon as it glides into the water, it first emits a certain tiny sound without any meaning, signifying its presence to those standing by. After that, however, while the water is now overflowing, certain thin sounds whisper a kind of prediction of the future. Such a spirit is found everywhere throughout the lands <note>The OCR reads "perras," likely a typo for "per terras" (through the lands).</note>, since it has obtained a solar order <note>This suggests a rank in the celestial hierarchy or a specific astrological alignment associated with the sun.</note>; and that kind of demon purposefully emits a thin, faint voice, so that because of the indistinct obscurity of the speech, its lies might be less easily detected. 

But can the bodies of demons be struck? They certainly can, and they feel pain when struck by a solid body. But in what way can this be, since they are spirits, and possess neither a solid nor a composite nature—and it is the nature of composite things to have sensation? Truly, in those things that feel, it is not the nerve itself that feels, but the spirit that dwells within them. For this reason, if a nerve is worn down, or if it grows cold, or suffers in any other way, pain occurs precisely because spirit is sent into spirit. To be sure, a composite thing would never feel pain by itself, but only when it participates in the spirit; once deprived of that spirit, it is also deprived of sensation. Therefore, the demonic body is naturally sensitive throughout its whole self; according to its individual parts, it sees, hears, and touches without an intermediary organ. It suffers through touch, and when divided, it feels pain just as solid bodies do. 

But there is this difference: when solid bodies are divided, they are restored only with great difficulty, or never at all. The body of demons, however, when it is cut, is soon recreated within itself and grows back together, just as the parts of water or air do when something solid falls between them; indeed, faster than words can say, the demonic spirit returns into itself. Nevertheless, it feels pain in the meantime while it is being divided. For this reason, it fears the edge of iron; those who strive to put demons to flight, having noticed this, set up spears and swords upright in the places where they do not want the demons to approach. They also devise other machines, sometimes repelling them with opposing passions, and sometimes soothing them with a certain agreeable affection.

<meta>This page transitions from the text of Michael Psellus on demons to a new dedicatory letter by Marsilio Ficino. # ON DEMONS

### MARSILIO ficino of florence to Filippo Valori, a noble and high-minded man. Sends many greetings.

He who commands "Know Thyself" <note>The famous Delphic maxim, *Gnothi Seauton*, which Ficino interprets here through a Platonic lens.</note> seems to admonish us to know the soul; for since the soul is the medicine of all things, it is surely everything. Therefore, once the soul is known, we shall easily come to know all things. I have, therefore, for a long time studiously applied myself to philosophers—not common ones, but the most excellent—so that I might primarily attain a knowledge of the soul, through which I might eventually attain everything else. 

However, as I anxiously questioned the Platonists on one side and the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, named for the "peripatos" or covered walkway where they studied.</note> on the other, and since their answers seemed to disagree with one another, I despaired from the beginning that I would ever fulfill my wish. But not long after, Themistius <note>A 4th-century philosopher and statesman known for his paraphrases of Aristotle.</note> offered me the greatest hope, affirming that such great philosophers do not actually disagree in their opinions, but only in their words; he claimed that the opinion of Plato, Aristotle, and Theophrastus <note>Aristotle’s successor as head of the Peripatetic school.</note> regarding the soul was the same, despite being expressed in different words. 

Finally, by a certain divine fortune, I happened upon a book by Theophrastus *On the Soul*, which was briefly but diligently explained by a certain Priscianus Lydus <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>—chiefly using the same reasoning by which Plutarch and Iamblichus, distinguished Platonists and Peripatetics, had explained the Aristotelian opinion on the soul. When, therefore, in reading these works, I noticed that the Platonists and Peripatetics were in agreement, I possessed almost everything my mind sought. 

And so that others might also have it as soon as possible, I have translated this book from the Greek language into Latin. I have furthermore added certain brief explanations devised by us during the reading and translating. However, I did not think I should labor too much or wander too far afield in this matter at present. For Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <note>The famous "Phoenix of the Wits," a brilliant young contemporary and friend of Ficino.</note>—truly a man to be wondered at—is already dealing with this at the highest level, where he most diligently discusses the minds of all philosophers on every subject. He wonderfully demonstrates that Plato and Aristotle are in harmony regarding the soul. 

I decided, my dear Valori, that this book should be dedicated chiefly to you. For you, alongside me, have for a long time vehemently desired this "concord of philosophers" <note>original: "concordia philosophorum" — a major Renaissance project seeking to reconcile seemingly contradictory ancient systems of thought.</note> on this subject. Our Medici patrons, to whom we are accustomed to give—indeed, to return—everything, will undoubtedly agree that this one little gift among many be dedicated to my Valori, who is the dearest friend of the house of Medici and always the most ready helper in the works of the Platonists. 

Furthermore, although we found only a single Greek manuscript, and even that was faulty and mutilated, nevertheless read it with confidence and offer it to others to read. For I have studied most diligently to correct and repair it, and our friend Angelo Poliziano <note>The renowned poet and scholar, another key figure in the Medici circle.</note>—a man of the sharpest judgment and vast learning—has approved this diligence of ours.

->Farewell, and read happily, and offer it to others to read. Farewell.<-

PSELLUS
3

Interpretation of Priscian Lydus on Theophrastus *On Sense*, translated and explained by Marsilio Ficino the Florentine. How the instrument of sense becomes like the things perceived by the senses.

### Chapter One. MARSILIO’S SUMMARY.

<margin>a</margin>
In order for sensation to occur, its instrument <note>The "instrument" usually refers to the sense organ or the "spiritus" (a subtle vapor) that connects the body to the soul.</note> must become like the things being sensed. This likeness is not in a material or natural physical form, but in a certain immaterial and purely representative **species** <note>original: "specie"; here meaning a formal image or mental representation</note> and **ratio** <note>original: "ratione"; meaning a formal principle or logic</note>. The physical form of a sensible thing, which is extended in space, is not sufficient for sensation, because the act of sensing happens suddenly and as a whole—all at once—concerning the whole object that can then be comprehended.

### PRISCIAN’S TEXT.

Next, it is Theophrastus's intention to discuss sensation. Indeed, because Aristotle considers the instruments of the senses—which are moved by sensible things—to be made like those sensible things through a certain "passion" <note>A "passion" in this philosophical sense is not an emotion, but the act of being acted upon or receiving an impression from the outside.</note>, Theophrastus rightly inquires how this similarity comes to be by nature. For it seems absurd that in the instruments of the senses—and much more so in the soul itself—any actual assimilation to colors, liquids, flavors, sounds, forms, or figures should occur. Therefore, he himself also says that such a likeness is produced according to **species** and **reasons** <note>original: "species rationesque"</note> without matter. We must therefore discuss whether the form falls upon us from the outside, what sort it might be, and where exactly it appears; and also whether a form extended and divisible across a body ever suffices for knowledge, especially if such a form falls upon us in a scattered way. All knowledge, however, consists of a certain gathering into one, and a comprehension of the whole knowable object in an indivisible way.

### Chapter II. That which senses already holds an immaterial and representative form of the thing it senses; but before it holds it, the instrument of sense must be moved and affected by the sensible object. MARSILIO’S SUMMARY.

<margin>q</margin>
To the extent that the substance of the soul accommodates itself to the **spirit** <note>original: "spiritui"; the subtle bodily fluid that acts as the vehicle for the soul's powers</note> through a certain inclination, the instrument of sense is explained in the act. The power of sensing, which lay hidden in the soul, when thus brought forth, concurs as one part with such a body to complete the "living being." Therefore, the substance of the soul is more separate, but this power is more joined to the body and does not act without the body. **Phantasia** <note>original: "Phantasia. i. imaginatio"; the faculty of the soul that processes mental images</note>—that is, the imagination—affects the spirit in various ways with its sharper movements, and from that, the rest of the body is affected. This is because the imagination directs its gaze inward toward its own images. Sensation, however, is directed toward external things; it does not perceive the "passion" (the impression) of the instrument, nor the form which the instrument brings to the sense, but through these two it perceives those things which are outside. Therefore, in its acts, it does not alter the spirit, for its act is not terminated at the internal, but at the external.

### PRISCIAN’S TEXT.

It is necessary, therefore, that that which knows acts according to the form of the knowable thing and displays its character; and this is called "assimilation." However, the "passion" (the receiving of an impression) occurs in the instrument of sensing...

<summary>Ficino introduces Priscian Lydus's commentary on Theophrastus, arguing that sensation involves an immaterial assimilation where the soul receives the "form" of an object without becoming physically like it. He distinguishes between the inward-looking imagination (phantasia) and the outward-looking senses.</summary>

This page delves deeper into the mechanism of sensation, distinguishing between physical movement and the internal formation of a mental image.</meta>

-> ON DAEMONS <- <note>original: "DE DAEMONIBVS". While the title suggests a treatise on spirits or demons, in this context, it refers to the Neoplatonic discussion of "spirits" (spiritus) as the intermediary substances between the physical body and the immaterial soul.</note>
y <note>This "y" is a signature mark used by early printers to track the order of the pages during binding.</note>

the act of sensing occurs, and it is necessary that this [power] precedes the actual sense perception. For the power of sensing is not entirely separated from bodies; rather, it finds its essence in the very inclination of the soul, or its movement toward the instruments of the senses, and is required for the completion of the living being. Nor can it act without these instruments. However, this power does not—like the imagination, which is primarily excited—move the instruments at the same time. This is because it is very extended and reaches out entirely toward external things, which always require the presence of sensible objects. Therefore, things that can be imagined are not outside us, even though they are (so to speak) made to resemble external things. But sensible things are truly external. For sensation occurs around these external things, not around the "passions" <note>In historical philosophy, a "passion" is the act of being acted upon or receiving an impression from the outside world.</note> prepared within the sense organ, even if the sense itself perceives the **species** <note>original: "species"; here meaning the formal images or mental representations of things.</note> which are in the bodies together with those passions.

<margin>Marsilio's summary</margin>
### Chapter iii.
The thing to be sensed moves the instrument of sense in a certain way—that is, the living **spirit** <note>original: "spiritum"; the "spiritus" was thought to be a subtle, vapor-like substance that connected the soul to the body.</note>. This motion is called a "passion" because the spirit is acted upon by a body; but it is also called an "action" because the spirit is alive, and the efficacy of life applied to that passion exerts a continuous action from itself.

<margin>e)</margin>
This kind of motion is similar to the objects, both because it is inflicted by them and because when the action continuous with this motion is applied by the life of the spirit, the spirit itself is already excited toward those objects. It appears that such motion—because it is more of a passion than an action, and is divisible in time and space—is not sensation itself. Sensation does not have the nature of a motion, but of a species; it acts indivisibly, suddenly, and through a species to comprehend the object as a whole. That such motion is not sensation is clear, because otherwise, every time we were moved physically, we would also experience sensation, and a more violent motion would not then offend the sense. It is necessary, after the motion and passion, to arrive at a certain species through which sensation occurs; the sense reaches this species and therefore perceives through it. This species is not located in the physical instrument [the organ]. If it were, it would be a motion and a passion rather than a species, and it would be spread out across the instrument. It is necessary, therefore, to proceed from that which is physically extended to a species that has been reduced to the smallest quantity, and through this to the **ratio** <note>original: "rationem"; meaning the formal principle, logic, or "reason" of the thing.</note> implanted in the soul, which has no quantity at all. Furthermore, the species itself does not reside in the "trace of life" <note>original: "vestigio vitae"; a Neoplatonic term for the lowest level of life that lingers in physical matter.</note> which the soul impresses upon the instrument; for every action of this trace is mixed with passion and is the same as the motion that agitates the trace and the instrument together. But the species is free from passion and motion. It is, in fact, the goal or "terminus" of motion. Therefore, it does not come from the trace of life (which is merely an accident), but from life which is a kind of substance—not life separated from the body, but the animal life proceeding from the higher soul. This higher soul is either separate or separable, a true and complete substance subsisting in itself. The life diffused from it through the body, although it is like a substance, is nevertheless the "animal part" and a kind of vital attachment of the soul to the body, divided along with the body as a kind of propagation of the soul.

<summary>This page explores the transition from physical stimulus (motion/passion) to mental perception, arguing that sensation requires an immaterial "species" rather than just physical movement. Ficino explains that while the body is acted upon, the soul provides a "vital attachment" that allows the living being to comprehend objects as whole forms.</summary>
