<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Priscian Lydus's interpretation of the philosopher Theophrastus. On the previous page, Ficino explained that for a sense organ to perceive, it must become physically similar to the object it encounters. Here, he explores the boundary between the physical reaction of the organ and the mental realization of the soul.</meta>

# PSELLUS OF PRISCIANUS <note>This title likely refers to Michael Psellos and Priscianus Lydus, whose works on psychology and sensation were often studied together by Renaissance scholars like Marsilio Ficino.</note>

<margin>
<unclear>...</unclear>
</margin>

They are affected by sensible things: the very instruments of the senses <note>The physical organs, such as the eyes or ears.</note>, not as if they were inanimate objects, but this is a **passion** <note>In this context, a "passion" (passio) refers to the state of being acted upon or receiving an external impression.</note> of a living body. Wherefore, it is not entirely a passion there, nor do all things occur from the outside. But it also acts according to its own proper **action**; it is not moved first and then acts afterward. Rather, it is not moved at all without acting at the same time, yet it does not act unless it is also moved. Therefore, such motion in the instruments is similar to the **species** <note>original: "speciebus"; the formal images or mental representations of things.</note> that are perceived, insofar as it was brought about both by those external objects and according to a certain arousal of a vital appearance or impression implanted in the instrument toward them. 

But this is not yet sensation: namely, that similarity brought into the instrument of the senses for the sake of perceiving things. Since this is a passion rather than an action, and is something corporeal, divisible, and extended in time, striving toward a species but not yet placed within a species, but still in motion. Sensation, however, comprises the beginning, middle, and end of the indivisible thing being perceived; it is a perfect action and judgment, and it exists simultaneously as a whole in the present moment. And it seems to have already been established according to the species of the sensible thing. 

For this reason, sensation is not brought about without some passion of the instrument; however, this passion is not sensation itself. From which it happens that we sometimes undergo [this passion] while both awake and asleep, yet we do not perceive anything. Therefore, after the passion, it must finally be perfected into a species and come to a limit—a species, I say, similar to the thing to be perceived. For sensation is brought about according to a perfect species, since it judges. 

Moreover, this species of the thing to be perceived is not placed in the instrument. For in the instrument, passion and motion are accustomed to occur. What is here involves division, and the species does not exist, nor again is it bound together in the very vestige of life which is granted to the instrument by the soul. For the vital action of even this vestige is performed along with passion. And there, a motion occurs common to both the instrument and the life gathered within it. But the species itself, according to which sensation occurs, is placed in the life—in life, I say, as it exists according to act, yet not separate, but in the animal life completing the animal and in its vital application, which is already divided around bodies.

### Marsilio's Commentary. Chapter 4.

The species produced in the animal life assigned to the body, since it is also co-extended simultaneously with this life, is not sufficient for the act of sensation, which is indivisible: in an indivisible moment, it grasps a certain whole sensible thing by a single stroke.

### PRISCIAN <note>Priscian of Lydia, a 6th-century philosopher whose work on the soul was highly influential in the Renaissance.</note>

<margin>u</margin>
But even this species is not sufficient for sensation. For a species perfected around a physical instrument according to an act—because it is divided across the body and has not been converted into a single indivisible thing—is not capable of cognition. But there is certainly in the soul a certain pattern of sensible things that exists before the act of sensing and before the species is grasped; this pattern also lives according to itself and is not merely a part of the composite. Therefore, it also acts in an indivisible way and is a certain power over particular things. It does not simply come into being in the soul at a specific time as if it were a single, particular, divided species. For the cognitive pattern of sensible things exists within the soul itself, not lying in the body. It is indeed one, but not in the way that singular objects are; rather, it possesses that "one" within itself, embracing many things and being adapted to each of them. For by one and the same pattern, the soul senses individual white things. Therefore, a pattern of this kind must be set forth and brought out if sensation is to occur. It is brought forth, however, when it is awakened toward a **vital species** <note>A mental image that is "alive" within the soul's own activity, rather than a dead reflection.</note> as if toward its own familiar species, and adapted to this species as if to the likeness of an external species, acting together with it. For that which judges is the pattern and the thought according to the sensory soul; and that very collection into a single indivisible point in substance is separated from physical bodies.

### ->PRISCIAN<-

<margin>a 2</margin>The soul, therefore, is said to possess the form of the thing to be sensed for this reason: because it brings forth the pattern of that thing. Nor does it in any way receive a shape or configuration from the object as if from a seal <note>The author is rejecting the common idea that the mind is like soft wax being stamped by external objects; he argues the mind is active, not passive.</note>, for judgment and action exist internally and through life. Thus, the pattern remains within and is essential to the soul. But the "life" which completes the animal depends on the essential patterns as if suspended from them. In accordance with a certain extension toward the body, this life itself subsists. This too is sensory, and is the boundary and perfection of the animal. Because of this, the likeness of the thing to be sensed is perfected in this life. In the instrument, however, it is imperfect and mixed with **passion** <note>In philosophy, "passion" means being acted upon by an external force.</note> and action; and a certain passion falls upon it from external things, while action proceeds from life. Likewise, the form is in the animal life, but judgment and thought consist in the very act of the pattern.

External things affect the instrument of sense in their own way with a certain material affection. But the life that is present transfers this affection into an immaterial form, through which the soul is excited to bring forth the pattern appropriate to the form.

### ->MARSILIO. Chapter 6.<-

<margin>p</margin>Through an issuance of this kind, the soul makes itself similar to the thing being sensed. Moreover, it can make itself similar to opposites at the same time through the issuance of different patterns. It would not, however, be able to become similar to opposites if it became such by being acted upon <note>Physical matter cannot be hot and cold at the same time, but the mind can think of both simultaneously.</note>. Again, if the soul touched heat with one of its parts and cold with another, it could not compare these two with each other—how they agree or how they differ. For it is necessary for the same judge to comprehend both opposites if they are to be compared. Therefore, the soul, through something **indivisible** in itself, reaches many things and opposites at the same time. It is, therefore, indivisible. For this very indivisibility suffices for knowledge, and therefore also for life.

### Chapter Seven
The sensory form <note>original: "species"</note> which arises in the primary life of the animal, arises from the innate pattern of the soul as if from a principal cause; it also arises from the life in which it exists, as if from an instrument. Moreover, a certain passion brought into the instrument of sense by the sensible object provides the occasion for this effect.

->MARSILIO<-

<margin>i</margin> The power of sensing itself is not in a state of potential to be formed by external things, but to produce its own acts concerning external things. The soul becomes like the things to be sensed insofar as it brings forth their patterns <term>rationes</term> from itself into action. But the instrument of sense becomes like them insofar as it is affected by them as a body, and insofar as a living thing performs some action agreeable to them.

->PRISCIAN<-

<margin>q</margin> Therefore, when even Theophrastus says that sensation becomes like the things sensed, according to forms and patterns <term>species and rationes</term> without matter, we shall admit it in this way: that forms are not simply brought in from external things, but are established from internal patterns in life according to the sensory act. Now, because sensation is extended toward external things and becomes like them, it is rightly named a certain "potential," as if it were bearing acts or actions. In the soul, indeed, assimilation occurs according to the act of the pattern; but in the instrument, it occurs both according to the passion brought in by the sensible thing, and at the same time according to a vital act or life-giving action.

### Chapter Eight
Since the instrument of sense is extended <note>meaning it takes up physical space</note>, it can indeed suffer one contrary in one part, and another contrary in another part. But it cannot compare these things among themselves. The soul, however, being indivisible, if it were to suffer from contraries at the same time, it would suffer entirely through the same part, which is impossible. Therefore, when it perceives contraries at the same time, it does not suffer from them, but rather acts upon them.

### Chapter Nine

->MARSILIO<-

There are those who think that number and motion are so formal and distant from matter that they do not suit the senses at all, and therefore are apprehended only by rational thought when it is appropriately stimulated toward these things through the senses—just as the essence of sensible things is apprehended by thought, not by sense. It is also permitted that the objects of perception <note>original: "sensibilia"</note> proper to each individual sense may exert a more intense action, while those common to all senses <note>The "common sensibles" usually include motion, rest, number, shape, and size.</note> exert a more relaxed one; the former are like those which are proximate and familiar, while the latter are more remote. Chapter Ten. ### PRISCIAN

### MARSILIO

It belongs to the same sense to judge between opposites; for instance, hearing judges both voice and silence. If it is pure silence, the external sense does not perceive it; rather, the internal sense perceives it through the memory of voice, noticing that it has fallen into the opposite of voice. However, for the most part, silence is not pure. In those cases, the hearing actually exerts itself around a very weak object, and barely perceiving anything, it is said to grasp silence, as if it were grasping what remains when the voice is absent. The sense judges a thing to be congruent, friendly, and pleasant when its innate pattern <term>ratio: the internal logic or organizing principle of the soul</term> agrees with it. It judges a thing to be alien when they disagree, during which time the sensory instrument is moved in a distorted <note>original: "perverse"</note> manner.

### PRISCIAN

Furthermore, since the sensory instrument is usually struck first and more forcefully by "proper" sensibles <note>Objects unique to one sense, such as color for sight or sound for hearing.</note>, but by "common" sensibles <note>Qualities like shape, number, or motion that can be perceived by multiple senses.</note> subsequently and more weakly, each sense is rightly accustomed to perceive its own specific objects. Sight, for instance, perceives color first, and subsequently magnitude and motion. For this reason, common sensibles may seem to relate more to the soul itself, and to be known by the sense as if by "accident" <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a quality that is not essential to the nature of the thing, but happens to be present.</note>. Yet certainly, as has been said, this common sensible becomes known to the sense as a consequence; it is not grasped by thought alone. 

It is also frequently asked how the eye perceives darkness and the hearing perceives silence. The answer is that they do not "sense" them so much as "consent" <note>original: "consentire"; here meaning a shared internal realization rather than an external impact.</note> to them. The sense does not lean upon or fix itself to such things at any time; rather, because action is inhibited during the very attempt to sense, the sense judges that something is lacking to them. Thus, it perceives what is distant and alien from the fact that its own innate pattern is minimally congruent with it. Meanwhile, the sensory instrument is moved in a somewhat distorted way due to a "passion" <note>In this context, a "passion" (passio) is a passive reception of an external impression.</note> brought in by a certain sensible object.

## Chapter Twelve. Since the soul is the mistress of the body, and therefore a far more excellent substance, the body is rightly made and arranged for its sake.

In the order of providence, therefore, the soul is both prior to and distinguished before the body. For the body receives exactly as many instruments <note>Physical organs.</note> as are necessary to serve the soul, which already possesses its various powers. These powers are "formal" <note>Pertaining to the "form" or essence of the being.</note> and are distinguished formally according to their species—a distinction that does not arise from matter. Therefore, a single internal sense derives the fruitfulness of its unity into five external senses. For these five, appropriate instruments are subsequently accommodated within the body.

<header>ON THE SOUL</header>

<margin>h</margin> So far, we have treated sensation in general. Concerning the individual senses, however, such as sight, hearing, and the others, we must first make this distinction. It is not the case (as some believe) that there is only a single sense which is somehow divided into different types by the participating physical instruments <note>original: "instrumentis," referring to the sense organs like eyes or ears</note>. For the diversity of instruments does not precede the differences in the powers of the soul, nor does it have the authority to divide those powers. Rather, sense itself, while being one within itself, distinguishes itself into five from within to perceive individual sensible objects. Indeed, the difference in the instruments then follows this distinction of the senses, appropriately adapted to each. For the formal and specific division <note>The design or "blueprint" of the soul's powers</note> precedes the material and instrumental division, and this diversity exists in those who use the instruments as if relying on a greater authority.

### *Chapter thirteen. The act of sensing is not brought about as if the sense naturally touches the object, or the object naturally forms the sense, but by a certain rational process in a spiritual manner.*

->MARSILIO<-

<margin>n</margin> Sight does not emit anything natural from itself—something quasi-corporeal <note>Almost physical</note>—by which it might touch color like a proboscis <note>A trunk or snout; Ficino is arguing against the "extramission" theory where the eye sends out physical rays to "feel" the world</note>. Nor does anything natural flow out from the color to be imprinted upon the sight; nor, again, does the color physically color the air, and the air color the sight. Species <term>species: the non-physical "form" or "image" of an object that conveys its appearance to the mind without the object's physical matter</term> separated from matter, because they are entirely free from place and excluded from the limits of matter, are therefore able to act upon all things and to act equally over any distance. However, species determined within matter and place, according to the mode of their nature, act only upon something specific and up to a certain distance, and similarly receive by being acted upon. There are, however, many actions of natural things belonging to the composite itself <note>The physical object made of both matter and form</note>, such as heating and similarly affecting something through smell and taste. Yet, beyond these, there are certain actions of this kind belonging to the species, attributed not so much to the composites as to the species themselves—specifically following the excellence and property of the species itself. These actions are, as it were, "spiritual" <note>In this context, "spiritual" means non-physical or refined, like light or thought, rather than religious</note>, and they extend further than the actions proper to the composite. They sometimes happen suddenly, yet only up to a certain distance, because these species exist in matter and are contained by a place. Such actions are not only in the soul regarding its actions upon things, but also in the species of things as they reach out in a certain way toward the soul. It is in such action and passion <note>In the philosophical sense, "passion" refers to the state of being acted upon or receiving an impression</note> that sensation occurs. Since the soul is a living and sensory form, it acts upon those things offered to it in a vital and sensory manner; and because it is within a body, it operates up to a certain distance.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the spiritual nature of sensation, specifically how the "species" (formal images) of objects interact with the soul's instruments. It identifies the philosopher Priscianus as a follower of the Neoplatonists Plotinus and Iamblichus.</meta>

ON THEOPHRASTUS

The species <term>formal images or patterns of objects</term> of things, by the very reason that they are forms of forms and images of divine things, act formally and, as it were, spiritually. They act primarily upon a thing that is itself formal and spiritual—namely, the instrument of sense, which is to say, the living being itself. And such an action leads properly and most directly to sensation, provided that the action of the soul (which I mentioned a moment ago) is added to it. However, the action of the composite being <note>The human being as a combination of physical body and spiritual soul</note>—which is proper, material, and natural—either hinders, or does not lead to, or is not sufficient for the effect of sensing. The souls of the heavens <note>The celestial intelligences believed to animate the stars and planets</note>, since they possess all sensible things through their causes within their own body, therefore look into all sensible things by a certain inward sense, using their body as both an instrument and a cause at once. On the contrary, since the principles of sensible things are not located within our human bodies, our sense is forced to look outward. From these points, it appears that this Priscianus is a Platonist. For what he touches upon regarding the sensation of the celestial soul belongs to the teachings of Plotinus, Iamblichus, and Proclus <note>Three major figures of Neoplatonism who emphasized the hierarchy of being and the spiritual nature of the soul</note>. Indeed, both through what preceded and what follows, it is everywhere clear that he is a Platonist and a diligent follower of Iamblichus.

## PRISCIANUS.

<margin>u</margin> But what, then, is seeing or hearing or smelling? And are all the senses brought about through a certain medium? Just as sight is achieved through the *diaphanum* <note>original: "diaphanum," the transparent medium such as air or water</note>—that is, something clear and passable to the eyes—or do certain senses rather touch the things to be perceived without a medium? Likewise, what exactly is the transparent medium? I personally judge that vision is perfected neither by some reception from external things (as if the sense were formed by the objects through a physical flow coming out of them), nor by an emission from the eyes (as if some physical body were sent out to touch the things to be sensed). Nor do colors move the transparent medium as if they were physically shaping it, and the transparent medium in turn move the sight in a similar way. Instead, the species <note>The formal, non-physical patterns of the objects</note> themselves possess an active power. Through this power, each species acts primarily upon that which is exposed to such a "passion" <note>original: "passioni," meaning the state of being acted upon or receiving an impression</note>—not only by touching it, but also acting upon things at a distance, provided there is a certain proportionate distance: for the one to act, and for the other in turn to be acted upon. For since a natural species is corporeal, is contained in something, and is circumscribed by a specific location, it does not act upon just anything placed anywhere. Rather, it acts only upon that which is distant from it according to a certain proportionate ratio—a ratio involving the effective power of the agents, the fit and exposed power of those being acted upon, and the measure of the impression itself. Indeed, the visible object acts upon the instrument of sight from a certain distance that is proportionate to the one seeing,

with the visible object, the former indeed for acting, and the latter for receiving the action <note>The author uses "passion" (passio) in the Aristotelian sense—the state of being acted upon by an external force.</note>. However, since the simple reception of the visual nature by a visible object does not by itself create sensation—for a too-powerful reception hinders it, being disproportionate to the measure of reception required for sense—it is clear that a certain distance is also required. This is why very bright things, if they are closer than the proper measure requires, hinder vision and eventually prevent it altogether. Since sensation is produced not only through the "passion" of the sense organ but also through a certain action (as has already been said), that which sees also acts upon that which it sees; not by altering it or inflicting some physical change upon it, but by acting "judicially" <note>Acting "judicially" (iudiciarie) means the soul is making a judgment or perception of the object's form rather than just reacting physically.</note> toward it. For it does not act as a mere body, but as something vital and visual. But because this vital and cognitive power resides in a physical body, it does not grasp sensible things according to their primary causes (as that celestial life and power of knowing does), but rather its work is perfected through a certain distance and extension toward those sensible things; thus, this proportion rightly requires a fitting interval.

### Chapter 14. How among the other senses, sight alone is most celestial, and how it uniquely and necessarily uses light—a truly celestial thing.

->OF MARSILIO FICINO<-

<insert>3</insert> Where there is light, there are luminous things and luminal <note>Ficino distinguishes between "luminosa" (things that generate light) and "luminalia" (things that are light-like or transmit light).</note> things. The first luminous thing is celestial <note>The sun, stars, and planets.</note>. The second is fiery. The third is found among composite bodies, which shine like fire. The first "luminal" thing is the eye, which is especially radiant in animals that see at night. But other eyes, though less radiant, are nevertheless luminal. The second luminal thing is color, which is created from a certain dominance of light in naturally composite bodies. The third luminal thing is the <term>transparent medium <note>original: "diaphanum"; the medium through which light travels, such as air or water.</note></term>, which we can call transparency. Indeed, this transparency seems to be so easily passable to oncoming light that it is a kind of beginning of light, possessing a supreme aptitude for receiving the fullness of the remaining light. Since, therefore, sight, color, and the transparent medium naturally possess a small amount of light within themselves, they rightly seem to strive toward a fuller light. By this means, they may emerge from being merely "luminal" to being "luminous," and having attained a perfect degree of that kind, they may be joined together: namely, the color with the eye through the transparent medium. The necessary medium between the eye and color is not air (specifically by reason of it being air, otherwise opaque air and the like would not be seen), but rather by reason of it being the "diaphanum"—that is, the transparent—which is passable by rays on all sides and friendly, like a welcoming host and something naturally...

luminous quality, which is surely required. Indeed, it is most necessary that light—already imbued with its own nature—illuminates the eye as well as the colors. There must always be a proper distance between these, for when either the eye or the object we are looking at is very luminous, it is not necessary for some third light beyond these to complete the medium, by which the act of sight is then perfected. Color is said to be the extremity of the transparent <term>diaphanum|The 'transparent'—an Aristotelian term for a medium like air or water that has the potential to receive light and color.</term> within a bounded body in two principal ways: first, by reason of the transparency itself; second, by reason of the object. You look at white snow; know then that this white color is the boundary of the transparency—specifically of the intervening air, for whiteness is at its extremity where it touches the snow—and also of a certain transparency that we understand to reside within the snow itself. But this whiteness appears in actuality <note>original: "actu". In philosophy, this refers to a quality being fully realized rather than just a potential.</note> not in just any part of this transparency, but only at the boundary—that is, always on the surface of the snow, no matter how deeply you cut into it. By these arguments, it is confirmed that color is something luminous.

### OF PRISCIAN <note>Likely referring to Priscian Lydus, a 6th-century philosopher who wrote a commentary on Theophrastus's work on the soul.</note>

<margin>h</margin> These things are indeed common to both hearing and sight, and to any of the other senses as well, if there is any other sense that is not forced to physically touch its own sensible object. But in sight, the use of light is primary and unique, perfecting the process from both sides: both preparing the one who sees to see, and the visible object so that it may be seen. For the visible object will not act upon the viewer without light, nor will the viewer act upon the visible object. For that which is visual within us is, in a certain way, naturally luminous; this is clearly demonstrated by certain animals that first illuminate the things they need to see for themselves. For this reason, they are even able to see at night. Colors are similarly luminous in a way, insofar as they are perceived at the boundaries of the transparency of bounded bodies. For these reasons, therefore, both are rightly perfected by light, since by their own nature they possess only a small luminous quality relative to what is needed for their perfect mutual action; for this reason, they require an additional external light—both the visual power itself as something luminous, and the colors, which are like certain lights. This is clearly indicated by their visual appearance <note>original: "spectaculum".</note>. For colors are the boundaries of the transparency. The transparent medium <term>diaphanum|A substance like air or glass that lacks color of its own but allows light to manifest.</term>, however, is a certain aptitude (if I may put it this way) for receiving light, or perhaps it is a faint trace of light, so slight that it cannot yet complete the middle interval for vision. And yet this very interval is adapted for vision, not merely as air, or water, or anything else, but as a transparency already made perfect by the illuminating source, and perfecting both that which sees and that which is seen.

### Chapter fifteen: whether vision occurs by the emission of a ray from the eye, or by the reception of a certain species <note>original: "speciei". In Renaissance philosophy, a "species" is a non-material likeness or image of an object that travels through a medium to the senses.</note> from the object. Likewise, concerning three rules generally pertaining to the senses.

### OF MARSILIO <note>Likely Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the influential Neoplatonist philosopher who translated and commented on these works.</note>.

Vision is an action that remains within the seer, just as shining and heating remain within a fire. Therefore, if vision were in some way located in the external object, then the seeing eye itself would also be present there (through the presence of a certain emitted visual ray). It also appears that vision occurs around the visible object placed outside of us, both because distance could not easily be judged otherwise, and because nothing physical from the object being seen comes to the eye, in the way that something seems to reach the other senses from their objects. On the other hand, there are those who believe that something does come to the eye from the object. For the eye suffers <note>In this context, "suffers" or "undergoes" (passio) means to be acted upon or changed by an external force.</note> something from it; for instance, the sight is contracted by black and dilated by white, and it is sometimes dazzled by brilliance. This kind of "suffering" is indeed perceived by the eye, but we shall discuss these matters elsewhere. There are three principal rules handed down by Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who integrated Pythagorean and Platonic thought.</note> that must be firmly maintained regarding every sense. First, something is produced by the sensible object upon the instrument of the sense; it is necessary that the instrument be affected by it in some way. This affection is both a "passion" brought in from external things—because this instrument is a physical body—and an "action" resulting within the instrument, because since it is a living thing, this kind of affection becomes in some way similar to the thing being sensed.

The second rule is that after this affection of the living instrument, there arises a certain <term>species|A spiritual or formal likeness of the object.</term> that is more spiritual in nature within the life of the animal itself. This is better suited for the sense and is also similar to the sensible object. The third rule is that at the presence of this species, a certain "reason" <note>original: "ratio". Here referring to a rational power or innate principle of the soul.</note> regarding the thing to be sensed—which was previously latent in the soul—is awakened. Once awakened, it aligns with the species, and through the species with the affection of the organ, and through that affection with the sensible object placed outside. This awakening and alignment is, in a general sense, the act of sensing.

### OF PRISCIAN.

Thus, much variety occurs in sight; for it seems to go out beyond itself. This is because it acts upon the sensible object outside its own location. Yet it also seems to receive something from the thing being seen, because it clearly undergoes some effect from that source. Now, indeed, the <term>diaphanum|The transparent medium, such as air or water.</term> and the medium seem to be traversed by both, as if...

### Chapter sixteen: how a medium is needed between the sensible object and the sense, and concerning the color of the transparent.

## OF MARSILIO.

The sensible object itself is excessively material, while the sense is quite spiritual. Therefore, they do not come together by themselves to complete the act of sensing; rather, there is need for a certain somewhat spiritual medium that may reconcile them to each other. In every sense, this medium is a certain species, such as we described shortly before. Regarding sight, however, as the most excellent sense, beyond the species there is an additional need for the transparent <note>original: "diaphano". This refers to the medium (like air or water) that allows light to pass through.</note> and for light, by which the material may be fully adapted to the spiritual. 

Where Aristotle says that the transparent is not seen through itself, but through a foreign color, Theophrastus wonders whether it is rightly said that something becomes visible through a foreign color and tastable <note>original: "gustabile"</note> through a foreign flavor. The answer is that Aristotle called light the "color" of a body that is luminous in itself, and by this light being communicated to it, the transparent becomes seen. There are those who think the transparent has its own color, but a very slight one. Otherwise, it would not be so easily passable and formable by foreign things. Therefore, they say this imperfect color is perfected by the light of a luminous body with a perfect color; however, those who deny the transparent has its own color...

### OF PRISCIANUS.

<margin>s</margin>But now let us return to Theophrastus. He himself also seems to think that no sense touches its sensible object by reason of itself: he says it is alien <note>That is, it seems contradictory or strange.</note>, since all senses are of the same kind, that they do not have something common and similar among themselves by condition. He adds this moreover concerning the transparent <term>diaphanum; the medium (like air or water) that allows light to pass through</term>, which could certainly disturb some by its novelty: in what way is this thing called "visible" when it is not so through itself, but becomes manifest to the eyes because of an external color? It is just as if it were said that something "tastable" becomes so through an external flavor. But the doubt is easily solved in this way: namely, that "external color" is called light, as if proceeding from elsewhere, that is, from an illuminator. For light is so familiar to things that are to be seen that it perfects them and leads them into act <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "act" (actus) is the realization or fulfillment of a potential; light makes the "potentially" visible object "actually" visible.</note>; therefore, even if the transparent itself possesses its own color, it is nonetheless perfected by light just as the colors of other things usually are. For light does not take away what is proper to a thing, but on the contrary leads it to act; or, as I said, if the transparent is by itself devoid of light, it is certainly perfected by light as if it were colored, and thus it emerges as something to be seen.

## Chapter seventeen: on the transparent and light.

### OF MARSILIO.

<margin>d</margin>Transparency or "perspicuity" <note>original: "perspicuitas"</note> is not a body. Otherwise, it would not be infused into other bodies without displacement <note>Ficino argues that if the transparent medium were a physical substance, two bodies would have to occupy the same space simultaneously, which was considered impossible in classical physics.</note>, nor is it some disposition brought into other bodies by some mode of "passion" <note>passive reception of a physical change</note> from one body to the others. Rather, it is a certain species and form in its own right, just like light, color, and heat. Indeed, the "species" of forms do not flow principally from corporeal matter or from bodies (as if from their own ineffective matter), but they are made and formally distinguished by the first Form—which is simultaneously uniform and all-forming <note>original: "omniformi"</note>—that is, by the Divine Mind. Moreover, Priscianus posits this from the mind of Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD).</note>, just as Julian <note>Julian the Apostate (331–363 AD), whose Neoplatonic "Hymn to the Sun" influenced this school of thought.</note> asserts in his book *On the Sun* from that same mind. The transparent exists not only in the ether, fire, air, water, and glass, but in the earth itself and in all composite bodies. Surely a certain intellectual soul is infused in all these things. From this soul, therefore, insofar as it is a certain life, heat proceeds through all things (though it may be hidden); and insofar as it is intellectual, light is diffused through all things (though in some places it is hidden). Thus the transparent is exhibited with light as the proper vessel <note>original: "susceptaculum"</note> for light. Furthermore, Julian says—following the mind of Iamblichus and the Phoenicians—that light is pure act <note>original: "purum actum"</note> extended through all things from the act of the divine intelligence. ...[neither a physical] thing, nor is it mixed with the qualities of bodies, although it is diffused through all these things. The exterior light placed by Plato in the tenth book of the *Republic* <note>Referring to the "Myth of Er" where a pillar of light binds the universe</note> signifies the same thing; he confirms this also in the *Timaeus*. But we speak of these matters more extensively in our commentary on Plotinus. Since color exists everywhere in composite things and even beneath the earth, and since color is a certain portion or participation of light, it follows that light is everywhere. Therefore, the transparent <term>diaphanum; the property of a medium that allows light to pass through it</term> is a necessary receptacle for light. If anyone, relying on the rule of the astrologers <note>In this period, "astrology" included what we now call celestial physics or astronomy</note>, considers how much power the innumerable rays of the immense machinery of the heavens have to penetrate the earth of the world, he will recognize that through this machinery and through composite things, celestial light and the transparent are diffused everywhere, as if through a single point. These powers may not be obvious to us here on earth, but perhaps they are clear to certain animals living there. They say also that just as cold relates to heat and blackness to whiteness, so darkness relates to light; thus darkness is not pure privation <note>A "privation" is the mere absence of a quality; here the author argues darkness has its own minimal reality</note>, but is instead minimal or opaque light. For the light of the celestial bodies is so powerful that a place for "pure" darkness is nowhere available.

## OF PRISCIANUS.

What then is the nature of the transparent (that is, the perspicuous and accessible to the eyes)? For it is not enough to say that this belongs to air, water, the ether, and the solid. He says it is necessary that the transparent be either a certain "passion" <note>In philosophy, a "passion" (passio) is an effect or quality produced in a subject by an external agent</note> or a disposition. For this is deep within the body; however, one body cannot be inside another body in such a way. But if it is a passion or a certain disposition, we must investigate by what it is produced. For it seems to proceed perhaps from one or from many of the simple bodies. However, if this cannot happen—for these simple bodies, namely air and water, are themselves transparent—earth too is transparent by means of fire; indeed, so are all composite bodies insofar as they are all colored. For color is the limit of the transparent <note>This follows the Aristotelian definition: color is the "boundary" or "limit" of the transparent within a solid body</note>. 

I assert, therefore, that the transparent is not a passion or a disposition brought upon bodies by something else, but is a certain conciliating form <note>original: "speciem quandam conciliatricem"</note> of those things which exist in the generation of bodies, meant for receiving the perfection of light. Likewise, it provides them with a certain aptitude for receiving light and for undergoing darkness, whether participating in either of these through its essence, or each in turn, or both simultaneously through some mixture. Indeed, the transparent which is in fire has essential light. But the transparent which is in earth has essential darkness. For this reason, just as fire is light-making, so the earth is dark-making; for darkness itself (if we may put it this way) is not a privation of light, but is itself also an act <note>original: "actus"; here meaning a positive reality or active state of being, rather than a mere void</note>. But have we perhaps erred just now in [placing darkness] in the earth also...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the "transparent" (diaphanum) and light. The previous page discussed how light and color permeate even the depths of the earth and the role of the celestial heavens in diffusing light through all things.</meta>

...positing the transparent: if indeed the transparent itself is the receptacle of light. But we have not erred; for this (as we have said) is the receptacle not only of light but also of darkness. Furthermore, the earth is also colored. Color, however, is the limit of the transparent itself within bounded bodies <note>In Aristotelian physics, a "bounded body" is a solid object with definite surfaces, as opposed to the "unbounded" air or water</note>. Therefore, the transparent is also in the earth, and there it is not only a receptacle for darkness according to its essence, but also, in a way, for light. For it receives darkness in its depths, but light at its boundaries—provided that colors are a kind of light, and if the earth also receives light on its surface. However, the transparency of air and water loses both in turn; it is this which we are more properly accustomed to call "the transparent" by definition. But the transparency inherent in composite bodies <note>Bodies made of a mixture of the four elements</note> contains both through mixture.

We ought not, therefore, to inquire from which of the simple bodies <note>The simple bodies are the elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire</note> the transparent arises. For forms <note>original: "species"; here meaning the metaphysical "blueprints" or formal appearances of things</note> are produced neither by the elements nor by any bodies at all. Rather, bodies themselves participate in these forms, and according to them, they obtain their proper characteristics. Wherefore those things which do not claim for themselves a luminous form by essence require light so that they may be seen. Fire and shining things, however, similarly do not require it at all, since they are participants in the luminous form through their essence, which is sufficient for this very purpose.

### Chapter 14. Of what thing light is the act, BY MARSILIO,

<margin>l</margin> Wherever light may be, it is the act <term>actus; the fulfillment or actualization of a potentiality</term> of the transparent; but in a natural, bounded body, it is an act like a form and a specific quality belonging to it. In a transparent medium that is not naturally luminous, however, light is introduced, not as its form or quality or a true "passion" <note>original: "passio"; in this context, it refers to the state of being acted upon or undergoing a change</note>, but as a quasi-passion.

### BY PRISCIANUS.

<margin>i</margin> Among these matters, Theophrastus <note>A student of Aristotle who succeeded him as head of the Peripatetic school</note> asks how light itself—which is extended through the illuminating body—can be the "act" of the transparent. For it could seem rather to be the act of *that* [the illuminating body]. But after he doubted, he resolved the question in this manner, saying that it behaves similarly to what happens in other "patients" <note>Things that receive an action</note>, showing perhaps by these words that just as heat is the "act" of fire as the agent, but the "act" of the thing heated as the patient, so also light is called the act of the recipient as a kind of passion. Nor is it named an "act" in the primary sense. On account of which he adds that we should not fuss over names, but it will be enough for us if we understand its nature. First, I think this must be distinguished: one kind of light is that which is produced from elsewhere; the other is that which produces it, just as light exists in the sun and fire. Now, however, the discussion is not about the cause, where properly...

ON THEOPHRASTUS:

The question is asked what light is: or rather, what it is as it proceeds from its cause. It is surely said to be the "act" <note>original: "actus"; in Aristotelian philosophy, "act" or "actuality" refers to a thing fulfilling its purpose or being in its completed state</note> of the transparent in air and water and other things that receive darkness and light in turn.

# Chapter Nineteen: How light is not present in the transparent as its quality, but is present rather as the very act of that which illuminates.

## MARSILIO [FICINO].

The Epicureans <note>Followers of Epicurus who believed the world was composed of atoms and void</note> think light is a body <note>meaning a physical, material substance</note>. Most of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>, however, believe it is not a body—otherwise, it would not penetrate other bodies so easily—but they want light to be in transparent things (which receive it from time to time) as their "passion" <note>original: "passio"; an "undergoing" or a state of being affected by an external force</note> and quality. Priscianus rejects this as foreign to the Platonists, whom he honors above all others. He therefore brings forward the arguments of Iamblichus, which Iamblichus himself received from Plotinus <note>Plotinus was the founder of Neoplatonism; Iamblichus was a later, influential Neoplatonist</note>. A quality that comes into a body and is properly received by it, becoming its form, has six conditions:

First, it enters through parts of the body gradually. Second, it brings a "passion" to the subject and changes its natural disposition, first accidentally and finally substantially. Third, it is propagated only up to a certain distance. Fourth, when the source of the form departs, the quality remains in the subject for some time, like heat in water after the fire is removed. Fifth, the quality itself moves when the body is moved from place to place. Sixth, it can be stained by the impurities of the body and be confounded there, mixing with other qualities into a single thing and becoming a composite.

Light, however, acts to the contrary: it comes suddenly <note>meaning instantaneously</note>; it does not change the nature of the subject; it appears as something capable of being spread through the infinite, provided there is something present able to receive it. When the thing that illuminates recedes, light leaves nothing of itself behind in that which seemed to have it. It does not move when the air or water moves; it is not stained when the transparent is stained, but either remains pure in itself or departs immediately, always continuous with the source of illumination. Furthermore, multiple lights do not merge into one. This is apparent because if you walk toward two lamps, twin shadows will result; if toward more, then more shadows. Likewise, if a large board is placed against three lamps with a hole in the middle, it will transmit three distinct lights to the opposite side through this hole. Finally, light is present in the transparent as a separable thing, just as the intellectual soul is present in the body.

## PRISCIANUS [LYDUS].

Therefore, following Iamblichus, I judge that light is neither a body, nor—as the Peripatetics think—a passion or quality of some body. For light does not have a "stained outpouring" <note>original: "effusuum... inquinamento"</note> in the air. For when the air moves, the light remains; when the air is changed in many ways, the light departs by its own impulse back into itself, and meanwhile maintains an indissoluble connection with its cause. Indeed, its presence is at once whole through all things capable of receiving it...

<meta>suddenly</meta>

<summary>Marsilio Ficino and Priscianus Lydus argue against the Aristotelian and Epicurean views of light, asserting that light is not a material body or a physical quality, but a separate, instantaneous activity of a source.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on the nature of light, specifically arguing against the Aristotelian view that light is a physical "quality" or "passion" of the air. ...[light is] made suddenly, namely in the presence of that which illuminates. And again when it departs, the sudden failing of light, leaving no trace of itself behind, serves as proof for us that light is not a "passion" <note>original: *passio*; a state of being affected or modified by an external force</note> of the air. For "passions" like heat do not arrive suddenly, and when the fire is removed, the heat leaves at least some small trace of itself in the subject. Furthermore, it is clear that the very act of light is separate from bodies, because it does not approach through a succession that progresses by degrees, nor by a change of the subject, nor is it confined to a certain limit. Instead, it diffuses itself as far as it encounters something that can receive it, and lights are never confused or mixed with each other. In what way, then, is light called the "act" <note>original: *actus*; the state of being active or the fulfillment of a potential</note> of the transparent? Certainly not as a kind of "passion," nor as its perfection made in it as in a subject, but as something that perfects it while remaining separate. Nor does this luminous act ever become a property of the transparent; rather, it brings it about that the transparent is its permanent abode, while the act itself remains continuous with the illuminating source and is carried around with it on all sides. Let this be summarized in this way, so that perhaps we do not suspect that light is made or received in something in the same way as an effect is usually produced in other things that undergo change.

### Chapter 20: Concerning light again and the transparent.

->MARSILIO [FICINO]<-

<margin>q</margin> Since it is clear from the above that light is something incorporeal <note>not consisting of physical matter</note> and not mixed with corporeal things, we can conjecture three points from this. First, indeed, that the celestial body—the first receptacle of light—is ruled by an incorporeal life and intelligence, from which it both possesses light and hands it down to others. Because light, as something incorporeal, cannot be birthed from a body. Second, that the celestial body does not have the kind of matter that mixes with other things. Third, that light is a most powerful cause in acting. For if it is not mixed with the things that receive it, it acts more freely, as if unhindered, and is most powerful by its own nature. Thus, miraculous actions proceed from it. Light does not flow out from a luminous source through a kind of "resolution" <note>original: *resolutionem*; a breaking down or dissolving of substance, like particles</note>, as a scent does from an apple, nor like heat from a fire (which becomes the property of the receiver and is not always continuous with the giver). Rather, it is like a visual ray from the eye—if indeed vision occurs through emission <note>Referring to the "extramission" theory, popular in antiquity, where the eye sends out rays to "touch" objects</note>. This ray is perhaps nothing other than sight itself stretched out toward external things, or the act of sight itself acting at a distance, not leaving the agent but always continuous with the agent and unmixed with external things. It is capable of doing harm, as is seen in the basilisk <note>original: *regulo*; a mythical serpent whose gaze was believed to be lethal</note>, and capable of doing good, as is established by instruction <note>likely referring to the spiritual or intellectual influence of a teacher's presence</note>. If we say that light is the visual rays of the celestial eyes living within themselves, through which rays of this kind all things vi- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, to be continued as "videnda" or "videntur" (seen)</note>

## PRISCIANUS

<margin>P</margin> After this, Theophrastus asks: if light is incorporeal, why does it only appear when fire or another body is present? For in this way, light might seem to be a certain corporeal flow and a body itself. Resolving this immediately, he says: it must not be understood in this way, but only by the logic of its natural state. Here, he certainly declares that the act of light exists as something specific and formal, since even heat comes from the form <note>original: *specie*</note>. Therefore, it is not a body. For light does not consist of a division or a cutting-off, nor of a flow, but it is, as it were, the very act of the luminous form—or whatever other name you wish to call the form which is the cause of light. Furthermore, if darkness is seen without light, then light will not be the cause for all things to be seen. But indeed, as Theophrastus says, darkness is not visible. For we do not perceive it by any firm ground of our gaze, but rather by the deprivation of seeing and by the fact that we do not see at all. Then truly, fire and anything similar is seen in the darkness because it is itself the cause of the <term>perfect transparent</term> <note>original: *perfecti diaphani*; the medium, like air, that allows light to pass through when it is "perfected" or activated by a light source.</note>. And for that reason, fire does not entirely need an external light to be seen. Fire, therefore, in order to be perceived, does not require a medium that is already in a state of transparency—that is, already illuminated. However, because it is necessary for there to be some medium (for vision does not occur by direct contact), this medium must be <term>transparent</term>, lest if it were solid or resistant, it might hinder the mutual action of luminous things through an opaque and "dark-making" property—I mean the action between the fire and the instrument of the senses <note>the eyes</note>.

### Chapter 21: Other senses do not require a perfect medium as sight does.

## MARSILIO [FICINO]

<margin>U</margin> It is clear that sight is the most excellent of the senses, because it perceives more quickly, further, more broadly, and more distinctly than the others. Likewise, the movement of apprehension <note>the mind's grasp of an object</note> and its progression is more perfect than its descent. Therefore, just as the soul and many instruments are needed to perform this more perfect movement (whereas they are not needed for imperfect movement), so a much more perfect medium is needed for this more perfect act of sensing. For this reason, a material, sensible path and a suitable interval between the senses is enough for the act of hearing and the rest. But for seeing, it requires not only a medium of this kind, but a "perfect" one—perfect, I say, in light, as if by a certain celestial virtue. Indeed, this light can be called a certain "color" of the luminous body...

### PRISCIANUS
<note>Priscianus Lydus was a 6th-century philosopher whose "Paraphrase of Theophrastus" served as a vital source for Renaissance thinkers like Ficino to understand earlier Greek theories on perception.</note>

<margin>C</margin> It happens moreover (as Theophrastus says) that the cause for seeing colors is color itself, and simply put, the cause for visible things to exist is the "visible." Indeed, since light exists as color, it is the cause of the diaphanous <note>original: *diaphani*; in Aristotelian physics, this refers to the "transparent" medium, such as air or water, which allows light and color to travel to the eye</note> and of the visible. He adds, again, that this is not absurd, but is also observed in other things; for instance, taste occurs through flavor. Perhaps, however, someone will say that flavor is the "proper sensible" <note>The specific object that a particular sense is designed to perceive—e.g., sound for hearing, smell for odors.</note> of taste, and sound is the proper sensible of hearing, and these two require no external medium at all through which the instrument of the sense may be moved. Unless, perhaps, one were to say that hearing requires a sounding body, just as color requires the diaphanous. But indeed, sound is suddenly sensible as soon as the intervening air has been measured <note>original: *commensuratus*; referring to the vibration or displacement of air necessary for sound to travel.</note>. We know that color requires an external illuminator if it is to be made visible. This is perhaps a unique property of sight—namely, to require light—not because sight is less perfect than the other senses, which require no other external thing to perfect them, but because it has a more excellent and sublime action. Sight does not possess enough "sensual power" on its own, but requires an additional, more divine form <note>original: *speciem*</note>. For just as our body, in order to be heavy and descend, does not require a soul, yet it does require a soul for the motion of walking and grasping—because the excellence of that motion surpasses the natural movement of the body—so too this motion made by the impulse of the imagination is not worse than natural movement, but better. In the same way, sight is more excellent than the other senses, and because it operates more excellently, it makes use of another "perfector" <note>In this context, light is the "perfector" because it brings the potential for sight into actual reality.</note>.

### Chapter 22. Sight, as the most perfect of the senses, and the visible, as the most perfect of sensible things, possess an order from the many toward the one, which the other senses and other sensible objects do not have.

### MARSILIO
<note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the leader of the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note>

<margin>N</margin> Neither are all tastes reduced to a single taste through which they are tasted, nor are all things that can be tasted reduced to a single "tastable" object through which they may be tasted. The same applies to similar senses. Visible things, however, become visible through a "primary visible"—that is, light—and therefore all acts of vision occur through a "primary vision." Since, indeed, those things which are divided among lower levels are united among higher levels, we can therefore conjecture that the primary visible and the primary vision are the same thing: namely, primarily the light of the sun. For this reason, Orpheus <note>The mythical poet and musician to whom a collection of mystical hymns was attributed; Ficino was famous for singing these hymns.</note> calls the sun the "eye of the world." Similarly, all intellects are referred back to the Primary Intellect, and all intelligible things are referred back to the Primary Intelligible. Indeed, the Primary Intellect and the Primary Intelligible are the same. Consequently, just as from the very center of the heavenly bodies—which many confirm is in the sun...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the nature of vision and the role of light. The previous page established that light is the cause of visibility in the diaphanous medium. # ON THEOPHRASTUS

A universal life is diffused through all things without any breaking down, thinning out, or mixing of that life itself. Similarly, light is diffused through all things, which indeed, coming from that life of all things, is life-giving to all. And here is a marvelous order in the very category of things seeing and things seen: they are brought back from a multitude into a unity, from which they had previously proceeded. There is also a marvelous abundance in that first visible thing <note>referring to light itself</note>, so that by its power all things are seen. Finally, there is a singular efficacy in sight, such that through one thing it perceives innumerable others. Since indeed the other senses and the rest of the things to be perceived ought not to lack order altogether, it is likely that both the other senses and the other sensible objects are contained within the power of the first sight and the first visible, so that if they are not ordered through themselves, they are at least ordered through its arrangement.

->BY PRISCIANUS<-

<margin>P</margin>erhaps someone might say that it is worthy of consideration whether that which is bright, and light itself, is the primary visible thing which moves the eye through itself and around which sight acts, needing nothing else from the outside to complete it. Colors, however, like certain tiny lights, cannot be seen through themselves, but require the primary visible thing itself to complete them immediately. But someone might say further: if this were so, light ought not to assist colors so they can be perceived, but on the contrary, it would confuse them. Just as a greater light usually overwhelms a lesser one—and even among objects, that which shines more takes over that which shines less—so the light of a lamp is hardly seen under the sun. However, the comparison of a greater to a lesser thing is not the same as that of a preceding thing to a following one. For a visible thing is not compared to light simply as a visible thing, nor is it visible at all without light. Therefore, it is compared to light as a "consequent visible" <note>Something that becomes visible only as a result of a prior cause—in this case, light.</note> insofar as it is perfected by it and becomes visible through it. But light itself is sufficient by its own nature to be perceived. If a similar proportion is not found in the other senses—whereby one thing is audible or gustable <note>original: *gustabile*; able to be tasted.</note> primarily and another consequently—this is certainly a kind of richness, both of the very first of all visible things (which we call light), as it perfects the other things to be seen, and of the power of seeing itself, which perceives not only light but also certain other things through the benefit of that light.

This medium should moderate the action and passion by means of distance and, by a certain property, adapt the agent to the patient <note>The "agent" is the object acting (like color), and the "patient" is the recipient (the eye).</note>. Let the medium, therefore, be a body of this kind, and certainly not opaque. For sight and color are, in a certain way, of the nature of light, and moreover they require a fuller light; therefore, that which is shadow-forming is not a medium, but an impediment to seeing. The medium thus becomes the <term>diaphanum</term> <note>The "diaphanum" is the transparent medium, such as air or water, that Aristotle and his commentators believed was necessary to transmit light and color.</note> which, located between the eye and the color, contributes when it is not already luminous—both by providing the space for the mode of action and passion <note>In this context, "action" refers to the object's influence and "passion" refers to the eye's reception of the image.</note>, and by its transparency for receiving a more abundant light and, furthermore, for displaying it. But where either the eye or the color is intensely luminous, the interval helps at least to temper the action and passion; indeed, it also helps to bind these two together by a certain property. For through its transparency and light, it agrees with the luminous color and the clear, shining eye at the same time. Remember, meanwhile, that the transparent medium is by itself something related to light.

### BY PRISCIANUS.

Since the transparent medium seems to be moved by colors, we wish to extend this question—namely, how it is moved, whether by a certain flow <note>original: "defluxu"; referring to the theory that objects shed physical films or particles that travel to the eye</note>, or from the fact that the colors act while the medium is affected—to those who think that vision occurs without a transparent medium (with colors merely brought to the eye), and even to those who think something is emitted from the instrument of the senses itself <note>The "extramission" theory, where the eye sends out visual rays to "touch" objects.</note>. Therefore, it is worthwhile to investigate: since the transparent medium is truly moved, how is it moved? It appears that colors are seen through a transparent medium, but when placed directly against the eyes, they are not seen. Regarding this, we said the transparent medium requires a medium so that the things to be seen may be illuminated. But when the spectacle itself shines by itself, is there never a need for some transparent medium? On the contrary, there is a need even then, as we said, so that there is a fitting interval. Furthermore, the medium must not be solid and opaque, lest it hinder the action by its shadow-forming property. But does the transparent medium contribute only to the extent that it hinders nothing? As if it were a vacuum? This is not consistent with reason; rather, it must contribute something, for the medium is not a body by mere chance. Now, it clearly assists in the case of colors, which we could not perceive unless the medium were illuminated; it follows, therefore, that in the case of shining things as well, it contributes to something.

This is true even if in those other senses the medium acts through a kind of "mixing" rather than a pure action. Again, everything that illuminates clearly acts upon the transparent medium. Therefore, colors that are perfected and "illustrated" <note>In this context, "illustrated" means "lit up" or "made clear" by a light source.</note> by an illuminant also move the transparent medium.

### Chapter xxv. How color moves and acts upon the transparent medium and the eye.

->BY MARSILIO<-

The fire of the thermal baths acts upon the air, and the air acts upon the man. Here there are two agents and two distinct actions. For the fire grants heat to the air, which then becomes a quality belonging to the air itself. The air, being thus heated, warms the man even after the fire has been removed. The sense of touch can feel the burning air, or at least the warm air, even if it does not directly perceive the fire. This is not the case with an illuminated or luminous color (such as celestial or fiery color). Such color does not "format" the transparent medium by mixing a kind of light into it until it becomes a permanent quality of the air—if it did, the air itself would become the agent that forms the image in the eye, independent of the original color's action. If that were true, we would perceive the *colored air* rather than the *color of the object*. As it is, however, we see the color clearly because its "lucid act" reaches all the way to us—and indeed, it does so in a single moment, and is present in its entirety in every portion of the air. For we see the whole thing suddenly and everywhere, from which it is clear that this light is not mixed into the air, nor does it become a part of it...

It almost shapes the transparent medium separately, and along with this shaped medium, it simultaneously moves our sight. Thus, the color itself even acts upon the sight, but in such a way that it meanwhile uses the transparent medium as a subject for its own action—not as something undergoing a physical change, but as something shaped separately by an action of that kind. For this reason, the act of color is present to the eye in an unmixed state, though it is present in no other way than by using the transparent medium like a <term>chariot</term> <note>original: "curru"; a common Neoplatonic metaphor for how a higher substance (like light or the soul) is transported by a lower medium.</note>, since it carries itself along unmixed.

## PRISCIAN.

<margin><unclear>...</unclear></margin> How then is the <term>transparent medium</term> <note>original: "diaphanum"; the medium (like air or water) through which light or sound travels.</note> brought to the act of seeing color, which falls upon it without being mixed? For this is the proof of absolute presence: that it exists as a whole in all and in each one of the listeners, and similarly fills all people according to the logic of a single form.

## Chapter 27. That which contributes most closely to sensation is not a material thing, but rather something spiritual.

## MARSILIO.

<margin>m</margin> Remember that what is immaterial, indivisible, and released from a physical subject—and which is therefore whole everywhere around those who sense—could not proceed from a material source. And so it is established that there is something spiritual and vital in its vigor, not only in our senses but in the universe. By the power of this vigor, spiritual acts, <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; here meaning the non-physical "forms" or "images" that the mind perceives.</note>, and images are produced whenever a material <term>impression</term> <note>original: "passio"; literally a "suffering" or "undergoing," referring to the physical impact on the air.</note> occurs in the air, whether from a sounding object, a colored object, or other objects of the senses. And yet, meanwhile, something immaterial reflects in the instrument of sensing, or even in the air itself. This is necessarily required for the act of sensing; this act does not properly arise from the material impression of the air or the instrument, but from a certain spiritual "species" which meanwhile reflects in them by a certain power of life. Nevertheless, such a species is not enough for sensation and judgment unless the soul, at its prompting, immediately brings its own innate <term>rational principles</term> <note>original: "rationes"; the internal logic or concepts the soul uses to understand the world.</note> into action.

Every type of sensory object affects the medium and the sensory organ through its own nature by a natural and, in a sense, material physical impression. Certainly, the natural form of the visual organ is minimally material; the natural form of hearing and sound is almost similar. Therefore, even with very little material physical change, the spiritual form—which is necessary for sensation—is very easily produced. In the other three senses, however, the form of both the organ and the object is judged materially; therefore, that form which contributes to sensation results more from a material impression, since it is itself almost material. Nevertheless, these objects can move the sense without an actual outflow of their own matter, and colors can do so even more easily.

### Chapter XXX. The intervening air contributes to sight, hearing, and smell, not properly because it receives a form from the thing to be sensed, but because it transmits an "act" flowing from the form of that thing to the sense.

## Chapter XXXI. That which is less material reaches an immaterial sense more powerfully, and a sense further removed from matter receives an immaterial object more powerfully.

### BY MARSILIO <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the Florentine philosopher who translated and commented on these works.</note>

There are four causes by which a sensible object reaches the sense more effectively and is more strongly perceived. First, when the object is more potent for this purpose. Second, when the sense itself is purer. Third, when the quality of the medium <note>The substance between the object and the eye/ear, such as air or water.</note> is more conformed to both, so that it may more aptly transmit the "act" from the object into the sense. Fourth, if a shorter distance is added. Sight and the visible object act upon one another across a greater distance because of their spiritual nature. The other senses, descending step by step into action—because a material nature gradually increases in both the instrument <note>The physical sense organ, like the ear or tongue.</note> and the object—act upon one another more clumsily and sluggishly. Nor do they proceed as far in the act of sensing as sight does.

### BY PRISCIAN <note>Priscian of Lydia, a 6th-century philosopher whose commentary Ficino is translating/adapting.</note>

After this, Theophrastus <note>Aristotle’s successor as head of the Peripatetic school.</note> asks whether every object to be sensed reaches the sense equally, or whether one reaches it more and another less. I indeed judge that they undoubtedly do not reach the sense in the same way. Rather, it depends on the extent to which that which is to be sensed has a greater or lesser power for acting. Again, it depends on the extent to which the sensory instrument possesses a more or less sincere purity. Furthermore, it depends on how much the medium itself is more or less apt for transmitting the "act" between the object and the sense. Finally, according to whether the interval is longer or shorter—by which the sensible object is made to be far off or close at hand—a certain difference in the reaching of the sense occurs.

## Chapter XXXII. Between the sensible object (which is overly material) and the immaterial sense, there is always a need for a certain medium that is, in some way, spiritual.

### BY MARSILIO.

When you see a spark across a very long distance, or hear the tiny sound of a cricket, or even very small animals; likewise, when bees and ants smell honey from the furthest distances; when even shellfish taste things at a distance; and when a torpedo <note>The electric ray fish, famous in antiquity for its ability to numb a fisherman's hand through a spear or rod.</note> often numbs you through a long rod just as if it were touching you—do you think, especially in the higher senses, that such a vast distance is broken through or materially affected by even the smallest object? Not at all. Instead, something "spiritual" <note>original: "spiritale"; here meaning a non-physical, ethereal transmission of information.</note> in a certain way intervenes, which acts through such a long distance upon the sense. This is a certain "special and specific act" proceeding from the species of the thing to be sensed. This happens whether it occurs within us (as in touch and taste) or even outside of us (as in sight, hearing, and smell), which arises from the power of the <term>common life</term> <note>original: "vitae communis"; the Neo-Platonic idea of a "World Soul" that connects all parts of the universe, allowing distant objects to affect one another.</note> by whose benefit all things are bound together, so that the sense is easily moved by distant things...

A body is affected by another that conforms to it, a principle that has been discovered through magic <note>Ficino often refers to "natural magic" as the study of hidden sympathies and antipathies between physical things.</note>. Although the medium and the instrument <note>The physical sense organ, such as the eye or the ear.</note> are more violently affected by a more material object—as occurs in touch, taste, smell, and often hearing—nevertheless, a safer and more efficient sensation results from that which arrives in a less material form. Regarding sight, a spiritual "act" arises immediately from the object, I believe by the benefit of light; thus, we see at the same moment that the process occurs. But sound, near the source of the noise, is a certain material physical affection <note>original: *passio*; here meaning a physical change or "undergoing" of an action rather than an emotion.</note> of the air and a "breaking" <note>A reference to the physical displacement or vibration of air particles.</note> that happens over time. This is soon followed by a "formal" <note>original: *specialis*; pertaining to the *species* or the formal image of the sound.</note> and somewhat spiritual act that reaches the hearing all at once, which results in the air thus "broken" by the duty of a more hidden power. Therefore, you do not hear a person striking something at the same moment you see them strike it. However, the formal act proceeds into voices, insofar as the physical affection of the air is not an affection that "breaks," but one that "affects"; for it proceeds far beyond the initial breaking of the air.

<margin>c</margin> Furthermore, just as in all the senses, some medium falls between the sensible object and the sense—although the medium appears more clearly in external objects and least in those things which are, in a way, within us—this has been sufficiently defined by Aristotle, and was not doubted by Theophrastus, even if he judged it somewhat less studiously. But one might first investigate this: if the presence of the voice (as we have said) suddenly arrives all at once, how is it that those closer to the sound hear it more clearly and more swiftly? Or why, when someone fells an oak, do we see the striker before we hear the sound? For it is certain that the sight of the percussion and the hearing of the sound do not happen at the same time. It must be said that this happens because the air must first undergo something and be moved. Once the air is so moved, the formal image <note>original: *species*; the non-material representation of the sound perceived by the mind.</note> of the voice soon becomes whole all at once. The physical affection and the motion occur over time; the *species*, however, certainly comes later, but it approaches the completed physical movement all at once. Therefore, regarding the voice, the *species* of its act occurs later within the physical affection, and it reaches only as far as that affection proceeds through the continuity of the air. For this reason, those who are closer to the object hear more quickly and more clearly, since those who are nearest to the sound-maker are affected more swiftly and more strongly. But as for what is seen, it does not act upon the transparent medium <note>original: *diaphanum*; the air or water that allows light to pass through.</note> through a physical affection, since not even the source of illumination itself does so. Thus, it acts without time, and it occurs simultaneously for everyone by whom it is seen. Although it is not the same for all, it reveals itself more expressively to those who are closer, since it acts more powerfully upon those things that are more "prepared"; and these are the things that are nearby in space, because both the things seen and the things that, in a way, see, are bodies.
