## Chapter 33. On the reflection of light, and images. BY MARSILIO.

<margin>1</margin>
When light falls upon a body that is somewhat dense, smooth, and shiny, it stops itself, gathers together, and immediately grows stronger within that body, which is both firmer and more suitable to it than others. Once gathered and made powerful, it acts again in the opposite direction; specifically, when it hits mirror-like bodies, it reflects <note>original: *resultat*; literally "leaps back."</note> toward the opposite wall and produces a brightness there. It reflects likewise into other things and into the eyes. It is therefore never <unclear>broken</unclear>, but first unfolds itself, then folds back and applies itself; in both directions it appears as one continuous act of light.

Similarly, a visual ray touching a mirror-like body in any way is strengthened, gathered, reinforced, and folded back. Having fallen back in the opposite direction from the mirror, it sees the things placed before the mirror. There are also those who believe that the illuminated forms of things produce rays toward the mirror, which are then reflected into the sight that sees the objects in this way. Theophrastus and Plato add that from the illuminated shapes of things, certain images go forth, which are called <term>Idola</term> <note>From the Greek *eidolon*, meaning an image, phantom, or ghostly double.</note>. For <term>Idos</term> <note>original: *eidos*; the Greek word for "form" or "type."</note> is a species; from this, by a diminutive, it is called an "idol," as if it were a specimen or a thin "species" coming from a more perfect species. These idols, being very weak, do not move the sight until they fall upon a mirror-like body; there they are stabilized, restored, and reinforced, and so offer themselves to the eyes. This happens whether the idols proceed from the mirror to the sight, or the visual ray itself leaps out toward them. However, the manner in which these idols—not only spiritual but also material—flow from things through light or without it, sometimes toward the sight and sometimes toward other senses, and especially how they grow strong in our <term>imaginal spirit</term> <note>The "imaginal spirit" was thought to be a subtle, vaporous substance in the brain that acted as a canvas for mental images.</note> as if in a mirror, showing themselves to us and acting upon us wonderfully, we discuss in our commentaries on Plotinus.

<margin>t</margin>
Theophrastus says next that we must treat refractions or reflections <note>original: *reuerberationibus*.</note>; for it is often said that a certain "squeezing out" of the presented form occurs as a reflection in the air. Perhaps Plato feels the same when he says a certain phantom-like or image-like appearance of bodily species occurs in a gentle light poured around a smooth body.

We must not, therefore, admit "breakings" <note>original: *fractiones*; referring to the physical breaking or refraction of a medium.</note> or "beatings" here as purely bodily things. For such a thing is a "passion" <note>original: *passio*; here meaning a passive undergoing of an effect, rather than an active force.</note> that differs from that which is naturally an "action." Especially where we deal with light alone, we must accept reflections that are active and effective; for both the source of illumination and the observer act more effectively around a dense, polished, smooth, and bright body. This happens to such an extent that the illuminating source further illuminates other things through this, and the observer...

### Chapter 34. There must be a communion between the agent and the patient.

->BY MARSILIO.<-

Where a destructive action <note>original: *actio peremptoria*; an action that consumes or destroys its object, like fire burning wood.</note> is to occur, a communion between the agent <note>The "doer."</note> and the patient <note>The "receiver."</note> is sufficient in matter alone, as between fire and water. But if some communion in quality is added, the action will proceed more easily, such as occurs between fire and air. Where, however, a perfecting action <note>original: *actio perfectoria*; an action that completes or improves the receiver, like a teacher instructing a student.</note> is imminent, communion in a certain property of nature is necessary. Thus, the rational teaches the rational; thus, the luminous illuminates that which is receptive to light. For the former perfects the latter above all others because there is a certain budding property in the receiver that matches the form of the giver. Therefore, there is a proportion in a certain property between this sense and this specific sensible object. The eye is something transparent and light-receptive; in that which it naturally began to possess, it is perfected to the highest degree by light through the transparent medium. In the spirit, likewise, vapor is smelled, for the spirit is most ready for the vapors of odors and is, as it were, already odorous. In taste, a certain natural saliva is most exposed, as if to similar liquids in flavor; in touch, a more solid nature exists, better suited to the primary qualities of the elements. And everywhere this sense-organ "suffers" <note>receives an impression</note> from the object, not because the organ is exactly equal to the object in likeness, but because it is in some way similar. ### OF PRISCIANUS.

He adds after these points that, in certain cases, the instrument of sense appears to be of the same nature as the things being sensed. For the tongue, through a certain moisture, tastes the moisture of flavor. Hearing, likewise, being "airy" in nature, hears a voice through the movement of air trapped inside the ear. The question is asked, therefore, why the situation is not similar in the other senses as well. Likewise, how is it that "like is affected by like"—namely, how the inner air is affected by the external air, and the innermost moisture by external moisture? Indeed, the reasoning is much the same in the other senses. Truly, in any sense, the instrument is of the same kind as its object. This is because the instrument is made subject to the actions of the objects. Thus, there is something <term>diaphanous</term> <note>original: *diaphanum*; transparent or translucent, like glass or clear water</note> in sight, and something resonant in hearing. For it is not by the nature of being "air" that the ear works, but by the nature of being something "resonant" that it drinks in sound. Similarly, something "scent-capable" lies hidden in the sense of smell. For this reason, there is also something here of a watery or airy nature, or rather a medium between them. For a watery moisture exists in the sense of taste. Finally, in the sense of touch, there is a certain power capable of receiving tangible qualities in a fitting way. Nor does like suffer from like in a simple way, but rather that which exists in <term>potential</term> <note>original: *potentia*; the capacity to become something</note> is affected by that which exists in <term>act</term> <note>original: *actu*; the state of being fully realized or active</note>. It is not, again, as if air is affected by air, but as something potentially resonant is affected by that which is actually resonating.

### Chapter 35. Doubts regarding sight, hearing, and smell.

### OF MARSILIO.

The medium necessary for seeing is not air or water, but simply the "transparent" itself, wherever it may occur. Nevertheless, a watery transparency is placed in the eye so that the aqueous humor <note>the clear fluid inside the eye</note> may restrain the thin <term>spirit</term> <note>original: *spiritum*; in Renaissance medicine, "spirits" were subtle vapors that carried sensation and life through the body</note> of vision itself, which would otherwise fly away entirely. The object of hearing is sound itself, whether it occurs in pure air or in water. However, air that is naturally trapped inside is most vital to hearing, because it is moved more easily than water. It is necessary for the instrument of hearing to be moved in order for us to hear. Since, therefore, the "airy spirit" is the instrument of hearing, it is impossible for anything to be heard unless this trapped air is moved; and perhaps for this reason, someone will think that nothing external is heard unless air is poured into it, or even surrounded by it. It is possible, however, for something to be smelled without breathing in air—namely, by animals that have a ready sense of smell, and by men who are similar to them.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the physical and metaphysical properties of the senses. Having previously discussed the "kinship" between the eye and light, it now addresses why specific elements (water for sight, air for hearing) are housed within the sensory organs, drawing on the commentaries of Priscianus Lydus and Marsilio Ficino regarding Theophrastus and Aristotle.</meta>

<header>ON THE SOUL</header>

Living creatures and humans who have their olfactory passages <note>original: *meatus ad olfatum*</note> filled by the act of breathing achieve two primary results: they draw in scent more abundantly, and by drawing air in forcefully, they immediately clear the passages.

->OF PRISCIANUS<-

Therefore, a certain watery fluid <term>humor</term> <note>original: *humor*; here referring to the "aqueous humor" of the eye, a clear liquid that maintains eye pressure</note> is placed within the eye. Yet, is it not rather a certain humor common to both water and air? Since, indeed, the property of being <term>diaphanous</term> <note>original: *diaphanum*; transparent or translucent, allowing light to pass through</note> is common to both elements. Again, why is there not something common to air and water placed within the sense of hearing? For sound occurs in water as well. A similar doubt arises regarding the sense of smell, but surely one of the two suffices. For even in external things, there is no need for a mixture; whether the medium is water or air, we see by a similar logic. Why then is the pupil located in water? Clearly, because water contains and preserves more effectively than air. For what reason, in turn, is hearing placed in air? Surely because air is more mobile. Indeed, motion contributes to the perception of sound. But if smelling can occur without breathing, what prevents—as Theophrastus <note>a Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle</note> asks—something from being heard without air? This certainly: because sound cannot occur without the striking <note>original: *pulsatione*</note> of the air deep within the ears. For air is the instrument of hearing; however, the breath drawn in through respiration is not the instrument of smell itself, but rather it is useful for opening the passages that lead to the sense of smell. This is the case, clearly, in those creatures that have blocked passages. In those where these passages are open, however, they can smell even without breathing at all.

### Chapter 36. On sound and the motion that is constant within hearing.

->OF MARSILIO<-

<margin>P</margin> The <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>original: *peripatetici*; followers of Aristotle's philosophy, known for walking while teaching</note> think that audible sound itself—that is, the sound which comes from outside to the ears—is created by a certain violent collision and breaking, where a less dense body striking a denser one is violently pushed back and shattered. Furthermore, they believe there is an "airy" substance within the hearing that is "cognate" <note>related by nature or "born together"</note> to it, which is perpetually in motion and makes a sound. But they hold that its motion is naturally removed from all violence, being a certain act of the <term>vegetative life</term> <note>original: *uitæ uegetalis*; the most basic level of the soul's power, responsible for growth and automatic bodily functions</note> perpetually exercising itself in that air, and from there generating a local motion in a sort of circular path. This motion of the air, brushing against the thicker parts of the head, produces a continuous sound with wonderful ease—so faint that it does not rouse our senses, chiefly because we are always accustomed to it. However, whenever we block our ears, that sound—previously diffused and able to escape—is compressed, grows stronger, reverberates, and is heard. Before, when it was not heard, it did not at all confuse other sounds, nor did its motion interfere with those motions coming from the outside; for it is both gentle and of a different kind than external motions.

<header>ON THEOPHRASTUS</header>

## OF PRISCIANUS.

<margin>i</margin>Among these matters, ask: Theophrastus <note>a Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle</note> asks whether sound absolutely requires something solid, or if it can also occur without a solid body, as the sound of the winds seems to be. But in truth, these winds also resonate by striking the earth; even thunder itself only happens when the spirit <note>original: *spiritus*; here referring to the air or vapor trapped in clouds</note> is broken around a cloud as if against something solid. Furthermore, if the air innate <note>original: *aer congenitus*; according to ancient theory, a chamber of pure air is sealed inside the ear from birth to act as the primary instrument of hearing</note> to hearing is heard, or if something is heard when the external air reaches it through a pulse, and if this [internal air] is also always in motion and always sounding, it follows that motion perceives motion, rather than sound itself perceiving sound—even if that which is within, whether agitated or resonating, usually prevents sensation, just as tends to happen in the other senses. However, that internal sound is not simply perceptible <term>sensibilis</term>. This is why we do not perceive the sound of our own ears unless we block them. For its motion is vital <note>meaning it is part of the living body's natural function</note>, unlike that of air that is pulsed and struck from the outside. But when the air that is most internal to us undergoes a striking and has now received the very "form" of sound <note>original: *soni speciem*; the philosophical "image" or essence of the sound conveyed through the medium</note>, then indeed hearing occurs in action. Thus, the prior [internal] sound, since it is not perceptible, does not confuse the hearing. Moreover, the vital motion itself not only does not hinder it, but even contributes to sensing the pulsed and broken air.

Chapter 37. How in seeing, hearing, and smelling there is a medium between the sensible object and the sense.

## OF MARSILIO.

<margin>f</margin>But it is certainly established that between a colored or luminous thing and the sight, there is a certain transparent <term>diaphanous</term> medium and a certain "act" or spiritual species <note>original: *speciem spiritalem*; a non-material representation of an object that travels through a medium to the sense organ</note>. Without this medium, sight would be hindered and overwhelmed. Indeed, when we hear or smell things from very far away, it is clear they are sensed through a temperate medium. But when broken air bursts upon us from a nearby source of sound, or a vapor flowing in from nearby incense reaches us, does not the sensible nature finally touch the sense without a medium? Answer: as far as the material nature of the sensible object is concerned, if it glides into the sensory instrument, it either hinders the sense (if it enters too sharply) or is not necessary for sensation at all (even if it flows in gently). But that which is both safe and necessary for sensation is not anything material, but rather a specific act—or a "spiritual species" of action—arriving from the object to be sensed to the sensory instrument in a spiritual manner. For the sense perceives just as it is moved; however, it is moved not *by* this medium in such an act, but *through* such a medium by the sensible object. Therefore, it does not sense this medium—that is, it does not sense this act or this species—but rather senses the sensible object through them. It is the sensible object that properly moves the sense, though it moves it through a medium of this kind.

This applies even to where spices smell sweet, and where color itself is; these things cannot be moved directly to the senses if they are to be known by the senses. Instead, a likeness of the action <note>original: *species actionis*; the "form" or "image" of an action transmitted through space</note> must be produced by them in the middle <note>the "medium," such as air or water</note>, and the instrument of these effects must be present. How this affection occurs was distinguished in the previous sections to the best of our ability. And yet, we do not truly perceive the medium, but rather the object that acts upon it. For "action" and the "agent" are not the same thing, nor is the "action" the same as the "thing acting." The acting object produces sensation through its effect; although the sensing subject undergoes an affection, it does not suffer in a literal sense, but rather functions according to that affection proceeding from another. Therefore, the act of sensing is an action coming from the sensible object, but it is the sensible object itself acting through that proceeding action. For this reason, we do not say we perceive the medium itself, but rather the object that produced it, by means of a certain "image of action" <note>original: *speciem actionis*</note> produced in the medium.

### Chapter xxxviii. The nature of light is more excellent than the nature of sound.

-> MARSILIO <-

Sound itself, as a category <term>genus</term>, is not strictly said to be distinct from high pitch and low pitch <note>original: *acumen* (sharpness) and *grauitas* (heaviness)</note>, which are its "differences," nor from a low or high sound, which are its "species" <note>sub-types</note>. For a category is never included within its differences, nor is the category itself included in the definition of such a classification. Light, however, is strictly said to be distinct from colors. Colors are the "differences" of light, yet they are not merely types of light; rather, they are certain "participations," images, and effects of light, and light itself transcends such things in its very essence. And for this reason, it is no less necessary to consider light itself in the defining and declaring of colors in nature than it is to consider sound (or any other category) in relation to its own specific differences.

-> PRISCIANUS <-

Aristotle says that the differences of sounds, such as low and high pitch, are revealed in the sound according to its actual performance. He further argues that just as colors are not seen without light, so too low and high pitch cannot be designated without sound; it is as if he were saying that light stands in the same relation to colors as sound stands to high and low pitch. Here, perhaps, someone might contradict Aristotle. For it is not light, but color, that stands in a similar relation to white and black, just as sound does to high and low pitch. One can respond on behalf of Aristotle: If these two are considered as categories <term>genus</term>, then color itself, as a category, can certainly be compared with sound as a category in this present comparison, but light cannot. Nevertheless, since colors are not discerned without light, just as high and low pitch are not [discerned without sound]...

### Chapter thirty-nine: On the nature of taste for the one who senses.

<margin>MARSILIO FICINO</margin>
Dry food must be liquefied in the mouth so that it does not cause harm and may slide down more easily. Therefore, it was necessary for the instrument of taste not to be dry, nor altogether unfit for moistening, but very easily moistened. It was also necessary for the tongue to be spongy, so that it might be irrigated by the small vessels <note>original: *follicidiis*; referring to the small ducts or sacs</note> of the stomach, lungs, and brain, and might drink up the liquids of the food. Yet it was not necessary for the tongue to have a viscous fluid <note>original: *humorem*</note> in itself, or a great deal of it. Otherwise, it would both dull the sense and would not perceive that the incoming liquid is moist; for a moist thing does not alter another moist thing, since it is necessary for the moist organ to be "perfected" <note>meaning the organ must be changed or completed by the quality it senses; if it is already identical to the object, no change occurs</note>. Moisture pertains to the sense of touch, and taste is either a certain type of touch or very close to it. Consequently, Nature did not give the tongue a manifest flavor or nature of its own, lest the judgment and discernment of flavors be confused by that one flavor; however, she gave it a certain fluid so affected and tempered that it is almost every flavor, and is most easily shaped by the flavors flowing into it.

<margin>PRISCIANUS</margin>
But since Aristotle thinks that the instrument of taste ought not to be moist, nor of such a kind that it cannot be moistened, because (as he says) that which is to be tasted <term>gustandum</term> will be moist, perhaps someone will respond to this very point: that which is "tastable" <term>gustabile</term> is not simply moisture, but moisture that is properly flavorful <note>original: *sapidū*</note>. Therefore, it was necessary for the instrument of taste not to have a flavorful liquid in itself. Or rather, since taste samples its own specific "sensible object" by a certain kind of touch, it must undergo an affection <note>original: *pati*; literally 'to suffer' or 'be acted upon'</note> not only from what is tastable, but also from what is touchable—and thus as if by a moist thing. For this reason, its instrument must not already be submerged in its own moisture.

### Chapter 40: On the instrument of taste and touch.

<margin>MARSILIO FICINO</margin>
The soul is the source of life and sense; it delivers these two first and most abundantly to the spirit <term>spiritus</term> <note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirit" was a subtle, vaporous substance that acted as the bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical body</note>, as if to its closest neighbor. Through the spirit, indeed, it communicates with the nerves and the flesh. Thus, the spirit is the primary instrument of the soul, both for imparting life and sense to the limbs, and for sensing those things that come from the outside. But it is necessary that this instrument, if it is to be acted upon by things sensed, be acted upon very gently. For a more violent "passion" <note>an external stimulus or physical impression</note> both dissolves the spirit and occupies the soul, disturbing its judgment. However, the passion of the spirit is tempered in sight, hearing, and smell by the distance and the medium of the air. But in taste and touch, where there is no such medium, why then is the sensation tempered? By the tongue and the nervous flesh; these two exist here as certain "mediums" between the sensible object and the spirit, which is the primary instrument for sensing. Nevertheless, these two can also be called instruments insofar as they participate in life and sense.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "medium" in sensation. While the previous page likely discussed how air and water act as bridges for sight and hearing, this page focuses on why touch and taste require an "internal" medium—the flesh and the tongue—and how the "spirit" (a physiological vapor) acts as the final instrument of judgment.</meta>

...they are named "media" <note>meaning a middle-ground or intervening substance</note> insofar as they are affected by a tempered passion <note>original: *passione*; in this context, "passion" means the experience of being acted upon by an external object</note> coming from the sensible object. Remember that in these two senses [taste and touch] the act of sensing does not flow from the material nature of the sensible object, but from a certain special act of it; and moreover, the act of sensing is performed through a sensory "species" <note>an image or impression of the object</note> resulting inwardly through a vital act. FROM PRISCIANUS.

<margin>|</margin> Accordingly, Aristotle—as also Theophrastus later thought—considers that neither the tongue is the true instrument of taste, nor the flesh the true instrument of touch. Instead, he believes these two have a certain proportion or comparison with those things which serve as media for us in seeing or hearing <note>referring to air and water</note>. For indeed, in touch and taste, there must also be some medium; for if a sensible object is placed directly upon the sense organ, it never moves the sense. However, in these cases, the medium is not external. For even when some medium intervenes from the outside, the sensation of taste or touch is not produced *through* it alone, but rather *together with* it. For example, if a shield is placed in between as a medium, a stone does not strike through the shield in the same way that a color moves the sight through the air; rather, the stone strikes the hand *along with* the shield, so that both are struck at once. Since, therefore, the medium serving touch and taste is not external, it follows that it must be internal. This, in a certain way, is the flesh and the tongue. It is clear that the flesh is "affected" <term>pati: to be acted upon by an outside force</term>. It is further clear that it is not affected in the same way as things that lack a soul. Therefore, it is affected "vitally"; and because the life of the flesh is sensory, it is also affected sensually. In what way, then, is it so affected, unless there is also something in it which judges? For even if there is some other instrument of touch that is more primary and perfect—such as the spirit <term>spiritus: a subtle, vaporous substance that Renaissance thinkers believed carried sensory information to the brain</term> itself—the flesh itself is nevertheless also sensory. In this regard, the flesh stands in a similar relation as the air does to sight, insofar as it is a medium for the more primary instrument. Because the flesh is not something that happens to be outside us, but is born with us, it is rightly a participant in the sense. Why then, if the flesh is sensitive, is it necessary to introduce another "primary" instrument of touch? Clearly because the flesh, being affected too violently when a sensible object falls upon it from such close range, would lose the act of sensing due to the harshness of the experience. For this reason, Aristotle also judges there to be a medium in touch and taste. Since he posits that this medium is innate to animals, he rightly defines it as a vital and sensory medium.

### Chapter 41: The instrument of sense must be a medium between its sensible contraries, such that it possesses neither of them, nor is a mixture of both.

-> MARSILIO FICINO. <-

If the spirit serving the sense of taste were naturally sweet, it would not be "altered" <note>changed or moved</note> by a sweet thing. Therefore, it would not perceive it, and it would confuse the judgment of what is bitter. If it were bitter, it would likewise fail to discern bitterness and would confuse sweetness. If it were a mixture of both, it would similarly fail to discern mixtures, and would confuse the extremes on both sides. Spirit is not the instrument of sense strictly because it is a "body" <note>a physical substance</note>, but because it is affected by a certain property that looks primarily toward such a sensible thing.

->FROM PRISCIANUS.<-

He also correctly judges that it is necessary for the instrument of sense to consist in a certain middle ground <note>original: *medio*; a neutral state of balance</note> between that contrariety which exists in the things to be sensed. It must be a middle ground that is not mixed from the extremes, otherwise it would have already been "affected" <note>original: *passum*; changed or acted upon</note>. Truly, it ought not to be something that has already undergone a change, but rather a judge of changes <note>original: *passionum*; the impressions made by objects on the senses</note>. For that which is mixed from extremes is not a judge of middle points, since like is not usually affected by like <note>a common ancient theory that a sense organ must be neutral—neither hot nor cold—to accurately judge temperature</note>. He adds, furthermore, that the instrument of sense is a body and a magnitude <note>a physical, three-dimensional thing</note>. Yet, it is not to be considered sensible simply because it is a magnitude, but through a certain ratio <note>proportion</note> and power. For this instrument consists in a certain ratio regarding sensible things, and is designated as a judicial form of life for bodies. Therefore, since all sensible things are "passions" or differences of bodies—for they are qualities and quantities through which each whole is knowable—it might seem to someone that the entire body consists in these passions and differences. But in truth, the body is usually known not by sense alone, but rather by "opinionative" reason. For in Plato's view, the body is known by opinion together with sense; thus, opinion perceives the corporeal essence.

### Chapter XLII. On the Number and Quality of the Senses.

Since an animal is defined by the capacity for sensation, it follows (according to Aristotle) that man, as the most perfect animal, possesses as many senses as can be found in the entire genus of animals. Therefore, there are no more than the five senses in the whole category of animals which man possesses. Perhaps it is also probable that there are five kinds of sensible things, since to be "sensible" belongs properly to the body. Now, there are five elements of the nature of bodies: namely, the four <note>earth, water, air, and fire</note> and the heavens <note>the fifth element or "aether"</note>. Furthermore, Aristotle thinks that there is a little fire and very little earth within the instruments of the senses. However, there is a great deal of air and water, so that these instruments can be said to be simultaneously "airy" and "watery." Likewise, if something is tasted and touched through the tongue, whatever animals have a tongue possess taste in addition to touch. Again, if movement is known through sight, hearing, and touch, any animal that has one of these will know movement in some way. Theophrastus adds—where it is said that the "airy nature" contributes to several senses—that this nature is not to be understood there in a simple sense

## FROM PRISCIANUS

<margin>p</margin>
Aristotle seems to have convinced himself that there are no more than five senses, primarily because all things are sensible to us. Indeed, things that can be touched are perceived by touch, while those sensed through a "medium" <note>The "medium" is the substance between the object and the organ, like air for sound or water for sight</note> are detected because we possess the organs through which that medium is recognized. It is known that this happens through only two of the "simple bodies," namely, air and water. Our sense instruments are formed from these two simple elements. For fire is either not present as a specific organ, or it is common to all senses; nor is earth used as a primary organ. However, if anything is perceived by touch, it is mixed with the elements in some way.

He further maintains that if several sensible things are accessible through one sense instrument, the one who possesses that organ is sufficient for sensing multiple things. But if the same thing is perceived through several instruments, he thinks that whoever has either one of them can sense the same thing. Since Aristotle said these things, Theophrastus consequently inquires: First, how can it be confirmed that the senses are perfected through only these two—namely air and water? Does it suit us through these alone because our organs are composed of them? Sight is attributed to water, and hearing to air, but smell might belong to either one.

Next, he asks if several things are known through the same medium, perhaps it is not necessarily the case that whoever has that medium knows several things for that reason. For example, if both odors and sounds are perceived through the air, it does not mean both are necessarily known through it; for not all animals that smell also hear. For it is not as if air is simply capable of smelling and hearing just by being air. For the air in a throat, like a pipe, has neither ability. Rather, the organ is capable through a <term>ratio</term> <note>original: *ratione*; here meaning a specific proportion or governing principle</note> rather than through the "matter" of sensing, and it must possess within itself a certain principle for sensing both. Therefore, he who does not possess the principle for both will not sense both.

### Chapter 43: Of what nature the instruments of the senses are.
## BY MARSILIO.

<margin>e</margin>
Although in the other senses besides touch, there must not be a quality formally similar to the objects—for there is no flavor in the sense of taste, nor odor in the sense of smell—yet in touch it is necessary for tactile qualities to be present. This is because a body is necessarily constituted from these qualities. But it will be enough if in the nerve of touch there is no "elemental quality" so dominant <note>For example, if the finger was extremely hot, it could not accurately judge the warmth of another object</note> that it prevents the discernment of the sensory quality it encounters. Therefore, this instrument will be composed of all four elements. But water will exceed earth, and air will exceed fire, and finally, air will also surpass water, so that this organ can be called "aqueous" in one sense and "aerial" entirely. But no one would say that "simple" <note>pure, unmixed</note> air is an instrument of sense for this very reason: because it is simple.

->FROM PRISCIANUS<-

<margin>i</margin> Furthermore, Theophrastus persists in doubting whether that Aristotelian view might be less than true—namely, that the instruments of the senses are "media" [middle-substances] so simply that they are not mixed with external things. Instead, he suggests they should be defined by us according to the quality that prevails within them. Indeed, we say that heat is common to all organs, and moisture is present in several. Moreover, if we require an instrument to be completely unmixed [pure], it would immediately follow that whatever is most unmixed would be most sensitive; thus, a substance separated from an animal would be capable of sensing. Added to this is the fact that a certain ratio [proportion] is the cause of sensation, for sensation is lost where the ratio is dissolved. Since ratio consists in the actual mixture of several things, then surely every instrument will be composed of several elements. Finally, why should the senses arise from only two elements? For living consists mostly in heat, and sensation is a function of life.

### Chapter forty-four: on the spirit, life, and sensation.

->FROM MARSILIO<-

<margin>f</margin> If the spirit <term>spiritus: in Renaissance medicine, a subtle, vaporous substance that carries life and sensation through the body</term> is a certain vapor of the blood, then like blood itself, it is composed of the four elements, though they are far more refined. The **vital spirit** in the heart is evidently fiery, appearing as such from the perpetual motion of the heart, its power, and from the nature of anger. The **natural spirit** in the liver is mostly airy, and thus perfectly suited for digestion and generation [reproduction]. The **animal spirit** <note>original: "spiritus animalis"; here "animal" refers to the "anima" or soul, meaning the spirit responsible for cognitive and sensory functions</note> in the brain is tempered almost equally by fire and water, and is thus placed at the service of the senses. For the instrument of sense must be very easily moved and shaped. Earth, indeed, resists the shaper; fire, however, shapes things itself rather than being shaped. Therefore, a temperament [mixture] of air and water is more suitable than the others for the instrument of sensation.

Now, light is a certain form <term>species: in this context, a formal image or essence that carries information to the senses</term> which, among all sensible forms, represents the intellectual form above all others. In the intellect, light exists through its cause; in the heavens, through the fullness of its form; in fire, through the fullness of its participation; and from there, it is derived into specific parts. However, all the senses do not exist wherever that temperament is found, unless all the formal properties for perceiving all things are also present in this temperament, and all the instruments <note>original: "instrumenta"; referring to the physical organs of the body</note> of the senses are present in the body. It is probable, indeed, that all such properties and all such instruments exist in the most perfect animal being—which is that which, besides sense, also possesses intellect, of which kind is man. Life itself, since it is the mistress of bodily generation and motion, and a pre-eminent form, does not sprout from a bodily mixture, but depends on an incorporeal substance. Therefore, all the worldly spheres, both the celestial and the elemental—being, as it were, among the simplest bodies and the first members of the world, and thus closest to the life-giving substance—are the first to live; therefore they are endowed with an abundance of life and sensation. But portions of the elements separated from their wholes <note>original: "universitatibus"; the elements in their pure, cosmic state rather than in small, mixed amounts</note> are mixed with foreign things, nor do they properly live, unless they are tempered within some animated body. Therefore, sensation is in a simple body, not because it is a body, but because it is close to life; and it is in a mixed body, not because it is mixed, but because it has been reduced to a harmony close to life. Sensation is not found in portions separated from the elements, because such a portion has neither simplicity nor harmony. Yet as long as they remain in their wholes, they are endowed with simplicity, life, and sensation.

...refuges from [others], and drives out foreign boundaries. Air and water, on the other hand, since they are easily bounded from elsewhere, rightly admit anything easily. They are affected by light causes and are easily formed, which results in the instruments of our senses being made from these two elements. How then is the instrument of sight considered both fiery and solar among the Pythagoreans? Clearly because it is a receptacle of light, both due to its thin, most shiny, and purest membranes, and due to the highly transparent fluids <note>original: "humores"</note> enclosed within such small films. For light is a fiery form <term>species: here meaning a visual image or formal essence that carries information</term>, not as a fiery body, but as a certain form shared from fire. In these two elements [air and water], therefore, the medium for sensing is placed, because of their nature which is very easily formed and bounded. Consequently, if many things are known through the same thing, the animal possessing that thing will also know many things—I speak of an animal that is neither mutilated nor imperfect. Therefore, Theophrastus <note>a Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle</note> rightly considers that several things are produced through one and the same thing according to reasons <term>rationes: here used as formal principles or proportions</term>, and towards many things according to different reasons. But what is truly perfect must necessarily have all reasons within itself, if indeed it is to be perfect. Now, a perfect animal is one which, besides sense, is also a participant in powers superior to sense, just as man is also a participant in the intellect.

But animals that indeed smell, yet do not hear, are considered imperfect. But if heat is common to all, and moisture to some, the instruments of the senses should not therefore be judged as mixtures. For neither external air nor water should be called mixtures because they participate in heat. For as long as they do not change their essence, they remain simple elements. But if they are proved to be mixed, mastery is nevertheless held through those two [air and water] which have been mentioned. And yet even if they are simple, it should not be said that they are sensitive because they are separate. Since they are sensitive not as simple things, but as things marked by a certain life; if they are deprived of this life, they are also deprived of sense. Unless perhaps we wish to think more in the Platonic way: namely, that those things which are truly simple possess sense in the highest degree. But those are truly simple which remain in themselves and in their own proper wholes, or (as I might put it) in their universalities, so that I am not forced to say "totalities."

->PRISCIANI<-
<note>Priscianus Lydus was a 6th-century philosopher whose paraphrases of Aristotle and Theophrastus were central to Renaissance psychology.</note>

In what way, then, is reason the cause of sense? For reason seems to consist in a certain mixing of several things, and in their mutual condition or proportion; but **Theophrastus** <note>Aristotle’s successor</note> solves this himself. He determines that reason itself consists not in the mutual condition of the elements, but in the proportion of the sensory instruments to the things to be sensed. I, however, think it more probable that Theophrastus does not place sensory reason principally in any condition or proportion, but in the vital essence and the judge of sensible things. And he places the "dissolution" of reason only insofar as the instrument intended to receive reason becomes inept. He considers it "ineptitude" even when a sensible thing, falling upon the sense incongruously, dissolves by this very incongruity the aptitude which the instrument requires to receive reason. Accordingly, if sense indeed pertains to life, and living is primarily occupied with heat, then heat will also be in the simple things within us according to their participation in life itself, by a certain added condition. But if the instruments of the senses are found to be mixed, mastery is nevertheless held, as we have said, through only two elements.

### Chapter 46. The proper, common, and accidental sensible.

->MARSILII<-
<note>Marsilio Ficino, the likely author/translator of this commentary, was a key figure of the Italian Renaissance.</note>

A **proper sensible** is that which is known by a single sense. Color by sight, voice by hearing, odor by smell, flavor by taste, heat by touch. A **common sensible** is that which is known by many; magnitude, for instance, by sight and touch; motion, however, by sight, hearing, and touch. The "proper" moves and is felt first because of its greater congruity with the sense; the "common" second. Thus, you see honey first as yellow, and soon after as large. For this reason, color deceives less at a distance than magnitude does. You do not truly "see" sweetness, however, unless perhaps you are said to see sweetness by **accident** <note>meaning you see the yellow color and *infer* the sweetness based on past experience</note>. For the eye is not moved by sweetness; it is moved, however, by the quality of color and the quantity of the object.

...but from quantity through quality as if through something more effective. In the path of generation <note>the process of a thing coming into being</note>, access is not made from motion to form, but from the form of the agent <note>the thing acting</note> through motion to the form in the patient <note>the thing being acted upon</note>. Therefore, in the path of knowledge, we do not perceive form through the knowledge of motion, but conversely. The quality of a natural thing brings a greater passion <term>passion: from the Latin 'passio,' meaning the state of being acted upon or receiving an impression, rather than an emotion</term> to the perceiver than quantity does, because it is more effective.
<note>The following line is struck through in the original manuscript:</note>
And both, namely quality and quantity, are known by some greater passion of the perceiver than form. 
That is, the species <note>original: "species," here meaning the outward appearance or visible form</note>, the specimen, the inner nature: something resulting from the proportion of colors and features. This is neither a composite body, nor the composition itself: but something given to the harmony of the composition as if a certain special and celestial gift; and because it arrives last, it is thought to stand far off from the coarseness of matter, and it corresponds to the higher forms understood in the upper world. For what is given last to matter is first in the informer <note>the shaping principle or soul that organizes matter</note>. Since, however, violence <note>sudden or overwhelming physical force</note> pertains to material things, and a form of this kind stands furthest from matter among these, the sense and its instrument exercise themselves more effectively in its presence, rather than suffering from something violent, as if like strengthened by like.

->PRISCIANI<-
<note>Priscianus Lydus was a 6th-century philosopher whose paraphrases of Aristotle and Theophrastus were central to Renaissance psychology.</note>

<margin>r</margin>
Again, Aristotle shows that regarding common sensibles <term>common sensibles: qualities like size, shape, and motion that are not restricted to one sense (like color is to sight) but are perceived by many</term>, we have no specific sense belonging to us, but we perceive common sensibles by motion. And for this very reason, we recognize these through several senses, such as magnitude by sight as well as by touch. Theophrastus, however, says it seems absurd if one arrives at the notion of form through motion, saying this, I believe, because he does not distinguish how that should be understood. Therefore, we ought not to say that we know common things by motion in such a way that we perceive motion primarily, and the rest accidentally <note>original: "contingenter," meaning by chance or as a secondary effect</note> or as a consequence. Instead, it must be said that we perceive all common things similarly, and all these entirely by motion. This is because we perceive from the fact that we are changed <note>original: "permutemur"</note> in some way. For if sight is moved by magnitude, it does not perceive it accidentally as it does sweetness; for sight does not suffer nor is it altered in any way by sweetness. But if magnitude belonged to some specific sense, it would be perceived accidentally by the others, like sweetness; but now that is not the case. Instead, by moving the sense, it offers itself to be perceived. There is, therefore, no specific sense for perceiving magnitude; similarly for other things, whatever the common sensibles are—they also move the sense by figure or form. However, the passion <note>the passive impression</note> brought from here is less apparent. Rather, a certain action of the sense itself shines forth more because of the nature of the form or figure, which is more specific than the others. And therefore, it moves the sense in us more specifically, more according to the act, and more stably.

[O]ught <note>original: "Portere" (Oportere). A space was left for a decorative initial 'O' which was never completed.</note> the five senses to be brought back to one common sense, and that this is indivisible, we prove sufficiently in our theology <note>referring to Ficino’s "Platonic Theology"</note> along with Plotinus <note>a major Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 204–270 AD)</note>. The common sense perceives the objects of the five senses as well as their actions and their periods of rest. To this sense properly belongs conscious attention <note>original: "animadversio"</note>; that is, when we notice that we are seeing or hearing something. From this, it often happens that we both see and hear things, yet we do not perceive that we are sensing them, because the common sense and the imagination are meanwhile turned elsewhere. In this common sense are sight, hearing, and the others. But here they are one form and one power; here they are derived to the five instruments <note>the eyes, ears, etc.</note> as if lines from a center to a circumference. That is, the specific forms and powers of the senses, which differ from one another on the circumference like lines, are one in the center. Therefore, the common sense is formally something different from the five that proceed from it. But by the power that collects these into one, it is the same. And insofar as this faculty notices, it can be said in a certain way that "sight sees" and "hearing hears," and then sight and hearing are said to pay attention, because the common sense is itself sight and hearing within itself. However, insofar as sight and hearing are separated from it—this one flourishing in the eye, that one in the ear—neither does the eye see itself seeing, nor does the ear hear itself hearing. For to turn back upon oneself and to double one’s actions <note>i.e., to act and to be aware of the action simultaneously</note> does not belong to powers so far removed from their source and therefore so weak. Furthermore, if hearing perceived its own action, it would also detect its own inactivity. Therefore, if placed in silence, it would perceive itself not sensing. It would then be acting and not acting at the same time. Truly, this diversity at the same time concerning the same thing does not belong to a sense that is ultimately divided and thoroughly weakened, but to a common form and faculty. Since this faculty turns back into itself and acts without a physical instrument and without being a "patient" <term>patient: the thing being acted upon or receiving an impression</term>, it is rightly considered separable from the body.

## PRISCIANUS

<margin>1</margin>
In those matters by which we sense that we sense in some way, he <note>Priscianus</note> proceeds by the same path as Aristotle, thinking that the common sense exists there to judge in this way, perceiving the work and the leisure <note>activity and rest</note> of each individual sense. For the same power perceives opposites. The common sense is neither the individual senses, nor is it entirely different from them; for since it is the collection of all the second senses and their height in one indivisible <note>original: "iptibilem," likely "impartibilem"</note> loftiness, it seems to be, as it were, the apex of them all. For this reason, each individual sense will also in a way perceive itself sensing—not by the reason that it is already divided, but insofar as it is joined to the one sense. Truly, it is the nature of a power separated from bodies to turn back upon itself and to know itself. Each individual sense, however, is more corporeal <note>bodily</note> insofar as it is divided. But it progresses rather into that faculty by which it separates itself according to a certain indivisible union with the other senses. For this indivisible union belongs to forms <note>original: "speciebus"</note> separated from the body. But if, as he himself rightly thinks...

# ON THEOPHRASTUS

It belongs to the same power to judge contrary things, and therefore it is within its scope to grasp them even when they are not active; for if there is indeed a period of rest, each individual sense is in a certain way separated from its instrument. Otherwise, sight would not perceive darkness, since the instrument <note>the eye</note> does not undergo any change there; yet it seems to act while the instrument is least affected. Much more so does the <term>common sense</term> <note>the faculty that unifies data from the five individual senses</note> itself, which perceives even the individual senses themselves during their periods of rest.

---

<margin>Chapter 48. Confirmation of the above. BY MARSILIO.</margin>

Numenius, Plotinus, Porphyry, and Iamblichus <note>a list of major Neoplatonist philosophers</note> believe that the <term>sensory soul</term> <note>original: "animam sensualem"; the part of the soul responsible for processing physical sensations</note> is separable from the body. Priscianus also touches upon this here because of the current conjecture: that the soul possesses a single and indivisible faculty that performs very different actions simultaneously. I set aside the <term>function of vegetation</term> <note>original: "vegetationis officium"; the basic biological functions like growth and nutrition</note> and speak instead of the <term>imagination</term>, which is one thing yet imagines such diverse things at the same time. Through this, the soul is also turned back into itself, where through that imagination it notices the actions of the senses; through this, it acts in a certain way without the instrument of the body, since it perceives darkness, silence, and the cessation of sensing. For at that time, the sense is not moved by the instrument, and thus it does not move the imagination; therefore, the imagination then acts as if separated in some way from the instrument. This common sense, therefore, flourishes in the soul as eternal according to its form and power; and when the powers of the bodily instruments are applied to it, it produces in itself those things which flourished in it before, distinct in their principles <note>original: "ratione"</note> but not separated by location or by their own specific actions. Therefore, when the body ceases, the senses do not entirely cease to be; they merely cease to be unfolded. Remember that these things are told by us according to the <term>Platonists</term>.

---

<margin>BY PRISCIANUS.</margin>

Why, then, will not each individual sense in truth—but rather the common sense itself—notice itself and its own action? For if any sense recognizes its action, it will also notice the absence of that action. If it recalls its own rest, it will simultaneously be at rest and yet active, as if perceiving itself. Does it not, therefore, rest insofar as it is divided and singular, yet act again insofar as it remains free from its own specific action and its cessation? Therefore, it acts according to the common sense, according to which each individual sense also acts—not by the logic by which they are individual and divided, but by the logic by which they are joined through the single unity of all. It is the office of this unity to grasp the sensory objects of all the senses at the same end, even while it acts through different principles. For this reason, the <term>judge</term> <note>the common sense acting as an evaluator of sensory data</note> remains one and indivisible in number, yet is also considered to be divisible insofar as it exercises different principles.

...adequates itself to the efficacy [of the object], so that it neither exceeds nor falls short. For when a thing is conforming on both sides, as we have said, we rest most pleasingly within it, embracing it most eagerly. This, moreover, is what it means to be affected by pleasure. There is, however, a double proportion in the instrument <note>the sense organ, such as the eye or ear</note>: one produced in the act of sensing through the congruence of the incoming object, and another more ancient one—that is, a certain affection naturally implanted in this instrument that is, so to speak, conformed and inclined toward one sensible object rather than another.

### FROM PRISCIANUS.

Following this, where Aristotle says that the voice is a harmony <note>original: "consonantia"</note>, it must be understood that this refers to when it is already a sensible thing in act, or placed in sensory action—that is, while it is actually being heard. It is heard, however, when both the voice and the hearing are made one in accord with each other, while they are thoroughly tempered together. For an excessive sensory object destroys or ruins the action of the senses; the sense itself consists in a certain measured proportion <note>original: "commensuratione"</note>, and we say those objects are "pleasant" which are tempered to the senses. Tell me then: when the sense is doing nothing, is it placed in no proportion within itself? Certainly, since the sense is not accustomed to act according to itself alone, but consists in a certain extension toward external things and in a certain relationship to things to be sensed; when it is idle, it will not have an active or effective proportion within itself. It will only have a proportion according to its potential. For the potential itself existed beforehand and is considered according to itself. But let us proceed next to those things which follow from another beginning, as we are about to treat the remaining matters pertaining to the book.

## THE END OF THE FIRST BOOK.

The interpretation by the Lydian philosopher Priscianus of the book of Theophrastus <note>a student of Aristotle and his successor at the Lyceum</note> on imagination and the intellect, translated by Marsilio Ficino the Platonist and explained by the same in chapters.

### Chapter One.

<margin>i</margin>
In the sense and the imagination, there are innate <term>principles</term> <note>original: "rationes"; these are the formal, formative patterns of things</note> that model themselves after sensible objects. In the sense, these are provoked into action by the "passions" <note>the physical impressions or changes</note> of the instrument. In the imagination, however, they arise from the actions of the senses. The <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "phantasia"</note>, acting as a mediator between sense and reason, is a certain activity within the sense. Iamblichus <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher</note> says of the imagination: it is born alongside all the powers of the soul. It shapes everything within itself, and translates forms from some powers into others, emulating the acts of all powers. The imagination does not receive forms from external things, but brings them forth from itself.

# PRISCIANUS ON THEOPHRASTUS

<margin>p</margin> It must be admitted from the books of **Theophrastus** <note>Aristotle’s successor as head of the Lyceum</note>—who follows **Aristotle** in this—that **Imagination** <note>original: "Phantasia"</note> is a power distinct from the senses. Furthermore, it differs from opinion and every kind of rational perception. Moreover, just as the sense is moved by sensible objects when vitally excited, and acts upon them according to the production of its own internal principles <note>original: "rationum"</note>, so too is imagination stirred by **sensory forms** <note>original: "speciebus sensualibus"; the mental representations derived from the senses</note>. It uses these as its immediate subjects and acts upon them; for this reason, imagination is also part of the bodily life and does not act without bodily instruments. This is because the sensory forms that move it are perfected from the impressions appearing in the sense organs. However, the following doctrines of **Iamblichus** <note>a prominent Neoplatonist philosopher</note> must be added: Imagination is innate to all the powers of the soul and shapes them all, fashioning likenesses of forms and appearances, and it transmits "visions" <note>original: "visa"</note> or impressions from some powers to others. Those impressions that flash from the senses, it arouses in opinion; those that come from the intellect, it offers to opinion in the second place. But within itself, it receives images from all sources. Through its own unique character, it is properly defined by its power of **assimilation** <note>the ability to make itself like something else</note>, both in acting and in receiving. These things are assimilated and appear in intellectual or general operations, or in those that lie between the two. Indeed, imagination fashions and expresses all actions of the soul; it accommodates external things to internal ones, and it imposes the impressions descending from the intellect upon the defects <note>original: "vitiis"; the limitations or "faults" of physical matter</note> that extend through the body. Since, therefore, imagination is in itself the power of assimilating other things to itself, it is rightly joined to the other powers, preceding them and providing the starting points for their actions. It is neither a "passion" <note>a passive undergoing or reception</note> nor a motion, but an impassive and definite action. It is not shaped by receiving something from the outside like wax; rather, it is stirred from within, following the production of assimilative principles toward the manifestation of **mental images** <note>original: "phantasmatum"</note>. These are the thoughts of Iamblichus.

->Chapter Two. BY MARSILIO.<-

<margin>i</margin> **Imagination** fashions the actions of reason under the condition of sensible things, and it can bring forth mental images more broadly than the acts of the senses can. Imagination agrees with sense because it perceives particular things. It surpasses sense, however, because it produces images even when nothing is moving [the sense organ]. Imagination is like **Proteus** <note>a Greek sea-god capable of changing shape at will</note> or a chameleon.

->BY PRISCIANUS.<-

<margin>u</margin> But if imagination expresses other "lives" (as Iamblichus says) and fashions intellectual and rational actions themselves, in what way will that Aristotelian saying still be true—namely, that "Imagination is stirred by sensory forms"? Perhaps indeed, even if it fashions all the more excellent acti-

# ON IMAGINATION AND THE INTELLECT

...it fashions images, while simultaneously imagining according to **sensory forms** <note>original: "species sensuales"; the mental images derived from our senses</note>, assimilating them through a certain formative condition. It is shaped and broken according to a certain relation to sensible things; for this reason, it fashions higher actions in the same way it is stirred by sensory forms. In what way, then, is the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia"</note> moved even when sensible objects are not present? For even if it is moved by sensory things, these are nevertheless brought into action when the senses are present or fail when they are absent. Perhaps it is not like the sense, which is usually moved only by present sensible objects; so it is always with imagination as well. But once it has been moved, it can now "awaken" of its own accord and produce **images** <note>original: "phantasmata"</note> according to a certain relation to the forms that originally moved it. Sometimes, however, it must be moved not just once or twice, but more often, so that it may offer those things within itself to those things that move in a similar way. Now, this formative power perhaps shares in a divisible nature with the sense; yet, by the faculty through which it produces images from itself—even if no further moving objects are present—it surpasses the sense. Again, by the condition through which it always refers itself to other things and assimilates itself to the different actions of the soul, it is indeed innate to all the powers of the soul. According to this assimilation, or this "likeness-making" property of the soul, it is judged to be a defining power.

### Chapter Three.

-> BY MARSILIO. <-

<margin>f</margin> Just as the sense and the imagination are formally different within the same substance of the soul, so the same substance of the **spirit** <term>spiritus: in Renaissance medicine, a subtle vapor that acts as the vehicle for the soul to move the body</term> is the instrument of both imagination and sense, according to its different qualities. Likewise, from the actions of the sense, certain marks representing them are impressed upon the spirit for the sake of the imagination. The imagination holds sensory forms as objects to which it refers its innate **principles** <note>original: "rationes"</note>. If the movements of reason and imagination produce manifest signs in the bodily humors and the solid body, how much more so in the spirit? Through these signs, it is known how **demons** <note>In the Platonic sense, these are intermediary spirits or entities that can perceive the subtle changes in a human's "spiritus"</note> perceive the thoughts of men. Regarding the same object, the sense can be truthful while the imagination is deceptive; and conversely, once awakened, the imagination can proceed further while the sense remains at rest.

-> BY PRISCIAN. <-

<margin>q</margin> Meanwhile, **Theophrastus** <note>Aristotle's successor as the head of the Peripatetic school</note> asks where the imagination should chiefly be placed. For it must not be placed in the sensitive power itself, since while the sense is truthful, the imagination itself sometimes lies. Nor, again, should it be placed in the instrument of the senses itself. For a "passion" <note>an impression or reaction</note> produced in the instrument only happens when a sensible object is present. But **phantasms** or **images** <note>original: "phantasmata siue imaginamenta"</note>—for one may interpret *phantasia* as **imagination**—I say these phantasms occur even when the sensible object is absent. I assert, therefore, that imagination is a power distinct from the sense, but very close to it. For that reason, it is moved in a certain way by the sense, and it uses sensory forms as its subjects. From these it is awakened, and toward these images...

# ON THEOPHRASTUS

...it reports images. Yet it varies these images in many ways because they surpass the sense; and from itself, once it has been moved toward formation, it fishes out whatever it has grasped. I believe, furthermore, that the signs or impressions of **forms** <note>original: "specierum"</note> emerging from the boundaries of the imagination can also be received by the instrument of sensing, just as formal and primary figures testify, though they do not indicate anything separate from bodies. Indeed, often while the body is moved toward imaginings and is affected according to them, I believe that **images** <note>original: "phantasmata"</note> appear in the instrument itself, but not as if it were performing a sensory act, since they do not fall upon it from external things; nor again as if we were changed by certain acting bodies, but rather as if in something receiving imaginative forms.

Nor should this seem strange, since certain signs and marks of our rational action also descend into the body, which is clearly seen when both the eyes and eyebrows are contracted during intense investigations. Now, if these solid members of the body follow along while the movements of the soul are affected, it is necessary that the instrument of the senses—being more vital—receive certain vestiges of life much sooner. In those things where life is merely sensory, the instrument is also merely sensory; but in those where there is additionally an imaginative, appetitive, or even rational life, the instrument is similarly adapted to receive life of that kind. It will therefore receive imaginative marks as something imaginative, even false ones if the imaginings are false. 

And just as we sometimes perceive true things while we are meanwhile able to produce false distorted images, so consequently the **spirit** <term>spirit: or "spiritus," the subtle, vaporous substance that medieval and Renaissance thinkers believed connected the immaterial soul to the physical body</term> itself, as we perceive it, receives true marks from the sensory powers; but as an imaginative faculty, it can receive false marks from the senses and true ones from the imagination. For instance, when seeing the sun, we perceive it to be a foot wide, while we meanwhile imagine it to be much larger than the earth, compelled by **geometric demonstration** <note>This is a classic philosophical example: our eyes see the sun as a small disk, but our reason/imagination knows its true, massive scale through mathematics</note>. Yet there is no sense of the imaginative faculty itself within us, even though an image exists in the instrument of sense; for sense properly pertains to and depends on sensible objects, while images emerge from the imagination. 

Therefore, it is not impossible for the underlying spirit to receive true and false appearances of the same things simultaneously, as appears to us in turn regarding the sun, since it receives input from different powers and according to different forms of life. Nor does anything prevent an image and the act of sensing from occurring together in the same subject, even if they are opposites, inasmuch as they are not of the same order or connection, nor are they works of the same power; for even opinion and sense regarding the size of the sun are opposed to one another in the same subject. To this, then, a response is made by reason; it has been said, moreover, that the presence of sensible objects is not always needed for the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia, i.e., imaginatio"</note> to be moved, but once it has been awakened and strives to give birth to such a form, it is sufficient unto itself. Let us proceed to the rest.

## ON IMAGINATION AND THE INTELLECT

<margin>f</margin>
<margin>i</margin>Our intellect is something proper to the soul, a kind of **form** <note>original: "species"; refers to the mental "blueprint" or image of a thing</note>, and in its actual operation and through its own essence, it contains within itself the forms of all intelligible things. However, because it has degenerated from the "first" <note>The "First Intellect" or God</note>, it requires the nourishment of that first intellect for three purposes: First, so that it may be most sharp-sighted. Second, so that its forms may be most clear and bright. Third, so that the intellect may be most perfectly united with those forms. Sensory perception is also a kind of form and, according to its essence, contains the **principles** <note>original: "rationes"; the underlying logic or patterns</note> of sensible things, which it brings forth whenever physical objects move its sensory organs. The "animal intellect"—which, due to the nature of the soul, inclines toward things that can be divided and are in constant motion—stands at a great distance from the unity and stability of the First Intellect and the primary things that can be understood. Note here that everywhere "the agent intellect" <note>The active part of the mind that produces thoughts</note> within our being is considered the First Intellect. These ideas are similar to those in Plato’s *Republic*, where the light of the "Good" itself joins intelligible forms with the minds that perceive them. There are people who write letters on paper using onion juice; these letters are not visible unless the paper is heated. The forms of things held by what we call the <term>possible intellect</term> <note>The mind's capacity to receive and store knowledge, like a blank slate or hidden ink</note> are like this. They come into view only through the presence of divine fire, just as colors are made visible by the light of the sun. Our intellect is not in a state of potentiality merely to *become* intellect and intelligible things, but rather to reach the ultimate perfection of understanding them.

THEOPHRASTUS, in the section where he later discusses the intellect, says that we should not accept this idea entirely, nor in the same way. For it would be a matter of dispute to accept these things simply—namely, that the intellect is a certain power entirely subject to something else, in the way that material powers usually are. Progressing a little further, he adds: "Perhaps this will appear absurd if the intellect possesses the nature of matter in such a way that it is nothing in itself, but is all things only in potential." Therefore, it must not be explained in that way, nor should this be assumed similarly for every kind of intellect. Instead, a distinction must be used. What then is this distinction? Matter is not a <term>this-something</term> <note>original: "hoc aliquid"; a specific, individual substance</note>, but if the intellect were not a "this-something," what else could truly be called a "this-something"?

->Thus far the words of Theophrastus.<-

<margin>q</margin>When, therefore, the intellect is compared with nature according to a certain proportion, this must be assumed: one intellect is in a state of potentiality relative to another. In this way, the animal intellect is rightly said to be "all things in potential" when compared to that intellect which is always "in act" <note>fully realized and active</note> and separate from matter. Sense perception, following this, is not strictly matter, but is called matter through a certain metaphor. For matter is thought of as the ultimate or lowest thing; however, sense is not the lowest of all things like matter is. Indeed, sense is a certain form, and it is said to contain the principles of sensible things according to its essence. In another sense, the sense is said to be "sensible things in potential," insofar as it is incited by them to act, and requires them—both being present and acting upon its instrument—for its own proper action. But the animal intellect is neither like matter nor like sense; for it is form, and it is a comprehender of forms solely according to its own essence. It acts from itself and within itself; indeed, it contains the things to be understood because of its kinship with them...

-># ON THEOPHRASTUS<-

...with the soul, and because of the soul's essential relationship to it, and finally due to its inclination toward the divisible <note>Meaning the physical world, which can be broken into parts, unlike the indivisible realm of pure thought</note>. Consequently, the intellect itself has fallen away from that intellectual essence which is entirely indivisible and purely united in its action. Furthermore, the "intelligibles" <note>original: "intelligibilia"; things that can be understood by the mind rather than perceived by the senses</note> within it seem to have degenerated from that first substance of intelligibles, which is super-radiant and self-shining. Similarly, the continuity between the animal intellect <note>The "anima" or soul-based intellect that governs the living body</note> and its intelligibles has been somewhat loosened; it is no longer entirely whole, unlike that unity which thrives constantly in the separate <note>meaning divine or transcendent</note> intellect. For this reason, the human intellect needs a "perfecter"—the intellect that is always in action—to reach a knowledge that is entirely indivisible. Likewise, the intelligibles within it need the illumination that shines from the separate intelligibles so that they too may become perfect. Hence, Aristotle says these intelligibles are like colors needing the splendor of the sun <note>Aristotle famously argued that just as colors exist but cannot be seen without light, thoughts exist in the mind but cannot be "seen" by the soul without the light of the active intellect</note>. The intellect itself, and its own intelligibles, when drawn back toward the indivisible, are joined by the most exact unity of the higher intellect and its intelligibles. For this reason, the animal intellect is said to be "in potentiality" <term>potentia: the capacity or "potential" to become something, as opposed to already being it in actuality</term>, insofar as it pertains to the separate intellect. For that higher intellect is entirely indivisible and purely united to the most excellent, primary, and perfect lights. 

It is also said to be in potentiality insofar as it is perfected by that kind of intellect. Therefore, when the intellect is described as a "tablet" <note>original: "tabella"; a writing board or slate</note> on which no letters are yet expressed, this should be understood according to a certain proportional comparison. This is not said as if the intellect has no forms <note>mental blueprints or concepts</note> in any way. Rather, just as the intellect is in potentiality—not in such a way that it is not an intellect at all, but rather an intellect that must be perfected by the First Intellect—so also the intelligibles placed within it are indeed intelligibles, but of the sort that must be illuminated by the separate intelligibles to be purely understood. This is why they are compared to colors, and this tablet is called "empty of letters" with respect to receiving those perfect forms. 

Rightly, then, Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle</note> cries out that it is absurd to give a material nature to the intellect and to think that, in the manner of matter, it is nothing in actuality but everything in potentiality. He forbids, above all, interpreting the words in this way. Moreover, he commands us to investigate in what way the intellect is said to be in potentiality by some other reasoning. But indeed, the manner in which it is said to be in potentiality has already been sufficiently discussed for our present purposes. Furthermore, we have distinguished not that every intellect is in potentiality, but what kind of intellect is in such a state.
