# ON PHANTASY AND THE INTELLECT
R iii

...turns [toward it], it is to that extent turned toward the primary intellect and its mental forms <note>original: "species"; refers to the conceptual shapes or patterns the mind perceives</note>. By that intellect and by those forms, the mind itself is shaped; it becomes more perceptive and the forms themselves become clearer. In this state, our intellect is most unified and is something consubstantial with the soul <note>Meaning the mind and the soul share the same underlying substance or essence</note>. They say something similar regarding the "free act" by which angels turn toward themselves, and through themselves toward God—a sign that these mental forms are innate, and that this intellect of ours is naturally joined to the divine. This is because when the intellect is turned toward itself, it finds all things and is perfected by the divine. Note here and below that our intellect is always coupled with the divine. External things do not form the sense, but the spirit does. The sense, however, brings forth from within itself forms or actions that conform to those external things. When we say that the "potential intellect" <note>The "intellectus possibilis," or the part of the mind that has the capacity to learn but has not yet learned</note> is formed by the active agent, we do not mean that it simply "receives" forms like a container, but that in the presence of that agent, it is more effectively joined to its own forms. Thus, in the potential intellect, there is no "motion" or "passion" <note>original: "passio"; here meaning the state of being acted upon or changed by an external force</note> in the proper sense of the word.

->PRISCIANUS<- <note>Priscianus of Lydia, a 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a commentary on the works of Theophrastus</note>

After these points, however, Theophrastus <note>Aristotle's successor as the head of the Peripatetic school</note> wonders how either our intellect becomes "intelligible things" <note>original: "intelligibilia"; things that can be understood by the mind</note>, or how those intelligible things themselves are made, and what it means to "suffer" or "be affected" <note>original: "pati"</note> in that process. For it is necessary that the mind itself somehow becomes the things it understands, and that a certain "passion" or reception occurs there—at least if the intellect proceeds into action in the same way that our physical senses do. Yet, it is a riddle: what kind of "passion" can be brought from a physical nature into an incorporeal <note>non-physical</note> thing? Or what change occurs between them? And is the starting point given by the external object, or rather by the mind itself? It certainly seems to "suffer" or be acted upon by the object, for among things that are affected, none is affected solely by itself. Yet truly, it is also fitting for this intellect to be the principle of all things, and it is appropriate that it understands by its own power. Nor is "knowing" attributed to the intellect from itself in the same way it is attributed to the senses; rather, it happens in a more excellent way. Thus far are the words of Theophrastus.

Nevertheless, in the meantime, it becomes the things it understands. Yet the mind is not exactly like the "separated intellect" <note>The divine or transcendent mind that exists apart from matter</note>, because its unity has been somewhat "relaxed," as we have said. It is more fully adapted to the things it understands. In this way, it "suffers" or undergoes change in a certain sense: when it falls away from that pure, entirely indivisible, and separate union of intelligible things. It is as if it has departed from that state because it was born together with the soul. It is perfected both by the "intellect in action" <note>The active part of the mind that is currently thinking</note> and by the intelligible forms that exist within it. Nevertheless, the mind also perfects itself insofar as it awakens from within itself, accommodates itself to that intellectual act, and receives perfection from that act through its own operation. This is especially true because it has not entirely withdrawn from that "intellect in action," but although it is lower than it, it remains joined to it, as something that is itself also intellect. And for that reason, it is not distracted by external things, but enters into itself and turns toward itself, joining itself to its own power as much as it can. Only then is it [perfected] by the intellect in action.

# ON THEOPHRASTUS

...is perfected by the intellect. For this reason, it is affected <note>original: "patitur"; often translated as "suffers," meaning to be acted upon by an outside force</note> in a different way than the senses do; and indeed, not in the proper sense of the word, but equivocally. Rather, it acts more than it is acted upon, since it receives its perfections from higher things through its own action, rather than receiving what it understands from the outside. For here, the mind is the thing itself in a second degree, insofar as the mind is perfected while it is joined to its own <term>intelligibles</term> <note>Objects of thought; things that can be understood by the mind rather than perceived by the senses</note> and is simultaneously adapted to higher realities. This is because the mind’s own contents are not severed from those higher realities.

Accordingly, objects of thought act upon the intellect in the same way that objects of sense act upon the senses—with this exception: objects of thought do not come from the outside to perform this action. Since they are never truly separated from the intellect, there is one single action shared by both: the intellect acting toward the objects of thought, and the objects of thought acting toward the intellect. This is possible because they are not distinct from one another; rather, the intellect is those very things that are offered to be understood. 

Furthermore, even in the case of the senses, a "passion" <note>An experience of being changed or affected by something else</note> occurs in the physical organ; however, the primary sensing power is perfected according to its own action and motion. It does not receive influence from sensible things passively, but actively. Much more, then, does the intellect act from within itself, receiving perfection from the things it understands not through "passion," but through action—if indeed we should say it "receives" at all, and not rather that it produces from itself. For it is perfected by beginning from itself. 

In truth, "passion" properly belongs to those things moved by another, as they are incited from the outside. But in things that operate entirely from within and are active through and through, we cannot suspect any "passion" unless we use the term in an equivocal sense. For the intellect—even that which is called the "potential intellect"—is, according to its essence, a kind of <term>act</term>, albeit in a second degree. This act, therefore, is the opposite of passion, and can never be affected in a passive way. 

Theophrastus says that absolutely no passion or change can happen to incorporeal things that are separate or separable from the body. He notes that while passions usually fall upon us from external things, the intellect is a principle and, moreover, comes from itself. Because of this, it can behave in a way *similar* to something being acted upon, even though in reality it is not "suffering" at all. For if one excluded every kind of "passion," he says, the intellect would be nothing. In this context, he clearly gives the name "passion" to the perfection conferred by the objects of thought, because he believes it is necessary to preserve the intellect as something entirely pure. Meanwhile, because the intellect is perfected by these objects according to its own action, he accepts the word "passion" here not in its specific sense, but as a more general term. 

For the intellect (as Theophrastus says) is devoid of passion, unless perhaps "passive" is defined differently than it usually is. It is certainly not "passive" like something that can be moved; for motion is imperfect, whereas the intellect is more like an action. These two things differ from one another, even if it is sometimes necessary to use the same words for them. These are the words of Theophrastus. You see, therefore, that "passion" is understood here in the intellect not as a defect, a transformation, a motion, or something from the outside, but rather as a specific kind of action. On the other hand, he thinks one must grant forgiveness...

...he considers that we might sometimes misuse terms. This is because I often transfer names from things pertaining to the senses to the very things pertaining to the intellect. And yet, in a certain way, this intellect perfects itself. For as has been said, it receives the gifts of the higher being through its own specific action.

### Chapter six.
->MARSILIO<-

<margin>d</margin> The intellect in the soul is twofold, and both are called "possible." <note>The "possible" or "potential" intellect is the capacity of the human mind to become all things by understanding them</note> The first is an individual essence shared in by the soul. The second is the power that moves through reasoning, which is properly called the "soul." The former always understands in actuality, having been formed by the divine mind; the latter understands only when it turns itself toward the former. It stops understanding, however, when it turns away from there toward the senses. In both, there is a proper and free act. <term>Phantasia</term> <note>Imagination; the faculty that forms mental images of physical things</note> is sometimes called "intellect," for this is the final trace of intelligence. The rational soul, because it is a particular kind of life, acts in different ways by turns. At some times it turns toward divine things, and at other times toward things that are fleeting and falling. Free will exists in the intellect, both the purely intellectual and the rational. The intellect—whether the purely intellectual or the rational, both of which are within us—begins its act from itself, and has nothing prior to itself (that is, in terms of time). If something from the outside were to move our intellect—which would otherwise be sluggish on its own—two absurdities would follow: first, something would be prior to it in time; and second, the intellect would not have its own independent action.

->PRISCIAN<-

<margin>q</margin> After this, it is asked why our intellect does not always receive from the higher intellect, and why it does not seem to always be understanding. But in truth, the intellect is always acting. The soul, however, does not always use the intellect that is always present to it, specifically because it turns toward bodies. It seems indeed that Aristotle and Theophrastus (as has already been said) sometimes call the entire rational life "intellect," even extending the name of intellect as far as the imagination. And so, not without reason, one might ask concerning the soul why it does not always understand. Certainly, intelligence is never interrupted because it lacks the power to understand; rather, it is because the soul is distracted toward subsequent things, toward bodies, and generally toward things outside itself, owing to the condition of a "particular life" that acts by turns toward both sides. For the entire perfection of the soul consists in its clear return to itself and its turning toward the intellect. Conversely, in its inclination toward bodies, a "fall" from the intellect occurs. ## Chapter seven. MARSILIO'S COMMENTARY.

<margin>i</margin> In our intellect, there are <term>intelligibles</term> <note>Abstract concepts or truths that can be grasped by the mind rather than the senses</note> in the manner of "knowable things" <note>original: "scibilia"</note> which are innate to us. But the higher intellect acts upon those things through a certain eternal act. Our soul acts upon its own objects through a temporal action, using the same activity of the intellect—namely, through understanding. At that point, the intellect is at its highest, and the intelligibles are most fully themselves, and vice versa. Therefore, the intellect is the very things it understands. Also, our intellect, according to its essence, is "act" <note>meaning it is always active and fully realized, never just a dormant potential</note>. Therefore, within it, "to be" is the same as "to act." For this reason, it always understands. 

But in the soul—that is, in the rational power—essence is one thing and action is another. Therefore, it does not always understand, and it does not always know. Just as our intellect *is* the intelligibles, so the rational power *is* the things that can be known, although it does not always hold these in a state of activity as the higher intellect does. Reason brings these knowable things into "act" <note>active realization</note> through its own specific action when the essence of the soul returns into itself. Where the soul is most individual, it is the intellect, and "to be" there is "to understand." In that state, it possesses an attached action of reasoning that is no less individual, yet distinct from the essence and the power of logical discourse. 

The essence of the soul is both stable and mobile; its action is similar. Stable action accompanies the stable essence, and mobile action accompanies the mobile essence. The soul remains still and moves all at once. Likewise, the mobile power revolves around that which is stable. Furthermore, within the permanent essence of the soul, a certain eternal action lies hidden. The attention of the soul is mostly turned toward things that can be imagined and sensed; but when it returns into itself, it finds knowables in the rational power. Through these, it is finally joined to the "intelligibles," which always flourish in the intellect, even the "animal" <note>referring here to the soul's role in giving life to the body</note> intellect. The rational power returns to the intellect; it does not act upon all things at once, but in a certain succession because of its divisible nature.

For if, he says, the intellect in the process of acting becomes the things themselves—and this is most true for both—certainly the thing itself will be the intellect. For not only are the things understood, but even the intellect itself...

# ON IMAGINATION AND THE INTELLECT

...of the intellect, they are then at their greatest when the intellect understands. For this reason, he speaks of both in this way: if, then, when the thing itself exists, the intellect also exists, surely the intellect will be the very things that are understood. Will it then be the case that when it understands nothing—since the thing itself is not present to it—the intellect likewise will not exist? But certainly that which is truly the intellect, and also that which is said to be intellect in potentiality—namely, that shared by the soul—surely understands, inasmuch as it is itself an "act" <term>actus</term> <note>original: "actus"; in Aristotelian philosophy, this refers to the state of being active or fully realized, as opposed to being merely a latent possibility (potentiality)</note> by its own essence, though in the second degree. In the individual soul itself, however, there is room for doubt, for this does not always understand.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But is the soul nothing at all before it understands? Or is it indeed something, but like a certain matter, which is formed when it knows by things falling upon it from the outside? But indeed the soul itself is both something before it knows, and it begins not from external things, but rather from itself; it produces the things that are to be known, finding the things themselves insofar as it enters into itself. The soul, therefore, is the things themselves within itself before it knows them. Since, however, the soul is also in a way divided by this reasoning—because it is clearly not an "act" by essence, but has an act of knowledge proceeding from its essence—it follows that just as it exists even when it does not know something in act, so also the things themselves exist, namely not according to act and action, but rather through essence. For it is necessary to accept the things themselves in the soul in the same order as the soul itself. Not indeed because these things are always understood, but because the mind acts in a "knowable" manner, and these things are made "knowable" <term>cognobilia</term> according to the action following and producing from its essence. Since in the soul neither being nor acting is simple and uniform, but one part is permanent while the other is mobile—as a mobile power proceeds around a permanent power—the whole soul is meanwhile weighed according to both; and for that reason, the soul at once remains permanent and is moved. At the same time, it also always acts according to a hidden action innate to its permanent essence, and according to a life progressing outward and changeable. When it is wholly turned toward subsequent and divisible things, it works upon them using opinion along with sense, neither turned toward those things which (as I might say) are called "knowable objects" <term>scibilia</term> <note>original: "scibilia"; objects that can be known by the human mind, often distinguished from higher "intelligibles"</note>—which are the things themselves in the soul—nor much less turned then toward those things called "intelligibles" <term>intelligibilia</term> <note>original: "intelligibilia"; pure spiritual or abstract truths that the higher intellect grasps directly</note>, to which it is joined through those very knowables as if by a single continuum or union. Now indeed, when it recalls to those things—which remain within it—the life and action that had been produced and at some time sent forth, it does not act upon all things at once, but now upon these, then upon those, clearly because of its divisible nature.

# ON THEOPHRASTUS

## Chapter Eight. MARSILIO.

**P**otentiality in the rational mind is said to proceed from potentiality into act <term>actum</term> <note>original: "actum"; in this philosophical context, "act" or "actuality" refers to the state of being active or fully realized, as opposed to "potentiality" which is the mere capacity to be something.</note>, not because it receives new forms <note>Ficino uses "forms" to mean the essential blueprints or ideas of things.</note>—for it always possesses all of them—but because it exercises now those which it did not exercise before. Theophrastus says that if the intellect were like matter, being simply in potentiality, then whenever it understood by receiving new forms, it would undergo a certain essential change—which is absurd. What Theophrastus says concerning our intellectual intellect, Priscianus <note>Priscian of Lydia, a 6th-century philosopher whose commentary on Theophrastus was translated and utilized by Ficino.</note> extends also to the rational intellect in a certain way: therefore, that intellect neither receives new forms nor is it "moved" <note>In ancient philosophy, "motion" often refers to any kind of change or alteration.</note> here; it does not indeed receive new ones, but it moves around its own forms.

->PRISCIANUS<-

**W**hen, therefore, we say that there is potentiality and act within the soul, we understand this according to a change, or certainly when that proceeding action is not present (according to which it is possessed and called knowledge); then we surely say that the permanent essence is the producer of this kind of action in potentiality. At that time, the soul also exists as the things themselves <note>The idea that the mind "is" what it knows.</note>, yet it does not act according to a proceeding action. Therefore, although it does not know all things at once, but some at one time and others at another, it is not on that account one thing at one time and another at another; nor is it ever not the same, since it is not changed in every respect, but there is also something meanwhile remaining in the soul, and according to this very thing, the objects of knowledge have always remained in the soul. Theophrastus says it would be absurd if the intellect were in potentiality in such a way that it existed as nothing in act, but when placed in act, it were someone else—and another again when it does not understand itself; for in this way, from the fact that it understands one thing after another, it would never be the same. But truly, a nature of this kind, becoming so indistinguishable and lacking order, would clearly refute those who thought that the intellect is indeed all things in potentiality, but nothing in act. First, indeed, when it does not understand, it would be nothing. Then, even if it does understand, when it understands other things and has not understood itself, it would be something else and not entirely the same, but different at different times, and thus it would be perpetually changed. For which reason he says that potentiality and act are not to be understood in this way in the intellect, but (as was said before) where he judged that these two must be placed according to a certain comparison of proportion. Nor must these things be affirmed in the intellect in any way as they are in matter <note>Matter is passive and changed by what it receives; the intellect is active and remains itself.</note>.

## Chapter Nine. MARSILIO.

**T**he animal intellect is not mixed with the body; therefore it is not formed by the senses. The rational power, born alongside this, also does not receive new forms, but exercises its own in a certain rotation. Ra-

...rational nature, by the unformed reason of its own essence, includes the forms of all knowable things. Even if the Soul passes from potentiality into act <term>actum</term> <note>In this context, "act" or "actuality" refers to the state of being active or fully realized, as opposed to "potentiality," which is the mere capacity to be or do something.</note>, it does not become something else, because it does not put on a new form; rather, it puts forth a new action.

->PRISCIANUS<-

Accordingly, when he says the intellect is "this certain thing" <note>original: "hoc aliquid"; a technical term in Aristotelian philosophy referring to a specific, individual substance.</note>, he adds that in this regard its name is equal to sense. For sense—as he now argues—does not exist without the body, whereas the intellect is separated from the body. For this reason, it does not require those things that proceed from the outside for its own perfection. Thus, even when the soul knows, nothing "in act" exists in the meantime; all things exist according to an essential and permanent perfection, even though the action and the act might meanwhile fail in terms of production and addition. Therefore, regarding this action, the soul is then judged to be in potentiality. But then, since it is innate <note>original: "congenita"; literally "born with." The soul does not learn from the world, but is born with the blueprints of all knowledge already inside it.</note> with knowable things, when it knows something, it exists "in act" as that very thing which is knowable; it is then no longer different from itself. Indeed, the soul determines its own essence for itself according to all knowable things. Nevertheless, it seems to "become" in a certain way, for when it becomes individual things in this way, it is said to be "knowing in act." We say this happens when it can act by its own power; then it is indeed in potentiality in a certain way, yet not in the same way as when it had neither learned nor discovered.

### Chapter ten.

->MARSILIO<-

In the intellect, nothing new is born; in the soul, at least a new act and a habit <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitus"; a stable disposition or quality that allows someone to perform an action easily, like a skill or ingrained knowledge.</note> through that act are born. For the intellectual nature is uniform and stable, but the nature of the soul, besides these two, also possesses their opposites. For it is furthermore multiform and mobile; motion belongs to the definition and nature of the soul. The rational soul, because it is both the "middle of things" <note>A core Neoplatonic concept: the soul acts as the "horizon" or bridge between the eternal, divine world and the changing, physical world.</note> and is mobile by its own nature, plays its part toward the extremes, especially because it is a particular life. The rational power sometimes turns itself toward the intellect, and sometimes toward sense.

->PRISCIANUS<-

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation from page 6 regarding the nature of the rational soul and its transition from a state of possibility to a state of active knowing. ...it plays both roles, since it is both in the middle of things and has a life defined by motion. For this reason, it is sometimes carried toward ignorance insofar as it leans toward the lower, and at other times it is perfected by the gift of knowledge insofar as it turns toward the higher. Thus, it becomes at times imperfect and, in turn, perfect. For whenever it is ignorant, it is judged to be imperfect and is therefore said to be "in potentiality" <note>original: "in potentia"; the state of having the capacity to do something without currently doing it.</note>, because even then it possesses the power of knowing; but whenever it knows, it is judged to be perfect.

Furthermore, insofar as it acts, it claims perfection for itself from that very act; but insofar as it does not act at all even when it knows something, it is still judged to be in potentiality. However, this is not the same condition as before it learned or discovered, since it now possesses a "habit" <term>habitus</term> <note>In medieval and Renaissance philosophy, a 'habit' is a stable, acquired disposition—like a skill or a piece of knowledge—that allows a person to act readily and easily.</note> and has perfected that power of its own which is accustomed to producing acts of knowledge. 

Therefore, when Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle.</note> asks how there occurs in the soul a generation or "habit" of both powers and essences, he should be understood to ask whether a change occurs in the soul only according to habit and power, or also according to essence <note>original: "essentiam"; the fundamental nature or "what-it-is" of a thing.</note>.

## Chapter eleven.
### MARSILIO’S [COMMENTARY].

<margin>a)</margin>
Our soul is also changeable, in a certain way, according to its essence. Otherwise, if its essence were entirely unchangeable, it would not produce actions so diverse and changeable that they tend toward opposites. Likewise, there is a single soul in us by essence; if it were entirely unchangeable in itself, it would not produce actions that are sometimes right and sometimes perverse. If there were two distinct essences of souls in us that were disconnected from each other, and one did not depend on the other, there would not be one single living animal. The intellectual soul would not be the ruler of the bodily life unless the latter depended on it. There is a single essence in which there is intellectual and rational power, as well as a power that wanders in various ways. He seems here to place intellect, reason, and imagination within the same essence of the soul; because of this union, the being is a single animal, and the lower powers are referred back to a single ruling principle in the soul. There is a single essence of the soul in each one of us, and this is at once unchangeable and changeable; in whatever change of the soul occurs, the rational life proper to itself remains.

### PRISCIAN’S [COMMENTARY].

<margin><unclear>n. 1.</unclear></margin>
Since, therefore, habits and acts come from the essence, it is impossible to posit a certain essence that is entirely permanent, separated from all change, and always in the same state, yet which meanwhile sometimes produces perfect and good actions, and at other times imperfect and perverse ones. For the essence is the cause of the actions; therefore, the quality of the actions [indicates] the quality of the powers at the same time...

# ON PHANTASY AND INTELLECT

...and we rightly conjecture that the form of the essence is the same. If someone were to imagine a **double essence** <note>original: "geminam essentiam"</note> within us, along with double powers and actions at the same time—some always perfect in themselves, others at times imperfect and at times perfect—if he understood these as disconnected, one animal would become many animals. He would completely discard the more excellent essence as if it neither governed life nor had anything in common with it. Indeed, it is through the second essence that an alternation occurs between the imperfect and the perfect, by which human life is defined. 

But if the one who devised such things in us says there are **double dispositions** <term>habitudines</term> <note>States of being or relationships between the soul and the body.</note>, or double reasons, or double paths, he must not break the union of the two. Otherwise, our nature might become like a choir or some other multitude; rather, everything should come together into one and, fused into a single principle, they should harmonize. We will immediately ask about this "one": whether it is uniform, immutable, and always whole. If that were admitted, it would follow that there is never any imperfection, wickedness, or passion in animals, either according to essence or according to action. For actions follow the essence. Nevertheless, it must not be conceded that this "one" is entirely changeable, for life itself remains constant throughout changes.

### Chapter twelve. MARSILIO'S [NOTES].

<margin>2</margin>
Because our soul is the **middle** between things that are entirely stable and those that are mobile, it possesses an essence that is both stable and mobile. Through this, it takes turns acting out the lives of everything inhabiting the world. Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who influenced Renaissance thought on the soul's journey.</note>, on the composition of the soul and the alternation of lives: in the soul, there is a certain change, not only according to dispositions, but in a certain way even according to essence, insofar as the variety of species changes the intellectual or rational fire. Now it lives as a terrestrial human, then as an aerial one, and at other times as an ethereal one. But to me, Marsilio <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the priest and scholar who translated these works from Greek to Latin.</note>, it does not seem that Theophrastus <note>Aristotle’s successor, whose views on the soul are being debated here.</note> places any change in the soul that touches its essence. Iamblichus, however, allows for the very minimum of such change.

### PRISCIAN'S [COMMENTARY].

The particular soul, therefore, as it is found in Iamblichus, encompasses both equally: both the **permanent** and the **mutable**, so that by this reasoning its "middle state" <note>original: "medietas"</note> may be preserved. For higher things are stable and consist only in themselves. Falling things <note>referring to physical, decaying matter</note>, however, are entirely mutable. But the particular soul, as the middle between these, is divided and multiplied together with all the classes of things around the world; it does not only remain, but is also changed, acting out just as many divided or particular lives...

# ON THEOPHRASTUS

...is changed not only according to its **dispositions** <term>habitus</term> <note>The acquired states or qualities of the soul, like knowledge or virtue.</note>, but also in some way according to its essence. Which indeed Theophrastus also (as I believe) wishing to signify, says: "It seems indeed that generation in the soul happens more according to disposition." For change according to disposition and its reaching of **perfection** <note>original: "perfectio," referring to the soul reaching its full potential or "act."</note> is quite manifest; for this reason, he uses the word "more." And by saying this word "more," he signifies a clear perfection that pertains in some way to the essence itself; for this reason he adds: "this, however, perfects nature," meaning the nature of the one performing the action, as if it were not perfect before. For if the essence were entirely perfect, certainly the disposition and the action—which proceed from the essence alone—would not be imperfect.

### Chapter Thirteen.

### MARSILIO'S VIEW.
<note>Likely referring to Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century Neoplatonist who translated and commented on these works.</note>

Immaterial things have nothing in themselves except what necessarily pertains to their essence. Material things, besides their essential qualities, undergo many **accidental** <note>Non-essential characteristics that can change without destroying the thing itself.</note> changes. Our intellect knows both of these through **innate forms** <term>formae inatae</term>, which represent things; it knows immaterial things as being of the same kind as themselves, but material things it knows as their causes. Aristotle and Theophrastus wrote concerning things separated from matter and things joined to it. Iamblichus and Plutarch were commentators on Aristotle. The **possible intellect** <term>intellectus possibilis</term> <note>The capacity of the human mind to receive knowledge.</note> in us is twofold: one, the first, is always in **act** <note>Fully active and realized.</note>; the other, the second, passes from potentiality to act—that is, the faculty of **reason** <note>original: "ratio".</note>. When reason does not wander through imagination and the senses but turns back toward itself, it finds the innate reasons of things. These innate reasons are kin to the **separated substances** <note>Angelic or divine intellects that exist without physical bodies.</note>, and they are either the causes of material things or are similar to those causes. The **active intellect** <term>intellectus agens</term>, seeing itself, beholds all things according to their cause.

### PRISCIANUS'S VIEW.
<note>Priscian of Lydia, a 6th-century philosopher who wrote a commentary on Theophrastus's work on the soul.</note>

Next, Theophrastus, just like Aristotle, posits two kinds of **species** <term>species</term> <note>In this context, "species" refers to the "forms" or "essences" of things that the mind perceives.</note>: some are immaterial, while others are material. Regarding species separated from matter, he says: "each thing itself and its very being are the same." When he says "its very being," he designates the formal reason and the species; but when he says "each thing itself," he signifies the whole substance. Indeed, in species existing without matter, he thinks the whole substance exists according to the formal reason and species alone. However, in material species, he maintains that "each thing itself" is one thing, and "its very being" is another. For the "first good" is understood according to both together <note>meaning the union of form and matter</note>, whereas the other is understood according to the species alone. Since, therefore, the intellect which is called "potential" contemplates both kinds of species, Theophrastus investigates, along with Aristotle, how it observes both, and how it knows species existing in matter through a certain process of **abstraction**. For material species are contemplated either according to the species alone—

It does this by contemplating the immaterial principles of material things that are implanted in its own nature.

## Chapter Fourteen. ->MARSILIO'S VIEW.<-

<margin>f</margin>
Sense-perception knows only **accidents** <note>Temporary or non-essential qualities, like the color of a leaf or the temperature of a stone.</note> and particular objects. The intellect, however, also knows things universally; through **essential reasons** <term>rationes essentiales</term> <note>The defining principles that make a thing what it is.</note>, it likewise knows all the resulting accidents through infinite reasons. It knows immaterial things as being joined to these reasons, and material things as being produced by them. The "reasons" or principles implanted in the soul regard material things as causes regard effects, and regard immaterial things as either siblings or as effects. Natural forms, although they do not exist outside of individual objects, are nevertheless truly thought of when their individual accidents are ignored. Likewise, if the reason thinks about mathematical figures without specific matter, it knows them even though it realizes they can never actually exist without matter.

## ->PRISCIAN'S VIEW.<-

Indeed, the intellect knows material things, but not in the same way as sense-perception. For sense-perception reaches them as particulars according to qualities—for instance, as "hot," or "cold," or "white," or something else of that kind. The intellect and the rational life, however, know the **essences** <note>The "whatness" or core identity of a thing.</note> according to the common forms of material things. Will the intellect then not know that fire is hot? Certainly, all qualities and accidents proceed from each essence; therefore, the intellect, which has known the essence, also knows the accidents through the very principles of that essence, even more excellently than sense does. Furthermore, those material things known through "abstraction" <note>The mental process of "drawing away" or isolating the essential form of an object from its physical, material qualities.</note> by removing their physical traits are, in a certain way, the same as the material forms; yet, we think of them as they are in themselves. This means they are not thought of alongside matter. Indeed, they do not exist in a separate state, nor are they understood as if they claimed their own essence in some separate way; rather, when we think of them together with matter, we call them "material." But when we recognize them as forms alone—acknowledging that they exist in matter and cannot exist otherwise, yet choosing to focus only on the form—then we are perceiving them through abstraction.

### Chapter Fifteen.
->MARSILIO FICINO<- <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was a central figure of the Italian Renaissance who translated and commented on the works of Plato and his followers.</note>

The same intellectual power within us knows both immaterial and material things, and it knows the latter both as general concepts and as individual objects. It performs all of this through its innate principles, which it uses to engage with immaterial things as if they were close relatives (or as if it were their effect), and with material things as if it were their cause.

->PRISCIAN OF LYDIA<- <note>Priscian was a 6th-century philosopher; here he is presented as a commentator on the earlier Greek philosopher Theophrastus.</note>

Does the soul, therefore, judge material and immaterial things by some other power, or perhaps by the same power acting in a different way? And does it use a different method for those things found entirely within matter compared to those perceived through abstraction? Or is it rather the same power acting in a similar way? Perhaps both are true. For the same judge can evaluate different things. Certainly, the intellectual faculty itself, remaining the same and acting in the same way, achieves this; for it acts according to its own internal principles. Yet, at the same time, it achieves this by a different faculty (in a sense) or by being in a different state. This is because it contemplates its own principles either as causes—when it thinks of material things through them—or as being joined to immaterial things, or as if they were produced by intellectual <unclear>forms</unclear>. In this way, it contemplates through its own principles, so much so that they have become, as it were, something else, or the soul itself exists in a different state.

That which is separated from matter immediately becomes "intelligible" <note>Capable of being understood by the mind rather than perceived by the senses.</note> as well as an intellect itself. The intellect appears to be indivisible because it turns back into itself; likewise, it is full of forms because, having turned inward, it finds all things within itself. There are three orders of separate substances, and three orders of intellects: first, there are the "super-mundane" <note>Existing beyond the physical universe.</note> intellects which are purely contemplators. ### FROM PRISCIAN
<note>Likely Priscian of Lydia (6th century AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a commentary on the works of Aristotle and Theophrastus regarding the soul.</note>

Generally, just as things themselves are separate from matter, so Aristotle and Theophrastus believe the conditions of the intellect to be. Perhaps, therefore, their opinion should be explained in this way: just as material forms <term>species</term> are separated from matter by thought alone—and thus are judged by a different faculty and in a different mode, as if they were apprehended and distinguished through thought alone—so too the forms innate to the "potential intellect" are separated by it through the act of understanding alone. This is because, according to its essence, the intellect always exists together with these forms. This is so much the case that even when the intellect is said to be "in potentiality" <note>The state of having the capacity for knowledge without currently thinking about it.</note> and we notice <note>original: "animaduertamus." The text transitions here to the catchword "animaduerti" for the next page.</note> nothing in actuality, it is evidently because we are operating through intelligence alone. Either those words of Aristotle and Theophrastus mean this (for this is how Plutarch <note>Referring to Plutarch of Athens, the Neoplatonist, rather than the more famous biographer.</note> explains it), or rather they mean what I shall soon add below. Just as those things said to be "separated from matter" are in some cases truly separate, while others exist in matter but are separated by the intelligence—just as those things perceived through abstraction are understood in both ways. Some are understood as truly separate, while others (if they are separated by some thought) are nevertheless not separate otherwise than by their material subsistence, so to speak. But perhaps we shall explain it better: just as we categorize things entirely separate from matter, so it is fitting to categorize the things concerning the intellect. This is lest these intellectual things be seen as existing only according to thought, when they actually exist in their own right and principally. For indeed, just as those immaterial forms are truly separated from matter, so too is the intellect entirely segregated from matter.

ON THEOPHRASTUS
<meta>catchword: illuminated</meta>

Truly, before and above material species <note>original: "species"; here meaning the formal qualities or "blueprints" of things.</note>, it is necessary for immaterial species to exist and to subsist intelligibly (so to speak) within themselves. Indeed, because these are indivisible and are entirely filled with life and knowledge through their whole being, they are said to possess neither a void of life nor ignorance by way of privation <note>Privation refers to the lack of a quality that ought to be present.</note>; for privation usually occurs only in the mingling of form with matter. Since, therefore, these species are free from matter, they are immediately intellectual. It is established that they exist in the intellect, and that the intellect itself is entirely free from matter, having received its very essence along with these immaterial species. For life and knowledge, which turn back into themselves, are indivisible—especially since the intellect, by entering into itself, finds beings that are both real and true. 

But because among things that are truly separate from the parts of matter, there is a certain hierarchy of descent: some are entirely indivisible, others exist with a certain "unfolding" <note>original: "explicatione"; the process of a simple unity expanding into complex parts.</note>, and others are intermediate between these, acting as indivisible principles that merely define what is unfolded. The intellect itself functions in this same way. In the first rank is that which is called the **intellect in act** <term>intellectus secundum actu</term> <note>The "intellect in act" is the mind in the moment of actually thinking or grasping a truth, as opposed to just having the capacity to think.</note>, which is fully separate. In the second rank is the **potential intellect** <term>intellectus secundum potentiam</term> <note>The capacity of the soul to receive knowledge.</note>, which is shared by the soul, and the rational soul itself. For although this soul exists in a state of unfolding, it nevertheless gathers both itself and other things into that which is indivisible. This soul begins its work from itself; it finds things—and true things—within itself. Therefore, the soul is separate from matter and full of separate rational principles.

# ON PHANTASY AND THE INTELLECT

...is illuminated from that source, and from there is united with its own forms. The **potential intellect** <term>intellectus possibilis: the capacity of the mind to receive or "become" the forms of all things through understanding</term> sees with a simple and stable intuition. The **rational power**, however, sees through a mobile and composite action <note>While the intellect grasps truth all at once, the "rational power" works through logic and sequences.</note>. The potential intellect is always and everywhere united to the agent <note>The "agent" or "active" intellect which provides the light or "spark" for understanding.</note> and is formed by it. But because it is formed through its own proper and free action, the potential intellect is rightly said to form itself; thus, the potential intellect is "all things" in a second degree, just as the agent is "all things" in the first degree.

### BY PRISCIAN.

<margin>t</margin>
Theophrastus again reminds us in a very philosophical manner how we ought to properly understand this very point: that the intellect is said to exist as the things themselves, both when the intellect is in potentiality and when it is in act. We must take care lest we understand "in potentiality" as a state of privation <note>original: "privationem"; a total lack or absence of a quality, like a blank slate</note>, as we are accustomed to do when speaking of matter. Nor should we suspect that what is called "in act" occurs according to a "passive perfection" brought in from external things. Furthermore, it does not happen as it usually does in sensation, where the production of formal patterns <note>original: "rationum"</note> occurs through the movement of physical instruments, and the sense itself perceives things placed outside it. On the contrary, he says that the state of things being both in potentiality and in act must be understood "intellectually" within the intellect itself.

For this very thing which is called **in act** <term>in actu: the state of being fully realized, operational, or "turned on"</term> must be judged according to an indivisible unity, a pure limit, and a thoroughly united perfection. For the intellect in act is truly the things themselves—not through participation, nor dividedly, nor as something "other," nor as if it were defined by them or perfected by them. Rather, it exists as the thing itself, and as the limit and perfection of all things.

However, we use the term **in potentiality** <term>in potentia: the capacity to become or know something that is not currently being thought about</term> to describe the state of contact made along with "otherness" <note>original: "alteritate"; the state of being different or separate from the object of thought</note>. This occurs through a certain descent toward that which is determined and perfected from elsewhere, while in the meantime this very "otherness" appears more clearly in the **rational soul**. Indeed, the contemplation of the soul reveals this, along with a certain explanation and "unfolding" <note>original: "euolutione"; the process of a single truth expanding into many complex thoughts</note> united to the things to be known. Yet, the soul is not entirely divided or distant from things; otherwise, it would not be gathered back toward that indivisible unity, nor would it ever have contemplated knowable things from itself and within itself. But because it possesses a "relaxed" union with things and therefore depends continually on that which is thoroughly united, it is said to be "in potentiality" for this very reason. Now, this relaxation appears more clearly in the soul, and from there in the intellect...

# ON THEOPHRASTUS

...through an act <note>original: "ctu"; the end of "perfectu" from the previous page</note> shared by the soul because of a certain subjection. This act depends on a healthy intellect, united by a completely impartible <note>original: "impartibili"; something that cannot be divided into parts</note> limit, and remains suspended there. It is perfected according to its essence by that higher intellect. For this reason, it is said to be **in potentiality** <term>in potentia: having the capacity for something but not yet expressing it</term> according to itself. However, because this too is impartible, and has not yielded to the first intellect through distance or through complete alterity <note>original: "alteritatem"; the state of being "other" or different</note>, it is not perfected as if moved from outside or by another at a specific time. Instead, it perfects itself, even though it achieves this through the limit of that higher intellect. In a second degree, it is this very thing which the higher intellect is in the first degree; it is united according to the union that follows next and looks toward that higher one. Thus, the term "in potentiality" should be understood in the way that properly suits the intellect.

### Chapter eighteen.

### BY MARSILIO. <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), a central figure of the Italian Renaissance who translated and commented on Plato and Neoplatonists.</note>

<margin>1</margin> When the **potential intellect** <term>intellectus possibilis: the mind's ability to receive and process thoughts</term> first exists, it is itself all the **forms** <term>species: the essential mental patterns or archetypes of things</term> according to its essence; therefore, it does not receive them from the agent <note>The "agent intellect" or "active intellect" which provides the "light" for understanding.</note>. Rather, it receives from eternity <note>original: "ab euo"; referring to *aevum*, the state of existence between time and eternity</note> the perfect union of itself to those forms and the union of the forms among themselves. **Reason**, however, receives its union from the intellect in a temporal way. The potential intellect is described as if it were "empty" of forms because, unless it is united to its forms by the agent, it behaves as if it did not have them. For it does not see them unless it is perfectly united to them. Note here and below that the potential intellect assumes perfection from the agent through its own free and independent act, and thus perfects itself. The potential intellect is always joined to the agent and always formed in act. Reason is not always joined to the intellect; similarly, reason is joined to the intellect through its own proper and free act, and from that point, it perfects itself.

We must explain this word "before," however, not according to the condition of time—though it may apply to time within the soul—but certainly not within the participated intellect. Rather, it should be understood according to a certain lowering and a conceived separation, and at the same time according to its own specific property. For this intellect, named "in potentiality" insofar as it is lower and is thought of only in itself, is not yet in act; but insofar as it is coupled with the first intellect, it is thus perfected by it—or rather, according to that higher intellect, it perfects itself from that source.

### Chapter nineteen. Every form separated from matter is far from privation, motion, and division.

Our human intellect always possesses a simple and stable intuition, whereas our **reason** <term>ratio: the logical, step-by-step thinking process</term> possesses **discourse** <term>discursum: the process of moving from one premise to another</term>. Within reason is "science," which is knowledge acquired through this step-by-step discourse. Reason, when it is about to know something, recalls its discourse to the **innate principles** <note>original: "insitas rationes"; literally "grafted" or "inborn" reasons</note>, through which it knows things and is said to possess the known things within itself. Indeed, Plotinus <note>The 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism</note> says that reason, through these innate principles, is all things according to potentiality. ### ON THEOPHRASTUS

...just as it knows material things through their causes as effects. Truly, it knows immaterial things through those same causes, as if they were joined by the same rational principles. Sight, in the act of seeing, merges with the visible object into a single thing. However, the object of sense comes from the outside. Knowledge merges into one with the thing known to a much greater degree, since it does not look outside itself. Even more so, the intellect and the intelligible <term>intelligibile: an object of pure thought, as opposed to a "sensible" object perceived by the senses</term> are entirely one, for they are not pulled apart by motion.

->PRISCIAN<-
<note>Priscian of Lydia, a 6th-century philosopher whose paraphrases of Aristotle and Theophrastus were central to Renaissance thought.</note>

After these things, where Theophrastus explains Aristotle’s claim that separate and immaterial things are identical to the intellect—whereas in material things, each intelligible object exists in a state of potentiality <term>in potentia: having the capacity to be understood, but not yet being actively thought about</term>—he distinguishes such sayings point by point, directs them, and meanwhile raises certain doubts. To grasp these points more clearly, we will first present Aristotle's words briefly and point by point. 

He says that some things exist in matter, while others exist without matter—such as the incorporeal and "separate" substances <term>substantiæ separatæ: entities like the soul or angels that do not require a physical body to exist</term>. In these separate things, the one who understands and the thing understood are the same. For the intellect is not stretched out toward external things, but, remaining within itself, it understands the things themselves. Therefore, it is the same as the things it understands. Indeed, since all immaterial things are indivisible and full of life and knowledge, they are certainly considered to be "intellectual." 

For sensible things <note>physical objects perceived by sight, touch, etc.</note>, because of their material division, must be perceived by others; for the most part, they cannot perceive themselves in any way. But things entirely free from matter, being intelligible, differ from sensible things in this way: they are not torn away from the one who understands, nor are they perfected by external things. Instead, by a perfect reason, they are intelligible of themselves. For this reason, they are both "understanders" and—since they are without parts—they are united without division to the one who understands. Moreover, since they are intelligible through and through, they are rightly united through and through to the intellect. They are not intelligible by accident, but according to their very essence <term>essentia: the fundamental nature that makes a thing what it is</term>. They are perfect according to their essence, and for this reason, existing as perfect according to their own essence, they are surely those very same intelligible things. They are simultaneously "understanders," so that by their own nature they are both things that are understood and the most perfect understanding subjects. 

Furthermore, Aristotle reminds us by the example of knowledge itself that in separate things, that which understands and that which is understood are the same. For he says that speculative knowledge <term>scientia speculativa: theoretical knowledge sought for its own sake</term> and that which is thus knowable are the same. That is, knowledge is not at all stretched out toward external things, but remains...

# ON IMAGINATION AND THE INTELLECT

acting within itself and from within, it exists simultaneously as an observer of things: and that which is thus "knowable" is there the same as the knower. For when we speak of things that can be known—both material things and those perceived by a certain stripping away through abstraction <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, abstraction is the process by which the mind "strips away" physical qualities to understand the universal essence of a thing.</note>—we do not call them "knowable" in the sense that this knowledge observes them as a separate, equal partner, but rather so that it might grasp them from the rational principles implanted in the soul, as if from their causes. Looking toward these things and distinguishing them from their opposite, he says that which is "knowable" in this way—namely, as an equal and joined partner—is that which is eternal and established within the soul itself. This is the same thing as knowledge. Indeed, it has already been said regarding the senses that cognition is not completed there unless the act of knowing coincides with the thing being known. Therefore, knowledge in its active state is the same as the object of knowledge in its active state. But the difference is this: that which is primarily knowable neither comes from the outside, nor is it placed outside the mind, as happens in the case of the senses. If, therefore, knowledge and the knowable are the same, the thinking mind is even more unified with the intellect. Surely the intellect must be considered identical to the things it understands.

## Chapter twenty. ->MARSILIO'S [COMMENTARY]<-
<note>Refers to Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the Florentine philosopher who translated and commented on these works.</note>

<margin>¶</margin>That which is material is not intelligible <term>intelligibile: something that can be grasped by the pure intellect rather than the physical senses</term> in itself, but only insofar as it is freed from material conditions by the intellect. Therefore, it does not become intelligible to itself, but to the intellect that performs the abstraction. Conversely, a thing that is by its nature separated from matter is intelligible in itself, and to its own self. In separate things, therefore, the intellect and the object of understanding coincide in the same form. The intellect knows material things, not through the objects themselves, but through the rational principles innate to the intelligence, as if through their causes. According to Theophrastus and Aristotle, the intellect is immaterial, and yet it is a certain potentiality <term>potentia: the capacity or "power" to become or do something, as opposed to "act" (the thing being done)</term> for material things. This is explained in three ways: two active and one quasi-passive. First, the intellect is a productive power of its own acts or actions regarding material things. Second, not by equality of nature, but through its superior power, it knows material things through its own forms as if through causes. Third, it also knows material things insofar as it is formed by the light of the "active intellect." Immaterial things are always naturally present to the intellect. Material things, however, become present insofar as they are resolved from matter by the intellect. Knowledge in its active state becomes the same as the thing known in its active state, even within the discourse of reason itself. Much more so, in the very state of intelligence, the one who understands and that which is understood are the same. Indeed, the intellect itself is, according to its essence, those very forms which are understood by it. Intel—

<meta>This page continues the technical exploration of Neoplatonic epistemology, specifically focusing on the hierarchy of the intellect and how it perceives different classes of reality. It builds on the previous discussion regarding the unity of the knower and the known, now distinguishing between the active intellect and the levels of the possible intellect.</meta>

[The intel]lect recognizes immaterial things as if they were conjoined to it. <note>In this context, "conjoined" means the mind and the object of thought are of the same substance and perfectly united.</note> However, it perceives material things as inferior, insofar as it notices the causes of those forms—which it possesses within itself—as the origins of material things. The **active intellect** <note>original: "Intellectus agens"; the part of the mind that actively produces thought or illuminates the "possible" intellect.</note> is in no way "made." The **first possible intellect** <note>original: "intellectus possibilis ... primus"; the highest receptive part of the human soul that is always in contact with divine truth.</note> within us is never in the process of "being made," but is "always having been made"—that is, it is constantly formed by the active intellect. The **second possible intellect** within us—which is to say, our **reason**—is "always being made"; that is, it is formed in action daily through the higher intellect and through its own discursive movement toward that higher power; or at least, it brings forth innate forms into active thought from a state of rest. This opinion concerning the threefold intellect and a certain eternal act of intelligence within us is frequently approved by **Plotinus** and **Iamblichus** <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) and Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) were foundational philosophers of Neoplatonism.</note>.
<margin>I</margin>

### OF PRISCIAN.
<note>Priscian of Lydia was a 6th-century philosopher whose commentary on Theophrastus is a primary source for this text.</note>

<margin>c</margin>**S**ince these things are so, he [Theophrastus] rightly signified the same point with these words in the appropriate middle of the discussion: "Why then," he asks, "do we not always think, since both the **knower** and the **known** are within us?" For both are the same thing. This, therefore, we must consider as a priority and with all our strength: in those things separated from matter, the knower and the known are the same, just as we said above. But in those things that exist with matter, each of the knowable things exists only "in potential" <note>original: "in potentia"; meaning they are not actually "thoughts" until a mind processes them.</note>. For material things are not knowable in their own right, nor according to their essence; they do not share the same rank as the intellect, nor are they known as if conjoined to it. How then are they called "knowable in potential"? For if they are such in potential, they will also be knowable "in act" at some point. They will certainly be so at some point, but perhaps not as things conjoined to the mind; rather, they will be known according to their causes which are placed within the intellect. And because they share the same properties as their causes, they too are called "knowable," but only by a certain potential, because he who understands them stands above them, and they are understood by him according to a surpassing cause. They are not knowable to themselves or by themselves, for they do not understand themselves. Wherefore he next introduces this: "In those things, therefore, there is no intellect"—namely, in material things. Therefore, they are not knowable to themselves or by themselves, because these things are indeed material, while the intellect exists as immaterial. For (as he says) the intellect of such things is itself the potentiality without matter. Of these things, the statement "without matter" shows the nature of the intellect to be entirely devoid of matter. But the intellect of material things is "in potential," either as the cause of actions—for so **Plutarch** <note>Likely Plutarch of Athens (d. 431 AD), a Neoplatonist who taught Proclus, rather than the more famous biographer.</note> explains it—or as something not conjoined, but understanding these things by a certain more eminent condition. This is because it contemplates these things from their cause; or the intellect itself in potential is also the potentiality of such things, as if also understanding these according to perfection granted by a higher [power...]

Therefore, the intellect is not found within material things, but the **object of thought** <note>original: "intelligibile"; that which is capable of being understood by the mind, as opposed to "sensible" things perceived by the body.</note> is found within the intellect; you will, however, distinguish this as being articulated. **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BC) was Aristotle’s successor and a key figure in developing the theory of the mind.</note> adds the following: but when they [material things] come to be and are understood, then the intellect will possess them. And it is that very thing which is said to be the "intelligible things." Material things, however, are present to the intellect only when they are understood; they are not understood by it as if they were of the same rank or order. For material things are never truly joined with the **immaterial intellect**, from which they might receive a union. But when the intellect perceives the things within itself—not merely as themselves, but as the **causes of material things**—then material things are also present to the intellect according to their cause. I would not assert, however, that these things were said concerning the intellect when considered "in act." For that intellect is not a mere potentiality, nor can it ever become so.

# ON THEOPHRASTUS

...the lusts of the body, all of which are fleeting and perishable; instead, they set out with a certain common zeal and with the whole fire of the mind to grasp and cultivate the one stable virtue of the soul. Our **Plato**, that master and leader of all philosophers, wished for this virtue of the soul to be called **wisdom**. Indeed, he considered wisdom to be the knowledge of divine things. Furthermore, in his books *On the Republic*, he demonstrates that divine things can become known to our mind in no other way than by God illuminating us, just as the forms of bodies are seen by the eyes in no other way than by the sun illuminating the eyes.

Therefore, it is God Himself whom we desire to see: He who illuminates the sharp edge of the mind <note>original: "acie mentis"; a common philosophical metaphor for the highest, most piercing part of the human intellect.</note> so that we may perceive, and who finally shows Himself to the clear mind. In showing Himself, He delights us; likewise, God is for us the way, the truth, and the life. <note>original: "via... et veritas... et vita"; a reference to the Gospel of John 14:6, which Ficino here integrates into a Platonic framework to show that the "God of the philosophers" and the "God of the Christians" are the same.</note> He is the **Way**, because He turns, leads, and carries us to Himself by His own rays. He is the **Truth**, because He shows Himself as true to us when we have turned toward Him. Finally, He is the **Life**, because He perpetually feeds and delights our soul—the spectator of Himself—with that blessed vision.

Therefore, all who desire to taste the sweetest waters of wisdom must thirst for this perennial fountain. It is necessary, indeed, that all who desire to obtain virtue of the soul pursue wisdom; from which it follows that whoever resolves to cultivate their own soul is compelled to worship God. Previously, we defined those as mutual friends who strive toward virtue with a similar and equal zeal, and who cultivate their souls with mutual favor. The cultivation of the soul consists of virtue alone. Virtue is wisdom, and wisdom is the knowledge of divine things; divine light grants us knowledge of this kind.

Thus, the cultivation of the soul is the worship of God Himself. Therefore, since friendship strives by the agreement of two people to cultivate the soul through virtue, it seems to be nothing other than the highest harmony of two souls in worshipping God. Moreover, whoever worships God with a pious mind is loved by God. For this reason, there are necessarily always **three friends**, not just two: namely, two human beings and one God. God, I say—**Jupiter the Hospitable**, **Jupiter the Friendly**, **Jupiter the Savior** of human life—whom Plato always worshipped and Socrates always honored. He is the leader of human life; He unites us as one; He is the indissoluble knot of friendship and its perpetual guardian.

### Chapter Three: The philosopher is engaged in three things: namely, in the contemplation of things, in moral action, and in the skill of discourse.

Plato intended for the philosopher's study to focus chiefly on three areas: the speculation of things, the action of virtues, and the consideration of speech. Thus, the knowledge of things is called **contemplative**; the study of morals is **active**; and the care of speech is **dialectic**.

Dialectic, in turn, is divided into many species: division, definition, induction, and reasoning. This reasoning is further divided into:
*   **Demonstration**, which is necessary reasoning;
*   **Ostension**, which is called probable reasoning;
*   **Rhetorical enthymeme** <note>original: "enthymema"; a logical argument where one premise is implied rather than stated</note>, that is, a cautious thought, which is called imperfect reasoning;
*   And finally, **sophisms**, to which the true philosopher will apply effort—not because he approves of them as primary, but because he deems them occasionally necessary <note>The philosopher studies fallacies (sophisms) to avoid being deceived by them.</note>.

Furthermore, of that philosophy which is concerned with action, the first part cares for the **morals** of the person himself. The second governs the **household**, and the last protects the **state** <note>original: "rempu." for "rempublicam"</note>. The first is called **moral** <term>moral: here referring to individual ethics</term>, the second **domestic**, and the third **civil**.

In that philosophy which pursues contemplation, one part investigates immobile and divine things and the first causes of things, which we call **theology**. Another part observes the movement of the stars, the circuits and returns of the celestial bodies, and the order of the world, which is named **natural knowledge**. This is followed by **mathematics**, which contains geometry and arithmetic. Since philosophy is distributed into these three main species—contemplative, active, and dialectic—we must first treat dialectic itself, what Plato thought of it, and specifically of the **judicatory** faculty first.

### Chapter Four: Concerning the faculty of judgment, and the powers of the soul pertaining to judgment.

Since there is something which judges and something which is judged, it is necessary that something also arises from both, which we can properly call **judgment**. Thus, the judgment itself is named **judicatory**; more commonly, however, that which judges is also called such. Furthermore, that which judges appears to be twofold: one *by which* <note>original: "a quo"</note> and the other *through which* <note>original: "per quod"</note> judgment is made. The former is our **intellect**, while the latter is a **natural organ**; it judges true things in the first place, and false things in the second. Nor is this anything other than **natural reason**. If we wish to explain this even more clearly: the judge should be called the **philosopher**, by whom the things themselves are judged; likewise, the judge is **reason**, through which the truth is also judged, which indeed we have called the "organ" <term>organum: the tool or instrument of thought</term>.

# ALCINOUS

Reason <term>original: "ratio"; the faculty of the mind that allows for logical thought</term> is twofold: one is entirely beyond our grasp and true, while the other is infallible regarding the knowledge of things. The first belongs to God and is not at all for man; the second is suitable for man. But this human reason is also twofold: one part looks toward things that can be understood by the mind <note>original: "intelligibilia"; abstract concepts or forms like "Justice" or "Circle"</note>, the other toward things that can be perceived by the senses <note>original: "sensibilia"; physical objects like a stone or a tree</note>. The first is called **knowledge** <term>original: "scientia"; certain, unchanging understanding</term>, and the second is called **opinion** <term>original: "opinio"; belief that may be true but lacks the certainty of proof</term>. Knowledge possesses stability, as it is concerned with stable things; opinion possesses only likelihood and imagination, since it tends toward things that are subject to change. Indeed, the principles of knowledge regarding the intelligible, and of opinion regarding the sensible, are intellection <term>original: "intellectio"; the direct grasping of a truth by the mind</term> and sensation.

Sensation is certainly an affection of the soul through the body, first announcing the capacity to receive an impression; afterwards, when the forms of things are impressed upon the soul through the sense organs, it remains so firm and indelible that its preservation is called **memory**.

Opinion, however, is a weaving together of memory and sensation. For when a certain sensible thing first meets us, a sensation is produced in us by it, and from that sensation comes memory. When the same thing is presented to us again, we join the preceding memory with the following sensation, and in these moments we say: "Socrates," "a horse," "fire," and other such things. This is called **opinion** when we combine a preceding memory with a recent sensation. Whenever these gathered elements harmonize with one another, a true opinion exists; if they clash, the opinion is false. 

For example, if someone keeps the form of Socrates in their memory but happens upon Plato, and thinks because of a certain resemblance that they are meeting Socrates again, they later draw the sensation of Plato into their memory of Socrates. Because they apply the sensation of Plato to the memory of Socrates, a false opinion results. Plato compares that in which sensation and memory occur to an image in a **wax tablet** <note>A famous Platonic metaphor from the "Theaetetus": the mind as a block of wax where experiences leave imprints.</note>. 

But when the soul, reshaping through thought the opinion conceived via sensation and memory, looks back at these as if at the original sources from which they flowed, Plato calls this a certain "painting," and also a mental image or **phantasia**. He calls **thought** <term>original: "cogitatio"</term> the internal discourse and reasoning of the mind with itself, while **speech** is the outflow from thought through the mouth along with articulated sound.

**Intellection** is the operation of the intellect as it contemplates primary intelligible things. This, too, appears to be twofold. One occurs before the soul descends into the body, for then it gazes upon the intelligible forms themselves. The other occurs after the soul has been immersed in this body. Of these, the first is properly called "intellection" itself; the second, in place of intellection, is now called **natural intelligence**, being a form of intellection residing within the soul. Whenever we call intellection the "principle of knowledge," we do not mean the second kind we just proposed, but rather that which belongs to the soul when it is released from the body, which indeed, as we have said...
