### Chapter 27. How virtue is voluntary, but wickedness is involuntary.

Since virtue is something that remains within our own power and is not coerced, it is of such a nature that it is especially voluntary. Indeed, it would not be considered worthy of praise if it occurred either by nature or by divine chance. It follows, then, that virtue exists as a voluntary act, arising through a certain fervent, noble, and perpetual disposition. From this, it is finally concluded that because virtue is voluntary, **wickedness** <note>original: "prauitatem"</note> must be involuntary. For who would ever willingly choose the ultimate evil for the most excellent part of themselves <note>referring to the soul</note>? 

If anyone falls into vice, they are inclined toward it not as an evil, but rather as if it were a good. And if someone rushes into evil, they are entirely deceived, acting so as to avoid a greater evil through a lesser one. In this way, they are driven involuntarily. For it cannot happen that someone turns toward evils with the intention of desiring them for their own sake, without being carried along by some hope of good or fear of a greater evil. For this reason, all things that a wicked man does are involuntary. Since **injustice** <note>original: "iniusticia"</note> is involuntary, it follows even more so that acting unjustly is involuntary, insofar as the actual operation of a vice is worse than the idle habit of it. 

Yet, although crimes are involuntary, criminal men must still be punished. There must also be different kinds of punishments, just as the damages inflicted through injury are different. Furthermore, that which is involuntary consists of a certain ignorance or **disturbance** <note>original: "perturbatione"; a passion or emotion that clouds judgment</note>. These can certainly be shaken off through reason, social custom, and diligent effort.

### Chapter 28. On injustice and the distinction of the passions.

Injustice is so great an evil that it is far better to suffer an injury than to inflict one. For to affect someone with an injury is the work of a wicked man, while to be affected by an injury is a **passive weakness** <note>original: "imbecillis passio"; a state of being acted upon rather than acting.</note>. Both are indeed shameful. However, to inflict an injury is worse to the degree that it is more shameful. 

Indeed, it is worthwhile to submit oneself voluntarily to a judge when one has been unjust, just as one commits oneself to a doctor when ill. For every punishment is a kind of medicine for the wandering soul. Since many of the virtues are concerned with the regulation of the **passions** <note>original: "affectus"; emotions or internal movements</note>, these passions themselves must now be distinguished. 

A passion is a movement of the soul without reason, caused by the perception of some good or evil. It is called an "irrational movement" because neither judgments nor opinions are passions; rather, passions are movements of the irrational parts of the soul. These movements occur in the part of the soul devoid of reason; and although they are our own doing, they are nevertheless not entirely within our power. Often, therefore...

-># ON IMAGINATION AND THE INTELLECT <note>original: "DE PHANTASIA ET INTELLECTV"; while the header mentions Phantasia (imagination) and Intellect, the text of this page focuses on the "perturbationes" or passions of the soul.</note><-

...tice, <note>original: "-tur"; completing the word or phrase from the previous page concerning "iniustitia" (injustice).</note> involuntary movements of this kind arise in us, and our voluntary ones resist them. For it sometimes happens that even when we recognize that the things we encounter are neither harsh nor sweet, neither to be sought after nor even to be feared, we are nevertheless pulled along by them. We would surely never suffer this if **disturbances** <note>original: "perturbationes"; often translated as "passions" or "emotions" in a Platonic/Stoic context, referring to movements of the irrational soul.</note> were the same as judgments. For we reject judgments whenever we refute them through deliberation, whether we do so properly or not.

Furthermore, it is added in the definition that [these movements occur] for the sake of some good or evil. For an **affect** <note>original: "affectus"; a general term for a feeling or state of mind.</note> is not stirred up by an indifferent encounter. From the fact that something appears either good or evil, all disturbances are born. If a good seems to be present, we are flooded with pleasure; if we desire it to be, [we feel longing]. Conversely, when an evil appears present, we grieve; if it is in the future, we fear.

There are two simple and principal emotions: namely, **pleasure** and **pain**. The others are composed of these as if from certain elements. We should not count fear and longing among the simple and principal ones. For one who fears is not entirely deprived of pleasure; indeed, if he utterly despaired of the repulsion or mitigation of evils, he would no longer fear, but rather, afflicted by a sharper passion, he would grieve rather than fear. But he who desires, insofar as he hopes for the achievement of what he seeks, is in a certain way delighted. Yet, when he lacks certain hope, he is distressed. If longing and fear are not at all simple, it will be granted without controversy that none of the remaining emotions is simple either—such as anger, emulation, and others of this sort. In these, pleasure and pain are observed as if in a compound.

Furthermore, some disturbances are **wild**, while others are **domestic**. Domestic ones are those which exist in humans according to nature. As long as these maintain a **measure** <note>original: "modum"; referring to the "Golden Mean" where emotions are balanced rather than suppressed.</note>, they are necessary and appropriate. But when they are carried beyond measure, they surely fall into fault. Of this kind are pleasure, pain, anger, pity, and shame. For it is fitting for humans to be delighted by things that happen according to nature, to grieve at their opposites, and anger is indeed necessary for repelling and avenging injury. **Pity** <note>original: "misericordia"</note> is characteristic of humanity and charity. **Shame** <note>original: "verecundia"</note> provokes us to turn away from disgraceful things.

But wild and savage disturbances are produced contrary to human nature from a perversion of life and the worst habits. Of this kind are excessive laughter, exultation in the misfortunes of others <note>The Greek concept of "epichairekakia," often translated as "Schadenfreude."</note>, and hatred of the human race. These, whether they are vehement and intense or relaxed, or however they may be, always go astray and never attain any praiseworthy moderation. Concerning pleasure and pain, **Plato** says this: that these disturbances are naturally excited in us from our very origin.

<meta>This page continues the translation of Alcinous's "Handbook of Platonism." The previous page concluded with a discussion of the "passions" or disturbances of the soul, specifically focusing on how they arise from judgments about good and evil. This page continues that classification by examining the nature of pleasure and its relationship to our natural state, before transitioning into a famous Platonic defense of free will within the framework of fate.</meta>

-># ALCINOUS<-

...[pain] indeed happens to those who are moved contrary to nature, while pleasure <note>original: "uoluptatẽ"</note> happens to those who are restored to their own nature. For he <note>Alcinous refers to Plato here, as this is a summary of Platonic doctrine.</note> considers the natural state of man to be a middle ground between pleasure and pain, occurring while one is moved by neither; we live the majority of our time in this state. He also relates many species of pleasures: some through the body, and some through the soul. Furthermore, among pleasures, some are mixed with pain, while others are pure. Some occur through memory based on hope, others are stirred up in the moment. There are also some that are shameful and others that are honorable; the former are taken up from lack of self-control and from injustice, while the latter arise from temperance or some other good—such as that joy perceived from the exercise of the virtues. 

Since the nature of most pleasures is shameful, he judges that it should by no means be argued whether pleasure can be a good in a simple and absolute sense. For it seems to be a thin and empty thing, whose nature is a **handmaiden** <note>original: "pedissequa"; literally a female servant who follows her mistress, implying that pleasure is a byproduct that follows an action rather than a primary goal.</note> and a successor to something else, not participating in its own principal substance. It is also encountered in opposition to its contrary, being always mixed with pain; these things would certainly never happen if pleasure could be an absolute good and pain an absolute evil.

### Chapter 29. Concerning Fate and Free Will.

Now, regarding fate <note>original: "fatum"</note>, these are some of the views held by Plato. He says that all things are *in* fate, <margin>d.</margin> but not all things are *decreed* by fate. For he does not speak of fate as being like those laws that say, "this man will do such things, and this man will suffer such things." For then there would be an infinite progression, since those who are born are infinite, as are the countless things that happen to them afterward. Furthermore, no freedom would remain, and praise and blame would be entirely abolished. 

Rather, he pronounces fate in this way: "Whatever soul chooses such a life and commits certain acts of this kind, consequently it will suffer such things." Therefore, the soul is free, and it is placed within its own **choice** <note>original: "arbitrio"; the power of the will to decide.</note> either to act or not to act, nor is it forced to do this by anyone. However, that which follows the action will be fulfilled by fate itself. 

Just as from the fact that Paris will kidnap Helen—which indeed will be within his power of choice—it will follow that the Greeks will fight over Helen. So too Apollo foretold to Laius himself: "If you beget a son, the one born will kill you." In the law [of fate], both Laius and the begetting of a son are included together. What is established by fate is that which follows the begetting of a son. 

But the nature of the **possible** <note>original: "possibile"; referring to things that may or may not happen.</note> itself falls in the middle between the false and the true; and by its own nature, it is undefined. The free power of the rational soul is carried along from every side. But that which is brought about by us choosing is immediately either true or false. This differs greatly from that which is in **potency** <term>potency: the capacity or potential for something to exist or happen, as opposed to its actual realization</term>—that is, what will eventually be in habit and in act. For "potency" signifies a certain faculty and aptitude for things that have not yet attained their order...

...just as a boy is a grammarian, a flute-player, or a scribe by a certain potentiality, and he will then be established in the stable habit of one or two of these when he has learned and obtained one of those habits. ### Chapter 30. On goods, and the highest good, and the virtues.

<margin>d</margin> **Next**, let us briefly touch upon what Plato held regarding morals. He believed that the most venerable and supreme good <note>original: "summum bonum"</note> could neither be easily found, nor once found, could it be safely revealed to just anyone. Therefore, he communicated the contemplation of this highest good only to a very few, and indeed to those most familiar and rightly chosen. Yet, if anyone examines his books diligently, they will find that he placed our human good in the very contemplation of the first good. This good one may call both God and the Primary Mind. For he wished all things that are called "good" by men to be named so for the reason that they participate in some way in the first good itself. Just as all things that are sweet or hot obtain such a name by a certain participation in the "first sweet" or "first hot." Among those things that are within us, however, he held that only the mind and reason attain a likeness to the good itself. For this reason, our good is called by him something beautiful, venerable, divine, lovable, proportionate, and "blessedness." 

Regarding those things that are commonly called goods—such as health, beauty, strength, as well as riches and high honors—he held that none of these are truly good unless they happen to be used for virtue. For if these are separated from virtue itself, they possess only the status of "matter" <note>original: "materiae sortem"; meaning they are the raw materials or tools that are morally neutral in themselves.</note> and are undoubtedly evils to those who use them badly. Nevertheless, Plato sometimes calls these things "mortal goods." However, he maintains that happiness <note>original: "Beatitudinem"</note> is by no means found in "good men" <note>meaning those merely possessing worldly goods</note> but in the divine and holy. Therefore, he proclaims that the souls of legitimate philosophers are filled with certain great and admirable goods. And after the death of the mortal body, they feast upon divine banquets and wander together with the gods through the "field of truth." They deserve this most of all because throughout their entire lives they burned with a desire for divine knowledge and cherished it above all other things as something most precious. By the gift of this knowledge, the "eye of their mind" <note>original: "mentis illorum... oculus"</note>—once blinded but now awakened and coming back to life—is more excellent than countless bodily eyes; it makes them masters of the entire rational nature. For indeed igno... <margin><image-desc>A cross-like symbol consisting of a vertical line intersected by two horizontal bars.</image-desc></margin>

# ALCINOVS

...[comparing] wandering men to those who have spent their entire lives in a certain subterranean cave, where they have never looked upon the bright light of the sun, but only upon the small and empty shadows of those bodies which we see above the earth. While they gazed at these, they thought they were seeing real bodies. For just as it is natural for these people, if they ever emerge from the darkness into the light, to find fault with everything they had seen before—and even more so with themselves, as if they had been utterly deceived—so too is it reasonable for those who betake themselves from the darkness of this life to divine things to despise what they once held in the highest esteem, and to love only the blessed contemplation <note>original: "speculationem"; in this context, it refers to intellectual or mystical vision rather than guesswork.</note> of divine matters. From this, it follows that we must say the "good" itself consists solely in the knowledge of the First <note>original: "scientia primi"; referring to the First Principle or God.</note>, which is also the Beautiful; this has been shown through all of Plato's books, yet it is always asserted according to a specific participation in that Good.

In the first book of the *Laws*, he speaks in this way: "There are indeed two kinds of goods, namely human and divine," and so forth. Moreover, if anything is possessed without virtue and is devoid of the essence of the First, it is called "good" only by those who are ignorant; Plato testifies in the *Euthydemus* that for one who possesses such things, they are actually a great evil.

That he considers the virtues to be chosen for their own sake is clear from the fact that only the beautiful and the honorable <note>original: "pulchrum honestūmq"; a translation of the Greek *kalon k'agathon*, referring to moral excellence.</note> is judged to be good. This is demonstrated in many of his dialogues, but especially in those he published *On the Republic*. For this reason, he considers the man who has attained the knowledge of God to be the most fortunate and most blessed. He does not call him blessed for the sake of the honors that follow such a man, nor for the sake of any other reward; rather, even if he remains hidden from all men, and even if those things commonly thought to be evils—such as infamy, exile, and death—should befall him, he will nonetheless be blessed.

Conversely, a man without the knowledge of God, even if he possesses everything the common people proclaim as "goods"—wealth, power, health, strength, and beauty—he considers to be in no way more blessed. To all of these points, he introduced a consistent and harmonious end: that is, to become **like God** <note>original: "dei similem fieri"; the Platonic doctrine of *homoiosis theoi*.</note>, as far as the human race can attain it. 

He attempts to establish this in various ways. Sometimes he says the "likeness to God" consists in being wise, just, and holy, as he declares in the *Theaetetus*. Whence he warns that we must strive to flee from here to divine things as quickly as possible; but this "flight" <note>original: "fuga"; a reference to *Theaetetus* 176a-b regarding the escape from earthly evils.</note> is the likeness to God, and the likeness to God is to become wise, just, and holy. Sometimes he also demonstrates that we can become like God through justice alone, as in the final book of the *Republic*. For he says that no one is ever despised by God who strives to become just, and through the duty of virtue itself, to render himself as like to God as possible. In the *Phaedo*, however, he asserts that the likeness to God is acquired through temperance and justice, saying: "Are they not blessed and holy, and [placed] in the best

Care for the body must also be maintained through gymnastics, by which one is made more ready for the works of both peace and war.

### Chapter 31. The definition and distinction of virtue.

Since virtue is a certain divine treasure, it is the perfect and best disposition of the soul, rendering a person orderly, harmonious, and stable, both in action and in speech, toward themselves and toward others. Of the virtues, some concern the rational part of the soul, while others concern the part devoid of reason. For since the nature of the rational part is one thing, the power of anger <note>The "irascible" part of the soul in Platonic psychology.</note> another, and the power of desire yet another, there must also be different perfections for each. Hence, <term>Prudence</term> <note>Latin: "prudentia"; the virtue of the rational part of the soul, often called practical wisdom.</note> pertains to the first; <term>Fortitude</term> <note>Latin: "fortitudo"; courage, the virtue of the spirited or angry part of the soul.</note> to the second; and <term>Temperance</term> <note>Latin: "temperantia"; self-control, the virtue of the desiring part of the soul.</note> to the last. And Prudence is the knowledge of things good, evil, and those which are neither. Temperance is the order regarding pleasures and lusts, making them obedient to reason. When we attribute "order" and "obedience" to temperance, we wish it to be understood that it is a certain power by which the desires become followers of their natural master [reason]. # ALCINOUS

...of a difficult or easy preservation—that is, the conserving and executive power of a lawful and rational purpose. Justice is a certain harmony of all the parts of the soul. Indeed, it is a certain force through which the three powers of the soul <note>Plato divided the soul into the Rational, the Spirited (emotional), and the Appetitive (desire-driven) parts.</note> harmonize with one another, and each performs its own duty according to its dignity. Thus, justice is a kind of common and complete perfection of these three virtues—prudence, fortitude, and temperance—while reason leads and commands, and the remaining parts stay subject and obedient to the duty of their higher nature. Therefore, it must be thought that the virtues follow one another in a certain interlinking <note>original: "coniugatione"; this refers to the Stoic and Platonic idea that the virtues are inseparable; if you truly have one, you have them all.</note>. For since fortitude is the preservation of lawful instruction, it will be the preserver of right reason. Moreover, right reason proceeds from prudence. Furthermore, prudence stands with fortitude, for it is the knowledge of good things; no one can discern the good while he is blinded by fear and the disturbances that follow it. In the same way, the prudent man has no dealings with intemperance. Generally, whoever, stirred by disturbance, performs anything contrary to reason, always wanders astray because of ignorance. Prudence, however, administers personal, domestic, and public affairs. And as it governs the state, it is called "civil science," of which there are two duties: to establish laws and to execute those that have been established. <margin><unclear>nomothetike</unclear></margin> The first is <term>legislative</term> <note>original Greek: νομοθετικὴ (nomothetike); the art of law-making.</note>, that is, the power of making laws; <margin><unclear>dikastike</unclear></margin> the second is called <term>judicial</term> <note>original Greek: δικαστικὴ (dikastike); the art of judging and administering the law.</note>, that is, the power of judging. Finally, civil expertise considers those things which pertain to peace and to war; and in this, among many other things, it especially considers whether a war should be entered into or rather refused.

### Chapter 32. On Friendship.

<margin><unclear>ali...</unclear></margin> Friendship is properly nothing other than mutual benevolence. This exists when each desires the good for the other just as much as for themselves. <margin><unclear>...y...</unclear></margin> This equality is preserved in no other way than through a similarity of character. For "like is a friend to like" <note>A common Greek proverb cited by Plato in the *Lysis* and the *Gorgias*.</note> and to the moderate. Those who are immoderate can agree neither with one another nor with the moderate. Certain other things are also called friendships, though they are not truly so, but are in some way colored by virtue. Such is the natural benevolence of parents toward children and of kinsmen toward one another; and also that which is called civil and rhetorical friendship. These indeed do not always have a reciprocity of benevolence. Furthermore, a certain species of friendship is the affection of love. Honorable love belongs to the noble soul; base love to the lowly; and middle love to the middle soul. Indeed, just as there are three dispositions of the rational soul—namely, good, bad, and middle—so there are three effects of love, differing from one another in kind. That there are three loves is shown by their different ends. Base love is for the pleasure of the body alone...

...[the third kind] follows pleasure. And so it is a passion of beasts <note>original: "brutorum"; referring to non-rational animals who act on instinct rather than reason.</note>. The noble type, however, looks at the bare soul, prompt toward the duties of virtue. The middle type loves both the beauty of the body and the beauty of the soul. And that type which is chosen is neither entirely honest nor dishonest. For this reason, it is more fitting to call a love that declines toward the body in some part a **daemon** <note>In Platonic thought, a "daemon" is a mediating spirit between humans and gods, neither fully divine nor fully mortal.</note> rather than a god; it is never submerged in earthly bodies, but carries divine things to humans and human things back to the gods. Since the movement of love is distributed among the three forms <note>original: "ideas"</note> we have mentioned, the love of a good man, being devoid of passion, is in some way skillful; thus, it resides in the irrational part of the soul, and its thoughts are of this kind: to discern who, by the gifts of the soul, is worthy of goodwill, and to win him over. Then, he praises and approves the thoughts and desires of the one he loves if they are noble and carried toward the good with a certain fervor of soul. But if they are the opposite, he will neither agree with him nor charm him with sweet words and compliance, but will rather deter him and teach him that he should by no means live in such a way until he becomes better. He will always promise and provide those things by which the one he loves, through exercise, may turn out for the best. Finally, the goal of this is that friendship may be formed from love.

### Chapter xxxiii. On the types of the Republic

<margin>r</margin> He [Plato] says that certain republics <note>The Latin term "res publica" refers to the state or the organized political community.</note> must be presupposed, which he taught in his books on the *Republic*. For in these, he described the first as harmonious and the second as distrustful, inquiring which of these were superior and in what way they were established. There is also in his work a republic modeled after the division of the soul, divided into three members: the **guardians**, the **helpers**, and the **craftsmen**. To the first, he assigns deliberation and leadership. To the second, defense when needed, whom he compares to "anger" <note>original: "iracundiae"; this refers to the "spirited" or emotional part of the soul (thymos) that acts as an ally to reason.</note>, as they bring aid to reason. To the last, he assigns the arts and other services. He considers that the leaders should be **philosophers** and devoted to the contemplation of the Good itself. For only in this way will they govern all things correctly, since the human race will never cease from evils unless either philosophers rule or those who dominate become philosophers through some divine fate. For the republic is administered best and with justice when each portion of the city performs its own duty: the leaders of the people deliberate and decide; the military obey and protect them; and the rest willingly obey their superiors. He introduced the forms of the republic: first, the **government of the best** (aristocracy), when the best men are in charge; second, the **ambitious** (timocracy), in which men inflated with pride dominate; third, the **popular** (democracy).

### Chapter XXXIIII. On the Sophist.

Thus far, it has been said what kind of man the philosopher is. The **Sophist**, however, differs from the philosopher both in his method and his material. In method, he follows the wages of young men <note>Sophists were famous—and often criticized—for being the first to charge high fees for education.</note>, and prefers to seem good and famous rather than to actually be so. In material, however, the philosopher is concerned with those things which are always the same and behave in the same way <note>The eternal "Forms" or "Ideas."</note>. The Sophist contends and labors around that which "is" least of all <note>original: "id quod minime est"; referring to the realm of appearance and non-being.</note>, retreating into a province that is difficult to see because of its darkness. For to "that which is," "that which is not" is by no means opposed as a direct contrary. For the latter [absolute non-existence] neither exists, nor shares in any substance, nor can even be understood. If anyone were forced to utter or think it, he would wander and waver, since he would be fighting against and distrusting himself. 

But "that which is not," in terms of how the spoken word is heard, is certainly not a bare negation of being, but carries a certain suspicion and insinuation of **something else** <note>original: "alterius"; referring to the Platonic category of "The Other" or "Difference."</note>, which in some way accompanies "that which is." Unless things themselves also participated in "that which is not," they would in no way be distinguished from one another. Now, however, there are as many ways "that which is not" is expressed as there are things that exist. For "that which is not" is simply not any *one* of those things that exist.

### Regarding the final section: On the Epilogues.

Let these things suffice as a certain introduction to the Platonic discipline. Some things have been treated in their proper order; some have been introduced scattered about without a fixed order. Nevertheless, they have been handed down in such a way that by following these traces, one may also hunt down the remaining thoughts of Plato.

->THE END OF ALCINOI.<-

### The Book of Speusippus, Disciple of Plato, on the Definitions of Plato.

**Eternal**, that which has existed through all time, both previously and now, and is subject to no corruption. ¶ **God**, a living being, immortal through himself, sufficient for happiness, an eternal essence, the cause of the Good itself. ¶ **Generation** <note>original: "Generatio"; in a Platonic sense, this refers to "becoming" or the process of coming into existence, as opposed to eternal being.</note>, motion toward essence, the receiving of essence, the process into being. ¶ **Sun**, celestial fire, which alone can be seen by the same observers from its rising to its setting; an eternal living thing, an animated star, diurnal, and the greatest. ¶ **Time**, the motion of the sun, the measure of progression. ¶ **Day**, the journey of the sun from its rising to its setting, a light contrary to night. ¶ **Dawn**, the first beginning of the day, the first light from the sun. ¶ **Midday**, the time in which the shadows of bodies are at their shortest. ¶ **Sunset**, the end of the day. ¶ **Night**, a shadow contrary to day, the privation of the sun. ¶ **Fortune** <note>original: "Fortuna"; often implying "luck" or "chance."</note>, a motion from the hidden to the hidden, the cause of a successful action by a certain chance. ¶ **Old Age**, the decrease of life caused by time. ¶ **Wind**, the agitation of air around the earth. ¶ **Air**, the element whose changes of place are all according to nature. ¶ **Heaven**, a body embracing all bodies except for the supreme air <note>original: "supremum aerem"; referring to the "aether," the fifth element believed to occupy the highest regions of the universe.</note> itself. ¶ **Soul**, that which moves itself, the cause of vital motion for living things. ¶ **Power**, that which is effective through itself. ¶ **Sight**, the habit or state by which bodies are discerned. ¶ **Bone** <note>original: "Os"; here meaning bone rather than mouth. This definition draws from Plato’s *Timaeus*, where bone is described as being formed from marrow hardened by fire and cooled.</note>, marrow consolidated by heat. ¶ **Element**, that from which things are composed, and into which composed things are dissolved. ¶ **Virtue**, the best disposition or habit of a mortal living thing, praiseworthy through itself; the habit according to which that which possesses it is called good. ¶ **Fellowship** <note>original: "Communio"; here meaning civic community or commonality.</note>, the just institution of laws, through which that which is endowed with it is called upright; a habit providing harmony. ¶ **Prudence** <note>original: "Prudentia"; representing the Greek *phronesis* or practical wisdom.</note>, a power which leads through itself to human happiness; the science of good and evil, providing a happy disposition, by which we judge what must be done and what must not. ¶ **Justice**, the agreement of the soul with itself, and the mutual order of its parts toward one another; a habit distributing to each according to their dignity; a habit by which he who is endowed with it always chooses what seems just; a habit obedient to the laws of life; communicative equality; a habit which always obeys right laws. ¶ **Temperance**, the moderation of the soul regarding natural desires and pleasures; the composition and order of the soul toward natural pleasures and pains; the harmony of the soul for commanding and obeying; the voluntary action of those things which are according to nature; the conversation of the rational soul regarding what is honorable and what is base; the habit by which one chooses what is becoming...

### Speusippus

...we [gather] and preserve. ¶ **Fortitude**, an intrepid habit of the soul, a military boldness, and a skill in those matters which pertain to war; the constancy of the soul against those things that are usually terrifying. Boldness as the handmaid of prudence. Fearlessness in the expectation of death. A disposition preserving a rational purpose in dangers. A strength resisting danger, and a vigor enduring all things for the sake of virtue. The perseverance of the soul in those things which, according to right reason, seem worthy to be dared or feared. The observance of what reason dictates in terrifying matters. Skill in military affairs, and a habit remaining immovable within the law. ¶ **Constancy**, the power of bearing the trouble following from what right reason has commanded; a power that is never cast down from the purpose of reason. ¶ **Sufficiency**, the perfect possession of goods, a habit by which each person becomes master of themselves. ¶ **Equity**, the tempering <note>original: "remissio"; here meaning a relaxation or softening of the strict letter of the law for the sake of fairness.</note> of just and profitable claims. Moderation in dealings, and the rational order of the soul regarding things honorable and shameful. ¶ **Tolerance**, the endurance of trouble for the sake of what is honorable; the endurance of labors for the sake of honor. ¶ **Boldness**, security by which one neither expects a future evil nor shudders at a present one. ¶ **Freedom from Suffering** <note>original: "Indolentia"; literally "indolence," but used here in the philosophical sense of *apatheia*, or the state of being undisturbed by pain.</note>, a habit by which we never fall into pains. ¶ **Perseverance**, a disposition which completes whatever it has chosen; that is, a voluntary endurance. An unshaken habit against labors. ¶ **Modesty** <note>original: "Pudor"; encompassing moral shame and a healthy respect for what is right.</note>, the restraint of boldness, a spontaneous and willing acceptance of what appears best, and the dread of true blame. **Liberty**, the mastery of life, an absolute authority in all things proper to one's life, and a disposition that is not at all stingy in the possession and use of things. ¶ **Liberality**, a habit which maintains decorum in seeking and spending money; the fitting acquisition and accumulation of wealth. ¶ **Gentleness**, a constitution of the soul that is immovable against the impulse of anger; a moderate tempering of the soul. ¶ **Propriety** <note>original: "Modestia"; used here to mean orderly conduct or self-restraint.</note>, a voluntary concession to that which is judged best, and the orderly arrangement of the body's posture. ¶ **Happiness**, a good accumulated from all goods, a power sufficient in itself for living well, perfection according to virtue, and a sufficient comfort of life. ¶ **Magnificence**, estimation according to right and honorable reason. ¶ **Industry**, the character of the soul by which whoever is equipped easily guesses what is fitting in individual cases; sharpness of mind. ¶ **Frugality**, the simplicity of a rational life, and the study of good morals. ¶ **Goodness**, a disposition by which we choose the best things. ¶ **Magnanimity**, the moderate use of circumstances, and polite conversation with men. Magnificence of the soul joined with reason. ¶ **Philanthropy** <gloss>that is, humanity</gloss> <note>original: "φιλανθρωπία" (philanthropia) and "humanitas."</note>, a disposition that wins over the friendship of men, a habit beneficial to people, and the returning of thanks. Beneficial gratitude.

¶ **Piety**: justice toward God; a disposition that worships God; voluntary veneration of God; the correct knowledge of divine honor. ¶ **The Good**: that which is to be sought for its own sake. ¶ **Fearlessness**: a habit through which we are moved by no fears. ¶ **Health of the soul**: a habit that does not succumb to the passions <note>original: "affectibus"; while often translated as humility, the definition "ease of soul free from all anger" suggests a gentle or meek temperament.</note>: a gentleness of the soul free from all anger. ¶ **Shrewdness**: a disposition by which we strive toward our own proper end. ¶ **Friendship**: agreement in honorable and just matters; the choice of the same way of life; consensus in deliberation and action; harmony in the sharing of life with goodwill; the sharing in giving and receiving benefits. ¶ **Nobility**: the virtue of a well-born character; a readiness of mind for both speaking and acting. ¶ **Choice**: a correct approval. ¶ **Goodwill**: the pleasing and accepted choice of one person toward another. ¶ **Kinship**: a shared participation in the same lineage. ¶ **Agreement**: a sharing of all things; a harmony of thoughts and expectations <note>original: "suspicionum"; here meaning 'anticipations' or 'conjectures' regarding the future rather than the modern negative sense of 'suspicion'.</note>. ¶ **Affection** <note>original: "Charitas"; the diligence of guarding. ¶ **Order**: the harmony of operations with one another; the proportion of communal life; the cause of change in all things; a tempering suitable for perception. ¶ **Attention**: the focusing of the mind for the sake of learning. ¶ **Natural Talent**: speed in learning; a good natural birth; a virtue implanted in one's nature. ¶ **Teachability**: the talent of the soul for perceiving quickly. ¶ **Judgment**: a settled declaration concerning that which has come into dispute. ¶ **Law**: the standard by which it is asked whether someone has caused injury or not. ¶ **Lawful Citizenship**: obedience to good laws. ¶ **Joy**: gladness found in the works of temperance. ¶ **Honor**: the granting of goods because of the duty of virtue; the esteem and dignity acquired by virtue; a form of veneration; the preservation of dignity. ¶ **Readiness**: the clear execution of a purpose for doing things. ¶ **Gratitude** <note>original: "Gratia"; this can mean grace or favor, but here "returning a good service" defines it as gratitude.</note>: voluntary beneficence; the returning of a good service at an opportune time. ¶ **Concord**: the agreement of those who hope and those who are subjects.

# Speusippus

the diligent observation of divine worship according to nature. ¶ **Divination**: knowledge predicting things without demonstration. ¶ **Prophecy**: knowledge which discerns what is present or what shall be for a living mortal. ¶ **Wisdom**: knowledge that presupposes nothing at all; knowledge of those things which always are; knowledge which contemplates the causes of all things. ¶ **Philosophy**: the appetite for wisdom; the contemplation of truth as it is; the care of the soul according to right reason. ¶ **Knowledge**: the soul's comprehension of what is unchangeable by reason; a power comprehensive of one thing or certain things by unchangeable reason; true reason in unchangeable thought. ¶ **Opinion**: perception with belief through the reasoning of the mind's discourse; a thought falling upon truth and falsehood through reasoning. ¶ **Sense**: the progress of the soul; a movement of the mind; the announcement of the soul through the body into the forms of men, from which arises an irrational power of the soul knowing through the body. ¶ **Habit**: an affection of the soul, according to which we are said to be of a certain quality. ¶ **The Voice**: an utterance from the mouth according to thought. ¶ **Speech**: a voice that can be written; the proclamation of any matter; a composition of word and name, without the harmony of song. ¶ **A Name**: a simple word signifying that which is predicated according to essence, and everything which is not said according to itself <note>original: "minime dicitur"; likely referring to accidental or relational naming rather than the core nature of a thing.</note>. ¶ **Diction**: the voice of a man which can be written; and a certain common sign signifying without the harmony of song. ¶ **A Syllable**: an articulation of the human voice that can be written. ¶ **A Definition**: speech composed from genus and difference <note>This refers to the classical method of defining something by its general category (genus) and the specific trait that sets it apart (difference).</note>. ¶ **Conjecture**: an indication of a hidden thing. ¶ **Demonstration**: true reasoning; speech showing something through things already known. ¶ **An element of voice**: a simple voice, and the cause by which other voices are indeed voices <note>original: "Elementum vocis"; referring to the basic sounds or letters (phonemes) that build up language.</note>. ¶ **The Useful**: the cause through which each thing is well affected; the cause of a certain good. ¶ **The Conducive**: that which leads toward the good. ¶ **The Beautiful**: that which is good. ¶ **The Good**: that which is the cause of safety in all things that exist; the cause of everything that tends toward it; that from which come whatever things are to be chosen. ¶ **Temperament**: the ornament of the soul. ¶ **Right**: the institution of law, from which justice proceeds. ¶ **The Voluntary**: that which leads itself; that which is to be chosen for its own sake; that which perfects thought. ¶ **The Free**: that which is master of itself. ¶ **The Moderate**: the middle between excess and defect, sufficient according to art. ¶ **Measure**: the middle of excess and defect. ¶ **The Palm**: the reward of virtue to be desired for its own sake. ¶ **Immortality**: a living essence, and everlasting preservation.

### On the Definitions of Plato

->On the Definitions of Plato<-

¶ **Holiness**: the worship of God, which is pleasing to God. ¶ **A Festival** <note>original: "Celebritas"; here referring to a religious observance or solemnity</note>: a time made sacred according to the laws.
¶ **Man**: a wingless, two-footed animal with flat nails; the only one among living creatures that is capable of participating in knowledge and reason. <note>This is a famous Academic definition. According to legend, Diogenes the Cynic mocked it by plucking a chicken and bringing it into the Academy, saying, "Behold, Plato's man!"</note> ¶ **Sacrifice**: the gift of a victim offered to God. ¶ **A Vow**: a prayer of men to God, by which they earnestly ask for either good things or what seem to be good things.
¶ **A King**: one who rules according to the laws, subject to no one, the blameless founder <note>original: "institutor"</note> of the civil order. ¶ **Sovereignty** <note>original: "Principatus"</note>: the providence of the whole. ¶ **License**: a concession of the law. ¶ **Lawgiver**: the author of the laws by which a city [state] ought to be governed. ¶ **Law**: a civil institution of the multitude, without a fixed limit of time. ¶ **Supposition** <note>original: "Suppositio"; likely referring to a hypothesis</note>: an indemonstrable principle, a formula of discourse. ¶ **A Decree**: a civil institution pertaining to a fixed time. ¶ **A Statesman** <note>original: "Civilis homo"</note>: one skilled in those things which pertain to the administration of the republic [state]. ¶ **A City**: a habitation of many men using common laws, with all other men subject to those same laws.
¶ **The Virtue of a City**: the right constitution of the republic. ¶ **Military Virtue**: experience in war. ¶ **Safety**: a defense secure from all harm. ¶ **A Tyrant**: one ruling a city according to his own opinion. ¶ **A Sophist**: a mercenary hunter of noble and wealthy youths. <note>Plato frequently described sophists as "hunters" who sought profit rather than truth.</note> ¶ **Opulence**: a possession of things so moderated that it contributes to happiness; an abundance of things contributing to blessedness. ¶ **A Deposit**: a giving in trust. ¶ **Purgation**: the separation of the worse from the better. ¶ **To Conquer**: to overcome an adversary.
¶ **A Good Man**: one who is of such a kind that he returns good things to man. ¶ **Temperate**: one who has moderate desires. ¶ **Continent**: one who restrains the parts of the soul that fight against reason.
¶ **Upright**: one who is perfectly good, possessing his own proper virtue. ¶ **Conscience**: a sorrowful thought without reasoning. <note>In this context, conscience is defined as the instinctive emotional pang of remorse that precedes intellectual reflection.</note> ¶ **Indocility**: slowness in learning.
¶ **Dominion**: a just sovereignty, subject to no one. ¶ **Misology** <note>original: "Aphilosophia"; the hatred of reasoning or discourse</note>: a habit by which one hates reasoning. ¶ **Fear**: a shaking of the soul in expectation of evil. ¶ **Spiritedness** <note>original: "Animositas"</note>: a violent, irrational impulse of the soul without the reason and order of the mind. ¶ **Dread**: a trembling in expectation of evil. ¶ **Flattery**: social interaction for the sake of pleasure without regard for the good; a habit tending toward the delight of custom and exceeding moderation. ¶ **Anger**: a provocation of the irascible part of the soul for the purpose of avenging. ¶ **Insult**: an injury inflicted through contempt. ¶ **Incontinence**: an affection drawing one toward those things that seem pleasant, contrary to the judgment of right reason. ¶ **Laziness**: a flight from the labors that arise from governing. ¶ **Timidity**: the primary cause of a failing impulse. ¶ **Calumny**: a disagreement among friends caused by words. ¶ **Opportunity**: a time in which each thing is fit either to be done or to be endured. ¶ **Inequity**: a habit that despises the laws. ¶ **Indigence**: a diminishing of good things. ¶ **Modesty** <note>original: "Verecundia"; often used as a healthy sense of shame</note>: a dread in expectation of disgrace. ¶ **Ostentation**: an affection that claims for itself those goods which it does not possess at all. ¶ **Sin**: an action contrary to right reason. ¶ **Envy**: a sadness arising from the good fortune of friends, whether present or past. ¶ **Impudence**: a habit of the soul undergoing disgrace for the sake of gain. ¶ **Ferocity**: an excess of audacity, not fearing those things which ought to be feared. ¶ **Ambition**: a habit of the soul accepting all expenses for the sake of honor, contrary to the norm of reason. ¶ **Degeneration**...

# The golden words of the philosopher Pythagoras.

<margin>1</margin> First, honor the immortal gods as the laws command; respect your oath, then the blessed heroes. Afterward, honor the spirits of the earth <note>original: "Terrestres demones"; in ancient philosophy, "demones" refers to tutelary spirits or the souls of the departed, not "demons" in the modern sense</note>. Observe what has been established by law. Honor your parents and your relatives. From other men, make him your friend who is most outstanding in virtue. Yield to gentle words and useful works. Do not turn against your friend for the sake of a small error; bear with him as far as you are able. For power dwells near necessity. Consider these things well. Moreover, abstain from these things: first from the belly <note>meaning gluttony</note>, then from sleep, lust, and anger. Commit nothing shameful, neither in the presence of others, nor by yourself. Above all, respect yourself. Practice justice, in word and deed alike. Accustom yourself to do nothing without reason. Know that death is ordained for everyone by fate. Learn to accumulate money in season, and again to spend it when the situation requires. And as for those adversities which happen to men by chance, whatever lot you have, bear it without disturbance. It is necessary to heal as much as you can. Know that fortune does not bring many of these [troubles] to good men. Many and varied speeches, partly good and partly bad, are spread among the common people; do not let these move you, nor allow yourself to be restrained by them. If something false is said, bear it with moderation. Completely fulfill what I now tell you. Let no one, by either deed or word, lead you to that which is not best for you. Deliberate before a task, lest you do anything rashly. For it is the mark of a wretched man to speak or act rashly. Do not do things which might eventually cause you regret. Do not do things you do not understand, but learn as much as is necessary. And in this way you will pass your life most pleasantly. Do not neglect the health of the body, but use measure in food, drink, and exercise; by measure I mean that which will cause you no distress. Accustom yourself to a pure diet without luxuries. Avoid those things which stir up envy. Do not squander your wealth out of season, nor be stingy <note>original: "illiberalis"</note>; for the middle way <note>original: "mediocritas"</note> is best in all things. Do not do things that might harm you. Consider before the deed. Do not surrender yourself to soft sleep before you have reviewed your daily deeds three times in your mind,

<meta>This page continues the "Golden Verses of Pythagoras," specifically focusing on the practice of nightly self-examination and the path toward divine transformation. # The Golden Words of Pythagoras the Philosopher

What have I done wrong? <gloss>What have I done?</gloss> What duty have I neglected? <note>This refers to the famous Pythagorean practice of reviewing one’s day every evening to maintain moral discipline.</note> Starting from the first, run through the rest. When you have done something base, punish yourself. But when you have accomplished good things, rejoice. You must practice these things, meditate on them, and love them: these will place you in the footsteps of divine virtue through him who handed down to our souls the fourfold source <term>the Tetraktys; the number ten represented as a triangle of dots, which Pythagoreans revered as the root of all nature</term> of ever-flowing nature. Go forth to your work, having prayed to the gods. For if you hold fast to these things, you will know the condition of the immortal gods and of mortal men—how all things proceed and are held together. You will know, as far as is right, that nature is similar in all things: so that you do not hope for things that cannot be hoped for, and nothing remains hidden from you. You will know that men are miserable because of their own evils. They neither see nor hear the good things that are near them. Indeed, very few understand the release from their evils. Such a fate harms the minds of men, who are carried from one thing to another by certain revolutions, subject to infinite evils. A deadly discord, planted within, harms them secretly; avoid it by yielding, and once it has come, do not increase it. O Father Jupiter, either deliver men from evils or show them what spirit <note>original: "daemone"; referring to a guiding spirit or the inner character of an individual</note> they possess. But you, take heart, for a divine race is innate in men; for to them, sacred nature brings forth and demonstrates all things. If any of these things are revealed to you, you will abstain from those things from which I command you to abstain. If you apply this medicine, you will free your soul from these labors. Truly, abstain from the mortal things we mentioned above in the purification and release of the soul. Consider each thing with right judgment. Then set the best understanding before you as a charioteer.

> Having laid aside the body, when you go free into the upper air,
> You will escape being human and become a god of the nourishing heavens.

### Symbols of Pythagoras the Philosopher.

¶ When you come into a temple, worship; in the meantime, do not say or do anything that pertains to daily life. ¶ One should not enter a temple or pray while on a journey by chance, even if you pass near the very entrance. ¶ Sacrifice and worship with bare feet. ¶ Flee the public roads; travel by the side paths. ¶ Abstain from that which has a black tail, for it belongs to the gods of the underworld. ¶ Above all, restrain your tongue, imitating God. ¶ When the winds blow, worship the Echo. ¶ Do not poke the fire with a sword <note>A metaphor for not provoking someone who is already angry.</note>. ¶ Put away every sharp thing from yourself. ¶ Help a man who is lifting a burden, but do not help him put down what he is laying aside <note>Encouraging industry and perseverance over sloth.</note>. ¶ Put your right foot into your shoes first, but your left foot into the bath. ¶ Do not speak of divine matters without light. ¶ Do not step over a yoke. ¶ Do not step over a balance-scale <note>A metaphor for not transgressing justice.</note>. ¶ When you have left home, do not turn back, for the Furies <note>original: "furiae"; the goddesses of vengeance</note> will meet you. ¶ Do not urinate facing the sun. ¶ Do not speak facing the sun. ¶ Do not wipe a seat with oil. ¶ Nourish the cock <note>a rooster</note> indeed, but do not <note>The text continues on the next page; the "cock" symbol typically forbids sacrificing the animal because it is sacred to the Sun or Moon.</note>

¶ Do not sit upon a bushel-measure. <note>original: "Super modium ne sedeas"; a warning against idleness or living only for the present day's rations.</note>
¶ Do not nourish animals with hooked claws. <note>A symbolic warning to avoid the company of predatory or grasping people.</note>

¶ Do not receive a swallow into your home. <note>Swallows were sometimes seen as symbols of talkativeness or wandering spirits.</note>
¶ Abstain from animals. <note>A reference to the Pythagorean practice of vegetarianism.</note>
¶ It is fitting to banish with all zeal and by every device, and to cut away by iron and fire: disease from the body, luxury from the diet, ignorance from the soul, discord from the home, sedition from the city, and finally, intemperance from all things.

### ¶ Preface of Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to his translation of the book of Xenocrates the Platonist, "On Death," dedicated to the most illustrious man Piero de' Medici.

Cosimo [de' Medici], the glory of Italy, O Piero de' Medici, happy not only in his deeds but also in having such a son as you, acquired for himself a marvelous glory, not only through kingly and human prudence, but also through divine wisdom. He passed no time in his life, even in his greatest business affairs, without the company of the Muses; and in his old age especially, he gave himself over entirely to the study of philosophy and sacred letters. So that he might be initiated into the first mysteries of philosophy, he wished for certain books of Aristotle to be translated by Ioannes Argyropylus <note>A Greek scholar and diplomat who was central to the revival of Greek learning in 15th-century Italy.</note>, a most learned man, and he read them most diligently. Then, lest the inner secrets of wisdom itself be lacking to him, he ordered ten books of the Divine Plato and one of Mercury <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, whom Renaissance scholars believed was a contemporary of Moses and a source of ancient wisdom.</note> to be translated from the Greek language into Latin by us. In these, all the precepts of life, all the principles of nature, and all the holy mysteries of divine things are revealed. Cosimo read all these things accurately and understood them perfectly. And when he had already finished Plato’s book on the single principle of all things and on the Supreme Good, on the twelfth day thereafter—as if about to return to that Principle and to enjoy that Good—he departed, called back from this shadow of life to the light above. At his passing, both his fatherland and the Academy <note>The Platonic Academy of Florence, founded under the patronage of the Medici.</note> would have mourned heavily, had Piero not been so like his father; in whose prudence and piety the fatherland strengthens its hope and the Academy finds its rest. ...as the sun was setting, he began to deplore the misery of this life. Indeed, he so railed against the errors of mortals that he claimed death was even a kind of gain. In this, he discussed the contempt for this life both sharply and at great length, as one who already aspired to heavenly bliss. When he had finished speaking, I said, "Cosimo, the holy and beloved Xenocrates, a disciple of our Plato, treated these same matters in his book on death." I have now translated it and dedicated it to your name <note>Ficino is addressing Piero de' Medici, son of Cosimo.</note>. Thus, when you read this brief but most precious little work, you may consider how much is to be hoped for in this life, and how much a person’s own death—or that of parents or children—ought to be mourned. Read these things, therefore, with joy, O pillar of the Academy. And may you live long, lest we should ever feel ourselves to be without Cosimo.

# The book on death by Xenocrates the Platonic philosopher
## Translated from the Greek language into Latin by Marsilio Ficino the Florentine, for the most illustrious man, Piero de’ Medici.

->Socrates. Clinias. Axiochus.<-

When I was setting out for the Cynosarges <note>A public gymnasium outside the walls of Athens.</note> and had already reached the Ilissus <note>A river in Athens.</note>, I heard the voice of someone calling me by name. Turning around, I saw Clinias, the son of Axiochus, running toward the Callirhoe spring, and with him Damon the musician and Charmides, the son of Glaucon. The former was a teacher of music, while the latter was joined to Clinias by a certain mutual goodwill. It seemed best to me, therefore, to turn back and meet them, so that we might come together more quickly and easily. 

But Clinias, in tears, said, "Socrates, the present moment demands that you show us that wisdom which you always preach. For my father has been struck by a sudden and unbearable illness; he is near death and seems to take it hard, although he used to mock those who feared death as if they were shivering at the sight of ghosts <note>original: "larvarum uultus"; literally "the faces of larvae/spirits," referring to masks or bogeymen used to scare children.</note>. Come, I beseech you, and encourage him as you usually do, so that he may bear this necessity easily. Join us, then, and together with the others, perform this pious work." 

Socrates: "You shall have your honorable wish granted, Clinias, as far as it lies within my power, especially since what you ask is a holy work. Let us hurry, then. For if things are as you say, there is need for haste." 

Clinias: "As soon as he sees you, O Socrates, he will grow stronger. For it has often happened that he recovered himself somewhat in your presence." 

So we went to him along the walls through the Itonian fields <note>Fields near the Itonian Gate of Athens.</note>. For he lived near the gates, toward the Amazonian column. We found him strong and robust in his limbs and body, but weak in spirit and greatly in need of consolation, breathing heavily and drawing sighs, with many tears and the striking together of his palms.

# Xenocrates the Platonist

When I had seen these things, I said, "What is this, O Axiochus? Where indeed is that former and boastful constancy of yours? Where are the constant praises for the virtues? Where is the wonderful greatness and boldness of your soul? For like a cowardly wrestler who appears noble in the gymnasiums but collapses in the matches, you have succumbed. Why do you not consider the order of nature itself? Since you are so great a man, imbued with so many disciplines, and if nothing else, at least an Athenian. Do you not hold to that common and well-worn proverb, which says that this life is a kind of pilgrimage <note>original: "peregrinationem"; the Latin term implies a temporary journey or stay abroad</note>, and that we ought to proceed as travelers—rightly and with a level head—approaching that which is owed and necessary not with a sick mind, but a joyful one? This softness is not suited to a mature age, but to an infant." 

**Axiochus**: "These things, O Socrates, seem to be said rightly. But I do not know how it is that when the crisis looms, those abundant speeches about endurance secretly vanish and are ignored. Instead, a certain contrary fear arises, shaking the soul from all sides. Alas! I shall be deprived of this light and these goods. I shall lie in darkness; deprived of taste and sight, I shall rot. I shall be turned into worms and beasts."

**Socrates**: "Without the examination of reason, O Axiochus, you are joining the deprivation of sensation with sensation itself <note>Socrates argues that Axiochus is mistakenly imagining he will be 'aware' of his own rotting, which is impossible if he has no senses.</note>, and you contradict yourself both in speaking and in your distress. You do not notice that you are simultaneously complaining about the loss of sense and grieving over the rot and the loss of goods, as if you were going to pass into another life, rather than migrating into a total lack of sensation—a lack, I say, such as that which preceded your birth. For just as under the government of Draco or Cleisthenes <note>Draco (7th c. BC) and Cleisthenes (6th c. BC) were famous early Athenian lawmakers. Socrates points out that Axiochus did not suffer under their laws because he did not yet exist.</note> nothing evil happened to you—for you were not there for whom the evil might exist—so after death there will be nothing adverse for you. For you will not be there for whom the future evil might be. Therefore, cast all such trifles away from you. And consider this: that once that which was composed is dissolved, and the soul departs to its own place, this which remains—the earthly and irrational body—is in no way the human being. For we are the soul, an immortal living being <note>original: "animal"; in this context, it refers to any 'animated' or living thing</note> shut in a mortal dwelling place. Nature constructed this shelter for us to our misfortune. Its pleasures are counterfeit, fleeting, and mixed with many troubles; its pains, however, are pure, long-lasting, and devoid of any joy. Add to this the swellings of bile and phlegm, the diseases of the senses, and the corruption of the internal organs. The soul necessarily suffers with these, spread as it is through every passage [of the body] so that it may bind each part. Thus it happens that the soul now longs for the celestial and kindred ether <note>The 'fifth element' of which the heavens and stars were thought to be composed.</note>, and thirsts for the life and the heavenly choir. For the loss of this life is a transition from evil to good." 

**Axiochus**: "Since you judge this life to be evil, O Socrates, why do you remain in it? Especially since you meditate on these things most of all, and you exist as a caretaker for others, and you excel the rest in mind?" 

**Socrates**: "Axiochus, you are not a very true witness for me. For you think..."

### On Death
4

The Athenian people certainly believe, since I have become a seeker of the nature of things, that I know something. I, however, would wish to understand those common things rather than being skilled in superfluous matters. What we have just spoken of are the declamations of Prodicus the wise <note>Prodicus of Ceos was a contemporary of Socrates, a Sophist famous for his lectures on linguistics and ethics, for which he charged high fees.</note>, bought some for two-thirds, some for two drachmas, and some for four; truly, he teaches no one for free. He always has that saying of Epicharmus <note>A Greek dramatist and philosopher</note> in his mouth: "Hand washes hand. Give something, receive something."

In recent days, he brought so many arguments against life that I was nearly driven to end my own life. And from that time on, my soul continually dies, O Axiochus. 

**Axiochus**: What then are the things he said? 

**Socrates**: I will recount everything that remains in my memory. For he said: what part of life is not full of evils? Does the infant, hardly born, not immediately wail? And does he not begin life from sorrow? Nor is any pain absent. Whether because of need, or cold, or heat, or a blow, does he not weep? He is not yet able to explain in words what he suffers, but he cries and shouts, and has this one voice as a sign of his distress. 

When he has fulfilled his seventh year, he is burdened with many labors. For there arise tutors <term>pedagogi</term>, grammarians, and physical trainers <term>pedotrivae</term> <note>These were the three standard instructors for a Greek boy: the pedagogue (a slave who supervised behavior), the grammaticus (literature and music), and the pedotriva (gymnastics).</note>. These men rule over him no differently than tyrants. When he has grown a little, censors, arithmeticians, geometers, distributors, and countless masters besides these are set over him. 

Indeed, fear surrounds and enslaves the young man <term>ephebum</term> <note>An ephebe was a young man aged 18–20 undergoing military training in Athens.</note>; the Lyceum and the Academy, the offices of the gymnasium, the scepters of authority, and an immoderate amount of evils truly occur. All the distress of the youth rests under the censors of morals and the chosen council of the Areopagites <note>The Areopagus was the ancient high court of Athens, which held significant power over the conduct of citizens.</note>. 

When he has been released from their command, cares and deliberations creep in, while it is debated which path of life it is proper for him to enter, so much so that in comparison with subsequent labors, those preceding ones seem light and to be feared only by infants. Military expeditions, wounds, and frequent struggles arise. 

At last, old age itself creeps in secretly, into which every foul and incurable evil of nature flows. And unless one immediately renders up life as a debt, nature, like a debt collector, insists and demands its pledges. From this man it takes sight, from that one hearing, and from another both. If anyone resists, it dissolves, corrupts, mutilates, and cuts them off. Some live until the very extreme of old age, but in mind they become decrepit, twice children <note>original: "bis pueri"; referring to the common Greek and Latin proverb that "old men are twice children" due to their return to a state of dependency and mental fragility.</note>. 

Therefore God, providing for the affairs of men, recalls those whom He loves early to Himself from this life. And so Agamedes and Trophonius <note>Architects of the Temple of Apollo at Delphi.</note>, when they had built a temple for the Pythian god and prayed for whatever might be best for them, were immediately weighed down by sleep and never rose again. The same also happened to the priests of Argive Juno <note>Likely referring to the famous story of Cleobis and Biton, though the text here calls them "priests" or attendants.</note>, when their mother requested some reward from Juno for her sons' piety. For as the yoke was slow, they themselves went under it and transported their mother into the temple—

### ->Xenocrates the Platonist<-

...truly. And since they had made a vow to the god, they departed from life in the night. <note>original: "Cumq: deo uouissent noctu e uita migrarunt." This likely refers to the story of Cleobis and Biton, two brothers who died in their sleep as a "reward" from the goddess Hera for their piety, illustrating the Greek theme that death is better than life.</note> It would be a long task to relate the opinions of the poets who, in their divine poems, deplore the calamities of human life. I will mention one most famous poet <note>The author is referring to Homer.</note> who speaks thus: "The gods have ordained that miserable mortals should live in perpetual sorrow. Nor is there anything on earth more wretched than man." <note>original: "Statuerunt dii, ut mortales miseri i moerore perpetuo uiuerent." A translation of the Iliad, 24.525-526.</note> And so they say that Amphiaraus <note>A legendary seer and hero whom the earth swallowed up to save him from a more shameful death in battle.</note> was beloved by Jupiter <note>Zeus</note> and Apollo with a certain supreme affection, yet he did not reach old age. What, moreover, do you think of that poet who commands the newborn to mourn the misery of his own life?

But now I shall stop, lest I seem to wander further beyond what was proposed. Who is there, indeed, who does not complain greatly about the pursuit and the craft they have chosen? Let us consider the hired laborers and the mechanical craftsmen, working from night to night and scarcely acquiring those things necessary for life; they live complainingly, filling their nightly vigils with weeping and tears. What shall I say of sailors? To how many dangers are they subjected? Rightly indeed did Bias <note>Bias of Priene, one of the Seven Sages of Greece, famously remarked that sailors were neither among the living nor the dead because they were separated from death by only a few inches of wood.</note> say that he counts a sailor neither among the living nor the dead; for a creature of the earth, as if a participant in a double and a doubtful life, plunges himself into the water, entirely subject to fortune.

But agriculture is sweet, you say. So be it—but does it not, as they say, like a sore <note>original: "ulcus"</note>, always find an occasion for sadness? Now indeed the farmer blames the drought and groans; now the rains; now the heat and the scorching sun; now the worms; now the warmth; now the untimely cold. The pursuit of the state <term>res publica</term> is truly to be honored, yet—to pass over much—by how many evils and hardships is it tortured? It has a joy that is like moving phlegm or seething bile <note>In ancient medicine, an excess of these "humors" caused illness and emotional instability; the author uses them here as metaphors for the volatile nature of political success.</note>—unstable, swollen, deceitful, and turbulent; but its loss is sad, and worse than a thousand deaths. Who, moreover, can be happy while he lives at the nod of the crowd, mocked and hissed off stage, like some game and a tale for the common people, shaken, whistled at, fined, wretched, and ruined?

Where now, O civic Axiochus, did Miltiades <note>The hero of the Battle of Marathon, who was later fined and died in prison.</note> die? Where Themistocles? Where Ephialtes? <note>Famous Athenian leaders who faced exile or assassination despite their great service.</note> Where are the rest of the generals? For my part, I never gaped after these things. For it does not seem to me honorable to perform the duties of a magistrate among a senseless people. Consider those who, concerning Theramenes and Callixenus, on the next day, acting as presiding officers, forced the schemers to condemn men to death indiscriminately. <note>original: "in discreta homines morte damnarūt." This refers to the illegal collective trial and execution of the Athenian generals after the Battle of Arginusae in 406 BCE. Socrates was the only member of the council who famously refused to vote for the illegal motion.</note> You, along with Euryptolemus, resisted these things before the three thousand assembled citizens.

**Axiochus**: You speak the truth, O Socrates. And yet from that time until this very day, I have avoided the public tribunal, nor has anything seemed more difficult and harsh than the governing of the state. This is clear to those who themselves handle civil matters. You, however, speak of these things as if you had observed them from afar, from some watchtower. We certainly understand those things more clearly, we who are engaged in the work itself. For the people, O friend Socrates, are ungrateful, irritable, hostile, cruel, envious, and unrefined, consisting of... <meta>The sentence continues onto the next page with the catchword "fluente" (flowing/crowding).</meta>

# On Death

...a flowing crowd, and is piled high with trifles; and whoever accommodates himself familiarly to this life is far more miserable than that. **Socrates:** Since, O Axiochus, you judge the most liberal discipline <note>original: "disciplinam liberalem." This refers to the life of a free citizen and the study of politics or statecraft, which was previously discussed as being full of vanity.</note> of all to be avoided above all others, what must be thought of the rest? Must they not be fled from with the greatest effort? I heard **Prodicus** <note>A famous Greek Sophist and contemporary of Socrates, known for his teachings on the "correctness of names" and the choice of Hercules.</note> saying once that death pertains neither to the living nor to the dead. **Axiochus:** By what reasoning? **Socrates:** Because death is not present to the living, and those who have died no longer exist. Therefore, it is not present to you now, for you are not yet dead. Nor, even if you depart, will it be present to you, for you will no longer be. It would be a hollow grief, therefore, if Axiochus lamented that which is neither present to Axiochus nor will be in the future. For you would be acting just as if you shuddered at a **Scylla** or a **Centaur** <note>Classic examples of mythical monsters that do not exist; Socrates argues that fearing death is like fearing a fictional monster.</note>. Since these monsters are neither around you now, nor will they ever be. For that which is fearful and horrible happens only to those who exist; but for those who do not exist, there is nothing to be feared.

**Axiochus:** You indeed gather these things from that light chatter which is already spread everywhere by loquacity. For from that source comes this abundance of empty words, composed for the sake of young boys. But I mourn because I am deprived of the goods of this life, even if you bring forward stronger reasons than the previous ones. For a wavering mind does not understand the ornament of words, nor does it reach the "colors" <note>original: "colores orationis." A rhetorical term referring to stylistic figures and emotional flourishes used to sway an audience.</note> of speech. The pomp and splendor of a sermon, even if the mind hears them, it ignores them, for it is far from the truth; it by no means tolerates the little traps of sophistries.

<margin>So</margin> It attends only to those things which can strike and penetrate the soul completely. **Socrates:** Without reason, Axiochus, you join the sensation of evils with the deprivation of goods, and it escapes you what it is to be dead. Clearly, the contrary passion of evils afflicts him who is deprived of goods <note>That is, you can only feel the loss of something if you are still alive to feel it.</note>. But he who is no longer, does not even notice the deprivation itself. In what way, therefore, can there be affliction where the awareness of the afflicting things is absent? For at the start, unless through ignorance you assumed some sensation remained, you would not dread death. But now you pervert your own reasoning, fearing lest you lose your soul, yet you assign a soul <note>Or "life/consciousness."</note> to the loss itself. You fear being deprived of sensation, yet you think that the state of non-existence is something perceived by the senses—even though there are many famous discourses on the immortality of the soul.

For mortal nature would never have risen to such excellence as to despise the violence of huge beasts, cross the sea, found cities, prescribe order for the republic, look up to the sky, and measure the circuits of the stars. It would not have noticed the movements of the sun and moon—their risings and settings, and furthermore eclipses, and the swift noon-day restorations, the double turnings of the **Pleiades** <note>A star cluster used in antiquity to mark the seasons for farming and sailing.</note>, and winter and summer alike. It would not have understood the blasts of the winds and the force of the rains, the passage of lightning and its flash, and finally, it would not have wonderfully captured the phenomena of the world in eternity, unless some divine spirit were present in the soul, through which...
