# Xenocrates the Platonist <note>Xenocrates was a student of Plato and the third leader of the Platonic Academy; his name here likely serves as an attribution for the philosophical school of thought being presented.</note>

...had attained an understanding of such great things. Therefore, my dear **Axiochus**, you do not migrate into death, but into immortality itself. Nor will you be deprived of good things, but you will enjoy the full possession of all that is good. You will no longer perceive pleasures mixed with the mortal body, but pleasures entirely free from all sadness. There, I say, you shall set out, free from this **prison** <note>original: "carcere." A common Platonic metaphor (soma-sema) viewing the physical body as a jail for the eternal soul.</note>, where all is quiet and removed from sadness and old age. Where there is holy exultation, and a life ignorant of evils, nourished by tranquil peace, beholding the nature of things and contemplating the secrets of philosophy—not indeed for the favor of a crowd or a theater, but toward the object of clear truth. **Axiochus:** Your speech has led me to a contrary feeling. For I no longer dread death, but desire it. To express something overflowing in the manner of the orators, even now, O **Socrates**, I am carried on high; I run through the divine circuit and the throne. Taking myself out of this weakness, I have been reborn. **Socrates:** I will relate to you further, if you please, what **Gobrias** the **magus** <note>original: "magus." Here referring to a Zoroastrian priest or a practitioner of Eastern wisdom.</note> passed on to me. For he said that at the time when **Xerxes** <note>The Great King of Persia who invaded Greece in 480 BCE.</note> crossed over, his grandfather, named **Gobrias**, had been sent to **Delos** to guard the island where the two gods were born. There, he said, he learned from certain bronze tablets—which **Opis** and **Hecaergos** <note>Mythical figures or "Hyperborean maidens" associated with the worship of Apollo and Artemis.</note> had brought from the **Hyperboreans** <note>A mythical people who lived in the far north "beyond the North Wind" in a land of perpetual sunshine.</note>—that at the release of the body, the soul migrates into a hidden place beneath the earth, in which is the palace of **Juno** <note>original: "Iunonis." Here Juno (Hera) likely represents the chthonic queen Persephone.</note>, a court no narrower than that of **Jove** <note>original: "Iouis." Jupiter/Zeus.</note>. Indeed, since the earth holds the middle of the universe, and the heaven is spherical, the celestial gods have been allotted one hemisphere, while the lower gods have the other—some being brothers of the sky-dwellers, and others the sons of those brothers. The vestibules of **Pluto’s** province are fastened on all sides by barriers and bronze chains. For the one who relates these things, first the river **Acheron**, and then the **Cocytus** <note>The "River of Woe" and the "River of Lamentation" in the Greek underworld.</note> receives them. Once these are crossed, one must be led to **Minos** and **Rhadamanthus** <note>Legendary kings of Crete and Aegina, respectively, who became judges of the dead for their legendary fairness.</note>, into that region which is known as the **Plain of Truth**. There the judges sit, examining the life of each one who arrives. Here, no one can protect themselves with lies. Therefore, for whomever a good **daemon** <note>original: "dæmon." Not an evil spirit, but a personal guiding spirit or "genius" assigned to a person at birth.</note> breathed upon in life, they pass through to the place of the pious. There, eternal spring abounds with every kind of fruit, and fountains of shining water gush forth. Moreover, there are pleasant meadows painted with various colors. Nor are there lacking assemblies of those practicing philosophy, and theaters of poets. There are circular dances there, and musical songs, and sweet harmonies. Joyful banquets, and holy and abundant gatherings of those drinking—an inviolable joy and sweet companionship. There is no excess of cold or heat there, but a healthy nature of the air, tempered by the gentle rays of the sun. This is the seat of purified souls, where they celebrate the divine mysteries. What then stands in your way, so that the first honor and reward should not be given to you there, since you derive your origin from God? For even those like **Hercules** and **Dionysius** <note>Dionysus.</note>, when they [descended] there...

# On death

[Those who] descend, reason dictates that they go cleansed, and from the rest of their devotion <note>original: "cultu." This refers to their religious conduct or way of life.</note> they take up the hope of a happy journey. On the other hand, those who have stained their life with crimes are suddenly snatched through **Tartarus** <note>The deepest abyss of the underworld, used as a dungeon of torment for the wicked.</note> by the **Furies** into **Erebus** <note>A region of the underworld representing personified darkness.</note> and **Chaos**. There lies open the province of the impious, and the useless labor of the **Danaid** girls <note>The daughters of Danaus, condemned in the afterlife to the endless task of filling a perforated vessel (or sieves) with water.</note> striving in vain to fill sieves with water. There is the thirst of **Tantalus** <note>A figure punished by being "tantalized" with food and drink he could never reach.</note>, the entrails of **Tityos** <note>A giant whose liver was perpetually eaten by vultures as punishment for his crimes.</note>, and the stone of **Sisyphus** <note>Famous for his eternal punishment of rolling a boulder up a hill, only for it to roll back down again.</note> that forever rolls back. There, biting beasts wrap themselves inseparably around bodies. There, unquenchable torches burn the flesh. There, wicked men, tortured by punishments of every form, are tormented with perpetual retribution. These things indeed I learned from **Gobrias**. But you, **Axiochus**, may judge these things for yourself. For I, compelled by reason, know only this clearly and firmly: that every soul is immortal, and that which departs pure from these places lives without sadness. Therefore, whether you tend upward or downward, **Axiochus**, it is necessary that you be blessed, if only you have lived piously and holily.

**Axiochus:** I blush, my **Socrates**, and I am afraid to speak further. So far is the fear of death from me now that I strongly long to die; to such an extent has your previous speech persuaded me, as if it were a heavenly oracle. Now therefore I despise this life, as one about to pass happily into a better place. Wherefore, for the present, I shall silently reflect upon these things that have been said. But you, **Socrates**, shall return to me after noon.

**Socrates:** I will do as you say. But meanwhile, I shall return to the **Cynosarges** <note>A public gymnasium in Athens dedicated to Heracles, where Socrates was known to frequent.</note> for the sake of a walk, from where I was brought here to you.

->The End of Xenocrates on Death.<-

# The Book on Pleasure by Marsilio Ficino the Florentine, written while still a youth, addressed to Antonio Canisiano, a Florentine citizen. Preface.

## THREE KINDS OF DISCOURSE.

I remember when I was together with you at your estate in **Campoli** <note>A rural area outside Florence where the Canisiano family held property.</note>; and as we were drawn by the particular beauty of that region and the sweetness of the various fruits in which that villa especially abounds, we happened upon a discussion about pleasure. You requested this discussion of me and asked that I commit it to writing as soon as I had the leisure. Therefore, I wrote this little work on pleasure for you as soon as I returned to **Figline** <note>original: "Figinum." This is Ficino's family home in the Valdarno; his name "Ficino" is derived from this town.</note>, with the greatest pleasure myself.

To begin here, there are three kinds of discourse among philosophers. The first is where we defend and approve a certain side of a question through argument, as the **Peripatetics** <note>The school of Aristotle, known for systematic and empirical study.</note> and **Stoics** <note>Philosophers who emphasized virtue and logic as the path to happiness, often opposing pleasure.</note> did. The second is where, once a question is proposed, we bring forward various opinions and reasons regarding what is being sought; thus, having presented several views and compared them in turn, we may choose what appears more probable and likely. This was the method used by the **Academics** <note>Members of the Platonic Academy; here Ficino refers to the "New Academy," which favored exploring multiple perspectives.</note> and nearly all **Socratics**. The third kind is most characteristic of the **Sceptics**, who, because they think all things are indifferent, hold nothing certain or even probable to follow. Indeed, they confuse and mix things that are separated and distinct by the order of nature, and they are rejected by all the more excellent philosophers.

I have therefore decided that, of all these, the method of the Academics and Socratics should be set forth by me in this discussion. For **Plato**, whom we follow and venerate as if he were a "god of philosophers," forbids those who are still in their tender years from offering their own opinion on any matter. He fears that, as often happens among younger men, what we most strongly approved in our early years might later—in a more mature age and with graver judgment—have to be revoked and turned into the opposite opinion. I thought it better, therefore, to run through the opinions of other philosophers on pleasure in a brief discourse rather than express my own, so that I might not shamelessly assert anything against what we are taught by our Plato, and so that I might satisfy your desire, which I know is most ardent for the study of philosophy. But so much for this; let us now come to the opinions of the philosophers.

<summary>In this preface, a young Marsilio Ficino introduces his treatise on pleasure, written at the request of his friend Antonio Canisiano. He explains his decision to use the "Academic" method of presenting multiple viewpoints rather than his own conclusion, citing Platonic caution regarding the shifting opinions of youth.</summary>

->¶ Chapter One. On the parts of the soul.<-
->¶ Likewise on gladness, joy, and pleasure, according to Plato.<-

**P**LATO therefore (to begin with the prince of philosophers <note>The author refers to Plato as "their prince," reflecting the high status of Platonic thought in the Renaissance</note>), since he divided the soul into two parts—namely, the mind and the senses—attributed <term>gladness</term> <note>original: "læticia"</note> and <term>joy</term> <note>original: "gaudium"</note> to the mind, and <term>pleasure</term> <note>original: "uoluptas"</note> to the senses. But he believes these first two differ from each other because all "joy" is worthy of praise, whereas "gladness" is partly to be praised and partly to be blamed. For he says that gladness is a certain elevation of the mind in the possession of some good, which can either exceed or maintain moderation. Joy, however, is that very delight received from contemplation or some other practice of the virtues. And so, in his *Phaedrus* <note>One of Plato's famous dialogues concerning the soul and love</note>, when he speaks of that first and true life which the soul enjoys in its heavenly seat, he says it is nourished by the contemplation of truth and "rejoices." For this reason, he often calls joy the "sustenance of the mind." For he wishes truth itself to be like a field, and the contemplation of that truth to be like the crops. Then, the sustenance taken from these two is the joy by which the mind fully enjoys the contemplation of truth. Therefore, in that same *Phaedrus*, when he discusses those shadows into which the soul has been cast and submerged from the highest and true light, he says: "where there is great effort to see where the plain of truth is; for from there comes the suitable food for the soul, and the nature of the wings by which the soul is raised up is nourished by this." Plato calls "wings" those things by which the soul flies back to the heights, from which it had descended due to the thought of earthly things. Now, since this can be achieved through two virtues—namely, the <term>contemplative</term> <note>Relating to deep thought or prayer</note> and the <term>moral</term> <note>Relating to behavior and ethics</note>—Plato understands these same virtues, as I interpret him, to be the very wings of the soul, which it recovers through the contemplation of truth and divine matters, just as it had lost them through the desire for these earthly things. But when, through the exercise of both natural and moral philosophy, it flies back to the heavens with its wings recovered, then he believes two rewards are returned to the returning soul: one is the contemplation of divinity, and the other is a certain perfect and absolute joy, which the soul enjoys in that very knowledge of God. Plato calls the former <term>ambrosia</term> and the latter <term>nectar</term> <note>In mythology, the food and drink of the gods</note> in the *Phaedrus* with these words: "the soul that has truly beheld [truth] and been nourished by these things, returning, enters again into its home within heaven. And when the <term>charioteer</term> <note>original: "auriga"</note> has returned, standing the horses at the manger, he sets before them ambrosia and, over it, nectar to drink." In the manner of Pythagoras, he calls the "charioteer" Reason; the "horses" are the other parts and natures of the soul which Reason leads. The rest...

...indeed be led entirely and ruled; and I think the same thing is generally signified by some of the more excellent poets <note>original: "uatibus"</note> when they mention either ambrosia, or nectar, or the charioteer concerning the soul. This, therefore, is the divine opinion of our Plato concerning the nature of joy itself, which Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius trismegistus," the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and magic</note> seems to have understood when he said these things about the highest God: "You grant us reason, sense, and intelligence. Reason, so that we may seek you out through inquiries; sense, so that we may recognize you; and intelligence <note>original: "cognitione"</note>, so that by knowing you we may rejoice because you have shown yourself to us in your entirety." ### ¶ Chapter II. What pleasure is, and that it is not a good in itself, for many reasons, according to Plato.

Plato, however, maintains that <term>pleasure</term> <note>original: "uoluptas," specifically referring to physical or sensory pleasure</note> is a certain sweet motion in the senses, which arises from the fulfillment of a lack <note>original: "indigentiæ repletione"</note>. For he says that lack and its fulfillment are, in a certain way, in conflict with each other; from the former (lack), desire and pain fall upon our senses, and from the latter (fulfillment), pleasure. Nor does he think that this very pleasure of which we now speak should be counted among the "goods." Although he has demonstrated this with many most true arguments, this one is the first and most powerful of all:

¶ Just as, by the presence of heat, those things to which heat comes are made hot, so also by that which is good assisting them, all things become good to which goodness itself is present. Yet no one is made better by the possession of pleasure, since pleasure exists in beasts even more than in humans; and yet these beasts are not only not better than humans, but are not even good at all. Furthermore, women and children, the foolish, and finally all the lazy pursue pleasure and embrace it with all their strength, much more so than good men and those of excellent character. And yet it would be absurd if that which is a "good" were more suited to the wicked and the lazy than to honest and excellent men.

¶ Nor, as he thinks, can opposites be mixed with one another. Yet pleasure is undoubtedly found even where there are evils, since it is not lacking in the wicked and the unjust. Therefore, it is in no way a "good," for it associates with that which is evil. But the good and the evil, because they are repugnant to each other, can in no way coincide. 

¶ Add to this what is said by Socrates in the *Gorgias* <note>One of Plato's dialogues exploring the nature of rhetoric, justice, and the soul</note>: that good and evil are never found at the same time in the same person. Yet the same person at the same time is frequently affected by pain and pleasure alike. For indeed, every lack is painful, and every fulfillment of it is pleasurable to the senses. He calls thirsting a "lack of nature," and drinking its "fulfillment." The former is therefore troublesome, while the latter—drinking—is pleasant.

<summary>This page concludes a discussion on spiritual joy as divine nourishment before defining physical pleasure as the mere fulfillment of bodily needs. It argues that pleasure cannot be an intrinsic good because it is experienced by the wicked and exists simultaneously with the pain of desire.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Platonic arguments against identifying pleasure with the "highest good." ->## ON PLEASURE<-

...furthermore, it happens that one hungers and thirsts at the same time, from which he wishes to conclude that it is possible for someone to possess pain and pleasure simultaneously. Indeed, he argues that desire, anxiety, suspicion, envy, and pity—all of which contain pain within themselves—are the companions of pleasure. From this, he says that "fearful desire" <note>original: "timens cupidinem"</note>, being permitted to both pain and pleasure at once, proceeds from the senses; thus it happens that pleasure is joined and confused with pain. And since "the good" is not mixed with "the evil," he denies that pain can be an evil or that pleasure can be a good <note>This refers to the Platonic view that if pleasure and pain can exist together, they cannot be absolute opposites like Good and Evil</note>.

¶ Moreover, since every "good" ought to be stable and permanent, who would say that pleasure—which has no stability—is a good? And yet, it cannot be denied, if one considers its definition, that pleasure is unstable and uncertain; for, in its definition (as we recorded above), it is called a "motion" <note>original: "motio." In Platonic philosophy, things that are "becoming" or in "motion" are less real than the eternal, "stable" Forms</note>. Nothing is more contrary to stability than motion, nor is there anyone who has ever tasted any pleasure of the body who does not know how fragile it is, how brief, with what speed it slips away and flows off, and how quickly it is turned into its opposite. Furthermore, that which is good can never be contrary to another good. Yet, since pleasure hinders many of the greatest goods, who could doubt that it is contrary to the good? For pleasures hinder <term>prudence</term> <note>original: "prudentiam," meaning practical wisdom or foresight</note>; they pour darkness into the mind, deprave judgment, and with their flatteries and enticements, like certain little prostitutes <note>original: "meretriculæ"</note>, they allure the minds of men to themselves and ensnare them, prostrating the entire nature of man in the mud and filth of vices and crimes. For the divine Plato, in his letter to Dionysius, says: "pleasure brings detriment to men, giving birth to ignorance, restlessness, foolishness, and petulance."

¶ Furthermore, there is no "good" that is not worthy of either praise or veneration. Yet no one of sound mind praises pleasure, nor is anyone judged worthy of honor and glory because he enjoys the greatest pleasures. Rather, honor is given to the one who is of such a character that he rejects and neglects them with a high and unconquered soul.

¶ Added to these points is the fact that no "good" seems able to be rightly called "ours" unless it is either inherent in the very nature of each thing or has proceeded from ourselves. And we are nothing other than <term>mind and reason</term> <note>original: "mentem & rationem"</note>. The body, however, is a prison and a tomb for us <note>original: "Corpus autem carcer, & sepulchrum est nobis." This is the famous Orphic and Platonic pun "Soma Sema" (the body is a tomb)</note>. The senses, indeed, are like certain henchmen and ambushers, who seem to care for and strive for this above all: to plunge and bind us more deeply in the darkness of this prison, so that the souls may not fly back to their own place and heavenly fatherland.

Truly, other things arise from fortune, or from that prison which is hostile to us <note>The "prison" here likely refers to the physical body, a common Platonic metaphor where the soul is 'imprisoned' in the flesh</note>, and they are not so much ours as they are of the body and of fortune. And Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a Roman scholar and writer</note> says rightly: "No one should call his own that which is outside of himself." 

Therefore, since pleasure is innate and implanted in the body and the senses, whoever counts it among our [true] goods will undoubtedly seem to be insane. Add to this, if you please, what Socrates says in Plato’s *Gorgias* <note>A dialogue by Plato exploring whether it is better to suffer or commit injustice; it contains a famous critique of pleasure as 'filling a leaky jar'</note>: that all the goods of the soul proceed from skill, rectitude, order, and choice. And in this, the entire discipline of moral philosophers also agrees: that the whole power of virtue and the goods of the soul consists in choice. But who would say that pleasure proceeds from choice? Is it not necessary that for those things which fall under choice, counsel and deliberation must have first taken place? For nothing is chosen unless it has been previously consulted upon and judged. But no one deliberates in order to have pleasure within himself, for it is innate to us. 

Therefore, Socrates thinks there are two ideas <note>original: "ideas." In this context, guiding principles or internal drives</note> in each of us which we follow wherever they lead. One is the opinion that strives for the best; the other is the desire for pleasures. He calls the former an "acquired idea," but the latter he calls "innate." Thus, pleasure follows neither skill, nor reason, nor any order whatsoever. Rather, it is stirred up within us by a certain sudden and rash impulse of nature and the senses, more than by any certain judgment or counsel; it flatters the senses, soothes and tickles the body with a certain ruinous sweetness, weakens the soul, and displaces the mind and reason from their proper state. 

¶ Furthermore, such is the nature of all goods that, while they are yet to come, they raise a man's hope. When they are present, however, they make the soul of the possessor tranquil and quiet, rendering it content with what is at hand; they fulfill the soul with their possession so that it lacks nothing further, seeks nothing, and desires nothing—as if one possessed that single thing which is by its own nature sufficient and perfect. But if someone who enjoys the possession of some good should desire anything beyond it, he nonetheless seems to be entirely free from anxiety and distress. Future pleasures, however, affect the senses with a certain intolerable heat of desire; they kindle worry, burden the soul with anxiety, and (to be brief) drive one into a kind of fury and madness. When someone embraces those pleasures as present—those for which he had burned with desire—they immediately bring fear and suspicion along with them, blinding us while we enjoy them, and reducing us to the wildness of beasts. ...strive for. And they should tend toward one thing, nor should they be separated from one another by any means, but should merge in a certain kind of fusion <note>original: *confusione*; here meaning a blending or union rather than disorder</note>, so that whoever possesses any one of them cannot lack any of the good things. Indeed, the virtues follow each other with such a strong connection that he who has acquired one already enjoys the possession of all virtues <note>A central Stoic and Platonic tenet: the "Unity of the Virtues" suggests that one cannot truly possess courage without also having wisdom, justice, and temperance.</note>. But truly, evils disagree and dissent among themselves, nor can they merge or be blended in any way. And rightly Aristotle says that evil destroys itself; for if it were entirely intact, it would be intolerable <note>Aristotle argues in the *Nicomachean Ethics* that while virtue is a "mean," vice is an extreme that often conflicts with other extremes.</note>. Nor do prodigality <term>prodigalitas: wasteful extravagance</term> and avarice, or boldness and cowardice, ever meet in the same person; in the same way, no other extremes of vice are connected to each other, since they are utterly opposed. Therefore, it seems that nature has applied the best remedy against the tendency to do wrong: that he who is more prone to a fall cannot fall toward every side of the precipice at once. Yet, he who ascends with the greatest difficulty necessarily attains the whole and entire summit. 

Since, therefore, such is the condition of evils and goods, it is concluded by necessary reasoning that those things which do not follow one another cannot be goods. Pleasures, however, far from coming together, seem to conflict with each other in a certain way and often bring about an obstacle. For while any bodily sense is moved by the greatest sweetness, the rest of them can scarcely perceive the delight of the things then offered to them. It also happens that one person perceives more and greater pleasures than another, and not all living creatures are delighted equally. Virtues, however—and indeed all things that are good—are so joined together for the reason we mentioned a little before, that all are present to the same person at once, and no more of these can be present to one man than to another. Since it is clear, then, that the nature of goods and the nature of pleasures are so different, surely no one would call bodily pleasure a good thing, unless they were too great a friend to it.

¶ Then, another argument of Plato proves it to be a property of good things that they tend <insert>toward</insert> the common utility and safety of the human race. But he says that pleasure breeds its own lust and love, and he who is subject to it always focuses only on his own desire, nor does he have any care for anyone else, provided he may more vigilantly obey his own "whirlpool" <note>original: *uoragini*; a metaphor for a bottomless or devouring appetite</note> of greed. And everything he does, he directs toward that sweetness and delight perceived by the senses.

->### ON PLEASURE<-

<page-type>text</page-type>
<sig>Y iii</sig>

...they say it is, while the "end" <note>original: *finem*; the ultimate goal or purpose of an action</note> is that toward which a certain ultimate <term>appetitio: a natural desire or reaching-out of the soul toward an object</term> is directed. Therefore, since the natural appetite of man desires pleasure solely for the sake of something else, who of sound mind would think this is the end, or a "good" at all? Indeed, they believe that nature gave a sweet perception of this kind to living beings for this reason: so that they might acquire and prepare those things which are necessary for living. For that which lives requires two things above all: that it might reject and repel those things which can harm it, and take and adopt those things which are profitable. 

But because repelling the former and pursuing the latter is laborious and difficult, nature has woven a certain pleasure into every action of this kind, lest living beings be too slow to procure what they need because of that very difficulty. Thus it happens that, soothed and thoroughly captured by this sweetness—as if by a bait <note>original: *esca*; a common philosophical metaphor for pleasure as a hook used by nature</note>—they neither flee any dangers or labor, nor do they perceive the difficulty of preparing their food. They are made more ready to prepare the necessities of life. Moreover, they demonstrate that pleasure was given to us by nature for the sake of these things by this sign: that all living creatures, when they expel from the body what is superfluous or take in what is necessary, are moved by this sweetness we have so often mentioned; and the more effectively they do these things, the greater the delight they perceive. 

However, when they have entirely filled the deficiency of their nature, they feel no further pleasure. But we see them moved only so long as they are refilling that deficiency, as if nature referred the pleasure of the senses to the fulfilling of needs and the attainment of life's necessities. Pleasure, therefore, was handed down for the sake of both preserving life and propagating the species; it is not to be sought for itself, nor is it the "end," and for that reason, it ought not even be called a "good," as we have frequently demonstrated. 

¶ Archytas the Pythagorean <note>A 4th-century BCE Greek philosopher and mathematician, known as a friend of Plato and a leader in Tarentum.</note> also used this argument against bodily pleasure: that causes and the things that follow from those causes ought always to be related. Therefore, he thinks no one should doubt that if a thing is the source of many evils, it cannot itself be a good. It is clear that for the sake of pleasure, all the pestiferous disturbances of the mind are born: adulteries, debaucheries, homicides, thefts, dissensions, and finally all crimes. From these things it is concluded (as he thinks) that pleasure seems not only not a good, but a certain maximum and detestable evil. By the same reasoning, Antisthenes the Socratic <note>A pupil of Socrates and a foundational figure for the Cynic school of philosophy.</note> proves that bodily pleasure is the extreme and highest of evils, because that which is the cause and origin of all evils can rightly be judged the worst of all. And since all sins proceed from ignorance, and there can be nothing which is equally...

We see that those virtues placed in action are of the first kind. For it is their specific property to render the soul free from all the tumult of the <term>perturbations: in Stoic and Platonic philosophy, these are the irrational passions—fear, lust, grief, and joy—that disturb the mind's peace</term> and to make it tranquil. Yet it is evident that the condition of pleasure is contrary to both. For it agitates the soul with countless and most burning passions, as if by certain furies, so that it is far removed from that tranquility which nature so greatly requires. And since the human race holds a middle position between God and the beasts—and for that reason seems to deservedly share in the nature of both—Trismegistus believes that one can migrate and, as it were, be transformed into either one. 

For he who uses his mind primarily surely leads the most blessed life of the immortal gods, while he who uses his body and senses leads the life of beasts. Therefore, since the use of pleasure exists in the body and the senses, he who is most devoted to it not only does not ascend to those things which are better and more divine, but does not even retain the station and dignity of his own nature; he slips, as it were, from soul to body, from mind to senses, and from man to beast.

In the same way, all things that are good follow from that which is the highest and primary good,

### Chapter III. Objections of the Peripatetics against the Platonic definition of pleasure.

This, then, is Plato’s divine opinion on pleasure, in which Hermes Trismegistus, all the Pythagoreans, and all the more excellent followers of Socrates agree without any doubt. But the <term>Peripatetics: the followers of Aristotle, so named because they walked about (*peripatein*) while teaching</term>—men who are certainly sharp, but perhaps more fond of argument in this matter than of truth—strive to subvert and deprave Plato’s excellent and divine opinion with certain subtleties of their own. 

There are three points on which they attempt to criticize the Platonists. First, because Plato called pleasure a **motion** in his definition; for they say that every motion is either fast or slow, but no pleasure can be called fast or slow. Rather, it must be called either brief or long-lasting. Nor can any motion exist as a whole all at once; instead, one part of the movement must always succeed another, so that as one part ends, another is born, and two parts of a motion cannot wait for each other. Pleasure, by contrast, becomes a whole all at once, and all its parts—if we may...

Next, they find fault with Plato because he called pleasure the "filling of a deficiency" <note>Plato’s theory that pleasure is like drinking when thirsty: the "filling" of a hole or need.</note>. They think this is false because pleasure resides in the soul, whereas "filling" occurs in the body; nor do they agree that all pleasure is of such a kind as to coincide with the filling of a deficiency. Indeed, those pleasures perceived by the eyes, ears, and nostrils from shapes, sounds, and smells do not fulfill any prior deficiency. Furthermore, there is a certain ineffable pleasure in contemplation <note>The act of deep intellectual or spiritual thought</note> that fills nothing lacking. For that is proper to the mind, and the mind truly neither lacks any support nor can it be refilled by any means; for being filled and, conversely, being emptied, is appropriate for bodies, which can be both full and empty. But since the soul is simple and incorporeal <note>without a physical body</note>, those things can in no way happen to it. 
In the third place, they argue against the fact that Plato said no pleasures are good, and most are bad. But they believe many are excellent and most worthy of praise—those that are undertaken from honorable actions. For such actions seem most pleasant, and the pleasure inherent in them is the best and purest.

<meta>This page continues the technical philosophical debate regarding the nature of pleasure and the soul. The previous page established that the Peripatetics (Aristotelians) argue pleasure is an instantaneous state rather than a time-consuming "motion." This page counters that argument by distinguishing between the divisible nature of the body and the simple, indivisible nature of the soul, and clarifies Plato’s specific definitions in the "Gorgias" and "Timaeus."</meta>

-># ON PLEASURE #<-

It is necessary that what remains in the undivided <note>The author is distinguishing between the physical body, which can be divided into parts, and the soul or mind, which is a single, unified entity.</note> has already stripped off the nature of the body. For this reason, since every body is extended and divisible, it is necessary that whenever it acts or undergoes something, or is moved from one place to another, the closer and front parts must either suffer, act, or be turned before the rest. Therefore, all motion of bodies requires a span of time and is stretched out by a certain succession from what is prior to what is later. The soul, however, is indivisible and simple, having no internal distinction or distance between parts. Therefore, the motion of the soul is indivisible and simple, and is completed as a whole in a single point of time. Hence, Thales of Miletus <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher often cited as the first Western philosopher.</note> said that nothing is faster than the mind. When, therefore, pleasure was defined by Plato not as a motion of the body, but of the soul, nothing truly prevents it from being a motion and also existing as a whole all at once. This is especially true since in the Platonic books, "motion" signifies not only flux and succession (as the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: Followers of Aristotle’s school, known for their focus on empirical observation and formal logic.</term> would have it) but also every operation and act.

Next, as for their claim that Plato called pleasure the "filling of a deficiency" and deficiency "pain," this might perhaps seem less than true. For in the *Gorgias* <note>One of Plato’s dialogues focusing on rhetoric and ethics.</note>, he himself maintains that pleasure consists in the act of filling. But no one—except those most unlike Plato—would say that "pleasure consists in pleasure," or that any other thing produced by nature consists in itself. Furthermore, in the same book, he says that the process of filling is "pleasurable," and deficiency is mostly "painful." But who speaks so foolishly as to call pleasure "pleasurable" or pain "painful"? Who would likewise say "beautiful beauty" or "just justice"? In the same way, Plato would not have called pleasure "pleasurable" nor pain "painful." Therefore, he did not intend for pain to be the deficiency itself, nor for filling to be pleasure itself. 

Moreover, he says that pleasure arises *from* the act of filling, and pain *from* want or lack. He himself, however, believes that nothing can be produced from itself. How then could pleasure, if it were the filling, be produced by the filling itself? Or how could pain, if it were the lack, be born from the lack? Furthermore, in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the nature of the physical world and human biology.</note>, he places pleasure in the senses and calls it a motion and an affection. A man of such stature would never say that an affection or the motion of the senses is a "filling." If someone reads in the *Gorgias* that pleasure is the filling of the body, they should consider that passage more carefully; they will eventually find that Plato does not hold this view himself, but that it is the opinion of Callicles—a most pleasure-seeking man—against whom Socrates disputes most sharply.

But the Peripatetics grant us this much: some nevertheless deny that all pleasure comes from the filling of a deficiency. This is especially true of that pleasure which contemplation brings us, and which resides in the mind...

It further clarifies that Plato viewed pleasure as a result of replenishment, rather than the act of replenishment itself, distancing him from the hedonistic views of Callicles.</summary>

For those words of Plato, in which he says pleasure is born from the filling of a lack, can (as it seems) be interpreted in two ways. For these two—lack and desire—are so mutually connected that one cannot be separated from the other. For we desire those things which we lack, nor do we desire anything that we did not lack before the longing; nor is anyone lacking without desiring, nor does one ever desire who does not lack. Thus it happens that both seem to be so mutually joined that one always accompanies the other. Therefore, among all the most excellent philosophers, this is the custom: that they frequently signify "desire" by the name "lack," and in the same way, they wish "lack" to be understood by the name of "desire." 

Whence Cicero rightly says: "He does not lack who does not desire" <note>original: "non caret... is, qui non desiderat"</note>. Socrates also used to deny that he lacked the riches and delights of ours for which others strive most ardently, because he by no means desired them. Epicurus <term>Epicurus: An ancient Greek philosopher who taught that the highest good is the absence of pain and fear, often misunderstood as advocating for luxury.</term> moreover, said that he who lacks is not the one who has little, but the one who desires more. Therefore, if anyone wishes to drive away lack, one must not add to their money, but rather subtract from their greed. 

And in the same way, when Plato says the "filling of a lack," he wanted it to be understood as the <insert>filling of desire</insert>. Now, longing is filled when it attains that which it was desiring; moreover, the filling of desire is nothing other than a certain attainment of that which had come into longing. <meta>This page continues the defense of the Platonic definition of pleasure as the "filling of a deficiency." ...[we] interpret Plato. The filling of a deficiency exists as the cause of pleasure. This occurs when a desire, which is in need—and which we call a "deficiency"—attains that which it longed for, enjoys its presence, and is, as it were, filled. That motion is immediately born in the senses, which we call sweetness, delight, and pleasure. Hence the Delian epigram <note>original: "epigramma deliacum"; an ancient Greek inscription at Delos famously stating that the most pleasant thing is to obtain what one loves.</note> says that it is most pleasant to possess the thing loved. Moreover, by this interpretation, in all the senses, those who have obtained the very thing they previously desired are soothed by a certain ineffable pleasure. 

And this is the first mode of responding by which the Platonists might escape the snares of the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: Followers of Aristotle, who often used rigorous logic to "trap" their philosophical opponents in contradictions.</term>. And if perhaps this interpretation seems too harsh to anyone, come, let us try another, lest our side seem to have succumbed to their darts. 

To fill a deficiency, then, what else is it but to attain that which you lack? Now, what do we lack but those things which can either preserve our well-being while it is present, restore it if lost, or in some other way bring us some utility? But we are humans. Now, "man" is, as the Peripatetics and Stoics believe, that which consists of a rational soul and a body. The Pythagoreans and Platonists, differing slightly from the others, think that man is a certain divine mind bound by earthly chains. Thus it happens that among other philosophers, the soul has the nature and name of a "part" of man, whereas among the Platonists, our soul stands as the whole man. 

Therefore, when Socrates was asked by Crito how he ordered himself to be buried, he said: "As you please, provided you catch me and I do not escape you" <note>A reference to Plato's *Phaedo*, where Socrates argues that his true self—his soul—cannot be buried in a grave.</note>. And the same man, disputing with Alcibiades in Plato, proves by many arguments that man is nothing other than the soul. The body is not the man, but the man's property. External things, however, belong not to the man, but to fortune. Yet he does not call our soul "man" always and everywhere; rather, as long as it lives in the celestial seats, it is called by the Platonists now a "god," now even a "daemon" <note>In the Greek sense, a *daemon* is a tutelary spirit or a being between gods and men, not necessarily evil.</note>. 

But when it is enclosed in earthly dwellings, it receives the name of "humanity" <note>original: "humanitatis"; here the author plays on the Latin etymology of *homo* (man) coming from *humus* (earth/ground).</note> from the very nature of the ground in which it is submerged. Thus the most noble Platonic Origen used to assert that a man can be converted into a daemon or a god, and sometimes even migrate into beasts. Seneca likewise, a great student of Plato, called our soul a god guest-hosting in a human body. But all these followed Heraclitus, Empedocles, and Pythagoras. For Pythagoras asserts in these words that our soul is transferred from a man into a god:

> Having laid aside the body, when you go free to the upper air,
> You shall escape being a man, having become a god of the nourishing ether.

¶ Therefore (to return to our subject), since a human being is, in the opinion of the **Aristotelians**, a creature consisting of a rational soul and a body, but according to **Plato**, a certain divine mind that makes use of the service of an earthly body, it follows that we must certainly undertake the care of two things: the soul and the body. The care of the soul (as Plato commands) should be for its own sake alone, while all care for the body ought to be directed toward the soul, like a servant to a master. Therefore, there are two kinds of things that we need. We lack those things which will benefit the soul, and those which will benefit the body. Those things benefit the body which either restore or preserve life, health, strength, beauty, or its own specific nature. However, all those things are fitting for the soul which contribute anything toward the best character and toward the knowledge of reality. To these, add above all others those things that benefit both soul and body, which seem similar and related to either one. For "like is preserved by like" (as the saying goes), and each individual thing seeks its own well-being. These, then, are the things that humans require. For this reason, when these things are present—or at least those which have a certain appearance and likeness to them—we are moved by pleasure. Indeed, if things that seem good to us are present, they bring delight. From this, it follows that **opinion precedes pleasure**; for as the **Stoics** <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that taught that our internal judgments and opinions determine our emotional responses to the world.</note> believe, nothing can be pleasant to anyone unless each person considers it related to themselves and good.

¶ Since bodily pleasure is perceived through the senses, and there are five types of these, there will similarly be five kinds of pleasures: one is perceived by **touch**, another by **taste**, **smells** provide another, and the **ears** and **eyes** supply the remaining ones. And these senses are related to each other in such a way that they maintain a certain order of both location and nature. The eyes are the purest and—as the Platonic *Timaeus* <note>original: "timaeus platonicus"; referring to Plato’s dialogue regarding the creation of the universe and the nature of the physical world.</note> discusses and proves—are related to the nature of fire and light. The ears hold the second rank in order of purity and are compared to air. The nostrils then possess the third degree of refinement and, being composed of a denser nature, hold a middle place between air and water. Next, the organ of tasting is denser and very similar to the nature of water. Finally, in the last degree of refinement <note>original: "tenuitatis gradu"; the author is ranking the senses from the most "ethereal" (fire/light) to the most "solid."</note>, those parts with which we touch are assigned; for these approach the nature of the body more closely and are attributed to the density of the earth. You see these five senses, arranged step by step, relating to each other so that those placed in the more eminent part of the body also obtain a higher order of purity, and different senses are related to different elements. Because we have discussed this more extensively in the commentaries we published on Plato’s *Timaeus*, it will suffice to have touched on it briefly here. Since, therefore, certain solid things [pertain] to the sense of touch...

For it is delighted by those flavors that have the nature of a cooked and ripe moisture. Indeed, since the sense of taste itself (as the **Platonists** <note>Followers of Plato who believed that the physical world is a reflection of higher mathematical and spiritual truths.</note> believe) is composed of the same proportion, it follows that when a similar and, as it were, familiar substance approaches, the sense rests most sweetly within it. Furthermore, the power of **smell** is greatly refreshed by those odors that are mixed between the nature of water and air, which is perceived in fruits and flowers; for smell itself was allotted that same nature from its origin. **Hearing**, moreover, is delighted by sounds of the sort that are fashioned from the purest air and consist of the same harmony by which the ears themselves are composed. Thus we see that, due to the diversity of nature, some people are delighted by gentler harmonies, others by more intense ones, some by deeper tones, and others by clearer ones. To the **eyes**, however, because they are most familiar with light, those things seem most pleasing whose nature is tempered by a light most similar to their own; such things are all those that result from the most beautiful tempering of colors, which all proceed from light. 

Nor do we require these things, which we draw in through the senses, only for the sake of increasing life and repairing our nature, but also for attaining the skill of the mind. From this it follows that the senses require certain excellent things offered from the outside for two reasons: first, because they are kindred and similar to themselves (for it is necessary that individual things be preserved and perfected by their likes); and second, because they can provide instruction for the knowledge of things and arts—the pursuit of which is most greatly desired by us. Whenever, therefore, those things of which we have spoken are offered to the senses and admitted deep within for our enjoyment, that lack <term>indigentia</term> <note>original: "indigentia"; refers to a state of being "unfilled" or lacking a necessary component for wholeness.</note> of the senses, which previously gave birth to desire, is filled. And that pleasure which we seek occurs from this filling of the lack <term>repletio</term>. 

This is, therefore, the second interpretation of the **Platonic definition**, which I believe no one, provided they are of sound mind, will find fault with. For this reason, enough has been said of these things; let us proceed to the rest. ¶ There are three questions proposed by the **Aristotelians** <note>Followers of Aristotle, who often focused on empirical observation and logic to challenge Plato’s more metaphysical theories.</note> against **Plato**: the first is that he falsely called pleasure a "motion" <term>motio</term>; another is that not every pleasure can be a "filling" <term>repletio</term>, nor can it arise from a filling. To all these points, I believe a sufficient answer has already been given—not indeed by my own meager wit (for I do not claim so much for myself), but by those things which have been most extensively disputed by Plato himself. The final objection of **Aristotle**, however, was that very many pleasures exist contrary to what Plato had denied...

### Chapter 5. Various opinions on what pleasure is. The first opinion, that of Aristotle.

<margin>a</margin>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**Aristotle**, however—to come to his opinion—uses the name of "pleasure" more broadly, and thus he intends to signify not only that delight which inheres in the senses, but also that which resides in the mind. But as to what pleasure itself is, he seems to hint at it rather than express it clearly. Nevertheless, what he disputes concerning this in the seventh and tenth books of the *Ethics* <note>Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*, the foundational text for Western virtue ethics.</note> can be interpreted in the way I shall describe. There are (to use Aristotle's words) three powers of the soul, one of which is common to us and to plants, which they call the **vegetative power** <term>vegetative power: the basic biological functions of growth and reproduction</term>. Its duties are three: to nourish its own body, to grow it, and finally to produce another like itself. The second nature of the soul he calls the **sensing power**, which exists in common between us and the other animals. Of the senses, some are internal and others external. The external ones, which are more relevant to our purpose, are five—very well known by the common division. The third power of the soul belongs only to humans out of all the types of mortal living beings, and this he calls the **intellect** and the **mind**. To these he adds the power of movement; but let us set that aside, as it has no bearing on our current purpose. Regarding the first nature of the soul, which belongs to plants, the ancient philosophers held diverse views. Indeed, **Plato** thinks that the souls of trees and herbs have a certain silent appetite, which he calls the "striving of nature" <note>original: *naturae nixum*</note>. **Empedocles** <note>A Pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed that the world is composed of four elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note> maintained that not only a natural inclination, but even sensation is present in plants. **Anaxagoras** and **Democritus**, however, believe that they are affected by pleasure and pain, and that they possess the power not only of sensing, but also of thinking and understanding. But **Aristotle** thinks they are endowed with neither reason nor sensation at all, and that they do not participate in any pleasure. Consequently, that power of nourishing and growing contributes nothing to Aristotle’s [opinion]...

Therefore, the remaining powers of the soul to which he attributes **pleasure** <note>original: *uoluptas*</note> are two: one of which (to use his own words) he calls the **intellect**, and the other the **sense**, and to these he assigns their own actions, which he calls "cognitions" <note>The author is explaining that for Aristotle, both thinking and sensing are ways the soul "knows" or processes the world.</note>. He intends the operation of the intellect, or (to speak in Latin) of the **mind** and **reason**, to be called intelligence, thought, and contemplation. 

Truly, he calls the operation of sight "vision," of hearing "audition," of smell "smelling," of taste "tasting," and finally of touch "touching." Thus, sight is the power and nature of the soul itself by which one is able to see, while vision is the action itself—that is, the act of seeing. He follows the same logic for the other senses. 

Regarding vision (to follow one example for all), he says it has two principal origins from which it arises as if from causes: namely, the **sight** itself in which the power resides, and furthermore the **external object** which is perceived, by which the sight is stimulated so that it may see. Aristotle calls "sight" the power and faculty of the soul, and that which is perceived by sight the "object." He says that "perfect vision" occurs when both the power of the soul is in its best state and the object to be seen is by its own nature the best and, moreover, in harmony with the nature of the soul. But if either of these is lacking, the vision will be imperfect; however, when both concur as one, it is perfect. 

Furthermore, he argues that whatever vision is perfect is also pleasant; that which is more perfect is more pleasant; and that which is most perfect is most pleasant. Therefore (to repeat the same point often), because vision is perfect, it is pleasant; thus, the **perfection of vision** appears to be a certain pleasantness. For this reason, conversely, the pleasantness of vision is its perfection. 

Since "pleasantness" and "pleasure" <note>original: *iocunditas, ac uoluptas*</note> signify the same thing regarding the present topic, he concludes that **pleasure** is the perfection of vision. We wish it to be understood that what has been said of sight applies also to the other senses and to the mind itself. For in all of them there is a proper <term>operation</term> <note>original: *operatio*; in Aristotelian philosophy, this refers to the active exercise of a faculty, like "thinking" being the operation of the "intellect."</note>: in hearing, audition; in smell, smelling; and similarly for the others. 

Therefore, according to the common definition in Aristotle, **pleasure** is nothing other than a certain perfection of the operation of the soul, which is the same as the perfection of cognition. Since pleasure inheres in all the senses, the pleasure of sight will be the perfection of vision; of hearing, the perfection of audition; of taste, the perfection of tasting; and so on for the rest, so that the pleasure of each is the perfection of its own proper operation. 

However, according to Aristotle, there is a twofold perfection: one is **primary**, the other is **annexed**. That is "primary" which exists as a part of the nature of that which it completes—such as the human soul, for this is the perfection of a human being and a certain part of human substance. We call that "annexed" perfection which, while it is not a part of the substance, nevertheless follows the substance itself, and as if it co-

Wherefore, it is not without reason that pleasure is defined as a certain attached perfection of that operation to which it belongs—such as **contemplation**, vision, hearing, and all the rest. And if the action is honorable, Aristotle calls the pleasure itself honorable. But if it is shameful, the pleasure is also shameful. If it is neutral, the pleasure is indeed neutral. In this matter, Aristotle differs from most of the ancient philosophers. 

¶ For some have thought pleasure to be the nature of a certain thing that suits us, imposed upon the senses, like the sweet taste of honey absorbed by the tongue. Others, however, define pleasure as the **perception** of a suitable thing. For example, when the sweetness of a liquid is applied to the taste, they called neither the sweetness itself, nor the liquid, nor the sense of taste "pleasure," but rather the tasting itself—that is, the perception of the sweetness. **Avicenna** <note>original: *Auicenna*; a Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works were foundational to the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> seems to approve of their opinion. 

Some, however, did not want even the perception of the sweet liquid itself to be pleasure, but rather that **judgment** of the mind which follows the first apprehension of the senses, which most call the **imagination** <note>original: *phantasia*; here referring to the faculty that forms a mental image of an object before the intellect judges it.</note>. For first, the sense knows that the taste is sweet; afterwards, it judges that it is good and to be accepted. Most think that this judgment is signified by the name of "pleasure." 

Nor were there lacking those who called neither the sweet quality imposed on the senses, nor the perception of that quality, nor the judgment "pleasure." Instead, they called it a certain commotion of the body and sense, which follows the perception and judgment themselves—such as a **melting**, a pouring forth, an elevation, an exultation, petulance, and similar things. ### Chapter 6. Opinions of the Peripatetics concerning pleasure.

<margin>a</margin>
Aristotle, however, seems to call none of these things "pleasure." Instead, he views it as a certain perfection of apprehension itself. Just as the perception of sweetness comes first, from this something else is born as its companion and an attached perfection; and this very thing is pleasure. But what exactly this kind of perfection is, which he calls pleasure, he never (it seems) sufficiently explained. The **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, named for the "peripatos" or covered walkway in the Lyceum where they walked while discussing philosophy.</note>, however, who followed Aristotle, wishing to explain and bring to light what had been obscurely stated by their leader, were divided into various opinions. For some placed pleasure in the senses, while others placed it in the **appetite** <note>original: *appetitus*; referring to the faculty of desire or the soul's drive toward a goal.</note> that follows the senses. And those who placed it in the senses also interpret Aristotle in different ways. Indeed, some think there are two perceptions in the senses: the first seems to proceed and flow into the mind from things offered from the outside, while the second, having originated more from the mind, extends toward those external things. For first, the mind perceives sweetness (for example), and this first perception seems to arise from the pleasantness of the object itself. Then the mind considers that it has obtained that sweetness—that it perceives it, possesses it, and enjoys it. They judged that this pleasant perception of the mind—whether called a thought, a meditation, or an observation—was what Aristotle named pleasure. Thus, pleasure is that very consideration through which one realizes they are enjoying the presence of good things.

¶ Some think that it is not the sense itself, but rather when it notices it has obtained sweetness, it presents itself and is (so to speak) lifted up, conceiving and carrying a certain cheerfulness; they believe this is what Aristotle called pleasure. Therefore, they define pleasure as an **elevation** or **cheerfulness** of the mind that has already attained the good it desired. 

¶ But those who placed pleasure in that part of the soul with which we desire think there are two properties of appetite. One is that we are moved and inclined toward those goods which are far from us and which we have not yet reached. The other consists in that which we have already gained and attained. They call the first **desire** <note>original: *cupiditas*</note> and the second **rest** <note>original: *quies*</note>. They claim the first is full of trouble, worry, care, and anxiety, but the second is infused with an ineffable sweetness. This, they say, is what the leader of the Peripatetics called pleasure, so that pleasure is nothing other than a certain boundary or "rest" of the appetite in a good that has already been achieved. Hence **Lucretius** <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), Roman poet and Epicurean philosopher.</note> says: "The rest of men and the pleasure of the gods." <note>original: "requies hominum divumque voluptas." A variation on the opening of Lucretius's *On the Nature of Things*, which famously addresses Venus as the pleasure of men and gods.</note>

¶ However, as to what this "rest" itself is, not everyone [agrees] in the same way...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the followers of Aristotle (the Peripatetics) define pleasure, moving from the idea of "rest" to the psychological process of "diffusion" and "assent" toward a good. It transitions into a comparison between Aristotle's views and those of Plato.</meta>

...have explained. For others define rest itself as a kind of cessation or end of desire. They argue that the **appetite** <note>original: *appetitus*; the faculty of the soul that drives a person toward a perceived good.</note>, once it has obtained the good it desired, stops its seeking. Therefore, to be free from worry and anxiety—a state of rest—is what Aristotle calls pleasure. Thus, as these thinkers define it, pleasure is the freedom from all the worry and anxiety of desiring, once the sought-after good has been acquired.

¶ Some **Peripatetics** <note>The "Walkers," followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note>, however, added something else to this idea of freedom. They argue that to simply be without trouble does not yet possess the full and perfect nature of pleasure. Instead, it becomes whole and absolute if, in that very state, every desire comes to rest in such a way that it not only seeks nothing further, but clings to this good it enjoys with all its strength and power, agrees within itself that it is enough, and is deeply poured out into it. Therefore, as these men believe, pleasure is the **assent** <note>original: *assensio*; a mental agreement or "yes" to the present state.</note> and the **diffusion** <note>original: *diffusio*; a spreading out or expansion of the soul toward an object.</note> of the appetite into the good it possesses. This is why, in the midst of pleasures, the whole body seems to melt and flow away; for all the power and movement of the mind and body is inclined toward and utterly seized by the object presented from the outside. Indeed, this kind of diffusion must exist not only in the limbs and parts of the body, but also in the appetite and the very nature of the soul. For the body is never "poured out" into anything unless by the impulse of the appetite and the power of the mind. For this reason, it is necessary that the appetite and the mind themselves also be diffused and most greedily fixed and clinging to that which seems to suit their own nature. Therefore, every such effort of the mind and appetite—to couple with, cling to, and be fixed upon the good already possessed—contains pleasure. In the view of these thinkers, pleasure seems to be nothing other than to assent to, cling to, and be fixed upon a present good, and to flow into it and be deeply poured out within it. You must understand that this occurs in the mind, and specifically in that part of the mind called the "power of desiring." For while a similar movement is found in heat, blood, spirits, and the whole body, that is neither pleasure nor any part of pleasure. Rather, from that diffusion and assent which is in the mind (which they call pleasure), those physical effects—the liquefying and pouring out of the body—proceed as if they were certain "footprints" of inward pleasure. For as these things appear in the body, such is the nature of pleasure as it exists in the soul.

...opinion of our **Plato** <note>Plato (c. 427–348 BCE), the Greek philosopher. The author refers to him as "ours," a common way for Renaissance Humanists to show reverence.</note> does not differ, except that **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE), Plato's student who often used broader categories in his natural philosophy.</note> speaks more broadly using the same name for "pleasure," calling both the delight that is in the mind and that which is in the senses by that name. Plato, however, calls "pleasure" <note>original: *uoluptatem*</note> that which happens to the senses; but that which is in the mind, he names "joy" <note>original: *gaudium*</note>. Furthermore, sometimes Plato himself confuses the names of pleasure and joy, using either term to signify both. In name, therefore, they differ either not at all, or barely and in the smallest degree; that they agree in the actual reality, several of Plato's books can be witnesses, as well as many Platonists—philosophers by no means to be looked down upon. For **Apuleius**, **Calcidius**, **Contius**, and the noble Platonist **Ptolemy** <note>These are later commentators and followers of Plato; Calcidius is famous for his commentary on the *Timaeus*.</note> interpret Plato’s opinion (placed in very obscure words in the *Timaeus*) in the following manner, which I will briefly relate. They say that by "sense," Plato certainly means the first perception of the soul which is born from a **passion** <note>original: *passione*; here meaning an impression or something "suffered" or experienced by the body from the outside.</note> of the body itself. For they say that certain "species" <note>original: *species*; used here as "images" or "forms" of things.</note> of all things that are to be known flow toward us, are drawn in through the openings of the senses, and are imprinted and sealed upon the **spirit** <note>original: *spiritu*; the "animal spirit," a refined vapor believed to reside in the brain's ventricles and act as the bridge between body and soul.</note> which is in the ventricles of the brain. These species of things, shaped in the spirit (which is a most thin and translucent body), strike the soul and cause it to gaze upon and perceive those very external objects whose images these are. We see that this perception of the soul is born from that very passion and impulse of the body. Since the spirit is moved by external bodies, it strikes the soul with a similar image and forms it. Therefore, since a perception of this kind is born from the impulse of the spirit, it follows that it proceeds from a "passion" of the body—that is, from a strike and a motion. In this, the good Platonist **Aurelius Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine (354–430 CE), whom the author classifies as a Platonist because of his heavy use of Neoplatonic philosophy.</note> followed him in that book titled *On the Quantity of the Soul*. "Sensation is," he says, "a passion of the body that is not hidden from the soul." <note>original: *Sensus est passio corporis per se ipsam non latens animam.*</note> That is, through the very appearance of the body drawn in by the senses, the passion of that same body is perceived by a certain first and proper image. From these things it happens that we feel by a double passion of the body. For by the impulse of the brain and the spirit, we apprehend the passions of external bodies. But the Platonists divide that passion which our own body receives from the outside into two parts: one of which soothes and softens the body, and does not so much strike the limbs and vitals as it strokes and tickles them; the other, however, shakes them more roughly and harshly. When the soul consents to that first motion of the body, whose nature it is to soothe, **pleasure** is created. When it shrinks from and revolts against the other, which we call harsh, they say it brings **pain**. The soul, moreover, attends to the motion of the body when it gladly adheres to it, is fastened to it, joined to it, drenched in it, and in it most sweetly...

Therefore, **Saint Augustine** <note>Aurelius Augustinus (354–430 CE), the influential Christian theologian and philosopher whose works bridged Neoplatonism and Christianity.</note> defines pleasure as the union of desire itself with that which it loves. Indeed, in this they do not differ at all; for the soul never rests unless it consents, nor does it consent unless it also rests.

### Chapter VIII. How the Peripatetics divide pleasure, and on the powers of the soul.

<margin>9</margin>
**W**hat the Platonists and Peripatetics handed down regarding the definition of pleasure, and how their discussions agree on the same point, has now, I believe, been sufficiently declared. Let us now examine what the Peripatetics thought regarding the division of pleasure. The Peripatetics believe that the entire nature of man consists of **soul** <note>original: *anima*</note> and body. They distribute the soul into two parts, as pertains to the question at hand: namely, the **mind** <note>original: *mens*</note> and **sense**. Furthermore, they hold that the mind has a twin power and nature. One of these is engaged in the investigation of truth, the other in deliberation and action; the former (to use their words) they call the **contemplative intellect**, the latter the **active intellect**. They say it is the property of the former to investigate the causes, properties, and progressions of those things contained in the order of nature, and that it is content with the contemplation of truth alone. But they want the work of the latter to be called discerning through deliberation what should be done or avoided. Regarding the senses, they call some internal and others external. The internal senses (as **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), the medieval Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to Western university study.</note>, the sharpest of the Peripatetic interpreters, wishes) they divide into four types. The first of these collects and perceives all the images that are drawn in through the five external senses; for this reason, they call it the **common sense** <note>original: *communis sensus*. In Renaissance psychology, this was a specific faculty that combined data from the five senses into a single experience.</note>. Then, the second power is named by them the **imagination** <note>original: *vis imaginandi*</note>, whose duty it is—though it perceives nothing itself—to retain the images received from the prior senses and bring them to the third nature of sensing, which they call the **phantasy** <note>original: *phantasia*</note> or the power of estimating and thinking. They believe it is the work of this power, once those images are received, to judge and perceive what or of what kind that thing is whose images they are; and then to entrust those very things which it has discerned, joined, or conceived by judging, to the final part of the brain and sense itself, which they call **memory**, to be preserved. Those external senses...

...they divide those senses which are more powerful for what we seek into five types, which are known to all. They believe that these relate to one another in such a way that those which occupy a higher place in the body are purer and simpler. The remaining ones are coarser. Therefore, sight is seen to be purer than hearing, hearing than smell, the power of smelling than taste, and finally taste than touch. For light and colors belong to sight; sounds to the ears; odors to the nostrils; flavors to taste; while solidity, softness, heat, and cold belong to the power of touch. For this reason—just as light and color are purer than sound, sound than odors, and these than flavor, while flavors are purer than those things subjected to touch—so sight excels hearing, hearing excels the sense of the nostrils, this sense excels taste, and finally taste excels touch in purity and dignity.

To these five powers of sensing, five equal organs (as they call them) are attributed in the body as subjects and, as it were, certain foundations. These seem to be nothing other than certain states of the body, which some call "dispositions," others "qualities," and some "complexions" <note>original: *complexiones*; in the medical and philosophical tradition of the time, this refers to the specific temperament or balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—within a person or a specific organ.</note>, which arise differently in different parts of the body through various mixtures of the elements and are the foundations of the different senses. For there is one state of the body by which the power of seeing is sustained and flourishes, and another by which the power of hearing does; the same must be judged for all the rest. In addition to these five states or subjects, five equal instruments—the more solid members of the body—are established and devised as certain "receptacles" in which both the senses and the states themselves might reside. For the eyes, like small vessels, receive the state and power of seeing; and the other members of the body, as is clear, are assigned to the other qualities and senses in a certain fixed order. 

Furthermore, certain movements are innate to these members and instruments, which seem to demonstrate the innermost feeling of each. Thus, in the disturbances of the mind <note>original: *animi perturbationibus*; often refers to "passions" or "emotions" like fear, anger, or joy that agitate the soul.</note> itself, we see the body now turn red, now turn pale; in some cases it contracts and grows rigid, while in others it flows away and, as it were, melts. **Aristotle** <note>The famous Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) whose system of logic and natural philosophy dominated university education in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> considers pleasure to relate to all these things we have now listed in a long sequence in such a way that a certain perfect and absolute pleasure exists in that mind which he calls "contemplative." It then gradually degenerates in the other parts of man. For, as he thinks, for seven reasons, that first pleasure appears to be more perfect than the other pleasure which is placed in the "active" mind.

[investi]gation and contemplation is honorable and most worthy of praise. But when the other mind <note>The "active" or "practical" mind.</note> deliberates on things to be done or avoided, and rejoices in the choice of such things, not all that pleasure is usually praised. That which comes from these counsels and actions which oppose the best laws is rightly censured—as if the mind should rejoice in a plan undertaken against the safety of its country and parents, or against what is right. When it is delighted by honorable actions, the pleasure is honorable. But when it is delighted by neutral things <note>original: *mediis*; referring to morally indifferent actions that are neither inherently good nor evil, known in philosophy as *adiaphora*.</note>, that pleasure too is neutral. Thus it happens that in the first mind <note>The contemplative mind.</note> there exists only one kind of joy, and that is worthy of praise. In the other, however, three kinds (as we have said) are found: the honorable, the shameful, and the neutral.

¶ That reasoning too, which he [Aristotle] uses in the tenth book on ethics <note>original: *decimo de moribus*; referring to Book 10 of Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note>, is of no small value to the subject we are discussing. For he says that we are able to contemplate longer than we can perform any other kind of action. And since the inquiry into truth is firmer and more stable than any duty of acting, it is necessary that the pleasure which comes from it is also more stable and perfect.

¶ Add to this that the life and contemplation of the wise man needs fewer things than the civic life. Therefore his pleasure, since it is content with few and minimal things, will without doubt be more self-sufficient and be judged more perfect.

¶ There is, moreover, that part of the mind to which we attribute the contemplation of nature; it is more perfect than the other, as no one would deny, and for that reason it brings a pleasure superior to all others.

¶ And since the motion and activity of the active mind is directed toward something else—either to be chosen or rejected—but the contemplation of the first mind is content with itself and desires nothing at all besides itself, it is established by necessary reason that the pleasure proper to contemplation is desired only for its own sake. But the other pleasure seeks something besides itself as an end, and therefore that first kind is to be judged much more excellent.

¶ To these things is added the fact that the first and more perfect part of anything holds, as it were, the place and name of the whole. From this it follows that although each human is composed of many parts, yet that part assigned to contemplation—because it excels the others in dignity—encompasses almost the entire nature of man. Indeed, that part is what man most truly is, as Aristotle says. Wherefore, its action is especially suited to us and contains an ineffable pleasure; for those things which are more closely related by nature are accustomed to bring greater pleasure.
