# ON PLEASURE

¶ Aristotle’s final argument proves that the proper activity of the immortal gods consists in contemplation alone. For this reason, nothing in us—except for that "first mind" (as we have said) <note>Referring to the *intellectus* or the highest part of the soul capable of grasping eternal truths.</note> and contemplation, and the pleasure arising from it—appears to be akin to God. If pleasure of this kind is the most divine because it alone is suited to the immortal gods, it will rightly be judged superior to all other pleasures. ¶ Aristotle used these arguments so that he might place the pleasure of contemplation above that which is perceived through action. 

But let us now come to those pleasures which, as it were, tickle the senses and flow into them with a certain sweetness. We find these divided by Aristotle into two species: some appear to be natural, while others are against nature. He calls those "natural" which, because they restore our nature, are sought by all or by most people. He divides these natural pleasures into two equal parts: some are common to all living creatures alike, while others are in some way specific and related to individuals according to the diversity of their nature. 

For it is characteristic of a common and natural desire <note>original: *libidinis*; here used in the broad sense of "appetite" or "drive."</note> and pleasure that all creatures seek food, drink, and the use of Venus <note>original: *ueneris usum*; a common euphemism for sexual intercourse.</note>. However, the fact that individuals are delighted in various ways by specific and certain things according to the diversity of their nature—and that different things happen to be more pleasing to different beings—belongs to natural but "specific" pleasure. 

For since that which is agreeable to its nature seems pleasant to each thing, and since the inclinations and natures of various living creatures are different, it is necessary that those things which are agreeable to different animals also differ. And for that reason, a certain and, as it were, specific desire and pleasure (as Heraclitus says) belongs to individual living creatures. For what is suited to its own nature delights each one; "his own pleasure draws each man" <note>original: *trahit sua quenque uoluptas*; a famous phrase from Virgil’s *Eclogues* (2.65), here used to support the Aristotelian idea that nature dictates desire.</note>. 

And these are what he calls natural pleasures. He holds that those "against nature," on the other hand, are those from which almost the entire human race shrinks in horror. He divides these into three types: some arise from a shameful and corrupt nature, others from the worst habits, and some from diseases and unfortunate accidents. Aristotle writes that it happens through a perversity of nature that a certain woman was driven by an intense desire to cut open the wombs of pregnant women and devour the infants, or what they say of certain savage tribes <term>around the Pontus</term> <note>The Black Sea region, which ancient Greeks often associated with "barbaric" or "uncivilized" customs.</note>. For some are said to delight in raw meat, others in human flesh. Some are said to trade their children to be eaten at banquets. The <term>Troglodytes</term> <note>Literally "cave-dwellers"; legendary tribes often described by ancient geographers as having strange diets.</note> are said to feed on the flesh of serpents. It also happens to many through long-standing habit, such as the pulling out of hair or the biting of nails...

<margin>1</margin> These three types of pleasures that are against nature are considered by Aristotle to belong not to a human, but to a wild and monstrous <note>original: *immanis*; implying something vast, savage, or beyond the human scale.</note> nature; for this reason, he calls such pleasures "monstrous" in the seventh book of the work titled *On Morals* <note>Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book VII, which deals with continence and bestial states.</note>. From these things we have listed so far, there appear to be three kinds of pleasures according to Aristotle. The first consists in **contemplation**; the second is engaged in **deliberation and action**; and both indeed reside in the mind, though in a different way (as we have said). Then, we placed the third kind in the **senses**, and we divided it into two species: namely, the *natural* and those *against nature*. Of the natural ones, we call one "common" and the other "proper." Furthermore, we noted that of the monstrous pleasures, one arises from a corrupt and shameful nature, another from a vicious habit, and a third from disease. 

Therefore, the first pleasure, which is born from contemplation, he calls **divine** because it is most like God, and because it belongs to us not insofar as we are humans, but as we are like gods. However, that pleasure which is proper to the active mind, he calls **honorable** <note>original: *honestam*; referring to moral beauty and virtue.</note> indeed, but not divine. For honor <note>original: *honestas*</note> is not divinity itself, but a certain perfect likeness and image of divinity; thus the second mind and its pleasure descend from the first, because divinity is attributed to the first, but the likeness of divinity to the second. 

But those pleasures which soothe the body can no longer be partakers of divinity, nor any more of honor, since honor exists as the grace, beauty, and adornment of the mind alone. And yet, this adornment and the harmony of all parts is called *honor* in the disposition of the mind, *moderation* in the affections, *modesty* in actions, *order* in works, and *beauty* <note>original: *forma*</note> in the body by most Platonists. Nevertheless, even those pleasures which move the senses have a certain small image of honor. For those among them that obey the laws of the mind and reason, and for that reason become moderated, seem to imitate the nature of the honorable and the becoming because of this very moderation. In the same way, the others excel one another in purity and dignity according to that same order.

...those things in which we ought to rejoice or grieve, most of the ancient philosophers called "pleasure" and "pain." Others, however, judged that **pleasure** is the restoration of nature made manifest to the senses, while **pain** is the dissolution and lessening of that which is proper to nature. Besides these internal motions, certain external gestures follow which provide signs of hidden affections; indeed, there have been those who called these very outward signs by the names of "pleasure" and "pain."

But the brevity of this little work seems to require that we put an end to the Aristotelian discussion. This shall be done now, provided we first give this warning: whenever in this discussion "pleasure" is placed by us in the **mind**, it should be understood as being situated in that part of the mind which desires and wills something. For one part of the mind **thinks** and considers, another **remembers**, and a third **wills**; and though the mind might be divided in other ways, these categories will suffice for the present. Nor is the pleasure of the mind anything else but that very perfect and pleasing assent by which the **will** <term>will: the faculty of the mind that chooses a course of action or desires an object.</term> rests deeply in that which the mind considers, as if in something familiar and proper to itself.

->Chapter Ten. The opinions of the Stoics and others concerning pleasure and all the affections.<-

<margin>h</margin> These points should therefore be sufficient regarding **Aristotle's** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC) was a Greek philosopher whose "Peripatetic" school emphasized observation and the golden mean.</note> opinion. Let us move to the **Stoics**. The Stoics, then, whose leader was **Zeno** <note>Zeno of Citium (c. 334–262 BC), the founder of Stoicism, which taught that virtue is the only good and emotions should be governed by reason.</note>, define **joy** <note>original: *gaudium*</note> no differently than **Plato** does; however, they frequently confuse the names of **pleasure** <note>original: *uoluptas*</note> and **delight** <note>original: *lætitia*</note> with one another, designating the same thing by both names in their discussions.

For when we are moved in such a way that we are in some state of "good," they think this happens in two ways. When the soul is moved by **reason** <note>original: *ratione*</note> calmly and consistently, they want this to be called **joy**. But when it exults excessively and emptily, they call it **wanton delight** and **pleasure**. This they define as an irrational elevation of the soul that believes it is enjoying some great good. 

Nevertheless, **Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), a Roman statesman and philosopher who translated Greek concepts into Latin.</note> in the second book of *On Ends* <note>original: *De finibus*</note> wants us to use these Latin terms such that **joy** and **delight** reside only in the mind, while **pleasure**, though primarily attributed to the senses, can also be transferred to the mind. He states that **delight** is an elevation of the mind believing it enjoys a great good, while **joy** is a rational elevation of the mind. **Pleasure** is that sweetness perceived by the senses; and while it can be transferred to the mind, such pleasure in the mind is always to be censured.

### 1

<meta>catchword: Then; bleed-through throughout</meta>

He <note>original: "hæc ille"; referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator and philosopher mentioned on the previous page.</note> says these things when he disputes about philosophy and when he expresses the difference between these matters. Indeed, in other places, he often uses the name of **pleasure** <note>original: "voluptas"</note> for both **joy** <note>original: "gaudium"</note> and **gladness** <note>original: "lætitia"</note>. ¶ **Aristotle**, however, seems to differ greatly from **Cicero** and the **Stoics**, since he maintains that neither joy nor any pleasure should be called "gladness." For when he enumerated the *affections* <term>affections: "affectus" in Latin, referring to emotions or passions of the soul.</term> in that book which is titled the second on ethics <note>Referring to Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book II, where he categorizes the passions.</note>, he included gladness. He then added that those are affections which pleasure or pain follow. From which it follows that pleasure cannot be an affection according to Aristotle; otherwise, what he had said shortly before must necessarily be false. For since pleasure cannot follow itself, whoever calls it an affection will seem to deny what Aristotle had asserted: that pleasure follows all affections. Furthermore, since in that same second book he called affections "movements of the soul," but in the tenth volume of the same work he demonstrates that pleasure is by no means to be called a "movement," who would not understand that Aristotle utterly denied that it is an affection? Therefore, since in his opinion pleasure is neither a movement nor an affection, whereas he intended gladness to be an affection, it is concluded by necessary reasoning that pleasure and gladness differ greatly from one another. 

Nor indeed is gladness among the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, named for the "peripatos" or covered walkway where they studied.</note> such that it is present in the soul while it enjoys a present good. For no one among the Peripatetics doubts that it is a movement of the soul. For indeed, since affections are defined by them as certain passions of the appetite, and in their opinion a passion is a flow and a movement, they will be motions. And so gladness, being an affection, will necessarily be seen as a movement. But the soul, having now attained that which it had desired, is no longer moved, but all excitement of seeking ceases, and it rests most sweetly in the good it has acquired; wherefore, while the appetite enjoys it, it is necessary to remove all affections that concern the very thing which has been attained. Therefore, we shall also remove gladness from it when it enjoys some good. 

¶ Someone might perhaps ask, then, what gladness is, if it is neither pleasure nor joy, nor consists in the appetite while it enjoys a present good; and if this has not been sufficiently explained by the Aristotelians, I think I shall nevertheless interpret Aristotle in this way, by no means absurdly. When something that appears good is presented to us, the soul first judges that it must be taken, then the appetite is inclined toward that very thing which was judged; this we may call **desire** or **longing** <note>original: "cupiditatem, seu libidinem"</note>.

### ON PLEASURE

Next, the soul itself inquires whether it can easily obtain what it desires—a concern and anxiety we call **solicitude**. If the soul finds it is less able to achieve its goal, this very opinion is called **mistrust**, which is followed by **despair**. This occurs when the soul no longer expects to easily enjoy what it desires. From this arises **sorrow** <note>original: "tristitia"</note>; that is, a depression and casting down of a despairing and mistrusting soul. However, this term is applied to the expression of the face no less than to the state of the mind by those who care for speaking Latin correctly.

But if someone believes they will easily attain what they desire, this very faith is called **confidence**. **Hope** then follows confidence; that is, a firm and easy expectation of a future good. From this is born **gladness** <note>original: "laetitia"</note>, a certain lifting up and elation of a soul hoping that it will, without any doubt, possess what it has sought. Indeed, a certain confidence and a very firm hope—along with the intense contemplation of that very thing we hope for—represents the object of our quest to the soul in such a way that it is not far from appearing entirely present.

The result is that something very similar to pleasure is born from this hope and thought. I believe **Aristotle** called this **gladness** a certain image and appearance of future pleasure. **Lucretius** the Epicurean <note>Lucretius (c. 99–55 BC) was a Roman poet and philosopher who explained Epicurean physics and psychology in his poem *On the Nature of Things*.</note> called it a "drop of Venus" <note>original: "guttam ueneris"</note>, because it is a small and light perception of the beloved thing; whereas **pleasure** <note>original: "uoluptas"</note> is the perfect and absolute enjoyment of the desired thing (to speak in the manner of **Plato**). For this reason, the same Lucretius, in the fourth book of *On the Nature of Things*, when speaking of this first "drop of Venus," says:

> For mute desire foretells pleasure.
> From this comes Venus to us; from this the name of love;
> From this, that drop of Venus’s sweetness first
> Dripped into the heart, and burning care followed.
<note>original: "Nanque uoluptatem præsagit muta cupido..." Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura*, 4.1057-1060. The author uses this to show how the "drop" (gladness) precedes the full "pleasure" of possession.</note>

That is to say, when desire itself—which we call "venereal love"—is mute (still hidden and reflecting within itself with an internal motion), it senses and, as it were, pre-tastes future pleasure because of hope and confidence. In that moment, that first "drop of Venus" arises, which we call **gladness**.

Therefore, let it be held among the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: Followers of Aristotle's philosophy, so named because they walked about the Lyceum while discussing.</term> that gladness is a certain sweet presentiment of future pleasure born from hope itself. Just as pleasure is in the appetite while it enjoys, so gladness is in the same appetite while it hopes. And this is the controversy regarding these names—gladness, joy, and pleasure—among **Plato**, **Aristotle**, **Zeno**, and **Marcus Tullius**. ¶ But let them use their own terms as they please; let us return to the **Stoics**.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of human emotions and psychological states, specifically moving from the previous definitions of confidence and hope into a formal Stoic classification of the four primary "disorders" or "perturbations" of the soul, contrasting rational responses with irrational passions.</meta>

->**BOOK**<-

<meta>catchword: but</meta>

A **disorder** <note>original: "perturbatio"; in Stoic philosophy, this refers to a "pathos" or a distressing emotion that clouds judgment.</note> (as the **Stoics** <note>The Stoics were a school of Hellenistic philosophy that taught that virtue is the highest good and that emotions/passions are often the result of errors in judgment.</note> define it) is an agitation of the soul that is turned away from right reason and is contrary to nature; they believe that such a state is born from an opinion. For as soon as the appearance of something is presented, the soul judges it to be either a destructive evil or a good. From this opinion, four disorders of the soul arise. For the things presented to us—whether they be good or evil—seem to be either in the future or in the present. 

If the soul considers a certain evil to be in the future, it immediately attempts to turn away from it. If this turning away is done in accordance with reason, it is called **caution** <note>original: "cautio"</note>, and this is neither a disorder nor is it foreign to the soul of a wise person. However, that which is done without reason, and with a lowly and broken loss of spirit, is called **fear**. **Fear** is thus a turning away from reason, or an anxious expectation of a future evil. 

But when that which is seen as an evil is already imminent and affects the soul in the present, there arises that disorder which they call either **distress** <note>original: "aegritudinem"</note> or **pain**. **Distress** is a contraction of the soul that opposes reason; however, in the wise person, there is no such affection caused by a present evil. 

On the other hand, when the appearance of something that seems to be a future good is offered, the very opinion of it impels one to attain it (to speak in the Stoic manner). When this is done with constancy and prudence, we call such a desire the **will** <note>original: "uoluntatem"</note>; they believe this exists only in the wise person and should in no way be called a disorder. They define it thus: **will** is that which desires something in accordance with reason. But when it is incited in opposition to reason, it is a more violent **lust** <note>original: "libido"</note> or unbridled **craving**, which is found in all foolish people. 

Furthermore, when we are moved in such a way that we enjoy some good, it happens in two ways. For either the soul is moved gravely and calmly, which they call **joy** <note>original: "gaudium"</note>, or it exults lightly and excessively; then they call it **exultant gladness** and **pleasure**. They define this as an irrational and exultant elation of the soul, which believes it is enjoying a great good. On this point, they agreed with the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for walking about while lecturing.</note>, whose opinion we reported in the second place earlier when we were speaking of **Aristotle**; for both groups agree that **pleasure** is the very elation of a soul that believes it has attained some supreme good.

¶ The **Stoics** divide **pleasure** into several parts. They have judged there to be five in the senses, and four in the mind, provided the mind agrees with the senses. Those things that move the senses do not have distinct or specific names among the Stoics, except for that which is perceived by hearing; this they call **delight** <note>original: "delectationem"</note>, and they define it as follows: **Delight** is a pleasure that soothes the soul through the sweetness of hearing, while others entice the remaining senses.

<meta>This page continues the Stoic classification of emotions, specifically detailing the sub-categories of pleasure as a "disorder" of the soul. <meta>catchword: which</meta>

But besides those things by which the body is affected, four additional types have been identified that are also found in the mind once it has been corrupted by desire. These are **delight**, **effusion**, **exultation**, and **malevolence**. **Delight** <note>original: "oblectatio"</note> is an inclination of the mind toward a softening pleasure. I do not believe this to be anything other than a certain softness and assent of the mind, by which it most willingly joins itself to, agrees with, obeys, and submits to the sweetness offered by the senses. By **effusion** <note>original: "effusio"</note>, however, they define the relaxation and dissolution of the soul's virtue. For the mind itself is not only inclined and drawn by a certain softness to obey the pleasures of the senses—which we said happens through delight—but what is greater, the entire force of our mind and every intention melts and flows away in the sweetness of a present good, lifting itself up and spreading itself deeply to enjoy it. This, then, is what the **Stoics** <note>A school of philosophy that viewed such "effusions" of emotion as a loss of rational self-control.</note> call (as I believe) **effusion**. Next follows **exultation** <note>original: "iactatio"</note>, a pleasure that rejoices and lifts itself up quite insolently. This too is a sickness of the mind, when it triumphs in the possession of what appears to be a good and boasts in an empty manner. **Malevolence** <note>original: "maliuolentia"</note>, however, is pleasure taken from the misfortune of another without any personal benefit. For when someone is affected by pleasure at another's misfortune for the sake of their own utility, it seems to be more a matter of benevolence toward oneself than any malevolence toward others. Therefore, that phrase "without any personal benefit" was rightly added to the definition.

### Chapter 11. The Cyrenaics on pleasure, that it is the ultimate goal.

Let these things said concerning the opinion of the Stoics be sufficient. Let us now hear from the **Cyrenaic** <note>A Greek school of philosophy founded in the 4th century BCE that emphasized immediate physical pleasure.</note> philosophers, who descended from **Aristippus**, a disciple of **Socrates**. The Cyrenaics established two disturbances: **pain** and **pleasure**. They called pleasure a "smooth motion" and pain a "rough motion." They claimed that one pleasure does not differ from another, nor does one delight more than the other; and while all living creatures seek pleasure, they reject pain. They understand pleasure to be of the body, which they also say is the **end** <note>original: "finis"; the ultimate goal or purpose of life, often called the *summum bonum*.</note>, not the kind of pleasure that exists in a stable state or consists in the absence of pain and acts as a rest from disturbance, which **Epicurus** <note>A later philosopher who defined the highest pleasure as "ataraxia" or freedom from fear and bodily pain, rather than active physical indulgence.</note> adopted and established as the goal. They believe the proof that pleasure is held as our goal is that nature has reconciled us to it from childhood, even without the judgment of reason; for when the mind's judgment is neither corrupted by custom nor shaped by opinion, it happens that by the instinct of nature alone we seem to consider pleasure the highest good. And when we enjoy it, we seek nothing else besides it, as if seeking...

...[evils] of all, and that it stands as the last, extreme, highest, and final goal; nor is there anything which we naturally flee as much as pain. Therefore, we seek pleasure most of all. [They hold] furthermore that pleasure is a good even if it arises from the most shameful things; for even if the act is foul, the pleasure itself is nevertheless to be chosen for its own sake <note>original: "per se ipsam esse eligendam"</note> and considered a good. Moreover, that removal of pain which **Epicurus** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher (341–270 BCE) who taught that the absence of pain (aponia) was the height of pleasure—a view the Cyrenaics, discussed here, rejected as being merely a "neutral" state.</note> defends does not seem to be pleasure, nor is the deprivation of pleasure [merely] pain, for both are rooted in fear. However, pleasures are not only of the body, but also of the mind—specifically those perceived from the memory of past events, the hope of future goods, or the study of disciplines. Yet, they believe the pleasures of the body are far more excellent than those of the mind, and bodily pains are worse than those of the mind. Indeed, they hold that virtues and everything else besides pleasure is good and desirable only for the sake of pleasure. Whatever evils there are seem to be evils of pain and are to be avoided. Truly, pleasure alone is good and desirable for its own sake, while pain is evil for its own sake and to be rejected. They also claim that pleasure and pain occur from the mind’s assent to and suffering with the body. For the body is moved by various and diverse motions; if these are gentle and smooth, the mind assents, and that is pleasure. But if the body is struck by a harsher sensation, the mind contracts and suffers with it, which is pain. For this reason, in this definition of pain and pleasure, they agree with most of the **Platonists** <note>Followers of Plato's Academy.</note> and **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, who often taught while walking (peripatētikos).</note>. Nevertheless, they disagree in certain other matters, as can be seen from what we have related, and additionally because they did not think anything was [inherently] pleasant or unpleasant. Furthermore, regarding the power of any thing, some are delighted by its novelty, variety, or abundance, while others are distressed by them.

### Chapter 12. The opinion of Eudoxus that pleasure is the supreme good.

<margin>c</margin> The opinion of **Eudoxus** <note>Eudoxus of Cnidus (c. 390–337 BCE), a renowned astronomer and mathematician who argued that pleasure is the goal of all living things.</note>, the pupil of **Archytas** <note>A Pythagorean philosopher and mathematician who was a friend of Plato.</note>, is nearly the same. For he proves that pleasure is the supreme good <note>original: "summum bonum"</note> through the following arguments that I shall set forth. That which is desirable, he says, appears to be good; and that which is more desirable is better; and finally, no one would doubt that what is most desirable is the greatest and highest good. He judges that pleasure is sought above all others for two reasons. First, there is nothing among all things that living beings desire more vehemently and ardently than pleasure; nor is there any good besides it that is sought by all. Indeed, not only humans, but all other animals, and even infants immediately as they are born, and later youths and old men, strive for pleasure. Moreover, nothing...

which is present in all other virtues, or which suits all animals by nature.
But pleasure is mixed into all virtues, and no virtue at all can be found without
pleasure. Yet pleasure itself is found without virtue in many cases, and there can be no
possession of a good without pleasure. From these points, it is concluded that it is infused
into all goods, and for that reason, it is the most ample and the best.
¶ Moreover, there is nothing except pleasure that we do not expect for the sake of something

pleasure itself. For we do not strive for what is good for any other reason than that, once it
is acquired, we may finally enjoy <note>original: "fruamur"</note> it in whatever way possible. For the sake
 of enjoyment <note>original: "fruitionis ... gratia"</note> (so to speak), all goods are sought out.
Pleasure, however, since it is nothing else but a certain sweetest enjoyment of a good
already acquired, who would deny that the remaining goods are desired for its sake?
There is no one who seeks anything of the good except to obtain that very thing according
to his strength, nor does he wish to obtain it except to possess it and to rest most
sweetly in it. That sweet rest, or that sweetness of rest by which we enjoy the good
already obtained, has been called pleasure by almost all those who practice philosophy, 
and it is for its sake, as we have proved.

### Chapter 13: Aristotle's arguments against Aristippus and Eudoxus concerning pleasure prove that the pleasure of the mind is superior to the pleasure of the body.

<margin>a</margin>
Aristotle weaves together the truest and most approved arguments against both of these opinions. In the first place, he demonstrates with many reasons that the pleasure of the mind is superior to that of the body. ¶ For among all bodily pleasures, the most intense are those perceived through touch and taste. The nature of these, however, is such that without a sense of lack <note>original: "indigentia" - a state of needing or wanting something</note>, they can either not move the body at all, or only with great difficulty. Hence <term>Socrates</term> used to say that the seasoning for food is hunger, and for drink, thirst. Since every lack is an enemy to nature, it brings pain. And because pleasures of this kind cannot exist without a sense of lack, they must always share in pain. For that reason, they are considered neither whole nor pure, especially since they breed regret, over-satiety, and disease. The pleasure of the mind, however, has no mixture of want within it; for that reason, it shares no part of pain, nor does it affect the mind with any surfeit or distress. ¶ What of this: that the delights of the senses, the more and more greedily they are drained, the more quickly they fall back into their opposite <note>meaning they turn into disgust or pain</note>. But the joy of the mind, the more it is sought, the greater and more perfect it is held to be.

¶ Furthermore, the causes—or as it were, the principles—of pleasure are two: namely, the very power of the soul which receives such a movement, and additionally, that which is presented to us from the outside. They call the former the "subject" of pleasure and the latter its "object." The subject of bodily pleasantness is the sense, while the object is the quality and nature of the body, which the forms drawn in by the senses present. But of that joy which the soul enjoys, the subject is the mind, and the object is something incorporeal, simple, absolute, eternal—namely, truth. Therefore, to the extent that the principles of this pleasure are more divine than those of the former, this one is more perfect than that. ¶ And (as <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina, c. 980–1037) was a Persian polymath. His philosophical works attempted to reconcile Aristotelianism with Neoplatonism and Islamic theology.</note> argues), the senses only touch upon the surfaces of things, or certain properties from the outside...

<header>ON PLEASURE</header>

[The senses] are not joined to the things themselves, but rather to their images <note>original: "imaginibus" – in Aristotelian terms, these are the sensory impressions or "phantasms" rather than the essence of the object.</note>. The mind, however, examines the inner and absolute nature of that which is presented to it, and is so joined with what it considers that either one entity is made from two (as <term>Averroes</term> <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a medieval Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle argued for the "unity of the intellect."</note> claims), or (as <term>Aurelius Augustine</term> <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 CE). The text refers to his views on the soul's mystical or intellectual union with truth.</note> says) they cohere in an indissoluble connection. From this comprehension and union, a much greater pleasure reaches the mind than the senses, which cannot attain such a thing.

¶ Add to this that the nature of the mind always exists as one and the same, and therefore its likeness to itself is always constant and proper. From this it follows that for the mind, the same thing is always delightful, and the same pleasure is present. The nature of the body, however, either never remains in the same state (as <term>Heraclitus</term> <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher famous for the idea that "everything flows" (panta rhei).</note> and **Plato** believe) or is quickly transformed into many different conditions (as **Aristotle** thinks), and its quality varies from one state to another. For this reason, the same thing does not suit the body at all times. That which now seems to agree with its nature will immediately, or certainly shortly after, disagree and differ; thus, the same thing is not always pleasurable to it. By these facts, it is understood that the pleasure of the mind is certain and stable, while that of the body is brief, fleeting, and fragile.

¶ Likewise, the senses are moved only by the sweetness of present things, nor do they receive pleasure from any things except those that are physical. The mind, however, is equally delighted by the memory of the past, the hope of the future, and the contemplation of the present; nor can it only rejoice in the knowledge of those things that lack a body, but even in the knowledge of bodies themselves.

¶ And since the soul <note>original: "animus"</note> is the most excellent part of all that makes a human being, there can be no doubt to anyone that what is agreeable to the mind must be judged more kindred and similar to man than what is suitable to the senses. Since whatever is most kindred to each thing is undoubtedly the most pleasant, it is understood that the joy of the soul is greater and more excellent than the sweetness of the body.

¶ Added to this is the fact that the soul is indivisible and simple, and the knowledge of truth is likewise indivisible. Therefore, the pleasure of the mind—since it flows from these two as if from certain causes—will be seen to be simple, nor can it become smaller or greater than itself, especially since its principles suffer no variety of any kind. The senses, however, are scattered and distributed through the limbs. Because of this, they are composed of a manifold variety. The objects of the senses also seem to be nothing other than certain forms and qualities of bodies, which arise from a certain harmony of their parts, such as shapes, colors, sounds, smells, and other things of this kind. And when that very proportion of bodies by which the senses are moved is harmonious and similar to the proportion of the senses themselves, the senses adopt it as something proper, familiar, and good, and [attain] pleasure...

<meta>This page continues the technical comparison between mental and physical pleasure, building on the previously established Aristotelian view that the mind’s simplicity makes its joys more stable than those of the body. It specifically addresses why we seek physical pleasure: as a biological necessity, a remedy for pain, and a subservient tool for the mind.</meta>

...they are affected. But since the harmony of such bodies can approach the likeness of the harmony of the senses more or less, it follows that the sense receives a greater pleasure at one time and a lesser at another, depending on the proportion of the body. This can be observed in songs and sounds; for at the same moment of time (so to speak), the very delight perceived from the same song is rendered more intense or more relaxed by voices emitted now more sweetly, now more discordantly. Therefore, since the pleasure of the mind remains simple and immutable, while the delight of the body is mixed and becomes greater or lesser, no one of sound mind will deny that the former is more excellent and more perfect than the latter.

¶ Indeed, the final argument of **Aristotle** on this same point is clear: things which are sought for their own sake (he says) seem more powerful than those sought for the sake of another. The joy of the mind is shown to be loved for itself most especially because the mind and its activity greatly surpass all other things within us in dignity. From which it follows that nothing exists within us to which we might refer the mind as if to some end; and by the same reasoning, we shall not seek the pleasure inherent in it for any other reason.

¶ However, we desire the pleasure of the body for three main reasons. One of these is the mind; another is the deficiency of nature; the last is deep-seated and perpetual pain. For since nature has referred the inferior things to those which are superior—so that there might be an inexplicable order of things and a perfect connection of parts among themselves—it is necessary that the senses of the body and their motions also be referred to the mind as if to a mistress and queen.

¶ Next (as we also said above), nature implanted such vehement pleasure in the senses for this reason: so that by these allurements, we might be more inclined to acquire those things necessary for life. This is most evident from the fact that as long as we admit into the body that which nature lacks, we are moved by this sort of sweetness. But after every natural need has been fulfilled, not only do we taste no further pleasure, but—what is more significant—we are affected by either <term>regret</term> <note>original: "pœnitētia" – in this physiological context, it refers to the physical revulsion or "after-pain" of over-indulgence rather than moral remorse.</note> or satiety. I believe nature established this for the following reason: just as we are enticed by pleasure to dispel deficiency, so we might be deterred by regret and satiety, so that we do not harm nature by admitting more than is necessary.

¶ Also for the sake of soothing hidden pain (as **Aristotle** argues in the seventh book of the <term>Ethics</term> <note>original: "de moribus" – literally "On Morals," the common title for Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics.</note>), we seek pleasant movement of the body as if it were a kind of medicine. For not only manifest pains occur, but also certain hidden and intermediate ones. Violent movements brought in from the outside cause manifest pain. Natural agitations that occur within, however, cause a silent and intermediate pain. ->**ON PLEASURE**<-

Furthermore, the mind transfuses humor <note>The "humors" were the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to control health and temperament.</note> and spirit from the limbs of the body to other limbs in an alternating and perpetual motion. It then utilizes the instruments of the body for sensing, and the senses themselves for contemplation. It seems reasonable, indeed, that these motions—so great, so varied, and so constant—should weary nature and affect it with a certain hidden pain (if I may call it that). We notice this pain less because we endure it perpetually from our very birth until our final day. Thus, long-standing habit makes it, in a way, familiar to our senses and dissolves the mind’s focus upon it. 

However, it was ordained by Nature herself—the master and architect of all things—that what long habit has erased should not lead to the animal’s destruction through negligence. Instead, the animal is stirred by a certain necessary and blind instinct, by which all things are, as it were, compelled to desire the pleasure of the body as a medicine opposed to this inward pain. For this reason, even those who experience no obvious or manifest lack still pursue pleasure because of this innate and blind deficiency. Thus, that saying of **Plato**—which we discussed above—is most true: namely, that all pleasure proceeds from the filling up of a deficiency. For even those in whom no open lack appears, an inward and hidden one can never be absent so long as they live. 

This same innate deficiency of which we have spoken occurs most especially in the young and in those of a "melancholic" temperament. In the young, it is because they are stirred by many violent motions due to the necessity of the body growing and reaching its perfection; it happens that they require a greater medicine, and for this reason, they pursue pleasures most of all. However, in those whom <term>black bile</term> <note>original: *atra bilis*, which the Greeks call *μελαγχολίαν* (melancholian)</note> dominates, the body (as the author says) is continually consumed and gnawed away by the intense dryness of that humor. Because of this, they too greatly indulge in pleasures. Therefore, the young and the melancholic tend to be the most incontinent <note>In this context, "incontinent" refers to a lack of self-control or the inability to resist physical impulses.</note> and intemperate of all.

¶ What might be called "middle pain," however, is hunger, thirst, and any other such desire of the body. This pain is not entirely hidden, yet it does not torture the body with an open or more violent motion. Hence it is not undeservedly called "middle pain," and as everyone can see, we seek pleasures for the sake of driving this pain away as well.

<margin>1</margin>
We have already declared in a long series of arguments Aristotle’s judgment that the pleasure of the mind is superior to the sweetness of the body. There now remains another discussion by Aristotle against Eudoxus <note>A Greek astronomer and mathematician who argued that pleasure is the supreme good because all creatures seek it.</note> and the **Cyrenaics** <note>A school of philosophy founded by Aristippus of Cyrene, which taught that the pleasure of the moment, especially physical pleasure, is the only certain good.</note>, through which he demonstrates that the pleasure of the body is by no means the "highest good" <term>summum bonum (the ultimate goal or end of human existence)</term>.

Indeed, by the authority of all philosophers, the highest good must be of such a kind that there is nothing better beyond it, nor is it referred to anything else as a means to an end. However, the pleasure of the body is considerably inferior to the joy of the mind (as we showed a little while ago), and it is desired for the sake of the mind and the other things we have mentioned. Moreover, that which is the highest good in itself ought to always appear good and desirable to everyone, and be approved in all its parts. Yet, not every physical delight is sought always, nor is it sought by all people. For what often provides pleasure to one person frequently provides distress to another; what seems pleasant to children seems bothersome to men; and what we crave while we are sober, we later find nauseating to even look at once we have been filled. 

To this we must add the fact that such is the nature of the highest good that whatever we do, we choose it for its own sake, as if compelled by necessity. Yet there are many most laborious tasks and duties full of danger which—even if we know for certain they will bring us no physical pleasure—we do not hesitate to undertake for the sake of honor, virtue, or the joy of the mind. Indeed, many of the bravest and wisest men have committed themselves to certain death for the sake of what is honorable, for their country, or for their parents. If anyone should say they did this because they were ensnared by physical sweetness or inflamed by lust, or if a critic prefers the judgment of the common crowd and of beasts over the character of these men, he must surely be judged the most foolish of all.

Furthermore, anyone, even the most abject person, can enjoy physical pleasures no less than the best of men. But no one would say that "happiness" <term>felicitas (the state of flourishing or true well-being)</term> belongs to the abject. Nor is it reasonable to assert that the lowliest, "half-alive" little men <note>original: "homunculos"</note> are equally blessed as great and wise men.

Likewise, the highest good of any nature ought to be unique to that nature. Since physical pleasure is shared with even the lowliest living creatures <note>original: "bestiolis"</note>, it should in no way be judged the highest good of man. 

Or would you truly call that the "highest good" which does not even seem to be good? Indeed, I believe it has been sufficiently discussed above by our **Plato** how foul, how base, and how pestilential such "elation of the senses" <note>original: "sensuum elatio"</note> can be. As for the point upon which **Eudoxus** and **Aristippus** especially relied—namely, that pleasure...

...physical pleasure is sought by everyone, this seems to the followers of Aristotle to carry little weight for what they strive to prove. For Aristotle believes that there are various dispositions of different bodies; therefore, the things naturally related to these bodies—which, through that very relationship, produce pleasure—differ greatly among themselves. From this, it is understood that various and differing pleasures occur for different living beings. If you were to run through all the pleasures of the body, you would ultimately find none that is sought by everyone above all else. However, it is established that the mind is either one in all things, or at least very similar. Therefore, what is proper to the mind appears proper and related to the minds of all who use reason. 

The proper work of the mind is the investigation and knowledge of truth. It is clear, therefore, that this is agreeable to all people and is thus to be desired for that reason. For this reason (as Aristotle says), all men by nature desire knowledge <note>original: "omnes homines scientiam natura desiderant." This is the famous opening line of Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>. Moreover, that which is sought usually causes distress if it is absent, but produces pleasure if it is present. To all men, therefore, there is one thing naturally akin, one thing to be sought by all, and finally, one thing most delightful. And yet all this consists in the contemplation of truth, which (as Plato says) is the food <note>original: "pabulum." Plato frequently describes truth or "forms" as the nourishment of the soul, notably in the *Phaedrus*.</note> of the mind, and it fills the soul with a certain ineffable pleasure. Thus, while some physical pleasures are sought by some and others by others, the joy of the mind is one and the same, loved by all.

In place of that pleasure toward which nature’s primary intention is directed, we follow this one which charms the senses, deceived by this similarity, and we embrace it greedily.

But to return to our proposal: pleasure is varied and uncertain according to the diversity of men, but a single joy of the mind is naturally sought by everyone. Since both of these—namely, the contemplation of truth and its accompanying pleasure—reside in the mind, and the nature of the "highest good" seems to consist of these, the ancient philosophers doubted which of them was more essential or excellent for reaching blessedness. 

For Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of wisdom texts; often cited by Renaissance scholars as a source of ancient theology.</note>, and Theodorus (the disciple of Dionysius the Dialectician), Democritus, Pyrrho, Eurilochus, Philotimon, Phliasius, Nausiphanes, Theius, Epicurus, Origen, Avicenna <note>The Latinized name for the Persian philosopher Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037).</note>, and Al-Ghazali <note>Latinized as Algaizel; a major Persian theologian and philosopher (c. 1058–1111).</note> seem to judge that the "joy" which is the companion of contemplation is the chief part of the nature of blessedness. 

However, Thales, Bias, Anaxagoras, Socrates, Euclid of Megara, Aristotle, Herillus of Chalcedon, and Averroes <note>The Latinized name for the Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd (1126–1198).</note> prefer contemplation itself. Indeed, this debate and controversy has flourished right up to our own age and is even debated among Christian theologians. But regarding this, we will speak elsewhere. For now, it will suffice to have warned how Aristotle differs from Eudoxus and Aristippus in two primary ways (as we declared above).

### Chapter XVII. What the Epicureans believe regarding the origins of things, Pleasure, the passions, and morals.

<margin>a</margin> In truth, the Epicureans establish the name "pleasure" as a kind of genus, of which there are two species. Furthermore, they consider one pleasure to consist in motion and the other in state <note>Modern scholars refer to these as "kinetic" pleasure (the joy of satisfying a desire) and "katastematic" pleasure (the peaceful state of having no pain or want).</note>. That which is placed in motion they divide into two parts: one indeed is in the mind, the other in the senses. They mostly call the former "joy" and the latter "delight." They define joy as a sweet commotion of the mind enjoying what it had sought. But delight they define as a pleasant motion by which the senses open up and overflow. They teach that this very pleasantness, which is placed in motion, arises in this way: they say that the origins of all things that exist are certain very small and entirely indivisible bodies, which for this reason—because they are "uncuttable"—they call atoms <note>original: "ἀτόμους" (atomous).</note>. They say these differ among themselves in size and shape, so that some seeds are larger, others smaller; some are round and smooth, others are curved, hooked, and rough. All these fly through the immense void in perpetual motions, touch each other, and, clinging together by chance collisions, constitute whatever exists in the nature of things. They believe three principal kinds of things are made by the grouping of these: some are produced by those atoms which are round, small, and smooth; others by larger...

...rougher [particles]. They believe that some things truly hold a middle ground between these two, being neither smooth nor entirely rough. They also hold that our body and soul are composed of these same <term>seeds<note>The author uses "seeds" (semina) to refer to what we now call atoms—the tiny, indivisible building blocks of matter in Epicurean philosophy.</note></term>, with this difference: the body is filled with larger and thicker seeds, while the soul is filled with minute, smooth, and round ones. Furthermore, they say there is a <term>void<note>original: "inane"</note></term> mixed within all bodies and natures, which they call passages or pores. Through these, it happens that bodies can receive one another and, as it were, drink each other in. 

Therefore, when those primary types of seeds are presented to us, because (as we have said) they are the smallest that exist, they penetrate the body and soul from all sides without any offense. Because they are round and smooth, and therefore kindred to the nature of the soul, they immediately soothe it and flatter the senses. They believe that sweet fruits, the liquids of honey and milk, songs, the sweetest smells, and other things of this sort are of this kind. For this reason, when the seeds from which the soul is woven are touched by these smooth and pleasant little bodies, they assent to this sweet commotion; they pour themselves out with a certain great greed into those little bodies that have been drawn into the senses and passages, adhering to them joyfully, binding to them firmly, and embracing them most sweetly. They believe that this very assent, effusion, joining, and embracing is <term>pleasure placed in motion<note>original: "uoluptatem in motu positam." This refers to "kinetic pleasure," the active delight felt during the process of satisfying a desire or being stimulated by a pleasant sensation.</note></term>. 

On the contrary, it happens that when that third kind of body, which is constructed of rough and heavy seeds, is moved toward the senses, it causes pain. Because the elements of which they consist are large, they are thrust into the openings of the body and soul with difficulty, and they strike, break through, and pull apart the soul’s particles with a certain force. Because they are rough and <term>hooked<note>original: "hamata." Epicureans believed that "bitter" or "painful" atoms had physical hooks that literally snagged or tore at the sensory membranes.</note></term>, they bite the soul sharply in a way and prick the body. They judge such things to be wormwood, bile, unpleasant colors, sounds, and smells—and finally, all other things that touch the senses with some roughness and bitterness. Indeed, the first principles of the soul, provoked by the seeds of these things, are pulled apart; they shudder, flee, and quickly contract themselves. They define such dispersion and contraction as the movement of <term>pain<note>original: "dolorem"</note></term>. 

The noble Epicurean Lucretius expresses this in these verses in the second book of *On the Nature of Things*:

> *So that you may easily recognize that those things*
> *Which can touch the senses pleasantly are made of smooth and round [seeds].*
> *But on the contrary, those things which seem hooked and rough,*
> *Are held bound to each other by more hooked [seeds],*
> *And for that reason are accustomed to tear open the paths*
> *To our senses and break into the body by their entry.*
> <note>original Latin: "Ut facile agnoscas de leuibus atque rotundis / Esse ea, quae sensus iocunde tangere possunt. / At contra quae hamata atque aspera, cumque uidentur. / Haec magis hamatis inter se nexa teneri, / Proptereaque solere uias rescindere nostris / Sensibus introitūque suo perrumpere corpus." But in truth, those things which are joined by certain middle elements are divided into several kinds. The first type entices the soul to pleasure through a certain silent motion; the second seems to incite it gradually and secretly toward sadness and pain. Those that are called <term>indifferent<note>In this context, "indifferent" refers to things that do not immediately cause a strong reaction of either extreme pleasure or extreme pain.</note></term> produce a motion that is ambiguous and doubtful. For this reason, the mind grows sluggish and numb under their impulse, and is not stirred to action unless some new motion arrives. 

Nor do I think it should be passed over in silence that between those things which are entirely smooth and round, and those that are completely hooked and rough, a certain middle category of bodies is placed. These do not soothe the mind, nor do they scatter it, nor do they cause it to grow weary; rather, they prick it lightly and moderately, and, as it were, titillate it, producing pleasure. ### BOOK

...they remove pains, nor do they increase pleasure. For once the needs of nature are satisfied, and the pain that follows such need is removed, Epicurus thinks that the highest limit of bodily pleasure is reached. While pleasure can afterwards be varied and distinguished, it cannot be increased or amplified. Therefore, in this second category, the Epicureans place those pleasures which are perceived through various seasonings and the exquisite delicacies of banquets. He then added a third category of those pleasures which are neither natural nor necessary, such as those derived from public spectacles of external things—which contribute nothing to one’s livelihood or skill—and generally all those pleasures taken from an immense pile of riches and wealth. 

The logic regarding all these pleasures is that the desire for those that are necessary can be satisfied without much labor or expense. Nor do the cravings for natural pleasures require much, because nature itself holds the riches with which it is content to be both easily obtainable and limited. However, for empty desires—which pursue pleasures that are neither natural nor necessary—no limit or end can be found (as he believes). Hence, Epicurus says: <note>original: "si ad naturam uixeris, nūquam eris pauper. fi ad opinionem, nunquam diues."</note> "If you live according to nature, you will never be poor; if you live according to opinion, you will never be rich." For nature itself enriches the wise man, and its riches are easily obtained. Indeed, pleasures perceived from the simplest and most humble food are no less than those from the most exquisite things for feasting. For nature is content with few and very small things.

¶ Nor does Epicurus pursue only that pleasure which moves nature with some sweetness (about which we have already said enough), but he considers that to be the greatest pleasure which is perceived when all pain is removed. He says this is "pleasure in a stable state" <note>This refers to *katastematic* pleasure, the state of tranquility or "being" rather than the "kinetic" pleasure of "doing" or consuming.</note>. When the <term>Cyrenaics<note>A rival school of philosophy founded by Aristippus of Cyrene, who believed that pleasure was only found in active, "kinetic" movement and denied that the absence of pain was a pleasure in itself.</note></term> denied, on the contrary, that this was pleasure, Epicurus taught that it must be called pleasure for this reason: because when we are deprived of pain, we rejoice in the very liberation and vacancy from all trouble. 

Now, everything in which we rejoice is pleasure, just as everything by which we are offended is pain. The removal of all pain is rightly named pleasure. For just as when hunger and thirst are driven away by food and drink, the very removal of the trouble brings the attainment of pleasure. So, in every matter, the removal of pain effects a succession of pleasure. Therefore, it did not please Epicurus that there should be some middle state between pain and pleasure. For he believed that very thing which seems to some to be a middle state—when we lack all pain—is not only pleasure but even the highest pleasure. For whoever is aware of how they are affected must necessarily be either in pain or in pleasure. Furthermore, they divide this pleasure "in a stable state" into two parts: they place one in the soul and the other in the body; the latter they call 

->**freedom from pain**<-
<note>original: "indolentiā"</note>

# ON PLEASURE
L

...<term>absence of pain<note>original: "indolentiam"; referring to the Greek concept of *aponia*, or the state of being free from physical suffering.</note></term>. This latter state they indeed call <term>tranquility<note>original: "tranquillitatem"; referring to the Greek *ataraxia*, the ideal state of mental serenity.</note></term>. Now, as these thinkers see it, "absence of pain" in the body is the removal of all suffering. "Tranquility," however, is a certain peaceful and constant freedom of the mind from every disturbance. Sometimes, they even encompass both types of pleasure under a single name, calling it "absolute and complete tranquility." Because of this, tranquility is twofold: one belongs to the mind alone, while the other is that which is entirely perfect and absolute.

---

## Chapter XVIII. Moderation in pleasures, and how happiness lies not in 
## active pleasure, but in tranquility according to Epicurus and Democritus.

<margin>o</margin>
Furthermore, every pleasure is by its own nature good and something to be sought after, yet it must sometimes be avoided for the sake of something else. For those pleasures which arise from immoderate and shameful actions ought to be avoided for this reason: they are very brief and fragile, and they bring with them regret, care, anxiety, and pain. Likewise, all pains are to be avoided for their own sake, yet they should sometimes be endured for the sake of another thing—specifically, those pains which, though they are light and very brief, will provide us with certain great pleasures and advantages. 

And even if all pleasures are good, a happy life does not consist in all of them. For that pleasure which occurs through motion—<term>active pleasure<note>original: "uoluptate concitata"; often called "kinetic pleasure," it involves the active stimulation of the senses, like eating or drinking, rather than the state of being satisfied.</note></term>—is not sufficient in itself for a happy life, nor is it strictly necessary for its own sake for living happily. On the contrary, they believe that "absolute tranquility," which contains peaceful rest for the mind and the absence of pain for the body, is the highest good of all. ¶ For they believe that through these two things, the entire nature of a human being—namely, the body and the mind together—is made perfect, and that this is the state to which all our affairs should be directed. 

Indeed, we undergo all labors so that we may eventually be in leisure and rest. We pursue those pleasures which we have categorized as "in motion" only so that they may drive away pains and satisfy the needs of nature. We seek to drive away pain and satisfy need so that we may be released and free from all the suffering that comes from the body's lack of something. And this is that "absence of pain" which they want understood as a stable state; they consider this one part of happiness, while the other part is governed by the "tranquility of the mind," for the sake of which all virtues are sought. Indeed, the virtues desire nothing else except to free the mind from every disturbance. That very thing is tranquility itself. For this reason, they maintain that all the virtues were sought for the sake of tranquility, as were all other human actions. ¶ Furthermore, since...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the "highest good," building on the previous discussion of pleasure and the absence of pain. It focuses on proving that tranquility is the ultimate goal of human life because it represents a state of total fulfillment.</meta>

->BOOK<-

...other human goods are either proper to the mind alone or to the body. <margin>a</margin> But among all of these, that absolute and perfect tranquility encompasses the whole of human nature. Therefore, it ought to be rightly judged as the most excellent of all goods. <margin>b</margin> To this point, it is also of no small importance that it is confirmed by the authority of all philosophers: namely, that the "highest" <note>original: "summum"</note> is seen as that to which nothing further can be added. But what will you add to tranquility? Or how would you do so, unless it lacked something? Yet if any good is lacking, it is necessary for the one who lacks it to desire it; and one who feels desire can in no way be tranquil. Therefore, where there is tranquility, there is no desire. Where nothing is desired, there is no lack. Where there is no want, there finally is a perfect state, an abundance of things to be sought, and an absolute embrace of all goods. Therefore, where there is tranquility, there are all goods. Where all things and tranquility are present, it is understood that nothing is missing, nothing at all can be added, and that it encompasses within itself the nature and reason of all goods. For this reason, it is the perfect and ultimate good, toward which the desire of all nature is directed. <margin>c</margin> Since there are many goods, <term>happiness<note>original: "beatitudo"</note></term> is either one of these, or all of them gathered together, or rather something that is fashioned from the accumulated possession of all other goods. However, any single good separated from the rest—since many other things could be added to it—can in no way be seen as the highest good. Nor even all of them simply collected together. For happiness exists as the final and ultimate <term>end<note>original: "finis"; the Greek *telos*, or the ultimate purpose of life.</note></term> of human life. But an ultimate end ought to be one and simple. Therefore, the highest good will be that which results from the accumulation of all others. Truly, this can be nothing other than tranquility. For the nature of goods is twofold: they both fill the mind and free it from all distress. This kind of fulfillment and liberation is, without a doubt, tranquility itself.

<margin>d</margin> Since this follows the possession of other goods, it follows that it should rightly be seen as their end and ultimate limit, and for that reason, the highest. For the mind never rests unless it has attained all goods. Now, rest and tranquility are one and the same. It follows, therefore, the possession of other goods. Thus, all goods seem to be sought for its sake, as if this were the ultimate and best end to be desired by all. For this reason, Epicurus judges that a happy life consists in the tranquility of the mind—specifically, in that most blessed tranquility which contains the <term>absence of pain<note>original: "indolentiam"; referring to the state of *aponia* (physical) and *ataraxia* (mental).</note></term> of both mind and body simultaneously. <margin>e</margin> But lest I seem to assert these things regarding Epicurus on my own authority, first...

<meta>Continuing the discussion from the previous page regarding the nature of the "highest good," this page moves into a specific defense of Epicurean philosophy, clarifying that true pleasure is found in tranquility rather than physical excess.</meta>

# ON PLEASURE

That pleasure, which is the companion of motion, is not the highest good <note>original: "summum bonum"</note>, he himself testifies in his own words in his letter to Menoeceus <note>Epicurus’s *Letter to Menoeceus* is a foundational text of Epicurean ethics, focusing on how to achieve a happy life.</note>, saying: "Therefore, when we say that pleasure is the goal, we do not mean the pleasures of the dissolute, nor those found in the taste [of food], as some who are ignorant and disagree with our opinion think, but we mean the absence of pain in the body and being tranquil in the mind, and to be free from disturbance. For it is not banquets and revelries, nor the company of boys and women, nor the consumption of fish and other things offered by a costly table, that produce a sweet life; but rather sober reasoning, searching out the causes for why everything should be chosen or avoided, and driving out opinions through which the greatest turmoil occupies the soul." Likewise in the same letter: "The absence of pain and disturbance," he says, "are constant pleasures. But joy and gladness are said to be actions according to motion <note>The author distinguishes between "kinetic" (moving) pleasures, like eating, and "static" pleasures, like the state of being full or at peace.</note>. The highest pleasure is the privation of pain, and the pleasures of the mind are indeed greater than those of the body. For the flesh is bathed only in present sweetness, but the mind rejoices together in the thought of past, present, and future things." Likewise in the same letter: "One cannot live pleasantly unless one lives prudently, honorably, and justly; nor prudently, honorably, and justly, unless one lives pleasantly." From these things Epicurus shows that the highest good does not consist in pleasures according to motion, nor in those taken from shameful actions, but that these two—namely, <term>indolentia<note>Literally "painlessness." In this context, it refers to the Greek *aponia*, the absence of physical pain.</note></term> of the body and tranquility of the mind—produce the most blessed life. The Epicurean Lucretius also testifies to the same in the second book of *On the Nature of Things* <note>original: "De rerum natura"</note>. There, while he censures the empty desires and luxurious delights of men, he says:

> O wretched minds of men, o blind hearts!
> In what darkness of life and in how great dangers
> This lifespan, such as it is, is spent! Do you not see?
<margin>1</margin>
> That nature barks for nothing else for herself except that
> Pain, separated from the body, may be absent, and that [the mind] may enjoy
> A pleasant sensation, with care and fear removed.

Here, therefore, censuring the luxury of men, he calls them blind and wretched because they burden themselves with all kinds of troubles, and do not see what nature desires as the supreme end and good. What that truly is, he himself explains, saying that nature seeks this: that pain be absent from the body (which signifies that painlessness we spoke of), and that care and fear be removed, by which words he certainly intends tranquility of the soul to be understood, and that [the soul] might enjoy the benefit and sense of these two...

<meta>This page concludes Ficino’s treatise on pleasure, continuing from the previous discussion of Epicurean ethics. Having established that pleasure is not merely physical indulgence, the text now argues that the highest state of being is a combination of mental peace and physical ease, supported by the deathbed testimony of Epicurus himself.</meta>

# BOOK [ON PLEASURE]

...and in the mind, as if to say, that in these things consists the greatest delight of both body and soul.

Therefore, that the most blessed life consists in these two things—namely, freedom from pain <note>original: "indolentia"</note> and tranquility of the mind—these testimonies of Epicurus and Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus, the Roman poet who popularized Epicureanism in his work *On the Nature of Things*.</note> ought to be sufficient. Indeed, that the man in whom there is tranquility of mind remains blessed even if his physical limbs are tortured, Epicurus is a witness. In his letter to Metrodorus <note>Metrodorus of Lampsacus was one of the four major figures of Epicureanism and a close friend of Epicurus.</note>, he says that he who has once become wise cannot pass into the opposite state, nor can he stray by yielding to disturbances; and whether he is tortured or even flayed, the wise man will nonetheless be happy. Also, in that letter which he wrote to Hermarchus <note>Hermarchus succeeded Epicurus as the head of the Epicurean school.</note> while dying, he says: "While we were spending this blessed and final day of our life, we were writing these things; such great pains of the bladder and intestines were present that nothing could be added to their severity. Yet, the joy of my mind, which I derived from the memory of our reasonings and discoveries, compensated for all of these things." In these words, he says that he is spending a blessed day, and yet he is tortured by the greatest pains. The same is said to have been the opinion of Leucippus, Democritus, and Theodorus <note>Theodorus "the Atheist," a philosopher of the Cyrenaic school who emphasized mental joy.</note>: that happiness lies in the tranquility of the mind. But if freedom from bodily pain is joined to this, then in this combined state of mind and body, absolute and perfect happiness consists.

These things regarding pleasure, disputed by various philosophers, we have written down for you. Which of these opinions you should follow, however, I wish for you to be persuaded by the authority and reasons of those who debate here, rather than by my own judgment. For it will have been enough for me to have recounted the opinions of nearly all the philosophers for the sake of exercising the memory. **THE END**
